Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.

Moggallāna pañcikā ṭīkā

Moggallāna's Pañcikā Sub-Commentary

Sāratthavilāsinīnāma

Sāratthavilāsinī

Pañcikāṭīkā

The Pañcikā Sub-Commentary

Paṇāmādikathā

The Chapter on Homage and So Forth

Vijjādhanassa [M 0.0001] samanussaraṇampi yassa,

Paññāvisuddharatanānayanekahetu;

Taṃ dhammarājamamalujjalakittimālaṃ,

Sāmodamādaramaye hadaye nidhāya.

Having placed in my heart, filled with joy and reverence, / That Dhamma-king, whose garland is immaculate, radiant fame, / Whose wealth is knowledge, and even the recollection of whom / Is the manifold cause for bringing forth the jewel of pure wisdom.

Laddhammahodaya mahādaya (sampasādā) japaso (potthake),

Sakkā(di) sakkataguṇaṃ ratana (dvayañca) ttayatā (potthake);

(Yāpañcikā) guruvarappa(bhavātyagāhā) hapā tya gāyā (potthake),

Taṃ sādhu sissajana majjavagāha yāma.

Having obtained profound serene confidence in the Dhamma, / And the virtues honored by Sakka and others, and the two jewels; / That Pañcikā, which is a profound grasp arising from the excellent teacher, / Let us, the community of disciples, immerse ourselves well in that.

Jayatīha mahāpañño, so moggallāyano muni;

Yassa sādhuguṇubbhūta,kitti sabbattha patthaṭā.

Here triumphs the greatly wise one, the sage Moggallāna, / Whose fame, arisen from good qualities, is spread everywhere.

Icceva manavasesa mattano bhayādyūpaddavopaghābhakarasāmatthiya yogena sakalajjhattikabāhiyantarāya nivāraṇa madhippetasiddhi visesa mabhikaṅkhiya ratanattaya visayabhūtaṃ taṃsādhane kantanidāna bhūtassa [M 0.0002] ālokiyayātisayaguṇavisesayuttassa mahato pyatimahanīyassa ratanattayassa sappasādānurūpaṃ pūjāvisayaṃ tadanussa(raṇaṃ katvā) gurusanniyogamanuṭṭhātuṃ–

Thus, desiring the special attainment of the intended goal, having averted all internal and external obstacles by means of the power to ward off all dangers, fears, and calamities from oneself; and having recollected, in accordance with one's serene confidence, that object of worship—the Triple Gem, which is the object of the Triple Gem itself, the beloved foundation for its accomplishment, and which is endowed with incomparable and exceedingly great virtues, being truly great and venerable—one should undertake the teacher’s instruction.

Kintehi pādasussūsā, yesaṃ natthi gurūniha;

Ye tappādarajokiṇṇā, teva sādhū vivekinoti.

What use is foot-service to those who have no teacher here? But those who are covered with the dust of his feet, they alone are truly virtuous and discerning.

Vacanato attano gurupūjā purassaraṃ pañcikāvivaraṇaṃ pathi’yā pañcikā’tiādinā katapaṭiññattā sampati mahādayotiādino ganthassa sādhujanavaṇṇanaṃ vaṇṇanamārabhissāma.

In accordance with the statement concerning the exposition of the Pañcikā, which is preceded by homage to one's own teacher, and due to the declaration made with the words 'This is the Pañcikā,' and so forth, we shall now commence the commentary on the text beginning with 'Mahādaya,' a commentary esteemed by virtuous people.

Nanu ca vuttiganthassa vaṇṇanāyaṃ katābhiniveso-yamācariyoti kathamihānadhikate mahādayotiādike paṭipannoti ratanattappaṇāmaganthakattuganthanissayaganthārambhaphalaabhidheyyasaṅkhāta- payojanasotujanasamussāhanānaṃ sandassanatthaṃ. Tattha ratanattayappaṇāma karaṇaṃ antarāyakarāpuññavighātakarapuññavisesuppādanena kattu micchitassa ganthassa anantarāyenaṃ parisamāpanatthaṃ. Vacīpaṇāmo panettha sotūnampi yathāvuttatthanipphādanako ācariyenāpyaya mattho dassitoyeva’tattha ratanattayappaṇāmasandassana’ntiādinā, vācasikasatthādhikāratopi vacīpaṇāmoti kāyappaṇāmo manopaṇāmo ca. Na kato, ganthakattusandassanaṃ ganthassa pamāṇa bhāvavibhāvanatthaṃ, ganthanissayasandassanaṃ attaniyabhāvasandhassanena tabbisuddhidassanatthaṃ, ganthārambhaphaladassanaṃ tappaṭikkhepakajananisedhāya, abhidheyyasaṅkhātayayojanasandassanaṃ vīmaṃsāpubbakārīnaṃ payojano pālambhapubbikā satthe pavattatīti sotujanasamussāhanaṃ (katvā) ādarena ganthe pavattanatthaṃ, yadāhu –

Indeed, is it not so that this teacher, being committed to commenting on the stated text, has undertaken here what is not directly related, such as the verse beginning 'Mahādaya'? It is for the purpose of demonstrating the homage to the Triple Gem, the author of the text, the basis of the text, the fruit of commencing the text, the meaning designated as the purpose, and the encouragement of the listeners. Herein, the act of paying homage to the Triple Gem is for the flawless completion of the text desired to be composed by the author, by generating special merit that overcomes obstacles and destroys demerit. And here, verbal homage also brings about the stated meaning for the listeners. This meaning has also been shown by the teacher, as in 'therein the demonstration of homage to the Triple Gem,' and so forth. And because of the authority of the verbal teaching, it is verbal homage; physical homage and mental homage, however, are not performed. The demonstration of the text's author is for clarifying the authoritative nature of the text. The demonstration of the text's basis is for showing its purity by revealing its connection to oneself. The demonstration of the fruit of commencing the text is to prevent those who would reject it. The demonstration of the meaning designated as the purpose is for the benefit of those who investigate beforehand, since the teaching proceeds for those who take up the purpose beforehand; and for encouraging the listeners to engage in the text with reverence, as it is said—

Sabbasseva hi satthassa, kammassāpi ca kassaci;

Kenetaṃ gayhate tāva, yāva-vuttampayojanaṃti.

Indeed, for every teaching, and for any action whatsoever, how can it be grasped at all, until the purpose is stated?

Nanu [M 0.0003] satthappayojanānaṃ sambandhopi vattabbo idamassa payojananti yato–

Indeed, should not the connection between the teaching and its purposes also be stated, with the words 'This is its purpose,' since—

Siddhappayojanaṃ siddha,sambandhaṃ sotumicchati;

Sotādo tena vattabbo, sambandho sappayojanoti.

The listener desires to hear of an established purpose and an established connection; therefore, to the listener, the connection with its purpose should be stated at the outset.

Tatredamuttaraṃ–

Herein, this is the response—

Sattaṃ payojanañceva, ubho sambandhanissayā;

Taṃ vuttantogadhattā na, bhinno vutto payojanāti.

The teaching and the purpose, both are based on connection; because that is included within the stated content, the purpose is not stated separately.

Payojanappayojanampana sāmatthiyaladdhabbaṃ sayamācariyena “ko pana saddalakkhaṇassa ajānane doso”tiādinā vuttanayena viññātabbaṃ.

The purpose of the purpose, however, should be understood by oneself through the proficiency gained, according to the method stated by the teacher, such as: 'What, indeed, is the fault in not knowing the characteristics of sound?' and so forth.

Tattha‘mahādayo’tyādinā gāthādvayena ratanattayapaṇāmo dassito, ‘yo iddhimantesū’tiādinā ganthakattā, ‘saddasattha’ntiādinā ganthanissayo, ‘saṅkhepanayenā’tica ‘sārabhūtaṃ vipulatthagā hiṃ anākula’nti ca imehi ganthārambhaphalaṃ sotujanasamussāhanañca, abhidheyyasaṅkhātappayojanampana‘saṃvaṇṇana’nti iminā dassitaṃ anvattha byapadesena saṃvaṇṇīyati vivaritvā vitthāretvā kathīyati attho etāyāti saṃvaṇṇanābhi katvā, tampana vivaritvā kathanaṃ saddānusāsanasatthasannissayattā abhidheyyo nāma samuditena satthena vacanīyattho taṃ vacanīyatthoti (potthake) vuttasaddānusiṭṭhisaṅkhātapayojanamevāti ayamettha samudāyattho.

Herein, homage to the Triple Gem is shown by the two verses beginning with 'Mahādaya'; the author of the text by the phrase beginning with 'yo iddhimantesū'; the basis of the text by the phrase beginning with 'saddasattha'; and the fruit of commencing the text and the encouragement of the listeners by these phrases: 'by way of conciseness' and 'essential, containing extensive meaning, and unambiguous'. But the purpose designated as the subject matter (abhidheyya) is shown by 'saṃvaṇṇana' with its etymological designation, meaning that the meaning is explained, elucidated, and expounded by this, hence it is called saṃvaṇṇanā. And that explanation is called abhidheyya because of its reliance on the Saddānusāsana teaching; the meaning to be conveyed by the collected teaching is that very purpose designated as instruction according to the spoken words. This is the collective meaning here.

Ayampanettha avayavattho-yoti aniyamavacanaṃ dhammarājasaddā pekkhāya cettha pulliṅgatā, tenettha vuccamānaguṇavisesā dhārapuggalavisesanidassanaṃ, dayati dukkhaṃ apanetvā paresaṃ sukhaṃ dadāti, dayīyati vā sappurisehi gamiya(ti sa) santāne pavattīyati, dayati vā paradukkhaṃ hiṃsati, dayati vā paradukkhaṃ gaṇhāti taṃvasena attano hadayakhedaṃ karotīti dayā, “daya=dānagati hiṃsādānesu” iccasmā “itthiyamaṇattikayakyāce”ti (5-49) appaccayo, visayamahantatāya [M 0.0004] mahatī pasatthā vā dayā assāti mahādayo, visesana samāse “saddhāditva” (4-84) vakkhamānapāramitāsambharaṇadukkhānubhava nānamidaṃ hetuvacanaṃ, kammakilesehi janitāti janā sattaloko, iminā khīṇāsavāpi saṅgayhanti tesampi diṭṭhadhammikasukhavihārasaṅkhāta hitassa dānato, janānaṃ samūho janatā tassā hitāya abhivaḍḍhiyā sakalavaṭṭa dukkhanissaṭanibbānasukhabhāgiyakaraṇāyāti vuttaṃ hoti, assaca’sampūraya’nti iminā’dukkhamanubhavī’ti iminā ca sambandho, sambodhīti ettha saṃsaddo sāmanti imamatthaṃ dīpeti, tasmā saṃsayameva anaññabodhito hutvā cattāri saccāni bujjhati paṭivijjhati etāyāti sambodhi, saṃpubbā budhadhātuto “i”iti ṇvādi (ko) ippaccayo, savāsanasakalasaṃkilesappahāyakaṃ bhagavato arahattamaggaññāṇaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇantipi vadanti, sampāpayatīti sampāpakaṃ, sambodhiyā sampāpakanti chaṭṭhīsamāso, kinti dhammajātaṃ dhammasaddenettha pāramidhammā pañcamahāpariccāgādayo ca adhippetā, tepi hi attānaṃ dhārentaṃ dhārenti sambodhi sampāpanasāmatthiyayogena parepi dhārenti nāmāti dhammāti vuccanti, ‘dhara=dhāraṇe’iccasmā khīsu, viyādisuttena ṇvādi(ko) mappaccayo, dhammānaṃjātaṃ, dhammāevavā jātaṃ, sambodhisampāpakañca taṃ dhammajātaṃ ceti visesanasamāso, ‘sampūraya’nti massetaṃ kammaṃ, sampūrayanti payogasampattiyogā dīpaṅkara (pāda)mūle hatthopagatampi nibbānampahāya yathāvuttakaruṇāguṇayogasītalībhūtahadayatāya “kathannāmete accanta dussahavaṭṭadukkhopagate satte taṃmahādukkhā mocessāmī”ti vaṭṭadukkhanissaraṇekahetutāya sammā pūrento vaḍḍhento vuḍḍhiṃ virūḷhaṃ vepullaṃ gamentoti vuttaṃ hoti, hetuyevedamapi dukkhānubhavanassa, mahādayatā panassa paramparahetu, duṭṭhu khanati kāyikaṃ assādanti’dupubbā khanismā’ “kvī”ti (5-4) kvi, dukkhaṃ kāyikadukkha vedanā, kīdisanti āha-’anantarūpa’nti, sabhāvavacano yaṃ rūpasaddo “piyarūpa”ntiādīsuviya, te ca dukkhasabhāvā (anantā) anantakāraṇānaṃ vasena, tasmā anantaṃ rūpaṃ sabhāvo assāti anantarūpaṃ, taṃ dukkhaṃ anubhavī vindī, kimivāti āha-‘sukhaṃ vā’ti, suṭṭhu khanati kāyikaṃ ābādhanti [M 0.0005] sukhaṃ, ivasaddo sadhammattasaṅkhātopamājotako, sadhammattañhi upamā, vuttañhi “upamānopameyyānaṃ, sadhammattaṃ siyo pamā”ti, kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti “aniṭṭhānubhavanasabhāvāyāpi dukkhavedanāya anubhavanasabhāvasāmaññena ajjhāsayasampattivisesayogā mahākāruṇikassa sukhena sadisatāpattihotīti dukkhampi samānaṃ taṃ sukhamiva vindī”ti. Kathamaññathā vaṭṭadukkhato sakalalokassa samuddharaṇaṃ siyāti, athavā sukhamiva sukhaṃ vindanto viya anaññavindiyamapi tādisaṃ dukkhaṃ sakalalokahitāva hitamanatāya vindīti attho, tenāha ‘akhinnarūpo’ti, akhinnaṃ parissamamappattaṃ rūpaṃ sabhāvo assāti viggaho.

This is the explanation of the component part here—it is an indefinite term. With reference to the word 'dhammarāja', its gender is masculine. Therefore, the special qualities described herein indicate the characteristics of the person who bears them. He removes suffering and gives happiness to others; or, it is attained by good people, being cultivated in their lineage; or, he harms the suffering of others; or, he takes upon himself the suffering of others, thereby causing distress to his own heart—this is compassion (dayā). From the root 'daya' in the senses of giving, going, harming, and taking, the 'a' suffix is used, according to the rule 'itthiyamaṇattikayakyāce' (5-49). He whose compassion is great or praised due to the vastness of its object is one of great compassion (mahādayo). In a descriptive compound, according to the rule 'saddhāditva' (4-84), this is a causal term for the knowledge of experiencing suffering while accumulating the perfections to be mentioned. Beings (janā) are so called because they are generated by kamma and defilements; this refers to the world of beings. By this, even the taintless ones (khīṇāsavā) are included, because of the giving of benefit to them also, which is known as the happy abiding in the present life. The multitude of beings is 'janatā'; for their welfare, for their growth, for making them partakers of the happiness of Nibbāna, which is the escape from all the suffering of the cycle of rebirth—this is what is meant. And there is a connection with 'he fulfilled' and with 'he experienced suffering'. Regarding 'sambodhi', the prefix 'saṃ' here indicates the meaning 'completely'. Therefore, because one awakens to and penetrates the four truths by means of it, being completely without doubt and not enlightened by another, it is called 'sambodhi'. From the root 'budh' preceded by 'saṃ', the 'i' suffix is applied from the ṇvādi group. Some also say that the Blessed One's knowledge of the path to Arahantship, which eradicates all defilements together with their latent tendencies, is omniscient knowledge. That which brings to accomplishment is a 'sampāpaka'. 'Sambodhiyā sampāpakaṃ' is a genitive compound. What is this collection of dhammas (dhammajātaṃ)? Here, by the word 'dhamma', the perfection-dhammas, the five great sacrifices, and so on, are intended. Because they uphold the one who upholds them, and because they also uphold others through their capacity to bring about the attainment of sambodhi, they are called 'dhammas'. From the root 'dhara' (to uphold), the 'ma' suffix is applied from the ṇvādi group, according to the viyādi sutta. 'Dhammānaṃ jātaṃ' or 'dhammā eva jātaṃ'; and 'sambodhisampāpakañca taṃ dhammajātaṃ ca' is a descriptive compound. 'Sampūraya' is its action. 'Sampūrayanti' means: through the perfection of his application, having abandoned Nibbāna even when it was within his grasp at the feet of Dīpaṅkara, with a heart cooled by the quality of compassion as described, he thought, 'How shall I liberate these beings, who have fallen into the utterly unbearable suffering of the cycle of rebirth, from that great suffering?' Being the sole cause for escape from the suffering of the cycle, he was perfectly fulfilling, increasing, causing it to grow, develop, and reach abundance—this is what is meant. This is also the reason for his experiencing of suffering; his great compassion, however, is the remote cause. 'It digs badly' (duṭṭhu khanati) into the body; from 'du' and the root 'khan', with the 'kvi' suffix, comes 'dukkha', which is painful bodily feeling. What is it like? He says, 'anantarūpaṃ'. Here the word 'rūpa' means nature, as in 'piyarūpa'. And those sufferings are endless in nature because of their endless causes. Therefore, 'anantarūpaṃ' means 'that which has an endless nature'. He experienced that suffering. Like what? He says, 'as if it were happiness' (sukhaṃ vā). 'It digs well' (suṭṭhu khanati) into the bodily affliction; this is 'sukha'. The word 'iva' indicates a simile based on a common quality. For it is said: 'A common quality between the standard of comparison and the object of comparison is a simile.' What is meant? Although painful feeling has the nature of an undesirable experience, for the great compassionate one, due to the commonality of the nature of experience and the excellence of his disposition, it attains a state of similarity to happiness. Thus, though it was suffering, he experienced it as if it were happiness. Otherwise, how could the deliverance of the entire world from the suffering of the cycle of rebirth be possible? Alternatively, the meaning is: just as one might experience happiness, he experienced such suffering—which could not be experienced by another—with a mind intent on the welfare of the entire world. Therefore, he says, 'akhinnarūpo'. The analysis is: 'he whose nature (rūpa) is untiring (akhinnaṃ), not having reached exhaustion'.

Taṃ dhammarājanti yoti aniyamaniddiṭṭhassa vuttaguṇavisesādhāra puggalassaniyamanavacanaṃ, dhammena rājati no adhammenāti vā, attanā paṭividdhassa sāmibhāvena dhammassa rājā sāmīti vā, attanā paṭivijjhiyamāne dhamme paṭivijjhantova tattha rājati dippatīti vā, parūpakāravasena tadatthāyeva paṭipannattā paresaṃ dhammaṃ rājeti pakāsetīti vā dhammarājā, taṃ dhammarājaṃ namitvāti sambandho, namassitvāti attho, kīdisanti āha-‘jitamāravīraṃ sudhanta sovaṇṇanibha’nti. Tattha māro ca so vīrocāti māravīro jito vidtedhastabalo māravīro nāti jitamāravīro, taṃ, kiñcāpi devaputtakilesābhisaṅkhāramaccukkhandha mārā-nena jitā eva, tathāpi vīrasaddasannidhānena devaputtamāre gahite taṃvijayā aññepi jitā eva nāma hontīti viññeyyaṃ, suṭṭhu dhantaṃ dhamitaṃ uddharitaṃ sudhantaṃ, suvaṇṇameva sovaṇṇaṃ, sudhanta ca taṃ sovaṇṇañca, tasseva nibhā sobhā asseti samāso, athavā sudhantañca taṃ suvaṇṇaṃ ceti samāse tassidanti “ṇo”ti (4-34) ṇappaccaye “majjhe”ti (4-126) majjhavuddhiyaṃ sudhantasovaṇṇaṃ paṭimārūpaṃ, tena nibho sadiso, taṃ.

Regarding 'that King of Dhamma' (taṃ dhammarājaṃ): this is an indefinite expression for the person, indefinitely indicated, who is the repository of the special qualities mentioned. Or, he is King of Dhamma because he reigns by the Dhamma, not by what is not the Dhamma; or, because he is the king, the master of the Dhamma he has penetrated by himself; or, because while penetrating the Dhamma, he reigns and shines therein; or, because, having undertaken the practice solely for the benefit of others, he causes the Dhamma to reign for them, that is, he proclaims it. The connection is 'having paid homage to that King of Dhamma'. The meaning is 'having revered him'. What is he like? He says: 'who has conquered the hero Māra, who is like well-purified gold'. Herein, Māra, who is also a hero, is 'Māra the hero' (māravīro). He by whom Māra the hero was conquered, his power destroyed, is 'one who has conquered the hero Māra' (jitamāravīro). Although the Māras of the deity's son, defilements, formations, death, and the aggregates have been conquered by him, nevertheless, from the proximity of the word 'hero', it should be understood that when the deity's son Māra is taken, the others are also indeed conquered by that victory. 'Sudhantaṃ' means well-smelted, refined, extracted. 'Sovaṇṇaṃ' is gold itself. 'Sudhantañca taṃ sovaṇṇañca' (that which is well-purified and is gold). 'Tasseva nibhā sobhā assā'ti' (whose radiance or beauty is like that) is the compound. Alternatively, in the compound 'sudhantañca taṃ suvaṇṇaṃ ca', the 'ṇa' suffix is applied according to the rule 'tassidaṃ' (4-34), with middle vowel strengthening according to 'majjhe' (4-126), forming 'sudhantasovaṇṇaṃ', meaning a golden image. 'Tena nibho' means similar to that. Him (taṃ).

Ettāvatā ca –

Thus far—

Hetu phalaṃ parattho ca, sabbopi thutisaṅgaho;

Hetu sambodhito, pubbeva, yamaññaṃ tatoparīti.

The cause, the fruit, and the welfare of others—this is the entire collection of praise. The cause is that which is before awakening; whatever is other than that comes after.

Vuttahetuphalasattopakāravasena [M 0.0006] buddharatanassa thutipubbakampaṇāmaṃ dassetvā idāni dhammarājena tenāpi pūjanīyassa dhammaratanassa nipaccakāraṃ dassetuṃ‘dhammañca mohandhatamappadhaṃsi’nti āha, tattha ca saddo ‘dhammañca namitvā’ti namassitvā (potthake) namassanakriyāya dhammaṃ sampiṇḍeti, kimbhūtanti āha, ‘mohandhatamappadhaṃsi’nti, muyhatīti moho=aññāṇaṃ, andhayati samatthacakkhuviññāṇaparihānenāti andhaṃ, andhañca taṃ tamañceti andhatamaṃ=bāḷhatimiraṃ, mohoyeva taṃsadisatāya andhatamanti mo handhatamaṃ, taṃ padhaṃseti pakārena nāseti sīlenāti mohandhatamappadhaṃsī, pasaddassapakāsanatthaṃ hitvā pakāratthasseva gahaṇato pariyattiyā saha–

Having shown the homage preceded by praise to the Buddha Gem, based on the cause, fruit, and benefit to beings as stated, now, to show reverence for the Dhamma Gem, which is worthy of worship even by that King of Dhamma, he says: 'And the Dhamma, the dispeller of the darkness of delusion.' Here, the word 'ca' connects the Dhamma with the act of homage, implying 'having paid homage to the Dhamma also'. What is it like? He says: 'the dispeller of the darkness of delusion' (mohandhatamappadhaṃsi). One is deluded (muyhati), thus it is delusion (moho), which is ignorance. It makes one blind (andhayati) through the loss of effective eye-consciousness, thus it is blinding (andhaṃ). That which is blinding and is darkness (tamaṃ) is blinding darkness (andhatamaṃ), i.e., dense gloom. Delusion itself, being similar to it, is the darkness of delusion (mohandhatamaṃ). That which destroys (dhaṃseti) it thoroughly (pakārena) by its nature (sīlena) is the 'dispeller of the darkness of delusion'. The meaning of 'thoroughly' for the prefix 'pa' is taken here, abandoning its meaning of 'proclaiming', in accordance with the scriptural teaching—

Sotāpattādayo maggā,cattāro tapphalānica;

Cattāri atha nibbānaṃ, dhammā lokuttarā navāti.

The four paths, beginning with stream-entry, and their four corresponding fruits, and then Nibbāna—these are the nine supramundane dhammas.

Vuttanavalokuttarammo gahitāti viññātabbaṃ, aññathā arahattamaggova gayheyya, kasmā panettha mohasseva pahānaṃ vuttaṃ, netaresanti tammūlakattā sabbakilesānaṃ, tappahānasmiñhi vuccamāne tammukhenetaresampi pahānaṃ vuttameva hotīti.

It should be understood that the nine supramundane states mentioned have been taken; otherwise, only the path to arahantship would be apprehended. Why is only the abandoning of delusion mentioned here, and not the others? Because it is the root of all defilements. For, when its abandonment is stated, the abandonment of the others is also stated in effect.

Evaṃ dhammaratanassa namakkāraṃ dassetvā idāni tadādhārabhūtasaṅgharatanaṃ namassituṃ ‘saṅghaṃ tathā saṅghaṭitaṃ guṇehī’ti vuttaṃ, tattha tathāsaddo samuccaye vā, vacoyuttiyaṃ vā, vacoyuttipakkhe ca saddo ānetvā sambandhitabbo, kilesādayo saṃhanati hiṃsatīti saṅgho, saṃpubbato hanatismā kvimhi “kvimhi ghoparipaccasamo hī”ti (5.100) hanassa gho, kilesahiṃsanañcettha tadaṅgādivasena gahitaṃ, guṇehīti sāmaññaniddesato sammutisaṅghena saddhiṃ

Having thus shown reverence to the Dhamma Jewel, now, in order to revere the Sangha Jewel, which serves as its foundation, it is said: 'The Sangha, likewise, well-assembled with qualities.' Herein, the word 'tathā' can denote either conjunction or appropriateness of expression. In the case of appropriateness of expression, the word 'ca' should be brought in to connect it. The Sangha crushes and destroys defilements and so forth; therefore it is called 'Sangha.' From the root 'han' (to strike, kill) with the prefix 'saṃ' and the suffix 'kvi', according to 'kvimhi ghoparipaccasamo hī' (5.100), 'gha' comes from 'han.' And here, the destruction of defilements is included in the sense of temporary abandonment (tadaṅga) and so forth. 'With qualities' is a general designation, so along with the conventional Sangha...

Cattāro ca paṭipannā, cattāro ca phaleṭhitā;

Esa saṅgho ujubhūto, paññāsīlasamāhitoti.

Four are those practicing for attainment, four are those who have attained the fruit; this Sangha is upright, composed of wisdom and virtue.

Vuttaaṭṭhaariyapuggalā [M 0.0007] gayhanti, guṇehīti lokiyalokuttarehi sīlādiguṇehi, saṅghaṭitanti saṃhataṃ.

The eight noble individuals mentioned are included here. 'With qualities' refers to worldly and supramundane virtues such as morality, etc. 'Well-assembled' means well-combined.

Evamanantarāyena ganthaparisamāpanatthamananta guṇavisiṭṭhalokattayaggasīkhāmaṇibhūtassa ratanattayassa paṇāmaṃ dassetvā idāni gantha kattādiyathāvuttatthopadassana pubbaṅgamamattanā samārabhitabbaṃ gantha karaṇaṃ paṭiññātukāmo’yo iddhimantesū’tiādimāha, tattha ‘yo’ti imassa ‘tannāmadheyyenā’ti iminā sambandho, etāya sattā ijjhanti iddhā vuddhā ukkaṃsagatā hontīti iddhi=iddhividhādayo lokiyā lokuttarā ca sā etesamatthīti iddhimanto, tesu iddhimantesu, iddhimantānaṃ mahāsāvakānaṃ majjheti attho, mahattappattoti mahattaṃ mahantabhāvaṃ gato, tannāmadheyyenāti tasseva nāmadheyyamassāti tannāmadheyyo, tena, tapodhanenāti muninā, kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti- “etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ iddhimantānaṃ yadidaṃ moggallāno”ti bhagavatā iddhimantesu etadagge ṭhapito mahāmoggallānatthero nāma yo dutiyo aggasāvako… (tena samānanāmadheyyenāti) tamapadisanto-yamācariyo anuddhatabhāvena ujunākkamena nāmādikamavatvā vaṅkavuttiyā attano moggallānoti nāmaṃ mahāsāmiṭṭhānantarappattiṃ kālocitapaññā veyyattiyaṃ buddhasāsanopakāritādiñca vibhāveti. ‘Yaṃ racita’nti sambandho, racitanti kataṃ, kinti āha saddasattha’nti, saddasatthaṃ nāma sutta, saddalakkhaṇabyākaraṇādyaparanāmadheyyaṃ, suttaṃ(hi) ‘saddā (lakkhīyanti) sāsīyanti anusāsīyanti pakatippaccayādivibhāgakappanāya etenā’ti saddalakkhaṇanti ca ‘byākarīyanti saddanipphādanavasena kathīyanti etenā’ti byākaraṇanti ca vuccati, aparampana vutyādi tadupakaraṇabhāvena saddasatthaṃ saddalakkhaṇaṃ byākaraṇanti ca vuccatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ, anunanti tabbisesanaṃ, asesalakkhiyopasaṅgāhakabhāvena vattabbassāparassābhāvā sampuṇṇanti attho, athāti anantaratthe nipāto, saddasattharacanānantaranti attho, tasseti saddasatthassa, vutti ca [M 0.0008] samāsā katāti sambandho, suttaṃ vivarīyati etāyāti vutti, samassate saṅkhipīyatīti samāsā.

Having thus paid homage to the Three Jewels, which are the crest-jewel of the three worlds, distinguished by infinite virtues, for the purpose of completing this treatise without interruption, now, desiring to declare the composition of the treatise to be undertaken by himself, which is preceded by an indication of the author of the work and so forth, and its purpose as previously stated, he begins with ‘yo iddhimantesū’tiādimāha.’ Herein, ‘yo’ is connected with ‘tannāmadheyyenā’ti. By this, beings succeed, prosper, and become exalted—thus, ‘iddhi’ refers to psychic powers, such as the various kinds of worldly and supramundane attainments. ‘Iddhimanto’ means those who possess such powers. ‘Iddhimantesu’ means among those possessing psychic powers, that is, among the great disciples. ‘Mahattappattoti’ means having attained greatness, the state of being great. ‘Tannāmadheyyenāti’ means bearing his name; ‘tena’—by that ascetic. What is meant? The Blessed One declared, ‘Among my monk disciples who possess psychic powers, Moggallāna is the foremost.’ Thus, the Elder Mahāmoggallāna, the second chief disciple, was established as the foremost among those with psychic powers… By indicating him (tena samānanāmadheyyenāti), this teacher, being free from arrogance and straightforward in approach, without directly stating his name and so forth, but rather by an indirect expression, reveals his own name as Moggallāna, his attainment of the position of great master, his timely wisdom and skill, and his service to the Buddha’s Dispensation, etc. ‘Yaṃ racita’nti is the connection. ‘Racitaṃ’ means composed. How? He says ‘saddasattha’nti. ‘Saddasatthaṃ’ refers to the Sutta, also known as ‘saddalakkhaṇa’ (characteristics of sounds) and ‘byākaraṇa’ (grammar). For the Sutta is called ‘saddalakkhaṇa’ because sounds are characterized, instructed, and guided by it through the classification of natural conditions, suffixes, etc. It is called ‘byākaraṇa’ because sounds are explained and spoken through it for their production. Furthermore, it should be understood that ‘saddasatthaṃ,’ ‘saddalakkhaṇa,’ and ‘byākaraṇa’ are also used in relation to their auxiliary functions, such as the commentary (vutti) and so forth. ‘Anunanti’ is its adjective, meaning complete, as there is nothing else to be characterized or supplemented. ‘Athāti’ is a particle meaning immediately after. The meaning is ‘immediately after composing the saddasattha.’ ‘Tasseti’ refers to the saddasattha. ‘Vutti ca samāsā katāti’ is the connection. ‘Vutti’ means that by which the Sutta is explained. ‘Samāsā’ means that by which it is condensed.

Tassāpīti vuttiyāpi, saṅgahetvā saddavasena saṅkucitaṃ viya katvā khipanaṃ saṅkhepo, tassa nayo kamo saṅkhepanayo, tena, bhovāti yo saddasatthassa vuttiyā ca kattā so eva, idāni suttavuttiracanānantaramavasarappatte imasmiṃ kāle, samārabheyya sammā ārambhaṃ kareyya bahunnaṃ kriyākkhaṇānamādibhūtaṃ kriyākkhaṇamanutiṭṭheyya, kinti saṃvaṇṇanaṃ, saṃvaṇṇīyati attho etāyāti saṃvaṇṇanā, pañcīyati vipañcīyati byattī karīyati vutti attho etāyāti vā, taṃ pañcayatīti vā laddhanāmapañcikā, taṃ.

Even of that commentary (vutti), a summary (saṅkhepo) is a composition made by compiling and, as it were, contracting it through words; the method of that is the sequence of summarization (saṅkhepanayo); by that (method). ‘Bhovāti’ refers to the one who is the author of both the grammar (saddasattha) and its commentary (vutti); he himself, now, at this opportune time, immediately after composing the Sutta and its commentary, should properly begin, undertake the right start, and pursue that initial moment which is the beginning of many action-instants. What is the explanation? Because the meaning is explained by this, therefore it is called an explanation (saṃvaṇṇanā). Or, because the meaning of the commentary (vutti) is elaborated, expanded, and made clear by this, or because it elaborates that, it is called the Pañcikā, the commentary which has obtained that name. That.

Evamattanā karaṇīyasatthampaṭijānitvā tadanantaraṃ “dve me bhikkhave paccayā sammādiṭṭhiyā uppādāya (katame dve) parato ca ghoso (ajjhattañca) yoniso manasikāro”ti vacanato sammāsavanapaṭibaddhā sabbāpi sāsana (ppaṭi) sampattīti sāsanappaṭipattiyā byākaraṇassa mūlakāraṇattā taṃ savane sādhujane niyojento ‘taṃ sārabhūta’ntiādimāha, tattha tanti yasaddavirahepi adhikatattā saṃvaṇṇanaṃ parāmasati, taṃ suṇantū’ti sambandho, sādhūti savanakriyāvisesanaṃ, atthānurūpaṃ byañjanaṃ, byañjanānurūpañca atthaṃsallakkhetvā anaññamanā hutvā sakkaccaṃ suṇantūti attho suvaṇṇabhājane nikkhittasīhavasāviya avinassamānaṃ katvā hadaye ṭhapanavasena, sakkaccasavanameva hi sotūnamatthāvahaṃ hotīti, santoti savanakriyāya kattāro dasseti, tathā sātisayabyākaraṇaṃ… tathāvidhā eva sappurisā sādhukaṃ sotukāmā hontīti, kimbhūtanti āha ‘sārabhūta’ntiādi, bhūtasaddo ettha “bhūtasmiṃ pācittiya’ntiādīsu viya vijjamānattho, phegguttābhāvena apariccajanīyatāya sāro thiraṃ so attho byañjanañca assā atthīti sārā ca sā bhūtāca, atha vā lokiyalokuttaraguṇātisayasādhanekasādhanabhāvato seṭṭhaṭṭhena sārañca sā bhūtācāti sārabhūtā, taṃ gantho yevettha saṅkhepito, attho pana nayaggāhitatāyapi sabbathā dassitoyevāti [M 0.0009] vipulaṃ atthaṃ gaṇhātīti vipulatthagāhī, taṃ, vidhīyamānavaṇṇanākkamavisesena byākulassa vaṇṇanākkamassa nirasanato natthi ākulaṃ kiñci assāti anākulaṃ, taṃ, iminā ca kaccāyanavuttivaṇṇanāsu na tathābhāvaṃ dasseti.

Having thus acknowledged the treatise to be composed by himself, immediately after, from the statement, “Monks, there are two conditions for the arising of right view: the voice of another and proper attention,” all the attainments of the Dispensation are connected with right listening. Therefore, since grammar (byākaraṇa) is the root cause of success in practicing the Dispensation, directing the virtuous to listen to it, he says, ‘taṃ sārabhūta’ntiādi. Herein, the word 'taṃ' (that), even in the absence of the relative pronoun 'ya', refers to the commentary (saṃvaṇṇanaṃ) because it is the subject under discussion. ‘Taṃ suṇantū’ti is the connection. ‘Sādhū’ti qualifies the act of listening. Having discerned the meaning according to the expression and the expression according to the meaning, and being undistracted, they should listen carefully—this is the meaning. Like placing lion’s fat in a golden vessel without letting it spoil, so should it be held in the heart. For listeners, careful listening alone brings benefit. ‘Santoti’ indicates the agents of the act of listening. Likewise, such a grammar is exceedingly advantageous… such virtuous ones are indeed eager to listen well. What kind? He says, ‘sārabhūta’ntiādi. Here, the word ‘bhūta’ conveys the sense of existence, as in ‘an offense exists’ (bhūtasmiṃ pācittiya). Because it is not to be discarded due to being pithless, its essence is firm. Both the meaning and the expression are substantial—thus, it is ‘sārā ca sā bhūtā ca’ (essential and existing). Or, because it is supreme by nature, being the sole means to achieve worldly and supramundane excellences, it is both essence and existing—thus, ‘sārabhūtā’. Here, the text itself is concise, but the meaning is fully shown even by the method of logical inference. It grasps a vast meaning—thus, ‘vipulatthagāhī’ (grasping vast meanings). This, by the elimination of a confused sequence of the commentary when being composed, has nothing confusing—thus, it is ‘anākula’ (free from confusion). Moreover, by this he indicates that such is not the case in the commentaries on Kaccāyana’s Vutti.

Tadevamadhikatattāyevāyamācariyo ganthārambhe’mahādayo yo’tiādike paṭipajjitvā dāni attanā vaṇṇanīyassa ganthassādi bhūtaṃ vākyamanadhikataparihāramukhenevopanyasya byākhyātumāha- ‘idhā’tiādi, tattha idhāti imasmiṃ māgadhikasaddalakkhaṇaviracanādhikāre, māgadhānaṃ saddānaṃ idanti māgadhikaṃ, māgadhikaṃ saddalakkhaṇanti visesana samāso, viracayitukāmoti kattukāmo, ratiṃjanetīti ratanaṃ, ramayatī ra tayatī (potthake) ti (vā) ratanaṃ anappaccayena, athavā yaṃ loke cittīkatādikaṃ ratananti vuccati, idampi taṃ sadisatāya ratananti vuccati, tathācāhu–

Therefore, precisely because of its importance, this teacher, having undertaken the composition with ‘mahādayo yo’ and so forth at the very beginning, now introduces the initial sentence of the work to be commented upon by himself, presenting it in a manner that avoids excess and deficiency, and proceeds to explain, saying, ‘idha,’ and so forth. Therein, ‘idha’ means in this matter of composing the characteristics of Māgadha words. That which belongs to the words of the Māgadhas is ‘Māgadhika.’ ‘The characteristic of Māgadha words’ is a descriptive compound. ‘Viracayitukāmo’ means desiring to compose. ‘Ratiṃ janeti’—that which generates delight is a ‘ratana’; or ‘ramayati’ is a ‘ratana’ with the suffix ‘ana.’ Alternatively, that which in the world is called a jewel, such as something esteemed, this too, because of its similarity, is called a ‘ratana.’ And thus they said—

Cittīkataṃ mahagghañca, atulaṃ dullabhadassanaṃ;

Anomasattaparibhogaṃ, ratanaṃ tena vuccatīti.

Esteemed and of great value, incomparable, rare to see, and enjoyed by beings of peerless worth—for that reason it is called a jewel.

Buddhādīnametamadhivacanaṃ, tayo avayavā assāti tayaṃ, samudāyo, ratanānaṃ tayaṃ ratanattayaṃ, avayavavinimmuttassa pana samudāyassa abhāvato tīṇi eva ratanāni vuccanti, paṇamanaṃ paṇāmo, ratanattayaguṇaninnatā, paṇamanti etāyāti vā paṇāmo, paṇāmakriyānipphādikā kusalacetanā, ratanattayassa paṇāmoti chaṭṭhīsamāso, abhidhīyati paṭipādīyatītyabhidheyyo samuditena satthena vacanīyattho, yena ca yo paṭipādīyati so tassa attho hotīti, so ca pakatippaccayādivibhāgakappanāya saddānaṃ saṅkharaṇaṃ, saddasatthena hi saddasaṅkharaṇameva paṭipādīyati, (ratanattayappaṇāmo ca abhidheyyo ca) ratanattayappaṇāmābhidheyyanti catthasamāso, tassa sandassanaṃ attho yassāti aññapadattho, kintaṃ vākyaṃ, tā vāti vākyālaṅkāre, nanucevamadhikatattepi abhidheyyamattamevadassetabbaṃ [M 0.0010] siyā kiṃ vācāpaṇāmena, kāyamanomayenāpi puññāti sayappattiyā abhisamīhitatthasiddhi hotevāti codanaṃ manasi nidhāya vacīpaṇāmassa paratthasannissayatañca tasseva vibhāgena payojanañca dassetumāha- ‘tattha’iccādi, guṇasaddo ettha “sataguṇā dakkhiṇā pāṭikaṅkhā”tiādīsu viya ānisaṃsaṭṭho, guṇānamānisaṃsānaṃ anukūlaṃ anuguṇaṃ, hetumantavisesanametaṃ, padhānabhāvaṃ nītaṃ paṇītaṃ atiuttamanti attho, atīsayena paṇītaṃ paṇītataraṃ, cittassasantānaṃ pabandho cittasantānaṃ, paṇītatarañca taṃ cittasantānañca, anuguṇañca taṃ paṇītataracittasantānañcāti visesanasamāso, tappaṇāmakaraṇena anuguṇa…pe… santānaṃ yesanti aññapadattho, tesaṃ, yathā te sotāro ratanattayassa paṇāmakaraṇena puññātisayappaṭilābhā anekānisaṃsātisayappaṭilābhānukūla cittasantānatāya padhānataracittasantānā honti, tathā pavattānanti adhippāyo, idampi adhigatā…pe… ntarādhānantīmesaṃ hetubhāvena tiṭṭhati, adhigatā pattā aneke bahū ānisaṃsavisesā āyu vaṇṇasukhabalapaṭibhānādayo yesanti viggaho, visositā sukkhāpitā antarāyā bhayādayo ajjhattikā bāhiyā vā yesaṃ tathāvidhānaṃ sotūnaṃ, etepi abhi,pe,ddhatthanti iccassa hetū, abhisamīhitassa anuṭṭhitassa kataniṭṭhitassa ganthassa avabodhoyeva phalaṃ, tassa sijjhanatthaṃ, kintaṃ ratanattayappaṇāmasandassanaṃ.

This is the designation of the Buddha and others. 'Having three parts' means a triad, an aggregate. A triad of jewels is the Triple Gem. However, since there is no aggregate separate from its parts, it is simply called 'the three jewels.' Bowing (paṇamana) is reverence (paṇāma), an inclination toward the qualities of the Triple Gem. Or, it is called 'reverence' because one bows with it; it is the wholesome volition that accomplishes the act of bowing. 'Reverence to the Triple Gem' is a genitive compound. That which is expressed or conveyed is the 'expressible' (abhidheyya), the meaning to be stated with its collected substance. And that by which something is conveyed is its meaning. And that is the composition of words through the arrangement of divisions such as roots and suffixes. For by the science of words, only the composition of words is conveyed. 'Reverence to the Triple Gem and the expressible' is a copulative compound. That of which the meaning is the showing of this, is a relative compound. What is that? A sentence. The words 'tā vā' are sentence-ornaments. But surely, even though it is important, should only the expressible meaning be shown? What is the use of verbal reverence? Having kept in mind the objection that 'the desired goal is certainly accomplished through the attainment of an abundance of merit by bodily and mental reverence also,' he says 'Therein' (tattha), etc., to show that verbal reverence is dependent on others and to show its purpose by way of its distinction. Here, the word 'quality' (guṇa), as in passages like 'a hundredfold gift is to be expected,' has the meaning of 'benefit' (ānisaṃsa). Favorable to qualities and benefits is 'anuguṇa.' This is an adjective indicating a cause. 'Brought to a state of prominence' (padhāna-bhāvaṃ nītaṃ), 'paṇītaṃ' means 'most excellent.' Exceedingly excellent is 'more excellent' (paṇītataraṃ). The continuity of the stream of consciousness is the 'mental continuum' (cittasantāna). 'And that more excellent mental continuum, and that favorable more excellent mental continuum' is a descriptive compound. 'Of those for whom, by making that reverence, there is a favorable... [more excellent mental]... continuum' is a relative compound. The meaning is: just as those listeners, by making reverence to the Triple Gem, through gaining an abundance of merit, become possessed of a more pre-eminent mental continuum due to having a mental continuum favorable to gaining an abundance of many benefits, so it proceeds. This also stands as a cause for those who have attained... [and for whom] obstacles are removed. The analysis is: 'those by whom many various benefits such as long life, beauty, happiness, strength, and analytical knowledge have been attained.' Of such listeners for whom internal or external obstacles, such as fear, have been dried up. These too are causes for the meaning of 'accomplished.' For the sake of accomplishing its fruit, which is precisely the understanding of the work that has been desired, undertaken, and completed—what is that? The demonstration of reverence to the Triple Gem.

Saccaṃ punapi saccanti, bhujamukkhippa vuccate;

Sakattho natthī nattheva,parassatthamakubbatoti.

Truth, and again truth, it is declared with arm upraised: 'For one who does not act for another's benefit, there is no benefit for oneself, truly no benefit.'

Vacanato paratthova sappurisehi kattabbo, paratthe sampādite pana sakattho sampannova nāma siyāti manasi katvā āha- ‘etadevā’tiādi. Kāyamanosamācaraṇena sampajjamānañca vacīsamācaraṇena sampajjatevāti aneneva vākyena viññāyatīti avagantabbaṃ, buddhi pubbā yasmiṃ karaṇe taṃ buddhi pubbaṃ, taṃ sīlena karontā buddhipubbakārino, abhidheyyassa adhigamo jānanaṃ pubbo yassa so abhidheyyādhigamapubbako[M 0.0011], avatāro pavatti, ekadesadassane “samuddo diṭṭho”ti viya ekadesepi samudāyavohāradassanato pacchima pādenāti vuttaṃ, pacchimapādassekadesabhūtena ‘saddalakkhaṇa’miccanenāti attho, sādhiyaṃ saddānaṃ saṅkharaṇaṃ, sādhanaṃ byākaraṇaṃ, taṃ lakkhaṇaṃ sabhāvo assāti sādhiyasādhanalakkhaṇo, sādhiyassedaṃ sādhanaṃ, sādhanassa cedaṃ sādhiyanti evamassedambhāvahetusabhāvo sambandhoti vuttaṃ hoti, payojanaṃ abhidheyyasaddopadassitaṃ saddasaṅkharaṇaṃ, tattha sambandhassantogadhattaṃ… sādhiyopadassanamukhena sādhanassāpi dassitattā nissayopadassanato, ussukkaṃ sammāvāyāmaṃ, buddhattaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ, pūretvāti–

From the saying, 'What is for another's benefit should be done by the virtuous,' and having kept in mind that 'when another's benefit is accomplished, one's own benefit may be considered accomplished,' he says, 'This very thing...' and so forth. And it should be understood from this very statement that what is accomplished by bodily and mental conduct is also accomplished by verbal conduct. That action in which wisdom is first is 'preceded by wisdom.' Those who perform it with virtue are 'those who act preceded by wisdom.' He for whom the attainment of the expressible is preceded by knowledge is 'one whose attainment of the expressible is preceded by knowledge.' 'Entry' (avatāro) means 'occurrence' (pavatti). Just as upon seeing a part one says, 'The ocean is seen,' so too, because of the convention of referring to the whole by a part, it is said 'by the last quarter.' The meaning is: by 'the characteristic of words,' which is a part of the last quarter. 'What is to be accomplished' (sādhiya) is the composition of words; 'the means of accomplishment' (sādhana) is the grammar. That of which this is the characteristic and intrinsic nature is 'that which has the characteristic of what is to be accomplished and the means of accomplishment.' It is said that the connection is one of cause and intrinsic nature, in the sense that 'this is the means for what is to be accomplished, and this is what is to be accomplished by the means.' The purpose is the composition of words, indicated by the word 'expressible.' Therein, the connection is included because, by way of indicating what is to be accomplished, the means is also shown, due to the indication of dependence. 'Zeal' (ussukkaṃ) is right effort. 'Buddhahood' is the knowledge of omniscience. 'Having fulfilled...'

Manussattaṃ liṅgasampatti, hetu satthāradassanaṃ;

Pabbajjā guṇasampatti, adhikāro ca chandatā;

Aṭṭhadhammasamodhānā, abhinīhāro samijjhatīti.

Human existence, perfection of gender, the right cause, and seeing the Teacher; the going forth, the perfection of qualities, meritorious service, and strong aspiration; with the convergence of these eight conditions, the resolve is accomplished.

Vuttaaṭṭhadhammasamannāgatena abhinīhārena samannāgatā hutvā yathāvutte pāramitādayo dhamme pūretvāti attho, āgatāti sattattiṃsabodhipakkhiyadhammānubrūhanena āgatā, idhāti imasmiṃ loke, āgatāti pattā uppannā, tathāgatoti yathā sampati jātā te bhagavanto sattapadavītihārena gatā, tathā ayampi uttarābhimukhaṃ gatoti attho, muhuttajātovāti sampatijāto eva, jātasamanantaramevāti vuttaṃ hoti, vikkamīti agamāsi, satta padāni gantvāna disā vilokesīti idaṃ “dhammatā esā bhikkhave sampati jāto bodhisattā samehi pādehi patiṭṭhahitvā”ti eva mādikāya pāḷiyā sattapadavītihārūpariṭhitassa sabbadisānuvilokanassa vuttattā vuttaṃ, disā vilokesi samantatoti idampana ‘samehi pādehi phusī vasundhara’nti etassa anantaraṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ… pādehi vasundharāphusanānantarameva dasadisāvalokitattā, aṭṭhaṅgāni nāma–

The meaning is: having become endowed with the resolve that is endowed with the eight factors spoken of, he fulfilled the qualities such as the perfections as they have been described. 'Come' (āgatā) means come by way of cultivating the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment. 'Here' (idha) means in this world. 'Come' (āgatā) means arrived, arisen. 'Tathāgata' means: just as those Blessed Ones, newly born, went with a stride of seven steps, so too did this one go facing north. 'Just born' means newly born; that is to say, immediately after birth. 'Strode' (vikkami) means he went. 'Having gone seven steps, he looked upon the directions'—this is said because it is stated in the Pāli text beginning, 'This is the nature, monks, that a Bodhisatta, newly born, having established himself on his feet…' that he looked in all directions after standing upon the seven-step stride. 'He looked upon the directions all around'—this, however, should be understood as occurring after 'with even feet he touched the earth,' because he looked in the ten directions immediately after touching the earth with his feet. The eight factors are—

Visaṭṭhaṃ mañju viññeyyaṃ, savanīyā-visārino;

Bindu gambhīraninnādi,ccevamaṭṭhaṅgiko saroti.

Clear, sweet, intelligible, melodious, coherent, rounded, deep, and resonant—thus is the eight-factored voice.

Vuttāni [M 0.0012] aṭṭhaṅgāni, tathāgatoti imasseva visuṃ atthapariyāyaṃ dassetuṃ ‘athavā’tiādimāha, ariyena setunāti samathavipassanāsaṅkhātena uttamena maggena, evamādinātiādisaddena tesaṃ tesaṃ dhammānaṃ sabhāvasarasalakkhaṇaṃ tathaṃ āgato yathāvato adhigato’yegatyatthā te buddhyatthā, ye buddhyā te gatyatthā’titathāgatoti evamādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti, tatthatatthāti tesu tesu dīghāgamādīsu, tathāgatabhāvoti tathāgatoti bhavanaṃ nipphatti namassanakiriyābhisambandhāti’namassitvā’ti ettha namassanakiriyāya abhisambandhā iminā tathāgatādīnaṃ kammattaṃ vibhāveti, namassanakiriyāvisesanattāti ‘namassitvā’ti namassanaṃ katvāti vuttaṃ nāma siyāti namassananti vuttanamassanakiriyāya visesanattā, bodhiyāti bodhivuccati catūsu maggesu ñāṇaṃ, taṃ bhagavā ettha pattoti (bodhi, tassā) bodhirukkhassāti attho, mūleti mūlasamīpe “yāva majjhanhike kāle chāyā pharati nivāte paṇṇāni patanti etāvatā rukkhamūlaṃ”tiādīsu viya, nanu aññepi khīṇāsavā ‘aggamaggene’ccādinā vakkhamāna nayena nipphannā evāti anuyogaṃ manasikatvā vuttaṃ ‘saheva vāsanāyā’ti, na hi bhagavantaṃ ṭhapetvā aññe saha vāsanāya kilese pahātuṃ sakkonti, etena aññehi asādhāraṇaṃ bhagavato arahattanti dasseti, teneva iddhasaddassa atthaṃ dassento’tepi hi’ccādikaṃ vakkhati, kāpanāyaṃ vāsanā nāma pahīnakilesassāpi appahīnakilesassa payogasadisapayogahetubhūto kilesanihito sāmatthiyaviseso’āyasmato pilindavacchassa vasalasamudācāranimittaṃ viya’, aggamaggenāti arahattamaggena, sabbakilese rāgādike, arahattaṃ aggaphalaṃ, sammuti upapattidevabhāvato aññena visuddhi devabhāvenātinipphannattā āha-‘visuddhidevabhāvenā’ti, sakalakilesakālussiyāpagamena visuddhippattiyā sabbaññuguṇā laṅkārena visuddhidevabhāvenāti attho.

The eight factors are spoken of. To show the distinct meaning of this very word 'Tathāgata,' he says 'or,' and so on. 'By the noble bridge' means by the supreme path known as serenity and insight. By the word 'etc.' in 'evamādinā,' it encompasses such meanings as: 'he has come to the intrinsic nature, essence, and characteristics of those very phenomena as they are, he has realized them as they truly are'; 'those who have understanding as their goal, for them understanding is the goal; those who have understanding, for them the goal is attained'—thus, 'Tathāgata.' 'There, in those' means in the various long discourses and so on. 'The state of a Tathāgata' means the becoming, the accomplishment, of a Tathāgata. The connection with the act of homage: here, in 'having paid homage,' because of the connection with the act of homage, by this he clarifies the objecthood of the Tathāgata and others. Because it is a specification of the act of homage: 'having paid homage' means 'having performed homage.' Or, it might be said, because it specifies the act of homage which is called 'homage.' 'Of enlightenment': enlightenment is said to be the knowledge in the four paths. The Blessed One attained it here; therefore, 'of the Bodhi tree' is the meaning. 'At the foot' means near the root, as in 'until midday the shade spreads, in a windless place the leaves fall, thus far is the foot of the tree,' and so on. Now, are not other destroyers of cankers also perfected by the supreme path, and so on, in the manner to be explained? Considering this inquiry, it is said, 'together with the latent tendencies.' For indeed, apart from the Blessed One, no others are able to abandon defilements along with their latent tendencies. By this, he shows that the Blessed One’s arahantship is unique from others. For that very reason, explaining the meaning of the word 'iddha,' he will say, 'for even they,' and so on. And what is this 'latent tendency'? It is a particular capacity rooted in the defilements, which is a cause for conduct similar to the conduct of one who has not abandoned defilements, even for one who has abandoned them—like the venerable Pilindavaccha’s habit of addressing people as 'outcaste.' 'By the supreme path' means by the path of arahantship. All defilements means lust and so on. Arahantship is the supreme fruit. Because he is perfected by a state of purity as a deva that is different from the state of a deva by convention or by birth, he says, 'by the state of a deva of purity.' 'By the state of a deva of purity' means: through the removal of the stain of all defilements, by the attainment of purity, and by the adornment with the qualities of an omniscient one. This is the meaning.

‘Idha=saṃsiddhiyaṃ’ iddhavanto iddhāttappaccayena, ‘guṇa=āmantaṇe’ bhūvādiseso, guṇīyanti paricīyanti seyyattikehīti guṇā kappaccayena, tepīti sāvakapaccekabuddhāpi, hi saddo hetumhi, yasmā aggaṃ…pe… anūnaguṇā[M 0.0013], tasmāti attho, sabbaññutādīnantiādikaṃ tesaṃ sabbaññubuddhehi ūnaguṇatāya hetuvacanaṃ, keci ‘siddho middhaguṇo assāti siddhamiddhaguṇanti duṭṭhamatthaṃ parikappetvā vākyamidaṃ dūsenti, te pana ‘middho nāma koci guṇo natthī’ti ca, ‘tathāgato nāma middha guṇo na hotī’ti ca, ‘tādiso ce siyā na ñāṇanissitapūjā pakatopayoginī bhavatī’ti ca ajānitvā vadatha tumhehi vatvā uyyojetabbā, maṅgalatthañcetthādo siddhasaddopādānaṃ, maṅgalādīni hi satthānyabyāhatappasarāni hontyāyasmantabyākhyātusotukāni ca, dhammasaṅghānampīti iminā avayavena viggahepi samudāyassa samāsatthattā aññapadatthasamāsoyaṃ tagguṇasaṃviññāṇoti dīpeti, tenāha- ‘aññapadatthe’ccādi, guṇībhūtānampīti appadhānabhūtānampi visesanabhūtānampi aññapadatthassa padhānattā, kiriyātisambandho vagamyate dhammasaṅghānaṃ guṇībhūtānampi tadavinābhāvittena namassanātisambandhā, tadeva samattheti ‘tathāha’ccādinā, puttena saha vattamānoti tagguṇasaṃviññāṇaaññapadatthasamāsattā tulyamubhinnampi āgamananti puttopi āgatoti patīyate, tatthāti niddhāraṇe sattadhī, attānanti dhammaṃ dasseti, dhārenteti attani ṭhapente pavattente uppādente, cattāropi apāyā sāmaññavasena’apāye’ti vuttā, kilesavaṭṭa kammavaṭṭa vipākavaṭṭavasena tayo vaṭṭā, tesu dukkhaṃ, tasmiṃ, dhāretīti vuttadhāraṇaṃ nāma atthato apāyādinibbattakakilesaviddhaṃsanaṃ, tañca yathārūpaṃ kilesasamucchindanatappaṭippassaddhi ālambanabhāvena hotīti āha- ‘so…pe… vasenā’ti, navannampi, te samadhigamahetutāya dhammoyeva nāmāti ‘dasā’tiādi vuttaṃ, tattha kāraṇamāha- ‘tammūlakattā’tiādi, tammūlakattāti taṃ kāraṇattā, sīladiṭṭhisāmaññenāti ariyena sīlena ariyāya ca diṭṭhiyā samānabhāvena, ariyānañhi sīladiṭṭhiyo maggenāgatattā sabbathā samānāva, tena te yatthakatthaci ṭhitāpi sahagatāvāti saṃhatoti imasmiṃ atthe saṅghoti padasiddhi daṭṭhabbā, adhippetavasena panetaṃ vuttaṃ, lokiyasīladiṭṭhiyā sāmaññena saṃhatattā sammutisaṅghopi paṇāmārahoyevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

‘Here’ means ‘for success’; ‘possessing psychic power’ (iddhavanto) is by means of the condition of psychic power (iddhāttappaccayena). ‘Quality’ (guṇa) is in the sense of ‘invitation’ (āmantaṇa); this refers to the remainder of the bhūvādi group of verbs. They are cultivated and esteemed by those who are superior, hence they are ‘qualities’ (guṇā), by means of the suffix ‘ka’. ‘They too’ means the disciples and Paccekabuddhas. The word ‘hi’ is in the sense of a reason: because they are supreme… and so on… possessed of undiminished qualities, therefore—this is the meaning. The phrase beginning with 'omniscience, etc.' is a statement of reason for their having qualities inferior to the Omniscient Buddhas. Some, imagining a corrupt meaning, ‘let him be one whose quality is sloth, thus he is established-sloth-quality’ (siddhamiddhaguṇa), corrupt this statement. But they, not knowing that ‘there is no such quality as sloth,’ and ‘the Tathāgata does not possess the quality of sloth,’ and ‘if he were such, the homage based on knowledge would not be naturally applicable,’ should be dismissed by you, saying to them thus. Here, the inclusion of the word ‘siddha’ at the beginning is for the sake of auspiciousness, for treatises that begin with auspiciousness are unhindered in their spread and are pleasing to venerable commentators and listeners. And by this part, ‘of the Dhamma and the Sangha,’ he indicates that even in the analysis of the compound, since the collective is the meaning of the compound, this is a compound whose meaning refers to another word (aññapadattha-samāsa) that implies the qualities of the referent (tagguṇa-saṃviññāṇa). Therefore he says: ‘in the sense of another word,’ etc. ‘Even of those that are secondary’ means even of those that are not primary, or that are attributes. Because the meaning of the other word is primary, the connection with the action is understood. For the Dhamma and the Sangha, even though they are secondary, their connection with the homage is due to their inseparability from it. He confirms that very point with ‘thus he says,’ etc. When it is said ‘present with the son,’ because it is a tagguṇa-saṃviññāṇa aññapadattha-samāsa, the coming of both is understood as equal, and thus it is perceived that ‘the son also has come.’ Here, the locative case is in the sense of determination. ‘Self’ indicates the Dhamma. ‘Upholds’ (dhārenti) means establishing, maintaining, or producing in oneself. All four lower worlds (apāya) are spoken of as ‘lower world’ (apāye) in a general sense. The three rounds are the round of defilements, the round of kamma, and the round of results. Suffering is in them, in that round. The ‘upholding’ thus spoken of means, in essence, the destruction of defilements that produce the lower worlds, etc. And that, in its true nature, occurs by way of an object for the uprooting and subsequent calming of defilements—thus he says: ‘that… and so on… by means of.’ Of all nine (transcendent states). Because they are the cause of attainment, they are indeed called ‘Dhamma’—thus it is said, ‘the ten,’ etc. There, he states the reason: ‘because it is rooted in that,’ etc. ‘Because it is rooted in that’ means because it has that as its cause. ‘By the commonality of virtue and view’ means by the equality of noble virtue and noble view. For the virtues and views of the noble ones, having arisen from the path, are in every way equal. Therefore, wherever they may be, they are ‘gone together’ (sahagatā), thus ‘united’ (saṃhata). In this sense, the derivation of the word ‘Sangha’ should be understood. But this is said according to the intended meaning. And it should be understood that even the conventional Sangha (sammuti-saṅgha) is worthy of homage due to its being united by the commonality of worldly virtue and view.

Atha [M 0.0014] kete saddā, yesamidaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ bhāsissanti paṭiññātanti āha-‘saddā ghaṭapaṭādayo’ti, ādisaddena rukkhādayo, nanu santi meghasaddasamuddasaddādayopīti na niratthakānamidhānupayogittā, ye lokasaṅketānurodhenātthappakāsakā tesaṃ sātthakāname vidaṃ lakkhaṇanti, apica ‘saddā ghaṭapaṭādayo’ti vadanto vedikānaṃ viya unti ñatthi (potthake) ādīnaṃ anupubbīniyamāvatthānamasambhavā tadanukkamena nipphādiyamānanampi saddānaṃ lokiyattānabhivattanañca bodhetīti daṭṭhabbaṃ, nu tattha pakāsakatthaṃ saddassa samudāyavasena vā siyā paccekavaṇṇavasena vā, tattha yadi paccekavaṇṇā pakāsayeyyuṃ, ghaṭasadde ghakāroyeva ghaṭatthaṃ, pakāsayeyya, tathā cāññesamakārādīnamanattha katā siyā, atha samuditā pakāsayeyyuṃ, tadā vaṇṇānamuccāraṇānantaravināsittā samudāyoyeva na siyā, tathā sati katha matthaṃ saddo pakāsayatīti ce kamena sotacittādigahitakkhara pāḷiyā ca yo saddoti viññeyyo sātthako cittagocaro, cittagocarassāpi saddassa pana bālajanappabodhāya kappanāmattena pakatyādivibhāgato, na sabhāvenānvākhyānaṃ, tenāha-‘pakatyā’di ādi, nanu goiccādisādhusaddaniyame sati gotādayo asādhu saddāti viññāyanti gantabbamagganiyame agantabbamaggo viya, gotādi asādhusaddaniyame vā goiccādayo saddā sādhavoti agantabbamagganiyame gantabbamaggo viya, kiṃ saddānamanvākhyānenā tidamāsaṅkiya payojanamāha- ‘lakkhaṇābhidhānaṃce’ccādi, saddānampaṭipattiyaṃ paṭipadapāṭhassānūpāyattaṃ dassetumāha- ‘aññathe’ccādi, aññathāti asati lakkhaṇābhidhāne, sakkatādītiādisaddena pākatādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti, bahuvidhattaṃ sakkatapākatapesācikaapabbhaṃsavasena, magadhesu viditāti imasmiṃ atthe “aññasmi”nti (4-121) māgadhānaṃ idanti atthe “ṇo”ti (4-34) ṇappaccaye māgadhā māgadhanti ca padanipphatti veditabbāti dassetumāha- ‘magadhesmi’ccādi, magadhesu viditātiādino adhippāyaṃ vivaritumāha- ‘idaṃ vuttaṃ hotī’tiādi, tattha idanti idāni vakkhamānaṃ māgadhaṃ…pe… hotīti etaṃ vuttaṃ hotīti magadhesu…pe… lakkhaṇaṃ māgadhanti [M 0.0015] vadatā pakāsitaṃ hotīti attho, hisaddo’magadhesvi’ccādinā vuttaṃ samatthayati, lakkhaṇaṃ visesayatāti saddalakkhaṇa saddassa uttarapadatthappadhānattā māgadhanti iminā lakkhaṇaṃ visesayatā byavacchedayatā vuttikārena, atthatoti sāmatthiyato, sadde ca visesito hotīti saddalakkhaṇasaddo māgadhe eva saddeeva (potthake) byavacchedito hoti, ayametthādhippāyo ‘magadhesu viditā māgadhāti sadde gahetvā tesamidaṃ māgadhanti māgadhasaddena yasmā saddalakkhaṇasadde lakkhaṇaṃ visesitaṃ, tasmā saddalakkhaṇasadde saddo yadi amāgadho kathaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ māgadhaṃ siyāti sāmatthiyā saddopi visesito hotī’ti, nanu māgadhanti lakkhaṇassa māgadha saddasambandhittajhāpanato saddalakkhaṇanti ettha saddasaddassa niratthaka tāpatti hotīti, na hoti gammamānatthassa saddassa payogampati kāmacārattā saddalakkhaṇasaddassa vā samāsatthe niruḷhattā “tatridaṃ sugatassa sugatacīvarappamāṇa”ntiādīsu viya, kopanātiādisaddalakkhaṇanti iminā abhidheyyasaṅkhātapayojanassa dassitattā tappayojanapucchanaparā codanā, vuccateccādi parihāro, yathā sabbathāttaparahitakāmena.

Then what are sounds? Those whose characteristic will be declared as ‘acknowledged’—he says: ‘Sounds such as ghaṭa, paṭa, etc.’ The term ‘etc.’ includes trees and so forth. Indeed, are there not also sounds like thunder and ocean waves? No, because meaningless sounds are not useful here; this characteristic applies only to those meaningful sounds that convey meaning in accordance with worldly convention. Moreover, when one says ‘sounds such as ghaṭa, paṭa, etc.,’ it should be understood that, just as in the case of ‘unti’ and so on for Vedic scholars, the impossibility of a fixed sequential arrangement and that sounds produced in sequence do not attain the status of worldly phenomena are also indicated. Now, is the meaning conveyed by the sound as a whole or by individual letters? If individual letters conveyed the meaning, in the sound ‘ghaṭa,’ only the letter ‘gha’ would convey the meaning ‘pot,’ and the other letters like ‘ṭa’ would be meaningless. If the whole conveyed the meaning, since letters vanish immediately after utterance, the whole would not exist. In that case, how could the sound convey meaning? It is said that the meaningful sound is to be understood as the object of the mind that grasps the letters heard by the ear, etc., in sequence. However, for the sound as an object of the mind, its analysis by way of division into base, etc., is merely a convention for the sake of instructing ordinary people, not an explanation according to its intrinsic nature. Hence, he says: ‘by base,’ etc. But when there is a rule for correct words like ‘go,’ are not words like ‘gotā’ understood as incorrect, just as the wrong path is understood as not to be taken when there is a rule for the right path? Or, when there is a rule for incorrect words like ‘gotā,’ are not words like ‘go’ understood as correct, just as the right path is understood as to be taken when there is a rule against the wrong path? What is the purpose of explaining sounds in this way? Anticipating this, he states the purpose: ‘for the sake of defining characteristics,’ etc. To show that reciting sounds one by one is not the proper method for understanding them, he says: ‘otherwise,’ etc. ‘Otherwise’ means without defining characteristics. The term ‘Sanskrit, etc.,’ includes Prakrit, etc., in various ways—as Sanskrit, Prakrit, Paisācī, and Apabhraṃśa. ‘Known among the Magadhans’—to indicate that in this sense, the word formation of ‘māgadhā’ and ‘māgadhaṃ’ should be understood, as in “in another place” (4-121) for the Magadhans, and “ṇo” (4-34) for the suffix ṇa in the sense of ‘this belongs to them’—he says: ‘among the Magadhans,’ etc. To clarify the intention of ‘known among the Magadhans,’ etc., he says: ‘this is said,’ etc. Here, ‘this’ refers to what is now being explained as Māgadha… it is said. That is, ‘this is said’—the meaning is that by saying ‘the characteristic is Māgadha’ among the Magadhans… it is made clear. The word ‘hi’ confirms what is said in ‘among the Magadhans,’ etc. ‘Characteristic’ is specified: because the word ‘saddalakkhaṇa’ (sound-characteristic) has the meaning of the latter word as primary, the commentator, by specifying or delimiting the characteristic with ‘māgadhaṃ,’ implies it. And by implication, the sound is also specified: the word ‘saddalakkhaṇa’ is delimited only to Māgadha. The intention here is this: ‘Taking the sounds known among the Magadhans as “māgadhā,” and since the characteristic in the word “saddalakkhaṇa” is specified by the word “māgadhaṃ,” therefore, if the sound in the word “saddalakkhaṇa” were non-Māgadha, how could the characteristic be Māgadha? Thus, by implication, the sound is also specified.’ But since ‘māgadhaṃ’ indicates the connection of the characteristic with the Māgadha sound, would not the word ‘sadda’ in ‘saddalakkhaṇa’ become meaningless? No, it would not, because there is freedom in using a word whose meaning is understood, or because the word ‘saddalakkhaṇa’ is established in a well-known compound sense, as in ‘here, this is the Sugata’s robe-measure,’ etc. ‘Kopa, etc., is a sound-characteristic’—by this, the intended purpose is shown as the object of definition. The subsequent question is a challenge regarding that purpose. The reply is given: ‘it is said,’ etc., by one who in every way desires the welfare of oneself and others.

Piyo ca garu bhāvanīyo, vattā ca vacanakkhamo;

Gambhīrañca kathaṃ kattā,nocā ṭhāne niyojakoti.

Dear and respected, worthy of cultivation,

A speaker who is patient with words,

One who speaks profound teachings,

And does not assign one to an inappropriate task.

Vuttehi tato parehi ca pasatthatarehi guṇavisesehi samupetaṃ guruṃ.

A teacher endowed with special qualities more praiseworthy than those already mentioned and others besides.

Tasmā akkharakosallaṃ, sampādeyya hitatthiko;

Upaṭṭhahaṃ guruṃ sammā, uṭṭhānādīhi pañcahīti.

Therefore, one seeking their own benefit should develop skill in letters, rightly attending upon the teacher with the five kinds of service, such as rising.

Vacanato uṭṭhāna-upaṭṭhāna-paricariyā-sussūsā sakkaccasippapaṭiggahaṇehi sammā upaṭṭhahantena savana,uggahana-dhāraṇa-paripucchā-bhāvanā hi kaṅkhāvicchedaṃ katvā viññātabbaṃ saddalakkhaṇaṃ, tathā aviññātaṃ saddalakkhaṇamanenāti [M 0.0016] aviññātasaddalakkhaṇo puggalo, hisaddo avadhāraṇe, so ‘dhammavinayesu kusalo na hotī’ti ettha daṭṭhabbo, kusalo dakkho na hoti, tattha dhammavinayesu suttantātābhidhammasaṅkhātesu dhammesu ceva vinaye ca, kasmā–

By obedience to his word, by rising, attending, serving, listening eagerly, and respectfully receiving the teaching, one who rightly attends upon the teacher should understand the characteristic of sound, having dispelled doubt through hearing, learning, memorizing, questioning, and developing. Thus, a person by whom the characteristic of sound is not understood is a 'person with an ununderstood characteristic of sound'. The particle ‘hi’ is for emphasis; it should be understood in the phrase ‘he is not skilled in the Dhamma and Vinaya’. He is not skilled, not proficient, in the Dhamma and Vinaya, that is, in the Dhammas classified as Suttanta and Abhidhamma, and in the Vinaya. Why?

Yo niruttiṃ na sikkheyya, sikkhanto piṭakattayaṃ;

Padepade vikaṅkheyya, vane andhagajo yathāti.

One who does not learn the language, while studying the Tipiṭaka,

Would be doubtful at every step, like a blind elephant in the forest.

Vacanato, ayametthādhippāyo “yathā vuttanayena sambhūtapada byāmohavasena padatthepi byāmohasambhavato suttantopadassitāya diṭṭhiviniveṭṭhanāya ca abhidhammāgate nāmarūpaparicchede ca vinaya niddiṭṭhe saṃvarāsaṃvare ca akosallaṃ siyā”ti, yathādhammanti dhammavinaya saddassa yo-ttho vinayasuttābhidhammasaṅkhāto, tassa so-ttho, tadanatikkamena, paṭipajjitumasakkontoti tatthatattheva vuttāsu adhisīla adhicitta adhipaññāsikkhāsu pavattituṃ asamattho, kusalo pana samattho paññāvisesālokapaṭilābhato, vuttaṃ hi–

By 'vacanato,' this is the intended meaning here: 'As explained in the manner described, because confusion regarding the meaning of terms can arise from confusion concerning compound words, unskillfulness may arise in the disentangling of views as shown in the Suttantas, in the analysis of name-and-form found in the Abhidhamma, and in the restraint and non-restraint taught in the Vinaya.' 'In accordance with the Dhamma' (yathādhammaṃ): the meaning of the term 'Dhamma-Vinaya' is that which is reckoned as the Vinaya, Suttas, and Abhidhamma. It means not transgressing that meaning. One who is unable to practice accordingly is incapable of engaging in the higher training in virtue, higher training in mind, and higher training in wisdom as stated in those respective places. However, one who is skillful is capable, through the attainment of the light of special wisdom. For it is said:

Yāva tiṭṭhanti suttantā, vinayo yāva dippati;

Tāva dakkhanti ālokaṃ, sūriye abbhuggate yathāti.

As long as the Suttantas endure, as long as the Vinaya shines forth,

So long will they see the light, as when the sun has fully risen.

Paṭipattinti paṭipajjīyatīti paṭipattīti yathāvuttaṃ tividhampi paṭipattiṃ, virādhetvāti nāsetvā, nassati hi paṭipatti tesuyevā ko sallatamagatattā, tathā cāhu–

'Practice' (paṭipatti) is so called because it is practiced; that is, the threefold practice as stated. By 'having transgressed' (virādhetvā) is meant 'having destroyed'. Indeed, practice perishes in those very ones due to their having gone to the state of unskillfulness. And thus it was said:

Suttantesu asantesu, pamuṭṭhe vinayamhi ca;

Tamo bhavissati loke, sūriye atthaṅgate yathāti.

When the Suttantas are no more, and the Vinaya is forgotten,

Darkness will be in the world, as when the sun has set.

Saṃsāradukkhasseva bhāgī hoti… yathāvuttā-nukkamapariccāgena anurūpapaṭipattiyā paṭilabhitabbattā adhigamavisayassa visathattā (potthake) yo gakkhemassa, vuttañhi tassānulomapaṭipattimūlakattaṃ–

He becomes a partaker only of the suffering of saṃsāra… because security from bondage (yogakkhema), the object of attainment, is to be obtained by appropriate practice and by abandoning things in the sequence as stated. For it has been said that this is rooted in practice that is in conformity:

Suttante rakkhite sante, paṭipatti hoti rakkhitā;

Paṭipattiyaṃ ṭhito dhīro, yogakkhemā na dhaṃsatīti.

When the Suttantas are preserved, the practice is preserved;

Steadfast in the practice, the wise one does not fall away from security from bondage.

Etāvatā [M 0.0017] aviññātasaddalakkhaṇassa sakatthaparihāniṃ dassetvā idāni sakatthasampattimūlikā paratthasampattīti tadabhāvā tādiso puggalo paresampi paccayo bhavituṃ na sakkotīti dassetuṃ ‘nacā’tiādi vuttaṃ, patiṭṭhāti dhāraṇaṃ, tañcettha tesaṃ tesaṃ kula puttānaṃ dhammavinayasikkhāpanaṃ taṃtaṃ kammato nittharaṇādi ca, tadubhaya mevā-nhasaṅgikaṃ patiṭṭhaṃ, mukhyabhūtampana tammūlake suparisuddhasīle patiṭṭhāpanameva, tadupakaraṇattho sikkhāpanādi, idha pana taṃ sādhanabhūto puggalo upacārato patiṭṭhāti gahetabbo, hisaddo yathāvutta samatthanatthe nipāto, saddalakkhaṇaññūyevāti avadhāraṇampana tesu tabbidūyeva samatthoti dassanatthaṃ pakaraṇavasena vuttaṃ, attano pana suguttasīlakkhandhavirahena kadāci koci yathāvuttānaṃ patiṭṭhābhavituṃ na sakkoti… tammūlakattā saddhammaṭṭhitiyā saparapatiṭṭhā bhāvassa ca, teneva vinayadhare ānisaṃsaṃ dassentena bhagavatā tappadhānaṃ tappamukhaṃva katvā “pañcime bhikkhave ānisaṃsā vinayadhara puggale, katame pañca attano sīlakkhandho sugutto hoti su rakkhito, kukkuccapakatānaṃ paṭisaraṇaṃ hoti, visārado saṅgha majjhe viharati, paccattthike sahadhammena suniggahitaṃ niggaṇhāti, saddhammaṭṭhitiyā paṭipanno ca hotī”ti vuttaṃ, atthānurūpanti attano vacanīyassatthassa vācakattena yogyaṃ, byañjanānurūpanti attano vācakassa vacanīyattena yogyaṃ, parivāsādīsūtiādisaddena abbhānādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti, taṃtaṃkammanti parivāsādikaṃ taṃtaṃkammaṃ, aññoti asaddalakkhaṇaññū, na kevalamanena sakatthaparatthāva nāsitā, atha khoti vidho saddhammopi nāsitoyevāti vatthumāha ‘ajānanto panā’tiādi, ayathāpaṭipajjamānoti saddalakkhaṇaññunā yathā yena pakārena atthānurūpaṃ byañjane byañjanānurūpañca atthe paṭipajjitabbaṃ, tathā appaṭipajjamāno, tathā ca vakkhati– tathā hi so saddalakkhaṇa majānanto’tiādi. Tividhampi saddhammanti pariyattipaṭipattiadhigamavasenati vidhameva saddhammaṃ, tattha tipiṭakabuddhavacanaṃ pariyattisaddhammo nāma, terasa dhutaguṇā cuddasa khandhakavattāni dve asīti mahāvattānīti ayaṃ paṭipattisaddhammo nāma, cattāro maggā cattāri ca phalāni ayaṃ adhigamasaddhammo [M 0.0018] nāma, tathāhiccādinā vuttamatthaṃ samattheti, tampi pāḷiyā thirīkātuṃ ‘vuttaṃ heta’ntiādimāha, tattha dhammāti hetū, saddhammassāti yathāvuttassa tividhassa saddhammassa, padabyañjananti padañca byañjanañca taṃ, tattha padaṃ nāma syādyantaṃ tyādyantañca, byañjīyati attho etenāti byañjanaṃ-vākyaṃ athavā pajjate gamyate attho etenāti padaṃ-syādyantādi, vākyaṃva byañjanaṃ, sithiladhanitādipadamevavā vuttanayena byañjananti padabyañjanaṃ, taṃ, dunnikkhittaṃ duṭṭhu nikkhittaṃ ṭhapitaṃ virādhetvā kathitaṃ, attho ca dunnītoti dunnikkhittattāyeva padabyañjanassa tabbacanīyopi duṭṭhuviññāto hoti, vuttapaṭipakkhatoti ‘aviññātasaddalakkhaṇohi’ccādinā vuttassa viññātasaddalakkhaṇattādinā paṭipakkhabhāvato, bhāvappadhāno hi ayaṃ niddeso,ttappaccayalopo vā, na hi attāva attanā veditabboti yuttanti.

Having thus shown the loss of one's own welfare due to not understanding the characteristics of language, it is now stated, beginning with ‘na ca,’ to indicate that such a person cannot become a support for others either, because the welfare of others is rooted in one's own welfare, and that is absent. ‘Patiṭṭhā’ means sustaining. Here, it refers to the teaching of the Dhamma and Vinaya to the sons of good families and their completion of various disciplinary actions. Both of these constitute a secondary foundation. Primarily, however, it is an establishment upon the root of supremely purified virtue. The teaching of training and so forth serves as an aid to that. In this context, the person who is the means for this is to be understood as a foundation in a metaphorical sense. The word ‘hi’ is a particle in the sense of confirming what has been said. The emphatic statement ‘only one who understands the characteristics of language’ is said in accordance with the context to show that among them, only such a one is capable. But due to the absence of the well-guarded aggregate of virtue, no one at any time can become a foundation for those described above, because the stability of the true Dhamma and the state of being a foundation for oneself and others are rooted in that. Therefore, the Blessed One, showing the benefits of a Vinaya-holder, made that the chief and foremost, saying: ‘Monks, there are these five benefits for a person who is a Vinaya-holder. What five? His own aggregate of virtue is well-guarded and well-protected; he is a refuge for those afflicted by scruples; he dwells confidently in the midst of the Saṅgha; he restrains his opponents righteously and thoroughly; and he is one who has undertaken the practice for the stability of the true Dhamma.’ ‘Atthānurūpaṃ’ means that the expression conforms to the meaning to be conveyed. ‘Byañjanānurūpaṃ’ means that the meaning conforms to the expression used. In ‘parivāsādīsu’ (in probation, etc.), the word ‘ādi’ (etc.) includes rehabilitation and so forth. ‘Taṃtaṃkammaṃ’ refers to those particular disciplinary actions, such as probation. ‘Añño’ means one who does not understand the characteristics of language. Not only are one's own welfare and that of others destroyed by this, but the threefold true Dhamma itself is also destroyed. Therefore, the text states the case beginning with ‘ajānanto pana.’ ‘Ayathāpaṭipajjamāno’ means not practicing in the way that one who understands the characteristics of language should practice—with the expression conforming to the meaning and the meaning conforming to the expression. Thus it will be said: ‘For indeed, not knowing the characteristics of language…’ and so forth. The threefold true Dhamma refers to the Dhamma classified as learning (pariyatti), practice (paṭipatti), and realization (adhigama). Herein, the Buddha’s words in the Tipiṭaka are called the true Dhamma of learning. The thirteen ascetic practices, the fourteen rules of the Khandhakas, and the eighty-two major rules are called the true Dhamma of practice. The four paths and four fruits are called the true Dhamma of realization. With ‘tathā hi’ and so forth, the stated meaning is supported. To establish this with the Pāḷi, it is stated: ‘vuttaṃ hetaṃ’ (this has been said), and so forth. Therein, ‘dhammā’ refers to causes. ‘Saddhammassa’ refers to the threefold true Dhamma as described. ‘Padabyañjanaṃ’ refers to both ‘pada’ (word) and ‘byañjana’ (expression). Herein, ‘pada’ refers to terms with nominal or verbal endings. ‘Byañjanaṃ’ is that by which the meaning is expressed, i.e., a sentence. Alternatively, ‘pada’ is that by which the meaning is reached, such as terms with nominal endings and so forth. A sentence itself is ‘byañjanaṃ.’ Or, terms indicating unaspirated, aspirated, and so forth are also called ‘byañjanaṃ’ in the stated manner; thus ‘padabyañjanaṃ.’ ‘Dunnikkhittaṃ’ means poorly placed, badly arranged, or spoken erroneously. And ‘attho ca dunnīto’ means that because the words and expressions are poorly placed, the meaning to be conveyed by them is also poorly inferred. ‘Vuttapaṭipakkhato’ means from being the opposite of what was stated, that is, from being the opposite of ‘one who does not understand the characteristics of language,’ which is ‘one who understands the characteristics of language,’ and so forth. Indeed, this exposition is primarily concerned with the state. Alternatively, there is an elision of the ‘-tta’ suffix. For it is not fitting that the self should be known by the self.

Tadevantiādinā yathāvuttaṃ nigametvā saññāvidhāne payojanaṃ dasseti, tanti hetvatthe nipāto, yasmā saddalakkhaṇassa jānanaṃsāni saṃsaṃ tasmāti attho, evanti nidassanatthe nipāto, evaṃ sappayojananti sambandho, tadevanti vā nipātasamudāyo yaṃ, vuttena pakārenetyasmiṃ atthe vattate. Nanuca saññīnaṃ saññānaṃ vattabbatte “aādayo titālīsavaṇṇā”tiādīnaṃ vākyānaṃ visuṃvisuṃ mahantattā kuto lāghavaṃ satthassāti maññamāno ‘tathāhi’ccādinā saññāvidhāne lāghavasabbhāvaṃ samattheti, hotevāti avadhāraṇena katthaci parasatthe viya no na hotīti dasseti, paṭipattilāghavampi cettha hoteva, tathāhi “vaṇṇaparena savaṇṇopi”ccādo (1-24) vaṇṇādisaññāsamuddharitā nāttānamattāvagametumalanti pare pucchitvā jānitabbā assa, tato saññā-vaseyā, tatossa saññāti saññāsaññīvivecanaṃ tadanuṭṭhānanti paramparāpekkhāya bhavitabbaṃ paṭipatti gāravābhāvā. Idāni saṅkhepato satthakkamaṃ dassetumāha-evaṃ tāvi’ccādi, tāvāti paṭhamaṃ, upayujjamānattāti byāpāriyamānattā, visayo gocaro yatthete syādayo vidhī yante, saha visayenāti savisayā, paṭhamaṃ karīyatīti pakati yato syādayo vidhīyante, saha pakatiyāti sappakatikā, liṅgādikanti [M 0.0019] ādisaddena‘salabhacchāya’miccādo ekattādi, liṅgebhavā liṅgikā-itthividhayo, ekatthībhāvo samāso, tena, sāmaññato samānattā, samānattantuṇādivuttiyā “rājādivisiṭṭhe purisā doviya’vasiṭṭhādivisiṭṭhe apaccādimhi atthe pavattanato.

Having thus concluded what was stated with ‘tadevaṃ’ and so forth, he shows the purpose in the rule of designation. ‘Taṃ’ is a particle in the sense of ‘reason,’ meaning ‘because the knowledge of the characteristics of language has benefits, therefore.’ ‘Evaṃ’ is a particle in the sense of ‘illustration.’ The connection is ‘thus with purpose.’ Or, the collection of particles ‘tadevaṃ’ is used in the sense of ‘in the manner stated.’ And indeed, since statements like ‘the letters beginning with “a” are forty-three’ are each extensive for those to whom designations apply, one might think, ‘How can there be brevity in the treatise?’ To counter this, he shows through ‘tathā hi’ and so forth that brevity is indeed possible in the rule of designation. By the emphatic ‘hoteva’ (it is indeed), he shows that it is not absent here as it might be in some other treatises. Indeed, even here, ease of application is certainly present. For example, in a rule like ‘vaṇṇaparena savaṇṇopi,’ if the technical terms such as ‘vaṇṇa’ were not established, one would not be able to understand by oneself but would have to learn by asking others. Then, one would be dependent on the designation, and from that, the distinction between the designation and the thing designated, and its application, would have to be considered in a long sequence; thus, there is an absence of difficulty in application. Now, to briefly show the order of the treatise, he says ‘evaṃ tāva’ and so forth. ‘Tāva’ means ‘first.’ ‘Upayujjamānattā’ means ‘being employed,’ i.e., ‘being engaged.’ The scope (visaya) is the domain where these rules, such as those for suffixes (syādayo), are prescribed. ‘Savisayā’ means ‘together with the scope.’ ‘Pakati’ is the base from which the suffixes are first prescribed. ‘Sappakatikā’ means ‘together with the base.’ ‘Liṅgādikaṃ’ (gender, etc.)—by the word ‘ādi’ (etc.), singularity and so forth, as in ‘salabhacchāyaṃ,’ are included. ‘Liṅgikā’ means rules pertaining to gender, such as the rules for feminine forms. ‘Ekatthībhāvo’ is compounding, the state of becoming one meaning. By that, ‘sāmaññato’ means ‘generally,’ from similarity. Similarity, as in the case of the ‘uṇādi’ suffixes, is due to operating in the sense of ‘a person distinguished as a king,’ or in the sense of ‘a descendant distinguished as a Vasiṭṭha,’ and so forth.

Iti moggallānapañcikāṭīkāyaṃ sāratthavilāsiniyaṃ

Thus in the Sāratthavilāsinī, a subcommentary on the Moggallāna-pañcikā.

Ratanattayapaṇāmādikathā samattā.

The discourse beginning with the homage to the Triple Gem is concluded.

1. Paṭhamakaṇḍavaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the First Section

Saññādhikāra

The Chapter on Designations

1. A ādayo

1. A, and so forth.
