Sabbavacanānaṃ sātthakaniratthakattabyabhicārittā ‘ida’ntiādinā sadiṭṭhantena saṃsayamupadassiya sātthakattamassa dassetuñca ‘na tāva…pe… sātthakattā’ti vuttaṃ, ummattakādivākyamiti ‘dasa dāḷimā, cha apūpā, kuṇḍamajājinaṃ, palālapiṇḍo’iccādikaṃ, avayavatthāna maññamaññanāti sambandhā samudāyatthābhāvato anatthakattaṃ, ādivākyanti “manoseṭṭhā manomayā”tiādivākyaṃ, sātthakattaṃ panassa padatthāna maññamaññābhisambandhassa patītito.

Since all speech can be either meaningful or meaningless, a doubt is first raised with an example such as ‘this.’ Then, to demonstrate that speech is indeed meaningful, it is said, ‘na tāva… sātthakattā’ (not until… it is meaningful). An example of meaningless speech is that of a madman, such as: ‘ten pomegranates, six cakes, a goat-skin water-pot, a ball of straw,’ and so forth. This is meaningless because there is no mutual connection between the parts and therefore no collective meaning. In contrast, the initial statement, such as ‘manoseṭṭhā manomayā’ (mind is the forerunner, mind-made), is meaningful because the mutual connection between the meanings of the words is perceived.

Atha aādyādisaddānaṃ sādhuttānvākhyānāya idaṃ vacanamiccādivikappantarasambhave kathaṃ niyamo vuttiyaṃ vuttenatthena sātthakattamiccāsaṅkiya tesamihānupayogittaṃ kamena paṭipādayitumāha ‘vakkhamānatthamevida’miccādi,’ ākārādayo niggahītantā’iccādinā vuttiyaṃ vakkhamāno attho yassa taṃ tathā vuttaṃ, sādhūnaṃ sādhusaddānaṃ anusāsanaṃ ākhyānaṃ attho payojanaṃ yassa tanti viggaho.

Now, for the explanation of the correctness of words such as 'a' and so forth, this statement is made. Given the possibility of other interpretations, such as 'iccādi,' how is the rule established? Having suspected that it is meaningful by the sense stated in the commentary, and in order to gradually demonstrate their inapplicability here, he says, 'This has the very meaning that will be explained,' and so forth. That which has its meaning to be explained in the commentary by 'ākārādayo niggahītantā' and so forth, is thus stated. The analysis is: that whose meaning or purpose is the instruction or explanation of correct words.

Sādhusaddānusāsanasaṅkāpettha “katthettha kutrātrakvehidhā”ti (4-100) ādinā katthādisaddānaṃ sādhuttānusāsanassa dassanato, lakkhaṇantarena sādhubhāvassa anvākhyātattāti āpubbādāiccasmā “dādhātvī”ti (5-45) ippaccaye ākāralope ca ādīti [M 0.0020] aādiyesanti aññapadatthasamāse yomhi “yosu jhissa pume”ti (2-93) ‘ṭe aādayo’ti, tayo ca cattālīsā cāti cattha samāse “tadaminādīni”ti cata lopeca rasse ca titālīsāti, ‘vaṇṇa-vaṇṇane’iccasmā “bhāvakārakesva ghaṇa ghakā”ti (5-44) appaccayeyomhi ṭādese vaṇṇāiti ca sijjhanato, payoganiyamatthanti titālīsavaṇṇasaddesu paresu eva aādisaddo payujjīyatīti evaṃ payoganiyamatthaṃ, ayampi vikappantara sambhāvanā “abhūtatabbhāve karāsabhūyoge vikārā cī”ti (4-119) payoganiyamassā jhāyamānassa diṭṭhattā, ṭhānyādesatthanti aādisaddassa ṭhāne titālīsavaṇṇasaddā ādesā honti tesaṃ vā so iti, tadanurūpāyāti ṭhānyādesānurūpāya chaṭṭhī vibhattiyā, atoyevāti agamāgamianurūpāya chaṭṭhiyā abhāvato yeva, agamāgami bhāvatthanti aādisaddassa titālīsa vaṇṇasaddā āgamā honti tesaṃ vā so iti, etesupi saṅkā, “yavāsare” (1-30) “suña sassa”iti (2-53) ādesāgamānaṃ dassanena, āgama liṅgābhāvatoti ukāra kakāra makārānaṃ abhāvato, visesanavisessa bhāvatthanti titālīsavaṇṇasaddānaṃ aādisaddo visesanaṃ, te vā tasse-ti, etthāpi saṅkā ‘nīluppala’miccādīnamaññattha visesanavisessa bhāvadassanā, saddalakkhaṇā nupayogatoti saddalakkhaṇena saddasaṅkharaṇassa pakatattā vuttaṃ, tattha kāraṇamāha- ‘rūpavisesūpa lakkhaṇābhāvā’ti, rūpavisesassa upalakkhaṇa nimittaṃ tassaabhāvāti attho, na hi visesana visessabhāve paṭipādite aādyādisaddānaṃ rūpavisesassa saṅkharaṇaṃ kataṃ siyāti, yadi esova saddasaṅkharaṇanti gayheyya, tathā sati ‘nīluppala’miccādīnampi vattabbatā āpajjeyyāti nāssa tadattha tāpi sambhāvīyate, loke sīhaguṇassa mānavake dassanato upacārena ‘sīho-yaṃ mānavako’ti tagguṇajjhāropopi dissati, tadatthampetaṃ na hotīti dassanatthaṃ ‘tagguṇajjhāropanatthampetaṃ na hotī’ti vuttaṃ, tassa aādisaddassa, tesaṃ titālīsavaṇṇasaddānaṃ vā guṇo aādittādi, tassa ajjhāropanaṃ-titālīsavaṇṇasaddesu [M 0.0021] vā aādisaddeyeva vā āropanaṃ, tadatthampetaṃ suttaṃ na hotīti attho, tattha kāraṇamāha- ‘atoyevā’tiādi, atoyeva rūpavisesūpalakkhaṇā bhāvatoyo, pakataṃ saddasaṅkharaṇaṃ, yathāvutta vikappantarābhāve ubhayatthamidaṃ siyā, tattha paribhāsatthaṃ na hoti… tallakkhaṇattābhāvā uparivakkhamānattā cāti pārisesamālambiyāha ‘saññāsaññi’ccādi.

Here, a doubt regarding the instruction of correct words arises from seeing the instruction of the correctness of words such as 'kattha' by 'katthettha kutrātrakvehidhā' (4-100) and so forth, and because the state of correctness is explained by another characteristic. From the root 'dā' preceded by 'ā,' in accordance with 'dādhātvī' (5-45), with the 'i' suffix and the elision of 'ā,' 'ādi' is formed. Then, 'aādi' in a different compound meaning; as in 'yosu jhissa pume' (2-93), 'ṭe aādayo.' And 'three' and 'forty' together, in a compound, according to 'tadaminādīni,' with the elision of 'ca' and shortening, becomes 'titālīsa' (forty-three). And from the root 'vaṇṇa-vaṇṇane,' in accordance with 'bhāvakārakesva ghaṇa ghakā' (5-44), with the 'a' suffix and the substitution of 'ṭa' in the nominative plural, 'vaṇṇā' is formed. The purpose is the restriction of usage, meaning that the word 'aādi' is used only when the forty-three 'vaṇṇa' words follow. Thus, the purpose is the restriction of usage. This is also an alternative possibility, a presumption, as in 'abhūtatabbhāve karāsabhūyoge vikārā cī' (4-119), because the restriction of usage is seen being contemplated. The purpose is substitution in place, meaning that in place of the word 'aādi,' the forty-three 'vaṇṇa' words are substitutes, or that 'so' (it) is for them. 'In accordance with that' means in accordance with the substitution in place, in the sixth case. 'From this alone' means due to the absence of the sixth case in accordance with augmentation and what is augmented. The meaning is the state of augmentation and what is augmented, meaning that the forty-three 'vaṇṇa' words are augmentations to the word 'aādi,' or that 'so' is for them. Here too, there is doubt, as seen in 'yavāsare' (1-30) and 'suña sassa' (2-53), showing substitution and augmentation. There is no sign of augmentation, meaning due to the absence of the markers 'u,' 'ka,' and 'ma.' The meaning is the state of qualification and qualified, meaning the word 'aādi' qualifies the forty-three 'vaṇṇa' words, or they qualify it. Here too, there is doubt, as seen in examples like 'nīluppala,' showing the state of qualification and qualified in another sense. Due to its inapplicability to the characteristic of a word, it is said, because the formation of words is being dealt with through the characteristic of the word. There, the reason is stated: 'due to the absence of a distinguishing mark of a particular form.' The meaning is the absence of a characteristic mark of a particular form. For when the qualification and qualified are explained, the formation of words like 'aādi' with a particular form would not have been done. If one were to hold that this is indeed the formation of words, then in that case, examples like 'nīluppala' would also have to be stated, but that would not be its meaning. In the world, due to the perception of the lion's qualities in a young man, it is said, 'This young man is a lion,' and the superimposition of those qualities is also seen. To show that this is not its meaning, it is said, 'The superimposition of those qualities is not intended here.' For that word 'aādi,' or for those forty-three 'vaṇṇa' words, the quality is 'aādittādi,' and its superimposition is either on the forty-three 'vaṇṇa' words or on the word 'aādi' itself. The meaning is that the sutta is not for that purpose. Therein, the reason is stated: 'from this alone' and so forth. From this alone, due to the absence of a distinguishing mark of a particular form, the formation of words is being dealt with. In the absence of the aforementioned alternative possibility, this would apply to both. There, the purpose is not a paribhāsa rule... due to the absence of that characteristic and because it will be stated later. By elimination, it is stated 'saññāsaññi' and so forth.

Mariyādāyampakāreca, samīpe vayave tathā;

Catubbidhappakāroyaṃ, ādisaddassa dissateti.

In the sense of limit and manner, likewise in proximity and part; this fourfold kind of the word 'ādi' is thus seen.

Mariyādattho ettha ādisaddoti āha-‘ādimariyādā bhūto’ti, upalakkhaṇattāti upalakkhiyamānānamākārādīnaṃ gahaṇe kāraṇabhāvena appadhānattā, tenāha-‘upalakkhaṇassupasajjanīyabhūtassā’ti, kāriyenāti vaṇṇasaññābhavanādinā, na gunnampi ānayanaṃ bhavati..gunnamupasajjanīya bhūtattā aññapadatthasseva padhānattā, saññāyā bhāveti akārassa vaṇṇasaññāya abhāve, rūpantiti tālīsārūpaṃ, titālīsā+vaṇṇātipadacchedo, titālīsa+vaṇṇātivā, suttāvayavassāpi suttasambandhittā “byañjane dīgharassā”ti (1-33) pana vuttaṃ, rassattantu “dīgharassā”ti yogavibhāgena, itarathā byañjanaparasseva rassatte dassite titālīsaiti abyañjane padaṃ na sampajjeyyāti viññāyati, itarītarayogacatthe bahuvacanena bhavitabbanti āha-‘ekavacanampanā’tiādi, vippaṭipatti aññathābhāvo, rassa e okārehi tecattālīsakkharānanti sambandho, e okāre hīti sahatthe tatiyā, sakkatānusārenāti sakkate “sandhi yakkharānaṃ rassā na santī”ti vuttassa anusārena, kocīti sā sanappasādakacoḷiyabuddhappiyācariyaṃ dasseti, na hiccādiṃ vadato-yamadhippāyo ‘rassāivāti ivasaddo sādhammopamājotako vā siyā vedhammopamājotako vā, yadi tāva vedhammopamājotako, rassadhammassa e okāresva sambhavā tesaṃ dīghakālappavattito te dīghāyeva siyuṃ, yadi pana sādhammopamājotako[M 0.0022], tesu rassadhammassasambhavā rassakālappavattito rassāeva te siyunti ‘etthātiādīsu e okārānaṃ uccāraṇakālakataṃ rassattameva hotī’ti, rassakālavantoyevāti evasaddo sogate vaṇṇavinimmuttassa kālassevābhāvā vaṇṇānañca paccakkha siddhattā pamāṇasiddhaṃ pāramatthika me okārānaṃ rassakālavantataṃ dīpeti, atthāti vadato panāyamadhippāyo ‘etthātiādīsu yadi ekārādayo dīghāeva saṃyogapubbattā rassāva siyuṃtathā sati atthāti etthāpi dīghova ākāro saṃyogapubbattārasso iva uccatīti āpajjeyya, tasmā uccāraṇakālakatova rassadīghabhāvo gahetabbo’ti, kaccāyanavuttivaṇṇanā ñāso, taññāpaneti bahiddhā aññesamakkharānaṃ ñāpane, payojanābhāvāti tena sādhetabbassa kassaci iṭṭhassa abhāvamāha, kimettha samudāye vākyaparisamatti, udāhu avayaveti āha- ‘pacceka’nti, aññathā ‘rukkhā vana’ntiādīsu viya samudāye vākyaparisamattiyaṃ “iyuvaṇṇā jhalā namassante” (1-9) iccādikaṃ na sijjhatīti, paccekaṃ vaṇṇā nāmahontīti akāro vaṇṇo nāma hoti ākāro vaṇṇo nāma hotītiādinā, avayaveccādinā vuttiyaṃ avuttepi ‘pacceka’nti vacane sadiṭṭhantaṃ kāraṇamāha, diṭṭhantopanīto tyattho sukhena paṭipattuṃ sakkāti, ettha hi paccekanti avuttepi devadatto bhojīyatūtiādinā paccekaṃ bhuñjikiriyā parisamāpīyate, tenāha-‘na coccate’ iccādi, athavā samudāyepi vākyaparisamā pattiyaṃ sati samudāye pavattā saddā avayavesupi vattantīti ‘samuddekadesadassanepi samuddo diṭṭho, khandhekadesa bhūtāyapi paññāya paññākkhandhotiādīsu viya na doso, teneva vuttiyaṃ ‘pacceka’nti na vuttaṃ, vaṇṇasaddassa guṇādyanekatthattepi pakaraṇato akārādayovettha vuccantīti āha-‘vaṇṇīyati’ccādi, pakaraṇatopi attho vibhajjate, vuttaṃ hi–

Here, the word 'ādi' has the meaning of 'boundary,' thus he said, 'it is the initial boundary.' Due to its indicative nature, it is secondary as a cause for grasping the indicated forms, etc.; therefore, he said, 'of that which is secondary, serving as an indicator.' By 'kāriyena' is meant by the production of letter-perception, etc. The inclusion of qualities does not occur, because qualities are secondary and the meaning of the other word is primary. In the absence of the letter-perception of 'a', 'rūpaṃ' (form) is produced; 'rūpaṃ' is forty-threefold. The word division is 'titālīsā+vaṇṇā' (forty-three letters) or 'titālīsa+vaṇṇā'. Even for a part of a sutta, because of its connection to the sutta, it is said, 'long and short vowels occur before a consonant' (1-33). Shortness, however, is by the division of the rule 'dīgharassā'; otherwise, if shortness were shown only for what is followed by a consonant, the word 'titālīsa' would not be formed without a following consonant, it is understood. In the sense of reciprocal connection, it should be in the plural; therefore he said, 'but the singular,' etc. 'Vippaṭipatti' means contradiction. The connection is 'with the short 'e' and 'o,' there are forty-three letters.' 'e okāre hīti' is the instrumental case in the sense of 'with'. 'Sakkatānusārenāti' means according to what is said in Sanskrit, that 'short sandhi vowels do not exist.' 'Kocīti' indicates the teacher Sāsanappasādaka Coḷiya Buddhappiyācariya. The intention of one saying 'na hi...' etc. is this: the word 'iva' in 'rassā iva' (as if short) could be an indicator of a simile of similar property or a simile of dissimilar property. If it indicates a simile of dissimilar property, since the characteristic of shortness does not exist in 'e' and 'o' due to their prolonged pronunciation, they would be long. But if it indicates a simile of similar property, since the characteristic of shortness is present in them due to their short pronunciation, they would be short. Thus, in cases like 'ettha...' etc., the shortness of 'e' and 'o' is only due to the time of pronunciation. 'Rassakālavantoyevāti' (they possess a short duration) means that the word 'eva' indicates that the possession of a short duration by 'e' and 'o' is ultimately real and established by valid means of knowledge, because in the Saugata system, there is no time separate from letters, and letters are established by direct perception. The intention of one saying 'atthāti' is this: in cases like 'ettha...' etc., if 'e' and so on were inherently long, they would become short due to being preceded by a conjunct consonant. If that were so, then even in 'attha', the long 'ā' would be pronounced as if short due to being preceded by a conjunct consonant, which would be an undesirable consequence. Therefore, the state of being short or long must be taken as determined by the time of pronunciation. This is the Nyāsa, a commentary on the Vutti of Kaccāyana. 'Taññāpaneti' means in making other, external letters known. 'Payojanābhāvāti' states the absence of any desired result to be achieved by that, meaning there is no purpose. Does the completion of the sentence here apply to the collective, or to the individual parts? He said, 'individually.' Otherwise, in cases like 'rukkhā vanaṃ' (trees are a forest), if the completion of the sentence were in the collective, rules like 'iyuvaṇṇā jhalā namassante' (1-9) would not be accomplished. Thus, 'each is called a letter' means 'a' is called a letter, 'ā' is called a letter, and so on. By 'avayave...' etc., he states the reason with an example for the word 'paccekaṃ' (individually), even though it is not stated in the Vutti, for a meaning introduced by an example can be easily understood. Here, even if 'individually' is not stated, in 'Devadatta should be fed,' etc., the action of eating is completed for each one individually. Hence, he said, 'na coccate...' etc. Alternatively, even if the completion of the sentence is in the collective, words that apply to the collective also apply to the individual parts. Just as in 'the ocean is seen even when seeing a part of the ocean,' and 'the aggregate of wisdom is so-called even for wisdom which is a part of the aggregate,' there is no fault. For that reason, 'individually' is not stated in the Vutti. Although the word 'vaṇṇa' has multiple meanings such as quality, etc., from the context, 'a' and the other letters are meant here. Thus, he said, 'vaṇṇīyati...' etc. The meaning is also distinguished by context, for it is said—

Atthā pakaraṇā liṅgā, ocityā desakālato;

Saddatthā vibhajīyante, na saddāyeva kevalāti.

The meanings of words are distinguished by context, implication, propriety, place, and time—not from the words alone.

Nanu [M 0.0023] jhalādisaññā viya lahusaññaṃ akatvā kasmā gurusaññā katāti codanaṃ manasi nidhāya ruḷhi anvatthavasena dvippakārāsu saññāsu jhālāti ruḷhi saññātthābhāvena vohārasukhamattapayojanā, anvatthasaññā pana tappayojanāpi hoti tadaññappayojanā pīti dassetumāha- ‘eva’miccādi, vaṇṇīyatī attho etehīti vuttamatthaṃ anugatā anugatatthā vaṇṇasaññā taṃ, saddādhigamanīyassāti saddena viññātabbassa, vaṇṇaṃ mūlamassāti vaṇṇamūlako-attho, tassa bhāvo vaṇṇamūlakatā, atthassa vaṇṇamūlakataṃ sādheti ‘sāpi’ccādinā, vaṇṇaṃ rūpaṃ sabhāvo etesanti vaṇṇarūpāni-padāni, samudāyo pādānaṃ rūpamassāti samudāyarūpaṃ vākyaṃ, vibhatyantamatthajotakaṃ padaṃ, padasamudāyo vākyaṃ, sabbañcetamupacārena vaṇṇasaddavacanīyattaṃ gacchati vaṇṇamayattāti sabbopi sammutiparamatthabhedabhinno attho vākyādhigamanīyo vaṇṇeneva viññāyati nāma tasmā yathā vuttamattha visesadassanaṃlahusaññāya na sakkāti tadatthamakārādīnaṃ gurubhūtā vaṇṇasaññā katāti adhippāyo, sammuti saṅketavasena pavatto vohāro, paramattho sanibbāno pañcakkhandho. Ubhohi panetehi bhinno tatiyo koṭṭhāso nāma natthi, tathāca vuttaṃ–

Why, without making a 'light' designation like the 'jhala' designation, was the 'heavy' designation made? Having considered this objection, to show that designations are twofold—conventional and etymological—and that of these, a conventional designation like 'jhala' is merely for ease of communication as the designation itself lacks an intrinsic meaning, whereas an etymological designation serves its own purpose and also other purposes, he says, 'evaṃ...' etc. That letter-designation follows the stated meaning, having a meaning that follows the etymology 'meaning is designated by these.' 'Of that which is to be understood by sound' means 'of that which is to be known by sound.' 'The root of meaning is the letter' means meaning is rooted in letters; the state of that is being rooted in letters. He establishes that meaning is rooted in letters by the phrase 'sāpi...' etc. Words are 'vaṇṇarūpāni' (letter-forms) because they possess letters, form, and nature. A sentence is a 'samudāyarūpaṃ' (collective form) because a collection of parts is its form. A word is that which illuminates meaning and ends in an inflection. A collection of words is a sentence. All this, by metaphorical extension, becomes expressible through the word 'vaṇṇa' because it is made of letters. Thus, all meaning, distinguished by the division of conventional and ultimate, which is to be understood through sentences, is known by letters alone. Therefore, since a special insight into the stated meaning cannot be achieved through a 'light' designation, the 'heavy' designation 'vaṇṇa' was made for letters like 'a', etc., for that purpose—this is the intention. Convention is usage established by agreement. The ultimate is Nibbāna and the five aggregates. But apart from these two, there is no third category. Thus it is said—

Duve saccāni akkhāsi, sambuddho vadataṃ varo,

Sammutiṃ paramatthañca, tatiyaṃ nupalabbhatīti.

The Fully Enlightened One, the best of speakers, declared two truths: conventional and ultimate; a third is not found.

Nanu ca–

But surely—

Appakkharamasandiddhaṃ, sasāraṃ gūḷhaniṇṇayaṃ;

Pasannatthañca suttanti, āhu tallakkhaṇaññunoti.

With few letters, unambiguous, essential, profound in meaning, and clear in its purpose—this, those who know its characteristics say, is a sutta.

“Ādayo titālīsa vaṇṇā” “titālīsādayo vaṇṇā”ti vā vattabbanti na tathā sati sandiddhaṃ suttaṃ siyāti, nanu satthādo maṅgalavacanena bhavitabbaṃ, akāro paṭisedhatthopi hotīti (na) satthādo siddhasaddassopahitattā, atha hotva pubbā jhālādi saññā, saddasādhanamattappayojanattā pana sabbavidhānassa pubbācariya saññāvālametthāti kiṃ punāpi vaṇṇādisaññāvidhānena ganthagārava karaṇenāti saccametaṃ, pubbācariyesu pana gāravaṃ tadanugamanañca dīpetuṃ kāci [M 0.0024] saññāyopyanvākhyāyante, yajjevaṃ saṃyogasabbanāmalopādayopi saññā pubbācariyehi vuttā vattabbāti nanu bho vuttamevāmhehi’kāci saññāyo ākhyāyante’ti, kintadākhyānadvārena bhavatā tāpi viññātuṃ na sakkāti, kesañci sātthakattopi pativaṇṇamatthānupaladdhito vaṇṇānamadiṭṭhānamakārādīnamanukatiyo ihopadiṭṭhāityanukāriyenātthenātthavantatāya hotevākārādito vibhatti, lopena niddiṭṭhattā panassā assavanaṃ sannikaṃsavacanicchābhāvā saṃhitāyāniddeso, anukkamoti ādonissayā sarāvuttā, tato nissitā byañjanā, saresupi ekaṭṭhāniyā akārādayo bahuttā paṭhamaṃ vuttā ṭhānānukkamena, tato dvijā ṭhānānukkamena, tesupi rassāva lahuttā paṭhamaṃ vuttā, tato dīghā, byañjanesupi vaggā bahuttā ṭhānappaṭipāṭiyā paṭhamaṃ vuttā, tato yakārādayo, vaggesu ca aghosā paṭhamaṃ vuttā, tato ghosā, tesu ca sithilā paṭhamaṃ vuttā, tato dhanitā, tatthāpi appakattā dvijā pañcamā vuttā, tato yaralavā ghosabhūtā ṭhānānukkamena, tato dhanitā sakāraha kārā, tesupihakāro kesañci orasopi hotīti dvijattā pacchā vutto, kehici “laḷānamaviseso”ti dvinnamavisese vuccamānepi lipibhedena ṭhānabhedena ca bhinnattā ḷakāro visuṃ akkharabhāvena gahito, sopi ghosabhāvena ṭhānānukkamenaca hakārato paraṃ vutto niggahītaṃ pana sarattādisabbavinimmuttattā sabbapacchā vuttanti akārādīnamayamanukkamo, imassevānukkamassa manasi vipassa vattamānattā titālīsāti gaṇanāparicchedassa dassitattā ca ‘niggahītantā’ti vuttiyaṃ vuttaṃ, pakataṃ sādhusaddānvākhyānaṃ, na vaṇṇīyate, ti saddasaṅkharaṇa saṅkhāta mukhyappayojanābhāvā, kiñcāpi na vaṇṇīyate, amhehi pana kathamakārādīnamayamanukkamo uppannoti sissānaṃ kaṅkhā vicchedappayojanampati anukkamasaddassa atthakathanabyājena vaṇṇito yevāti, karīyante uccārīyante etenāti karaṇaṃ, tattha jivhāmajjhaṃ tālujānaṃ, jivhopaggaṃ muddhajānaṃ, jivhaggaṃ, dantajānaṃ sesānaṃ sakaṭṭhānaṃ karaṇaṃ, payatti payatanaṃ, tampana vaṇṇuccāraṇato abbhantaro bāhiyo ca ussāho, tattha abbhantarapayatanaṃ-saṃvutattamakārassa, vivaṭattaṃ sarānaṃ [M 0.0025] sakārahakārānañca phuṭṭhattaṃ vaggānaṃ, īsaṃphuṭṭhattaṃ yaralavānaṃ, bāhiyapayatanantu saṃvutakaṇṭhatādi, ṭhānato paccāsattiyā vidhīyamānakāriyasambhavena payojanasambhavā āha-‘ṭhānampanā’tiādi, tiṭṭhanti ettha uppattivasena vaṇṇāti ṭhānaṃ, “e onama vaṇṇe”ti (1-37) sutte vaṇṇeti kathanameva vaṇṇasaññākaraṇe payojanaṃ, yathāvuttamatthamaññatra byāpadisati’ eva’miccādinā, tasmā “dasādo sarā”iccādo ‘tenā’tiādīsu ‘tena saraiccanena kvattho kasmiṃ sutte payojanaṃ taṃ dasseti “sarolopo sare”ccādī’ti evamādinā attho daṭṭhabbo, ñāpeti vaṇṇalopanti ñāpakaṃ, kasmā pana’so cemināva ñāpakena siddho’ti vuccati nanu ‘tadaminādīni”ti (1-47) suttaṃ dissatīti, (saccaṃ) tathāpi pakārantaroyampi vaṇṇalope dassitoti viññātabbaṃ, evasaddo pana ‘yadi ñāpakena vaṇṇalopo siyā so imināva ñāpakena siddho, nāññenā’ti avadhāreti.

It should not be stated as, 'The forty-three are the initial letters,' or 'The initial are the forty-three letters,' for if it were so, the rule would be ambiguous. But should not the beginning of a treatise be an auspicious utterance? The letter 'a' can also have a prohibitive sense, but not here, as the word 'siddha' is prefixed at the beginning of the treatise. Or, let there be the designations of former teachers like Jhāla. However, since the sole purpose of all instruction is the formation of words, this follows the designations of the ancient teachers. What then is the use of making the text heavy by again laying down designations for letters and so on? This is true, but to show respect for the ancient teachers and adherence to them, some designations are also explained. If so, then designations like conjunction, pronoun, elision, and so on, which were stated by the ancient teachers, should also be stated. Sir, have we not already said, 'some designations are explained'? Why then can you not understand them through that explanation? For some, their usefulness is also from their meaning, but since the meaning of each letter is not found, the forms of unseen letters like 'a' and others are taught here by imitation. Thus, through an imitative sense, they are meaningful, and from 'a' and so on, there is an inflection. However, because it is indicated by elision, its sound is not heard. Due to the absence of a desire to express a close connection, it is not specified in euphonic combination. The sequence is as follows: the vowels, which are the basis, are stated first; then the consonants, which are dependent on them. Among the vowels, those with a single place of articulation, 'a' and so on, being numerous, are stated first according to the sequence of their place of articulation. Then those with two places of articulation, in sequence of their place of articulation. Among them, the short vowels, being light, are stated first, then the long ones. Among the consonants, the classified consonants, being numerous, are stated first according to the order of their place of articulation; then 'y' and so on. And among the classified consonants, the voiceless are stated first, then the voiced. And among them, the unaspirated are stated first, then the aspirated. Therein, the fifth letters, being few, are stated as having two places of articulation. Then 'y', 'r', 'l', 'v', being voiced, according to the sequence of their place of articulation. Then the aspirated 's' and 'h'. Among them, the letter 'h', for some, is also pectoral, and being of two origins, is stated later. Although for some, 'there is no difference between l and ḷ' is said, despite the lack of difference between the two, because they are different in script and place of articulation, 'ḷ' is taken as a separate letter. It too, being voiced, is stated after 'h' in the sequence of place of articulation. The nasal resonance (niggahīta), however, being entirely free from being a vowel and so on, is stated last. This is the sequence of 'a' and the other letters. Because this very sequence is present in the mind, and because the numerical limit of forty-three is shown, it is stated in the commentary as 'ending with the niggahīta.' The subject is the analysis of correct words. It is not described, because there is no primary purpose known as the description of sounds. Although it is not described, the question 'How did this sequence of 'a' and the other letters arise for us?' is indeed explained by us under the pretext of commenting on the meaning of the word 'sequence' for the purpose of dispelling the doubts of students. 'It is made, it is uttered by this,' thus it is the articulator. Therein, the middle of the tongue is the articulator for the palatals; the front of the tongue for the cerebrals; the tip of the tongue for the dentals; for the rest, their own place is the articulator. Effort is exertion. That, in the utterance of a letter, is both internal and external exertion. Therein, internal effort is: the closedness of the letter 'a'; the openness of the vowels and of the letters 's' and 'h'; the contact for the classified consonants; the slight contact for 'y', 'r', 'l', 'v'. External effort, however, is the constriction of the throat, and so on. Because of the possibility of a purpose due to the possibility of an action being prescribed based on proximity of place, he says: 'The place, however...' and so on. 'Letters stand here by way of origin,' thus it is the place. In the rule 'e o are bent before a letter' (1-37), the statement 'before a letter' is the purpose in making the designation 'letter'. He points out the aforesaid meaning elsewhere with 'thus' and so on. Therefore, in 'the ten initial are vowels' and so on, and in 'by that' and so on, the meaning should be seen in this way: 'by that, which is

2. Dasā

2. Ten

Nanu aādayoti paṭhamantenuvattante kathamettha’tatthā’ti sattamīniddiṭṭhatāti āha-‘tañcā’tiādi, atthavasāvibhattivipariṇāmenāti aādayoti paṭhamantassa‘ādo dasā’tyanena sambandhā sambajjhamāne cādhāratthena bhavitabbanti ādhāratthavasena sattamī vibhattiyā parivattanenāti attho, atthavasā sattamiyā vipariṇāmasambhavāyevasutte avijjamānepi‘tatthā’ti vuttiyaṃ vuttaṃ, ādodasannamanaññatthapavattisambhavato tesaṃ aādayo visayabhāvenapi sakkā parikappetunti vuttaṃ-‘tesu visayabhūtesū’ti, niddhāraṇatthopi yujjateva… vaṇṇasamudāyato tadekadesabhūtāna mādo vaṇṇānaṃ dasasaṅkhyāguṇena niddhāriyamānattā, ādimhi dasa vaṇṇāti vutte avuttānampi avassaṃ vattabbānaṃ ūnapūraṇatthamajjhāhāro hotīti vuttaṃ- avaṭṭhitā niddiṭṭhā vā’ti, ekādīna maṭṭhārasantānaṃ saṅkhyānaṃ saṅkhyeyye vattanato āha-‘dasasaṅkhyāya paricchinnattā’ti, gayhupagānaṃ rassae ovaṇṇānampi kaccāyane viya apariccāgā anūnā, agayhupagānaṃ tadaññesaṃ kesañci sarānaṃ pariccagā anadhikā, dasasaddassa saṅkhyeyya vuttittā [M 0.0026] dasannampi adhikatavaṇṇānaññattā vuttaṃ-‘dasannampī’tiādi, sayaṃ pubbā’rāja=cittiyaṃ’tīsmā kvimhi antalope samāse ca tadaminādittā niruttinayena vā sarasaddo nipphajjatīti, ‘sara-gatihiṃ sācintāsu’ iccasmā appaccayena vā nippajjatīti dassetumāha=‘sayaṃ rājantī’tiādi.

But do not 'a and the others' follow in the nominative case? How then is the locative case indicated here by 'tatthā' (therein)? He says: 'tañca' and so on. This means: by a change of case ending according to the sense. The nominative 'a and the others', being connected with 'the initial ten', should have a locative sense, and thus there is a change to the locative case ending according to the sense of location. Although not present in the rule, 'tatthā' is stated in the commentary. Since it is possible for other things not to occur among the first ten, they can also be conceived of as the domain, hence it is said: 'among them, which have become the domain.' The sense of determination is also suitable, because from the collection of letters, a portion of them, the initial letters, are determined by the quality of the number ten. When it is said 'ten letters at the beginning', it is stated that there is a supplying of an ellipsis to complete what is deficient, for what is unstated but must be said, hence 'established or specified'. Because the numbers from one to eighteen refer to what is countable, he says: 'being defined by the number ten'. Due to the non-abandonment of the short 'e' and 'o' vowels, which are to be included, as in Kaccāyana's grammar, they are not deficient. Due to the abandonment of certain other vowels which are not to be included, they are not excessive. Because the word 'dasa' refers to what is countable, and because there are more than ten letters, it is said: 'of the ten also' and so on. To show that the word 'sara' is formed from 'sayaṃ pubbā’rāja=cittiyaṃ' with the elision of the final letter in the compound with 'kvi', and because of 'tadaminādi', or by way of etymology; or that it is formed from the root 'sara-gatihiṃsācintāsu' with the suffix 'a', he says: 'sayaṃ rājantī' and so on.

3. Dvedve

3. In pairs

Teti’ādo’ti sattamyantattā apare dve parāmasati, heṭṭhā viyāti heṭṭhā vuttaṃ atthavasā vibhattivipariṇāmaṃ upameti, atova viññāyamānatthavasena tesu’ti vuttaṃ, tesuti pana niddhāraṇattavivacchāyaṃ tampi sambhavatīti tesaṃ vaṇṇānaṃ majjhe dvedveti dvisaṅkhyāya niddhāraṇatthopi veditabbo, vicchāyaṃ vutti yassa so vicchāvutti-dvisaddo, vicchāvuttitā cāssa savaṇṇattaguṇena dvinnaṃ (‘byāpitu) miṭṭhattā, kamenāvaṭṭhiteti iminā akārādivaṇṇappabandhassa anādikālasiddhaṃ kamasiddhattamāha. Nanu samānā vaṇṇā savaṇṇātyanvatthe savaṇṇasadde sati kataṃ rassadīghānaṃ savaṇṇasaññā siyā… asamānattā etesanti, netadatthivaṇṇappabandhassa kamasiddhattā vacanabalenevāsamānānampi hotevāti, nevampi vattuṃ yuttaṃ“dvedve savaṇṇā”ti suttassa tādisasāmatthiyasabbhāve sabbhāvena (potthake) visesakāraṇābhāvāti āha‘samānattampanā’tiādi. Tiṭṭhanti ettha vaṇṇā cittajattepi abhibyatti vasenāti ṭhānaṃ kaṇṭhādi, tena katanti samāso, kaṇṭhatātu iti catte pāṇyaṅgattā napuṃsakattaṃ. Pañcamehi vaggapañcamehi. Antaṭṭhākīti vaggānamante tiṭṭhantīti antaṭṭhā, tāhi, yuttassāti brahmacariyā, guyha’ntiādīsu yuttassa. Kecīti aniyamena vuttaṃ, te pana–

The phrase ‘teti’ādo’ (those, etc.), being in the seventh case ending, refers to the other two. The phrase ‘heṭṭhā viyāti’ (as below) compares it to the transformation of case endings based on meaning, as stated below. Therefore, ‘tesu’ (in them) is stated by way of the understood meaning. However, in the sense of specification, ‘tesu’ is also possible. Thus, among those letters, ‘dvedve’ (two by two) should also be understood as having the purpose of specification by the number two. The word ‘dvi’ (two) has a distributive application (vicchāvutti) because its application is distributive. Its distributiveness is due to the quality of being homogeneous letters, making the two compatible. By ‘kamenāvaṭṭhite’ (arranged in sequence), it states that the arrangement of letters beginning with ‘a’ is established by a sequence that has existed from time immemorial. Now, when the word ‘savaṇṇa’ (homogeneous letter) has the etymological meaning ‘similar letters,’ how can short and long vowels be designated as ‘savaṇṇa’… since they are dissimilar? It is not so, for due to the established sequence of the series of letters and by the force of the statement, even dissimilar ones can be so. Nor is it appropriate to say this, for if the rule ‘dvedve savaṇṇā’ (two by two are homogeneous letters) had such capability, there would be no special reason. Therefore, it is said: ‘samānattampanā’ (but similarity) and so on. The place (ṭhāna), such as the throat, etc., is where letters stand by way of manifestation, even when mind-born. The compound is ‘tena kataṃ’ (made by that). The word ‘kaṇṭhatālu’ (throat and palate) is neuter because it is a limb of a living being. With the fifths of the classes. The ‘antaṭṭhā’ (semivowels) are so called because they stand at the end of the classes. With them. Of that which is conjoined, as in ‘brahmacariyā’, ‘guyha’, and so on. By ‘some’ (kecī), it is stated without restriction. They, however, say—

“Hakāro pañcameheva, antaṭṭhāhi ca saṃyuto;

Oraso iti viññeyyo, kaṇṭhajo tadasaṃyuto”ti vadanti.

“The letter ‘ha,’ when combined with the fifth letters and with the semivowels (antaṭṭhā), should be known as ‘orasa’ (chest-born); when not combined with them, it is ‘kaṇṭhaja’ (throat-born),” they say.

4. Pubbo

4. Former

Vattateti atthavasā vibhattivipariṇāmena vattate, nanu cetyādicodanā, nesadosoccādi parihāro, dosābhāve kāraṇa māha-‘yoyo…pe… [M 0.0027] patīyate’ti, vuttaṃ samatteti-‘nahi’ccādinā, nanu ca pubbasaddo yamekattā ekaṃ pubbamācikkhati na sakalanti kathaṃ “pubbo’ti vutte yoyoti ñāyati ‘yoyo pubbo’ti ca vutte ‘tesu dvīsu’ti ettha’dvīsu dvīsu’ti idaṃ kathaṃ sukheneva patīyate tadidamasiddhenāsiddhasādhananti āsaṅkiya tadabhāvamubbhāvīya pubba saddassa vicchāgamakattamavagamayitumāha-‘naceda’miccādi. Taṃyogāti upacāravasenāha, tabbantatāyavāti atthiyatthe appaccayavasena, evamuparipi.

It is construed by way of alteration of inflection according to the meaning. The objection is 'but isn't it so?' etc. The refutation is 'this is not a fault,' etc. In the absence of a fault, he states the reason: 'whichever... is understood.' The statement is concluded with 'not so,' etc. But does not the word 'pubba' (former), because of its singularity, denote one prior thing and not the whole? So how, when 'pubbo' is said, is it understood as 'whichever'? And when 'yoyo pubbo' (whichever former) is said, how is 'in those two' understood here as 'in each of the two' so easily? Suspecting that this is proving the unproven with what is unproven, he brings forth its absence in order to make known the distributive function of the word 'pubba.' He says, 'if not this,' etc. 'Because of its connection'—he speaks by way of figurative usage. 'Because it ends in that'—it is said in the sense of existing by way of the 'a' suffix. Likewise, above as well.

5. Paro

5. Latter

Sesamiccādinā‘tesu dvīsūti savaṇṇasaññakesu dvīsu’ iccādi kamatidissati. Lahusaññā rassassa, saṃyogapubbassa rassassa dīghassa ca gurusaññā na vattabbā… uccāraṇavasenevānvatthasaññāti viññāyati, pubbācariyavasena vā ihāvuttāvasesasaññāviya.

By 'the rest,' etc., the sequence 'among those two, that is, among the two designated as homogeneous,' etc., is indicated. The designation 'light' is for a short vowel. The designation 'heavy' for a short vowel preceded by a conjunct consonant, and for a long vowel, need not be stated... It is understood to be a designation conforming to its meaning by way of pronunciation, or like the remaining designations not stated here, according to the former teachers.

6. Kādayo

6. Kādayo (K, etc.)

Kevala byañjanānamatthappakāsattābhāvā sarānamatthappakāsane accantopakārā byañjanāti ‘etehī’ti karaṇattena vuttaṃ, tenāha ‘sarāna’miccādi. Vipubbā ‘añja-byattiyaṃ’tīmasmā karaṇe anappaccaye rūpaṃ, napuṃsakattampissāvagamayituṃ ‘upakārakānī’ti vuttaṃ, byañjanattaṃ diṭṭhantena phuṭayati ‘yathā’iccādinā, yathā odanassupakārakāni sūpādīni byañjanāni, tathā sarānamupakārakānīti adhippāyo, byañjanampana addhamattikaṃ, vuttaṃ hi–

Because mere consonants do not have the ability to reveal meaning, they are extremely helpful in revealing the meaning of vowels. Thus, 'by these' (etehī) is stated in the instrumental sense. For that reason, he says 'of the vowels' (sarānaṃ), etc. The form is from the root 'añj' meaning 'to make clear,' preceded by 'vi,' with the 'ana' suffix in the instrumental sense. To also indicate its neuter gender, 'upakārakāni' (helpful things) is stated. He clarifies the nature of a consonant with an illustration, 'just as,' etc. Just as condiments (byañjanāni) such as soup are helpful to rice, so too are consonants helpful to vowels—this is the meaning. Moreover, a consonant is half a mora, for it is said:

Ekamatto bhave rasso, dīgho mattadvayāyuto;

Pluto timatto viññeyyo, byañjanaṃ tvaddhamattikaṃti.

A short vowel has one mora; a long vowel has two morae; a prolated vowel is to be known as having three morae; but a consonant is half a mora.

Anvatthāti anvatthato, ‘anvatthā byañjanā’ti sambandho.

'Anvatthā' means 'according to the meaning.' The connection is 'the consonants are etymologically significant.'

7. Pañca

7. Five

Sajātyapekkhāya samudāyavācittepi kādayotī anuvattanato vaggasaddena kakhagaghañādayova gayhanti, pañca parimāṇamassa pañcakovaggo, “tamassa parimāṇaṃ ṇiko cā”ti (4-41) ko, sutte ādibhūto [M 0.0028] pañcasaddo pañcasaṅkhyāparicchedaṃ kurumāno māvasānānaṃ vaggānaṃ bahuttaṃ gametīti ‘pañcakā’ti vuttaṃ, vaggāti bahuvacanato paccekanti viññāyati, vajjenti yakārādayobhi vaggā, paṭhamakkharavasena pana kavaggādivohāro.

Although it is a collective term, with reference to its own class, because 'k, etc.' is carried over, by the word 'vagga' (class), only 'ka, kha, ga, gha, ña,' etc., are understood. Its measure is five, hence a fivefold class. By the rule 'That is its measure, and ṇika' (4-41), the suffix is 'ka'. In the rule, the initial word 'pañca' (five), defining the number five, prevents the implication of a multitude of classes ending with 'ma'; hence, 'pañcakā' (fivefold) is stated. Because 'vaggā' (classes) is plural, it is understood as 'each one'. The letters 'ya,' etc., are excluded from the classes. However, based on the first letter, the usage is 'ka-class' (kavagga), etc.

8. Bindu

8. Bindu (The Dot)

Anekatthattā dhātūna muccāraṇatthopettha gaṇhātīti nipubbā tato kammanti ttappaccaye ññimhi pādisamāse dīgheca rūpaṃ dassento ‘rassā’tiādīmāha, pīḷanatthato niggahanaṃ niggaho, ‘i-ajjhena gatīsu’iccasmā kattari kammani-iti vattabbaṃ, itaṃ uccāritanti attho ttappaccaye itaṃ, niggahena itanti amādisa māse rūpaṃ dassento ‘karaṇaṃ niggahena vā’tiādimāha, pacchimapakkhaṃ sādhetumāha-‘vuttaṃ hī’ti.

Because roots have many meanings, here the meaning of 'pronunciation' is also taken. Therefore, showing the form with a long vowel in a compound with a prefix, when the suffix 'tta' is applied to the root 'gam' preceded by 'ni' in the sense of 'action,' he says 'short,' etc. In the sense of pressing, 'niggahana' is 'niggaho' (restraint). From the root 'i' in the sense of 'going' in the 'ajjhena' group, the suffix 'tta' is applied in the agent sense, forming 'ita.' Showing the form in a compound like 'am,' etc., as 'niggahena itaṃ' (gone with restraint), he says 'the act of restraining or...' etc. To establish the latter view, he says, 'for it is said.'

9. Iyu

9. I and U

Catthasamāsoti itarītarayogadvandasamāso. Atteti muni saddādivacanīye atthe, namatītīmassetaṃ kammaṃ,

'A compound in the sense of "and"' is an itarītarayogadvanda compound. 'Atte' is in the sense expressible by words like 'muni,' etc. 'namati' (it bends)—this is its object.

Yaṃ sabbavacanaṃ sabba, liṅgaṃ sabbavibhattikaṃ;

Taṃ sabbatthe namanato, viduṃ nāmanti tabbidū.

That which has all numbers, all genders, all case endings; That, because it bends to all meanings, those who know it know as 'nāma' (noun).

Idha nāmasaññāyābhāvepi anvatthabalāyeva nāmasaññā siddhāti (āha) ‘anvatthabyapadesenā’ti, syādyantapakatirūpanti paccayā paṭhamaṃ karīyatīti pakati, sā eva rūpanti pakatirūpaṃ, syādyantassa pakati rūpaṃ munisaddādi syādyantapakatirūpaṃ, atthavantamadhātukamappaccayampāṭipadikaṃ, padaṃ padaṃ pati paṭipade, paṭipadaṃ niyuttaṃ pāṭipadikaṃ. Visesanenāti sutte ‘namassante’ti vuttena ivaṇṇuvaṇṇānaṃ visesanena. Ākhyātassāti pacatiādino. Ādimajjhavattinoti inda udakasaddādīnaṃ ādo, pakhumādīnaṃ majjheca vattino. Padesesūti “jhalā sassa no”ti (2-83) ādikesu suttappadesesu, aniṭṭhapasaṅga (saṅkaṃ) nivattetīti sambandho, aniṭṭhappasaṅgonāma nāmāti (potthake) pacati-inda (udaka pakhuma) saddādīna manta ādimajjhabhūtaivaṇṇādīnaṃ [M 0.0029] jhalasaññā vidhāya tato parāsaṃ sādi vibhattīnaṃ “jhalā sassa no”ti (2-81) ādīhi ‘no’ ādesādimhi kate ‘pacatino, indano, udakano, pakhumano’tiādi rūpappasaṅgo, nanucādiādi codanā. Vattabbanti sutte vattabbaṃ. Byāsaniddesenāti asamāsaniddesena. Tadayuttantiādi parihāro, tanti taṃ codyaṃ, satihītiādinā ayuttattaṃ samattheti, dvīsuttaresu yogesūti uparimesu “pitthiyaṃ” “ghā”ti dvīsu suttesu. Itthiyanti idanti “pitthiya”nti sutte itthiyanti idaṃ padaṃ. Vaṇṇavisesanaṃ siyāti “pitthiya”nti sutte ‘iyuvaṇṇā’ti anuvattanato ‘itthiyaṃ ivaṇṇuvaṇṇā’ti evaṃ ivaṇṇu vaṇṇā “gho”ti sutte ‘itthiyaṃ ā’tievaṃ avaṇṇassa ca visesanaṃ bhaveyya. Vaṇṇavisesane virodhamāha ‘evañce’ccādi, nāmassanteti asamāsaniddese tvavirodhamāha- ‘byāse’ccādi. Sakkānāmavisesanaṃ kātunti dvīsu suttesu itthiyantiādinā vakkhamānakkamena. Nāmassa anto nāmantoti samāsassa uttarapadatthappadhānattā samāse guṇībhūtassa nāmassa itthiyanti idaṃ visesanaṃ kātuṃ na sakkāti adhippāyo, vacanamantarenāti pāṇiniyānamiva “yathāsaṅkhyamanudeso samānaṃ”ti (1-3-10) suttaṃ vinā, samāsaṅkhya etesanti samasaṅkhyakā, itisaddo ādyattho, tena–

Here, even in the absence of a name-designation, the name-designation is established by the force of its meaning; thus it is said, ‘by designation according to meaning.’ The base (pakati) is that from which suffixes are first made; that very form is the base-form (pakatirūpa). The base-form of that which ends in 'syā', etc., is like the word 'muni', etc. A meaningful, non-root, non-suffixal element is a nominal stem (pāṭipadika). 'Paṭipade' means 'for each word'; that which is connected to 'paṭipada' is a nominal stem. 'By specification' means by the specification of the vowels 'i' and 'u', as stated in the sutta 'namassante'. 'Of a verb' refers to 'pacati', etc. 'Occurring at the beginning and in the middle' refers to those at the beginning of words like 'inda', 'udaka', etc., and in the middle of 'pakhuma', etc. 'In the sections' refers to the sections of the suttas, such as 'jhalā sassa no' (2-83), etc. It prevents an undesirable consequence (saṅka); this is the connection. An undesirable consequence is the contingency of forms such as 'pacatino', 'indano', 'udakano', 'pakhumano', etc., which would arise if, after prescribing the designation 'jhala' for the final, initial, and middle vowels 'i', etc., of words like 'pacati', 'inda', 'udaka', 'pakhuma', etc., substitutions like 'no' were made for the following case-endings 'sa', etc., by rules such as 'jhalā sassa no' (2-81). 'nanu', etc., are objections. 'What should be said' refers to what is to be stated in the sutta. 'By uncompounded designation' means by designation without forming a compound. 'That is inappropriate,' etc., is the refutation; 'taṃ' refers to that objection. With 'sati hi', etc., he establishes its inappropriateness. 'In the application of the two suttas' refers to the two subsequent suttas, 'pitthiyaṃ' and 'ghā'. Regarding 'itthiyaṃ': this word 'itthiyaṃ' is in the sutta 'pitthiyaṃ'. 'There could be a specification of a vowel': because 'iyuvaṇṇā' is carried over into the sutta 'pitthiyaṃ', it would become a specification of the vowels 'i' and 'u' as in 'the vowels i and u in the feminine'; similarly, in the sutta 'gho', it would become a specification of the vowel 'a' as in 'ā in the feminine'. He states the contradiction in specifying a vowel with 'evañce', etc. He states the absence of contradiction in an uncompounded designation with 'byāse', etc. 'It is possible to specify the name' means in the two suttas, by the word 'itthiyaṃ', etc., in the manner to be explained. Regarding 'nāmanto', it means 'the end of a name'; the intention is that because the meaning of the latter member is primary in a compound, this word 'itthiyaṃ' cannot function as a specifier for the name, which has become subordinate in the compound. 'Without another statement' means without a sutta like Pāṇini's 'yathāsaṅkhyamanudeso samānaṃ' (1.3.10). 'Samasaṅkhyakā' means 'they have an equal number'. The word 'iti' has the sense of 'etc.' Therefore—

“Ālāpahāsalīlāhi, muninda vijayā tava;

Kokilā kumudānī vo, pasevante vanaṃ jalaṃ” (260).

“O King of Sages, through pleasant talk, laughter, and charm, yours are the victories; cuckoos and water lilies frequent the forest and the water for you.”

Iccādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti.

Thus, he includes this and so forth.

10. Pitthi

10. Back

Itthiyaṃ nāmassāti ca, ante ivaṇṇuvaṇṇāti ca vutte tesamā dhārādheyyasambandho ādheyyassādhāre pavattiṃ vinā na sambhavatīti ajjhāhāravasena ‘vattamānā’ti vuttiyaṃ vuttaṃ. Ivaṇṇu vaṇṇāti apekkhiya‘visesīyantī’ti bahuvacanametaṃ sambandhassa purisādhīnatāya nāmantīminā sambandhe sati‘visesīyatī’tekattena pariṇamati.

And when it is said, 'of a name in the feminine gender,' and 'the vowels i and u at the end,' their relationship as container and contained is not possible without the existence of the contained within the container. Therefore, by way of supplying an ellipsis, 'vattamānā' (existing) is stated in the commentary. With reference to 'the vowels i and u,' this is the plural form 'visesīyantī' (they are specified); because the relationship is dependent on the person, when there is a connection with this end of the name, it transforms into the singular 'visesīyati' (it is specified).

11. Ghā

11. Ghā

Itthiyaṃ [M 0.0030] nāmassanteti ca vattate. Heṭṭhā sabbattha saññino niddisiya saññāya niddiṭṭhattā tattha viya visuṃ saññino paṭhamamaniddese asanto viyāti dosalesamālambiya codayati nanhace’tyādinā. Tattha setoti vijjamānassa saññino. Kāriyenāti saññākāriyena. Pariharati ‘nāyaṃ doso’tiādinā. Pacchāvuttamattenāti “ghā”ti sutte kāriyino ākārassa pacchā vuttamattena. Nacāti ettha casaddo vattabbantarasamuccaye, aparampi kiñci vattabbamaniyamarūpamatthīti attho. Aniyamarūpamācariyappavattito sādhetumāha ‘ubhayathāpi’ccādi.

And the phrase 'in the feminine, at the end of a name' is carried over. Because below, in all cases, the possessor of the designation is indicated, and it is indicated by the designation, as if the possessor of the designation were non-existent when not separately indicated in the first instance, he raises an objection, seizing upon a slight fault, with 'Is it not so?' etc. Therein, 'sato' means 'of the existing possessor of the designation'. 'Kāriyena' means 'by the effect of the designation'. He refutes this with 'This is not a fault,' etc. 'By being merely stated later' means by the mere later statement of the vowel 'ā', the effect, in the sutta 'ghā'. In 'na ca', the particle 'ca' serves to include other things to be said; the meaning is that there is something else to be said, which is of an indeterminate form. To establish the indeterminate form from the teacher's usage, he says, 'in both ways,' etc.

12. Gosyā

12. Gosyā

Āsaddo ābhimukhye, anabhimukhamabhimukhaṃ katvā lapanaṃ kathanamāla panaṃ, tasmiṃ ālapane, ālapanatthe vihito sīti attho.

The word 'ā' has the sense of 'facing towards'. Addressing (ālapana) is speaking or uttering after making one who is not facing towards face towards. In that address, in the sense of address, 'si' is prescribed; this is the meaning.

Iti moggallānapañcikāṭīkāyaṃ sāratthavilāsiniyaṃ

Thus in the Sāratthavilāsinī, the sub-commentary on the Moggallāna-pañcikā.

Saññādhikāro samatto.

The section on designations is completed.

Paribhāsādhikāra

The Section on Governing Rules

13. Vidhi

13. Rule

Vacanārambhayojanamāha–‘yaṃ visesanabhāvene’ccādi, yanti aniyamena “ato yonaṃ ṭāṭe”ti (2-43) ādīsu atotiādikaṃ visesanabhāvena vattumicchitaṃ parāmasati, tenāti vise sanattenu-pādiyamānena yaṃ saddaniddiṭṭhena atotiādikena karaṇabhūtena, yathākathañcitabbatoti ādo majjhe-nte vā sabbhāvato yenakenaci ākārena abhedopacārena akārādivisesanavato nāmādino, tadantatthanti taṃ atotyādi visesanamante, nādo na majjhe yassa taṃ tadantaṃ, taṃ attho payojanaṃ yassāti aññapadattho, vattāyattāti vattuno āyattā… attāvāttano vacane padhānanti, tassāti vattuno, sāti vacanicchā, payogānusā renāti [M 0.0031] jinavacanānusārena, itīti kāraṇatthe nipāto, iminā kāraṇenāti attho, na sabbatthappasaṅgoti saṃhitādividhimhi sabbattha tadanta vidhippasaṅgo na hoti, tathāhi “saro lopo sare”ti (1-26) ettha saroti visesanabhāvena vacanicchāya sabbhāve saroti tatrā’dīnaṃ visesananti yathākathañcisarādisaramajjhasarantānaṃ tatrādīnaṃ lopappasaṅge “vidhibbisesanantassā”ti (1-13) sarantassapasaṅgo siyā, na “chaṭṭhiyantassā”ti (1-13) antassa… chaṭṭhīniddesābhāvā, tathā sati ‘tatrime’tiādimhi ‘ime’tiādinā vattabbatā āpajjeyyāti payogaṃ nānusaṭā nāmasiyunti na sabbattha tadanta vidhippasaṅgo, tathā “gatibodhā” (2-4) disuttādimhipi ‘gamayati māṇavakaṃgāmaṃ tyādippasaṅgotiādi ca yathāyogamavagantabbaṃ, vuttiyaṃ “ato yonaṃ ṭāṭe”ti suttodāharaṇaṃ dassitaṃ, “narā nare”ti lakkhiyodāharaṇaṃ.

He states the purpose for commencing the statement: 'that which is in the nature of a qualifier,' etc. 'Yaṃ' (which) refers without restriction to that which is intended to be stated as a qualifier, such as 'ato' in rules like 'ato yonaṃ ṭāṭe' (2-43). 'Tena' (by that) means by that which is indicated by the word 'yaṃ', i.e., by 'ato', etc., which is taken as a qualifier and functions as an instrument. Of a nominal stem, etc., which possesses a qualifier like the vowel 'a', etc., in some way—that is, existing at the beginning, middle, or end—by any means whatsoever, through the metaphor of non-difference. 'Tadantattho' means its purpose is to apply to that which ends in it (the qualifier). 'Tadanta' is that which has it (the qualifier) at the end, not at the beginning or in the middle. That whose meaning or purpose is that, is a possessive compound (aññapadattha). 'Vattāyattā' means dependent on the speaker... the speaker is primary in their own speech. 'Tassa' means of the speaker; 'sā' is the desire to speak. 'Payogānusārena' means in accordance with the usage in the Jina's words. 'Iti' is a particle in the sense of cause; the meaning is 'for this reason'. 'Na sabbatthappasaṅgo' means the rule concerning that which ends in the qualifier does not apply everywhere, in rules such as those concerning euphonic combination (saṃhitā). For instance, in 'saro lopo sare' (1-26), if 'sara' (vowel) were intended as a qualifier, then 'sara' would be a qualifier for 'tatra', etc. In that case, there would be the contingency of elision for 'tatra', etc., which have a vowel at the beginning, middle, or end. The rule 'vidhi visesanaṃ antassa' (1-13) would apply to that which ends in a vowel, but not the rule 'chaṭṭhiyantassa' (1-13) to the end... because there is no specification by the sixth case-ending. If that were so, in 'tatrime', etc., it would have to be stated as 'ime', etc., and thus the usage would not be followed. Therefore, the rule concerning that which ends in the qualifier does not apply everywhere. Similarly, in suttas like 'gatibodhā' (2-4), the contingency of 'gamayati māṇavakaṃ gāmaṃ', etc., should be understood as appropriate. In the commentary (vutti), the sutta 'ato yonaṃ ṭāṭe' is shown as an example, while 'narā nare' is an illustrative example.

14. Sattadhī

14. Sevenfold wisdom

Vacanaphalamupadasseti‘yatthe’ccādinā, yattha yasmiṃ “saro lopo sare”tyādike sutte, sattamiyāti ‘sare’tiādinā sattamiyā, yassāti sarotiādinā niddiṭṭhassa, kāriyaṃ lopādi, sambandhā visesāti saretyādo opasilesikamadhikaraṇaṃ, tañcopasilese bhavamadhikaraṇaṃ pubbassa vā paraṃ siyā parassa vā pubbanti pubbaparopasi lesassāvisiṭṭhattā pubbaparānaṃ sambandhassa avisesā, parassāpīti na kevalaṃ pubbasseva, satītyasmiṃ atthe jotanīye sattamī saṃsattamī santasaddassa samādesena, sattañcetyādivacanamevaṃ sati ghaṭate, santi vā santasaddatthe pādi, sutte avuttepi vuttiyaṃ ‘niddese’ti vacane kāraṇamāha-sattañcā’tiādi, niddesamantarena sattaṃ na sambhavatīti sambandho, sattamiyā niddese satiyeva taṃ sambandhāya sattāya sambhavo, aññathā kimaññantassā patiṭṭhāti adhippāyo, pubbasaddassa sambandhisaddattā kinnissāya pubbattamiccāha-‘sattami’ccādi, tanti “saro lopo sare”ti suttaṃ, ukārassāti ‘veḷu’iccatra ukārassa, pubbassa…pe… karitvā taṃmanasikatañcodanaṃ dassetumāha-‘tamaha’nti [M 0.0032] ccāditi evamettha sājjhāhāro sambandho veditabbo. Pubbassāti sattamī niddiṭṭhato pubbassa, anantarassāti abyavahitassa, vuttaṃ kiñci natthīti sambandho, ayamadhippāyo “tasminti niddiṭṭhe pubbassā”ti (1-1-66) pāṇiniyavacane “disirayamuccāraṇakriyo nisaddopyaya miha nerantariyaṃ joteti, tattha‘nirantaraṃ diṭṭho’ti pādisamāse kate phuṭamevānantaramuccāritetyamattho-vagamyateti “pubbasaddassa byavahitepi payogadassane byavahitepi kāriyaṃ pappotī”ti bhassakārādayo vaṇṇenti, iha tādisavacanābhāvena vaṇṇādi byavadhānepi siyā”ti, sareccādiparihāravacane-dhippāya mubbhāvayati ‘yadipi’ccādinā, mathurāya pāṭaliputtakassa cāntarāḷe gāmādīnaṃ sabbhāvā byavadhānepi pubbasaddassa pavattiyā diṭṭhantamāha-‘mathurā’ iccādi, yasmā sareti opasilesikādhāre sattamyantaṃ padaṃ, tasmā byavadhāne saralopo na hotīti evaṃ saṅkhepabyākhyānena vuttiya mattho veditabbo, na kevalaṃ sareti etthevāti āha- ‘kāriye’ccādi, opasilesikeyevādhāre bhavatīti seso, kāraṇamāha-‘vatticchānhavidhānato saddassā’ti, vattuno yā icchā vacanicchā tassā anutūlena vidhānato atthassa kathanatoti attho,yena hi yamatthaṃ vattātidhātumicchati satīpyabhidhānasā matthiye na tato-ññamatthaṃ saddobhidadhātītyadhippāyo, vatticchā vasāye kāraṇamāha’vatticchāpi’ccādi, vattuno suttakārassa icchā vatticchā, kathamupadesato vatticchā-vasīyate’ kathañca sāmatthiyatoti āsaṅkiya tamupadassetumāha-‘atocetyādi, ato vakkhamānakāraṇā upadesato vasīyateti sambandho, kintaṃ kāraṇa miccāha-‘yasmā’iccādi, anvayasaddenettha gurupārampariyo-padeso vivacchito, yasmā kāraṇā anvayo gurupārampariyo padeso gurukulamupagamma pañhakaraṇādinā anvicchīyate gavesīyati, ato kāraṇā guruparamparā gataupadesato vasīyatoti attho, sāmatthiyato-vasāyappaṭipādayitumāha- ‘sāmatthiyampi’ccādi, sāmatthiyampi vuccatetiseso, laghunopāyena saddānamupalakkhaṇe pavattīti byavahitanivattiyā vacanantaraka-raṇamanupannaṃ[M 0.0033], upapannaṃ vacanantarakaraṇaṃ, tassa ca opasilesikādhāra mantarena aññathānupapattiyā ādhāravisesappaṭippattīti idamettha sāmatthiyaṃ, ādhārantareccādinā yathāvuttaṃ sāmatthiyaṃ vibhāveti, ādhārantarepīti sabbattha pāṭho dissati, pasaṅgābhāvato atthanta-renāpi ādhārantarepi opasilesikādhārepi vacanantarappasaṅgo siyāti sambandhasambhavā opasilesikādhāranissayanepi ānisaṃso na dissatīti samuccayatthenāpi natthi payojananti vajjetabbo yampi saddoti, nanu kimevaṃ vaṇṇīyate pubbasseveti vacana mevopasilesikamadhikaraṇaṃ viññāpayati… tattheva pubbaparatta sambhavāti yomaññate, tassesā kappanā na saṅgatāti dassetumāha-‘pubbassāti’ccādi, ayuttatte kāraṇamāha-‘sāmīpikepi tassa sambhavā’ti, ‘gaṅgāyaṃ ghoso’ti vutte ghoso gaṅgāyaṃ pubbo vā paro veti gammamānattā sāmīpikepyadhikaraṇe pubbaparattassa sambhavāti attho, etāvavuccateti pubbasseva hoti na parassāti ettakameva vuccate, tathāca vakkhati-‘kinta’ntiādi, adhikaṃ byavahitanivutyādi na vuccateti sambandho, ādisaddenettha chaṭṭhīpakappanā gahitā, chaṭṭhīpakappanāpi sāmattiyā katāti sambandho, pakappanaṃ pakappanāvidhānaṃ, evaṃ maññate ‘pāṇiniyā “chaṭṭhīṭṭhāneyogā”tyato (1-1-49) “tasminti niddiṭṭhe pubbassa” (1-1-66) “tasmā tyuttarassa” iti (1-1-67) paribhāsāsuttadvaye chaṭṭhīgahaṇamanuvattiya ‘tasminti niddiṭṭhe pubbassa chaṭṭhī’ ‘tasmātyuttarassa chaṭṭhī niddiṭṭhe pubbassa chaṭṭhīti pubbassa kāriyittapaṭipādanayoggo chaṭṭhī tabbodhakapade bhavatityattho, eva dhuttarassetu vi. ujjotaṭīkā ti chaṭṭhīpakappanaṃ paṭipādenti ‘yasmiṃ sutte chaṭṭhīniddeso natthi, tattha chaṭṭhīpakappanāyathā siyā’ti, idha pana vacanantarābhāvepi yattha chaṭṭhīniddeso natthi, tattha sāmatthiyeneva chaṭṭhīpakappanā siddhā’ti, sāmatthiyamupadasseti ‘sattamīniddese’ccādinā, aññavibhattiniddiṭṭhopi paṭipajjateti sambandho, kāriyayo ganti kāriyasambandhaṃ, yathā “vagge vagganto”ti etthānuvattamānaṃ niggahīta’ntidaṃ chaṭṭhīyantaṃ viññāyate, kathaṃ vaggetesā sattamyakatatthā “niggahīta”nti (1-38) pubbasutte katatthatāya paṭhamā vibhattiyā [M 0.0034] chaṭṭhīvibhattimpakappeti sattamiyaṃ pubbasse’ti tathetyavagantabbaṃ. Etāva vuccateti vutte idanti na viññāyateti āha ‘kinta’ntiādi, yadāhiccādinā pariyāyapasaṅgakkamaṃ dasseti. Kimidamuccate pariyāyappasaṅge niyamatthaṃ vacananti nanu pubbaparānaṃ yugapaduppattiya mācariyavacanappamāṇenāppaṭipattiyaṃ vijjhanatthaṃ vacananti kasmā nocca teccāha- ‘yugapadupasiliṭṭhāna’ntyādi, yugapadupasiliṭṭhānamasambhavoti sambandho, kutoccāha-‘aparassūpasilesikassābhāvato’ti, atoti yugapadubhinnampattiyā abhāvato, vacanaṃ “saro lopāsare”ccādikaṃ (1-26) suttaṃ.

He shows the result of the statement with 'yattha,' etc. 'Yattha' means 'in which,' that is, in the sutta such as "saro lopo sare." The locative case is indicated by 'sare,' etc. 'Yassa' refers to that which is specified by 'sara,' etc. The operation is elision, etc. The relation is specific, thus 'sare,' etc., is the proximate locus (opasilesika-adhikaraṇa). And that proximate locus is the locus which consists in proximity. It could be that which is subsequent to the prior, or that which is prior to the subsequent. Because the proximity of the prior and subsequent is not distinguished, the relation between the prior and subsequent is non-specific. 'Also for the subsequent' means not only for the prior. When the meaning 'being present' is to be indicated, the locative is the locative absolute (sati-sattamī), by the instruction of the word 'santa.' The statement 'sattañca,' etc., is thus applicable. Or, 'santi' is in the meaning of the word 'santa,' etc. Even though it is not stated in the sutta, in the commentary (vutti), he states the reason for the word 'niddese' with 'sattañca,' etc. The connection is: without specification, existence is not possible. Only when there is specification by the locative is the existence related to it possible. Otherwise, on what would something else be based? This is the intention. Because the word 'pubba' (prior) is a relative term, he says 'sattami,' etc., asking, "In relation to what is it prior?" That is the sutta "saro lopo sare." 'Of the u-kāra' means: of the u-kāra in 'veḷu.' To show the objection which has that in mind, having said 'of the prior... etc.,' he says 'tamahaṃ,' etc. Thus, the connection here is to be understood by supplying what is missing. 'Of the prior' means: of that which is prior to what is specified by the locative. 'Of the immediate' means: of that which is not separated by an interval. The connection is that nothing specific is stated. This is the intention: In Pāṇini's rule "tasminti niddiṭṭhe pubbassa" (1.1.66), the term implies immediacy. Thus, the commentators (bhāṣyakāra) and others explain that "due to seeing the usage of the word 'pubba' even for what is separated by an interval, the operation would apply even to what is separated." Here, in this grammar, due to the absence of such a statement, it might apply even when there is an interval of a sound, etc. He clarifies the intention in the statement that resolves this, 'sare,' etc., with 'yadipi,' etc. He gives the example 'Mathurā,' etc., for the application of the word 'pubba' even with an interval, because villages and so on exist in the space between Mathurā and Pāṭaliputta. Because 'sare' is a word ending in the locative case in the sense of a proximate locus, therefore, when there is an interval, the elision of the vowel does not happen. Thus, the meaning of the commentary should be understood by this concise explanation. He says 'kāriye,' etc., to show that it is not only here in 'sare.' The rest of the meaning is: it occurs only in the proximate locus. He states the reason: "Because the word is established in accordance with the speaker's wish." The meaning is: because the meaning is stated by an establishment that is in accordance with the speaker's wish, which is the desire to speak. The intention is: for whatever meaning the speaker wishes to express, even if the word has the capacity to denote another meaning, it does not express that other meaning. He states the reason for determining the speaker's wish with 'vatticchāpi,' etc. The speaker's wish is the wish of the author of the sutta. Raising the doubt, "How is the speaker's wish determined from the teaching? And how from capacity?", he shows it with 'ato ca,' etc. The connection is: from this, that is, from the reason about to be stated, it is determined from the teaching. He says 'yasmā,' etc., asking, "What is that reason?" Here, by the word 'anvaya,' the instruction of the lineage of teachers is intended. Because 'anvaya,' the instruction of the lineage of teachers, is sought after and investigated by approaching the teacher's school, asking questions, and so on, for that reason, the meaning is: it is determined from the instruction that has come down through the lineage of teachers. To explain the determination from capacity, he says 'sāmatthiyampi,' etc. The rest is: 'capacity is also stated.' The grammar proceeds to characterize words by a concise method. Therefore, making another statement to exclude what is separated would be illogical. However, making another statement is logical, and since that is otherwise inexplicable without the proximate locus, a specific locus is understood. This here is the 'capacity' (sāmatthiya). With 'ādhārantare,' etc., he clarifies the 'capacity' as stated. The reading 'ādhārantarepi' is seen everywhere. Since there is no other occasion, there would be the occasion for another statement even for another meaning, for another locus, and for the proximate locus. Because this connection is possible, no advantage is seen even in relying on the proximate locus. Therefore, even with a conjunctive sense, there is no purpose. Thus, this word 'api' should be rejected. "Well, why is it explained thus? Does not the statement 'of the prior alone' itself make known the proximate locus, since only there is the state of being prior and subsequent possible?" To show that this assumption of one who thinks thus is not correct, he says 'pubbassa,' etc. He states the reason for its incorrectness: "Because it is also possible in the case of the locative of proximity (sāmīpika)." The meaning is: when it is said, "A village on the Ganges (gaṅgāyaṃ ghoso)," because it is understood whether the village is prior to the Ganges or subsequent to it, the state of being prior and subsequent is possible even in the case of the locative of proximity. 'This much is stated' means: only this much is stated, that it applies to the prior, not to the subsequent. And so he will say 'kintaṃ,' etc. The connection is: nothing more, such as the exclusion of what is separated by an interval, is stated. Here, by the word 'ādi,' the positing of the sixth case (genitive) is taken. The connection is: the positing of the genitive is also done by capacity. Positing is the establishment of a rule. Thus it is thought: In Pāṇini's grammar, from "chaṭṭhī ṭhāneyogā" (1.1.49), the word 'chaṭṭhī' is carried over into the two interpretive rules (paribhāsā-sutta) "tasminti niddiṭṭhe pubbassa" (1.1.66) and "tasmāt uttarassa" (1.1.67), and they establish the positing of the genitive as 'tasminti niddiṭṭhe pubbassa chaṭṭhī' and 'tasmāt uttarassa chaṭṭhī', so that where there is no specification of the genitive in a sutta, the genitive may be posited. Here, in Kaccāyana's grammar, however, even without another statement, where there is no specification of the genitive, the positing of the genitive is established by capacity alone. He shows the capacity with 'sattamīniddese,' etc. The connection is: even what is specified by another case is understood as genitive and enters into connection with the operation. For example, in "vagge vagganto," the word 'niggahītaṃ' which is carried over is understood as ending in the genitive. How? Because the locative 'vagge' has its purpose fulfilled, it causes the nominative case of 'niggahītaṃ' (whose purpose was fulfilled in the previous sutta, 1.38) to be posited as the genitive case. Thus it should be understood, as in 'sattamiyaṃ pubbasse.' When it is said, "This much is stated," since 'this' is not understood, he says 'kintaṃ,' etc. With 'yadāhi,' etc., he shows the order of the application by turns. "What is this that is said? That the statement is for the sake of restriction when there is the occasion of application by turns?" "Well, why is it not said that the statement is for the sake of refuting the non-understanding of the simultaneous arising of the prior and subsequent, an understanding which is authoritative due to the teacher's statement?" To this he says: 'yugapadupasiliṭṭhānaṃ,' etc. The connection is: simultaneous proximity is impossible. Whence? He says: "Because of the absence of the subsequent's proximity." Therefore, because of the absence of the simultaneous attainment of both, the statement is the sutta "saro lopo sare," etc. (1.26).

15. Pañca

15. Five

Avadhibhāvenāti ‘ato’ccādinā avadhittena, yassāti yo ādino, kāriyanti ‘ṭāṭe’ādikaṃ, pubbaparāpekkhattenāvisesāti yathā- ‘gāmā devadatto’ti vutte so tato pubbo parogeti viññāyatītyavadhibhāvassa pubbaparāpekkhattenāviseso, tathehāpi “ato yonaṃ ṭāṭe”ti (2-41) vuccamāne ato pubbesaṃ yonaṃ athavā paresanti pubbaparāpekkhattenāvadhibhāvassāvisesāti maññate, pure viyātyanena sattamiyanti ettha vuttaṃ niddesavacane kāraṇamatidisati, vuttiyaṃ ‘narānamere’ti ettha apavādavippaṭisedhe satiparattā ṭāṭeādesānaṃ pavattiṃ “ādissā”ti ettha vaṇṇayissāma, atha kimiminā vacanena nanu yato yattha pañcamī niddeso tattha sabbattha “mānubandho sarānamantā paro” (1-21) tyato ‘paro’tyanuvattetuṃ sakkāti tassānuvattitassa yonamiccanena sāmānādhikaraṇyā‘paresaṃ yonaṃ’tyayamattho viññāyate, tato pubbesaṃ pasaṅgoyeva natthīti, netadatthi, paroti tyanuvattamānaṃ ‘ato’ti pañcamyantena sambajjhamānaṃ na koci vāretā atthīti parato-kārato pubbesampi yonaṃ ṭāṭeādesā pappontīti vacaneneminā bhavitabbamevāti dassetumāha-‘vacane’ccādi, evañcarahi tadevodāharitabbaṃ, kiṃ ‘narānare’ tyudāhaṭanti ce, nesadoso, aññadatthaṃ kārīyamānamihā-pyatthavantaṃ hotīti, pubbako parihāroti byava hitanivattiyā [M 0.0035] pubbasutte vutto “saretopasilesikādhāro”ti parihāro, na sambhavatīti iha sattamiyā abhāvā na sambhavati, vacanānantaranti pāṇiniyānaṃ niddiṭṭhaggahaṇamiva byavahitanivattiyā suttantaraṃ, te hi “tasmātyuttarassā”tyettha (1-1-67) niddiṭṭhaggahaṇamanuvattiya tena pubbe viya byavahitanivattimpaṭipādenti. Anantaretivacanā paccāsattiyā nissayanaṃ viññāyate, katatthatāyāti vacanā jātiyātyāha- ‘paccāsatyā jātiṃ sannissāyā’ti jātiṃ sannissāya paccāsatyā karaṇabhūtāya nivattimāheti sambandho, iminā paccāsatti ñāyabyāpanañāyajātipadatthabyattipadatthesu paccāsattiñāyo jātipadatthoceha nissīyateti dasseti, na hi kevalaṃ jātiṃ nissāya byavahitanivatti vattuṃ sakkā, tathāhi yadettha paccāsattiñāyo na nissito, tadā byāpanañāyena byavahite cābyavahite cāsajjatīti jātiyā nissayane satyapi byavahitepi byāpyamānā jāti kena nivārīyate nāpi kevalaṃ paccāsattinnissāya byavahitanivatti vattuṃ sakkā, tathāhyasati jātisannissayena byattinissīyate, byattiyañca padatthe paṭilakkhiyaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ pavattatīti paccāsatti ñāyanissayanepyabyavahitampati yaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ bhinnaṃ tadabyavahite pavattaṃ, yampana byavahitampati bhinnaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ, tañca vacanappamāṇato mābhavatvassa byatthatāti byavahitepi pavattate, tasmā ubhopi nissāya nīyāti. Visayadassanappasaṅge visayidassanamatthabyattikāraṇanti vākyantogadhapadānamatthampaṭhamaṃ dassetvā pacchā samāsādikaṃ dassetuṃ ‘kato’tyādikamāraddhaṃ, jātilakkhaṇoti abyavahitattajātisabhāvo, ‘osadhyo’ti ettha sakāre akārā parassa dhakārena byavahitassa yossa viyāvasesānampi sabbhāvato vuttaṃ-‘yoppabhutīna’nti, jāti sāmaññaṃ, yāvati visayeti gavādike yattake visaye, kāmacārato visaya parisamattiyā diṭṭhantamāha-‘taṃ yathe’ti, bhojayetīti ettha bhojayeitīti padacchedo, katohi jātyattho kasiṇoti yasmā sakalo brāhmaṇa jātisaṅkhāto attho parisamatto, tasmāti attho, idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti- [M 0.0036] ‘yāva diṭṭhambhojaye’ti vutte vuttena (potthake) santāya sāmaññavutti brāhmaṇasaddappayogasāmatthiyā paccekambhojanakiriyā katā nāma hoti, yato kasiṇopi jātyattho parisamatto nāmāti. “Byañjane dīgharassā”ti (1-33) sutte byañjaneti sattamī pubbassa dīghādividhimhi caritattā “saramhā dve”ti (1-34) ettha saramhāti pañcamyaka tatthā, tato pañcamīniddesassa balīyattaṃ, tato “sattamiyaṃ pubbassa” “pañcamiyaṃ parassā”ti dvinnaṃ parassa samuṭṭhāpane ‘byañjane’ti sattamī parassa kāriya yogitāya atthato vibhattivipariṇāmena chaṭṭhībhāvena pariṇamatī… dvinnaṃ suttānaṃ vippaṭisedhe parassa balī yattāvāti etādisasāmatthiyasabbhāvato vuttaṃ-‘chaṭṭhīpakappanāpi pureviya sāmatthiyā’ti.

The term 'avadhibhāvena' means 'by means of the limit,' as in 'ato,' etc. 'Yassāti' refers to that which is the beginning; 'kāriyanti' denotes operations such as 'ṭāṭe,' etc. There is no distinction due to the expectation of what precedes or follows, just as when it is said, 'Devadatta from the village,' it is understood that he is either before or after it; thus, there is no distinction in the state of being a limit due to the expectation of what precedes or follows. Similarly here, when it is said, 'from this, the substitutions ṭā and ṭe for yonaṃ' (2-41), it is considered that there is no distinction in the state of being a limit due to the expectation of what precedes or follows, whether it be the 'yonaṃ' of those preceding 'ato' or of those following. By 'pure viya,' he indicates that the locative here is the cause in the directive statement. In the commentary, concerning 'narānamere,' we will explain under the rule 'ādissa' the application of the 'ṭāṭe' substitutions when there is a conflict with an exception, due to the strength of the subsequent rule. Now, what is the purpose of this statement? Is it not possible to carry forward 'paro' from the rule 'mānubandho sarānamantā paro' (1-21) wherever a fifth case is specified? If so, by its syntactic agreement with 'yonaṃ,' the meaning 'the yonaṃ of the subsequent ones' would be understood, and thus there would be no occasion for it to apply to the preceding ones. This is not so. Since there is nothing to prevent the carried-forward 'paro' from connecting with the fifth-case form 'ato,' the 'ṭāṭe' substitutions for 'yonaṃ' would also apply to those preceding 'ato.' To show that this statement is therefore necessary, he says 'vacane,' etc. If so, then that very case should be exemplified. Why is 'narānare' given as an example? This is no fault, for what is done for another purpose can also be meaningful here. The earlier remedy, stated in the previous rule 'saretopasilesikādhāro' for the prevention of application across an intervention, is not possible here due to the absence of the locative case. 'Vacanānantaram' refers to another rule for the prevention of application across an intervention, similar to the Pāṇinians' 'niddiṭṭhaggahaṇa.' For they, by carrying forward 'niddiṭṭhaggahaṇa' in the rule 'tasmādityuttarasya' (1-1-67), establish the prevention of application across an intervention as before. From the word 'anantare,' reliance on proximity is understood. Regarding 'katatthatāya,' he says it is due to the category, stating: 'relying on the category through proximity.' The connection is that it brings about cessation by means of proximity, which is the instrument, while relying on the category. By this, he shows that among the principles of proximity, pervasion, category-meaning, and individual-meaning, the principle of proximity and the category-meaning are relied upon here. Indeed, it is not possible to speak of the prevention of application across an intervention by relying solely on the category. For if the principle of proximity is not relied upon here, then by the principle of pervasion, it would apply to both the intervened and the non-intervened. Even when relying on the category, what is to prevent the category from pervading even the intervened? Nor is it possible to speak of the prevention of application across an intervention by relying solely on proximity. For in the absence of reliance on the category, one relies on the individual. And when the individual is the meaning of the word, the rule applies to what is perceived. Thus, even when relying on the principle of proximity, a rule that is distinct with respect to the non-intervened applies to the non-intervened. But a rule that is distinct with respect to the intervened would also apply to the intervened, by the authority of the statement, lest it be pointless. Therefore, it is determined by relying on both. In the context of showing the scope, showing the intended object is the cause of the clarification of meaning. Having first shown the meaning of the words contained in the sentence, he then begins with 'kato,' etc., to show compounds and so on. 'Jātilakkhaṇa' is the inherent nature of the category as being non-intervened. In 'osadhyo,' the statement 'yoppabhutīnaṃ' is made because of the existence of the remaining parts of 'yo,' which is intervened by 'dh' from the 'a' after 's.' 'Jāti' is generality. As far as the scope extends, in whatever domain, such as cows, etc., he gives an example for the completion of the scope by free application, saying: 'taṃ yathā.' In 'bhojayetīti,' the word division is 'bhojaye iti.' Because the meaning of the category is complete—since the entire meaning designated as the Brahmin category is complete—therefore is the meaning. This is what is said: when 'yāva diṭṭhaṃ bhojaye' is stated, by the power of using the word 'brāhmaṇa' with its general application, the act of feeding each one is considered done, because the entire meaning of the category is considered complete. In the rule 'byañjane dīgharassā' (1-33), the locative 'byañjane' has served its purpose in the operation of lengthening, etc., of the preceding. In 'saramhā dve' (1-34), 'saramhā' is in the fifth case, and it is stated there. Therefore, the specification in the fifth case is stronger. Thus, when there is a conflict between the two principles 'in the locative, of the preceding' and 'in the fifth case, of the subsequent,' the locative 'byañjane,' in order to be connected with the operation on the subsequent, is by implication transformed in meaning into the genitive case... In a conflict between two rules, the subsequent one is stronger. Due to the existence of such capacity, it is said: 'even the construing of the genitive is by capacity, as before.'

16. Ādissa

16. Having pointed out

Kiñci antassa sampattanti yaṃ ṭānubandhamanekavaṇṇaṃ na hoti, taṃ “chaṭṭhiyantasse” (1-17) tyantassa pattaṃ, kiñci sabbasseti “ṭānubandhānekavaṇṇā sabbasseti” (1-19) ṭānubandhamanekavaṇṇañca kāriyaṃ sabbassa pattaṃ. Yadantabhāvikāriyaṃtyādinā vacanaphalamupadassento ‘chaṭṭhīyantasse’tīmassāpavādo yaṃ yogoti dasseti, tassāyama pavādo hotu ṭānubandhādikāriyaṃ kathanti āha-‘ṭānubandhe’ccādi, vippaṭisedhāti apavādavippaṭisedhā, “chaṭṭhiyantasse’ti hi ussaggo, tassāpavādā “ādissa” “ṭānubandhānekavaṇṇā sabbasse”tyete, “ādissā”tīmassāvakāso ‘terasā’ti, “ṭānubandhānekavaṇṇā sabbassā”tīmassāvakāso ‘esu, anenā’ti, ihobhayampappoti “ato yonaṃ ṭāṭe” (2-41) “narānare” “atena” (2-108) “janenā”ti (tattha) “ṭānubandhānekavaṇṇā sabbasse”tīdampavattatīti tesamapavādānaṃ vippaṭisedhā sabbādeso bhavati. “Chaṭṭhiyantassā”ti dasasadde-ntassa pattopi tadapavādattā “ādissā”tiādibhūtassa dakārassa hotīti āha ‘dakārassaro’ti.

Some operation applies to the end: that which is not marked with 'ṭa' and does not consist of multiple letters, that applies to the end by the rule 'chaṭṭhiyantasse' (1-17). Some operation applies to the whole: an operation that is marked with 'ṭa' and consists of multiple letters applies to the whole by the rule 'ṭānubandhānekavaṇṇā sabbasse' (1-19). By showing the result of the statement with 'yadantabhāvikāriyaṃ,' etc., he shows that this rule is an exception to 'chaṭṭhīyantasse.' Let this be its exception. How does the operation concerning what is marked with 'ṭa,' etc., proceed? He says, 'ṭānubandhe,' etc. 'Vippaṭisedha' means a conflict of exceptions. For 'chaṭṭhiyantasse' is a general rule, and its exceptions are 'ādissa' and 'ṭānubandhānekavaṇṇā sabbasse.' The scope for 'ādissā' is 'terasā.' The scope for 'ṭānubandhānekavaṇṇā sabbassā' is 'esu, anenā.' Here, in the cases of 'ato yonaṃ ṭāṭe' (2-41), 'narānare,' 'atena' (2-108), and 'janenā,' both exceptions are applicable. There, 'ṭānubandhānekavaṇṇā sabbasse' prevails. Due to the conflict of those exceptions, a substitution of the whole occurs. Although application to the end of the word 'dasa' is obtained by 'chaṭṭhiyantassā,' because 'ādissa' is an exception to that, the operation applies to the initial 'da'-sound. Thus, he says, 'of the 'da'-sound.'

17. Chaṭṭhī

17. Sixth

Kotthonta [M 0.0037] saddasseccāha-‘antovasāna’miccādi, “vaṇṇassantassa”ti (1-1-52) sutte vaṇṇaggahaṇamantavisesanāyopadiṭṭhaṃ pāṇininā-antassa padassa vākyassa vā mābhavī’ti, iha tvanatthakaṃ vaṇṇaggahaṇaṃ byavacchejjābhāvāti dassetumāha-‘so ce’ tyādi, nanu brahmassāti visesanatthena vattumicchito mahābrahmasaddo chaṭṭhīniddiṭṭho nāmāti “brahmassu vā”ti (2-194) uādeso “chaṭṭhiyantassā”ti antabrahmasaddassa pappoti, tathā sati ‘na hi chaṭṭhī niddiṭṭhassa antaṃ padaṃ vākyaṃ vā sambhavatī’ti kasmā vuttanti, vuccate- na visesanatthenākkhepamattena mahābrahmasaddo chaṭṭhī niddiṭṭho nāma bhavatīti na brahmasaddassa sabbassādesappasaṅgo, mahābrahmasadde vā brahmasaddo atthīti tassāntassa uttaṃ vidhīyate.

He asks, 'What is the end of the sound?' and says, 'antovasāna' (the final part), etc. In the rule 'vaṇṇassantassa' (1-1-52), the taking of 'vaṇṇa' (letter) is taught by Pāṇini as a specification for the end, so that it does not apply to the end of a word or a sentence. Here, however, to show that the taking of 'vaṇṇa' is not meaningless due to the absence of anything to be excluded, he says, 'so ce' (if that), etc. Now, is it not the case that the word 'mahābrahma', intended to be stated with the specifying meaning 'of Brahma', is designated by the sixth case? Thus, the substitution of 'u' in 'brahmassu vā' (2-194) would apply to the end of the word 'brahma' by the rule 'chaṭṭhiyantassā' (of that which ends in the sixth case). If so, why is it said, 'For an end which is a word or a sentence is not possible for that which is designated by the sixth case'? It is answered: The word 'mahābrahma' is not designated by the sixth case merely by implication for the purpose of specification; therefore, the substitution for the whole of the word 'brahma' is not entailed. Or, the word 'brahma' exists within the word 'mahābrahma,' hence the substitution of 'u' is prescribed for its end.

18. Vānu

18. Vānu
