“Chaṭṭhiyantasse”tyanenevāvisesena vānubandhakāriyepyantassa siddhe kimatthoyamārambhotyāsaṅkiya ṭānubandhātyādinā vacanaphalamupadassento ‘bādhakabādhanattho-yamārambho’ti-vadati, tathāhi “chaṭṭhiyantasse”tyassa bādhako “ṭānubandhānekavaṇṇā sabbasse”ti, tassa ca “vānubandho”tyayaṃ yogo bādhakoti bādhakabādhanattho sampajjate, apaiccayamupasaggo vajjane nīvāraṇe, panayane vā vattateti apodyante ussaggalakkhaṇāni vajjīyante nīvārīyante apanīyante nenetyapavādo, suttekadesena suttamevopalakkhitanti antassa‘chaṭṭhiyantassā’ti suttassa apavādo antāpavādo, ussajjate nivattīyatyapavādenetyussaggo, ussaggāpavādakkamo panettha evaṃ veditabbo “chaṭṭhiyantasse”tyussaggo, tadapavādā “ṭānubandhānekavaṇṇā sabbassa” “ukānubandhādyantā” “mānubandho sarā namantā paro”ti, “ṭānubandhānekavaṇṇā sabbasse”tyussaggo, tada pavādā “vānubandho” “mānubandho sarānamantā paro”ti.

If, by 'of that which has the sixth case ending,' the action connected with 'vānu' is established for the ending without any specific qualification, what is the purpose of this undertaking? Having raised this doubt, and showing the result of the statement through 'ṭānubandha,' etc., it is said, 'This undertaking is for the purpose of obstructing an obstructor.' For the obstructor of 'of that which has the sixth case ending' is 'ṭānubandha with multiple letters for all,' and this application of 'vānubandha' obstructs that. Thus, the purpose of obstructing the obstructor is accomplished. The prefix 'apa' occurs in the sense of rejecting, preventing, or removing. Hence, that by which the characteristics of a general rule are rejected, prevented, or removed is an exception (apavāda). By a portion of the sutta, the sutta itself is indicated; thus, an exception to the sutta 'chaṭṭhiyantassa', which applies to the end, is an 'antāpavādo' (exception to the final part). That which is set aside or turned back by an exception is a general rule (ussagga). The order of general rules (ussagga) and exceptions (apavāda) here should be understood thus: 'Of that which has the sixth case ending' is the general rule. Its exceptions are: 'ṭānubandha with multiple letters for all,' 'ukānubandhādyantā,' 'mānubandho sarā namantā paro.' 'ṭānubandha with multiple letters for all' is the general rule. Its exceptions are: 'vānubandho,' 'mānubandho sarānamantā paro.'

19. Ṭānu

19. Ṭānu

Chaṭṭhīniddiṭṭhasseccādinā [M 0.0038] vacanārambhappayojanākhyānenāntādesāpavādo yaṃ yogoti bravīti, paccekamabhisambandhoti so ṭakārānubandho cādesotiādinā, kassa sabbassa bhavaticcāha-‘chaṭṭhī niddiṭṭhasse’ccādi, nanu ca ṭeādesopyanekavaṇṇoeva dvivaṇṇasamudāyattātyāsaṅkiyāha-‘upalakkhiye’ccādi, anubadhyate payoge asuyyamānepi payojanavasenānusarīyatītyanubandho, upadese yevopalakkhiya nivattatetyanenetaṃ dasseti ‘uccāritavināsinonubandhā’ti, upadese paṭhamuccāraṇe.

By 'of that which is specified by the sixth case ending,' etc., by explaining the purpose of commencing the statement, he says that this rule is an exception to the final substitution (antādesa). He says that there is a connection to each, and thus the 'ṭa' anubandha is also a substitute, etc. To the question, 'Of what does it replace the whole?', it is said, 'of that which is specified by the sixth case ending,' etc. Now, having raised the doubt that the 'ṭe' substitution also has multiple letters, being a combination of two letters, he says, 'it is to be indicated,' etc. An anubandha is so called because, even if not heard in usage, it is followed due to its purpose. By this, 'it is discerned in the initial instruction and then ceases to function,' it is shown that 'anubandhas perish upon utterance.' Upadesa means the first utterance.

20. Ñakā

20. Ñakā

Ādyantāti vutte kathamavayavātyayamattho labbhatī tyāha-‘ādyantasaddānami’ccādi, ādyantasaddānaṃ niyatavayavavācittā avayavassa cāvayavināmantarenā sambhavato sāmatthiyāvayavī lakkhīyati, chaṭṭhiyātyanuvuttito vāvayavāvayavisambandhesā chaṭṭhī, tāya niddiṭṭhassātyayamattho viññāyateti vuttiyaṃ-‘chaṭṭhīniddiṭṭhassā’ti (vuttaṃ), teneva paccayavidhimhi kūppaccayādayo na dosā bhavantīti, atoyevāti tadavayavācittatoyeva, taggahaṇeneti avayavaggahaṇena, katākatappasaṅgittāti otte katepi akatepi vukāgamassa pasaṅgato, bhūyattattā hi ottassa bhūggahaṇe sati katepi otte vukāgamena bhavitabbamakatepi tatova “katākatappa saṅgī yo vidhi sanicco”ti niccattā ottaṃ bādhitvā vukāgamo hoti, atha vukāgame pacchā tena na bhavitabbanti āha-‘antāvayave’ccādi.

When 'beginning and end' is stated, how is this meaning 'the whole' obtained? He says: 'by the words "beginning and end," etc.' Because the words 'beginning and end' denote fixed parts, and because a part cannot exist without a whole, the whole is indicated by capacity. Alternatively, from the continuation of 'by the sixth case', that sixth case is in the relation of part and whole; by that, the meaning 'of that which is specified' is understood. Thus, in the commentary, it is stated: 'of that which is specified by the sixth case ending.' For this very reason, in the prescription of suffixes, suffixes like 'kū' and others are not faults. From this very fact, namely, that it denotes its parts, by the taking of that (i.e., by the taking of the part), the state of 'being entailed whether done or not done' arises, because the augment 'vu' is entailed whether 'otta' is done or not. For, since 'otta' is dependent on 'bhū', when 'bhū' is taken, the augment 'vu' must occur whether 'otta' is done or not. Because of the principle 'A rule which is entailed whether another operation is done or not done is a constant rule', due to its constancy, having overridden 'otta', the augment 'vu' occurs. Then, lest it [otta] should not occur afterwards, after the augment 'vu', he says: 'at the end of the part,' etc.

21. Mānubandho

21. Mānubandho

Yadiniddhāraṇe chaṭṭhī antassāvisesitattā avisesena yato kutoci antato bānubandho paro siyā, na hi dutiyaṃ saraggahaṇamatthi, yenānto visesīyateccāha-‘niddhāraṇa’miccādi, kāraṇamāha-‘sutattā’ti, ‘sarāna’nti sutattāti attho, tena “sutānumitesusutasambandhobalavā”ti rundhatītetthadhakārassā numitassa [M 0.0039] maṃ na hotīti dīpeti, samāna jātiyasseva loke niddhāraṇappatīti hoticcāha-‘tathā hi’ccādi, yathā’kaṇhā gāvīnaṃ sampannakhīratamā’ti vutte avisesitattepi kaṇhāya kaṇhāgāvīyeva patīyate, tathehāpi sarānaṃ majjhe antātyantattena niddhāriyamāno samānajātiyo saroyeva patīyate, tena sarānaṃ yevāntāparo bhavissatīti bhāvo, visesanattoti “ñilatasse”ti (5-163) sutte assāti vutte ayameveti niyamābhāvā yassakassaci akārassa ñippatti, tenāniṭṭhappattīti lānusaṅgisseva assāti lassa yaṃ visesanattaṃ taṃ attho payojanamassa “kattarilo”ti (5-18) lakārassāti visesanattho lakāro, idhevāti imasmiṃ “mānubandho”tiādisutteyeva.

If this were the sixth case of determination, because the end is not specified, the anubandha 'ma' would occur after any end whatsoever without distinction—for there is no second taking of 'vowel' by which the end might be specified—he therefore says 'determination,' etc. He states the reason: 'because of being heard.' 'Of the vowels' means 'because of being heard.' By this he shows that, according to the principle 'between what is heard and what is inferred, the connection with what is heard is stronger', the inferred 'a' of the 'dha' in 'rundhati' does not become 'ma'. In the world, the understanding of determination is only of something of the same class—hence he says, 'for thus,' etc. Just as when it is said, 'The black one is the most abundant in milk among cows,' even though it is not specified as a cow, a black cow is understood. Similarly here too, that which is being determined as the end from among the vowels is understood to be a vowel, being of the same class. Therefore, the sense is that it will come after an end which is itself a vowel. Because it is a qualifier—as in the sutta 'ñilassa' (5-163), when 'assa' is stated, due to the absence of a restriction that it is only this one, the production of 'ñi' would occur for any 'a' whatsoever, leading to an undesired result. Therefore, so that 'assa' is connected only to 'la', the qualification of 'la' is its purpose, as in 'kattari lo' (5-18), where the 'la' has the meaning of a qualifier. This is stated here, in this very sutta, 'mānubandho,' etc.

22. Vippaṭi

22. Contradiction

Paroti vattate, so cāññādhikyaiṭṭhādyanekatthopi idha iṭṭha vācī daṭṭhabbo, kammabyatihāreghaṇiti kammabyatihāro kiriyāparivattanaṃ bhāvaviseso tasmiṃ ‘bhāvakārakesvaghaṇghakā”ti (5-44) sāmaññena vihitattā vippaṭisedhananti atthe ghaṇi vippaṭī sedho, tenāha-‘sāmaññe’ccādi, vippaṭisedhasaddassa atthamāha-‘aññamaññapaṭisedho’ti, saṃsiddhiyaṃ vattamānopi sidhi upasaggasambandhe nātthantarepi hotīti aññamaññavirodhotyattho, vippaṭisedhasaddassa loke virodhavācittena pasiddhattamāha ‘tathā hi’ccādinā, kathampana pamāṇabhūtassācariyassa vacanesu aññamaññavirodho sambhavatīccāsaṅkiya ubhinnaṃ sāvakāsatte sati sambhavati nāññathāti ‘dvinna’miccādi vuttigantho pavattoti vattuṃ ‘socā’tiādimāha aññamaññānajjhāsiteti aññamaññenānakkante apariggahiteti vuttaṃ hoti, anubhayatāginīti yo visayekadeso ubhayanna bhajate tasmiṃ anubhayabhāgini visayekadese, sāmaññavisayo dvinnaṃ vidhīnaṃ sādhāraṇo visayo, tattha pavattippasaṅge sati soca vippaṭisedho jāyatīti sambandho, iminā vippaṭisedhassa visayo pavattippasaṅgo visayavisayīnamabhedena sutte ‘vippaṭisedho’tivuttoti [M 0.0040] ‘dvinna’miccādinā vuttigantho racitoti dīpeti, paro hotī tividhidassitoti iminā yadi niyamo-bbhūpagato siyā, tadā ‘parovahotī’ti vadeyyāti dasseti, pāṇiniyā hi jātiyaṃ padatthe sakimeva lakkhaṇaṃ pavattatīti caritatthattā visayantare dvinnampi lakkhaṇānamappavattiyaṃ paraṃ pacchimaṃ kāriyanti vidhyatthamidaṃ vacanaṃ, byattiyantu padatthe latvādīnamiva pariyāyappasaṅge niyamatthanti paṭipannā, idha pana jātiyaṃ byattiyañca dvinnampi suttānamappavattiyameva vidhyatthamevidaṃ vacanaṃ, na niyamatthampīti paṭipādetumāha-‘tathāhi’ccādi, kāmacārato parisamāpīyateti sambandho, kāmato parisamāpanañcetissā sabbasmiṃ attano gocare avicchedabyāpanena pavattisabbhāvato. Kathampanekassāpi pavatti na bhaveyyātyāsaṅkiya kāraṇamāha‘ubhayampi’ccādi, hisaddo yasmātthe, yasmā ubhayampidamācariyavacanaṃ, tatoyeva pamāṇaṃ, abhimatakāriyavidhāne liṅgabhāvena saddikānumatattā(tesaṃ) vidhīnaṃ vidhāyakañca tasmāti attho. Pamāṇattā dvinnampi appattiyaṃ kāraṇamāha-‘anubhayabhāgimhi’ccādi, yato laddhāvakāsā tato samānabalāti, itisaddo hetumhi, viruddhācāti ettha itisaddaṃ datvā ‘anubhayabhāgimhi…pe… viruddhācāti dvinnaṃ vacanānaṃ pamāṇattā ubhinnampi appavattīti sambandho veditabbo. Samānabalānaṃ dvinnaṃ lokepi virodhittaṃ ekakkhaṇeyeva ubhinnampi kāriye appavatti ca dissatīti diṭṭhantamāha ‘lokece’tyādi, ettha ca pessassa (a)virodhatthino kāriye appavattiriva appavattiyeva (potthake) samānabalāna mubhinnaṃ vacanānaṃ kāriye appavattīti sukheno pamāsaṃsandanaṃ viññātabbaṃ.

The word 'paro' is used. And though it has many other meanings, such as 'other,' 'excess,' and 'desired,' here it should be understood as denoting 'desired.' In the sense of reciprocal action (kammabyatihāra), the suffix 'ghaṇ' is applied. Reciprocal action is a specific state of reciprocal activity. Since the suffix 'ghaṇ' is generally prescribed by the rule 'bhāvakārakesvaghaṇghakā' (5-44) for states and agents, in the sense of 'vippaṭisedhana' (mutual opposition), the suffix 'ghaṇ' yields 'vippaṭisedha.' Therefore, he says, 'generally,' etc. He states the meaning of the word 'vippaṭisedha' as 'mutual opposition.' Although the root `sidh` is present in `saṃsiddhi` (perfect accomplishment), in connection with a prefix, it does not take on a different meaning; thus, the meaning is mutual opposition. He states that the word 'vippaṭisedha' is well-known in the world as expressing opposition, saying 'for example,' etc. Having raised the question of how mutual opposition can occur in the statements of the teacher who is an authority, he states 'socā,' etc., to say that the commentary passage 'of two,' etc., proceeds because it occurs when both have scope, and not otherwise. It is said that 'mutually unoccupied' means 'not encroached upon or grasped by each other.' The phrase 'anubhayatāginī' (not belonging to both) refers to that part of the domain which does not belong to either; thus, 'in that part of the domain not belonging to either.' The common domain is the scope common to both rules. There, when the occasion for application arises, that very conflict arises—this is the connection. By this, it is shown that the scope of conflict is the occasion for application, and that in the sutta, 'conflict' is stated without distinguishing between the scope and that which has the scope; thus the commentary passage 'of two,' etc., is composed. By 'paro hotī tividhidassito' (the latter is shown in three ways), he indicates that if a restrictive rule had been accepted, then one would say 'parova hoti.' For according to Pāṇini, in the case of a word's meaning in a genus, a rule operates only once, and since it has thus fulfilled its purpose, in another domain, when the rules of both do not operate, the latter, the subsequent one, is to be applied—this statement is for the purpose of prescription. However, in the case of a word's meaning in an individual, as with 'latvādi,' when there is an occasion for alternation, it is understood to be for the purpose of restriction. Here, however, in the case of both genus and individual, this statement is only for the purpose of prescription, not for restriction, precisely when both suttas do not operate—thus, he states 'for example,' etc., to establish this. The connection is 'it is completed by free will.' And this completion by will is due to the inherent possibility of its operation through uninterrupted pervasion in all its own sphere. Having raised the question of how the operation of even one could not occur, he states the reason: 'both,' etc. The word 'hi' means 'because.' Because both are the teacher's statements, therefore they are an authority. And because they are accepted by grammarians as indicative in establishing the desired action, and are determiners of those rules, that is the meaning. Because they are authoritative, he states the reason for the non-application of both: 'in the part belonging to neither,' etc. Since they have obtained scope, therefore, they are of equal strength. The word 'iti' is used in the sense of a reason. Here, by inserting the word 'iti' after 'viruddhā ca,' the connection should be understood as follows: 'in the part belonging to neither... and because they are contradictory, due to the authority of both statements, there is non-operation of both.' He gives an example, saying 'in the world,' etc., that for two of equal strength, opposition is seen in the world, and the non-application of both actions is seen in a single moment. And here, just as there is non-application of action for a servant who desires no opposition, so too the non-application of action for both authoritative statements of equal strength—this comparison should be easily understood.

Jātipakkheyeva bhassakārena dvinnaṃ yugapadippattiyaṃ ‘latvādīnamiva’ pariyāyappasaṅgo vaṇṇito, tassāyuttattamupadassento āha ‘nacāpi’ccādi, bhinnavisayattāti dvinnaṃ vidhīnaṃ bhinnavisayattā. Abhinnavisayatte hi pariyāyakappanā yuttimatī, atoca latvādīnamabhinnavisayattampaṭipādayitumāha- ‘latvādayo hi’ccādi, anavayaveneti dhātu mattato vidhānenāvayavabyatirekasabbhāvato sabbadhātupariggahena, yattha yasmiṃ dhātvatthekadese pavattā samānā pavattā santo laddhāvakāsā [M 0.0041] siyuṃ tassekadesassa parihārenāpi pariccāgenāpi na vidhīyanteti sambandho, latvādīna mekakkhaṇe asambhavā ekasmiṃ kate satītaravacanāna mānatthakyappasaṅgāca pariyāyena bhavantīti yantaṃ yuttanti sambandho. Ihāti imasmiṃ yugapadippattiyaṃ, iha tathābhāvassa kāraṇamāha-‘sāvakā…pe… vacana’nti, tatthāti yugapadippattiyaṃ. Jātiyampadatthe “punappasaṅgavijānanā siddhaṃ, vippaṭisedhe yaṃ bādhitaṃ tambādhitamevā”tīmāsamubhinnaṃ paribhāsanampavattiṃ paṭipādento āha- ‘parasmiṃ ce’tyādi, parasminti iṭṭhe, paribhāsanampana ayamattho ‘punappasaṅgavijānanāti dvinnaṃ suttānamekatthappa saṅgasaṅkhāte vippaṭisedhe satiparamiṭṭhaṃ paṭhamaṃ hoti, hontena tena yadītarassa nimittopaghāto na kato tadā tassāpi punappasaṅgo tassa vijānanā siddhanti, vippaṭisedhe yathāvutte sati paṭhamaṃ hontena yaṃ suttaṃ bādhitaṃ tassa punappavattiyā yadi nimittaṃ natthi taṃ bādhitameve’ti. Byattiyampi vidhyatthamevidaṃ vacanaṃ, na niyamatthanti dassetumāha-‘byattiya’miccādi, evaṃ maññate ‘byattiyaṃ paṭilakkhiyaṃlakkhaṇappavattiyaṃ dvinnaṃ sādhāraṇaṃ ṭhānampati yāni vacanāni bhinnāni tesampi niravakāsattena tulyabalattā dvinnampaṭipattiyevasiyā, natu pariyāyappasaṅgo’ti. Byattiyampi yathāvuttānaṃ paribhāsānaṃ pavatti vuttavidhinevāti dassento ‘paribhāsānampi’ccādimāha.

In the context of genus, the commentator described the occasion for alternation, 'like latvādi,' for the simultaneous application of two rules. Showing its inappropriateness, he says 'nor indeed,' etc., because the two rules have different domains. For if they had the same domain, the postulation of alternation would be appropriate. Therefore, to establish that latvādi, etc., have the same domain, he says, 'for latvādi, etc.' 'Without parts' means encompassing all roots through prescription from the mere root, due to the exclusion of parts. The connection is that wherever, in some part of a root's meaning, they, being operative and having gained opportunity, are not prescribed by the omission or abandonment of that part. The connection is that since latvādi, etc., cannot exist simultaneously in a single moment, and since there would be the problem of meaninglessness for the other statements if one were applied, they occur by alternation; thus, that is appropriate. 'Here' means in this simultaneous application. Here, he states the reason for such a state: 'disciples... up to speech.' 'There' means in the simultaneous application. In the meaning of a word in a genus, establishing the application of these two maxims: 'through repeated application, knowledge is established; in a conflict, what is superseded remains superseded,' he says, 'if in the latter,' etc. In 'parasmiṃ,' it means 'in the desired.' The meaning of this maxim is this: 'through repeated application, knowledge is established'—when there is a conflict, designated as the application of two suttas to one object, the desired (latter) one comes first. If the condition of the other is not destroyed by that which occurs first, then for that too, repeated application and its knowledge are established. When a conflict as described occurs, if there is no condition for the re-application of the sutta that was superseded by the one that occurred first, then it remains superseded. To show that this statement is for the purpose of prescription even in the individual, not for restriction, he says, 'in the individual,' etc. Thus, one thinks: 'In the individual, in the application of a rule to its specific object, even those statements that differ regarding the common ground of the two, due to having no scope and being of equal strength, would certainly entail the application of both rules, not the occasion for alternation.' To show that even in the individual, the application of the stated maxims follows the prescribed method, he says, 'even of the maxims,' etc.

Jātiyampadatthe “vattamāneti anti, si tha, mi ma, te ante, se vhe, e mhe”ccādīnaṃ lakkhaṇānamekamekatthepi vattamāneti anti, vattamāne si tha iccādīnaṃ vākyekadesānaṃ gacchaticcādo gaccha siccādo ca lakkhiye sakimpavattiyā sabbasmiṃ sake visaye paṭhama majjhimapurisekavacanajāti parisamattāti caritatthattā tumhe gacchathāti ettha dvīhi dvinnaṃ purisāna mekakkhaṇe pavattiyaṃ na kassaci, byattiyampi paṭilakkhiyaṃ lakkhaṇāni bhijjantīti sādhāraṇaṃ ṭhānaṃ patibhinnehi lakkhaṇehi dvinnampekatthe-kakkhaṇe pavattiyaṃ na kassaci, tathā vuttanayeneva tiṇṇaṃ purisānamekakkhaṇe pavattiyanti sabbathā appavattiyaṃ sampattāyaṃ vacanamidaṃ, paro hotīti majjhimuttamaṃ bhavatīti adhippāyena ‘yathe’ccādinā vuttaṃ vuttiganthampañhamukhenā haritvā [M 0.0042] dassetuṃ ‘kvapanā’tiādimāha, nedamudāharaṇamamhaṃ manaṃ bhoseti-yato vippaṭisedhavisayamevedaṃ na hoti, kuto yato “vattamāneti anti”ccādippabhutīnaṃ vattamāneti anticcādīhi vākyekadesehi niddiṭṭhānameva pubbaparacchakkānaṃ purisavacanavisesavidhāyakena “pubbaparacchakkāna mekānekesu tumhāmha sesesu dvedve majjhimuttamapaṭhamā” (6-14) tīminā vākyāvayavena tumhāmhasesesu payujjamānesu appayujjamānesu vā yathākkamaṃ pubbacchakkānaṃ paracchakkānañca majjhimuttamapaṭhamānaṃ paccekaṃ dvedve vacanāni yathākkamaṃ bhavantīti ‘gacchatha gacchāmā’ti ettha ekakkhaṇe pavattiyeva natthi, dvinnampana sāvakāsāna mekakkhaṇe pavattiyeva hi vippaṭisedhoti, tathāpi vuttanayena vippaṭisedhappakappanāpi sakkā kātuntīdamudāhaṭaṃ siyāti daṭṭhabbaṃ, imissā pana paribhāsāya nirākulappavatti “ādissā” tīmissā vuttanayena veditabbā, katākatappasaṅgī yo vidhi, so nicco, yotvakateyevāyamaniccoti vuttaniccāniccesu antaraṅgabahiraṅgesu cātulyabalattā nāssa yogassa byāpāro, tathāhi niccāniccesu niccameva balavanti niccāniccānamatulyabalatā, antaraṅgabahiraṅgappakāra(mpana) upari “lopo”ti (1-39) sutte pakāsissāma.

In the meaning of the word 'jāti' (grammatical category), regarding the characteristics such as 'vattamāne ti, anti; si, tha; mi, ma; te, ante; se, vhe; e, mhe', even when each is present in a single meaning, and when parts of sentences like 'gacchati' and 'gaccha si' are observed, the grammatical category of person and number—third, second, and singular—is fully established in its entire domain by a single application, its purpose having been accomplished. Thus, in 'tumhe gacchatha', there is no simultaneous application for two persons at a single moment. Even in an individual instance, the characteristics are differentiated. Thus, it is a common principle that with differentiated characteristics, there is no simultaneous application for two [rules] in one meaning at one moment. Similarly, by the method stated, there is no application whatsoever for three persons at a single moment. When this statement is arrived at, with the intention that 'paro hoti' (what follows takes precedence) means the second and first persons take precedence, he states 'kvapanā' etc. to present the commentary text spoken of as 'yathe' etc. by way of a question. This example does not please our mind, for this is not a case for the rule of conflict (vippaṭisedha). Why? Because for the rules beginning with 'vattamāne ti, anti', which are indicated by parts of sentences such as 'vattamāne ti, anti', the prescription of the specific persons and numbers for the first and second sets of six endings is established by the sentence fragment 'pubbaparacchakkānaṃ ekānekesu tumhāmhasesesu dvedve majjhimuttamapaṭhamā' (6-14). This states that when 'tumha' and 'amha' are used or not used, respectively, for the first and second sets of six endings, the second, first, and third persons each have two numbers respectively. Therefore, in 'gacchatha gacchāma', there is no simultaneous application. For, conflict is indeed the simultaneous application at one moment of two [rules] that both have scope. Nevertheless, it should be understood that even the postulation of conflict can be made by the method stated, and thus this example might be cited. However, the unimpeded application of this maxim is to be understood by the method stated for 'ādissā'. A rule that has the potential to apply to both what has been done and what has not been done is permanent; that which applies only to what has not been done is impermanent. Among the aforementioned permanent and impermanent rules, and internal and external rules, because of their unequal strength, this principle has no application. Indeed, between permanent and impermanent rules, the permanent is stronger; thus, the permanent and impermanent have unequal strength. The nature of internal and external rules, however, we will explain later in the sutta 'lopo' (1-39).

23. Saṅketo

23. Convention

Vacanārambhassa phalamāha-‘anubandhoti yaṃ vuttaṃ’tyādi, vuttiyaṃ “yonavayavabhūto saṅketo”ti sāmaññena vuttepi “bhāsissaṃ māgadhaṃ saddalakkhaṇa”nti saddalakkhaṇā bhidhānappakaraṇato saddassānavayavabhūtoti viññāyateti dassetumāha-‘kassa’tyādiltuppaccaye lakāro udāharaṇaṃ, pakatiyādi samudāyassātiādivākyassa sāppāyamatthaṃ vivarituṃ ‘evamaññate’ccādi vuttaṃ, keci saddasatthakārāti pāṇiniṃ sandhāyāha, vacananti “tassa lopo”ti (1-3-9) vacanaṃ, payogāsamavāyitāti kattāiccādippayoge asamavāyitā appayogitāti adhippāyo, evampissa lopo vaseyo… anupubbo bandhivināsatthoti āhu uccāritapadhaṃsittā [M 0.0043] anubandhyate vinassatetyanubandhoti imāya sadda byuppattiyāvasena.

He states the result of commencing the statement: 'what is called anubandha', etc. In the commentary (vutti), although it is generally stated, 'the convention which is a component part', he says this to show that it is understood as 'not a component part of the sound' from the treatise designating the characteristics of sound, as in 'I will speak the Māgadha language with its sound characteristics.' The letter 'la' in the suffix 'tu' is an example, as in 'kassa' etc. The statement beginning with 'evamaññate' is said to explain the suitable meaning of the phrase beginning 'of the collection of the base, etc.' By 'some grammarians' he refers to Pāṇini. 'Vacana' refers to the rule 'tassa lopo' ('its elision'). 'Payogāsamavāyitā' means non-concomitance, that is, non-usage, in a form such as 'kattā'; this is the intention. Thus, its elision is better... They say it has the meaning of being attached and disappearing. Because it is destroyed upon being uttered, it is called 'anubandha' (that which is attached and perishes), according to this etymology of the word.

24. Vaṇṇa

24. Letter

‘Atenā’ti (2-108) ettha atoti rassabyattiniddeso vā siyā rassajātiniddeso vā sakalanissayabyāpī atthajāti niddesovā, tattha rassabyattiniddese sati buddhasiddhādīsu yatthakatthaci akāro gayhateti neṭṭhappasiddhi… kesañci asijjhanato, rassa jātiniddese pana buddhasiddhādisabbākārantānaṃ lakkhaṇikagavādyakā rantānañcākāro gayhatīti sabbathā iṭṭhappasiddhi, nāñño dīgho byattantarattāti nāniṭṭhappatti ākārato nāssenābhāvā, tasmā atoti rassajātiniddese nissite sabbamidamiṭṭhaṃ nipphajjatīti nātthajāti nissīyate, na rassabyattica, “yuvaṇṇāname oluttā”ti (1-29) ādīsu pana rassabyattiyā rassajātiyā vā niddese ‘tassedaṃ nopeti’ccādīsu eoādikamiṭṭhaṃ katthaci bhaveyya, na sabbattha, sabbattha vā bhaveyya ‘vāteritaṃ samonā’tiādīsu byattanta rattā, tasmā sabbathā iṭṭhappasiddhiyā ittajātyādi nissīyate, athavā vaṇṇuccāraṇampati kesañci vaṇṇuppattiṭṭhānānaṃ uccanīcatadubhaya saṃhāravasena vaṇṇavisesuppatti dassanato tesaṃ vasena rassa byattiniddese rassajātiniddese vā vuttanayena iṭṭhāniṭṭhappattiyaṃ sabbathā sabbathā iṭṭhappasiddhiyā ittajātyādi nissīyate, tattha vaṇṇa parena savaṇṇaggahaṇaṃ niyamituṃ vacanamidamāraddhanti ‘sabbatthevā’tiādinā vacanārambhaphalamāha, sabbatthevāti sabbasmiṃyeva suttappadese. Nanu sayañcāti vuttepi pariyattaṃ, na hyaññaṃ rūpā sayamatthi, aññaṃ vā (saya)to rūpanti siddhepyevaṃ sati atthettha paro koci visesoti ñāpetuṃ sañca rūpa’nti vuttikāro āhāti sambandho, rūpassa visesitabbattā ‘sañca rūpa’nti vuttiyaṃ niddisīyamānattā ca rūpanti viññāyatīti ‘sañca gayhatī’ti vuttaṃ, saṃrūpaggahaṇāyāpisaddaṃ karoto-dhippāyo-yanti vattumāha-‘aññathe’ccādi, aññathāti aññenappakārena saṃrūpaggahaṇāya apisaddābhāveti adhippāyo, aññapadattheti [M 0.0044] aññapadattha samāsavisaye, guṇībhūtassāti appadhānabhūtassākāre kārādino, samāsena vuttattā padhānatū tattepi guṇo bhavati aññapadattho-kārekārādi vidhāya kattā, vidhīyamāno savaṇṇova padhānaṃ… idamatthitāya tappavattiyāti. Nanu vuttiyamapisaddassātthaṃ vadatā sayañceti vattabbaṃ, “tathā sayamattanī”ti nighaṇḍuto sayañca-ttākārekārādiñca gayhatītyamattho sambhāvīyatīti codanampanasi nidhāya ‘sañca rūpa’nti vadanto sādhippāyāruḷhaṃ kiñci atthavisesaṃ pakāsetuṃ tathevāhāti dassetuṃ vuttaṃ-‘sayañce’tyādi, “dhanaññātīsu saṃsaddo, tathāttattaniyesupī”ti nighaṇḍuvacanato ‘sa’nti attāpi gayhati, ko so saddarūpaṃ sādhāraṇaṃ, ‘sa’nti attaniyampi, kintaṃ saddāna masādhāraṇaṃ saddarūpaṃ, tathā sati attaniyaṃ rūpaṃ nāmāttasaṅkhātasaddasambandhīti āha-‘saṃrūpaṃ saddānamasādhāraṇaṃ rūpa’nti, etañca idantīminā sambandhitabbaṃ, asādhāraṇanti asādhāraṇaṃ saddarūpaṃ, sati sambhave byabhicāre ca visesanassa sātthakatāya asādhāraṇanti rūpaṃ visesatā sādhāraṇassāpi sambhavo vuttoyeva nāmāti āha-‘duvidhaṃ hi’ccādi, kintaṃ sādhāraṇamasādhāraṇañcarūpanti sāmaññena rūpaṃ niddisitumāha-‘tatthā’tiādi, tatthāti niddhāraṇe sattamī, saddānanti sātthakaniratthakānaṃ yesaṃkesañci saddānaṃ, taṃtaṃ saddattādīhi tesaṃtesaṃ buddha aiādīnaṃ saddānaṃ saddattādi, ubhayattha ādisaddena attho saṅgahito, tena sādhāraṇaṃ saddarūpamattharūpaṃ tathā-sādhāraṇanti catubbidhaṃ saṃrūpanti dasseti, catūsupi cetesvasādhāraṇassa saddarūpassevopānaṃ dassetumāha-‘tatthā’tiādi, sādhāraṇarūpabyudāsenāti sādhāraṇarūpassa pariccāgena, upādiyanto rūpameva saddassasaṃ, nātthoti ca dassetīti sambandho, ca saddo panettha ‘idaṃ dassetī’ti heṭṭhā vuttaṃ samuccinoti, asādhāraṇassevopādiyane kāraṇamāha-‘tanta’miccādi, itaranti ye saṃkesañci saddānaṃ saddattādi, parassāpīti aññassa yassakassaci saddassāpi, iti idaṃ, patitaṃ pasiddhaṃ, ettha pana itisaddo hetumhi, yasmā idaṃ yathāvuttaṃ pasiddhaṃ tasmā pubbācariyaparamparāyāgato padesato [M 0.0045] upādiyantoti pakataṃ, saṃsaddavisesanasāmatthiyena asādhāraṇarūpopādiyanepi asādhāraṇaṃ saddarūpamevopādīyati nāsādhāraṇamattharūpaṃ… iminā vakkhamānakāraṇatā tāya (potthake) vasenāti āha-‘saddasse’ccādi, āsannaṃ…saddato saddabhāvasā naññattā, vipariyayatoti vipariyāsena anāsanna bhāvenāti attho, cakkhuvisayopi hi attho kathaṃ sotavisayasaddassa na āsanno saṃrūpambhavitumarahatīti, kāraṇantaramāha-‘aheyyattācā’tiādi, aheyyattāti apariccajanīyattā, idampi niccasambandhitte kāraṇavacanaṃ, taṃ saddarūpaṃ, niccasambandhīti nirantarasaṃyogī, vipariyayatoti heyyattā, tathāhiccādinā atthassa heyyattaṃ bodheti, aparaṃ kāraṇamāha-‘asādhāraṇañca rūpaṃ’tyādinā, sādhāraṇo pariyāya saddānaṃ, paccetabbattāti viññātabbattā, idāni kāraṇattayaṃ samodhānetvā imehi kāraṇehi rūpameva saddassa saṃnāma, nātthoti niyametvā dassetuṃ ‘tadeva’ntiādi āraddhaṃ, tadevanti yasmā evaṃ, taṃ tasmāti attho, sarūpappadhāneti “gossā vaṅa” (1-32) tyādo gossātyādike sarūpappadhāne.

Here, regarding 'Atenā' (2-108): 'ato' may be an indication of the short vowel as an individual instance (byatti), or an indication of the short vowel as a class (jāti), or an indication of the class of meaning (atthajāti) that pervades all bases. Therein, if it is an indication of the short vowel as an individual instance, wherever the 'a'-sound is taken—such as in 'buddhasiddha', etc.—the desired outcome is not achieved, because for some it is not accomplished. But if it is an indication of the short vowel as a class, the 'a'-sound of all words ending in 'a' like 'buddhasiddha', etc., and of characteristic words ending in 'a' like 'gavādi', etc., is taken, thus the desired outcome is achieved in every way. There is no other long vowel, due to being a different individual instance, so an undesired result does not occur, because of the absence of elision of 'ā'. Therefore, when 'ato' is based on the indication of the short vowel as a class, this entire desired outcome is accomplished. It is not based on the class of meaning, nor on the individual instance of the short vowel. However, in cases like 'yuvaṇṇāname oluttā' (1-29), whether the indication is of the short vowel as an individual instance or as a class, in phrases like 'tassedaṃ nopeti', etc., the desired 'e', etc., might occur somewhere, but not everywhere. Or, it might occur everywhere, as in 'vāteritaṃ samonā', etc., due to being a different individual instance. Therefore, for the achievement of the desired outcome in every way, that class of sound, etc., is resorted to. Alternatively, with respect to the pronunciation of sounds, due to the production of specific sounds by means of the high, low, or combined articulation of the places of origin of sounds for some, based on them, whether the indication is of the short vowel as an individual instance or as a class, in the manner stated, there is the occurrence of desired and undesired outcomes. For the achievement of the desired outcome in every way, that class of sound, etc., is resorted to. Therein, to regulate the taking of a homogeneous sound by a following sound, this statement is begun. By 'sabbatthevā', etc., he states the fruit of beginning the statement. 'Sabbatthevā' means in every single passage of the suttas. Now, even when 'sayañca' is stated, it is sufficient. For no other form exists by itself, nor does form exist apart from itself. Even when this is established, to make known that there is some other distinction here, the commentator says 'sañca rūpa'; this is the connection. Because the form is to be specified, and because it is indicated in the commentary as 'sañca rūpa', it is understood as 'rūpa'. Thus, it is said, 'sañca is taken'. To state the intention of the one who uses the word 'api' for the inclusion of its own form, he says 'aññathe', etc. 'Aññathā' means in another way; the intention is 'in the absence of the word 'api' for the inclusion of its own form'. 'Aññapadatthe' means in the domain of a compound having another term as its referent. 'Guṇībhūtassa' means of the subordinate, of the non-primary 'a'-sound, 'e'-sound, etc. Because it is stated by a compound, even though it is primary, it becomes subordinate. The agent which prescribes the 'a'-sound, 'e'-sound, etc., is the referent of the other term. What is prescribed, the homogeneous sound alone, is primary... because its operation is for the sake of this meaning. Now, should it not be said 'sayañceti' by the one stating the meaning of the word 'api' in the commentary? From the lexicon 'tathā sayamattanī', the meaning that 'sayañca'—one's own 'a'-sound, 'e'-sound, etc.—is taken, is considered possible. Having set aside this objection, in saying 'sañca rūpa', he reveals some special meaning that is intended, to show that it is just so. Thus, it is said, 'sayañce', etc. From the lexicon statement 'dhanaññātīsu saṃsaddo, tathāttattaniyesupī', the word 'saṃ' also takes the meaning of 'self' (attā). What is that? The common form of a sound. 'Sa' also means one's own (attaniya). What is that? The uncommon form of sounds. Thus, 'one's own form' (attaniyaṃ rūpaṃ) is that which is related to the sound designated as 'self' (atta). He says: 'saṃrūpaṃ is the uncommon form of sounds'. And this should be connected with 'idaṃ'. 'Asādhāraṇaṃ' means the uncommon form of a sound. Since a specification is meaningful when there is possibility and deviation, the form is specified as 'uncommon' because the possibility of a common one has also been stated. Hence, he says, 'duvidhaṃ hi', etc. What is that common and uncommon form? To indicate the form in general, he says, 'tatthā', etc. 'Tatthā' here is the seventh case in the sense of determination. 'Of sounds' means of any sounds whatsoever, whether meaningful or meaningless. The 'soundness', etc., of those respective sounds, 'buddha', 'a', etc., is their 'soundness', etc. In both places, the meaning is included by the word 'ādi'. Thus, it shows that 'saṃrūpa' is of four kinds: common sound-form, meaning-form, and likewise uncommon sound-form and meaning-form. Among these four, to show the inclusion of only the uncommon sound-form, he says, 'tatthā', etc. 'Sādhāraṇarūpabyudāsena' means by the exclusion of the common form. Taking it, he shows that the form is only the sound's own, not the meaning; this is the connection. The word 'ca' here conjoins what was stated below, 'idaṃ dassetī' (it shows this). He states the reason for taking only the uncommon: 'tantaṃ', etc. 'Itaraṃ' means the 'soundness', etc., of any sounds whatsoever. 'Parassāpi' means of any other sound whatsoever. 'Iti idaṃ, patitaṃ pasiddhaṃ' means this is established, well-known. Here, however, the word 'iti' is in the sense of reason. Because this, as stated, is well-known, therefore, it is taken partially according to the region, as has come down through the lineage of ancient teachers; this is what is under discussion. By the power of the specification of the word 'saṃ', even when taking the uncommon form, only the uncommon sound-form is taken, not the uncommon meaning-form... by means of this reason that will be stated, he says, 'saddasse', etc. 'Āsannaṃ' (proximate)... because from the sound, there is no otherness due to its nature as sound. 'Vipariyayato' means by the opposite, by the state of not being proximate. For how can the meaning, which is an object of the eye, not be proximate to the sound, which is an object of the ear, so as to be able to become its own form? He states another reason: 'aheyyattācā', etc. 'Aheyyattā' means because it is not to be abandoned. This too is a statement of the reason for the constant connection. That sound-form is constantly connected, meaning it has uninterrupted conjunction. 'Vipariyayato' means by the opposite, because it is to be abandoned. By 'tathāhi', etc., he explains the abandonability of the meaning. He states another reason: 'asādhāraṇañca rūpaṃ', etc. The common is a synonym of sounds, because it is to be cognized. Now, having combined the three reasons, by these reasons, it is determined that the form alone is the 'saṃ' of a sound, not the meaning. To show this by determining, 'tadeva', etc., is begun. 'Tadeva' means 'since it is so, therefore'. 'Sarūpappadhāne' means in cases where the inherent form is primary, such as in 'gossā vaṅa' (1-32), in 'gossa', etc.

25. Ntu

25. Ntu

Ntusutiyā jantvādīnampi “ntantūnaṃnto yomhi paṭhame” (2-215) tyādinā gahaṇappasaṅge jātiyamabhippasaṅgabādhanatthaṃ byattiyaṃ vantvādi sambandhīnamupādānattamidamāraddhaṃ “vantvavaṇṇā” (4-79) “tametthassattīti mantu” (4-78) “kattari bhūte ktavantu ktāvī” (5-55) ti vihitā vantvādayo nāma.

Regarding the sutta on Ntu, when there is the contingency of taking even 'jantu', etc., by the rule 'ntantūnaṃnto yomhi paṭhame' (2-215), this is begun in order to prevent the contingency of over-application to the class (jāti), for the inclusion of those related to 'vantu', etc., as individual instances (byatti). 'Vantu', etc., are namely those prescribed by 'vantvavaṇṇā' (4-79), 'tametthassattīti mantu' (4-78), and 'kattari bhūte ktavantu ktāvī' (5-55).

Iti moggallānapañcikāṭīkāyaṃ sāratthavilāsiniyaṃ

Thus in the Sāratthavilāsinī, the sub-commentary on the Moggallāna-pañcikā.

Paribhāsādhikāro samatto.

The section on Definitions (Paribhāsādhikāro) is finished.

Saralopādi vaṇṇanā

Exposition on the Elision of Vowels, etc.

26. Saro

26. Vowel

Ādhāravisesāpassayananti opasilesikādhāravisesassa nissayanaṃ, opasilesikādhāraṃ vinā ādhārantare gahite sati vacanantaraṃ [M 0.0046] suttantaraṃ vinā byavahitanivatti kātuṃ na ca sakkāti sambandho, kecīti buddhappiyācariyādayo dasseti, te hi yadi vaṇṇena kālena vā byavadhānepi sandhi bhaveyya tadā sareti nimittasso pādānaṃ niratthakaṃ bhaveyyāti sareti nimittopādānasāmatthiyenānena vaṇṇādibyavadhāne no sandhīti maññamānā ‘nimitto’ccādikaṃ vākyamāhu, tadayuttanti tehi’nimitto’ccādinā yaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ ayuttanti attho, ayuttatte kāraṇaṃ byabhicārasabbhāvena sāmatthiyābhāvoyevāti byabhicārandassetvā sāmatthiyābhāvandassetumāha-‘avasāne,ccādi, kāriyābhāvepīti ettha na kevalaṃ ‘idameva saccaṃ, sumanā bhavantu athopi’tyādo vaṇṇakālabyavadhāneyeva, atha kho ‘ete na saccena suvatthi hotū’tyādo avasāne ‘pamādo maccuno padaṃ’ tyādo anta bindu saṅkhātanimittantare vā kāriyābhāvepi nimitto pādānassa sātthakatoti apisaddassattho, sātthakatoti bhāvappaccayalopena bhāvappadhānavasena vā vuttaṃ, sātthakattatoti vuttaṃ hoti, aññathā nimittopādānameva sātthakaṃ nāmāti ‘nimitto pādānassa sātthakato’ti na yujjati, ayametthādhippāyo ‘avasāne nimintare vā kāriyābhāvena byabhicārasabbhāvā aññathānupapattilakkhaṇaṃ sāmatthiyaṃ natthi, nimittantubyavadhānepi catthi, yathā’dārunimittaṃ vanopasaṅkamana’nti tasmā vaṇṇakālabyavadhānepi sareti nimitte sati lopakāriyaṃ pappote vā’ti. Luppatīti ‘tatrime’ccādinā kathanakāle na dissatīti attho, adassanamattameva hi lopo, aññathā ‘tatrā’disaddarūpābhāvappattiyā atthappatīti kārittamesaṃ na siyāti, paṭhamāya niddiṭṭho… vuttattā kammassa, sarassāti vadeyya… bhāve khādippaccayena avuttakammattā, ihāti iminā satthantare bhāvasādhanavasena gahaṇaṃ vibhāveti, gantha lāghavo… sarassa lopoti vā lopaṃ pappotīti vā avattabbattā, saroti paṭhamāya niddiṭṭhattā saro lopo nāma hotīti saṅkāpi siyāti āha-‘na ce’ccādi, ihāti imasmiṃ sutte, honticcādopi pubbasaralope hanticcādikampi siyātyāsaṅkiyāha-‘soce’ccādi, ussaggato āgato sambhūto tassa vā ayaṃti ossaggiko pubbalopo[M 0.0047], tassa bhāvo ossaggikattaṃ, ossaggikattā pubbalopassa kāriyantarehi paralopādīhi apavādavidhīhi ābādhito eva, so ca pubbalopo hotīti sambandho, “paro kvacī”ti (91-27) kvaciggahaṇena pubbaparalopānaṃ tulyabalattābhāvā yathā gamappattito paralopassāpavādarūpattaṃ, ajjhāsiteti paviṭṭhe, na hoti… paralopāpavādena bādhitattā, tehīti paralopādīhi, sabbathā muttavisayo saddhindriyanti, vikappena muttavisayo late vāti.

“Reliance on a special basis” means dependence on the specific adhering locative (opasilesikādhāra). Without the adhering locative, when another basis is taken, it is impossible to prevent interruption without another word or another rule; this is the connection. “Some” indicates the teacher Buddhappiya and others. They state the sentence beginning with ‘nimitto’ thinking that if sandhi were to occur even with an interruption by a sound or by time, then the employment of the sign ‘sare’ would be meaningless; therefore, by the very power of employing the sign ‘sare,’ there is no sandhi when there is an interruption by a sound and so forth. “That is inappropriate” means that what was said by them with ‘nimitto,’ etc., is inappropriate. The reason for its inappropriateness is simply the absence of capability due to the presence of deviation. To show the deviation and to show the absence of capability, it is said: “at the end,” etc. “Even in the absence of the effect”: here, the meaning of the word ‘api’ is that the employment of the sign is meaningful not only in cases like ‘idameva saccaṃ, sumanā bhavantu athopi,’ where there is an interruption by a sound and time, but also in cases like ‘ete na saccena suvatthi hotū’ at the end, or in the absence of the effect in another sign known as the final dot, as in ‘pamādo maccuno padaṃ.’ The word ‘sātthakato’ is stated either through the elision of the abstract suffix or by way of the predominance of the abstract sense; thus, ‘sātthakattato’ (meaningfulness) is what is said. Otherwise, the employment of the sign itself is indeed meaningful, so the statement ‘the employment of the sign is made meaningful’ would not be fitting. This is the intention here: because of the presence of deviation due to the absence of the effect at the end or in another sign, there is no capability characterized by invariable concomitance (aññathānupapatti). But it exists even with an interruption by a sign, as in ‘the sign of wood for entering the forest.’ Therefore, even with an interruption by a sound or time, when the sign ‘sare’ is present, it attains the effect of elision. “It is elided” means that at the time of stating ‘tatrime,’ etc., it is not seen. For elision is merely non-appearance. Otherwise, due to the non-existence of the word-forms ‘tatrā,’ etc., their function of causing the understanding of the meaning would not exist. It is indicated by the first case… because the object has been stated. One might say ‘sarassa’… because the object is unstated by the khādi-suffix in the sense of state. “Here,” by this, he clarifies the understanding in another treatise by way of establishing the abstract sense. For the sake of textual brevity… because ‘elision of the vowel’ or ‘it attains elision’ should not be said. Because ‘saro’ is indicated by the first case, the doubt might arise that the vowel itself is called elision; thus, he says: “na ce,” etc. “Here” means in this rule. Suspecting that with the elision of the preceding vowel, ‘honti,’ etc., could also become ‘hanti,’ etc., he says: “so ce,” etc. The preceding elision is ‘ossaggika’ (general) because it comes from, arises from, or belongs to a general rule. Its state is ‘ossaggikattaṃ’ (generality). Due to its generality, the preceding elision is indeed obstructed by other operations, such as the elision of the following vowel, etc., which are rules of exception. And that preceding elision occurs; this is the connection. In “paro kvacī” (91-27), by the inclusion of ‘kvaci,’ because of the absence of equal strength of the preceding and following elisions, the following elision has the nature of an exception, just as it is obtained. “ajjhāsite” means when entered. It does not occur… because it is obstructed by the exception of the following elision. “tehi” means by the following elision, etc. “saddhindriyaṃ” has its sphere completely released. Its sphere is released optionally, like a creeper.

27. Paro

27. The following

Itisaddo idamatthe, kvaci lopanīyo hotīti idaṃ vacanaṃ dīpetīti sambandho, kinti āha-‘payogānusārita’nti, kassāti āha-‘kāriyassa paralopassā’ti, kena hetunāti āha ‘kvaciggahaṇenā’ti, katthāti āha-‘iha imasmiṃ sutte’ti, tenāti tena payogānusāritādīpanena, yathāpayoganti āgamapayogānatikkamena, niccaṃ pakkhevā paralopo siyāti honticcādo niccaṃ, latāvātiādīsu pakkhe vā paralopo bhaveyya, evaṃ maññate “kasminti atthe kvāti nipphannenāniyamavuttinā aniyamatthasseva visesakato vacane sabbatthevāniyatatthavuttittā kvacisaddo-yaṃ yathāgamaṃ niccamaniccamasantañca vidhiṃ dīpeti, tattha honticcādiko nicca pakkho paralopasseva visayo, latāvātiādiko aniccapakkho ubhayasādhāraṇattā pubbalopassāpi visayoti iminā niccaṃ pakkhe vā paralopo hoti, asantapakkho pana saddhindriyantiādiko pubbalopasseva visayo sabbathānena pariccattattā”ti, tīsupi cetesu pana pakkhesu niccāniccapakkhesu yevassāpavādarūpatā… pubbalopassa sabbathā honticcādo nivārakattā vā vidhāyakattā vā paralopassa, na tvasantapakkhe… pubbalopasseva sabbathānena dinnā vasarattā, lokaggotiādi tu kvacisaddassa payogānusāritā dīpakattā nicce asantevāpi vidhimhi dīpite paralopena vā nipphajjatīti neṭṭhabyāghāto, evaṃ tāva kvaciggahaṇe sabbathāniṭṭhaparihārena iṭṭhappasiddhi [M 0.0048] siyā, tadabhāvekathanti tadabhāve virodhamāha-‘aññate’ccādi, pariyāyena bhavantīti kvaciggahaṇābhāve ‘paro’ti suttaṃ siyā tathā sati suttadvayamekavisayaṃ tulyabalañca siyā, tattha vippaṭisedhābhāvā pamāṇabhūtānamācariya (vacanā)naṃ niratthakatā mā bhavīti vārena bhavantīti attho, itīti iminā pariyāyabhavanakāraṇena, pakkheyeva siyāti latāvātiādīsu pubbalope pariyāyappavatte pariyāyena paralopassāppavattito latāvāti pakkheyeva paralopo bhaveyya, honticcādo niccaṃ na siyāti sambandho, tañcāti taṃ pariyāyabhavanañca, kho vākyālaṅkāre, paṭipadanti padampa dampati hoti, nekadesaparihārenāpi, tenāha ‘na katthacī’ti, iminā idaṃ dīpeti “sabbattha vikappappasattiyā hanti, saddhandriyaṃtyādikaṃ “na dvevā”ti (1-28) suttepi hanticcādikañcāniṭṭharūpampi sampajjatī”ti. Nacevamiṭṭhanti evamidaṃ yathāvuttaṃ vikappavidhānaṃ saddalakkhaṇaññūhi nevābhimatanti attho, tameva sādheti ‘paralopo hi’ccādinā, athā niccapakkhe vā paralope kate-nena pariccattaṭṭhāne ussaggappavattiyā latāva latevāti rūpadvayaṃ sampajjati tasmā payogānusāritādīpakena kvacisaddeneva honti saddhindriyaṃ latāva latevāti payoga sambhavopi, tathāpi aniccapakkhe latāivāti tatiyarūpappasiddhiyā pariyāyena bhavitabbanti parikappeti ‘nanu cetyādinā, atha “paro kvacī’ti kvaciggahaṇe sati apa(vādarūpa)ttā kathampariyāyappavattīti manasi nidhāyāniccapakkhe pariyāyappavattidīpanatthaṃ “na dvevā”ti suttitanti apavāde rūpattayepi pariyāyappavattiyaṃ dosābhāvamāha-‘nāyaṃ doso’ccādi, tathāhiccādinā “na dvevā”ti sutteneva pariyāyassāpi dīpitattaṃ sādheti, sā ca ekatthappavatti pariyāyaṃ vinā na sambhavati… ekakkhaṇe pavatyasabbhāvāti adhippāyo, nanu ca kvacābhāve pariyāyappavattiyaṃ yathāvutta dosassevāppasaṅgato mā hotu pariyāyo, bhinnavisaye pana pubbaparalopappavattiyā “na dvevā’ti nisedhe lateva latāva latāivāti rūpattayaṃ nipphajjatīti codanaṃ manasi nidhāyāha-‘nace’ccādi, tattha dosamāha-‘tathā ca sati’ccādinā, katthaci demiccādo niccaṃ pubbalopasseva, katthaci honticcādo niccaṃ paralopasseva[M 0.0049], vikappena vā katthaci yathodakaṃ yathāudakaṃ tyādo pubbalopasseva katthaci itipi iccapiccādo paralopasseva katthaci lateva latāva latāivāccādo pariyāyenubhayalopasseva dassanatoti sambandho, etthaca itipīti vavatthitavibhāsatta dīpanena kvacisaddena paralope kate-ññatra pubba lope sampatte “na dvevā”ti etthānuvattamāna kvacānubhāvena niccaṃ nisedhe iccapicceva bhavati. Sambajjhati tesu tesu suttesu. Paricchedoti kammatthavasena ādhāravasena vāti āha-‘paricchijjati’ccādi.

The word 'iti' here is in the sense of 'this'; the connection is that this statement indicates that sometimes elision is to occur. What does it say? — 'following the application.' For what? — 'for the operation of subsequent elision.' By what reason? — 'by the inclusion of the word "kvaci" (sometimes).' Where? — 'here in this rule.' Therefore, by that indication of following the application, according to the application—without transgressing the traditional usage—subsequent elision may be constant, as in `honticcādo`, or optional, as in `latāvāti`, etc. Thus, one thinks: 'In what sense? When the word "kva" is formed with an unrestricted meaning, since the unrestricted meaning is specifically stated, and because it has an unrestricted meaning everywhere, this word `kvaci`, according to tradition, indicates a rule that is constant, inconstant, and non-existent. Therein, the constant case, such as `honticcādo`, is the domain of subsequent elision. The inconstant case, such as `latāvātiādiko`, being common to both, is also the domain of prior elision. Thus, subsequent elision occurs constantly or optionally. The non-existent case, however, such as `saddhindriyantiādiko`, is the domain of prior elision, being entirely abandoned by this rule.' However, in all three of these cases, its nature as an exception exists only in the constant and inconstant cases, because it either entirely prevents prior elision, as in `honticcādo`, or prescribes subsequent elision; but not in the non-existent case, because the opportunity is entirely given to prior elision. `Lokaggotiādi`, however, because the word `kvaci` indicates following the application, is formed by subsequent elision even when a constant or non-existent rule is indicated, so there is no contradiction with what is desired. Thus, with the inclusion of `kvaci`, the desired result is achieved by completely avoiding the undesired. If it is absent, how? In its absence, it states a contradiction, beginning with `aññathā`, etc. They occur alternatively. In the absence of the inclusion of `kvaci`, there would be the rule `paro`. If so, the two rules would have the same scope and equal force. Therein, since there is no conflict, lest the authoritative words of the teachers become meaningless, it means they occur in turn. Therefore, by this reason of alternative occurrence, it would occur only optionally. In `latāvātiādīsu`, when prior elision occurs alternatively, since subsequent elision does not occur alternatively, in `latāvāti` subsequent elision would occur only optionally. The connection is that `honticcādo` would not be constant. And that alternative occurrence... `kho` is an expletive. `Paṭipadanti` means it occurs at every step, not even with partial avoidance; hence it is said 'not anywhere.' By this it is shown: 'Due to the application of option everywhere, undesirable forms like `saddhindriyaṃtyādikaṃ` and `hanticcādikaṃ` are also produced, even in the rule `na dvevā` (1-28).' And this is not desired. The meaning is: this aforementioned rule of option is not approved by those who know the characteristics of language. This very point is established by 'for subsequent elision,' etc. Now, in the inconstant case, when subsequent elision is made optionally, in the place abandoned by this rule, due to the application of the general rule, the two forms, `latāva` and `lateva`, are produced. Therefore, by the word `kvaci` itself, which indicates following the application, the possibility of the usages `honti`, `saddhindriyaṃ`, `latāva`, and `lateva` also exists. Nevertheless, in the inconstant case, due to the establishment of the third form `latāiva`, it is conjectured that it must occur alternatively, beginning with 'nanu ca,' etc. Then, since `paro kvacī` is an exception when `kvaci` is included, how can alternative application occur? Bearing this in mind, to show the alternative application in the inconstant case, the rule `na dvevā` is stated. It states that there is no fault in alternative application even with three forms in the exception, with 'nāyaṃ doso,' etc. By 'tathāhi,' etc., it proves that the alternative is also indicated by the rule `na dvevā` itself. And that application to a single object is not possible without alternation; the intention is that occurrence at a single moment is impossible. But if `kvaci` is absent, in the alternative application, since the aforementioned fault would not arise, let there be no alternation. However, with the application of prior and subsequent elision in different domains, and the prohibition `na dvevā`, the three forms `lateva`, `latāva`, and `latāiva` are produced. Bearing this objection in mind, it says 'nace,' etc. Therein it states the fault, with 'tathā ca sati,' etc. The connection is that it is seen that: somewhere, as in `demiccādo`, there is always only prior elision; somewhere, as in `honticcādo`, there is always only subsequent elision; or optionally, somewhere, as in `yathodakaṃ yathāudakaṃ`, there is only prior elision; somewhere, as in `itipi iccapiccādo`, there is only subsequent elision; somewhere, as in `lateva latāva latāivāccādo`, there is elision of both alternatively. And here, in `itipi`, by indicating a restricted option, when subsequent elision is performed by the word `kvaci`, and when prior elision is obtained elsewhere, upon reaching `na dvevā`, due to the influence of the `kvaci` that continues into this rule, the prohibition is constant, and it becomes only `iccapi`. It is connected in those respective rules. `Paricchedo` (delimitation) is either in the sense of the object or in the sense of the location; thus it says 'it is delimited,' etc.

28. Nadve

28. Na dve

Tatthacāti casaddena bhavitabbaṃ, tathā ca sati aññoññānajjhāsi taṃ yathodakaṃ yathāudakaṃtyādi itipi iccapiccādica saṅgahitaṃ bhavatīti, pubbalope paralope ca pariyāyena sampatte dvinnampi pakkhe abhāve sati kathamidaṃ yujjatīti codeti‘yajjeva’miccādinā, yajjevanti hi ayaṃ nipātasamudāyo aniṭṭhāpādanārambha vattate, evañce gayhatīti attho, tadeti atthato viññāyati, niccaṃ sandhikāriyābhāve kāraṇamāha-‘upasilesā bhāvato’ti, tadeva samattheti īdisesu hi’ccādinā, vattumiṭṭhattāti iminā sannikaṃso vaṇṇāna maddhamattakālabyavadhānā paccāsatti, sannikaṃsassetassa vacanicchāyaṃ satiyeva sandhikāriyaṃ hotīti dīpeti, upasilesābhāvo vāti upasilesābhāvo eva bhavati, nāññathāti adhippāyo, tadabhāvecāti tassa upasilesassa abhāve ca, sandhikāriyābhāve kāraṇamāha-‘kālantarena byavadhānā’ti, kālantarenāti ubhayattha ṭhitavaṇṇāna muccāraṇakālato aññena majjhappatitakālena, sandhi hoteva… sannikaṃsavacanicchāvasena upasilesabhāvato, buddha vīra atthurājaputtaṃ ajarāmaroti chedo, yadipi sabbampetaṃ yajjevaṃtyādinā vuttaṃ kvaci saddappabhāveneva sijjhati, tathāpi pakāro-yampi satthe yojetabbo vāti dassetuṃ vutto.

Therein, `ca` should be taken as the word `ca`. And if so, that which is mutually un-elided, such as `yathodakaṃ yathāudakaṃ`, and also `itipi iccapiccādi`, is included. When prior elision and subsequent elision are obtained alternatively, and both cases are absent, how is this justified? It questions with 'yajjevam,' etc. For this particle combination `yajjevam` is used to begin the adducing of an undesired consequence. The meaning is 'if it is taken thus'; `tadā` (then) is understood from the meaning. It states the reason for the constant absence of sandhi operation: 'due to the absence of close contact.' It supports that very point with 'in such cases,' etc. The desire to speak indicates this: proximity is the nearness of sounds without the interval of even half a mora's time. It shows that the sandhi operation occurs only when there is a desire for speech characterized by this proximity. Or the absence of close contact means it is indeed an absence of close contact, not otherwise—this is the intention. And in its absence, that is, in the absence of that close contact, it states the reason for the absence of sandhi operation: 'due to the interval of another time.' `Kālantarena` means by another time that falls in the middle, other than the time of pronunciation of the sounds situated in both places. Sandhi certainly occurs due to the existence of close contact by means of the desire for proximate speech. The phrase `buddha vīra atthu rājaputtaṃ ajarāmaro` is an instance of separation of words. Although all this which is said with `yajjevam`, etc., is accomplished by the power of the word `kvaci` itself, nevertheless, it is said to show that this method should also be applied in the teaching.

29. Yuva

29. Yuva

Nanu [M 0.0050] sutte ‘luttā’ti pañcamī niddesā ‘paresa’nti hotu, ‘yathākkamaṃ’ti tu vacanābhāve kathaṃ yathākkamantīdaṃ vuttanti āha-‘same’ccāti, samā saṅkhyā gaṇanā yesu te samasaṅkhyā-uddesino anudesino ca, uddisanaṃ paṭhamaṃ niddisanaṃ uddeso, anudisanaṃ pacchā kathanaṃ anudeso, uddeso anudeso esamatthīti uddesino anudesino, tesaṃ samasaṅkhyānamuddesīnaṃ anudesīnañca, ivaṇṇuvaṇṇāhi uddesino dve, e okārā anudesino ca dveti uddesīnamanudesīnañca ṭhānyādesānaṃ samasaṅkhyā siyā, satiyañca tassaṃ yathākkama mādasā vidhīyante, lokato siddhimupadasseti ‘tathāhi’ccādinā. Ava…pe… e oti paresaṃ mataṃ, vippaṭipattīti viruddhā paṭipatti paṭijānanaṃ, pare “satipi heṭṭhā vāggahaṇe‘kvacāsavaṇṇaṃ lutte’ti sutte kvaciggahaṇakaraṇato avaṇṇe eva lutte asavaṇṇo vidhi hoti, tato idha na hoti diṭṭhupādāna”nti vadanti, kvacīti adhikāro idha na hoti mahussavo mātūpaṭṭhānanti, patisaddo ādhārattho, tena samānādhikaraṇo urasaddopīti urasminti nicca samāsattā asakapadena viggahe kate “asaṅkhyaṃ vibhatti”ccādinā (3-2) suttena asaṅkhyasamāsoti dassetumāha-‘vibhatyatthesaṅkhyasamāso’ti, ettha pana yuvaṇṇānanti saṃsāmi samīpasamūha vikārāvayavādīsu ṭhānyādesasambandhe chaṭṭhī, tasmā ivaṇṇuvaṇṇānaṃ ṭhāne e oādesā hontīti attho, ṭhānampana tidhā apakaṃso nivatti pasaṅgo ceti, tattha gunnaṃ ṭhāne assā sambandhīyantu bajjhantu (jinindabuddhi) ti apakaṃso ṭhānasaddassattho, “semhassa ṭhāne kaṭukamosadhaṃ dātabba”nti nivatti “dabbhānaṃ ṭhāne sarehi attharitabba”nti pasaṅgo, tesu idha paṭhamadutiyā na yujjanti… niccattā saddatthasambandhassa apanayanavināsā na yujjantīti, tatiyo tu (yujjati)… sutte atthābhidhānāya ivaṇṇuvaṇṇānaṃ pavattippasaṅge tadatthābhidhānāyeva eoādesā bhavantīti.

Is it not so that in the sutta, due to the specification in the fifth case as 'luttā', it should be 'paresaṃ'? But in the absence of the statement 'yathākkamaṃ', how is this 'yathākkamaṃ' stated? He says: 'same'ccāti, meaning those in whom the number and counting are equal; they are the designators and counter-designators of equal number. Designation is the first pointing out, the designation; counter-designation is the subsequent statement, the counter-designation. Those who have designation and counter-designation are the designators and counter-designators. Of those designators and counter-designators of equal number, the designators are two, the i-vowel and u-vowel; and the counter-designators are also two, e and o. Thus, the originals and substitutes of the designators and counter-designators should be equal in number. And when that is so, the substitutions are prescribed in order. He shows the establishment from worldly usage with 'tathāhi' and so on. Ava…pe… e and o are the opinion of others. 'Vippaṭipatti' means a contrary practice or acknowledgment. Others say, “Although there is the inclusion of 'vā' below, in the sutta 'kvacāsavaṇṇaṃ lutte', because of the inclusion of 'kvaci', the rule for a dissimilar vowel applies only when the a-vowel is elided. Therefore, 'diṭṭhupādāna' does not occur here.” 'Kvacīti'—this governing rule does not apply here, as in 'mahussavo' and 'mātūpaṭṭhāna'. The word 'pati' has the meaning of a locative. Therefore, the word 'ura' also has the same referent. In 'urasmiṃ', because it is always a compound, when the analysis is done with non-constituent words, he says 'vibhatyatthesaṅkhyasamāso' to show that it is an 'asaṅkhyasamāsa' by the sutta 'asaṅkhyaṃ vibhatti' (3-2) and so on. Here, however, 'yuvaṇṇānaṃ' is in the sixth case, which denotes the relationship between the original and the substitute, among its various meanings such as owner, proximity, collection, modification, part, and so on. Therefore, the meaning is that in place of the i-vowel and u-vowel, the substitutes e and o occur. 'Ṭhāna' is threefold: 'apakaṃsa' (removal), 'nivatti' (replacement), and 'pasaṅga' (application). Among these, 'apakaṃsa' refers to taking away the attribute of the original, 'nivatti' means replacement, as in “in place of phlegm, bitter medicine should be given,” and 'pasaṅga' means application, as in “in place of kusa grass, reeds should be spread.” Here, the first and second do not apply… because of the permanence of the relationship between word and meaning, removal and destruction do not apply. The third, however, applies… In the sutta, for the expression of meaning, on the occasion of the application of the i-vowel and u-vowel, the substitutes e and o occur for the very expression of that meaning.

30. Yavā

30. Barley

“Sattamiyaṃ [M 0.0051] pubbasse”ti (1-14) pubbassa kāriyavidhānato sattamī niddiṭṭhassa paratā viññāyatīti vuttiyaṃ ‘pare’ti vuttaṃ, evamuparipi, parehi iccassa ajjhiṇamutto’ti sādhetuṃ “sabbocanti” “ajjho adhī”ti ca suttitaṃ, tesamidha paccakkhātabhāvadassanatthamāha-‘ida’miccādi, abbhakkhānanti abbhuggabho imināva siddhanti “abbho abhī”ti ca na vattabbaṃ, iti+assa iti ṭhite paralopoti dassanatthaṃ ‘iti assa paralopo’ti āha, anvagamātiādīsu niccaṃ.

By the rule 'Sattamiyaṃ pubbasse' (1-14), since an operation is prescribed for what precedes, the subsequence of that which is specified by the seventh case is understood; thus, in the commentary, 'pare' is stated, and similarly above. To establish 'ajjhiṇamutto' (freed from adherence) from 'parehi', the suttas 'sabbo ca...' and 'ajjho adhi' are formulated. Here, to show that these are rejected, he says 'idaṃ', and so on. Since 'abbhakkhānaṃ' (denial) is established by this alone, 'abbho abhi' should not be stated. Thus, to show that when 'iti' and 'assa' are juxtaposed there is elision of the following vowel, he says, 'iti assa paralopo'. In 'anvagamāti' and so on, it is constant.

31. Eo

31. E o

Puttā me+atthi, asanto+etthāti padacchedo.

The word division is: 'Puttā me atthi, asanto ettha'.

32. Gossa

32. Gossa

Antādesatthoti “chaṭṭhiyantassā”ti (1-17) bādhakassa “ṭānubandhānekavaṇṇā sabbassā”ti (1-19) bādhakena “vānubandho”ti (1-18) suttena antādesattho, teneva vuttaṃ-‘bādhakabādhanatthoyamārambho’ti, avavādese pubbasaralope dīgheca gavāssaṃ, gavacchanti niccaṃ. Idaṃ kathaṃ sijjhatīti sambandho, idanti yathariveccādikaṃ, kiṃ vinā sijjhatīti āha-‘evādissā’tiādi, evassa ādiekāro evādi, tassa, riādesamantarenāti sambandho, casaddo aṭṭhānappayutto, rassavidhānañcāti yojanīyo, katepi tasminti tasmiṃ sutte vihite ca, na sijjhatīti evādissa riādeso na katoti katvā vuttaṃ, bhusaṃ+evāti (pana) ṭhite mahāvuttinā evādissa iādese rūpasiddhi hoteva, idha pana pakārantarena ‘bhusāmive’ti sādhetumāha ‘tampi’ccādi.

The purpose of the final substitution is that the rule 'vānubandho' (1-18) obstructs the rule 'ṭānubandhānekavaṇṇā sabbassā' (1-19), which in turn obstructs 'chaṭṭhiyantassā' (1-17). Therefore, it is said: ‘This undertaking is for the purpose of obstructing the obstructor.’ In the case of the ‘ava’ substitution, with elision of the preceding vowel and lengthening, ‘gavāssaṃ’ and ‘gavacchaṃ’ are always formed. The connection is the question: 'How is this accomplished?' 'This' refers to forms such as 'yathariva'. Without what is it accomplished? He says: ‘evādissā’ and so on. The initial vowel of ‘eva’ is ‘e’, thus ‘evādi’. The connection is: without the ‘ri’ substitution of that (evādi). The particle ‘ca’ is used inappropriately; it should be connected with ‘rassavidhāna’ (the rule for shortening). Even if it is made, and even if it is prescribed in that sutta, it is said that it is not accomplished because the ‘ri’ substitution for ‘evādi’ is not done. However, when ‘bhusaṃ+eva’ stands, the form is certainly accomplished by the Mahāvutti with the ‘i’ substitution for ‘evādi’. Here, however, to establish ‘bhusāmiva’ by another method, he says: ‘tampi’ and so on.

33. Byañja

33. Consonant

Rassadīghānanti sutte avutte kathaṃ rassadīghānanti labhati uddesinoti āha-‘dīghassā’tiādi, dīghassāti rassassāti ca ṭhānasambandhe chaṭṭhī, paccāsatyāti ṭhānaso paccāsatyā, idañca nissaya vasena [M 0.0052] vuttaṃ, nissayakaraṇameko satthāgato ñāyoti, idha niccaṃ-vītināmeti thullaccayaṃ, idha na hoti-jano sāyaṃ.

When 'short and long' are not stated in the sutta, how does one obtain 'short and long' for the designators? He says, 'dīghassā', etc. 'Dīghassā' and 'rassassā' are in the genitive case by connection to place. 'Paccāsatyā' means by proximity of place. And this is stated on the basis of dependence. The method of dependence is a principle that has come from the Teacher. Here, 'vītināmeti' always constitutes a grave offense. Here, it does not happen in 'jano sāyaṃ'.

34. Sara

34. Vowel

Ṭhānasambandheti ṭhiti ṭhānaṃ pasaṅgo, sambandhanaṃ-sambandho, ṭhānyādesabhāvalakkhaṇo ṭhāneyoganimittabhūto sambandho ṭhānasambandho tasmiṃ, dve rūpāni hontīti iminā na sarūpappadhānoti dassitaṃ hotīti sambandho, hetumāha-‘bahuvacananiddesā’ti, dve rūpānihontītyādi vacanamidaṃ padamidaṃ (potthake) dasseti “sarūpappadhānepi dvisadde dvisaddasāmaññena saṅkhyādvisaddānusiṭṭhaṃ nappayujjate, tassa (pana) saṅkhyeyyavacanasaṅkhyābhāvā ekavacanameva ( ) (pana) (potthake) hotī”ti, iminā ca-tthappadhāno-yaṃ niddeso na sarūpappadhānoti dasseti, adhipatipaccayo adhipatippaccayoti aniccaṃ, idha na hoti idha modatīti, taṃ khaṇanti ettha ekaṅgavikalaṃ paccudāharaṇanti saramhā parattābhāvā na dvittaṃ.

Regarding 'ṭhānasambandhe' (in connection with place): 'ṭhiti' (state) is 'ṭhāna' (place), an occasion; 'sambandhanaṃ' is 'sambandho' (connection). The 'ṭhānasambandho' is that connection characterized by the state of being an original and a substitute, and which is the cause for the application in a place. By this statement 'two forms exist', it is shown that this is not primarily about the form itself; this is the connection. He states the reason: 'because of the indication by the plural.' The phrase 'two forms exist' and so on indicates this: 'Even when the form is primary, with the word 'dvi' (two), due to the general sense of the word 'dvi', the numerical instruction for the word 'dvi' is not applied. Because of the absence of a number representing the numbered, only the singular occurs.' And by this, it is shown that this indication is primarily about the meaning, not primarily about the form. 'Adhipatipaccayo' becoming 'adhipatippaccayo' is optional. It does not happen in 'idha modati'. In 'taṃ khaṇaṃ', this is a counter-example lacking one component; because there is no consonant following the vowel, there is no doubling.

35. Catu

35. Four

Tabbagge tatiyapaṭhamāti kasmā vuttaṃ catuttha (dutiya) saddehi vaggakkharesveva gayhamānesu tathā niddeso yutto, na hi catunnampūraṇo catuttho dvinnampūraṇo dutiyoti akkharāyeva vuccantīti āsaṅkiya ‘vināpī’tiādimāha, akkhare akkharavisaye catutthādi vohāro karīyamāno vaggaggahaṇaṃ vināpi vaggakkhareyeva ruḷho pasiddhoti sambandho, hetumhi itisaddo, yato evaṃ, tasmā kāraṇā ‘tabbagge tatiyapaṭhamā’ti vuttanti adhippāyo, tabbaggeti catutthadutiyā yasmiṃ, tasmiṃyeva vaggeti attho, paccāsattīti pati āpubbā ‘sada-visaraṇagatyavasādanesu’iccasmā itthiyaṃ bhāvettimhi nipphajjatīti dassetumāha-‘paccāsīdana’miccādi, yathāyogganti catutthakkhare catutthassa tatiyo dutiyakkhare dutiyassa paṭhamoti evaṃ yoggamanatikkamma, dhassa dabhāvoti imināva pubbassa dhassa dattamupalakkheti, tathā yasattheroti. Theroti ettha ekāro vaggakkharo [M 0.0053] na hotīti tasmiṃ tavaggadutiyakkharassa tassa to paṭhamo na hoti. Panthoti ettha tavagga dutiyakkharena thakārena tabbaggabhūte nakāre satīpi na so tabbaggadutiyakkharoti na tassa paṭhamo to, ettha nigghoso nighosotiādi aniccaṃ, daḍḍho niṭṭhānanti niccaṃ.

Why is it said, 'in that group, the third and the first'? Because when by the words 'fourth' and 'second' only the group letters are taken, such a specification is appropriate. For it is not that 'fourth' means 'completing four' or 'second' means 'completing two' that the letters themselves are spoken of. Suspecting this, he says, 'even without,' etc. The connection is: the usage of 'fourth,' etc., being made in the domain of letters, is conventionally established for the group letters themselves, even without the explicit mention of 'group'. The word 'iti' is in the sense of reason. Since it is so, for that reason, the meaning is that 'in that group, the third and the first' is said. 'In that group' means in that very group in which the fourth and second letters are. 'Paccāsatti' (proximity): to show that it is formed as a feminine noun in the sense of state from the root 'sad' (in the sense of 'scattering, movement, descent,' etc.) with the prefixes 'pati' and 'ā', he says, 'paccāsīdana' (approaching), etc. 'As appropriate' means without transgressing the suitability, thus: for the fourth letter, the third of the fourth; for the second letter, the first of the second. By this very 'the state of da for dha', he indicates the 'da-ness' of the preceding 'dha'. Likewise, 'yasatthero'. Here, in 'thero', the 'e' is not a group letter; therefore, in its presence, the second letter of the ta-varga, 'tha', does not become the first, 'ta'. In 'pantho', even when the letter 'na' is present, which belongs to the same group as the second letter of the ta-varga, 'tha', it is not the second letter of that group, so its first, 'ta', does not occur. Here, 'nigghoso' becoming 'nighoso', etc., is optional; 'daḍḍho' and 'niṭṭhānaṃ' are constant.

36. Vitissa

36. Vitissa

Itisaddo-nukaraṇaṃ. Nipātassa pakativiyā-nukaraṇaṃ bhavati, anukaraṇañca dvidhā asādhusaddarūpaṃ sādhusaddarūpanti, tesu bhāravāhako koci tena pīḷito ‘aho bhāro’ti vattabbe sattivekallā ‘aho bāla’ iccāha, taṃsamīpavattī ‘kimayamāhe’ti kenaci puṭṭho samāno ‘aho bāla iccayamāhe’ti vadati, idhamasādhusaddarūpaṃ, itīti pana sādhusaddarūpaṃ, tasmā tato-nukāriyenātthena sātthakattā ṭhānasambandhe chaṭṭhī.

The word 'iti' is an imitation. It functions as an imitation of the original form of a particle, and imitation is of two kinds: that which has the form of an incorrect word and that which has the form of a correct word. Among these, a certain burden-bearer, oppressed by his burden, when he should say, 'aho bhāro' (oh, the burden!), due to a lack of strength, says, 'aho bāla' (oh, fool!). Someone nearby, being asked by another, 'What does this one say?', replies, 'This one says, 'aho bāla'.' This is the form of an incorrect word. But 'iti' is the form of a correct word. Therefore, because it is meaningful through the meaning which is imitated by it, the sixth case ending is used in the sense of relation.

37. Eo

37. Eo

Nanu “vitisseve vā”ti (1-36) votyanuvattiya avaṇṇe eonaṃ vo hotīti ca sakkā viññātuṃ, tathā sati ‘avaṇṇe kvaci vo hotī”ti vattabbaṃ ‘ahoti vā’ti kasmā vuttanti codanamāsaṅkiyāha-‘okārassapi’ccādi, ṭhānibhāvena niddiṭṭhattāti “eona”nti (1-31) vakārādesassa vijjamānattā vakārādesampati puna okāro ṭhānibhāvena niddisitabbo na siyāti adhippāyenāha, na nimittanti eonaṃ vakārādesatthaṃ avaṇṇo kāraṇaṃ na hotīti attho, aññathāti avaṇṇassa nimittatte, okāraṃ na paṭheyyāti sambandho, makārāgame’yāca kamāgate aggamakkhāyatī’ti, sve bhavanti viggayha tanappaccaye taddhitavuttiyaṃ vibhattiyā “ekatthatāyaṃ”ti (2-119) lope akārādese dīgheca syādimhi svātanaṃ dvitte hiyyattanaṃ. Svātanantiādīsu niccaṃ, idha nahoti pareca na vijānantīti.

Now, is it not possible to understand that by the continuation of 'vo' from the rule 'vitisseve vā' (1-36), 'eo' becomes 'vo' when a non-'a' vowel follows? If so, it should be stated, 'Sometimes 'vo' occurs when a non-'a' vowel follows'; why then is 'ahoti vā' said? Anticipating this objection, he says, 'okārassapi,' and so forth. Because it is indicated as the original (`ṭhānin`). With the intention that, since the substitution of 'va' for 'eo' already exists by the rule 'eonaṃ' (1-31), 'o' should not again be indicated as the original for the substitution of 'va'. It is not a cause (`nimitta`), meaning that a non-'a' vowel is not the cause for the substitution of 'va' for 'eo'. Otherwise, if a non-'a' vowel were the cause, he would not have taught 'o'—this is the connection. In the case of the insertion of 'm', 'and what has come in due course is declared supreme'. They become 'sve', having been analyzed in the `taddhita` formation with the `tana` suffix, with the elision of the case ending by 'ekatthatāyaṃ' (2-119), with the substitution of 'a' and lengthening. When `sya`, etc., is added, `svātanaṃ` is formed; with doubling, `hiyyattanaṃ`. In `svātanaṃ`, etc., it is constant. Here it does not occur, and others do not understand.

38. Nigga

38. Nigga

Katha‘māgamo [M 0.0054] hotī’ti vuttaṃ yadi niggahītamāgamo siyā sutte āgamaggahaṇena vā bhavitabbaṃ ña-ma-kādya nubandhavisesena vā tyāsaṅkiyāha-‘asati pi’ccādi, āgamāvasāye kāraṇamāha-‘ādesattāyogā’ti, ādesattāyogo kathaṃ viññāyati ccāha-‘ṭhāniniddesābhāvato’ti, tathā sati āgaminiddesābhāvā āgamattampi na siyāti codeti ‘yajjeva’miccādinā, na-iti codanaṃ paṭikkhipitvā tassa āgamattameva sādhetumāha-‘tassā’tiādi, tassāti niggahītassa, rassānuppavattito rassasarameva anugantvā pavattito, ayamevattho vuttiyampi dassitoyevāti vattumāha-‘etadeve’ccādi, purimā jātīti visesanasamāsekate rasse ca bindvāgamo, paranimittassāniddiṭṭhattā bahusadde-ntassa bindvāgame bahuṃ, satipi payogānusārittadīpakassa kvacisaddassāpi vavatthitavibhāsatte vāsaddassāpi tādisattasseva paṭipādakatta sabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ ‘vavatthitavibhāsattā vādhikārassā’ti vuttiyaṃ vuttaṃ, vavatthitassa lakkhiyassa anurodhena lakkhaṇappavattikā vibhāsā vavatthitavibhāsā, abhedena tu vādhikāro vavatthita vibhāsā, tassā bhāvo vavatthitavibhāsattaṃ, tasmā, idha na hoti idha modati, imasmiṃ ṭhāne āgamattappakāsako ṭhāninidde sābhāvā ādesattāyogasaṅkhāto kāraṇaviseso samattho, tassa bhāvo sāmatthiyaṃ-atthabala-maññathānupapattilakkhaṇaṃ, sacāti so āgamo ca.

How is it said, 'an augment occurs'? If the `niggahīta` were an augment, it should be indicated in the rule either by the term 'āgama' or by a special affix like `ña`, `ma`, `ka`, etc. Anticipating this, he says, 'asati pi,' and so forth. He states the reason for determining it as an augment: 'due to the unsuitability of being a substitute.' How is the unsuitability of being a substitute understood? He says: 'due to the absence of indication of the original (`ṭhānin`).' If that is so, due to the absence of indication of that which receives the augment (`āgamin`), it would not even be an augment. He objects with 'yajjevam,' and so forth. Refuting this objection with 'na', he establishes that it is indeed an augment by stating: 'tassā,' and so forth. 'tassa' means 'of the `niggahīta`'. Because it occurs following after a short vowel. To say that this very meaning is also shown in the commentary, he says, 'etadeve,' and so forth. In 'purimā jāti', when a compound of adjectives is formed and there is a short vowel, the `bindu` is an augment. Due to the non-indication of a subsequent cause, in the word 'bahu', the `bindu` is an augment at the end, making it 'bahuṃ'. To show that the nature of the particle 'vā' is also of this kind—even though the word 'kvaci' is an indicator that follows usage—it is stated in the commentary, 'because of the established optionality of the governing rule with `vā`'. `Vavatthitavibhāsā` is an option that operates in accordance with the established example. The governing rule with `vā`, however, is identical to `vavatthitavibhāsā`. Its state is `vavatthitavibhāsattaṃ`. Therefore, [we have] 'idha na hoti' and 'idha modati'. In this case, the special cause—designated as the unsuitability of being a substitute due to the absence of indication of the `ṭhānin`—is capable of revealing its nature as an augment. Its state is capability, characterized by the force of meaning and the impossibility of being otherwise. And that is the augment.

39. Lopo

39. Elision

Lopasaddassa bhāvasādhanamattameva sādhetumāha-‘tene’ccādi, lopoti yadi kammasādhano siyā tadā tena samānādhikaraṇaṃ katvā upari “parasaro”ti suttamārabhīyeyyāti byatirekamāha ‘na parasaro’ti, idha na hoti saṅgaro.

To establish that 'lopa' is merely a verbal noun, he says 'tena,' and so forth. If 'lopa' were a passive participle, then, having made it co-referential with that, the rule 'parasaro' should be begun above. He states the exclusion by 'na parasaro'; here there is no conflict.

40. Para

40. Subsequent

Tvaṃsi [M 0.0055] tvamasīti vikappo, idha na hoti tāsāhaṃ.

The alternative forms are 'tvaṃsi' and 'tvamasi'. Here, this rule does not apply, as in 'tāsāhaṃ'.

41. Vagge

41. In the group

Nanu vaggevaggantoti ettakeyeva vutte yasmiṃ (kismi)ñci vaggakkhare pare binduno yokoci vagganto aniyamena bhaveyya tathā sati aniṭṭhampi siyātyāsaṅkiya paccāsattiṃ sannissāyāniṭṭha nivattindassetumāha-‘vagge vagganto’ticcādi, sovāti vaggantova, tasminti vaggakkhare.

Now, if only 'vagge vagganto' were stated, then, when any class-consonant follows, any class-nasal whatsoever might replace the `bindu` without restriction. If that were the case, fearing that an undesirable form might also arise, to show the prevention of the undesirable by relying on proximity, he said 'vagge vagganto,' and so forth. `so` refers to the class-nasal itself; `tasmiṃ` refers to that class-consonant.

42. Yeva

42. Indeed

Nanu saddattā byabhicārittā evassa tāva saddo hotu, saṃyato, saṃhitoti saddekadesabhūtānampi sambhavā tepi gahe tabbā siyunti ‘yaevahi saddesu’ti yahīnampi kathaṃ saddavohāro katoti āha ‘evā’tiādi, etthāyamadhippāyo ‘abyabhicārinā byabhicārī niyamyate’ti.

Now, because it is a sound and because it is variable, let 'eva' first be a sound. Since even parts of a sound, as in 'saṃyato' and 'saṃhito', are possible, they too should be taken. He says, 'evā,' and so forth, asking how the term 'sound' is used even for those that are deficient, as in 'yaevahi saddesu'. Here the intention is: 'The variable is restricted by the invariable'.

43. Yesaṃ

43. Of whom

Yasadde pubbasutteneva saṃssapyādese siddhe so ( ) (tassa) (potthake) ya kāramatteyeva pare saṃsseva (yathā) siyāti suttamidamāraddhaṃ.

Although the substitution for the word 'ya' was established by the previous rule, this rule was begun so that the substitution might occur only when the letter 'ya' alone follows.

44. Vana

44. Forest

Ṭhāninamāsilissa gacchati pavattatīti āgamo nāma, ko-yamettha ṭhānīti āha-‘sarassāti, sutte anuvattassa ca avijjamānattā ‘sarassā’ti kuto labbhatīti codeti ‘nanu ce’tyādinā. Āgamasutiyā vanādīnaṃ ṭhānisutiyā abhāvepi sāmatthiyā byañjanassa vā āgamo siyā sarassa vā, yadi byañjanassa vā siyā (na) “padādīnaṃ kvacī”ti (5-92) suttita mācariyena, tasmā tadeva ñāpeti ‘saro yevettha ṭhānī bhavitumarahatī’ti.
