Kiñci vikāriyaṃ kammaṃ pakatiyā kāraṇassa ucchedena sambhūtaṃ, yathā [M 0.0074] kaṭṭhaṃ bhasmaṃ karotīti kaṭṭhassāccantaparāvatti parāvattiyā (potthake), kiñci pana guṇantarānamuppattiyā, yathā suvaṇṇaṃ kaṭakaṃ keyuraṃ vā karotīti evaṃ dvīdhā sā vikati hotīti attho, na vibhāvīyanteti na gamyante, sā patti‘pāpīyati visayīkarīyatī’ti katvā.

Some alterable object is produced by the destruction of its causal nature, as when wood is made into ash—this is the complete reversal of the wood. Some, however, is produced by the arising of other qualities, as when gold is made into a bracelet or an armlet. Thus, that alteration is of two kinds—this is the meaning. ‘They are not distinguished’ means they are not apprehended. That ‘attainment’ (patti) is so called because it is ‘attained’ or ‘made an object’.

Yatra kriyākato koci, viseso nāvagamyate;

Dassanā vānumānā vā, sā pattīti pakittitā.

Where no distinction made by the action is apprehended, whether by direct perception or by inference, that is declared to be ‘attainment’ (patti).

Yattha kiriyākato kiriyāsampādito viseso atisayo koci nāvagamyate nappatīyate dassanā vā paccakkhappamāṇena anumānappamāṇena vā yathā nibbattivikatīnamatisayo paccakkhānumānā vagamanīyo, tatra hi nibbattiyaṃ visesasiddhiratipasiddhā… atthalābhākhyassa visesassāvijjamānassa kiriyākattā, vikāriye ( ) (eva) (potthake) tu kvaci paccakkhavisayo… kaṭṭhaṃ ḍahatīti kaṇhattādibhāvassa paccakkhenevopalabbhanato, kvacidanumānagammo… devadattaṃ roseti pasādayati veti visiṭṭhamukhavaṇṇādikāriyānumeyyattā rosādino, evaṃ yattha na visesasiddhi api tu pattimattaṃ, sā pattīti pakittitā kathitā, ādiccampassati dhammamajjhetīti ayamettha attho, kathañcarahi asantassa santassa (potthake) pattikammassa kiñci (akaronta)ssa kārakattaṃ, na hi kiñci akarontaṃ kārakambhavitumarahatīti uccate-

Where no distinction or excellence, brought about by the action, accomplished by the action, is apprehended or understood, whether by the means of direct perception or by the means of inference—unlike the excellence of production and alteration which is to be apprehended by direct perception and inference. There, indeed, in production, the establishment of a distinction is exceedingly well-known, because the action creates a non-existent distinction called 'attainment of the goal.' In the case of an alterable object, however, it is sometimes an object of direct perception—as when one burns wood, the state of blackness, etc., is perceived directly—and sometimes it is accessible to inference—as when one angers or pleases Devadatta, for anger, etc., are to be inferred from the effect of a distinct facial expression, etc. Thus, where no establishment of a distinction occurs, but only mere attainment, that is declared and spoken of as ‘attainment’ (patti). ‘He sees the sun,’ ‘He studies the Dhamma’—this is the meaning here. How then can there be the status of an agent for an attainment-object which is non-existent and does nothing? For indeed, that which does nothing cannot be an agent—thus it is said:

Dassanakkhamatābhāso, pagamabyattiādayo;

Visesā pattikammassa, kriyāsiddhiyamicchitā.

Suitability for seeing, appearance, approach, manifestation, and so forth—these distinctions of the attainment-object are desired for the accomplishment of the action.

Atra daṭṭhuṃ sakkā iti dassane khamatā ābhāsopagamo visayattopagamo visayattopagamanaṃ byatti ceti evamādayo visesā yathāyogaṃ pattikammassa kiriyānipphattiyaṃ icchitā, tato tassa kārakattanti attho, ādiccaṃ passatīti ettha hi ādicco daṭṭhuṃ sakkā, tatova so dissati abhibyattiñcopayātīti dassanakiriyānipphādakatthenāssa kārakattamupapajjate, tathā ññatrāpyādisaddagahitavisesavasena kiriyāsiddhito kārakattaṃ veditabbaṃ[M 0.0075], nanu vikāriyampi nibbattikammameva… tena rūpenāsatoyeva jananato, pattikammampi kiriyāsambandharūpenāsantameva pacchā tathā bhavatīti nibbattiyevāti saccaṃ-

Herein, ‘it can be seen’ means suitability for seeing; appearance, approach, becoming an object, and manifestation—these and other such distinctions are desired, as appropriate, for the accomplishment of the action of the attainment-object. Therefore, its status as an agent is the meaning. For instance, in ‘He sees the sun,’ the sun is capable of being seen, and for that reason it is seen and comes to manifestation. Therefore, its status as an agent is established by its being the accomplisher of the act of seeing. Similarly, elsewhere as well, its status as an agent should be understood from the accomplishment of the action by means of the distinctions grasped by the word ‘ādi’ (etc.). But is not even the alterable object just a productive object, since it is generated from that very form which was non-existent? And is not the attainment-object also, being previously non-existent in the form of a relation to the action, only afterwards productive, since it becomes so? This is true—

Atthesā vatthuṭṭhiti, sukhumabuddhigocarapatītyanurodhena,

Tatra yampetaṃ ghaṭate, yathā patīti saddatthāvattānato.

This is the objective situation. In accordance with the apprehension that is the domain of subtle understanding, whatever is suitable in that case occurs as it is apprehended, due to the application of word and meaning.

Visesānupādānatoti “kamme dutiyā”ti sāmaññena vuttattā vuttaṃ. Karīyati kaṭo, kato kaṭo ccevamādīsu tyādippabhutīhi atihitakammādinissayesupi ekattādīsu dutiyādayo papponti niyamābhāvā, tathāhi pañcake nāmatthe kaṭādivacanīyassa sambandhī kammādyattho, tyādippabhutīti anabhi hitassa saṅkhyākhyassāparassa vibhatyatthassābhidhānāya abhihitesupi kaṭādīsu kammādīsu dutiyādayo siyunti pāṇiniyā “kamme dutiyā”ccādīsu (2-3-2) “anabhihite”ti (2-3-1) vacanamadhikaronti, veyyattiyāyeva dutiyādīnappasaṅgepi tannissayabhūte-kattādyatthe jotanāyābhihitesu dutiyādayo siyuṃ, tike pana saṅkhyākammādayo vibhatti vacanīyā, tattha yajjapi kammādino paccayenābhidhānaṃ, tathāpyekattādayo nābhihitāti tassa saṅkhyākhyassāparassa vibhatyatthassāti dhānāya abhihitesupi kammādīsu dutiyādayo siyunti pāṇiniyā “kamme dutiyā”ti “anabhihite”ti vacanamadhikaronti, tamupadassento āha-‘tatridaṃ siyā’tiādi, tatra tasmiṃ dutiyādi vibhattividhāne idaṃ codyaṃ siyā, kinti āha-‘pañcake’iccādi, anabhihitakammādinissayesuti anabhihitā kammādayo nissayā yesamekattādīnaṃ, tesūtyattho, dutiyādayo vibhattiyo yathā siyunti jotanāyābhidhānāya cāti yujjamānavasena attho veditabbo, abhihitakammādinissayesupīti apisaddena anabhihitakammādinissayamekattādiṃ samuccinoti, āsaṅkiyāti pubbakiriyāya vuttanti aparakiriyā veditabbā, pañcake tike cā bhihitakammādinissaye sekattādīsu dutiyādippattimāsaṅkāvasena dassetvā catukkavādīnampi pakkhamubbhāviya pariharituṃ ‘yadiccā’dimāha, ayantesamadhippāyo [M 0.0076] “yadesā saṅkhyā pāṭipadikattho tappaṭipajjane kammādayo vibhattivacanīyā, tadā ‘anabhihite kamme’tiādinā anabhihitaggahaṇaṃ kammādivisesānamanubhavantamanatthakaṃ… abhihite vibhattivāccābhāvato, yadā panāyaṃ pakkho ‘saṅkhyā vibhattivacanīyā’ti tadā “kamme dutiyā” tyevamādayo niddesā visayasandassanamattāyeva veditabbā”ti, sabbathāti pañcakatikavādīnaṃ catukkavādīnañca matavasena sabbappakārena, saddatthābyatirittatthamattoyevāti byatireko byatirittaṃ, napuṃsake bhāve kto, na vijjate byatirittaṃ byatireko bhedo yassa taṃ abyatirittaṃ, abyatibhinnanti attho, saddatthato sakatthato abyatirittaṃ atthamattaṃ atthasāmaññaṃ yassa odanādisaddassa so tathā vutto.

Because a specific is not taken up, it is stated generally, 'the second case ending for the object,' as has been said. In expressions such as 'karīyati kaṭo' (a mat is being made) and 'kato kaṭo' (a mat is made), the second and other case endings might apply to singularity etc., even when their basis, the object etc., has been expressed by verbal endings like ti etc., because there is no restrictive rule. Indeed, in the five-fold view of the meaning of a nominal stem, the meaning of object etc. is related to what is to be expressed by 'kaṭa' etc. Thus, to denote another meaning of the case ending, namely the unexpressed number, by means of verbal endings etc., the second and other case endings might apply even when the object etc. in 'kaṭa' etc. are expressed. Therefore, the Pāṇinians, in rules such as 'the second case ending for the object' (2.3.2), make the word 'anabhihite' (when not expressed) (2.3.1) a governing rule. Even when the second and other case endings are inapplicable due to their distinctness, they might still apply for the sake of indicating the agent etc. which are their basis, when these are expressed. In the three-fold view, however, number, object etc. are to be expressed by the case ending. There, although the object etc. are expressed by a suffix, singularity etc. are not expressed. Therefore, to denote that number, which is another meaning of the case ending, the second and other case endings might apply even when the object etc. are expressed; thus, the Pāṇinians, in 'the second case ending for the object,' make the word 'anabhihite' a governing rule. To illustrate this, he says: 'Herein, this might be so,' etc. There, in that prescription of the second and other case endings, this objection might arise. What is it? He says: 'In the five-fold view,' etc. 'In those whose basis is the unexpressed object etc.' means: in those [numbers] like singularity, for which the unexpressed object etc. are the basis. The meaning should be understood according to the context, that the second and other case endings might apply for the sake of indication and denotation. And by the word 'api' (even) in 'even in those whose basis is an expressed object etc.,' it includes singularity etc. whose basis is an unexpressed object. 'Having suspected' is stated as a prior action, but it should be understood as a subsequent action. After showing, by way of raising a doubt, the potential application of the second and other case endings to singularity etc. whose basis is an expressed object etc., according to both the five-fold and three-fold views, he says 'if it is said' etc. to introduce and refute the view of the proponents of the four-fold view as well. This is their intended meaning: 'When this number is the meaning of the nominal stem, and in its application, the object etc. are to be expressed by case endings, then in the rule 'when the object is not expressed' etc., the inclusion of 'not expressed' is meaningless, as it does not experience the specifics of the object etc., because when [the object is] expressed, there is no denotation by a case ending. But when this view holds that 'number is to be expressed by the case ending,' then statements like 'the second case ending for the object' are to be understood as merely indicating their scope.' 'In all respects' means in every way, according to the views of the proponents of the five-fold, three-fold, and four-fold views. 'Merely a meaning non-distinct from the word-meaning': 'byatireka' is 'byatirittaṃ' (distinct); in the neuter gender, the suffix 'kta' denotes a state. That which has no distinction (byatireka), no difference (bheda), is 'abyatirittaṃ' (non-distinct), meaning 'abyatibhinnaṃ' (non-different). A word like 'odana' (cooked rice) is so called because its meaning is merely a general meaning, non-distinct from its own meaning.

Kiñcāpi vuttiyaṃ tabbādiṇādisamāsehi abhihitamavuttaṃ, tathāpi tehi abhihitepyevameva daṭṭhabbanti nidassento āha-‘eva’miccādi, kara-karaṇe karīyitthāti kato‘kto bhāvakammesu’ti (5-56) kamme kto, satikoti ettha kītoti kammatthe “dissantaññepi paccayā”ti (4-120) iko, kammatāgamyate kitappaccayādīnaṃ kamme vihitattā, evañca dhuhi kimekamudāharaṇaṃ dattamācariyene tyato āha- ‘udāharaṇa’iccādi, anabhihiteti vacanaṃ vināpīti vacanaṃ vinā evāti avadhāraṇe-apisaddo, sambhāvanevā, yadyabhihitehi vacanaṃ vināpi dutiyādīnamappavatti bhaveyya, vacanasabbhāve tu kathāyeva natthīti attho, evañca panettha dutiyādīnamabhihite pasaṅgābhāvo jānitabbo “paccate odano, kato kaṭoccādopi yadi dutiyādayo siyuṃ paṭhamāvidhānassāvakāso na bhaveyya tato sāmatthiyānabhihiteyeva kammādo dutiyādayo sakiriyā (yaṃ tada)bhibyattiyā bhavissanti, paṭhamevatvabhihite”ti, na nuca paṭhamāyākārakamavakāso rukkho pilakkhoti rukkho pilakkhoti kriyāpadaṃ na sūyateti vibhatyantarassappatti maññatebhassāpadīpa kimidamuccate akārakanti yadya kārakaṃ nedampayogamarahati tato yattha visesakiriyāna massavanaṃ tattha padatthasahacaritāya sattāya patītiyā ‘rukkho atthi [M 0.0077] pilakkho atthī’ti apekkhīyatīti kārakattaṃ rukkhādīna mattheveti attheveti ññataṃ vatthuṃ paraṃ patipādayituṃ saddo payujjate ññaṇañca satoiti yatra kriyāpadantarassa appayogo tatra ussaggato sattā patītitutthīti kriyāpadānusaṅgara kattari tatiyappasaṅgaranavakāsā paṭhamā tyattho-bhassapadīpa, na ca uccaṃ nīcaṃtyadhikaraṇavācitte vācikā nipātassa atthītyanena natthi sambandhoti uccamatthītyādheyyasseva kattuttaṃ nādhārassātya kārakattamādhārassātyavakāso-tthi paṭhamāyāti “paṭhamāvidhā nassāvakāso na bhaveyyā”ti yathāvutto-yaṃ hetu asiddhoti ca sakkā vattuṃ, asaṅkhyato paṭhamātyavatvā “paṭhamāttha matte”ti (2.39) sāmaññavidhānato siddhoyeva, yaṃ hetuttānabhihitavacanamanatthakamicceva ṭhitaṃ.

Although in the commentary, it is not stated regarding what is expressed by compounds beginning with tabba, iṇa, etc., nevertheless, illustrating that it should be understood in the same way even when expressed by them, he says: 'evaṃ' (thus), etc. The form kato (done) has the suffix kta in the sense of object, according to the rule 'kta in the sense of state and object' (5-56). In 'satiko', the form 'kīto' is in the sense of object, with the suffix 'ika' according to the rule 'other suffixes are also seen' (4-120). Object-ness is understood because suffixes like kita etc. are prescribed in the sense of the object. And thus, why has the teacher given only one example? Therefore, he says: 'udāharaṇa' (example), etc. 'Anabhihite' (when not expressed) means 'even without the word.' The particle 'api' here is used in the sense of emphasis or possibility. If, when [the object is] expressed, the second and other case endings do not apply even without the word [anabhihite], then when the word is present, there is no question at all. And here, it should be understood that there is no occasion for the second and other case endings to arise when [the object is] expressed. 'If, in examples like 'paccate odano' (rice is being cooked) and 'kato kaṭo' (a mat is made), the second and other case endings were to apply, the rule for the first case ending would have no scope. Therefore, by implication, the second and other case endings will apply only to an unexpressed object etc., for the manifestation of its connection with the action, whereas the first case ending applies when [the object is] expressed.' But is it not the case that the first case ending has scope in a non-kāraka, as in 'rukkho pilakkho' (a tree, a fig tree)? Why is this said to be a non-kāraka? If it were a kāraka, this usage would not be appropriate. Therefore, where a specific action is not heard, there, through the understanding of existence that accompanies the meaning of the word, 'rukkho atthi, pilakkho atthi' (a tree exists, a fig tree exists) is expected, and thus the kāraka-status of 'rukkha' etc. certainly exists. And it is not that the particle, when denoting a location as in 'uccaṃ nīcaṃ' (high, low), has no connection with 'atthi' (is). In 'uccamatthi' (there is height), agent-hood belongs to the content (ādheyya), not to the base (ādhāra); thus, the base is a non-kāraka, and so there is scope for the first case ending. Therefore, it can be said that this afore-mentioned reason, 'the rule for the first case ending would have no scope,' is unproven. Because, without stating 'the first case ending when number is not expressed,' it is already established by the general rule 'in the mere sense of the nominal stem' (2.39). For which reason, the statement 'anabhihite' (when not expressed) stands as meaningless.

Yañcāti casaddo vattabbantarasamuccaye aparampi kiñci vattabbamatthīti attho, yañca phalaṃ maññateti sambandho, yadetthāna bhihitādhikāro natthi tadā yathā ‘kato kaṭo’ccatrattena kammassābhihitattā dutiyā na hoti tathā ‘kaṭaṃ karoti vipulaṃ dassanīya’nti kaṭasaddato uppannāya dutiyāya (vipulādigatassa) kammassā bhihitattā vipulādīhi visesanehi dutiyā na siyā, tato tyādi tabbādiṇādisamāsehi kammassāna bhihitattamattevāti vipulādīhipi dutiyāvidhānasaṅkhātaṃ anabhihite”ti (2-3-1) anabhihita vacanassa adhikāre yañca phalaṃ cintayatīti attho, yuttassātimassa attho sambandhassāti, paccekaṃ karotyabhisambandhatāyāti ‘kaṭaṃ karoti vipulaṃ karoti dassanīyaṃ karoti’ccevaṃ paccekaṃ paccekaṃ karotissābhisambandhatāyāti attho, kammatā atthīti seso, evaṃ maññate-“kaṭaṃ karomīti pavatto vipulaṃ karomī dassaniyaṃ karomīti ca pavattovāti vipulādīnampi paccekaṃ kammatā attheva, tatthekassābhidhāne parekassa sukhamavalokayantīti tadabhidhānāyapi dutiyā bhavissatī”ti, pakārantarāvatāro nācariye noparodhitoti tampi panettha dassayissāma-“kaṭasaddā uppajjamānā dutiyā [M 0.0078] kaṭajāti kammamabhihitavatī, na vipulādiguṇakammaṃ, tato tadabhidhānāya ca dutiyāyeva bhavati, athavā kaṭova kammaṃ, taṃ sāmānādhikaraṇyena vipulādīhipi dutiyā bhavissati, kaṭaṃ karoti vipulo dassanīyoti hi vuccamāne vipulādayo kattusamānādhikaraṇatāyeva patīyeyyuṃ tasmā kaṭasaddasāmānādhikaraṇyampaṭipādayatā vassamettha dutiyā karaṇīyā”ti. Nanvemiccādicodyaṃ, evanti evaṃ guṇayuttassa kammatāya sati, pappotīti kaṭa kamme-bhidhāniye (kato) ti ktappaccayassa katattā udārādito karotyabhisambandhā dutiyā pappotīti attho, evaṃ maññateccādi parihāro, avayavena kammaṃ na vadatīti sambandho, avayavenāti visuṃvisuṃ, kiñcarahīti āha-‘sabhāvato sabbaṃ kammaṃ vadatī’ti. Hotu kāmaṃ udārāditopi vuttena vidhinā paṭhamā, katasaddato kā pavattatīti āha-‘katasaddato pi’ccādi, antobhūto antogadho nāmassa saddassa attho yasmiṃ kammalakkhaṇattheso attho kammalakkhaṇo abhihito kathito sampanno sampajjatīti attho, nanu ‘kato kaṭo’ccādo sabhāvato sabbakammavuttiyā antobhūtanāmatthavuttiyā cātthamatte hoti sabbattha paṭhamāti ‘kaṭaṃ karoti uḷāraṃ sobhanaṃ dassanīya’nti kaṭāditopi uppannāya dutiyāya kammassābhihitattā uḷārādīhi paṭhamāppasaṅgo siyāti abhihitābhidhānappasaṅgopagataṃ codanaṃ manasi nidhāyāha-‘kaṭādisaddo tvi’ccādi, sāmaññenāti visuṃ visuṃ kaṭādisāmaññena.

In `yañca`, the particle `ca` is for the accumulation of another thing to be said; the meaning is, 'there is something else to be said.' The connection is with `yañca phalaṃ maññate` (and whatever fruit one imagines). When there is no governing rule of the unexpressed here, then just as in `kato kaṭo` the accusative does not occur because the object is expressed by the suffix, similarly, in `kaṭaṃ karoti vipulaṃ dassanīyaṃ`, the accusative should not arise from the adjectives `vipula`, etc., since the object is already expressed by the accusative arising from `kaṭa`. Therefore, with suffixes like `-tva`, compounds with `tabba`, `aṇīya`, etc., since the object is merely unexpressed, the accusative is prescribed even for `vipula`, etc., under the governing rule of the word `anabhihite` (2-3-1), which refers to the unexpressed, meaning 'and whatever fruit one contemplates.' The meaning of `yuttassātimassa` is 'of connection.' The phrase `paccekaṃ karotyabhisambandhatāyāti` means 'because of being related to `karoti` individually,' as in `kaṭaṃ karoti, vipulaṃ karoti, dassanīyaṃ karoti`—each is related to `karoti` individually. The remainder is `kammatā atthi`, meaning 'there is objecthood.' Thus, one thinks: 'When one proceeds saying, “I make a pot,” and also proceeds saying, “I make it extensive,” “I make it beautiful,” then objecthood exists individually even for `vipula`, etc. There, when one is expressed, anticipating the ease of the other, the accusative will occur for expressing that too.' The introduction of another method is not opposed by the teacher, so we will show that here as well: 'The accusative arising from the word `kaṭa` has expressed the object of the pot-class, but not the object which is the qualities such as `vipula`, etc. Therefore, the accusative arises for expressing that. Alternatively, only the pot is the object. By co-referentiality, the accusative will occur even with `vipula`, etc. For if one were to say `kaṭaṃ karoti vipulo dassanīyo`, the words `vipula`, etc., would be understood as being in co-referentiality with the agent. Therefore, to establish co-referentiality with the word `kaṭa`, the accusative must necessarily be applied here.' The objection begins with `nanu evaṃ`. Thus, when there is objecthood endowed with such qualities, it is obtained. The meaning of `pappoti` is: because the suffix `-kta` is used when the object `kaṭa` is to be expressed (as in `kato`), the accusative is obtained from `udāra`, etc., due to the connection with `karoti`. The refutation begins with `evaṃ maññate`, etc. The connection is 'it does not express the object by a part.' `Avayavena` means 'separately.' What then? He says: 'By its nature, it expresses the whole object.' Let it be so, the nominative also occurs from `udāra`, etc., by the stated method. But how does it arise from `katasaddato`? He says: 'from the word `kata` etc.' The meaning is: that in which the meaning of the nominal word is included, inherent, that meaning characterized by the object is expressed, stated, accomplished, becomes accomplished. But in `kato kaṭo`, etc., by virtue of expressing the whole object by its nature and by virtue of the meaning of the name being inherent, the nominative occurs everywhere in the sense of the mere stem-meaning. So, in `kaṭaṃ karoti uḷāraṃ sobhanaṃ dassanīyaṃ`, since the object is expressed by the accusative arising from `kaṭa`, etc., would there not be the undesirable consequence of the nominative for `uḷāra`, etc.? Keeping in mind this objection concerning the undesirable consequence of expressing what is already expressed, he says: 'But the word `kaṭādi`, etc.' `Sāmaññena` means `visuṃ visuṃ` (separately), by the generality of `kaṭa`, etc.

“Katturicchitatama”ntyanena (1-4-49) kattuno kiriyāya sambandhi tumiṭṭhatamaṃ tasmiṃ icchitatame kammasaññaṃ vidhāya nibbatyādikesutīsu kammesu dutiyā vidhīyate pāṇinīyehi, icchitatamattañca tadatthattā kiriyāya, odanaṃ pacati gāvumpayo dohatityādo(hi) odanādyatthā pacanādikiriyārabbhateti odanapayādīnamicchitatamattaṃ, tadupadassento āha-‘yaṃ kattu’ccādi, vibhattiṃ vidhāya dutiyābhimatāti sambandho, puna payādinipphattinimittaṃ yaṃkiñci dohanādikiriyā yuttaṃ [M 0.0079] karaṇādirūpena akathitaṃ gavādikamicchitaṃ kārakaṃ, tatthāpi “akathitañcā”ti (1-4-51) kammasaññaṃ vidhāya teneva dutiyā vidhīyate, tadupadassetumāha-‘upayujjamāne’ccādi, atra cevamakathitaniyamo kato vāttikakārena-

By this rule ‘Katturicchitatama’ (1-4-49), having prescribed the designation of object for that which is most desired by the agent in relation to the action, the accusative case is enjoined by the Pāṇinīyas in the case of objects of actions like ‘producing’ etc. And the state of being most desired is because it is the purpose of the action—for example, in ‘he cooks rice,’ ‘he milks the cow for milk,’ the actions of cooking, etc., are undertaken for the purpose of rice, etc., and thus rice, milk, etc., are the most desired. Illustrating that, he says: ‘what the doer...’ etc. Having prescribed the case-ending, the connection is that the accusative case is intended. Again, whatever desired kāraka (participant) like the cow, etc., which is unstated in the form of an instrument, etc., and is connected with the action of milking, etc., for the purpose of producing milk, etc., there too, by the rule ‘akathitañca’ (1-4-51), having prescribed the designation of object, the accusative case is enjoined by that very rule. To illustrate this, he says—‘when employed,’ etc. Here, this rule regarding the unstated is made by the author of the Vārttika—

Pucchicibhikkhīnaṃ duhi,yācīnaṃ nimittamupayoge;

Pubbavidhimhi-kathitaṃ, brūsāsīnañca guṇāsattanti.

For the verbs `pucch` (to ask), `ci` (to gather), `bhikkh` (to beg), `duh` (to milk), and `yāc` (to request), the secondary object (`nimitta`) in application; and for `brū` (to speak) and `sās` (to instruct), that which is connected to the secondary element (`guṇa`), when unstated by a prior rule.

Upayujjate iṭṭhatthasiddhiyaṃ byāpārīyatītyupayogo-payoppabhuti, tasmiṃ, nimittaṃ gavādi, apubbavidhimhi apādānādhikaraṇādi pubbasaññā vidhānābhāve, vidhāne hi māṇavakā maggaṃ pucchati, rukkhā phalānyavacinātyādi yathārahaṃ bhavati, guṇāsattanti guṇena sattaṃ sambandhī, guṇasaddenettha padhānasādhanaṃ dhammādikaṃ vattumicchitaṃ padhānasādhanañhi kiriyāyopakārakamupakāriyaṃ padhānabhūtaṃ kiriyamapekkhiya guṇo bhavati, co-nuttasamuccaye, padhānantu dhammādino pavattiyā tadatthattā, upayujjamānañca taṃ payopabhuticeti visesanasamāsaṃ katvā upayujjamānapayoppabhutino nimittanti chaṭṭhīsamāso, pabhuti saddena gavādino gahaṇaṃ, ādisaddena gomantādino, dutiyenādi saddena adhikaraṇādino, catutthena vinayādino, vidhānanti dutiyā vidhānaṃ, dutiyāvidhānamabhimatanti yojanīyaṃ. Pāṇiniyehi “tathā yuttañcānicchitaṃ” (1-4-50) iccanena kammasaññaṃ vidhāya “kamme dutiyā” (2-3-2) tyaneneva dutiyā vidhīyate, tandassetumāha-‘yene’ccādi, “tathā yuttañcānicchita”ntīmassa attho yeneveccādipañcikāpāṭhānusārena veditabbo, yujjateti kiriyābhisambajjhate, yuttanti kiriyābhisambandhaṃ, atra tu–

`Upayoga` refers to that which is used, that which is engaged for the accomplishment of a desired purpose, such as milk and so forth. In that, the secondary object (`nimitta`) is the cow, etc. `Apubbavidhimhi` means in the absence of a prior rule, i.e., in the absence of a prior designation such as ablative (`apādāna`) or locative (`adhikaraṇa`), etc. For when there is such a rule, examples like `māṇavakaṃ maggaṃ pucchati` (he asks the young man the path) and `rukkhaṃ phalāni avacināti` (he gathers fruits from the tree) occur as appropriate. `Guṇāsattanti` means `guṇena sattaṃ`, connected by a secondary element (`guṇa`). Here, by the term `guṇa`, the principal means (`padhānasādhana`), such as Dhamma, etc., is intended to be stated. For the principal means is indeed helpful to the action, being instrumental and fundamental, and it becomes a `guṇa` (secondary) in relation to the principal action. The particle `ca` is for the inclusion of what is unstated. The principal, however, is the Dhamma, etc., because the activity is for that purpose. And that which is being used is milk, etc. Having formed a descriptive compound (`visesanasamāsa`), `upayujjamāna-payoppabhuti` (that which is being used, beginning with milk), the genitive compound (`chaṭṭhīsamāsa`) is `upayujjamānapayoppabhutino nimittaṃ` (the secondary object of that which is being used, beginning with milk). By the term `pabhuti`, the cow, etc., is understood. By the first term `ādi`, Gomanta, etc., is included. By the second term `ādi`, the substratum (`adhikaraṇa`), etc., is included. By the fourth, the Vinaya, etc., is included. `Vidhānaṃ` (rule) refers to the rule for the accusative case; it should be construed as 'the rule for the accusative case is intended.' By Pāṇini’s rule `tathā yuttañcānīpsitaṃ` (1-4-50), having prescribed the designation of object, the accusative case is enjoined by the rule `kammaṇi dutiyā` (2-3-2). To show this, he says—`yena`, etc. The meaning of `tathā yuttañcānīpsitaṃ` should be understood according to the reading of the Pañcikā, beginning with `yena eva`, etc. `Yujjate` means 'it is connected with the action.' `Yuttaṃ` means 'connected with the action.' Here, however—

Yadyabuddhyāhilaṅghādi, tadāhyādimanicchitaṃ;

Yadā lajjābhayādīhi, tadecchi tatamaṃ mataṃ.

If one crosses a snake, etc., unintentionally, then the snake, etc., is undesired; but when one acts due to shame, fear, etc., then that very thing is considered the most desired.

“Tathā yuttañcānicchita”nti suttenassa pariyudāsavuttito icchitā aññamanicchitamanabhimatamitarañca, tatoyeva‘gāmaṃ gacchanto rukkhamūlamupasappatī’tyatra nevicchitanānicchitassapi rukkhamūlassa kamma saññā [M 0.0080] siddhāti tattha “kamme dutiyā”ti dutiyā vidhīyate, tandasseti’nevicchitanānicchitasmā’iccādi, rukkhamūlaṃ nevicchitaṃ pubbamanabhimatattā, nāpyanicchitaṃ appaṭikūlattā, gāmagamena hyassa tapparatā, rukkhamūlopasappanantu pasaṅgāgatanti rukkhamūlānampi kiriyābhisambandho attheva, atrāpi-

By the sutta `Tathā yuttañcānicchitaṃ` (Thus connected and not desired), since it is stated as a qualified negation (`pariyudāsa`), it refers to that which is other than the desired: the undesired, the disliked, and the indifferent. Therefore, in the example 'while going to the village, he approaches the foot of a tree,' the designation of object is established even for the foot of the tree, which is neither desired nor undesired. There, the accusative case is prescribed by `kamme dutiyā` (the accusative for the object). This is shown by 'from that which is neither desired nor undesired,' etc. The foot of the tree is not desired, because it was not previously intended; nor is it undesired, because it is not disliked. For his focus is on going to the village; approaching the foot of the tree, however, comes about incidentally. Thus, for the foot of the tree as well, there is indeed a connection with the action. Here too—

Nevicchitānicchitantu, mabuddhiyupasappane;

Mūlaṃ vissamanatthantu, tamicchitatamaṃ siyā.

When approaching unintentionally, it is neither desired nor undesired. But if the foot of the tree is for the purpose of resting, then it would be the most desired.

Brūsāsinañcāti casaddopasaṅgahite dassetumāha-‘eva’miccādi, ettha gāmadevadattagaggānamakathitasaññā, ajādayo tvicchitatamā, ādisaddena ‘pattheti gāvuṃ purisaṃ dvijo’tyādayo saṅgahitā, nayatinī=pāpuṇane, vahati vaha=pāpuṇane, harati hara=haraṇe, jayatiji=jaye, sabbatthaleca ette ayādese ca rūpaṃ, daṇḍa=daṇḍane curādittā ṇimhi rūpaṃ, atha “adhisīṭṭhāsānaṃ kammaṃ”tyādinā (1-4-46) tena tena kammasaññaṃ vidhāya ‘paṭhaviṃ adhisessatī’ti ādo (tattha) tattha “kamme dutiyā”ti (2-3-2) dutiyā vidhīyate tehi tehi sattha kārehi, sabbatthevettha lokassa kammavacanicchāti kamenetaṃññasaññāpubbakaṃ kammamupadassento āha-‘adhipubba’iccādi, yāya vatticchāya dutiyā siyā tāya vatticchāya kammatā kathaṃhināmāti sambandho, neva upalabbhantīti kadācikassaci siyāti sambandho, payatitabbanti suttantaramārabbhanīyaṃ, tatthevaṃ kiṃ bhavato manasi dosadhijambhanenāti attho, dhammeti etthāpi evaṃ saddaṃ yojetvā attho veditabbo, yathā ādhāre kammavacanicchā, tathehāpi ādhāravacanicchāti attho, tenevāha-‘dhammeti ādhāravacanicchā’ti, dhamme abhinivisateti sambandho, evaṃsaddasamānatthattā tathā saddassa tadatthānusāreneva viññāyatīti tathāsaddassa attho visuṃ na vutto, pānañca ācāroca pānācāraṃ, taṃpānācāramassa ādhārassa tasmiṃ tappānācāre, pānatthācāratthadhātusambandhī yo nadyādi ko ādhāro so pānācāravāyevāti āha- ‘pānatthācāratthānaṃ dhātūnamādhāre’ti[M 0.0081], kesañcīti aniyamena kesañci saddasatthakārānaṃ, etthāti etasmiṃ ādhāravacanicchāpakkhe, patiparīhi bhāgecetyavasiddhāti iminā patisaddassa dhātunā ayuttataṃ dasseti… yadi yujjeyya chaṭṭhiyābhāvā, tenāha-‘yadātvi’ccādi, vuttiyaṃ tenāti tasaddena, apisaddopasaṅgahitaṃ tatiyampi gahetvā vācāti bahuvacananiddeso.

To show what is included by the particle 'ca' in 'Brūsāsinañcāti', he says 'evaṃ' and so on. Here, 'village', 'Devadatta', and 'cows' have the designation 'unstated'. However, 'goats' and others are most desired. By the word 'ādi', expressions such as 'the brahmin desires a cow from the man' are included. Nayati (from the root nī) means 'to cause to reach'; vahati (from vaha) means 'to cause to reach'; harati (from hara) means 'to take'; jayati (from ji) means 'to conquer'. And in all these instances, the form is with the substitution of 'aya'. Daṇḍa means 'to punish'; being in the curādi class, the form is with 'ṇi'. Then, having established the designation of 'object' (kamma-saññā) in each case by the rule 'adhisīṭṭhāsānaṃ kammaṃ' (1-4-46) and so on, for example, in 'he will lie upon the earth' ('paṭhaviṃ adhisessatī'), the second case is enjoined by those respective grammarians with the rule 'the second case in the object' ('kamme dutiyā') (2-3-2). In all these instances, there is the world's desire to express the object. Thus, indicating an object preceded by another designation in this sequence, he says 'adhipubba' and so on. The connection is: by whatever expressive desire the second case would occur, how indeed can objectness exist by that same expressive desire? The connection is that 'it is not found' means it might occasionally exist for someone. 'Payatitabbaṃ' should be initiated by another sutta. Here, the meaning is thus: 'What is in your mind, venerable sir, with this obstruction by the poison of hatred?' In 'dhammeti' here too, the meaning should be understood by connecting the word 'evaṃ'. Just as there is a desire to express the object in the locative, so too here there is a desire to express the locative; this is the meaning. Therefore, he says, 'In "dhammeti" there is a desire to express the locative.' The connection is 'he is intent on the Dhamma'. Because the word 'tathā' has a similar meaning to the word 'evaṃ,' its meaning is understood according to the meaning of that word; therefore, the meaning of the word 'tathā' is not stated separately. Drinking and conduct constitute 'pānācāra'. That 'pānācāra' is its basis; in that 'pānācāra', whatever basis, such as a river, is related to the roots meaning 'drinking' and 'conduct', that is indeed 'pānācāravā'. Therefore, he says, 'in the basis of roots meaning drinking and conduct'. 'Kesañci' means 'of some', without restriction, of some grammarians. 'Ettha' means in this case of the desire to express the locative. With 'patiparīhi bhāgecetyavasiddhā', he shows the unsuitability of the word 'pati' with the root... If it were suitable, it would be because of the absence of the sixth case. Therefore, he says, 'yadā tu' and so on. In the commentary, 'tena' means by that word. Taking also the third case, which is included by the word 'api', the plural indication is 'vācā'.

3. Kāla

3. Time

Yadā kāladdhānamiccādinā‘māsamāsate kosaṃ sayati’ccādo akammakehipi yoge kālabhāvaddhadesānaṃ parehi kammattamanuññātanti ca, yadātviccādinā tu kiriyāva sabbenasabbaṃ na sūyati, tathā sati kuto ca kammattanti teheva vuttantī ca dasseti, gamma mānakiriyāyogopi na nissito… māsamāsateccādīsu āsanādi āsanādīsu (potthake) kiriyānaṃ māsādiyogo viya kalyāṇittaguṇādiyogo ca lokassa patītipathamupayātīti, na sijjhatīti kiriyā na honti guṇadabbānīti kiriyāsambandhābhāvā kammattābhāvoti na sijjhati, guḷena missā dhānā bhajjitayavā guḷadhānā. Ajjhayanakiriyāya pabbatena ca māsakosānaṃ sākallena sambandhābhāvā accantasaṃyogābhāvoti māsassātiādīsu na dutiyā. Pubbaṇhe samayanti iminā pubbaṇhe samayoti sattamīāmādisamāsaṃ dasseti, accanta mevāti iminā samayassa sākallena viharaṇakiriyāya sambandhamāha, yaṃsamayaṃ karuṇāvihārena vihāsi, taṃ ekaṃsamayanti sambandho, upasaṅkamanakiriyāyaccantameva yuttoti iminā nivāsanaviharaṇa kiriyāhipi pubbaṇhasamayādīnamaccantameva yuttataṃ upalakkheti, pakārantarenāpi siddhiyamāsaṅkamubbhāvayati ‘yadā tvi’ccādinā, vibhattiyā vipallāso yathāpakatamatikkamma aññathā bhavanaṃ, idha pana sattami yampattāyaṃ sattamyatthe bāhulakena “kamme dutiyā”cceva dutiyāppatti.

And when, by 'kāladdhānaṃ' and so on, as in 'he sits for a month' (māsamāsate), 'he sleeps for a kosa' (kosaṃ sayati), the objectness of time, state, duration, and place is allowed by others even in connection with intransitive verbs. But when, by 'yadā tu' and so on, the action is not heard at all, then how can there be objectness? This is also shown by those very grammarians. The connection to an implied action is also not relied upon... In phrases like 'māsamāsate' and so on, the connection of actions like sitting to a month, etc., is like the connection of qualities such as auspiciousness, etc., which comes to be understood by the world. 'It does not succeed' means: because qualities and substances are not actions, there is no connection to an action, and thus no objectness; therefore, it does not succeed. 'Guḷadhānā' are grains mixed with molasses, or roasted barley. Because there is no complete connection of the mountain with the action of studying, nor of the month and the kosa in their entirety, there is no absolute connection. Therefore, in cases like 'māsassa' (of the month), the second case is not used. With 'pubbaṇhe samayaṃ', he shows a compound like 'pubbaṇhe samayo' which has a seventh case member. With 'accantameva', he states the complete connection of the time with the action of dwelling. The connection is: 'the time when he dwelt with the abiding in compassion, that one time'. With 'the action of approaching is absolutely fitting', he indicates the absolute suitability of the morning time and so on, even with the actions of dressing and dwelling. He also raises a doubt about its success in another way, with 'yadā tu' and so on. The interchange of case endings is a becoming otherwise, transgressing what is natural. Here, however, for that which has attained the seventh case, the second case arises in the meaning of the seventh case, frequently by the rule 'kamme dutiyā'.

Tatiyābhimatāti “apavagge tatiyā”ti (2-3-6) vacanena pāṇiniyānaṃpapañcattamabhimatā, kathampana kāladdhānaṃ karaṇattamiccāsaṅkiya karaṇattamesampaṭipādento [M 0.0082] āha-‘tathāpi’ccādi, tathāpīti vuttakkamena karaṇattasambhavā tatiyāya vijjamānāyapi, siyāti tatiyā siyā, tañcāti taṃ karaṇañca. Kārakamajjheti ettha chaṭṭhī samāso kārakasaddena ca sattikārakaṃ gahitanti (āha) ‘dvinnaṃ kattusattīnaṃ majjhe’ti, abhinnassāpi hi ekassa devadattādikattuno bhinnānaṃ taṃsamavetānaṃ kattusattīnaṃ majjhe kāladdhānāni, sattibhedameva byañjayamāha-‘tathāhi’ccādi, ekatthāti ekasmiṃ devadatte, dvīhetīte (bhuñjikriyā) sādhananti sambandho, dvinnaṃ ahānaṃ samāhāro dvīhaṃ tasmiṃ. Isumasatīti vā, isumhi āso asseti vā nipphannena issāsasaddena gammamānaṃ kiriyaṃ dasseti ‘isvasane’ti, nanviccādi codyaṃ, dhanupañcasataṃ koso, evamaññateccādi parihāro, chaṭṭhiyāsampattāyanti kosassekadeseti evaṃ chaṭṭhiyā sampattāyaṃ, muttasaṃsayenedaṃ samānanti mutto saṃsayo yasmiṃ avadhyādo tenetaṃ tulyanti attho. Vuttiyaṃ abhimatāti “sattamī pañcamiyo kārakamajjhe”ti (2-3-7) vacanena sattamīpañcamiyo papañcattamabhimatā, dvīhe bhuñjissatīti dvīsu divasesu gatesu bhuñjissatīti attho, “yabbhāvo bhāvalakkhaṇa”nti (2-36) sattamī, sakasakakārakavacanicchāyevāti hi idaṃ bāhullaṃ nissāya vuttaṃ, dvīhā bhuñjissati kosā vijjhatīti dvīhā nikkhamma bhuñjissati, kosā nikkhamma ṭhitaṃ lakkhaṃ vijjhati upāttavisayo-yamavadhi, kose vijjhatīti kose ṭhitaṃ lakkhaṃ vijjhatīti attho.

'The third is preferred' means, by the statement 'the third in apavagga' (2-3-6), it is preferred by the Pāṇinians for its detailed explanation. But how can time and duration be instrumental? Having thus raised the doubt, he says 'tathāpi' and so on, explaining their instrumentality. 'Tathāpi' means, due to the possibility of instrumentality by the stated method, even when the third case is present, it may be—the third case may be. And that—that instrument. 'Among the kārakas'—here, it is a sixth case compound, and by the word 'kāraka', the agentive kāraka is taken. He says: 'between two agentive powers'. Indeed, even for a single undivided agent like Devadatta, time and duration are among the distinct agentive powers inherent in it. He says 'tathāhi' and so on, expressing the distinction of powers. 'Ekattha' means in one Devadatta. The connection is: 'two days having passed' is the means of the action of eating. 'Dvīhaṃ' is the aggregate of two days; in that. By the word 'issāsa', derived from 'isum asati' (he throws an arrow) or 'isumhi āso assa' (his is the throwing of an arrow), he shows the implied action as 'isv-asane' (in the throwing of an arrow). 'Nanvi' and so on is the objection. A kosa is five hundred bows. 'Evamaññate' and so on is the refutation. 'When the sixth case is attained' means, when the sixth case is attained in the sense of 'a part of a kosa'. The meaning of 'this is equal to that which is freed from doubt' is: it is comparable to that from which doubt is removed, such as the limit. In the commentary, 'it is preferred' means, by the statement 'the seventh and fifth among the kārakas' (2-3-7), the fifth and seventh cases are preferred for their detailed explanation. 'He will eat in two days' means, he will eat after two days have passed. The seventh case is by 'yabbhāvo bhāvalakkhaṇa' (2-3-36). Indeed, this is said relying on the abundance of the desire to express their respective kārakas. 'He will eat from two days, he shoots from a kosa' means, having departed from two days he will eat; having departed from a kosa, he hits the target placed there. This is the limit, the scope obtained. 'He shoots at a kosa' means he hits the target placed at a kosa.

4. Gati

4. Movement

Katacatthasamāsāti kato catthasamāso yesu te tathā vuttā, aññapadatthavuttayoti aññapadatthe vutti yesanti byadhikaraṇaññapadatthasamāso, cattasamāse gatyādīnaṃ visuṃvisuṃ padhānattā tehi paraṃ payujjamāno atthasaddo gatyādīhi paccekamabhisambajjhatīti maññate, atha sutte ‘payojje’iccetāvatyuccamāne payojjo sayaṃ kattāti kathaṃ viññāyati yena ‘payojje kattarī’ti vivaraṇaṃ katamiccāsaṅkiyāha-‘gatyādyattha’miccādi, ādisaddena bodhā dīnaṃ [M 0.0083] gahaṇaṃ, takkiriyāsamatthovāti tassā gatyādikāya kiriyāya samattho eva niyujjateti sambandho, kiriyākaraṇe samattho nāma kattāvāti āha-‘soca kattā’ti. Dutiyāya siddhāyāti vakkhamānanayena payojjassa kattuno kammattasiddhiyā “kamme dutiyā”ti sutteneva kamme dutiyāya siddhāya. Kiṃ lakkhaṇo-yaṃ niyamo yadatthami damārabhīyaticcāha-‘gatyādyatthāna’miccādi, paccudāharīyissate ‘etesameve’ccādinā, tathācābbhupagame, payojjo kattā na kammaṃ tyabbhupagamma payojje kattarī’ti vivaritanti attho, sāmatthiyampanaiccādinā sāmatthiyasarūpamāha, gati ādyatthānanti padacchedo, niyujjamāno payojakabyāpārasaṅkhātāya kiriyāya sambandhīyamānattā kammabhūtova bhavatīti attho, ayametthādhippāyo “gamanādikiriyāya sādhanattā yadipi payojjo kattā, tathāpi so payojakena gamanādīsu byāpāriyamāno payojakassa byāpāralakkhaṇāya kiriyāya sambandhīyamāno yadi kammaṃ na hoti aññathā kiṃ hotīti aññathānupapattilakkhaṇena sāmatthiyena kammabhūtova hotī”ti (attho) (potthake) ( ), patīyateti iminā patītivasenevāssa kammatā, sabhāvato tu payojjo kattāvātipi ñāpeti, payojakoti sabbattha devadattādiko viññeyyo, atthagahaṇassāti “saddākammakabhajjādīna”nti avatvā “saddatthākammakabhajjādīna”nti atthaggahaṇassa, bodhatthassa udāharaṇanti seso, nanu vacanappayojanaṃ dassayatā vacanamevopadassiya pañho kātabbo, atha ‘etesamevā’tyavijjamāneneva kathaṃ tyāsaṅkiyāha ‘etesameve’ccādi, heṭṭhā vuttakkamena niyamatthattā vacanassa evakāro labbhati, sambandhivacanattā etasaddassa tena yathāpaṭhitā gatyādayova visessabhūtā saṅkhepena parāmasīyantīti ete samevāti katanti maññate evosañcāti maññate (potthake), (gacchati devadattoti…pe… nahotīti) iminā imamatthañca joteti “yadipi kiriyābhisambandhā payojjassa viya kattunopi kammattampasajjati, tathāpi payojjeti vuttattā kattari devadatte dutiyā nappasajjatī”ti, abhimatāti “gatibuddhyā”di (1-4-52) suttena [M 0.0084] payojjassa kattuno kammasaññaṃ vidhāya tasmiṃ payojjedutiyābhimatā, carahisaddo pucchāyaṃ, payojetīti asmiṃ uddese tadā kathaṃ bhavitabbanti sesoti yadācarahiccādivākyassāvasāne payojetīti asmiṃ uddese vacanasamīpe’tadā kathambhavitabba’nti pāṭhaseso hotīti attho veditabbo, yāvatāti tatiyantapaṭīrūpako nipāto, yasmā dattho vattate, yasmā dutiyā pappoti tasmā ‘yaññadattene’ti bhavitabbanti sambandho.

Katacatthasamāsa means those compounds in which a fourfold compound has been formed; thus they are called. The expression 'aññapadatthavutti' means 'the expression of another word's meaning'; thus, a compound in which the meaning of another word is expressed is a 'byadhikaraṇaññapadatthasamāsa.' In a fourfold compound, because each of 'gati' (going) and others is principal, it is held that the word 'attha' (meaning), when used after them, is connected with each of 'gati' and others. Now, if in the sutta only 'payojje' (the one caused to act) is stated, how is it understood that the prayojya is himself the agent? To resolve the doubt as to why the explanation 'in the prayojya, the agent' was given, it is said: 'gatyādyattha' (the meaning of going, etc.). By the word 'ādi' (etc.), 'bodha' (understanding) and others are included. 'He who is capable of that action...'; the connection is that he is employed only if he is capable of that action, such as going. 'One capable of performing an action is called an agent.' Thus, it is said: 'And he is the agent.' Since the second case is established: according to the method to be explained, the object-ness of the prayojya (who is an agent) is established by the sutta 'kamme dutiyā' (the second case in the object). 'What is the characteristic of this rule, for what purpose is it begun?' To this, it is said: 'gatyādyatthānaṃ' (of the meanings of going, etc.). It will be counter-exemplified by 'etesameve' (just these) and so on. And if it is accepted that the prayojya is the agent and not the object, then the meaning is that it is explained as 'in the prayojya, the agent.' But by 'sāmatthiyampana' (but capability) and so on, the nature of capability is stated. The word division is 'gati ādi atthānaṃ' (of going, etc., the meanings). 'Being employed, he becomes the object because he is connected with the action designated as the activity of the causer.' The intended meaning here is: 'Even though the prayojya is the agent due to being the means for the action of going, etc., yet when he is engaged by the causer in going, etc., being connected with the action characterized by the causer's activity, if he is not the object, what else could he be?' Thus, by the impossibility of it being otherwise, he is indeed the object. By 'patīyateti' (it is understood), his object-ness is shown only in terms of perception. But by nature, the prayojya is indeed the agent—this is also indicated. 'Prayojaka' (the causer): everywhere, someone like Devadatta is to be understood. Regarding the inclusion of 'attha' (meaning): instead of saying 'saddākammakabhajjādīnaṃ' (of sounds, objects, shares, etc.), it is said 'saddatthākammakabhajjādīnaṃ' (of sounds, meanings, objects, shares, etc.). The remainder is an example for the meaning of 'bodha' (understanding). 'Surely, when showing the purpose of a statement, the question should be posed by presenting the statement itself?' 'But how is it [the question] posed by 'etesameva', which is not present [in the original sutta]?' To this doubt, it is said: 'etesameve' and so on. The particle 'eva' is obtained for the purpose of restriction, in the order stated below. And because it is a word of relation, the word 'eta' (these) in this context briefly refers to 'gati' and others, which are the specific entities as read [in the sutta]. Thus, it is understood that 'ete sameva' is stated. '(Devadatta goes… etc., that is not)'—by this, this meaning is also illuminated: 'Even though, due to connection with the action, object-ness would apply to the agent as it does to the prayojya, nevertheless, because 'payojjeti' (he causes to go) is stated, the second case does not apply to Devadatta, who is the agent.' 'Abhimatā' (it is intended): by the sutta 'gatibuddhyādi' (1-4-52), having prescribed the designation of 'object' for the prayojya who is an agent, the second case is intended for that prayojya. The word 'carahi' is for questioning. 'Payojeti' (he causes to act): in this section, the remainder is 'then how should it be?' This means that when the sentence 'carahi' and so on ends, the remaining part of the text near the word 'payojeti' in this section should be understood as 'then how should it be?' 'Yāvatā' is an indeclinable particle resembling a third case ending. Because the meaning is current, and because the second case is obtained [for the prayojya], therefore it should be 'by Yaññadatta' [for the prayojaka]—this is the connection.

5. Harā

5. Carrying away

Niyameneccādinā vacanārambhassa payojanamāha, sāpi tatiyāpi dutiyāpiti vattabba yadātviccādinā harati nāhāratthe naharatyatthe (potthake) tipi viññāpeti, ubhayatthāti dutiyāya pattāya appattāya ca, vibhāsā vikappoti attho, kāretikara-karaṇe, lettāyādesātilatta ettaayādessa, vada-vacane, abhivadanamabhivādo taṃ karotīti “dhātvatthenāmasmī”ti (5-12) imhi nāmadhātu ‘abhivādi’tisutte niddiṭṭhoti āha-‘abhivādismā’iccādi.

By 'niyamena' and so on, the purpose of beginning the statement is stated. And that third case, by 'yadātu' and so on, also conveys the meaning of 'harati' (to carry) in the sense of 'not carrying away' (nāhāratthe). The meaning of 'ubhayattha' is 'for both the obtained and not-obtained second case.' The meaning of 'vibhāsā' is 'option' or 'alternative.' 'Kāretikara' is in the sense of 'karaṇa' (instrument). 'Lettāyādesātilatta' is for 'ettaayādesa' (the substitution of etta and aya). 'Vada' is in the sense of 'speaking.' 'Abhivādana' is 'abhivāda' (salutation); he performs that. Thus, it is said: 'abhivādismā' and so on, as specified in the nāmadhātu sutta 'abhivādi' in 'dhātvatthenāmasmi' (5-12).

6. Nakhā

6. Nails

Khādayati ādayati khāda, ada=bhakkhaṇe, avhāpayati vhe=avhāne āpubbo, “payojakabyāpāre ṇāpice”ti (5-16) ṇāpimhi pubbasaralopo, kandayati kanda=avhānarodanesu.

He causes to eat, he takes; 'khāda' and 'ada' are roots meaning 'to eat/devour'. He summons; 'vhe' is the root 'to call' with 'ā' prefixed. In the causative activity, there is 'ṇāpice' (5-16), and in 'ṇāpi' the preceding vowel is elided. He causes to cry; 'kanda' is the root 'to call and weep'.

“Vahissāniyantuke”ti gaṇasutte ayamettho “vahissadhātussa payojje kattari niyanturahite dutiyā na bhavatī”ti, niyantā sārathi kiriyāsiddhiṃ niyāmakoti vatvā tameva pakāsetumāha-‘kiriyaṅga’miccādi, kiriyaṅga kiriyopakaraṇabhūtaṃ balī baddādiṃ kiriyākāraṇaṃ, niyametvāti ekasmiṃ karaṇīye kiriyā visaye patiṭṭhapetvā, vāhayati bhāraṃ devadattenetyatra hi devadatto paññavā puriso niyantāramantareneva bhāraṃ vahatītyaniyantuko kattā, vāhayati bhāraṃ balībadde iccatra tu balībaddā niyantā ramantarena na vahantīti saniyantukā.

The meaning of 'vahissāniyantuke' in the Gaṇasutta here is this: 'For the root `vah`, in the prayojya agent who is without a controller, the second case does not occur.' Having said that the controller is the charioteer, the regulator of the accomplishment of the action, to clarify that very point, it is said: 'kiriyaṅga', etc. 'Kiriyaṅga' means an instrument of action, the cause of the action, such as oxen and so forth. 'Having regulated' means having established the action in a single task or sphere. For in the example 'vāhayati bhāraṃ devadattena' (He has Devadatta carry the load), Devadatta, being a wise person, carries the load without a controller; thus, the agent is uncontrolled. But in 'vāhayati bhāraṃ balībadde' (He has the oxen carry the load), the oxen do not carry without a controller; thus, they are controlled.

“Bhikkhissāhiṃsāya”nti [M 0.0085] gaṇasuttassāyamattho “bhakkhissāhiṃsatthassa payojje kattari dutiyā na bhavatī”ti, atha kathamettha hiṃsatthatā bhakkhissa hiṃsā hi cetanāvati sambhavati, na cetthasassaṃ cetanāvantanti āha-‘sabbe’iccādi, sabbeti rukkhādayo, bhāvā padatthā, idāni sabbadassanānukūlahiṃsatthatamupadassetumāha-‘yadive’ccādi, nanu buddhavacana nissitamidaṃ byākaraṇaṃ, tathā sati sammatameve-ttho-padassetvā gantabbaṃ kinnāmāññadassanopagātādhirenāti tuṇhī hoti nikkāraṇissā nikkammissā (potthake) bhavato-pāyoti viññāyati, paratthānubaddhakicchaṃ pana mahāpuññapaññā na kiñci viya maññanti, hoti (hi) etena parattho “matantarepi siddhi sissānaṃ, taṃtaṃ mataññuno vā kadāci karahaci yadidamavalokeyyuṃ te cetthāvatāraṃ cetthakāraṃ (potthake) labheyyuṃ etādiso ca paññavā paṭiladdhabuddhavacanappasādo’ti tadavatārena ca buddhe bhagavati kamena daḷhaṃ pasādaṃ paṭilabheyyu”nti, evamevaṃ tattha tattha taṃtaṃbyākaraṇodāharaṇappasaṅgepi tadanusāreneva tantaṃpayojanaṃ veditabbaṃ, na niratthakakathāpasuto-yamācariyoti.

The meaning of the Gaṇasutta 'Bhikkhissāhiṃsāya' is this: 'For the root `bhakkh` with the meaning of non-harming, the prayojya agent does not take the second case.' Now, how is there a meaning of harming here? For harm occurs to a sentient being, and here the crop is not sentient. Thus, it is said: 'sabbe', etc. 'Sabbe' refers to trees and the like. 'Bhāvā' means 'things' or 'meanings of words'. Now, to illustrate the nature of harmfulness in a way that aligns with all views, it is said: 'yadive', etc. Surely, this grammatical explanation is based on the Buddha's words. That being so, having shown the accepted meaning, one should proceed. Why then remain silent, as if through adherence to another view without cause? It is understood that this is a means for the venerable one to be without reason. But those of great merit and wisdom consider the difficulty connected with the welfare of others as nothing. For by this there is benefit for others: 'Even in another teaching, success for disciples may occur. Those knowing a different teaching might, at some time or place, consider this and gain entry here. And such a wise person, having obtained confidence in the Buddha's words, might through that entry gradually obtain firm confidence in the Blessed Buddha.' Similarly, in each and every instance of grammatical explanation and example, the purpose should be understood according to its context, not thinking that this teacher is given to pointless talk.

Duhādīnaṃ tyevamādo amhākamparamagurunā ratanamatipañcikālaṅkārādikārena nānākārasāratthavedaveditu vedāvedita (potthake) mahāpaññāpāṭavānaṃ paññavantānaṃ sāminā mahāsāminā sambuddhasāsanaratanavaropakārakena ‘idamettha vicāraṇīyaṃ’tyabhidhāya nānāmatantaramākaḍḍhiya bahuṃ sampaveditamatthi, mayampanettha ācariyenādhippetamattamevālamba atthampa kāsayissāma. Satyapyanekadassanabhede siṭṭhappayogānusārena yattha padhānekammanityādippabhutayodissanti, yatra tvappadhānetyādī, yatrobhayatrapi, taṃsabbamiha bhassakārādyanumatakkamena paṭipādayamāha-duhādīna’miccādi, etthādisaddo pakāravācī, tena yācippabhutayo gayhanti, kammadvayayuttānanti niddhāraṇe chaṭṭhī, tena kammadvayayuttānaṃ majjhe duhādīnamappadhānepi gavādo kamme tyādippabhutayoti yojanā[M 0.0086]. Iccāditiādisaddena ‘avarundhati vajaṃ gāvaṃ avarundhīyate vajaṃ go’iccādīnaṃ pariggaho, gamanādyatthāna mityādisaddena bodhatthādīnaṃ gahaṇaṃ. Gamīyate gāmo devadattanti ettha kathaṃ payojjattasambhavoti āha-‘purise’ccādi, yajjapi gāmo tuṇhī hoti nibyāpārattā purisova tu gamanakiriyaṃ nipphādeti, tathāpi purisassa gamanakiriyāya yaṃphalappattilakkhaṇaṃ, tamubhinnampi gāmapurisānaṃ samānanti purisa kiriyātulyaphalattā gāmopi gamanakiriyāya kattubyapadese kāraṇaṃ bhavatīti adhippāyo, tathāhi gāmaṃ gacchanto koci gāme āsanne sati vadati ‘āgato gāmo patto gāmo’ti, atoññesanti ye kammadvayayuttā duhādayo gamanādyatthācodāhaṭā, etehi aññesaṃ, padhāne kammebhi ajādimhi padhāne kamme, padhānattampana ajādīnaṃ kiriyāya payojanattā, ajādyatthā hyānayanakiriyārabhyate. Ayampanettha saṅgaho-

Regarding 'duhādīnaṃ' and so forth, this was extensively explained by our supreme teacher—the great master, the excellent benefactor of the jewel of the Buddha's dispensation, adorned with such qualities as the fivefold brilliance of the Ratana-mati-pañcikā, possessing great wisdom and skill, and a knower of the essence of various meanings—who, after stating, 'This should be examined here,' drew out various alternative views. We, however, relying only upon the meaning intended by the teacher, will explain the meaning here. Although there are many different views, following the usage of the learned, where there is a primary object, where there is a secondary, and where there are both—all this he sets forth here in the order approved by the commentators, beginning with 'duhādīnaṃ.' Here, the word 'ādi' indicates class; thereby, roots such as 'yāci' are included. 'Kammadvayayuttānaṃ' is the genitive of determination; thus, the construction is: 'among those connected with two objects, in the case of the duhādi roots, the case ending is applied to the secondary object, such as the cow (`gavādo kamme`).' By the word 'iccādi,' examples such as 'avarundhati vajaṃ gāvaṃ, avarundhīyate vajaṃ go' are included. By the word 'gamanādyatthānaṃ,' meanings such as 'bodhattha' are included. Regarding 'gamīyate gāmo devadattena,' how is it possible for it to be the object of the action? He says, 'purise,' etc. Although the village is still, being without activity, and it is the man who performs the action of going, nevertheless, the attainment of the fruit of the action of going is common to both the village and the man. Because the village has a fruit similar to the man's action, it becomes a reason for the designation of agent in the action of going—this is the intention. Thus, someone going to a village, when the village is near, says, 'The village has arrived, the village has been reached.' Therefore, for others than these cited examples—those connected with two objects, such as the duhādi roots and those with the meaning of motion—the case ending is applied to the primary object, as in 'ajādimhi.' The primacy of the goat and so on is due to its being the purpose of the action, for the action of bringing is undertaken for the sake of a goat, etc. This, herein, is the summary:

“Duhi yāci rudhi pucchi, bhikkhi ci bruvi sāsi ca;

Ji daṇḍi patthi manthī ca, dhātū honti duhādayo.

"To milk, to beg, to obstruct, to ask, to live by begging, to gather, to speak, and to teach; to conquer, to punish, to spread out, and to churn—these are the roots known as duhādi (those beginning with 'duh').

Gatyādisuttapaṭṭhitā, gatyādyatthā bhavanti te;

Nīvahaharakasāca, nīvahādī bhavanti te.

Established by the rules concerning motion and so forth, they have the meaning of motion and so forth. And the roots 'nī', 'vah', 'hara', and 'kasa' become the group known as nīvādi (those beginning with 'nī' and 'vah').

Dvikammakesu cetesu, appadhāne duhādinaṃ;

Tyādippabhutayo honti, padhāne nīvahādinaṃ;

Ubhayattha payogānu, sārā gatyatthaādinaṃ”ti.

"Among these verbs that take two objects, for the duhādi group, the case endings are applied to the secondary object; for the nīvādi group, to the primary object; for those with the meaning of motion and so forth, according to usage, they are applied to both."

Payogo pana sambandhacintāyamiha ca vuttānusārena sabbathā viññeyyā.

However, the usage, in connection with the analysis of relations here, should be understood in every way according to what has been said.

7. Dhyādi

7. The word 'dhi' and so on

Pubbe kiriyānissayena kārakanissayena (potthake) dutiyāya vihitattā āha ‘idāni’ccādi, dhisaddassa atthappadhāna niddesena vā ādisaddena vā ‘hā devadatta’ntipi hoti, hā devadattadukkhanti tu dukkhena yogā devadattena na yutto hotīti paṭhamāvāmantaṇe. Nanuca antarāsaddena yoge yathārājagahanālandāhi [M 0.0087] dutiyā (tathā) antarā ca rājagahaṃ antarā ca nā landa(nti tathā) antarāmaggeti ettha maggatopi antarāmaggatopi kasmā na dutiyāti tenāyogā, yesañhi taṃmajjhaṃ te tena yujjantīti tehiyeva dutiyā, athavābbhupagatepi taṃyoge taṃsambandhīyeva maggoti mukhyattā tato sabbassa (potthake) na dutiyā, atrāpi chaṭṭhīyeva pappoti antarā tañca mañca kamaṇḍaluiti, tava mama majjhe kamaṇḍalutyattho, atha kamaṇḍalusaddato dutiyā kasmā na bhavati satīpyantarena yoge tassa padhānattā, tathāhi kamaṇḍaluno sakatthā pavatti, tumhamhānantu paratthā-kamaṇḍaluvisesanattena tesaṃ pavattattā, tatra kamaṇḍaluno sakatthe vattamānattā padhānattenāvatattā pāṭipadikato accutattā parattā paṭhameva bhavatīti jīnindabuddhinyāsa. Nindādi lakkhaṇassa sambandhassa sabbhāvā sabbattha sambandhachaṭṭhiyā sampattāyaṃ vacanaṃ, ākatigaṇo-yaṃ.

Previously, because the second case was prescribed by dependence on action, he says, ‘idāni,’ etc. Alternatively, by the primary indication of the meaning of the word ‘dhi’ or by the word ‘ādi,’ it can also be ‘hā Devadatta.’ However, ‘hā devadattadukkhaṃ’ is not so constructed, for due to the connection with 'suffering,' it is not properly connected with 'Devadatta'; thus, the first case or vocative is used. And is it not so that in connection with the word ‘antarā,’ as in ‘antarā ca rājagahaṃ antarā ca nālandaṃ,’ the second case is used? Why then, in the expression ‘antarā maggaṃ,’ is the second case not used with 'magga'? Because there is no connection with it. For only those things which are in the middle are connected with it, and thus the second case applies only to them. Or, even if a connection is accepted, the road itself is what is related, and so due to its primacy, the second case is not used. Here too, the sixth case is obtained, as in ‘antarā tañca mañca kamaṇḍalu,’ which means 'the water-pot is between you and me.' Then why is the second case not used with the word ‘kamaṇḍalu,’ even though there is a connection with ‘antarā’? Because it is primary. Thus, the water-pot functions in its own meaning, whereas ‘you’ and ‘I’ function in relation to another—existing as qualifiers of the water-pot. There, since the water-pot functions in its own meaning, it is primary; because it does not deviate from its nominal stem and because it is subsequent, the first case occurs—this is the system of Jīnindabuddhi. This rule is stated because the genitive of relation, characterized by blame and so forth, is obtained everywhere. This is a class-group.

8. Lakkhaṇi

8. Characteristics

Lakkhaṇādīsvatthesuti nāmassā kassā (potthake) yamatthaniddesoti āha ‘abhināyo yutto’ccādi, tenāti abhinā yuttassātthaniddesa kāraṇena, lakkhaṇasaddena hetu vattumicchitoti āha-‘tatthe’ccādi, duvidho hetu, vuttañhi subodhālaṅkāre “janako ñāpako ceti, duvidhā hetavo siyu”nti (252), samupalakkhayatīti samupalakkhaṇaṃ, saṅketamattaṃ ñāpakaṃ, na tu janakaṃ, saṅketopi lakkhaṇamuccate lakkhīyate kāriyamānenāti katvā, janakassāpyatra lakkhaṇattena gahaṇe payojanaṃ “anunā” (2-10) iccatra daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kañcipakāranti iminā itthaṃsaddassa atthaṃ vadati. Pattoti iminā bhūtasaddassa, ettha hi bhūdhātu pattiyaṃ vattate, rukkholakkhaṇanti rukkho ñāpakahetūti attho… rukkhena vijjuyā ñāpīyamānattā, ācariyajinindabuddhi pana aññathā vaṇṇayati, tassedaṃ mataṃ-

Regarding the phrase 'in the meanings of characteristic, etc.', this is an explanation of the meaning of the noun, so he says, 'abhināyo yutto,' etc. 'Tena' means: because of the explanation of the meaning connected with 'abhinā.' Because he wishes to express 'cause' by the word 'lakkhaṇa,' he says, 'tatthe,' etc. A cause is twofold, for it is said in the Subodhālaṅkāra: 'Causes are of two kinds: generative (janaka) and indicative (ñāpaka).' 'Samupalakkhayati' means 'samupalakkhaṇaṃ,' an indicative sign, which is a mere convention, not a generative cause. A convention is also called a 'lakkhaṇa' because 'it is characterized by what is done.' The purpose of including even a generative cause here as a 'lakkhaṇa' should be seen in the section on 'anunā' (2-10). By 'kañcipakāraṃ,' he states the meaning of the word 'itthaṃ.' By 'patto,' he states the meaning of the word 'bhūta'; here the root 'bhū' is used in the sense of attainment (patti). 'Rukkho lakkhaṇaṃ' means the tree is an indicative cause, because lightning is indicated by the tree. However, the teacher Jinindabuddhi explains it differently. This is his view:

Kriyāya jotako nāyaṃ, sambandhassa na vācako;

Nāpi kriyantarāpekkhī, sambandhassa tu bhedakoti.

This is not an indicator of action, nor a denoter of relation; nor is it dependent on another action, but it is a distinguisher of relation.

Ayamettha [M 0.0088] attho “ayamabhi abhinandatityādīsu viya kiriyāya jotako na hoti, chaṭṭhī viya sambandhassa vācako na hoti, nikkosambītyatra gamanakiriyāpekkhī nisaddo viya nāpi kiriyantarā pekkhī, kiñcarahi sambandhassa tu bhedako visesako bhavatī”ti tamupadassetumāha-‘aññe tvi’ccādi, ettha itisaddo nidassane, rukkhampatvā vijjotate itievaṃ pattikiriyāya patvātivuttarukkhapāpanakiriyāya janitoti attho, tathāhi rukkhassa vijjuyā pāpanābhāve vijjuyā lakkhiyāya tallaṇassa ca rukkhassa yo lakkhiyalakkhaṇabhāvo sambandho, so kena sampādito bhaveyya, nanu sambandhe abhinā jotīyamāne rukkhassa lakkhaṇavuttitā kathaṃ jotīyatīti āha-‘lakkhaṇatthoca visayabhāvenā’ti, tathācetyādinā tasmiṃ pakkhe sambhāvitaṃ dosamubbhāvayati, tatrāya miccādinā yathāvuttadosaparihārāya parehevābhidhīyamānamparihāramāha, parihāropadassanenāssāpi pakkhassāduṭṭhatākhyāpanenesopi pakkho-bbhupagatotyavaseyo, atoyevupari yathāvutta pakkhanissayeneva byākhyāyate, devadattassa sādhuttasaṅkhātaitthampakārappattiyā visayabhāvenāvaṭṭhitā mātā tattha vattati nāmāti āha-‘mātuyā’tiādi, mātā ca itthambhūte pavattā visaya bhāvena devadatto ca tattha visayībhāvena, tesañca visayavisayībhāvalakkhaṇo sambandho itthampattilakkhaṇāya kiriyāya jāto, so mātusambandho hoti kāraṇavasena, socātinā jotīyatīti mātu tenābhinā yogoti āha-‘yvāya’ccādi, mātusambandhoiti yojanā, itthampattiyāti itthampattilakkhaṇāya kiriyāya karaṇabhūtāya, evaṃ maññate “kiñcāpi so sambandho devadattenāpyavinābhāvīti tassa sobhinā jotīyate, tathāpi mātusambandhobhinā jotīyatīti ‘mātu tena yogo’ti ca (vuccati)… saddasattiyā taggatāyeva dutiyāya ubhayagatassāpi sambandhassa jotanato”ti rukkho rukkho tiṭṭhatīti sambandho, ṭhitimpaṭiccāti ṭhitinnissāya esaṃ rukkhānaṃ yo ca sambandhoti yojanā, rukkhānanti iminā rukkhā kiriyāya pare sambandhinoti ñāpeti, ṭhitimpaṭiccāti [M 0.0089] iminā pana tiṭṭhatisaddavacanīyā sādhyarūpā ṭhitikiriyā rukkhato pare sambandhīti, acetanānaṃ rukkhānamapekkhāvirahepi lokampatītivasena ‘pipatīsā’dīnaṃ viññāyamānattā viññāyamānaṭhānāpekkhaṇakiriyāyasādhyasādhanalakkhaṇo sambandho jātoti viññeyyaṃ, so ca rukkhasambandho-bhinā jotīyatīti āha-‘so’tiādi, dvibbacaneneva jotanīyāti vicchātthe vuttimatte satīpi vibhattiyā vicchatthe vutkimattetyādivacanaṃ vicāreretabbaṃvitattiyā abisaddassaca vicchatthe vuttiyā abhāvā, lakkhaṇitthambhūti hi pakativisesanaṃ jotetumasamatthattā vicchāya jotanāya dvibbavacanaṃ kattabbamevāti adhippāyo.

Herein is the meaning: 'In such phrases as ayamabhi abhinandati (this one delights in this), abhi is not an indicator of action; like the sixth case ending, it is not a denoter of relation; nor, like the prefix ni in nikkosambī (going out of Kosambī), which is dependent on the action of going, is it dependent on another action. What then is it? It is a distinguisher or qualifier of the relation.' To illustrate this, it is said, 'Others, however...' and so forth. Here, the word iti serves as an example. For instance, in 'it shines, having reached the tree,' the meaning is that the shining is produced by the action of reaching, that is, by the action of attaining the tree which is expressed by 'having reached.' Indeed, if there is no attainment of the tree by the lightning, by what would the relation between the lightning as the mark and the tree as that which is marked—the relation of being the mark and the marked—be established? If the relation is illuminated by abhi, how is the tree's function as a characteristic illuminated? It is said, 'And the meaning of characteristic is by way of being the object.' By 'and thus...' and so forth, a possible fault in that position is raised. Therein, by 'this...' and so forth, he states the refutation for the aforementioned fault, a refutation which is declared by others. By showing the refutation, the faultlessness of this position is also declared, and thus this position is accepted; this should be understood. Therefore, what follows is explained based on the aforementioned position. Devadatta's mother, who is established in the state of having attained such a quality designated as goodness, exists in that state as the object. It is said, 'of the mother...' and so forth. The mother, being in such a state, is the object, and Devadatta is the subject therein. The relation between them, which is characterized by the state of being object and subject, is produced by the action characterized by the attainment of such a quality. That relation is the mother's relation, by way of being the cause, and it is illuminated by ati. Thus, the connection of the mother with that abhi is stated. It is said, 'that which...' and so forth. The construction is 'the mother's relation.' 'By the attainment of such a quality' means by the action, which is the instrument, characterized by the attainment of such a quality. One might think thus: 'Although that relation is inseparable from Devadatta and is illuminated by him, nevertheless the mother's relation is illuminated by abhi, and thus it is said, "the mother's connection with that"... by the power of the word, because it pertains to that, and by the second case ending, because it illuminates the relation pertaining to both.' 'Tree by tree it stands' is the relation. 'Depending on the standing' means, based on the standing, the relation of these trees. The construction is thus. By 'of the trees,' it is shown that the trees are related to the action as the other party. By 'depending on the standing,' it is shown that the action of standing, which is to be accomplished and is expressed by the word tiṭṭhati, is related as the other party from the perspective of the trees. Although inanimate trees lack intention, due to worldly convention, such expressions as pipatīsā (desire to fall) are understood. Thus, it should be understood that the relation characterized by the means and the end is produced from the action of depending on the place where it is understood. And that relation of the trees is illuminated by abhi. It is said, 'that...' and so forth. 'It should be illuminated only by the dual number.' The intention is that even when there is only the sense of a distributive meaning, since the case ending alone is unable to illuminate it, the dual number must be used for the illumination of the distributive sense.

9. Pati

9. Paṭi

Upādiyamānoti abbhupagammamāno, yadi pana upādiyamāno bhāgo, anupādiyamāno kathanti āha-‘yo panā’tiādi, tagarakuṭṭhā gandhabbavisesā, mamābhajatīti maṃ ābhajati, mama koṭṭhāso hotīti adhippāyo.

`Upādiyamāno` means being approached or accepted. If one asks, 'But if `upādiyamāno` is a part, what is `anupādiyamāno`?' he says, beginning with 'But which...' and so forth. `Tagarakuṭṭhā` are a particular kind of celestial musician. `Mamābhajati` means 'he attends to me,' and the intention is 'he becomes my portion.'

10. Anu

10. Anu

Natulakkhaṇanti saccakiriyā vuṭṭhiyā hetu hoti, na tu saṅketoti attho, hetuttā lakkhaṇattābhāve saccakiriyāya kathaṃ lakkhaṇe dutiyāti hetuttepi lakkhaṇattamassa sādhento sādhammapayogenānvayamāha-‘yaṃ sakimpi’ccādi, ettha hi lakkhaṇaṃ sacca kiriyāti paṭiññā, pakkho (potthake) sakimpi nimittatāya kappanattāti hetu, yaṃ sakimpi nimittatāya kappate tampi lakkhaṇaṃ bhavati, yathā’api bhavaṃ kamaṇḍalupāṇiṃ sissamaddakkhī’ti sādhammapayogenānvayo daṭṭhabbo, kappateti samatthoti attho, kamaṇḍalu pāṇimhi asseti kamaṇḍalupāṇī, apīti pañhe, kadāci kenaci kamaṇḍalupāṇīsisso diṭṭho so tameva dassanaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ katvā pucchati ‘api’tyādinā, atha yathā vuttena hetunopi lakkhaṇattamattu tathāpi paravippaṭisedhena hetumhi tatiyā kasmā na siyāti codayamāha ‘na nvevampi’ccādi, pubbavippaṭisedhenāti apavādapubbavippaṭisedhena, tathāhi chaṭṭhiyā [M 0.0090] pavādo hoti hetumhi tatiyāvidhi… sambandhachaṭṭhiyā pattāya hetutatiyāvidhānato upapadavibhattividhipi chaṭṭhiyāpavādo… sambandhavisesābhibyattihetunopapadena yoge tasmiṃyeva sambandhe vidhānato, tattha hetutatiyāvakāso ‘dhanena kula’nti, upapadavibhattiyāvakāso ‘rukkhamanuvijjotate’ti, saccakiriyamanu pāvassīti tu hetumhi lakkhaṇe-pavādavippaṭisedhe sati pubbavippaṭisedhena dutiyā bhavati.

`Na tu lakkhaṇaṃ` means that a truth-act is the cause of rain, not merely a conventional sign; that is the meaning. If it is not a characteristic because it is a cause, how can there be the second case ending in the sense of characteristic for a truth-act? To prove that it has the nature of a characteristic even when it is a cause, he states the connection by means of an affirmative example, beginning with 'Whatever even once...' and so forth. Here, the proposition is that the truth-act is a characteristic. The reason is: 'Because it is fit to be a sign even once.' Whatever is fit to be a sign even once also becomes a characteristic, just as in, 'Sir, did you see the student with the water pot in hand?' The connection should be understood through this affirmative example. `Kappate` means 'is capable' or 'is fit.' `Kamaṇḍalupāṇī` means 'one who has a water pot in hand.' `Api` is used in a question. Someone has at some time seen a student with a water pot in hand; taking that very sight as the characteristic, he asks with 'Sir...' and so on. Then, raising an objection that even if a cause has the nature of a characteristic as stated, why should the third case ending not be used in the sense of cause by the principle of subsequent negation, he says, 'Is it not so...' and so forth. 'By prior negation' means by prior negation of an exception. Indeed, the rule for the third case ending in the sense of cause is an exception to the sixth case ending... because the third case ending for cause is prescribed where the sixth case ending of relation would apply, the rule for a case ending governed by a neighboring word is also an exception to the sixth... because it is prescribed in that very relation when there is a connection with a neighboring word which is the cause for the expression of a specific relation. There, the scope for the third case ending for cause is 'a family by wealth,' and the scope for the case ending governed by a neighboring word is 'it shines following the tree.' But in 'may it rain following the truth-act,' when there is a conflict of rules between cause and characteristic, the second case ending occurs by the principle of prior negation.

11. Saha

11. Saha

Sahatthe-nuno vattane pabbatena yogo kathanti āha‘pabbatene’ccādi.

When `anu` is used in the sense of `saha`, how is there a connection with the mountain? He says, beginning with 'with the mountain...' and so on.

12. Hīne

12. In the sense of inferior

Visayabhāvenātiādinā hīnattheti visayasattamittamāha, vijānanappakāramāha-‘hīne’ccādi, tenāti anunā, kathaṃ tena yuttattaṃ ukkaṭṭhassāti hīnukkaṭṭhasambandhamukhena vibhāvento’tatthā’tiādimāha, tatthāti hīneccādinā vutte tasmiṃ, yatoti ukkaṭṭhasāriputtādiko, hīnoti paññavattādi(to nikkaṭṭho, so sāriputtādiko ukkaṭṭho) hīnatthavisayo jāyate… tabbisaye tassa ukkaṭṭhatā pattito, hīnukkaṭṭhasambandho pana atisāyanādikāya kāyaci kiriyāya katoti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

By 'by way of being an object' and so on, he states that 'in the sense of inferior' is merely the seventh case ending in the sense of object. He states the manner of understanding, beginning with 'In the sense of inferior...' and so on. By `tena` is meant `anunā`. Explaining by means of the connection between the inferior and the excellent, by asking, 'How is the excellent connected with that?' he says, beginning with 'Therein...' and so on. 'Therein' refers to that which was stated by 'In the sense of inferior...' and so on. `Yato` means the excellent one, such as Sāriputta. `Hīno` means one who is inferior to the wise and so on. (He is base, so Sāriputta and others are excellent). The object in the sense of 'inferior' arises... because his excellence is attained in relation to that object. However, the connection between the inferior and the excellent should be understood as being made by some action, such as surpassing and so on.

14. Satta

14. Seventh

Kintaṃ ādhikyamiccāha- ‘adhikādhikīsambandho’ti, adhiko assa atthīti adhikī=khārī, athādhikīvinimutte adhikādhikisambandho kathamavasīyate nahyatrādhikī koci sūyaticcāha-‘navine’ccādi, iti saddo hetumhi yathāvuttasambandhasādhano, tadopasaddenayogoti tadā upasaddenādhikinoyogoti attho. Dviṭṭhattā sambandhassa adhikassāpyupasaddena yogā tatopi kasmā na sattamītyāha-‘adhikamhātvi’ccādi, yathā ekāyeva vibhattiyā ubhayagatassāpi sambandhassa jotitattā vijjusaṅkhātalakkhiyā sattamyabhāvo, evamidhā pīti pubbe vuttasamādhimatidisanto āha-‘lakkhitā viya sattamya bhāvo’ti, “māṇikā caturodoṇā, khāritthī catumāṇikā”.

What is that excess? he says. 'It is the connection of the excess with that which possesses the excess.' Because there is excess associated with it, it is `adhikī` (possessing excess); it is a `khārī` (a measure). 'But when that which possesses excess is absent, how is the connection of the excess and that which possesses it understood? For no possessor of excess is heard here,' thus he says, beginning with 'Not without...' and so on. The word `iti` is the means for establishing the aforementioned connection in the sense of cause. The meaning of `tadopasaddenayogo` is 'then there is a connection of that which possesses excess with the neighboring word.' Because the relation stands in two places, and because the excess also has a connection with the neighboring word, why is the seventh case ending not used for that? he says, beginning with 'But from the excess...' and so on. Just as, because the relation pertaining to both is illuminated by a single case ending, there is an absence of the seventh case ending for that which is marked, namely the lightning, so too here—extending the previously stated solution, he says, 'the absence of the seventh case ending is like for that which is marked.' 'Four `māṇikās` are a `caturodoṇa`; a `khārī` is four `māṇikās`.'

15. Sāmi

15. Lord

Kintaṃ [M 0.0091] sāmittamiccāha-‘sassāmisambandho’ti, kāya kiriyāya janitoti āha-‘paripālanādikiriyāya janito’ti, tañcāti sāmittāpekkho napuṃsakaniddeso, sambandhassānekavidhattā āha‘sabbattha sambandhe’ti, ākhyāyatetīmassa attho vidhīyate ñāpīyateti, diṭṭhanto-panītottho sukhena paṭipattuṃ sakkāti pasiddhamanuvadiyamānamappasiddhañca vidhīyamānaṃ diṭṭhantamāha-‘yathā yo kuṇḍalī so devadatto’ti, kuṇḍalittampasiddhaṃ, devadattattamappasiddhamiccāha-‘kuṇḍalittānuvādene’ccādi. Yathevobhayādhiṭṭhānattepyupasajjanatova chaṭṭhī ‘rañño puriso’ti, na visessato ‘purisassa rājā’ti, tathā sambandhābhibyañjanakenādhinā yogepi visesanatova bhavati, nāññatoti āha-‘tatthā’tiādi. Byatirekamāpādīyatīti kārakachakkato byatirittattā sambandho byatireko taṃ āpādīyati pāpīyatīti attho, ubhayatoti saṃto sāmito ca, adhibrahmadatte pañcālāti brahmadattassa pañcālā santakā sāmino (potthake) ti attho, santakā sāmino (potthake) hi pañcālā, na sāmi nasaṃ (potthake), adhipañcālesu brahmadattoti pañcālānaṃ brahmadatto sāmītyattho.

Why is it called ‘ownership’? He says, “It is the connection with an owner.” By what action is it produced? He says, “It is produced by actions such as protection.” And that (taṃ) is a neuter designation with reference to ownership. Because connection is of various kinds, he says, “in every connection.” The meaning of ‘ākhyāyate’ is ‘it is prescribed’ or ‘it is made known.’ An example is given so that this meaning may be easily understood. He gives an example that is well-known and being restated, and one that is not well-known and being prescribed, such as, ‘He who has earrings is Devadatta.’ Having earrings is well-known, but being Devadatta is not well-known; thus he says, “by restating the having of earrings,” and so on. Just as, even when both are the basis, the sixth case ending arises from the subordinate term, as in ‘rañño puriso’ (the king’s man), not from the principal term, as in ‘purisassa rājā’ (the man’s king); similarly, even in connection with a word like ‘adhi’ which expresses a relationship, it is applied to the principal term, not otherwise. Thus he says, beginning with “tatthā” and so on. Distinction is brought about.
