Because a relationship is distinct from the six kārakas, it is a ‘distinction’ (byatireka); the meaning is that this is brought about, is attained. ‘From both’ means from the property and from the owner. “Adhibrahmadatte pañcālā” means ‘the Pañcālas are the property of Brahmadatta.’ For the Pañcālas are the property, not the owner. “Adhipañcālesu brahmadatto” means ‘Brahmadatta is the owner of the Pañcālas.’

16. Kattu

16. The Agent

Kiṃ lakkhaṇo-yaṃ kattāiccāha-‘kattari’ccādi, gacchati devadattoccādo kattari patiṭṭhitaṃ, pacatyodanaṃ devadattoccādo kamme patiṭṭhitaṃ kiriyaṃ karotīti sambandho, karotīti ca iminā anvattha byapadesova siddho-yaṃ kattu vohāroti ñāpeti, kenaci payujjamānopi sake kamme sayameva padhānattamanubhavatīti‘payutto vā padhānabhāvenā’ti vuttaṃ hoti cettha-

What is the characteristic of this agent? He says, ‘in the agent,’ and so on. In ‘Devadatta goes,’ and so on, he performs an action established in the agent; in ‘Devadatta cooks rice,’ and so on, the connection is that he performs an action established in the object. And by ‘he does,’ it is shown that this designation ‘agent’ is established according to its meaning. Even when employed by another, he himself experiences the state of being primary in his own action. Thus, it is said here, ‘or employed, by way of being primary’—

Padhānatāya yo kattu, kammaṭṭhaṃ kurute kriyaṃ;

Sā kattā nāmappayutto, payutto vātyayaṃ dvidhāti.

He who, as agent, by virtue of being primary, performs an action established in the object; that agent is named ‘unprompted’ or ‘prompted,’ and is thus twofold.

Tattha purisena katanti appayutto, purisena karoti devadattoti payutto, nanu kiriyā-yamabyavadhānena karaṇādhikaraṇe heva [M 0.0092] sādhyate kattārā tu dūraṭṭhena, tathāsati kathamanekasādhanasādhanīyaṃ kiriyaṃ kattāva karoti mukhyabhāvenāparetvamukhyabhāvenāti vuccate-

Therein, ‘done by a man’ is an example of an unprompted agent. ‘Devadatta acts by means of a man’ is an example of a prompted agent. Now, is it not so that this action is accomplished directly by the instrument and the location, but by the agent who stands at a distance? If that is so, how can it be said that an action, which is to be accomplished by many means, is done primarily by the agent and secondarily by the others?

Kattutoññesamubbhūtyā, vivittālocanādinā vavivekeca dassanāti vākyapadīye, pavivekeca kārakantharāmabhāvedissabhe kattarikriyā atthi bhavati vijjaticcādo titaṭīkā, tatiyapāthānaṃpāta 100, naṃpāta 243;

Dūrādapyupakāritte, kattu vāttappadhānatā.

Through the arising of others from the agent, and through distinct consideration and so on; even when assisting from afar, the agent indeed has the primary role.

Ayamettha attho “kattuno sakāsā aññesaṃ karaṇādīnaṃ ubbhūtyā sambhavenaca, tathāhi pasiddhakaraṇasabhāvopi pharasu kattāyattavuttitāyādhikaraṇambha vati‘pharasumhi ṭhapetvā chindatī’ti, vivittassa karaṇādīhi puthabbhūtassa, kattuno kiriyāya ālocanena dassanena ca ‘devadatto atthi bhavati vijjatī’ti vuthabbhūtassānena ālocanena dassanenaca kattunodevadattenadevadattaṃ bhavati vijjatīti (potthake), ādisaddena karaṇādino (tadadhīna) pavattiādīnaṃ gahaṇaṃ, iminā kāraṇena dūrato upakārittepi kattuyeva sappadhānatā siyā”ti, punapi-

This is the meaning here: “Due to the arising and coming into being of other things such as instruments from the agent's presence; for thus, even an axe, whose nature as an instrument is well-known, becomes a location because its functioning depends on the agent, as in ‘he cuts, having placed it on the axe.’ And by the consideration and seeing of the action of the agent, who is distinct and separate from the instruments and so on, as in ‘Devadatta exists, is, is found.’ By the word ‘and so on,’ the functioning, etc., of the instruments (which is dependent on that) is included. For this reason, even when assisting from afar, the primary role would indeed belong to the agent.” And again—

Thālyādīnantu kattuttaṃ, hotevācetanānapi;

Yato saddassa vutyatthe, micchātyāsena-nādinā.

But for inanimate things like pots and so on, agency does indeed occur; because the application of a word to its meaning arises from beginningless wrong habituation.

Ayamettha attho “acetanānampi thālīasiādīnaṃ kattuttambhavati yathāvaṇṇitasappadhānattanimittābhāvepi, kasmāti ce yato kāraṇā atthe attano abhidheyyesaddassa vutti paṭipatti anādinā micchābhyāsenabhavati tasmā thālyādīnantiādi pakataṃ, kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti “aññathā saddattho, aññathā sabhāvattho, na hi saddo bāhye vatthumhi byāpāramāpajjati, tathāhi–

This is the meaning here: “Even for inanimate objects like pots, swords, and so on, agency occurs, even in the absence of the cause for being primary as described. If it is asked why, it is because the application and understanding of a word with regard to its own denotable meaning arises from beginningless wrong habituation. Therefore, ‘pots and so on’ is stated. What is meant by this? The meaning of the word is one thing, the meaning of its inherent nature is another. Indeed, a word does not exert influence on an external object. Thus—”

Aññathe vāggi saṃsaggā, dāhaṃ daḍḍhoti maññati;

Aññathā dāhasaddena, dāhattho sampatīyate.

In one way, through contact with fire, one experiences burning and thinks, ‘I am burned’; in another way, by the word ‘burning,’ the meaning of burning is understood.

Bāhyapadatthassa sabhāvo viya hutvā micchābhyāsena anādinā pana pavattena bāhye vatthūni avijjamānena karaṇabhūtena thālyādīnaṃ kattuttaṃ hotī”ti. Atha ca pana–

“As if it were the nature of an external object, it is, however, through beginningless and ongoing wrong habituation—which is non-existent in reality and serves as an instrument—that the agency of external objects like pots and so on occurs.” And yet—

Vatticchādo [M 0.0093] pavattehi, sappadhānatta hetuhi;

Kattudhammehi vuttehi, kattā saddāva ñāyate.

Ekassāmukhyavatthāhi, bhedena parikappane;

Kammattaṃ karaṇattañca, kattuttaṃ copajāyate.

When the properties of an agent, which have primacy as their cause, are stated, the agent is known from the word alone. When a single thing is conceived of differently through its secondary states, object-ness, instrument-ness, and agent-ness arise.

Vuttehīti ‘kattutoññesamubbhūtyā’ccādinā, saddāvāti sadde tedhammā hontu vā mā vā kattusambandhiyathāvuttadhammavacanicchāya saddatova kattā patīyate, niyamena na vatthutoti attho, amukhyā vatthāhīti buddhiyā tadākāratāya pariṇāmāvatthāhi, hantyatta nāvattānanti ekassevāttano kammattādi jāyate, atoyevāccantamasantopi aṅkuro jananakiriyāya kattā bhavati ‘aṅkuro jāyate’ti, vuttaṃ hi–

‘When stated’ refers to what was said in the verse beginning, ‘Through the arising of others from the agent.’ ‘From the word alone’ means that whether those properties exist in the object or not, the agent is understood from the word alone, due to the desire to state the aforesaid properties related to the agent. The meaning is that it is not necessarily from the object itself. ‘By secondary states’ means by the states of the transformation of the intellect into that form. As in the expression ‘one kills oneself by oneself,’ for one and the same self, object-ness and so on arises. For this very reason, even a sprout, which is utterly non-existent before arising, becomes the agent of the action of being born, as in ‘a sprout is born.’ For it has been said—

Purāsañjanito purāsañjātito bhāvā, buddhayavatthāni bandhano;

Avasiṭṭho satāññena, kattā bhavati jātiyāiti.

A state generated before, which is the basis for the states of the intellect; what remains, cognized by another being, becomes the agent in the act of being born.

Satā aññena devadattādinā.

By another being, such as Devadatta and so on.

Kintaṃ karaṇaṃ nāmāti āha-‘yo panā’tiādi, yoti yo padattho, iminā idaṃ dīpeti “karaṇabyapadesāya suttantarābhāvepi karotyaneneti karaṇantyanvatthato pasiddho-yaṃ karaṇavohāro”ti, atredaṃ paṭibhānaṃ–

What is this called ‘instrument’? He says, ‘But that which…,’ and so on. ‘That which’ refers to the meaning of the word. By this, he shows the following: “Even in the absence of another rule for the designation of ‘instrument,’ this usage of ‘instrument’ is established from its etymological meaning, as ‘that by which one acts is an instrument.’” Here is this insight—

Yaṃ vattumicchitaṃ kattu, kriyāyaccantasādhanaṃ;

Karaṇantaṃ dvidhā hoti, bāhyabbhantarabhedatoti.

That which the speaker wishes to express as the most effective means for the agent's action; that instrument is twofold, by the division into external and internal.

Tattha yaṃvattumicchitaṃtyādinā idaṃ dasseti-“na vatthuto kiñci karaṇaṃ nāma atthi, vacanicchāvasena pana pasiddhakaraṇānampi pharasuādīnaṃ ‘pharasu chindati, pharasumhi chindatī’ti kattuadhikaraṇattassapi, pasiddhādhikaraṇānampi tadanuttādivisesasambhave thālyā pacatī’ti karaṇattassapi dassanato vacanicchātoyeva karaṇaṃ kārakaṃ viññeyya”nti, tañca duvidhanti āha-‘dvidhā hotī’tiādi, tattha asinā chindatīti bāhyaṃ, cakkhunā passatītyabbhantaraṃ. Kiriyānimittattā kārakanti iminā kārakasaddassa nimittapariyāyattamāha. Pakati yābhirūpoccādo [M 0.0094] kiriyāyāvijjamānattā sambandhamattaṃ viññāyatīti sambandhalakkhaṇā chaṭṭhī siyā, samena dhāvatītyādo tu kiriyāya vijjamānattepi kammattaṃ vattumicchitanti dutiyā siyā, samaṃ dhāvati visamaṃ dhāvatītyattho, tathā dvidoṇenāti dvedoṇe kiṇātītyattho, pañcakenāti pañca parimāṇassa pañcako pañcakaṃ vaggaṃ katvā pasavo kiṇāti pañcapañca katvā kiṇātītyatthoti vāttikakārena ‘tatiyā vidhānāyopasaṅkhyānaṃ’kataṃ, taṃ dassetumāha- ‘pakatiādīhī’tiādi, yatthesaṃkaraṇabhāvoti yassaṃ kiriyāyame sampakatyādīnaṃ karaṇattaṃ, taṃ kiriyaṃ kathayatīti sambandho, sabbasseva padatthassa sattābyabhicārato āha-‘bhū’iccādi, pakatiyābhirūpoti sabhāvenāyamabhirūpo bhavati, na tu vatthālaṅkārādinetyattho, karotissa gammamānatte pana pakatiyābhirūpo katotiādi, tadā kattariyeva tatiyā, yaṃ yasmā aññagotto gotamo na hoti atoca gotamo bhavatīti sambandho, nanuca dvidoṇa pañcakā kayampaṭicca kammabhūtā honti dvidoṇādinā keyattā tato kimuccate‘kayampaṭicca dvidoṇapañcakā karaṇāni bhavantī’tyā saṅkīyāha-‘tathāhi’ccādi, idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti-“dvidoṇādisaddena hi na gayhupagaṃ vatthumuccati, tehi pana dvidoṇādyatthaṃ mūlaṃ tādatthiyā bhihitanti na vuttadosāvasaro”ti.

There, by 'that which is desired to be spoken,' etc., he shows this: "In reality, there is no such thing as an instrument. However, by the intention of speech, even for established instruments like an axe, the state of being an agent or a locative is possible, as in 'the axe cuts' or 'he cuts on the axe'; and even for established locatives, when there is a special connection such as not being otherwise expressed, the state of being an instrument is possible, as in 'he cooks with a pot'. Therefore, an instrument as a kāraka is to be understood solely from the intention of speech." And that is twofold, he says, 'it is twofold,' etc. Therein, 'he cuts with a sword' is external, while 'he sees with the eye' is internal. Because it is the cause of an action, it is a kāraka. By this, he states that the word 'kāraka' is a synonym for 'cause'. In 'naturally beautiful,' etc., as an action is absent, only a relation is understood; thus, the sixth case, which is characterized by relation, would be used. But in cases like 'he runs evenly,' etc., even though an action is present, the second case would be used because it is desired to express the state of being an object. The meaning is 'he runs evenly, he runs unevenly.' Similarly, 'by two doṇas' means 'he buys for two doṇas,' and 'by a group of five' means 'he buys cattle, having made a group of five,' or 'he buys having made groups of five and five.' Thus, the Vārttikakāra made the supplementary rule, 'an additional statement for the prescription of the third case.' To show that, he says, 'by nature,' etc. 'Where their state of being an instrument is' means: in which action the instrumentality of these, such as 'nature', exists; it speaks of that action—this is the connection. Since the meaning of every word is invariably connected with existence, he says, 'bhū,' etc. 'Naturally beautiful' means that this person is beautiful by nature, not due to clothes, ornaments, and so forth. However, when [the verb] 'karoti' is understood, as in 'made beautiful by nature', then the third case is indeed in the sense of the agent. The connection is: 'Because this person is not of another clan, he is therefore of the Gotama clan.' Now, is it not the case that 'two doṇas' and 'a group of five' are objects in relation to buying, because they are what is to be bought with two doṇas, etc.? Then why is it said, 'in relation to buying, 'two doṇas' and 'a group of five' are instruments'? Anticipating this doubt, he says, 'Thus indeed,' etc. This is what is said: 'By the words 'two doṇas,' etc., the object to be acquired is not stated. But by them, the price for the purpose of two doṇas, etc., is expressed. Therefore, there is no occasion for the stated fault.'

17. Saha

17. With

Yathākkamamāgamanakiriyāya thūlattaguṇena gomantadabbena ca sambandhaṃ dassetuṃ ‘taṃ yathe’ccādimāha, udāharaṇamattaṃ dassentopi iminā adhippāyenāpi dassetīti vuttaṃ ‘sabbattheva vā’tiādi, puttena sahāgatotiādīsu āgamanādikiriyampaṭicca dve kattāro padhānāppadhānavasena, tesu padhāne kāriyasampaccayañāyena vā bahulaṃvacanena vā padhāne kattari paccayo, itare’kattari tatiyā’tyeva tatiyā siddhā, tato-yaṃ vacanārambho-natthakoti maññamānoco deti ‘nanvi’ccādinā, ttenābhidhīyate piteti padhānakattā, tulyopi kiriyāsambandhe pitāputtānaṃ pitātra padhānaṃ saddacoditattā, putto-ppadhānamasaddacoditattā[M 0.0095], saddabyāpārāpekkhāya hi padhānāppadhānāya vavatthānaṃ, piturevātrāgatādisaddasāmānādhikaraṇyā āgamanakiriyā sambandho saddenoccate, netarassa saddasattisabhāvato, tathā vidhā hi saddassa satti yato piturevātra kiriyā sambandhaṃ sakkoti paṭipādetuṃ, na puttassa, evañcāgatoccādo ekavacanamupajjate, aññathā hi bahuvacanaṃ siyā, ‘pitā puttā āgatā’ti. (Yadi) vuttanayena tatiyā siddhā ‘siddhe satyārambho niyamāya vā vikappāya vā’ na cettha niyamo, nāpi vikappo, tato kimanena yogenā tyāsayenāha-‘appadhāneyeva’ccādi. Nayidamevamiccādi parihāro. Sahabhāvamattaṃ vattumiṭṭhaṃ vāti yojanā, sāmatthiyāti bhedādhiṭṭhānattā sahatthayogassa puttassāpi kiriyābhisambandho viññāyati kathamaññathā sahatthayogo siyāti iminā attha balena. Atthaggahaṇanti sutte “sahatthene”ti atthaggahaṇaṃ. Pariyāyatthanti parito ayanti avagacchanti atthamaneneti pariyāyo attho payojanaṃ yassāti viggaho, ettha ca pariyāyatthamevāti nāvadhāraṇaṃ, atoyeva vināpi sahasaddappayogaṃ tappariyāyappayogaṃ vā sahatthena yoge vidhānato asatyapi sahādisaddappayoge yattha tadattho gamyate tatthāpi bhavatyeva tatiyā… gamyamānena sahatthena yogā, yathā“syādi syāne”ti. (3-1) Saha pariyāyenāti sahasaddassa pariyāyato. Visesānupādānatoti “sahayutte-ppadhāne”ti (2-3-19) pāṇinīya sutte viya appadhāneti visesassānupādānato.

To explain the connection with the action of coming in due order, with the quality of grossness, and with the substance Gomanta, he says, ‘taṃ yathā,’ etc. Even when giving just an example, it is said that he also shows this intention, as stated in ‘sabbattheva vā,’ etc. In cases like ‘puttena sahāgato’ (came with his son), etc., in relation to the action of coming, etc., there are two agents—primary and secondary. Among them, for the primary agent, the case ending is applied by the maxim of the cause of the effect, or by the principle of frequent application. For the other, the non-agent, the third case is thus established. Then, considering that this commencement of the rule is meaningless, one raises the objection with ‘nanu,’ etc. Therefore, it is stated that ‘pitā’ (the father) is the primary agent. Even though the connection with the action is equal for father and son, here the father is primary because he is expressed by the word, while the son is secondary because he is not expressed by the word. The distinction between primary and secondary depends on the operation of the word. Here, the connection with the action of coming, etc., is expressed by the word for the father alone, due to its grammatical agreement with the word ‘āgata,’ etc.; not so for the other, due to the inherent nature of the power of the word. For such is the power of the word that it can establish the connection with the action here for the father alone, not for the son. Thus, the word ‘āgato’ appears in the singular. Otherwise, it would be in the plural, as in ‘pitā puttā āgatā’ (the father and sons came). If the third case is established by the stated method, then ‘when established, a new rule is for restriction or for option.’ Here, there is neither restriction nor option. So, what is the use of this rule? With this in mind, he says, ‘appadhāneyeva,’ etc. 'It is not so,' etc., is the refutation. Or, the interpretation is that it is desired to state merely co-existence. By its capacity, because the connection with the meaning of 'saha' is based on difference, the connection with the action is also understood for the son. Otherwise, how could there be a connection with the meaning of 'saha'? This is by the power of the meaning. The taking of the meaning is [indicated] in the sūtra by 'sahatthena' (with the meaning of 'saha'). ‘Pariyāyattha’ is defined as that by which one understands the meaning by going around it; that which has this as its purpose. And here, this is not an exclusive rule; therefore, even without the use of the word ‘saha’ or the use of its synonym, the third case still occurs wherever that meaning is implied, due to the rule concerning its connection with the meaning of 'saha'... due to association with the implied meaning of 'saha', as in ‘syādi syāne.’ ‘Saha pariyāyena’ means by way of a synonym of ‘saha.’ ‘Visesānupādānato’ means due to the non-inclusion of a specific qualifier, that is, due to the non-inclusion of the specific qualifier 'appadhāne' (in the secondary), unlike in the Pāṇinian sūtra ‘sahayukte 'pradhāne’ (2.3.19).

18. Lakkhaṇe

18. In a characteristic.

Lakkhīyatyanenāti lakkhaṇaṃ saṅketo, kintaṃ kamaṇḍaluppabhuti, atthe kāriyassāsambhavā taṃvācīhi vibhattīti maññamānena yaṃvivaraṇaṃ kataṃ ‘lakkhaṇe vattamānato’ti, tamullaṅgiyātthaṃ vadati ‘yo attho’iccādi, vattamānatoti viññāyati… nāmasmā paccayavidhānappa saṅgato, upāttoti gahito. Kañcippaṇaramāpannassa lakkhaṇe tatiyā yathā siyā ‘rukkhampati vijjotana’miccatra lakkhaṇamatte mā [M 0.0096] bhavīti pāṇinīyehi “itthambhūtalakkhaṇe”ti (2-3-21) itthambhūtaggahaṇaṃ kataṃ, tammanasi nidhāya codayamāha–‘nanvi’ccādi, itthambhūtassa lakkhaṇanti chaṭṭhīsamāso, āpannassāti bhūtassa, sāmaññassa bhedako viseso pakāro vuccate, tathāhi ‘tidaṇḍakena paribbājakamaddakkhī’ti manussattasāmaññassa paribbājakattampakāro, tamparibbājako patto, tassa tidaṇḍakaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ. Upalakkhaṇatteti iminā itthambhūtassa lakkhaṇattābhāvamāha, upalakkhaṇanti saṅketo. Nayidamatthiccādi parihāro, rukkhampati vijjotananti ettha kassaci itthambhūtassābhāvā itthambhūtaggahaṇe payojanaṃ na dissati tannivattanato, rukkhampati vijjotateti etthatu itthambhūtassa vijjusaṅkhātassa atthassa sabbhāvā tatiyāppattiyaṃ taṃnivattiyā yathāvuttaṃ ñāyamantarena nāññaṃ kiñci paṭisaraṇamatthīti saññāpayamāha-‘avassa’miccādi, aññathāti evamanabbhupagamma ‘itthambhūtalakkhaṇe’ti vacane karīyamāne sati, itthambhūtavādino uttaramāsaṅkiyāha-‘nacā’tiādi, vattunti vacanaseso, co-vadhāraṇe, neva sakkāti vuttaṃ hoti, dutiyāvidhānasāmatthiyāti “patiparīhi bhāge cā”ti (2-9) kasmā na sakkāti āha-‘atthi’ccādi, asati hi payojane sāmatthiyanti bhāvo. Atha kamaṇḍalu pāṇimhi assāti ādo tatiyā kasmā na siyā tyāha-‘kamaṇḍalu’iccādi, kamaṇḍalussa setassa ca upalakkhaṇa bhāvenānupādānatoti sambandho, iminā upādātuno savacasi satantatamāha, visiṭṭhāvayavādheyyenāti pāṇi kamaṇḍalunā visiṭṭhovayavo, tassādheyyo kamaṇḍalu tenāti attho. Yenāṅgena vikatena aṅgino vikāro lakkhīyate tato tatiyā yathāsiyāti parehi “yenāṅgavikāro”ti (2-3-20) āraddhaṃ, tadāha-‘yene’ccādi, tattha yasaddena vikatāvayavo hetuttena niddiṭṭho aṅgasaddo ca samudāyavacano upātto tenāha-‘yeneccādi, nanuca kāṇādīnaṃ niyataguṇīnamabhidhāyittā akkhisaddassa payogo na yutto byāvattiyābhāvāti, nesa doso, lokiyo-yaṃ saddassa vohāro, lokassa ca saddappayoge gurulaghumpatyadayo natthi, tathāhi lokena ‘sīsapāti’pi vuccate, rukkho [M 0.0097] sīsapātipi, yassa tu tatthādaro, so-kkhisaddaṃ payujjateva, athavā sāmaññupakkame viseso payogamarahati, akkhi(nāti) hi vutte sandeho siyā ‘kimassa vattumicchita’nti tato kāṇoti vuccate, nākkhinā nirūpayati sobhanoti, kiñcarahi kāṇoti, akkhikāṇamassetyādo kasmā na siyāti āsaṅkiya‘kamaṇḍalu pāṇimhi assā’tyatra yo vutto parihāro, ta metthopadisanto āha-‘heṭṭhā viya appasaṅgo’ti.

That by which something is characterized is a characteristic (lakkhaṇa), a sign (saṅketa); what is that? A water pot and so on. Because of the impossibility of the action in the meaning, thinking that the case ending is with those words that express the characteristic, the explanation given as 'from being present in the characteristic'—transcending that, he states the meaning 'yo attho,' etc. The meaning of 'being present' is understood... not connected with the rule for applying a suffix to a noun; 'upātta' means 'taken.' So that the third case may be used for the characteristic of one who has attained a certain state, as in 'lightning flashes towards the tree,' and so that it may not be used merely in the sense of a characteristic, the Pāṇiniyas have formulated 'in the characteristic of being thus' (2-3-21), including the term 'itthambhūta.' Reflecting on that, he raises an objection—'nanvi,' etc.; 'the characteristic of being thus' is a sixth-case compound, meaning 'of what has come into being,' i.e., 'of what has occurred.' A specific kind that differentiates the general is called a mode (pakāra). For example, in 'he saw the wandering ascetic with three staffs,' the state of being a wandering ascetic is the particular mode of the general human state; that wandering ascetic has attained it, and his characteristic is the three staffs. By 'upalakkhaṇatteti,' he states the absence of 'itthambhūta' being a 'lakkhaṇa' (primary characteristic); 'upalakkhaṇa' means a secondary mark. ‘Nayidamatthi,’ etc., is a refutation. In ‘lightning flashes towards the tree,’ due to the absence of any 'itthambhūta' (being thus), there is no purpose seen for the inclusion of 'itthambhūta,' hence its exclusion. But in ‘lightning flashes towards the tree,’ due to the existence of the meaning designated as lightning being 'itthambhūta,' when the third case would apply, to prevent it, there is no other recourse apart from the aforementioned rule; thus he declares—'avassaṃ,' etc. Otherwise, that is, not accepting this, when the statement 'in the characteristic of being thus' is made, the proponents of 'being thus,' anticipating a reply, say—'na ca,' etc.; 'vattun' is the remainder of the word, 'ca' is emphatic; it is said that it is indeed not possible. By the capacity of the rule for the second case, namely 'patiparīhi bhāge ca' (2-9), why is it not possible? He says—'atthi,' etc.; for when there is no purpose, there is capacity—this is the meaning. Then, in 'the water pot is in his hand,' etc., why should the third case not be used? He says—'kamaṇḍalu,' etc.; the connection is that the water pot and its whiteness are not taken as a secondary mark (upalakkhaṇa). By this, he states the independence of what is taken up in its own expression, by being the content of a distinguished part: the hand is a distinguished part by means of the water pot, and the water pot is what is contained therein; this is the meaning. So that the third case may be used for a limb by which, when it is deformed, the deformity of the possessor of the limb is indicated, others have formulated 'yenāṅgavikāro' (by which the deformity of the limb) (2-3-20); he states this—'yena,' etc. There, by the word 'yena,' the deformed part is indicated as the cause, and the word 'aṅga' is taken as denoting the whole; thus he says—'yena,' etc. But is it not so that since words like 'blind' denote a fixed quality, the use of the word 'eye' is not proper due to the absence of differentiation? This is no fault, for this is the worldly usage of words, and in the world's usage of words, there are no considerations of heavy or light, etc. For example, in the world, 'sīsapā' is said, and the tree is also called 'sīsapā'; but one who has regard for it, indeed uses the word 'eye.' Or rather, when beginning with the general, the specific is appropriate for use; for if 'with the eye' is said, there might be doubt, 'what does he wish to say?' Hence 'blind' is said. He does not describe it as 'beautiful by the eye,' but rather as 'blind.' Suspecting why it should not be 'he is blind in the eye,' etc., and teaching here the refutation stated in the case of 'the water pot is in his hand,' he says—'as in the preceding case, there is no application.'

19. Hetu

19. Cause

Kismiñci phale diṭṭhasāmatthiyetthe hetu niruḷho. Ekatra hi diṭṭhasāmatthiyottho taṃyoggatāya kāriya (ma)karontopi hetu vuccate sati saha kārinyasati ca vidhurappaccayo papā(ta) to, tena kāriyassa byabhicāro, tenevāha- ‘anipphādayantopī’ti, kāraṇe tatiyāyābhāve kāraṇamāha- ‘takkiriyāyoggatāmatte’ccādi.

The term 'cause' is established in the sense of that which has its capacity seen in some result. For a thing whose capacity has been seen in one instance is called a cause by virtue of its fitness for that, even while not producing the effect. When a co-agent is present, the effect is produced; when it is absent, due to a deficient condition, it is not. Thereby, there is a deviation of the effect. For this reason, he says: 'even while not producing.' In the absence of the third case for 'cause,' he states the reason: 'merely in the fitness for that action,' etc.

21. Guṇe

21. In the sense of quality

Upādhi visesanaṃ, parāṅgabhūteti parassa bandhattā(dino) vidhānā yāṅgabhūte jaḷattādihetumhīti attho, iminā guṇasaddo yamappadhānavacanoti vadati, yañcāppadhānaṃ tamparāṅgabhūtanti guṇetīmassa ‘parāṅgabhūte’ti atthamāha, yañhi paratthamupādīyate tadappadhānamanu vādarūpenopādīyamānattā, yathā ‘jaḷattā baddho, rukkho yaṃ sīsa pattā, aggi ettha dhumatte’ccādi, tenevāha-‘parattharūpāpanna’nti, vāvidhānanti “vibhāsā guṇe-thiyaṃ”nti (2-3-25) evaṃ vidhānaṃ, itthiyantiādinā pañcamīrūpassapi abhimatabhāvaṃ dasseti, tenevāha-‘ubhayatthā’tiādi, nanu ‘to pañcamyā”ti (4-95) suttena taddhitapaccayantassa kathaṃ pañcamyantatā tyāsaṅkiyāha-‘pañcaminiddese’ iccādi, iminā suttena pañcamiyā vināti yojanā, vā pañcamiyā vidhānato tatiyārūpenapi bhavitabbanti codanamanasi nidhāya pañcamyu dāharaṇeyeva kāraṇaṃ tatiyodāharaṇassa ca paṭhamodāharaṇānusārenānu mantabbatañcadassento āha ‘pañcamyāyevi’ccādi, abhāvena saṅkhāranirodhenāti tatiyantarūpāni.

An adjunct is a qualifier. The meaning of 'parāṅgabhūte' (in the subordinate) is: in a cause, such as dullness, which is a subordinate part for the prescription of another, such as being bound. By this, he says that the word 'guṇa' (quality) denotes that which is secondary. And because what is secondary is subordinate, he states the meaning of 'guṇe' as 'parāṅgabhūte.' For that which is taken up for the sake of another is secondary, as it is taken up in the form of a predicate. For example: ‘bound by dullness,’ ‘a tree which is a sīsapā,’ ‘fire is here because of smoke,’ etc. For this reason, he says: ‘having assumed the form for another’s purpose.’ The optional provision is the rule: ‘optionally in the sense of a quality, when not feminine’ (Pāṇini 2.3.25). By 'when not feminine,' etc., he also shows that the form of the fifth case is intended. For this reason, he says: ‘in both places,’ etc. Now, having raised the doubt as to how a word ending in a taddhita suffix can be in the fifth case according to the rule ‘to pañcamyā’ (4-95), he says: ‘in the exposition of the fifth case,’ etc. By this rule, the construction is 'without the fifth case.' Or, keeping in mind the objection that due to the optional provision for the fifth case, it may also appear in the third case form, and showing that the reason applies only in the examples of the fifth case, and that the examples of the third case should be understood in accordance with the first examples, he says: ‘even of the fifth case,’ etc. 'Abhāvena' (by absence) and 'saṅkhāranirodhena' (by the cessation of fabrications) are forms ending in the third case.

22. Chaṭṭhī

22. The Sixth Case (Genitive)

Sambandhavacanicchāyevettha [M 0.0098] chaṭṭhī siddhāti āsaṅkiyāha-‘hetumhi’ccādi, hetumāha-‘taṃ yoggatā’ iccādi, saddasattisāmatthiyāti saddasattisaṅkhātāya sāmatthiyā, tameva phuṭayati ‘yattha’iccādinā, hetvatthavācakehi antarenāti sambandho, samānādhikaraṇehīti hetvatthasamānādhikaraṇehi udarādīhi, tajjotanāyāti hetvatthajotanāyālanti sambandho, byatirekena tu hetvatthato tappavattimāha-‘yattha pani’ccādi, hetvatthehipiccādinā sāmatthiyamupadassitaṃ ‘vase dhammassa hetuno’ti tatthodāharaṇaṃ.

Having raised the doubt that the sixth case is established here merely by the desire to express relation, he says: ‘in the sense of cause,’ etc. He states the reason: ‘its fitness,’ etc. 'By the power of the word's potency' means by the power designated as the word's potency. He clarifies this very point with ‘where,’ etc. The connection is 'without words that express the meaning of cause.' By ‘co-referential,’ he means with words such as 'belly,' etc., which are co-referential with the cause. By ‘for its illumination,’ the connection is 'sufficient for illuminating the meaning of cause.' But by way of exception, he states its occurrence apart from the meaning of cause with ‘where but,’ etc. The capacity is shown even with words meaning cause, etc., and the example for that is ‘vase dhammassa hetuno’ (by the power of the Dhamma’s cause).

23. Sabbā

23. All

Nāmabhūtehīti sabbādīsu keci kesañci yadi nāmāni siyuṃ tehi, appadhānabhūtehīti piyasabbādīhi, kimpayojanantiādo payojanasaddo “payojanaṃ kāriyahetūsu”ti nighaṇḍuto hetuvacano.

By 'being nouns': if some among 'sabba,' etc., are names for certain things, then by those. By 'being secondary': by compounds such as 'piyasabba' (dear to all), etc. In 'what is the purpose?,' etc., the word 'payojana' (purpose) denotes a cause, according to the lexicon: 'payojana is used in the sense of effect and cause.'

24. Catu

24. Four

Yassa sacetanāyācetanāya vā kassaci, pūjānuggahakāmatta mantarena sammāpadānaṃ na sambhavatīti āha-‘pūjā’ iccādi, tenāti yathāvuttenatthena, cāgaṅganti dadātino dānakiriyāya kammena sambajjhamānañcāgakāraṇaṃ, idāni sampadānalakkhaṇaṃ sappabhedamāvikātukāmo āha-‘tadida’miccādi, nanirākarotītya nirākaraṇaṃ, ārādhayatītyārādhanaṃ, abbhanujānātītyabbhanuññaṃ, tesaṃ vasena, idha sampadānantidhā vuttaṃ kathitaṃ, keteti āha-‘rukkhayācakabhikkhavo’ti, rukkhādikaṃ taṃ sampadānaṃ vibhāgena dassetumāha-‘tattha hi’ccādi, ajjhesanenārādhanena sampadānaṃ bhavatīti sambandho, anumatiyā abbhanujānena, vijjamānepyanirākaraṇe bhikkhuno-dhikamanumatantyadhippāyenāha-‘so’ iccādi.

For whomsoever, whether with intention or without, proper giving does not occur without the desire for honor or favor, he says: ‘honor,’ etc. By that is meant by the aforementioned meaning. A factor of generosity means a cause of generosity connected by the action with the act of giving. Now, wishing to reveal the characteristic of the dative case with its divisions, he says: ‘that is this,’ etc. ‘He does not reject’ means non-rejection; ‘he gratifies’ means gratification; ‘he consents’ means consent. By means of these, the dative case is here said to be threefold. What are they? He says: ‘trees, supplicants, and monks.’ To show that dative case, beginning with trees, in detail, he says: ‘for there,’ etc. The connection is that the dative case occurs through solicitation and gratification, and through permission and consent. Even when non-rejection is present, with the intention of a higher consent from the monk, he says: ‘he,’ etc.

25. Tāda

25. Such

Payojanapariyāye atthasadde sati idanti payojanaṃ parāmaṭṭhuṃ sakkāti ‘tasseda’ntiādi vuttaṃ, tasaddenettha vikatiyātisambandho, atthasaddena [M 0.0099] tu pakatiyā, attha kathanametanti iminā vacanicchāya metissaṃ natthi samāsoti dīpeti, viggahe vāsmimimasmāyeva nipātanā samāso daṭṭhabbo,so vikatisaṅkhāto attho, pakatitvaññapadatthenākkhipīyate, tato tadatthasaddato, koyaṃ tadattha bhāvo ccāha-‘tadatthabhāvo nāmā’tiādi, nimittaṃ yūpādivikati, nimittīdāruādipakati tasaddenātthasaddena ca gahitā, tesaṃ sambandho tadatthasaddassa pavattinimittaṃ tadatthabhāvo nāmāti attho, hetu hetumantabhāvalakkhaṇo sambandho nāmāti vuttaṃ hoti, padhānāvacchedaguṇasmāti vidhīyamānattena padhānassa purisassa ācchedakā visesakā guṇā, yañhi vidhīyate ñāpīyate tampadhāna, mitaramappadhānamanuvajjamānattā, yadā upādīyateti vatvā upādīyamānappakāraṃ diṭṭhantena phuṭayitumāha-‘yathā’iccādi, yūpo nimittaṃ yassa dāruno taṃ tathā vuttaṃ nāññanimittanti yadā nimityavacchedakattenupādīyate tadā nimittasaddatova catutthī sambandho, tato aññanimittato, nimittanimittīnaṃ sambandhassa abhimukhabhāvena tattheva nimitte pavattīti sambandho, nimittasaddato hetutatiyāpi nāsaṅkanīyāti sambandho, kāraṇamāha-‘nimitta’ hetu iccādi. Ubhayatthāti yūpāya pākāyāti ubhayattha.

When, in the sense of 'purpose,' the word 'attha' is present, it is possible to refer to 'this' as the purpose; thus, 'tassedaṃ' etc., is stated. Here, by the word 'tassa', there is an excessive connection with the modification (vikati), but by the word 'attha', with the original form (pakati). By 'this is an explanation of meaning,' he shows that in this phrase, there is no compound, due to the speaker's intention. Or, in this analysis, the compound should be seen as formed by special rule from this very phrase. That meaning, designated as the modification, and the original form are implied by the meaning of another word. Then, from that word 'tadattha' (for that purpose), he asks, 'What is this state of being for that purpose?' and says: 'The state of being for that purpose is called...' etc. The sign (nimitta), the modification such as a sacrificial post, and the signified (nimittī), the original form such as wood, are grasped by the word 'tassa' and the word 'attha'. The connection of these is the cause for the usage of the word 'tadattha'; the meaning is 'the state of being for that purpose.' It is said that the connection is called 'cause,' characterized by the state of being cause and effect. 'From the quality that distinguishes the principal' means the qualities that distinguish and specify the principal person by being prescribed. For what is prescribed or made known is principal; the other is secondary because it is subordinate. Having said 'when it is taken up,' to clarify the manner in which it is taken up, he explains with an example: ‘just as,’ etc. The sacrificial post is the sign of that wood; it is so called, not the sign of another. When it is taken up as that which defines the signified, then the dative relation is from the word 'nimitta' itself, not from another sign. Because the connection between the sign and the signified is direct, the relation occurs right there in the sign—this is the connection. The instrumental in the sense of cause from the word 'nimitta' should also not be suspected—this is the connection. He states the reason: 'nimitta,' etc. 'Ubhayattha' means 'in both cases': for the sacrificial post (yūpāya) and for the wall (pākāya).

Piṇiyamānā kiṃ saddādivacanīyā paro sāduādiko yo-ttho so añño kattā yassa so aññakattuko-bhilāso, abhilāso rucīti iminā dityādyanekatthantopi rucisaddo-bhilāse ruḷhova gayhatīti vadati, sā ruci attho-bhidheyyo yesaṃ bhe tadatthā, tesaṃ sambandhino piṇiyamānassa, iminā ca kiñcāpi rucirayaṃ yassuppajjateyo vā tassā janako, tesamubhinnampi atthi, tathāpi yassuppajjate sova tassādhikaraṇaṃ, ajanakopi so tāya saṃsattoti tasseva piṇiyamānassa sampadānasaññā, natujanakassa tāyāsaṃsattassāti dīpeti, idhāti iminā sakkate udāharaṇānamasamānarūpakaṃ dasseti, iminā ca udāharaṇānamasamāna rūpattameva [M 0.0100] catutthīvidhāne kāraṇaṃ, aññathā chaṭṭhīyeva tehipi vidhīyeyya kāraṇāsambhavā kāraṇasabbhāvā hi dīpeti, īdisassa paccudāharaṇa(ssa) bhāve kāraṇamāha-‘anaññakattu kattā-bhilāsassā’ti, paresamidampaccudāharaṇambhavatu idha kathanti āha-‘ihatvi’ccādi, tvanti attamatte paṭhamāyeva, sambhave kāraṇantaramāha-‘athavā’tiādi, natthi añño kattā yassā sā anaññakattukā ruci, bhāya ruciyā sambandhino piṇiyamānassa sampadānasaññaṃ ye pana icchantīti sambandho, ye pana āhu cātisambandho, uppajjanamuppatti, kassa uppatti, ruciyā, uppattiyā ādhāro uppatyādhāro‘devadattāya rocate’ccādo devadattādiṃ upalakkhetīti uppatyādhāropalakkhaṇaṃ vacanaṃ, ettha ruciyā uppatyādhāropalakkhaṇameva vacananti sāvadhāraṇa mattho daṭṭhabbo… sabbesaṃ vākyānamavadhāraṇaphalattā, tena piṇiya mānavacanamabhilāsassa aññakattukatāsandassanaparaṃ na hotīti byavacchinnambhavati, tesaṃ kaccāyanassa cehāpi pasajjatīti sambandho, ihāpīti tvamiti etthāpi, aññathāsiddhattāti atthamatte paṭhamāya eva siddhattā, vacanassāti ubhinnampi catutthīvidhānavacanassa, atippasaṅgocāti “kassa vā tvaṃ dhammaṃ rocesī”tiādo tavāti anabhimataṭṭhānappattica.

What is 'being pleased'? That which is to be expressed by words like 'sound,' etc. The meaning which is pleasant, and so on, that which has another agent, is a desire whose agent is another. 'Desire is liking.' By this he says that although the word 'ruci' (liking) has many meanings such as 'light,' etc., it is taken here by convention only in the sense of desire. That liking is the meaning to be expressed by them; they are 'for that meaning.' [The dative is] for the one being pleased who is connected with them. And by this, although this liking exists for both the one in whom it arises and its producer, nevertheless, the one in whom it arises is its locus. Even if he is not the producer, he is associated with it. Therefore, he shows that the designation 'dative' applies only to the one being pleased, not to the producer who is not associated with it. 'Here': by this he shows the non-uniformity of the examples in Sanskrit. And by this, the very non-uniformity of the examples is the reason for the rule of the dative. Otherwise, the genitive would be prescribed by them, for he shows the impossibility of a different reason. He states the reason for the existence of such a counter-example: ‘of a desire whose agent is not another.’ Let this be a counter-example for others. How is it here? He says: ‘but here,’ etc. 'Tvaṃ' (you) is simply the nominative in the sense of self. He states another reason for its possibility: ‘or,’ etc. A liking whose agent is not another is 'anaññakattukā'. The connection is: those who desire the designation 'dative' for the one being pleased who is connected with that liking... And those who say so, this is the connection. 'Arising' is birth. Whose birth? Of liking. The locus of birth is the support of arising. In 'it is pleasing to Devadatta,' etc., it indicates Devadatta, etc., as the support of arising; thus, it is a phrase indicating the support of arising. Here, it should be understood that the meaning is emphatic: it is a statement indicating precisely the locus of the arising of liking, because all sentences have a determinative result. Therefore, it is established that the expression 'one being pleased' is not for the purpose of showing that the desire has another agent. The connection is that for them, Kaccāyana's rule would apply here too. 'Here too' means even here in 'tvaṃ'. 'Because it is established otherwise' means because it is established by the nominative in the sense of the mere meaning. 'Of the rule' means of the rule prescribing the dative for both. And 'over-application' means the undesired occurrence of 'tava' (your) in examples like 'Whose Dhamma do you approve?'

Dhārippayogeti dhāridhātuno payoge, uttamīṇo adhamīṇoti dhanikagahetūnaṃ ruḷhītyāha-‘uttamīṇo dhanasāmī’ti, uttamīṇamassāti uttamīṇo, dhārayatītimassatthamāha-‘vahatī’ti, dhāritoti dhāraṃdhātuto. Suttantarena (taṃ taṃ) niyamena niyamitānaṃ tesaṃtesaṃ sampadānasaññaṃ vidhāya catutthī vihitā parehi, tadāha ‘silāgha hanuṭṭhāsapāna’miccādi, sabbattha yogasambandhe chaṭṭhī, ñāpetunti silāghādike bodhetuṃ, icchitoti atimato. Tadatthavācīnañca dhātūnaṃ saṅgahaṇatthaṃ ‘kudhaduhissosūyatthāna’nti vuttaṃ, yampati kopoti iminā kopassa visayamāha, yassāti iminā yaṃkārakanti vuttameva parāmasati, yassāti rājādino, pucchatīti pucchiyate[M 0.0101], teneva vakkhati-‘yassa sambandhiṃ subhāsubhaṃ pucchati nemittiko’ti, yocānukūlattambha jatīti iminā idaṃ dasseti “patipubbako āpubbakoca suṇoti abbhupagame paṭijānaneca vattate, yadāyamabbhupagamo patthanā pubbato bhavati tadā patthanāya kattu patthayituno catutthī rūpambhavati, yadātvapatthatampi kevalamānukūlyena vattamānaṃdisvā deyyamabbhupagacchanti idamidaṃ vodassāmāti kopissasāmāti (potthake) tadānukūlyena pavattanasaṅkhātāya kiriyāya kattuno catutthīrūpambhavatī”ti, iminā ca pāṇiniyavuttikārassa jayādiccassamate byabhicāramāha, so hi “abbhupagamo nāma parena patthitassa bhavati tattha patthayituyeva catutthīrūpambhavatī”ti vadati, pubbassākiriyāya yo kattāti vedavākyena vihitathutikakaraṇa saṅkhātāya ussāhānujānanato pubbabhūtāya kiriyāya yo kattā hotā potā ca, sabbatthāpi‘tassā’ti idaṃ ‘catutthīyāyadabhimataṃ rūpa’ntiiminā sambandhitabbaṃ, chaṭṭhiyā sabbabyāpibhāvamālamba evanti atidesoti āha ‘evantī’tiādi, rūpasāmyato pana tādatthiyatthasabbhāvāca yathāyogaṃ tādatthha catutthīpi na virujjhati, vakkhati hi‘tādatthha vacanicchāyantu ‘iccādinā, icchito rājā, kamma vacanicchāti iminā vacanicchāya padhānattamāha… vacanicchābhimukhattā sabbesaṃ kārakānaṃ, appacurappayogattāti abahuppayogattā, hanute apanayati, upatiṭṭhate upaṭṭhānaṃ upagamanaṃ karoti, pihayanti patthenti, kujjha amarisaṃ karoti, duhanādayo kopappabhavā nānantarena te sambhavantīti dūbhādayopyudāhaṭā “byañjane dīgharassā”ti (1-33) rasse aparajjhāmi, issayanti nasahanti, ārajjhati pucchito nemittiko upaparikkhati, bhādatthhaṃ vibhāveti ‘yasse’ccādinā, pariyā loceti upaparikkhati, kiṃ lakkhaṇo-yamaniyamoccāha-‘nāvassa’miccādi, yācitusmāyeva yācituyeva (potthake) chaṭṭhīti nāvassamayanniyamoti attho, kutoccāha-‘sambandhe’ccādi, aññasmāpīti ayācitutoapi, thutikaraṇassa kattubhūtā hotāpotāro ussāhanānujānanānaṃ kammaṃ hotīti āha-‘paccanupubbassa giṇātissa kamme’ti. Hotupotusaddehiccādinā [M 0.0102] potusaddassapi chaṭṭhirūpaṃ dassitaṃ, vuttiyantu ‘hotu patigiṇāti’cceva pāṭho dissati, hotvevampityamhākamatropekkhā, ussāhayatītyatthe giṇāti antogataṇyattho. Anāvādoti nāvāannādivajjite. Ettha pana tathā paṭisedhābhāvepi bahulādhikārato ‘na taṃ nāvammaññe nataṃ annammaññe’ccādi bhavati, attheva hi bahulādhikāratovā tippasaṅgābhāvo, paṭhamantaṃ rūpanti maññamānoti paṭhamantaṃ rūpaṃ, etthaca yadā tiṇāditopi khikaṃsīyate tadā nindāvagamo, tattha ca niyogatova nañpayogo ñāthānupa pattiyāti sappaṭisedhamudāhaṭaṃ ‘na maññamāno’ti, avadhimhiyeva pañcamītiṇāti, nañpayogeva niyogato nindāvagamā tiṇanti kammeyeva dutiyā, athavā satīpi nindāvagame vacanicchāto savisayeyeva dutiyā, sammutippayogeti sammutisaddassa payoge, catutthiṃ icchantīti mattāyāti ettha catutthiṃ icchanti, puna ruttatte kāraṇamāha-‘atha sotivijjamānattā’ti, caṇḍassa kukkurassātiādisutte “atha so”ti pāṭhassa vijjamānattā ‘bhiyyoso mattāyā’ti ettha sokāro punaruttoti adhippāyo, caggahaṇenāti “silāghahanu…pe… sattamyatthesucā”ti sutte caggahaṇena, catutthībhimatāti “namo yogādisvapicā”ti suttena.

By 'dhārippayoga' is meant the use of the root 'dhāri.' 'Uttamīṇo adhamīṇo' is a conventional term for creditor and debtor, as stated: 'The creditor is the master of wealth.' 'Uttamīṇamassāti' means 'he is a creditor.' To convey its meaning of 'bearing,' it says: 'He carries.' 'Dhāritoti' is from the root 'dhāra.' By another rule, the fourth case is prescribed by others for those specifically governed by such rules, assigning to them the designation of 'sampadāna' (recipient). Thus, it is said: 'silāgha hanuṭṭhāsapāna,' etc. In all instances of connection by application, the sixth case is used. 'Ñāpetunti' means to make known 'silāgha,' etc. 'Icchitoti' means 'desired.' To include roots with those meanings, it is stated: 'kudhaduhissosūyatthāna.' By 'yampati kopo,' the object of anger is indicated. By 'yassāti,' the previously mentioned kāraka is referred to. 'Yassāti' pertains to kings, etc. 'Pucchatīti' means 'is asked.' Accordingly, it will be said: 'A diviner asks about good or bad omens connected to someone.' By 'yo cānukūlattaṃ paṭijānāti,' this is shown: 'When 'suṇoti' with the prefix 'pati' or 'ā' refers to agreement or acknowledgment, and when this agreement arises from a wish, then the fourth case form belongs to the agent of the wish, the wisher. When, however, even what is not wished for is seen to occur merely out of favor, and they agree to give, saying, 'We will give this and that,' then the fourth case form belongs to the agent of the action known as 'occurring out of favor'.' By this, a deviation from the view of Jayāditya, the author of the Pāṇiniya-vṛtti, is stated. For he says: 'Agreement arises from another’s wish, and thus the fourth case applies only to the wisher.' By 'pubbassā kiriyāya yo kattā,' it refers to the hotā and potā, who are agents of the action that precedes the act of praise-making prescribed by Vedic statements, namely encouragement and approval. In all instances, 'tassā' should be connected with 'the desired form for the fourth case.' The sixth case, relying on its all-pervading nature, is thus an 'atidesa' (extension of a rule), as stated by 'evanti,' etc. However, due to similarity in form and the existence of the meaning 'for the sake of that' (tādatthiya), the fourth case for 'tādatthiya' is also not contradicted, as appropriate. For it will be said: 'When there is a desire for the word 'tādatthiya',' etc. 'Icchito rājā' (the king is desired). By 'kamma vacanicchāti,' the primacy of the desire for the word is stated... because all kārakas are directed towards the desire for the word, and due to its infrequent usage (appacurappayogattā). 'Hanute' means 'removes.' 'Upatiṭṭhate' means 'attends' or 'performs attendance.' 'Pihayanti' means 'desire.' 'Kujjha' means 'becomes angry.' Actions like 'duhana' (harming), etc., arise from anger; they do not occur without it. Therefore, 'dūbhādayo,' etc., are also cited as examples. In 'byañjane dīgharassā' (1.33), 'I err in the short' (rasse aparajjhāmi). 'Issayanti' means 'they envy.' 'Ārajjhati' means 'is asked'; 'nemittiko' means 'an omen-reader'; 'upaparikkhati' means 'examines.' The meaning is clarified by 'yassa,' etc. 'Pariyāloceti' means 'examines.' What is its characteristic? This is stated by 'nāvassaṃ,' etc. The meaning of 'the sixth case is only from the asker' is 'this is not a necessary rule.' And why? It is stated by 'sambandhe,' etc. 'Aññasmāpi' means 'even from one not asking.' The hotā and potā, who are agents of the act of praise, become the object of encouragement and approval. This is stated by 'in the object of giṇāti preceded by paccanu.' By 'hotu-potu-saddehi,' etc., the sixth case form of the word 'potu' is also shown. In the Vṛtti, however, the reading 'hotu patigiṇāti' is seen. If it is so, we are indifferent here. In the sense of 'causes to exert,' 'giṇāti' has an inherent causative meaning. 'Anāvādo' means 'devoid of a ship, food, etc.' Here, even in the absence of such a prohibition, due to the governing rule of 'bahula,' 'na taṃ nāvaṃ maññe, na taṃ annaṃ maññe' (I do not regard that as a ship, I do not regard that as food), etc., occurs. Indeed, due to the governing rule of 'bahula,' there is no over-extension. 'Maññamāno paṭhamantaṃ rūpaṃ' means 'considering it a form ending in the first case.' And here, when even grass, etc., is held in contempt, blame is understood. And there, due to the necessity of the negative particle, because understanding would otherwise not occur, 'na maññamāno' (not regarding) is cited with a prohibition. The fifth case is only in the sense of 'avadhi' (limit). In the use of the negative particle, due to the necessity of understanding blame, the second case applies only to the object 'tiṇa' (grass). Or, even when blame is present, the second case applies to its own object due to the desire for the word. By 'sammutippayoge' is meant in the use of the word 'sammuti.' By 'they desire the fourth case for mattāya,' it means here they desire the fourth case. The reason for the repetition is stated: 'because 'atha so' exists.' In the sutta 'caṇḍassa kukkurassa,' etc., because the reading 'atha so' exists, the particle 'so' in 'bhiyyoso mattāyā' is considered redundant. By the inclusion of 'ca' in the sutta 'silāgha-hanu... sattamyatthesu ca.' The fourth case is intended by the sutta 'namo-yogādisu pi ca.'

26. Pañca

26. Five

Avadhīyate visilissate etasmātyavadhi, avapubbāya dhādhātuto avadhimhi“dādhātvī”ti (5-45) i.

It is called 'avadhi' because one delimits or separates from it. The term 'avadhi' is formed from the root 'dhā' with the prefix 'ava,' with the suffix 'i' according to the rule 'dādhātvī' (5-45), in the sense of a limit.

Yato-vadhīyate kiñci, kriyāpubbaṃ kutocipi;

Calañcācalamaññañca, taṃ vadantya vadhimbudhā.

That from which anything is delimited, from any place whatsoever, preceded by action, whether moving, unmoving, or other, the wise call a limit.

Etthāyamattho “yatokutocipi attho kiñci vatthuavadhīyate saṃyogassa vā kiriyānimittaṃ gamanadānādikiriyāpubbaṃ visilissate sayaṃ vā apeti aññena vā visuṃ karīyate, tamevaṃvidhaṃ calañcā calañca visilesaparicchedabhūtaṃ padatthamavadhiṃ vadanti budhā tabbiduno”ti, taṃ yathā dhāvatāssā puriso patati, purisaṃ pāteti vā, rukkhā paṇṇaṃ [M 0.0103] patati, paṇṇaṃ pāteti vāti, soca tidhāpyuccate visayabhedena, yathā–

Here, the meaning is this: 'That from which any object whatsoever is delimited, being separated from a prior conjunction, preceded by an action such as going or giving which is the cause of the action; or which departs by itself; or is made separate by another—such a thing, both moving and unmoving, which is the basis of separation and delimitation, the wise, the knowers of that, call a 'limit'.' For example: a man falls from a running horse, or one causes a man to fall; a leaf falls from a tree, or one causes a leaf to fall. And this is spoken of in three ways according to the distinction of its object, as follows:

Niddiṭṭhavisayo koci, upāttavisayo tathā;

Anumeyyavisayo cāti, tidhāvadhi samīritoti.

A specified object, an acquired object, and an inferable object—thus is the limit described in three ways.

Tattha niddiṭṭhā vacanopanītā kiriyā visayo yattha so niddiṭṭha visayo vadhi, yathā-‘gāmasmā āgato’ti, upāttājjhāhaṭā kiriyā visayo yattha so upāttavisayo, yathā-‘valāhakā vijjotate’ti, valāhakā nikkhamma vijjobhateti attho, anumeyyā kiriyā visayo yattha so anumeyyavisayo, yathā‘māthurā pāṭaliputtakehi abhirūpatarā’ti, ettha abhirūpaguṇena ukkaṃsanamanumeyyaṃ, atoyevetthāyameva saññā paripphuṭā viññāyatīti na kācidiha saññā paribhāsīyate byāmohakāriṇī, athāvadhismāti vuccamāne ‘padatthāvadhismā’ti kuto-vasīyate yenevaṃ vivaraṇaṃ katantyāsaṅkiyāha-padāna’miccādi. Yathā gāmasmātiādinā idaṃ dīpeti “na kevalaṃ kāyasaṃsaggapubbakova visileso, kiñcarahi buddhisaṃsaggapubbakopi, atthi ceha buddhisaṃsagga pubbako, tathāhi corehi bhāyatityādo yo (bhaya)pekkhaṇa sīlo bhavati, so yadi maṃ corā passeyyuṃ, dhuvaṃ me maraṇanti vicārento te buddhiyā pappoti pappuyya ca tato nivattate, tathā corehi tāyatityādo yo ekassa mitto bhavati so yadyetaṃ corā passeyyuṃ dhuvamassa maraṇanti passanto te buddhiyā patvā tato nivattayatītyavadhittā avadhismāva sabbattha pañcamī”ti, parehi pana etādisesu sabbattha paṭipattuvisesānuggahāya sutteheva papañco kato, idha pana sāmaññavacaneneva siddhattā tadanuggahāya udāharaṇeheva papañcitaṃ, bhītibhāyanatthānanti bhīti tāyanānaṃ attho yesaṃ te bhītitāyanatthā tesanti attho, nanu bhītyatthānaṃ payoge bhayahetu sambhavati natu tāyanatthānanti, nesa doso, tāyanañhi rakkhanamuccate sāyanāhi rakkhanamuppajjabhe (potthake) tañca bhayahetuto vetyāha-‘yo [M 0.0104] bhayahetu’tiādi, iminā ca “bhītyatthānaṃ bhayahetu”ti (1-4-25) pāṇiniyānamapādānasaññā suttampaṭikkhipati, tatoti bhayahetuto, tesanti bhayatāyanānaṃ, bhayamaniṭṭhapātasaṅkā, uttāsotyattho, tāyana maniṭṭhapātato parirakkhanaṃ, yathā dassanaṃ hontevātīminā vacanicchāyeva padhānattamāha, ko hi lokiyaṃ vacanicchamativattituṃ sakkoti, tathāhi sabbeva dabbādayo sabbakārakasattiyuttāva, tatthāyaṃ kārakavibhāgo vacanicchāvaseneva, taṃ yathā ‘valāhako vijjotate, valāhakena vijjotate, valāhake vijjotate’ti. Parāpubbassātiādinā “parājissāsayho”ti (1-4-26) saññāsuttaṃ paccakkhāti, asayho atthoti sahituṃ abhibhavitumasamattho attho, ajjhenasakāsāiccādinā udāharaṇatthamācikkhati, nanucevamatthaṃ vadatā yaññadattassāsayhattaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ kathaṃ ajjhayanassāsayhattaṃ, yenāsayhattassāvadhittaṃ paṭipādayati tyāsaṅkiyāha-‘yaññadattānabhibhavo’ccādi, asayhotīmassa paccudāharaṇaṃ paṭipādayati ‘yo pani’ccādi. “Vāraṇatthānamicchito”ti (1-4-27) suttitaṃ, tadāha ‘vāraṇatthāna’miccādi, vāraṇamattho yesaṃ te vāraṇatthā, avadhimattavacanicchāyanti visesato vidhānamantarenā vadhimatta vacanicchāyaṃ, visesavidhāneti icchitoti visesavidhāne, cittassāvadhivacanicchāyampana cittato pāpaṃ nivārayeti bhavati. “Rakkhanatthānamicchita”nti (2-6-3) suttitaṃ, tadāha-‘rakkhanatthāna’miccādi, kesañcīti kaccāyanādike dasseti. “Antaradhāne yenādassanamicchatī”ti (1-4-28) saññāsuttamāraddhaṃ, tadāha-‘antaradhāne’ccādi, ayamupajjhāyo yadi maṃ passatīti sambandho, dassane dosaṃ takketi ‘nuna’miccādinā, pesanamasakkārapubbako niyogo, ajjhesanaṃ sakkārapubbako, maññamāno sissā ahaṃ kathannāma byavahito bhavāmīti antaradhāne byavadhāna nimittaṃ, yena attano adassanamicchatīti sambandho, antaradhāneti nimittasattamīcāyaṃ, ato āha-‘byavadhānanimitta’nti, byavahitoti antarahito, māmaṃ upajjhāyotyādinā udāharaṇatthamāha, byavadhānatthaṃ byavahitatthaṃ, “antaradhāneti kiṃ core na didikkhatī”ti paccudāhaṭaṃ [M 0.0105] parehi, tampaṭipādayamāha-‘yatthādassana’miccādi, core na didikkhatī (tya), tra hi yo core na didikkhati tehi attano adassanamicchatīti na antaradhānanimittaṃ, kintupaghātanivatyatthaṃ, kintupaghātanivattiyāti evaṃ maññate “nātrāntaradhāname (vāvaseyaṃ), kintu tannimitto paghātanivattipi, ‘upajjhāyā antaradhāyatī’tyatra vināpyupaghātasambhavamantaradhānasampādanameva sambhavatī”ti. Icchatiggahaṇaṃ kimatthaṃ adassanicchāyaṃ sati satyapi dassane yathāsiyā”ti vuttaṃ, (taṃ) paṭipādayamāha-‘adassanicchāyampani’ccādi, satīpi dassaneti upajjhāyena dassane satīpi, tatoti upajjhāyato, avadhirūpatā evāti upajjhāyassāvadhirūpatā eva. “Ākhyāto payoge”ti (1-4-29) paravacanaṃ, tadāha ‘upayoge’ccādi, niyamapubbakaṃ vijjāgahaṇamupayogo trādhippeto, upayogavacanasāmatthiyā vijjāgahaṇatthaṃ sissavattaṃ niyamo, tatoti ākhyātuto. “Janikattuno pakatī”ti (1-4-30) saññāsuttaṃ kataṃ, tadāha-‘janyatthassā’tiādi, janino attho janyattho, kintaṃ jananaṃ, tatoti janikattuhetuto, pakatisaddena kāraṇamattaṃ gahitaṃparehi ‘puttā pamodā jāyate’ccādo puttāditopi yathā siyā’ti, duvidhaṃ (hi) kāraṇaṃ upādānakāraṇaṃ sahakārikāraṇañca, tattha kāriyenābhinnadeso ghaṭassa mattikāpiṇḍo upādānakāraṇaṃ, tasseva pana daṇḍacakkādi (kāriyena bhinnadeso) sahakārikāraṇaṃ, tesūpādānakāraṇasseha gahaṇe’siṅgā saro jāyate’ccatreva siyā, na tu ‘puttā pamodā jāyate’ccādo, kārakantaravacanicchāyanti ettha kārakantarādivacanicchāyanti pāṭhena bhavitabbaṃ… etthantare sambandha vacanicchāyapi sambhavato, tatra tiṭṭhantīti tatraṭṭhā, tesaṃ, loko-naññathāvādī vohārikajano, tattha bhavā lokiyā, navattu paṭibaddhāti lokavacanicchamullaṅgiya ahameva vadāmīti sakajjhāsayena vadanto vattā, tappaṭibaddhā na hotīti attho. “Pabhavo bhavatissā”ti (1-4-31) suttitaṃ, tadāha-‘bhavatissā’tiādi, paṭhamato upalabbhatīti atthakathanena janyattho-tra na sambhavatīti vadati, nahi himavā gaṅgāya kāraṇaṃ, sā hi aññehi evakāraṇehi uppannā[M 0.0106], himavati tu kevalaṃ paṭhamato upalabbhati. “Jigucchāvirāmapamādatthānumupasaṅkhyānaṃ”ti (1-4-24vā) vuttaṃ, tadāha-‘viramaṇatthe’tyādi, jigucchāpamādatthadhātuyoge pana kammādhikaraṇavacanicchā dissatīti vuttaṃ, avadhivacanicchāpi pana dissake ‘jigucchati nāhiriko pāpā’ti, dhammā pamajjatītipi hoteva paṭisedhābhāvā. “Aññārāditararite disāsaddāñcuttarapadācāhi yutte”ti (2-3-29) suttitaṃ, tadāha-‘aññasaddayoge’ccādi, yatoti devadattādito, “aññaityatthaggahaṇaṃ, tena pariyāyappayogepi bhavatī”ti aññehi byākhyātattā āha-‘bhinno devadattā’ti, ārāsaddassa dūratthattā āsavakkhayato ārā dūro bhavatī(tyattho u) pādīyatetyāha‘ārāsaddo dūrattho’ti, niddissamānapaṭiyogīti ‘devadatto sūro’ti niddissamānassa kassaci yo so dutiyo, so paṭiyogī. Disādesakālavuttīnaṃ disāsaddattena pariggahato āha‘disā desakālavācīnaṃ yoge’ti, pubbeva sambodhātiādīni kālavācīyoge udāharaṇāni, añcuttarapadaācaāhipaccayayo getviha nodāhaṭaṃ. “Pañcamīvidhāne lyaplope kammanyupasaṅkhyānaṃ “adhikaraṇe copasaṅkhyāna”miti (2-3-28-vā) vāttikaṃ, tadāha‘yattha’ccādi, lyappaccayassa yatrāppayogo, tassattho ce gamyate, so lyaplopo, tvālopo lyapalopotyaviseso, pāsāda māruyha pekkhati āsane upavisitvā pekkhatīti idaṃ visayo padassanaṃ pubbaṃ yassāti kiriyāvisesane samāso, vakkhamānasabbadassanesupi pāsādato-pakkamanalesasabbhāvā pāsādo (yevā) vadhirūpena vattumiṭṭhoti dassetumāha-‘tathāhi’ccādi, apakkamati tato taṃ dassananti tato pāsādato tassa daṭṭhuno dassanaṃ cakkhundriyaṃ apakkamatyapayātītyattho, avadhibhāvo pāsādassāti viññāyati, yesanti vesesikānaṃ, te hyevamācikkhanti “indriyesu cakkhundriyaṃ cakkhugoḷakato-ccantasukhumabhāvena nikkhamma visālībhavantaṃ visayadesamupagamma sakalamattanā diṭṭhaṃ passati raṃsirūpena, yathā kāhalā mūle kisā aggemahatī, tathā ñāṇindriyānī”ti, adhiṭṭhānadesanti indriyādhiṭṭhānabhūtaṃ cakkhugoḷakadesaṃ, visayappavattīti gocare [M 0.0107] pavatti, santatiyāti indriyapabandhassa, adhiṭṭhāna manindriyaṃ nāpajjateti sambandho, tatoti pāsādato, apakkantyāti apagamanena, yajjapi cakkhundriyaṃ cakkhugoḷakato bahi niggacchati, tathāpipāsādaṭṭhassacakkhugoḷakā niggacchatīti pāsādassāpyavadhibhāvo, yesantūti khaṇikavādīnantu, indriyādhiṭṭhānampatte visaye viññāṇalakkhaṇaṃ kāriyaṃ karonti sīlenāti pattakārīni, anindriyādhiṭṭhānadoso neti sambandho, tatoti pāsādato, yesampanāti khaṇikavādinova dasseti, atra hi cattāro pakkhā pattakārīnindriyāni, appattakārīni, cakkhusotāni appattakārīni sesāni vuttaviparitāni, cakkhuyeva pattakārī sesamaññatheti, catusveva tesu paṭhamapakkhadvayamupanyasya paṭipāditaṃ… tappaṭipādanenetaresampi paṭipāditattā, sabbasāmayikasādhāraṇattāsaddasatthassāti idaṃ ayuttamiva dissati… saddasatthassimassa buddhavacanopayogittena sogatasamayānuguṇappavattito, khaṇikavādino pana nissāyedaṃ sundarameva, manasikārādītiādisaddena cakkhuto cakkhunā (potthake) abhedo rūpāpāthagamo ca dassito, yoggadeseti dassanayogge padese. “Pucchanākhyānesu ca pañcamī vattabbā”ti (2-3-28vā) vuttaṃ, tadāha-‘pucchanasaddato’ccādi, pucchanākhyānesu sāmaññena pañcamīvidhāne-tippasaṅgaṃ dassetumāha-‘avassa’miccādi, kassāti pañho, devadattassetyākhyānaṃ, koso yañña dattoti pañho vidhirūpovāyaṃ, yo-ṅgadītyādyanuvādarūpamākhyānaṃ, aṅgadīkeyūrī. “Yatocāddhakālanimmānaṃ tato pañcamī vattabbā”ti (2-3-28vā) vuttaṃ, tadāha-‘addha’ccādi, nimīyate paricchijjate yena taṃ nimānaṃ, tadeva nimmānaṃ. “Addhassa paṭhamā sattamī ca vattabbā”ti (2-3-28) vuttaṃ, tatthāyamattho “taṃ yuttāti vattate, taṃ yuttā pañcamiyutthā parassāddhassa paṭhamā ca sattamī ca vattabbā”ti, pāṭaliputtasmāti pañcami yuttaṃ, etāpi na vattabbāti dassetumāha-‘sattayojanānī’tiādi, atra hi yadā rājagahassa yojanañcābhedo vattumicchīyate, tadā pāṭaliputtasmā rājagahaṃ sattayojanānīti, bhedavacanicchāyantu “sabbhāvo”tyādinā (2-34) sattamī siddhā‘sattasu yojanesu’ti. Tathāhi [M 0.0108] pāṭaliputtasmā sattasu yojanesu sati rājagahaṃbhavatītyayamattho patīyate, sattayojanasambandhibhavanaṃ rājagaha (bhavana)ssa lakkhaṇambhavati. Sambandhe chaṭṭhīti iminā “taṃ yuttā kāle sattamī vattabbā”ti (2-3-28vā) vacanampaṭikkhipati. “Karaṇeca thokappakicchakatipayassā sattavacanasse”ti (2-3-33) suttitaṃ, tadāha-‘yadā iccādi, kicchādayotiādisaddena thokaappakatipaye saṅgaṇhāti, asattarūpanti addabbarūpaṃ, guṇe hetumhīti guṇapadatthe hetubhūte “guṇe”ti (2-21) pañcamīti attho, yathāvuttavidhāneneti “guṇe”ti sutte vuttavidhānena, “guṇe”ti sutte vuttavidhānena, yadātviccādinā paresaṃ viya karaṇe visuṃ vidhāne payojanaṃ natthīti dasseti. Kattabbarūpassa calanassāti sambandho, samānādhikaraṇattena visesananti yojanā, samānādhikaraṇattenāti ca ‘rañño puriso’tyādo asamānādhikaraṇassāpi visesanattadassanato vuttaṃ, samānādhikaraṇattena visesanabhāvo cāssa thokaguṇānvite calane vattamāno thokasaddo asattavacanova visesananti, tenevākhyāyate ‘thokassa kammattā kamme dutiyā’ti. Pañcamītyanuvattamāne “dūrantikatthehi chaṭṭhī vā”ti (2-3-34) vuttaṃ, tadāha‘dūranti katthehi’ccādi, avadhisambandhalakkhaṇāti avadhisambandhāva lakkhaṇaṃ nimittamāsaṃ pañcamīchaṭṭhīnaṃ tā tathā vuttā, vattumiṭṭhoti iminā vacanicchāyeva padhānattamāha, evaṃ carahi taṃtaṃ kārakavacanicchāyamaññāpi vibhattiyo kasmā nappayujjeyyunti āha-‘lokiyā cetthā’tiādi, ettha vibhattīnaṃ niyame lokiyā eva vacanicchā nibandhanaṃ kāraṇanti attho, pañcamīcātyanuvattamāne “dūranti katthehi dutiyā ce”ti (2-3-35) vuttaṃ, “pañcamyadhikaraṇeca” (2-3-36) iccatra ca kārena dūranti katthehi sattamī ca vuttā pāṭi padikatthe sārasaṅgahakārādīhi, tadakkhippa aññāpadesena paṭikkhipituṃ kecityādi yaṃ vuttaṃ vuttiyaṃ, taṃ dassetumāha’kecīti sārasaṅgahādayo’tiādi. Dūrāpādāvasecananti ayaṃ tesampaṭikkhepana yoti sambandho, itisaddo panettha parihīno, nahitantiādīsu tasaddenāsattarūpaṃ dūrādi vattumicchitantyavaseyaṃ, na hi taṃ gamyate, na hi tato gamyate, na hi tena gamyate, na hi tasmiṃ ṭhīyate’ti visuṃ sambandho [M 0.0109] vaseyo. Patīyantecāti co vattabbantarasamuccaye, atoceti vakkhamānahetuparāmāso, yanti yasmā atthe nipāto, vākyakāro vararuci, taṃsāmānādhikaraṇyatoti dūrādisā mānādhikaraṇyato, taṃyuttatopīti dūrādiyuttā gāmādisaddatopi, paccakkhantoti vākyakāravacanaṃ paccācikkhanto, tathāhyatrāyaṃ mahābhāssa pāṭho “dūrantikatthehi pañcamīvidhāne taṃyuttā pañcamīpaṭisedho vattabbo dūrā gāmassa, tatrāpi dassanā anatthako-yampaṭisedho, tatrāpi hi pañcamī dissati–

Here, the scope of an action that is taught and presented is where that taught scope is the point of departure (avadhi), as in 'he came from the village.' The scope of an action that is taken up and implied is where that taken-up scope is, as in 'lightning flashes from the cloud'—the meaning is that having emerged from the cloud, it flashes. The scope of an action to be inferred is where that inferable scope is, as in 'the women of Mathurā are more beautiful than those of Pāṭaliputta.' Here, the superiority in the quality of beauty is to be inferred. For this very reason, it is understood that this designation (saññā) is pervasive here, so no designation that causes confusion is censured. Then, when 'in the sense of avadhi' is stated, how is 'in the sense of the word's meaning as avadhi' determined? Anticipating this question, which has prompted such an explanation, it is said: 'padānaṃ', etc. As shown by 'gāmasmā' and so forth, this illustrates: 'Separation is not only preceded by physical contact, but also by mental contact. And here there is that which is preceded by mental contact. For example, in "he fears the thieves," one who is of a fearful nature, thinking, "If the thieves were to see me, my death would be certain," reaches them with his mind, and having reached them, turns back from there.'

Dūrasmāvasathā muttaṃ, dūrāpādāvasecanaṃ;

Guruto kupitā dūrā,bhābyaṃ dūrā ca dassuhiti.

Released from a distant dwelling, far from the washing of feet; far from an angry teacher, and indeed, a villain should be far from what is proper.

Atra dūrantiketyādi vattabbaṃ vākyakāravacanaṃ, dūrā gāmassāti tassodāharaṇaṃ, tatrāpiccādi paccakkhānabhāssaṃ, dūrasmāvasathāti āvasathassa dūreti atthohi bhāssapadīpe keyyaṭo, paṭhamo puriso yassa so paṭhamapuriso bhavati “dūrantikā”di (2-6-5) kaccāyanasutte suddhādiyogopi saṅgahito, tenāha–‘suddhappa mocanavivittappamāṇayoge’ti, “dhātunāmānamupasaggayogādīsvapica” iti (2-6-2) sutte caggahaṇato pabhutiyogo ca gahito, tenāha–‘pabhuti yogecā’ti, pabhutiyogecāti iminā pabhutyatthayogopi saṅgahito, teneva ‘yatosarāmi attāna’nti udāhaṭaṃ.

Here, 'dūrantika,' etc., should be stated as the statement of the Vākyakāra, with 'far from the village' as its example. In that context, 'tatrāpi,' etc., is a gloss of rejection. 'Dūrasmāvasathā' means 'far from the dwelling,' as stated by Keyyaṭa in the Bhāssapadīpa. He whose person is first is the 'first person.' In the Kaccāyana Sutta (2-6-5) on 'dūrantikā,' etc., the application of purity, etc., is also included. Therefore, it is said: 'in the application of purity, release, seclusion, and measure.' And in the sutta (2-6-2) 'dhātunāmānamupasaggayogādīsvapica,' the application of 'pabhuti' (from) is also included due to the inclusion of 'ca.' Therefore, it is said: 'and also in the application of pabhuti.' By this 'pabhuti yogecā,' the application of the meaning of 'pabhuti' is also included; therefore, 'yatosarāmi attānaṃ' is cited as an example.

27. Apa

27. Apa

Nanu phuṭova tesaṃ sālādīnaṃ yogoti kimettha pañhena kassa panetehi yogo’tyāsaṅkiyāha-‘vajjanaṃ hiccādi, vajjanānanti kattari ano, vajjane sambandhe vattamānehīti vajjanasaṅkhāte sambandhe vatta mānehi apaparīhi, yuttasmāti yuttatova ekasmā, nāññato, kimettha vattabbanti iminā apaparīhi yuttasmāva pañcamībhavane pasiddhattamāha, pasiddhampetamāharitvā pakāsetumāha-‘kattuno’ccādi, yadatthoti yosālādi attho payojanaṃ yassa vajjanakiriyā rambhassa [M 0.0110] so yadattho. “Pañcamyapāparīhī”ti (2-3-10) āyuttepi pañcamī vidhīyate parehi, tadāha-‘mariyādāya’miccādi, avadhimā ettha vassanaṃ.

Is not their connection with sālā trees and so on established? What is the purpose of this question? Having wondered, 'Whose connection is this with these things?' he says: 'Avoidance,' etc. In 'avoidance,' the suffix `aṇa` is in the sense of the agent. 'In the connection of avoidance being present' means: by means of `apa` and `pari` which are present in the relation designated as 'avoidance.' 'From what is connected' means from the one thing that is connected, not from another. By asking 'What needs to be said here?' he states the established fact that the fifth case ending occurs after what is connected with `apa` and `pari`. Having brought up this established point to clarify it, he says: 'Of the agent,' etc. `Yadattho` means: he for whom the sālā tree, etc., is the object or purpose of undertaking the action of avoidance. By the rule 'Pañcamyapāparīhi' (Kacc. 2.3.10), the fifth case is also prescribed in connection with `pari` in the sense of a limit. He states this: 'In the sense of a boundary,' etc. Here, the rain is the limit.

28. Paṭi

28. Paṭi

Diṭṭhasambandhassāti pasiddhavasena diṭṭhakāriyakāraṇassa mukhyassa, tassa kāriyatthanti tassa mukhyassa yaṃ kāriyaṃ, tadatthaṃ mukhyakāriya karaṇatthanti vuttaṃ hoti, tasmiṃ paṭinidhimhi vattamānena pabhineti sambandho, vinimayeti parivattana nimittaṃ paṭidānecāti ca saddassāṭṭhānappayutti daṭṭhabbā, patinā tassa yogoti sambandho.

'Of the seen connection' means of the principal cause of a seen effect, by way of being well-known. 'For the purpose of its effect' means for the purpose of that which is the effect of that principal cause; that is to say, for the purpose of performing the principal effect. The connection is with `paṭi` when it is present in the sense of a substitute. `Vinimaye` means 'in exchange,' and `paṭidāne` ('in giving in return') is a sign thereof. The application of the word `ca` in an unsuitable place should be noted. The connection is its relation with `paṭi`.

29. Rite

29. Rite

Yadi vajjanakiriyāya sambajjhamānassa kammattā kamme dutiyā, kimatthaṃ carahi puna dutiyāvacananti āha-‘paṭipadavidhāne’ccādi, paṭipadaṃ ujukamevoccāritaṃ vidhānaṃ yassā sā paṭipadavidhānā, visesavidhāna vatītyattho, yajjatra dutiyāvacanaṃ na siyā tadā ritesaddena yoge ujukaṃ vidhīyamānāya pañcamiyā dutiyā bādhīyethāti maññate. Yadyatra pañcamiyā dutiyāya bādhābhāvo eva payojanaṃ, evañcarahi ‘rite vā’ti suttayitabbaṃ evaṃ sati pakkhe dutiyā ca bhavissati, lahu ca suttampaṇītambhavatī tyāsaṅkiya payojanantaramāha-‘uttaratthañce’ti, atoyevāti uttaratthattāyeva, puna payojanantaraṃdutiyā gahaṇassa dassayamāha-‘vibhatyantare’ccādi, āhacca kaṇṭhādiṭṭhāne vāyunāāhanitvā āharitvā vā vacanaṃ āhaccavacanaṃ, ujukavacananti vuttaṃ hoti, vibhatyantaraṃ chaṭṭhīvibhatti, tassa byudāsatthaṃ, nirāsatthantuttho, aññāpīti dutiyāya aññā chaṭṭhīpi, pakatāya pañcamiyā sambandhanattho pakatasambandhanattho.

If, for that which is connected with the action of avoiding, the second case is used because it is the object, then for what reason is the second case mentioned again? He says: 'For a direct prescription,' etc. That for which the prescription is uttered directly is a 'direct prescription'; the meaning is, it has a special prescription. It is thought that if the mention of the second case were not here, then the second case would be obstructed by the fifth case, which is prescribed directly in connection with the word `rite`. If the only purpose here were the non-obstruction of the second case by the fifth, then the rule should have been formulated as 'rite vā' ('or with rite'). Having raised the doubt that 'in that case, the second case would occur as an option, and the rule would be concise and elegant,' he states another purpose: 'and for a subsequent rule.' `Ato eva` means 'precisely because it is for a subsequent rule.' Again, showing another purpose for the inclusion of the second case, he says: 'another case ending,' etc. `Āhaccavacanaṃ` is speech produced by striking or bringing forth with the breath in a place like the throat; it means 'direct speech.' `Vibhatyantaraṃ` is another case ending, the sixth case ending. It is mentioned for the purpose of its exclusion; the meaning is 'for the purpose of its rejection.' `Aññāpi` means: another case besides the second, that is, the sixth. The purpose is to connect it with the natural fifth case; this is the meaning of 'connection with the natural'.

31. Putha

31. Putha

Na dutiyāpi yogavibhāgatoti evaṃ maññate “tatiyā ceti vattamāne tattha yadi cakārena ‘dutiyā ce’ti sambandhīyeyya, tatrāpi ca kārena pañcamītyevaṃ na kassāpyapakaṃsoti‘vināññatraputhanānāhi [M 0.0111] tatiyā ce’tyekayogamakatvā yogavibhāgasāmatthiyā ‘tatiyā ce’ti ca kārena jātu pañcamī”ti, asahāyatthatte sati ‘vinātthe hī’tyevamavatvā kiṃ visuṃ suttaracanāyetyāha-‘bhedo pādānantvi’ccādi.

He thinks thus: 'The second case is not brought in by splitting the rule.' When 'tatiyā ca' ('and the third') is stated, if 'dutiyā ca' ('and the second') were connected by the word `ca`, even then the fifth case would not be drawn down for anyone by the word `ca`. Because the rule 'vināññatraputhanānāhi tatiyā ca' is not formulated as a single rule, by the power of splitting the rule, the fifth case is never implied by the word `ca` in 'tatiyā ca'. This being the case, in the sense of 'without a companion,' instead of saying 'indeed in the sense of vinā,' why is there a separate formulation of the rule? He says: 'But the difference is at the end of the section,' etc.

32. Satta

32. The Seventh Case

Yantaṃ saddānaṃ niccattā sambandhassa yatthāti parāmaṭṭhaṃ soti, yoti parāmaṭṭhaṃ tassāti ca niddisati, yo yatthetyādikañca ‘kiriyādhārabhūte’ccādivuttigantha vivaraṇanti yoti kiriyādheyyabhūtādhippetā, etanevāha‘kiriyā cā’tiādi, tenāyamādhārīyati kattukamma samavetā kiriyāsmintyadhikaraṇe vā taṃ ādhārayatīti kattari vā ghaṇantena daṭṭhabbo, kattāraṃ kammañca kiriyānissayabhūtamādhāra yatītyādhāroti vā kattari ghaṇa, vuttaṃ hi–

Because of the eternality of sounds, the connection which is referred to by 'wherein' is indicated by 'that,' and that which is referred to by 'which' is indicated by 'of that.' And 'which, wherein,' etc., is an explanation of the commentary text 'being the locus of the action,' etc. 'Which' is intended as that which is the receptacle of the action. For this very reason he says 'and the action,' etc. Therefore, this word `ādhāra` should be seen as ending in the suffix `gha` either in the sense of locus, as in 'the action connected with the agent and object is supported in this,' or in the sense of agent, as in 'it supports that.' Or, `ādhāro` is derived with the suffix `gha` in the sense of agent, as in 'it supports the agent and the object, which are the basis of the action.' For it is said:

Ādhārayati yo kattu, kammaṃ kiriyanissayaṃ;

Ādhāraṃ kārakañcāhu, taṃ catubbidhameva ceti.

That which supports the agent and the object, which are the basis of the action, they call the Support and a Causal Factor. And that is of four kinds.

Nanu ca kiriyādhāraṇenādhārotyuccate, taṃ kimevamuccateti ce, nesadoso yadeva hi kiriyādhāraṇamassa, tantannissayabhūta kattukammadhāraṇaṃ, nahyaññatā taddhāraṇaṃ sambhavati tato kiriyā kāraṇenādhāraṇenādhārotya yamevattho, na kattukammapariccāgenādhārena ujukaṃ kiriyā gayhate, teneva vakkhati-‘kiriyāyayo ādhāro’ccādi, nanu yadyapyujukameva kiriyaṃ dhārayati kattā kattusamavāyiniṃ, kammasamavetañca viktedanādiṃ kiriyaṃ kammaṃ… tathā sati tānevādhāroti, na… loke satthe ca tesamādhāratthe nāppatītito, kattukammatāyeva hi tesampatītīti dassetumāha-‘kiriyā ce’tyādi, tathā ca vuttaṃ–

But is it not said that it is called a support because it supports the action? If it is asked, 'Why is it said so?', there is no fault. For whatever is its supporting of the action, that is the supporting of the agent and object which are its basis. For its support is not possible in another way. Therefore, the meaning is just this: it is a support by means of supporting for the sake of the action. The action is not grasped directly by the support, with the exclusion of the agent and object. For that very reason he will say: 'that which is the support of the action,' etc. But even if the agent directly supports the action inherent in the agent, and the object supports the action inherent in the object, such as softening, in that case, they themselves would be the support. No... because in the world and in the scriptures they are not understood in the sense of a support. To show that they are indeed understood only as agent and object, he says: 'And the action,' etc. And so it has been said:

Kattukamma byavahitaṃ, dhārentamanuju kriyaṃ;

Kriyāsiddhupakāri ca, satthe-dhikaraṇaṃ matanti.

That which is separated by agent and object, supporting the action indirectly, and which is helpful for the accomplishment of the action, is considered the Locus in the teaching.

Kattukammabyavahitanti kattukammehi taṃsamavetabhāvena byavahitaṃ, anuju pārampariyena, kriyāsiddhupakāriti kattukammasamavetāya kiriyāya pasiddhiyaṃ upakārī upakubbantaṃ, nanu ca na kiriyā dhāraṇenevāyamādhāro, kattukammānaṃ dhāraṇenāpyādhāroti sakkā [M 0.0112] vavatthapetunti codanammanasi nidhāyāha-‘na ce’tyādi, kiriyā nimittassevāti kattukammasamavāyiniyā kiriyāya nimittasseva, tadevaṃvidhamādhāraṃ catubbidhammatanti dassetumāha-‘ādhāro cāya’miccādi, cattāro vidhāpakārā assāti catubbidho, ādheyyena sahopasileso saṃyogalakkhaṇo-ssa atthīti opasilesiko ādhāro-‘kaṭenisīdati thāliyaṃ pacati’tyādo kaṭādi, tathāhi devadattasamavetaṃ nisīdanakiriyaṃ kaṭo devadattaṃ dhārayaṃ dhārayati devadattabyavahitaṃ, evaṃ thālīpi taṇḍulasamavetaṃ vikledanādikiriyaṃ taṇḍule dhārayaṃ dhārayatītyopasilesikādhārattaṃ kaṭādino. Yato-ññatrādheyyaṃ na vattate sabbathā bhiyyo vā, so vesayiko, visayohyādheyyassānaññatrabhāvo, yathā cakkhādippavattīnamaññatrābhāvā cakkhādīnaṃ rūpādayo visayāti vuccante, evamākāse sakunayotyādo sakunyādīnamākāsādito-ññatrābhāvāte tesaṃ visayātyuccante, visayo eva vesayiko. Yo ādhārādheyyānamabhibyāpetyādheyyamityabhibyāpako, tathā hi‘tilesu telaṃ, dadhimhi sappi,tyatra tilādikaṃ telādikamādheyyaṃ byāpetvā tiṭṭhatīti tilādi byāpakādhāro. Samīpe bhavo, samīpo eva vā sāmīpiko, yassa samīpadese ādheyyaṃ vattate so evamuccate, atrodāharaṇaṃ ‘gurūsu vasati gaṅgāyaṃ ghoso’ti. Nanu cātrāpyādhāre sattamī vidhīyate ādhāro ca nissayo vuccate, nissayo ca saṃyogasamavāyehi hoti, na ca sissādīnaṃ guruppabhutīti devadattasakunyādīnamiva kaṭākāsādīhi saṃyogo, telādīnamiva ca tilādīhi samavāyo vā atthi, tenāyuttaṃ te samādhārattanti, netadatthi, yadāyattā hi yassa ṭhiti so vināpi saṃyogasamavāyehi tassa nissayo bhavati, tathāhi purisassa na raññā saha saṃyogosamavāyo vātthi, atha pana tadadhīnaṭṭhitittā rājanissayo purisoti byapadissīyate, sissādīnañca guruppabhutina māyattā ṭhitīti tesamayaṃ tenassāyaṃ (potthake) yuttho te pati gurupabhutīnaṃ nissayabhāvo (jinindabuddhi) yutto guruppabhutinaṃ nissayabhāvoti, ettha [M 0.0113] pana yajjapi vesayikābhibyapakānamādhārādheyyopasileso atthi, tathāpi pakārantarasseva paripphuṭattā tatheva vacanicchā, nāññathā opasilesikena vā opasilesikeva visayābhibyāpakānamaggahaṇato upasilesasse vā upasilesasseva paribyattattā tatheva vohāroti na saṅkaro saṅkanīyoti.

'Separated by agent and object' means separated by the agent and object by way of being inherent in them. `Anuju` means 'indirectly.' 'Helpful for the accomplishment of the action' means helping, being beneficial for the accomplishment of the action that is inherent in the agent and object. Having kept in mind the objection, 'But is this not a support only by supporting the action? It can also be established that it is a support by supporting the agent and object,' he says: 'And not,' etc. 'Only of the cause of the action' means only of the cause of the action that is inherent in the agent and object. To show that such a support is considered to be of four kinds, he says: 'And this support,' etc. It is of four kinds because it has four modes or types. The support that has contact (upasilesa), characterized by conjunction (saṃyoga), with the supported object is the adhesive support (opasilesiko), as in 'he sits on a mat,' 'he cooks in a pot,' etc. For the mat supports the action of sitting, which is inherent in Devadatta, by supporting Devadatta, from whom it is separated. Similarly, the pot supports the action of softening, etc., which is inherent in the rice, by supporting the rice. Thus, the mat and so on have the nature of an adhesive support. That support from which the supported object does not exist elsewhere at all, or exists more so, is the locational support (vesayiko). For a 'domain' (visaya) is the non-existence of the supported object elsewhere. For example, forms, etc., are called the domains of the eye, etc., because the activities of the eye, etc., do not occur elsewhere. Similarly, in 'birds in the sky,' etc., because birds, etc., do not exist apart from the sky, etc., these are called their domains. The domain itself is the locational support. That which pervades the supported object by encompassing it is the pervasive support (abhibyāpako). For example, in 'oil in sesame seeds,' 'ghee in yogurt,' the sesame seeds, etc., exist pervading the supported oil, etc., so the sesame seeds, etc., are a pervasive support. That which occurs in the vicinity, or is the vicinity itself, is the proximate support (sāmīpiko). It is so called when the supported object exists in its vicinity. Examples here are 'he lives with the teachers,' 'a hamlet on the Ganges.' Now, here too the seventh case is prescribed in the sense of the support, and the support is called a dependence (nissayo). And dependence occurs through conjunction and inherence. But for disciples, etc., with teachers, etc., there is no conjunction as there is for Devadatta, birds, etc., with a mat, the sky, etc., nor is there inherence as there is for oil, etc., with sesame seeds, etc. Therefore, it is improper for them to be a support. This is not so. For one whose stability is dependent on another, that one is a dependence for him even without conjunction or inherence. For example, a man has no conjunction or inherence with a king, but because his stability is dependent on him, the man is designated as 'dependent on the king.'
