And since the stability of disciples and others is dependent on their teachers and so on, it is proper for those teachers and so on to be their dependence. Here, although for the locational and pervasive supports there is contact between the support and the supported, nevertheless, because another mode is more evident, the desire to express it is just so. Otherwise, due to the non-inclusion of the locational and pervasive by the adhesive, or due to the non-manifestation of the contact, the usage is just so. Thus, confusion should not be suspected.

33. Nimitta

33. Cause

Nimittabhāvamattetīminā kammasaṃyogābhāvepi sattamiyā pavatti māha, na paresaṃ viya kammasaṃyoge eva, teneva vakkhati-‘evamaññate’ccādi, bāhirānaṃ hi-‘nimittā kammena” (caṃ, 2-1-89) iti suttaṃ, tattha kammena yoge payojanā sattamībhavatītyattho, ajinamhi haññate dīpītidīpinohananassa payojanaṃ cammaṃ, tassa dīpinaṃhantīti kammena yo go, sutte kammenātyavacane payojanaṃ vattumārabhate ‘na pane’ccādi.

By this [phrase] 'by the mere state of being a cause,' he states the occurrence of the seventh case ending even in the absence of a connection with an object, not, as for others, only in connection with an object. Therefore, he will say: 'evamaññate,' etc. For the outsiders have the sutta 'nimittā kammena' (Cāndra 2.1.89). There, the meaning is that the seventh case ending occurs for a purpose that is in connection with an object. For example, in 'a leopard is killed for its skin' (ajinamhi haññate dīpī), the purpose of killing the leopard is the hide; its connection with the object is in 'he kills the leopard.' In the sutta, he begins to state the purpose of the word 'kammena' with 'na pana,' etc.

34. Yabbhā

34. Yabbhā

Yassa kiriyāti yassa gavādyatthassa sambandhinī dohanādikiriyā, kiriyantarassāti gamanādikiriyantarassa, etenāti lakkhaṇanti etena, tato-ccassa vivaraṇaṃ kiriyāvatāti, “kālabhāvesu ce”ti (2-6-43) kaccāyanehi suttitaṃ, tadāha-‘kālatthehi cā’tiādi.

'The action of which' means the action of milking, etc., related to that thing, such as a cow. 'Of another action' means of another action, such as going. 'By this' means 'by this characteristic.' And its explanation is 'by one possessing an action.' The sutta ‘kālabhāvesu ca’ (Kacc. 2.6.43) was formulated by Kaccāyana. Therefore, he says: ‘kālatthehi ca,’ etc.

35. Chaṭṭhī

35. Sixth Case

Sāmissarādiyoge chaṭṭhīsattamiyo yathā siyunti “sāmissarādhipatidāyādasakkhipatibhūpasutehi ca “iti (2-3-39) āraddhaṃ parehi, tadāha-‘sāmi’ccādi, atra ca jinindabuddhinā “sāmyādīnaṃ bhedeno pādānaṃ pariyāyantaranivatyatthamiha mā hotu gāmassa rājā”ti vuttaṃ vākyamupanyasya hassāpya yuttattamupadassayamāha-‘sāmissare’ccādi, kena nivārīyate, na kenāpītyattho, visayavacanicchāyaṃ ‘gāme rājā’tyapi bhavitabbamityanenāha, “āyuttakusalehyāsevāya”mīti (2-3-40) āraddhaṃ, tadāha-‘āyutte’ccādi, āsavā tapparatā, byāvaṭo niyutto, tatthedaṃ siyā “āsevāyanti vakkhāmī tyavassaṃ [M 0.0114] vacanamidamārabbhanīyamaññathā īsaṃyuttepi ‘āyutto go sakaṭassā’ti pasajjatī”tyāsaṅkiya natthevetampi payojananti dassetumāha-‘vināpi’ccādi, “sāmissarā”tyadikaṃ kaccāyanasuttaṃ, tenevāti kaccāyanasutte pasūtasaddānantaraṃ kusalasaddaniddeseneva, idhāti moggallānavuttiyaṃ. Kaccāyanena “kammakaraṇa nimittatthesu sattamī” (2-6-40) “pañcamyatthe ca” (2-6-41) iti ca suttitaṃ, tenāha-‘kamme’ccādi, gahaṇassa bāhā visayoti sambandho, kaccāyanānaṃ‘bhikkhūsū’tiādīni kammatthe udāharaṇāni, hatthesūtiādīni karaṇatthe, kadalīsūti pañcamyatthe. “Maṇḍitussukkesu tatiyā ce”ti (2-6-45) kaccāyanasuttaṃ, tadāha ‘pasannatthe’ccādi, pasannattheti maṇḍitatthe, ussukkattheti ussāhatthe.

So that the sixth and seventh cases may occur in connection with words like ‘sāmi’ (master) and ‘issara’ (lord), the sutta ‘sāmissarādhipatidāyādasakkhipatibhūpasutehi ca’ (Cāndra 2.3.39) was commenced by others. Therefore, he says: ‘sāmi,’ etc. Here, Jinindabuddhi, presenting the statement ‘sāmyādīnaṃ bhedeno pādānaṃ pariyāyantaranivatyatthamiha mā hotu gāmassa rājā,’ and having ridiculed it and shown its impropriety, says: ‘sāmissare,’ etc. By what is it prevented? The meaning is: by nothing. By this he says that, due to the desire to express the sphere, even ‘gāme rājā’ should be possible. The sutta ‘āyuttakusalehyāsevāyam’ (Cāndra 2.3.40) was commenced. Therefore, he says: ‘āyutte,’ etc. ‘Āsevā’ means devotion; ‘byāvaṭo’ means engaged, appointed. Here, it might be objected: ‘I will say “āsevāyam”; this statement must necessarily be commenced, otherwise, even in cases of slight connection, “āyutto go sakaṭassā” (the ox is yoked to the cart) would result.’ Having raised this doubt, to show that there is no purpose even in this, he says: ‘vināpi,’ etc. The sutta beginning ‘sāmissarā’ is Kaccāyana’s sutta. Therefore, it is only by the specification of the word ‘kusala’ after the word ‘pasūta’ in Kaccāyana’s sutta. ‘Here’ means in the Moggallāna-vutti. Kaccāyana formulated the suttas ‘kammakaraṇa nimittatthesu sattamī’ (Kacc. 2.6.40) and ‘pañcamyatthe ca’ (Kacc. 2.6.41). Therefore, he says: ‘kamme,’ etc. The connection is that the sphere of inclusion is wide. For the Kaccāyana school, examples like ‘bhikkhūsu’ are in the sense of object, those like ‘hatthesu’ are in the sense of instrument, and ‘kadalīsu’ is in the sense of the ablative. The sutta ‘maṇḍitussukkesu tatiyā ce’ (Kacc. 2.6.45) is Kaccāyana’s sutta. Therefore, he says: ‘pasannatthe,’ etc. ‘Pasannatthe’ means in the sense of adorned or delighted; ‘ussukkatthe’ means in the sense of zealous.

36. Yato

36. From which

Visuṃ karaṇaṃ niddhāraṇaṃ, jinindabuddhācariyena “kimatthampunaridaṃ vacanaṃ yāvatā niddhāriyamāno-vayavo samudāyabbhantaro, tattha yadā samudāyassā-dhikaraṇattaṃ vattumicchīyate, tadā sattamī siddhāva, yathā rukkhe sākhāti, yadā tvavayavasambandho tadā chaṭṭhī, yathā rukkhassa sākhāti saccametaṃ papañcatthantu vacana”nti vuttaṃ, tañceta mayuttantidassento āha-‘na sālayo’ccādisūkayuttānidhaññāni sūkadhaññāni, āhitā avaṭṭhitā, ādheyya bhūtāti vuttaṃ hoti. Yatoti āhitattakāraṇā, tatoti yato jinindabuddhivacanamevamayuttaṃ, tasmā kāraṇā. ‘Pañcamī vibhatte”ti (2-3-42) pāṇinīya suttaṃ, tadāha-‘samudāyato’ccādi, sutato sakāsā sīlaṃ atisayena seyyoti sambandho, “niddhāraṇe chaṭṭhī sattamīsu pattesu tadapavādo, yaṃ yogo”ti parehākhyāyate, tattha tāva niddhāraṇamevettha natthi kuto chaṭṭhīsattamīnaṃ tatthappavatti, yato tāsaṃ bādhanatthamidamārabbhateti dassayamāha-‘nātra jātyādīhi’ccādi, nahiccādinā jātyādīhi niddhāraṇābhāvaṃ dasseti, jaccādīnanti niddhāraṇe chaṭṭhī, kuto na bhavaticcāha-‘jaccādisambandhene’ccādi, ataṃ byapadesatoti sīlattādibyapadesābhāvato, puna niddhāraṇābhāve hetvantaramāha-‘tulyānañce”ccādi[M 0.0115]. Sādhunipuṇehi yoge pūjāyaṃ gammamānāyaṃ sattamī, tathā asādhuyoge, tathā pasitaussukkehi yoge tatiyāsattamiyo, tathā lopantanakkhattasaddā ca tena tena vacanantarena pāṇiniyehi vihitā, taṃ sabbaṃ taṃtaṃkārakavacanicchāyameva sādhetuṃ ‘mātari sādhu’ iccādayo udāhaṭā kesesu pasito pasatto, avabaddhoti attho, kesehi karaṇabhūtehi pasito bhavati, kattubhūtehi vā pasito katoti attho, phusseninduyuttena lakkhito kālo soyamityabhedena sambandhā phusse, tena karaṇabhūtena.

Distinguishing is determination. The teacher Jinindabuddhi said: 'What is the purpose of this statement? To the extent that when determining, the elements are within the aggregate, there, when one wishes to speak of the aggregate as the locus, then the seventh case is established, as in “a branch on a tree.” But when the connection is between the elements themselves, then the sixth case applies, as in “the branch of a tree.” This statement is true, though it serves for elaboration.' And showing that this is inappropriate, he says: 'Not the rice,' etc., referring here to grains with awns, which are said to be in the sense of being the object of placing, being placed or situated. The reason is their being placed. Therefore, because Jinindabuddhi's statement is thus inappropriate, for that reason. The Pāṇinian rule states: 'The fifth [case is used] in separation' (2-3-42). Hence, it is said: 'From the aggregate,' etc. The connection is that virtue is exceedingly superior to what is heard. Others explain: 'In determination, when the sixth or seventh case is obtained, then that is an exception, whatever the connection.' Here, first of all, determination itself does not exist—how then could the sixth or seventh case apply here? To show that this is initiated to refute them, it is said: 'Not here by birth,' etc. By 'na hi' and so on, he shows the absence of determination by birth and so on. The sixth case in determination is 'jaccādīnaṃ' (of birth, etc.). Why does it not occur? He says: 'Because of the connection with birth, etc.' Because there is no such designation, due to the absence of designations like 'virtuousness' etc. Again, another reason for the absence of determination is given: 'And if of equals,' etc. When there is a connection with 'sādhu' (good) and 'nipuṇa' (skillful), the seventh case occurs when honor is implied. Likewise, with the unskillful. Similarly, with eager and diligent connections, the third and seventh cases apply. Likewise, words ending in lopa (elision) and nakkhata (constellation) are prescribed by Pāṇini in various ways by various statements. All this is to establish the intention of the speaker regarding the respective case. Examples like 'good to his mother,' etc., are cited. 'Attached to the hair'—the meaning is 'bound.' He becomes attached by means of the hair as instrument, or the meaning is 'he is made attached by the hair as agent'. The time marked by the constellation Phussa, connected with the moon, is 'this one' without difference, in Phussa, by means of that instrument.

37. Paṭhamā

37. The First

Paṭhamātthamatteti ettake vuttepi vākyattho padattho vā na viññāyate nāmaggahaṇānuvattitoti dassetumāha-‘dvedvekānekādi suttato’tiādi, nāmenāttho paṭipādiyamāno nāmasaṅkhāte-ttani abhidheyyattenājjhāropya paṭipādayatyanapekkhita vibhattivisesanti āha-‘abhidhīyati’ccādi, pakatirūpenāti nāmena, tassa abhidheyyassa, mattasaddassātiādinā sāmaññantīdaṃ mattasaddassatthavacananti dasseti, idaṃ vuttaṃ hotīti nāmassābhidheyyamatteti iminā idaṃ vakkhamānaṃ vuttaṃ hoti. “Pāṭipadikatthaliṅgaparimāṇavacanamatte paṭhamā”ti (2-3-46) liṅgādīsu bhedena paṭhamāvidhānampaṭipannā, tadāha-‘liṅgaparimāṇe’ccādi, liṅgaṃ itthipunnapuṃsakāni, parimāṇaṃ paricchedo, saṅkhyā ekattabahuttāni, tabbantopi saddatthoevāti liṅgādivantopi sarūpā byatiritto saddattho eva, uccattanīcattasāmaññampurodhāya pavattiyā uccanīcasaddehi paṭhamā hoteva, taṃyuttassāpi saddatthabhāvato ‘uccaṃ gharāni’tyādīnipi uccattaṃ guṇaṃ nimittaṃ katvā soyamityabhedasambandha gharesu vattantīti. Palambate ajjhāgacchatityādo “asaṅkhyehi sabbāsaṃ”ti (2-119) lopavidhānasāmatthiyā pādīhyanatthakehipi paṭhamā siddhāyeva.

To show that when only 'in the mere meaning of the first [case]' is stated, the meaning of the sentence or the meaning of the word is not understood because it follows the taking up of the name, he says: 'from the sutta “dve, dveka, aneka,” etc.' and so on. The meaning conveyed by the name is presented by superimposing it as the denotation on the name itself, without regard for specific case endings. Thus he says: 'abhidhīyati' (it is denoted), and so on. 'By its natural form' means by the name. By 'of the word matta,' etc., he shows that 'generality' is the statement of the meaning of the word 'matta'. This is what is said: by this phrase 'in the mere denotation of the name,' the following is stated. 'The first [case ending] is used in the mere sense of the nominal stem, gender, measure, and number' (Pāṇini 2.3.46). The prescription of the first [case] is undertaken with distinctions in regard to gender, etc. Thus he says: 'in gender, measure,' etc. Gender is feminine, masculine, and neuter. Measure is limitation. Number is singularity and plurality. Even that which possesses these is just the meaning of the word; that is, even that which possesses gender, etc., is just the meaning of the word, distinct from its own form. Based on the generality of highness and lowness, the first [case] is indeed used with the words 'ucca' and 'nīca', because what is connected with them also has the meaning of the word. Thus, in expressions like 'uccaṃ gharāni' (high houses), etc., taking the quality 'highness' as the ground, they refer to the houses through a relation of non-difference, 'this is that.' In 'palambate,' 'ajjhāgacchati,' etc., on the strength of the rule for elision 'of all with uncountables' (Kaccāyana 2.119), the first [case] is established even with prefixes that are without meaning.

38. Āmanta

38. Addressing

Abhimukhaṃ katvātiādinā yogārambhassa phalaṃ dasseti, nāmattheti [M 0.0116] saddatthe, padatoti āmantaṇādhikaatthamattappakāsakapadato, honti cettha…

By 'having made it face,' etc., he shows the result of undertaking the formulation. 'In the meaning of the name' means 'in the meaning of the word.' 'From the word' means 'from the word that expresses only the additional meaning of addressing.' And here there are...

Siddhassābhimukhīkāra bhimukhībhāva (potthake), mattamāmantaṇaṃ siyā;

Attho katābhimukho hi, kriyāyaṃ viniyujjate;

Āmantaṇaṃ na vākyattho, padatova patītito;

Natthevāmantaṇaṃ loke, vidhātabbena vatthunā;

Taṃ yathā bhava rājeti, nippannattho bhaveti ca.

Addressing should be the mere act of making one who is established face [the speaker]; for the object, having been made to face, is employed in an action. Addressing is not the meaning of the sentence, as it is understood from the word alone. There is no addressing in the world of an object that is yet to be brought about. For example, in 'O king, be!', the meaning is accomplished by 'be!'

Siddhassāti devadattattādinā siddhassa, atthoti devadattādi, kataṃ ābhimukhyaṃ samādhānaṃ yenāti viggaho, kriyāyaṃ viniyujjate gaccha bhuñjāti, āmantaṇaṃ natthi… idāni vidhīyamānattenāladdhasattikassābhimukhayitumasakkarūpattā, vidhātabbenāti nipphādetabbena.

'Of one who is established' means established as Devadatta, etc. 'Object' means Devadatta, etc. The analysis is: 'that by which facing, i.e., attention, is done.' 'Is employed in an action,' such as 'go!', 'eat!'. There is no addressing... because it is impossible to make something face [the speaker] that has not yet acquired existence, as it is now being brought about. 'By that which is to be brought about' means 'by that which is to be produced'.

39. Chaṭṭhī

39. The Sixth

Kiriyākārakeccādivuttiganthassa atthasaṃvaṇṇanaṃ kattumārabhate ‘ekāyaṃ sambandho nāme’ccādi, kiriyāya kārakehi ca nipphāditoti iminā sambandhassa kiriyākārakasambandha pubbakattamāha, tatoyevāyaṃ nākasmīkoti na yesaṃkesañci dvinnaṃ bhavati, visiṭṭhānaṃyeva tu dvinnaṃ bhavatītyatippasaṅgābhāvo, kiriyākārakasambandhapubbako hi kārakehi añño sassāmibhāvādiko sambandho, tathā ca vuttaṃ–

He begins to explain the meaning of the Vutti text beginning 'action, agent,' etc., with 'this one connection by name,' etc. By this phrase 'accomplished by the action and by the agents,' he states that the connection is preceded by the action-agent connection. Therefore it is not accidental; it does not occur between any two things whatsoever, but only between two specific things. Thus there is no over-extension. For the relation of ownership, etc., which is other than the agents, is preceded by the action-agent connection. And so it has been said—

“Sambandho kārakehañño, kriyākārakapubbako;

Sutāyamassutāyaṃvā, kriyāyaṃ so-bhidhīyateti.

A relation other than the agents, preceded by the action and the agent, is expressed in connection with an action, whether that action is heard or unheard.

Tattha assutāyaṃ kiriyāyaṃ ‘rañño puriso’ccādo kiriyā kārakasambandhapubbako-ñño eva sassāmibhāvādiko sambandho patīyateti, ‘sarati rajjassa’tyādo tu suyyamāne kiriyāsadde, ettha pana santamapi kammaṃ vattumanicchitaṃ, visesanabhāvoyeva saraṇampati rajjassa paṭipādīyate’rajjasambandhisaraṇa’nti, kiriyākāraka sambandho hi sabbattha vatthuṭṭhitivasenevatthi, tannimitto ca sassāmi bhāvādi, tattha sassāmibhāvavivacchāyaṃ vijjamānopi kiriyākāraka sambandho [M 0.0117] na vattumicchito, yathā ‘anudarā kaññā’ti, so cāyaṃ sambandho sassāmibhāvajaññajanakabhāvā-vayavāvayavavibhāvādilakkhaṇo bahuvidhoti veditabbo, tattha sassāmisambandhe rañño puriso, jaññajanakasambandhe nigrodhassa bījaṃ, avayavāvayavisambandhe rukkhassa sākhā, idāni sambandhassetassa kiriyākārakasambandhasañjātattaṃ yathāyogamaññatrāpyavagamayituṃ kiñci udāharaṇamāha-‘tathā hi’ccādi, paripālanakiriyākato nesaṃ sambandhoti iminā paripālyaparipālanalakkhaṇo-yaṃ sambandhoti dasseti, sā ayampari pālanalakkhaṇā kiriyā sambandhamassedambhāvahetuṃ janayitvā nivattati, atthappakaraṇādinā tvimāya kiriyāyāyaṃ sambandhoti viseso vasīyate, na chaṭṭhiyā visesāvagamane sāmatthiyaṃ… tassā sabbatthekarūpattā, suyyamāne eva vā kiriyāsadde kārakabhāvassa hetuno vacanicchāyābhāve assedambhābhāvasaṅkhātasseva phalassa vattumicchitattā tatheva sambandho jāto chaṭṭhiyābhidhīyate ‘rajjassa saratī’ti, vuttaṃ hi–

Therein, when the action is unheard, as in 'the king's man,' a relation of ownership, etc., is understood, which is other than and preceded by the action-kāraka relation. But in 'he remembers the kingdom,' etc., the action-word is heard. Here, however, although the object exists, there is no desire to express it as such; rather, only its state as a qualifier in relation to the remembering is conveyed for the kingdom, as in 'remembering related to the kingdom.' For the action-kāraka relation exists everywhere by virtue of the objective situation, and the relation of ownership, etc., is grounded in that. Therein, when there is a desire to express ownership, even though the action-kāraka relation exists, there is no desire to state it, as in 'a girl with a slender waist.' And this relation should be understood as manifold, characterized by ownership, the generator-generated relation, the part-whole relation, etc. For example: in the relation of ownership, 'the king's man'; in the generator-generated relation, 'the seed of the banyan tree'; in the part-whole relation, 'the branch of the tree.' Now, to make it understood how this relation is produced from the action-kāraka relation elsewhere as appropriate, he gives an example, saying: 'For indeed...' By 'their relation is made by the action of protecting,' he shows that this is a relation characterized by the protected and the protector. This action, characterized by protection, having generated the cause for this genitive ('of this') relation, ceases. But by means of the meaning, context, etc., the specific determination 'this relation is from this action' is understood. The sixth [case ending] does not have the capacity to convey a specific meaning, because it has the same form everywhere. Or, even when the action-word is heard, since there is no desire to state the kāraka-role as the cause, but rather a desire to state only the result, designated as the genitive ('of this') relation, a relation is thus produced and is denoted by the sixth [case], as in 'he remembers the kingdom.' For it has been said—

Janayitvāna sambandhaṃ, kriyā kāci nivattati;

Suyyamāne kriyāsadde, sambandho jāyate kvacīti.

Having generated a relation, a certain action ceases; when the action-word is heard, a relation sometimes arises.

Paripālayatīti purisamparipālayati, tato pālanādikā upakāra sabhāvā kiriyādvinnampi tesaṃ sambandhinī bhavati, raññā hi kāriyamānā taṃsambandhinīpurisavisayattāvapurisayoginītyubhinnampikiriyāsambhavati, tatoyevatassā ubhayasambandhiniyā kiriyāya sambhaveassedanti buddhiyā hetubhūtassa aññamaññāpekkhasabhāvassa sambandhassa bhāvato kiriyājanitattamassa, aññamaññāpekkhālakkhaṇo… sabbathā nirapekkhatte sambandhābhāvā, sambandhi buddhisabbhavassāti sambandhīsu rājapurisādīsu assedanti evampavattāya buddhiyā sabbhavassa. Paresaṃ viya “guṇe chaṭṭhī”ti vacanantarābhāve ubhayatthapi (cettha) (yeva) (potthake) chaṭṭhippa- saṅgoti bodhetumāha-‘nanu ce’ccādi, saccanti yathā vuttaṃ codanamabbhupagamma codakampati yathāvuttaṃ sambandharūpaṃ tato-ññatrāpyupasaṃ haritvā [M 0.0118] tattha chaṭṭhippasaṅgaṃ codetumāha-‘devadatto’ccādi, atheva miccādināsatīpiaññamaññāpekkhālakkhaṇe sambandhe vacanicchāyevettha kāraṇanti codakādhippāyamatropanetvā tadeva visesato chaṭṭhiyā abhāve samupanetuṃ‘yajjevamihāpi’ccādikamāha, tattha athāti codakādhippāyappakāsanārambhe nipāto, evaṃ vattabbanti evaṃ yadipiccādinā vakkhamānanayena vattabbaṃ, paṭipādetabbatāyātyādinā idandīpeti “visessaṃ vidheyatāya na parādhīnanti appadhānabhāvato byatiriccate tato-ttaniṭṭhameva, na rūpantarambhajati‘purisasse’ti, visesanantu rājādikaṃ tadaṅgatāyānuvadiyamānamappadhānattā kārakarūpato byatiriccate, tato rūpantaraṃ bhajati ‘rañño’ti, tato byatireka lakkhaṇo sambandho hoti, ekassa sambandhittāsambhavā vatthuto dviṭṭho visesanagatattena patīyate tato chaṭṭhī visesanamevānudhāvati patītivisaye saddappavattī”ti, yo hi vikappanaṃ visayo so saddānanti, atoyeva sambandho niyamena visesanabhedamanuvidadhāti… vatthuto dviṭṭhassāpi taggatattena patītiyā yathā bhātūnaṃ dhananti, nāvassambhātūnaṃ dhananticceva bhavati, tathā satyapi visessa bhede visesanagatameva bhedamanu(vidadhā)ti ‘devadattassa assā’ti, tadetaṃ sabbaṃ visesanagatattena sambandhapatītito-vakappīyate, visessagatattenāpi tappatītiyaṃ niyamena taggatabhedānuvidhānaṃ siyā visesanagatabhedānuvidhānamiva, dviṭṭhattantu vatthuto cattuno na virujjhate, vattupaṭibaddhameva ca dviṭṭhattaṃ manasikatvā taṃvādīhi dviṭṭho sambandhobhidhīyate, atoyevāyaṃ byatirekavibhatti (yāgamyate)… byatiriccamānavisesanabhūtasambandhigatabyatirekalakkhaṇasambandhābhi- dhānappavattitoti, nīlādivisesanantu paratthattenāppadhānampi na kārakabhāvato byatiriccati… nīlādisaddenuppalādidabbābhidhānato, yathā ‘nīlamuppalampassa, nīlenuppalena ṭhitaṃ, nīlassuppalassa gandho’ti, yadā tu na visessapavatti tadā byatiriccateva ‘nīlassa guṇassa uppalannissayo’ti kārakabhāvalakkhaṇā padhānabhāvā byatiriccate eva nīlādi, tato visesanamevānekappakāratāyāva tiṭṭhate, tato vise- sanaṃ [M 0.0119] kiñcideva kārakarūpato padhānabhāvā byatiriccateti visesana mattenāpi sesaṃ sabbaṃ tathā siyāti nāsaṅkanīyanti.

'He protects' means he protects a person. Hence, the action of protection and other such beneficial actions pertain to both of them. For when an action is performed by the king, since its object is the person connected to him, it is associated with the person; thus the action is possible for both. Therefore, precisely because of the existence of a relationship whose nature is mutual dependence—which is the cause for the thought 'this is of that' when an action relating to both is possible—this relationship is produced by the action. It is characterized by mutual dependence, for in the case of complete independence, there is no relationship. The existence of the thought of a relationship means the existence of a thought that proceeds thus: 'this is of that' in relation to the related things, such as the king's men. To explain that, as with others, in the absence of another statement like 'the sixth [case] is for a quality,' the sixth case would apply to both, he says: 'nanu ce,' etc. Accepting the objection as stated, he addresses the objector. Applying the form of the relationship as described elsewhere, he then raises the objection of the application of the sixth case there, saying: 'devadatto,' etc. Then, with 'athevaṃ,' etc., he introduces the objector's opinion that even when there is a relationship characterized by mutual dependence, the desire for a particular expression is the reason here. To establish this especially in the absence of the sixth case, he says: 'yajjevam ihāpi,' etc. Here, 'atha' is a particle at the beginning of the exposition of the objector's opinion. 'Evaṃ vattabbaṃ' means it should be stated in this way, that is, in the manner to be explained with 'yadi pi,' etc. With 'paṭipādetabbatāyā,' etc., he clarifies this: 'The qualified, being what is predicated, is not dependent on another. Thus, it is distinguished from the non-principal state. Therefore, it stands on its own and does not take another form, as in 'purisassa' (of the man). The qualifier such as 'king,' however, being mentioned as an attribute of that, is distinguished from the kāraka-form due to its non-principal status. Therefore, it takes another form, as in 'rañño' (of the king).' Thus, the relationship is characterized by distinction. Since a relationship cannot belong to one thing, in reality it belongs to two, but it is perceived as belonging to the qualifier. Therefore, the sixth case follows only the qualifier, as speech operates in the domain of perception. For whatever is the object of conceptualization is the object of words. Therefore, the relationship invariably follows the distinction of the qualifier. Although in reality it belongs to two, this is because it is perceived as belonging to that [qualifier], as in 'the wealth of the brothers,' it is not necessarily the case that the form must be 'the wealth of the brothers.' Similarly, even when there is a distinction in the qualified, it follows the distinction belonging to the qualifier, as in 'Devadatta's mare.' All this is determined from the perception of the relationship as belonging to the qualifier. If it were also perceived as belonging to the qualified, it would invariably follow the distinction belonging to that, just as it follows the distinction belonging to the qualifier. The fact that it belongs to two is not contradicted in reality. And it is by considering that it belongs to two, which is connected to the thing itself, that those theorists state that the relationship belongs to two. Therefore, this is the case of distinction, which operates to express the relationship characterized by distinction, which belongs to the distinguishing qualifier-relatum. A qualifier such as 'blue,' however, although non-principal because it exists for the sake of another, is not distinguished from the kāraka-form, because the word 'blue,' etc., denotes the substance 'lotus,' etc., as in 'see the blue lotus,' 'standing with a blue lotus,' 'the fragrance of the blue lotus.' But when it does not function as a qualifier for a qualified noun, it is indeed distinguished, as in 'the lotus is the support of the quality of blue.' Here, 'blue,' etc., is indeed distinguished from the kāraka-form, which is characterized by being principal. Therefore, the qualifier stands in many different forms. Hence, it should not be suspected that because some qualifier is distinguished from the kāraka-form, which is principal, all other qualifiers merely by being qualifiers would be so.

Dvepīti rājapurisā dvepi, tatiye gehasaṅkhāte sambandhinī. Sahayuttampaṭicca evanti iminā purisassa appadhānattameva dīpeti, abhimatāti pāṇiniyānaṃ suttantarena abhimatā, yato chaṭṭhīya-mattano mate sambandhanissayā, tenāha- ‘sambandhamevi’ccādi, sambandho cettha mātu saraṇānamavaṭṭhānādikiriyānimittoti keci, aññe tu saraṇassa kiriyārūpattā kiriyantaramantareneva dabbena sambandhopapattimāhuyathā dvinnaṃ jatukato saṃsileso, jatuno tu kaṭṭhenāttanāyeva, na jatvantarakato saṃsilesoti. Paresaṃ tatiyatthe dutiyatthe ca kitakappayoge ññatrāpi (pañcamyatthe) sattamyatthe ca (“chaṭṭhī cā”) ti (2-6-20) dutiyā pañcamīnañcā”ti (2-6-29) ca suttantarehi chaṭṭhītimatā, tassāpi vatticchātova sādhitabhāvaṃ dassetumāha-yathācetthātiādi, etthāpyādo udāharaṇadvaye suttantaramantarena sampadānattābhāvā sambandhavacanicchāyameva paresampi chaṭṭhī, tenāha-‘etthā’tiādi, bahulantīmassa atthaṃ dasseti ‘yathā dassana’nti, avisaṃvādakālokassatyādikaṃ kamme udāharaṇaṃ, pañcamyatthe pana vatticchātova sabbe tasanti daṇḍassātyādīni udāharaṇāni veditabbāni.

'Both' means both the king and the man; the relationship is with the third, which is designated as the house. By this, 'sahayuttaṃ paṭicca evaṃ,' he shows precisely the non-principal status of the man. 'It is accepted' means it is accepted by the Pāṇinians through another sutta, because in his own opinion, the sixth case is based on the relationship. Therefore he says: 'sambandham eva,' etc. Some say that the relationship here is caused by actions such as remembering the mother. But others say that since remembering is itself a form of action, a connection with a substance is possible without another action, just as the adhesion of two things is from lac, but the lac adheres to wood by itself, not from another lac. For others, the sixth case is accepted in the sense of the third and second cases in connection with a verbal derivative, and also elsewhere in the sense of the fifth and seventh cases by other suttas, namely, 'chaṭṭhī ca' and 'dutiyā pañcamīnañca.' To show that its use is established simply by the desire to speak, he says: 'yathā cettha,' etc. Here too, in the first two examples, because there is no dative sense without another sutta, for others too the sixth case is used simply from the desire to express a relationship. Therefore he says: 'etthā,' etc. He shows the meaning of 'bahulaṃ' as 'according to usage.' An example in the accusative sense is 'avisaṃvādakālokassa,' etc. But in the sense of the fifth case, examples such as 'all are afraid of the stick' should be understood as arising simply from the desire to speak.

40. Tulya

40. Similar

Anabhimatāti ‘tulyatthehyatulopamāhi tatiyāññatarissa’nti (2-3-72) suttena tulopamāhi aññehi tulyatthehi yoge tatiyāya vidhīyamānattā pāṇiniyānaṃ anabhimatā, yasmā sadisā bhāvā tesaṃ nopamāti ‘ajjunassa tulā natthī’tyādikamuccate, tasmā evaṃ yathāvuttanayenāti tadevantīmassa attho veditabbo, tadevanti vā nipātasamudāyo yathāvuttanidassanattho, tulyesūti sadisesu, tathāvuttāti ajjunassatulānatthītyādinā tena pakārena vuttā.

'Not accepted' means it is not accepted by the Pāṇinians because by the sutta 'tulyatthehi atulopamāhi tatiyā aññatarassaṃ' (Pāṇini 2.3.72), the third case is optionally prescribed in connection with words having a similar meaning other than 'tulā' and 'upamā.' Since for them similar things are not a comparison, it is said: 'There is no equal to Arjuna,' etc. Therefore, the meaning of 'tadevaṃ' should be understood as 'thus, in the manner stated.' Or 'tadevaṃ' is a collection of particles with the meaning of illustrating what has been said. 'Among similars' means among those that are alike. 'Stated thus' means stated in that manner with 'There is no equal to Arjuna,' etc.

41. Ato

41. Ato

Sutte [M 0.0120] ‘ato’ti vuttaṃ ‘akārantato’ti kathaṃ vuttīti āha ‘ato’tiādi, ādesā hontīti seso, yakārānaṃyeva siyuṃ… āeādesānamekavaṇṇattā, lope kateti okārassa lope kate, tanneti yathāvuttaṃ dhacādyappaṭikkhipati, paṭikkhepe kāraṇamāha-‘paralopassā’tiādi, kāraṇantaraṃ vattumārabhate ‘kiñcā’tiādi, niccamparalopova siyā, na pubbalopopi āgamappayogānukūlyenātipi sakkā vattunti āha-‘nacā’tiādi, niccamparalopoyevāti na ca sakkā mantunti sambandho, evaṃ santetyādinā tattha virodhamāha, atosambhavāti ādesākārato sambhavā, jhissākāravidhānaṃ “yosu jhissa pume”ti (2-93) etadevapayojanantiādinā vuttappayojanābhāve kāraṇamāha-‘aniṭṭhattā’ti, anabhimatattāti attho, payojanābhāvānabhimatattameva dassesumāha-‘etadatthamevā’tiādi, imassāti “ato yonaṃ ṭāṭe”tī massa suttassa, jhismātvevāti ‘jhismā’ iti etādisaṃ suttameva, jhismā yonaṃ ṭāṭetivāti “jhismā yonaṃ ṭāṭe”ti suttaṃ vā, atoti ‘ato’ iti suttaṃ, tādisassapayogassāti aggā, agge iti payogassa.

To the question, 'In the rule, 'ato' is stated; how is it said to mean 'from the a-ending'?', he replies: 'ato,' etc. The remainder is 'substitutes occur.' They would be only for the y-sounds... because the substitutes 'ā' and 'e' are single letters. When elision is performed, that is, when the o-sound is elided, that rule rejects the 'dha,' etc., as stated. As for the reason for the rejection, he says: 'because of the elision of the following,' etc. He begins to state another reason: 'And further,' etc. The elision of the following should always occur, not the elision of the preceding. Because it is also possible to say this due to the suitability of applying an augment, he says: 'And not,' etc. The connection is: it is not possible to hold that only the elision of the following always occurs. With 'this being so,' etc., he points out the contradiction therein. 'Arising from 'ato'' means arising from the substitute a-sound. As for the absence of the stated purpose for the rule prescribing 'ā' for 'jhi' in 'yosu jhissa pume' (Kaccāyana 2.93), which is said to be for this very purpose, he states the reason: 'because it is undesired.' The meaning is 'because it is not intended.' To show that the very lack of purpose is what is not intended, he says: 'For this very purpose,' etc. 'Of this' means of this rule 'ato yonaṃ ṭāṭe.' 'Jhismā tveva' means just such a rule as 'jhismā,' or the rule is 'jhismā yonaṃ ṭāṭe.' 'Ato' means the rule 'ato.' 'Of such a usage' means of the usage 'aggā, agge'.

42. Nīnaṃ

42. Nīnaṃ

Yasmā ekameva rūpamudāhaṭaṃ, tasmā rūpārūpāni rūperūpānīti bhedo veditabbo, tena hi bahuvacane bahuvacanena (potthake) paṭhamādutiyāsu ‘aṭṭhīnī’ti ekameva rūpamudāhaṭanti dasseti.

Since only one form is cited, the distinction between 'rūpārūpāni' and 'rūperūpāni' should be understood. Thus, it shows that in the plural, in the nominative and accusative cases, only one form, 'aṭṭhīnī,' is cited.

44. Sassāya

44. Sassāya

Suñiti ñakāro kimatthoti āha-‘ñakāro’tiādi, asati hi ñakāre‘ñānubandho’ti ñakārena visesanena sukāro na visesī yeyya satiyeva tasmiṃ tena so visesīyeyya, tasmā “ñakānubandhādyantā”ti sutte ‘ñakānubandhā’ti visesanaṃ [M 0.0121] visesanabhāvo attho payojanaṃ yassa so visesanattho, bahulaṃ vacanenānabhimatamanavasesaṃ vavatthāpīyatīti vuttiyaṃ “bhiyyo”tyādikamupadiṭṭhanti dassetumupakkamate ‘sāmaññenā’tiādinā, chaṭṭhī bhavatīti (se)so, nanuca atthasaddenāññapadatthasamāse kathaṃ catutthyattho-vasīyatīti vuccate, catutthīekavacane attattha’nti ettha saddhammasavanādikamattanimittanti yo-ttho, so cattho-ñña padatthepi, tassā-ññapadatthabhūtassāpi attā attho payojanambhavati nimittabhāvenāti nātthabhedoti ta eta imavajjitānaṃ sabbādīnanti ta etaimasaddehi eva vajjitānamaññesaṃ sabbādīnaṃ, paṭisiddhesupi kassaci ādeso dissatīti dassetumāha‘tasaddassa cā’ti.

Regarding 'suñi,' what is the purpose of the letter 'ñ'? He says: 'the letter ñ,' etc. For if the letter 'ñ' were absent, the letter 'su' would not be specified by the qualifier 'having ñ as an anubandha.' Only when it is present is it specified by that. Therefore, in the rule 'ñakānubandhādyantā,' the qualifier 'ñakānubandhā' has qualification as its meaning and purpose. He begins to show with 'in general,' etc., that in the commentary it is taught with 'bhiyyo,' etc., that by the word 'bahulaṃ' (variously), what is not intended is fully established. The remainder is 'the genitive occurs.' But then, in a bahubbīhi compound with the word 'attha,' how is the meaning of the dative determined? It is said: in the dative singular 'attattha,' the meaning is 'for one's own purpose,' such as listening to the good Dhamma. That meaning also exists in the meaning of the other word. For that which has become the meaning of the other word, 'self' becomes the meaning and purpose in the sense of a cause; thus there is no difference in meaning. 'Of the 'sabba,' etc., group, excluding 'ta,' 'eta,' and 'ima'' means: of the other words of the 'sabba,' etc., group, which are excluded only by the words 'ta,' 'eta,' and 'ima.' To show that even among the prohibited ones, a substitute for a certain one is seen, he says: 'And of the word 'ta'.'

45. Ghapa

45. Ghapa

Itthiyā vadhuyāti pasaññānamī ūnamudāharaṇāni.

The forms 'itthiyā' and 'vadhuyā' are examples for the vowels 'ī' and 'ū' of stems with the technical term 'pa'.

46. Ssāvā

46. Ssāvā

Ghapasaññehīti idaṃ tetimāmūhi tīmassa aññapadatthasamāsena vā visesanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, vuttiyaṃ katanti ādikaṃ kattādippakāsanatthaṃ kataṃ, tāyāti sabbattha vikappodāharaṇaṃ.

'Ghapasaññehi'—this should be understood as a qualifier of 'tīmassa' either by a bahubbīhi compound with 'tehi imāmūhi' or as an adjective. In the commentary, 'katam,' etc., is used to indicate the agent and so on. 'Tāya' is an example of an optional form everywhere.

47. Namhi

47. Namhi

“Āgamā tagguṇībhūtā taggahaṇena gayhantī”ti paribhāsā vacanametaṃ tattha tagguṇībhūtāti tasmiṃ āgamimhi guṇībhūtā, avayavavasena pacchā bhavanto amukhyabhūtā, taggahaṇenāti āgamiggahaṇena taggahaṇena gahaṇatoti āgamibhūtassa naṃ iccassa gahaṇena gahaṇato, ‘namhi vibhattimhi’ti tu vattabbaṃ, vipallāso vā ettha daṭṭhabbo.

This statement, 'Augments, having become a quality of it, are taken by the taking of it,' is a maxim. Therein, 'having become a quality of it' means having become a quality in that which receives the augment; becoming secondary, they arise afterwards by way of being a part. 'By the taking of it' means by the taking of that which receives the augment; because it is taken by the taking of 'naṃ' which has become the augment. But it should be stated as 'in the inflectional ending namhi.' Or a transposition should be seen here.

(49) Ikārassevavātiādinā vuttameva vivarati tissa iccādinā, tassa tissa, niddiṭṭhattāti tissa niddiṭṭhattā, “namhi ticatunnamitthiyaṃ tissa catassā”ti (2-20) tissādeso “namhi nuka dvādīnaṃ sattarasanna”nti (2-47) nuka, tissannaṃ.

(49) With 'Ikārasseva,' etc., he explains what was just said with 'tissa,' etc. 'Of that, tissa'; 'because it is specified' means because 'tissa' is specified. By the rule 'namhi ticatunnamitthiyaṃ tissa catassā' (Kaccāyana 2.20), the substitute is 'tissā'; by the rule 'namhi nuka dvādīnaṃ sattarasannaṃ' (Kaccāyana 2.47), 'nuka' is the augment for 'tissannaṃ'.

51. Suña

51. Suña

Vibhattisutteti [M 0.0122] “dvedvekānekesvi”(2-1) ccādisutte, ssananti bahuvacanena sahitamekavacanamāha, suttamidanti “suñsassā”ti idaṃ suttaṃ, sutte pana satīti “suña sassā”ti sutte sati.

'In the rule about inflectional endings' means in the rule beginning 'dvedvekānekesu' (Kaccāyana 2.1). With 'ssānaṃ,' he states the singular together with the plural. 'This rule' means this rule 'suñassa ā.' 'But when the rule exists' means when the rule 'suña sassa ā' exists.

55. Ratyā

55. Ratyā

Ratti ca ādi ca ratyādayo, tehi.

'Ratti' and 'ādi' make 'ratyādayo' (the group beginning with 'ratti'); 'tehi' means by them.

56. Suhi

56. Suhi

Anukaraṇavasenāti anusadisaṃ karaṇaṃ vacanamanukaraṇaṃ.

'By way of imitation' means: imitation is a statement that makes something similar.

57. Ltu

57. Ltu

Tenāti yato ltuiti visesanattena vattumicchitassa paccayassa gahaṇaṃ, tenāti attho, paccayassa gahaṇā tadādigahaṇaṃ labbhate… “paccayaggahaṇe yato so vihito, tadādino gahaṇa”nti ñāyā, visesanattena vattumicchitattā tadantaggahaṇaṃ… “vidhibbisesanantassā”ti (1-13) vacanatoti manasi nidhāyāha- ‘yato’iccādi, so kriyattho ādi yassa so tadādi, so paccayo-nto yassa samudāyassa so tadanto, tādisassa tadā ditadantasamudāyavisesa(ssa) gahaṇaṃ, na tu tadantamattassetyattho, nanu ca ‘ltvī’ti visesanattena vattumicchite bhavatu “vidhibbisesanantassā”ti tadantassa gahaṇaṃ, paccayaggahaṇena pana tadādino gahaṇaṃ kathaṃ siyā vacanābhāvātyāha-‘tadavinābhāvittā’ti, yato vihito, tena vinā na bhavati sīlenāti tadavinābhāvī, tassa bhāvo tasmā. “Paccayaggahaṇe yato so vihito tadādino gahaṇa”nti ñāyassa yattha paccayaggahaṇaṃ tattha sādhāraṇattā ‘tadādino’ti vuttaṃ, tadādisamudāyassa gahaṇe panettha viseso na dissati… adhikattāti adhigatantāvāti (potthake) ādīsu visesadassanāsambhavā, ‘tuṃsmā lopo cicchāyaṃ te” tyatra (5-4) tu dissati viseso, vakkhatihi tattha “tuṃtāyetave bhāve bhavissati kriyāyaṃ tadatthāya”nti (5-61) tuṃpaccayaṃ vakkhati”ccādi.

By 'tena' is meant: because it is desired to state by means of the qualifier 'ltu', the suffix is taken. That is the meaning of 'tena'. By taking the suffix, the taking of that which begins with it is obtained... by the maxim: 'When a suffix is taken, that which begins with the element after which it is enjoined is also taken.' Because of the desire to state by means of a qualifier, that which ends with it is taken... Bearing in mind the statement (1-13), 'A rule applies to that which ends with its qualifier,' he says: 'yato,' etc. That which has the meaning of an action as its beginning is 'tadādi'; the aggregate which has that suffix as its end is 'tadanto.' The meaning is the taking of such a specific aggregate that begins with that root and ends with that suffix, not merely of that which ends with it. Now then, when it is desired to state by means of the qualifier 'ltvī,' let that which ends with it be taken, according to 'A rule applies to that which ends with its qualifier.' But how, then, could that which begins with it be taken by the taking of the suffix, since there is no statement to that effect? He says: 'Because of its inseparability.' That which is enjoined after a certain element cannot, by its nature, exist without that element; thus it is inseparable. Its state is therefore called inseparability. Because the maxim, 'When a suffix is taken, that which begins with the element after which it is enjoined is also taken,' is general wherever a suffix is taken, 'tadādino' is stated. But here, in the taking of the aggregate beginning with that, no distinction is seen... because it is impossible to see a distinction in cases like 'adhikatta,' etc. But in the rule 'After tuṃ, there is elision of te in the desiderative' (5-4), a distinction is indeed seen. For he will state there concerning the 'tuṃ' suffix: 'The suffixes tuṃ, tāye, tave occur in the sense of the infinitive and for the future, when there is an action for that purpose' (5-61), etc.

58. Ge

58. Ge

Aityevavattabbanti [M 0.0123] ‘gea’ityeva vattabbanti vuttaṃ hoti, pakkhe dīghavidhānenevāti iminā akārādese kate pakkhe dīghavidhāneneva, aññatthacaritatthatāyāti ltvantādito aññattha bhopurisā bhopurisaiccādo jātipadatthanissayanena katatthatāya, parisa mattatthatāyāti vuttaṃ hoti, avassaṃ dīghabhāve kāraṇamāha ‘yadicākāro’iccādi, yadica ākāroti padacchedo.

The statement 'It should be stated only as ā' means 'It should be stated only as ge ā.' By 'precisely by the optional rule of lengthening' is meant: when the substitution of 'a' is made, it is precisely by the optional rule of lengthening. By 'because it has found application elsewhere' is meant: because it has fulfilled its purpose elsewhere than in what ends with 'ltvā,' such as in 'bho purisā,' 'bho purisa,' etc., by relying on the meaning of a class-word. 'For the sake of completeness,' it is said. He states the reason for the necessary lengthening: 'yadi ca ākāro,' etc. The word-division is 'yadi ca ākāro.'

60. Ghabrahmā

60. Gha and Brahmā

Ghaitisaññā ghasaññā tāsaṃ, kaññāsaññātiādīsu ghasaññānaṃ bahuttā bahuvacanena niddeso, gharūpassāti ghassāti ghasaddarūpassa, tathā bho brahmāti ettha tathāti iminā brahmātirūpassa niruttiyaṃ niddiṭṭhattāva ettha saṅgahitabhāvaṃ dasseti. Evaṃ vivarantīti tasmā sa sakhato gassa akāraākārā”tiādinā evaṃ vivaranti, te hi aca āca ica īca ecāti dvande pubbasarānaṃ lopaṃ katvā ettupasilesaniddesaṃ vaṇṇenti, sāmaññavidhānanti ‘brahmakattuisi sakhato’ccevamavisesetvā sāmaññena kathanaṃ, kimatthanti kiṃ attho payojanaṃ yassa taṃ kimatthaṃ. Sāmaññavidhānaṃ kimatthampanevaṃ payojanāsaṅkāyaṃ payojanāsaṅkāvicāraṇaṃ manasi nidhāya ‘āgati gaṇoya’nti vuttattā āha– ‘atthato’ccādi, atthatoti sā matthiyato, anenāti‘āgatigaṇoya’nti iminā vacanena, idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti ‘āgatigaṇoyanti iminā tadākārasaṅkhātajātippadhānagaṇattappakāsanena yadi sambodhane ekārantākārantalābhīnaṃ kattu isi sakha muni bhadantādīnaṃ gahaṇaṃ payojanaṃ na siyā, aññathā anupapajjanaṃ siyāti evamaññathānupapattilakkhaṇasāmatthiyato sāmaññavidhāne payojanamāhe”ti, soyanti iminā vuttiyaṃ ‘āgati gaṇoya’nti vuttaṃ vacanaṃ nidasseti.

The term 'gha' is their designation. The designation of them is in the plural because of the plurality of the 'gha'-terms in cases like 'kaññā-saññā,' etc. 'Gharūpassa' means 'of gha,' that is, of the form of the word 'gha.' Similarly, in 'bho brahmā,' the word 'tathā' shows that the form 'brahmā' is included here because it has already been specified in the Nirutti. They explain thus: 'Therefore, sa from sakha becomes a or ā for gha,' etc. Thus they explain. For they explain the designation here by juxtaposition, after having elided the preceding vowels in the dvandva compound 'a ca ā ca i ca ī ca e ca.' 'General rule' means the statement in general, without specifying, as in 'brahmā, kattu, isi, sakha…' 'For what purpose?' means 'that which has what purpose or use?' Bearing in mind the question of the purpose of such a general rule, he says 'atthato,' etc., because it is said 'āgati gaṇo ayaṃ.' 'Atthato' means 'by implication.' By this statement 'āgati gaṇo ayaṃ,' the following is said: 'By this declaration that this is a class (gaṇa) whose primary characteristic is that form (tadākāra), if the inclusion of those that receive ī and ā endings in the vocative, such as kattu, isi, sakha, muni, bhadanta, etc., were not the purpose, then the statement would be untenable.' Thus, by the force of the argument from the untenability of the alternative, he states the purpose in the general rule. By 'soyaṃ,' he points to the statement made in the commentary, 'āgati gaṇo ayaṃ.'

63. Ghossaṃ

63. Gho, ssaṃ

Ssañca ssāca ssāyoca añca tiñcāti itarītarayoge cattha samāso,ssaṃ ssā ssāyaṃ tiṃsu.

In 'Ssaṃ ca ssā ca ssāyo ca aṃ ca tiṃ ca,' there is a dvandva compound in the sense of mutual connection. The forms are ssaṃ, ssā, ssāyaṃ, tiṃsu.

64. Eka

64. Eka

Ghoca [M 0.0124] oca gho ghāntaokārantā, natthi gho yesante agho, tesaṃ, sāmaññavidhānatoti kassaci liṅgassa aparāmāsā sāmaññena vidhānato, nādekavacanesūti nādīsu ekavacanesūti attho, hi hetumhi, yasmā kassaci evaṃ duṭṭhādhippāyo siyā, tasmā dutiyamudāharaṇanti attho, dutiyopi hetumhi, yasmā sabbesaṃ saṅgahaṇatthaṃ, tasmā na ca tathādhippetanti attho, sabbesamekavacanānaṃ saṅgahaṇābhāve suttānaṃ viracanappakāramāha-‘aññathā’tiādi, uparicātyādīsvayamadhippāyo “suttassa ‘aṃyosvaghona’nti viracitattā sāmaññene-kavacanesvaghassa narassattappatīti tappaṭisedhābhāvā’daṇḍi kula’nti rassattaṃ ‘sismiṃ napuṃsake’ti vidhisuttaṃ vadeyyā”ti, okārantappaṭisedhanti ‘aghona’nti okārantappaṭisedhaṃ, ādesantaraṃ “gossā gasihinaṃ sugāvagavā”tyādinā (2-67) karīyamānaṃ gāvādesādikaṃ, ettha pana napuṃsake ekavacanantaṃ daṇḍi kulanti vakkhamānattā nodāhaṭaṃ, yosu pana “yolopanisudīgho”ti (2-88) adīghassāpi dīghavidhānasāmatthiyā paṭhamameva dīghassa rassābhāvekāva kathāti nodāhaṭaṃ, daṇḍīdaṇḍīni icceva tu bhavati, nossavāti pāṭho dissati, ettha vijjamāne ge pare okārantassa vā rassāpajjanadosampasaṅgato nossā’ti pāṭhena bhavitabbaṃ.

'Gha and o are gho,' meaning stems ending in 'gha' and ending in 'o.' Those that do not have 'gho' are 'agho.' Of them... By 'general rule' is meant: because of the prescription in general, without reference to any particular gender. 'Not in the singulars of nā, etc.' means 'in the singulars of the nā-group.' 'Hi' is in the sense of a reason. Because someone might have such a wrong intention, therefore a second example is given; that is the meaning. The second is also a reason. Because it is for the inclusion of all, therefore it is not intended thus; that is the meaning. In the absence of the inclusion of all singulars, he states the way the suttas are composed: 'aññathā,' etc. In the above, etc., this is the intention: 'Since the sutta is composed as aṃyosvaghona, there is an understanding of the non-shortening of gha in the general singulars, and because there is no prohibition of that, one would need to state the prescriptive sutta sismiṃ napuṃsake for the shortening in daṇḍi kula.' 'Prohibition of the o-ending' means the prohibition of the o-ending by 'agho na.' Another substitution is the substitution of 'gāva,' etc., which is done by the rule 'Of go, ssā and si-hi naṃ become gāva, gava' etc. (2-67). But here, the neuter singular ending in 'daṇḍi kula' is not cited because it will be discussed later. In the case of 'yo,' however, because of the force of the rule prescribing lengthening even for what is not long in 'yo lopa ni su dīgho' (2-88), the only point is the non-shortening of what is already long in the first place; thus it is not cited. But it becomes only 'daṇḍī, daṇḍīni.' The reading 'nossavā' is found. Here, since the fault of the optional shortening of an o-ending would arise when 'ge' follows, the reading should be 'nossā.'

67. Gossā

67. Gossā

Gāvena gavenāti karaṇepi samānaṃ, gāvassa gavassāti chaṭṭhiyāpi.

‘Gāvena, gavena’ (by a cow, by a cow) is the same also in the instrumental case; ‘gāvassa, gavassa’ (of a cow, of a cow) also in the genitive case.

69. Gavaṃ

69. Gavaṃ

Senāti sutattā seiti vuttiyaṃ nimittaṃ parikappitaṃ.

Because it is so stated in the sūtra, it is 'senā'; in the commentary, 'seiti' is imagined as the derivation.

72. Gāvu

72. Gāvu

Saddantarattena koci dosoti sambandho, ādisitabbā ādesā kātabbā.

The connection is that there is some fault due to a difference in the word. Substitutions that are to be taught should be made.

73. Yaṃ

73. Yaṃ

Pena [M 0.0125] pasaññāya yuttā īpī, paca so īcāti vāpī abhedaggahaṇena, aññassāti ikāra ukāraūkārassa.

Endowed with perception by that which is drunk (pena), it is an īpī; or from 'paca so īca', it is 'vāpī' by means of undifferentiated grasping; 'of another' means of the sounds i, u, and ū.

77. Smi

77. Smi

Loke devadatto dattoti ekadesena samudāyavohāra dassanato sminotīmassa smiṃ vacanassātyayamattho dassitotyāha-‘smiti iminā’tiādi.

In the world, 'Devadatta' is called 'Datta,' a conventional expression of the whole by a part. In this way, for the verb 'sminoti', this meaning of the word 'smiṃ' is shown. Therefore, he says: 'by this "smi,"' and so on.

81. Jhalā

81. Jhalā

Brahmādīsu ‘ito kvaci sassa ṭānubandho’ti pāṭhāti sambandho, brahmādīsūti “ghabrahmādite”ti (2-60) sutte vuttabrahmādīsu, pāṭhāti ‘ito’tyādino gaṇasuttassa pāṭhā, ṭānubandhoti iminā (eṭādesaṃ) niddisati.

Among 'Brahmā' and others, the connection is from the reading: 'ito kvaci sassa ṭānubandho.' 'Among Brahmā and others' refers to the 'Brahmā,' etc., mentioned in the rule (2-60) 'ghabrahmādite.' 'From the reading' means from the reading of the gaṇasutta beginning with 'ito.' By 'ṭānubandho' it indicates this (the substitution of eṭa).

85. Kū

85. Kū

So bhasmā anto yassa so tadanto samudāyo, tassa, “cānukaḍḍhitaṃ nottaratrānuvattatī”ti viññūvacanaṃ, viduno vidūti kūpaccayantassa udāharaṇaṃ, viññuno viññūti “vito ñāto”ti (5-39) sabbaññuno sabbaññūti “kammā”ti (5-40).

The aggregate of which that is the end is 'tadanta.' Of that, there is a saying of the wise: 'What is drawn along by 'ca' does not continue further.' 'Vidu, vidū' is an example of a word ending in the suffix 'kū'. 'Viññu, viññū' is from the rule 'vito ñāto' (5-39). 'Sabbaññu, sabbaññū' is from the rule 'kammā' (5-40).

86. Lo

86. Lo

Lopotveva siddhattāti vomuttapakkhe lopotīmināva siddhattā.

Because it is already established by the rule 'lopo' itself: in the case where the rule for 'vo' is exempted, it is established by this very rule 'lopo'.

87. Nano

87. Na no

Amuyāti itthiyaṃ yādeso, nanotīmassidaṃ paccudāharaṇaṃ.

In the feminine form 'amuyā,' there is a substitution of 'ya'. This is a counter-example to this rule 'na no'.

88. Yolo

88. Yolo

Paṭhamādutiyāyonamekato udāharaṇāni aṭṭhī aṭṭhīniti, tānica yolopanilātisseva dassitāni, tathāyevāññānipi ñāyantīti.

Examples for the nominative and accusative 'yo' endings are given together, such as 'aṭṭhī, aṭṭhīni' (bones, bones); and these are shown precisely by the elision of 'yo' according to Nilātissa. In the same way, other examples are also to be understood.

92. Ntassa

92. Ntassa: Of -nta.

Ṭamuttapakkhoti [M 0.0126] asantaṃ kubbantassāti ṭādesena muttapakkho,ntussacevanti pasiddhattāva ṭādesamuttapakkhaṃ upameti, “sañjātaṃ tārakāditvito”ti (5-45) ito andhitā.

'Ṭamuttapakkha' means 'a case exempt from the substitution of `ṭa`,' as in 'of one who does what is non-existent.' And because it is established for '-ntu' itself, it is compared to the case exempt from the `ṭa` substitution. From the rule 'sañjātaṃ tārakādito' (5-45); from this, the word `andhitā` is formed.

93. Yosu

93. Yosu

Ṭādeso-tippasajjatīti kasmā vuttaṃ nanu tadantassa samudāyassa patte “chaṭṭhiyantassā”ti (1-17) antasseva hoti, tathāsati nevātippasaṅgo, tasmā kasmātippasajjatīti vuttanti, saccaṃ, tathāpi ‘jhissā’ti vattuṃ sakkuṇeyyatte issāti vuttatta vuttanthi sāmatthiyato tadantassa ṭādeso-tippasajjatīti tathā vuttanti, nanu ‘jhissā’ti vuttepi sovātippasaṅgo tadavatthoyevāti saccaṃ, tathāpi yadi samudāyassa ṭādeso-bhimato siyā ‘tathā sati kiṃ jhaggahaṇena issatveva vadeyyāti nātippasajjatīti, jhaggahaṇe nāmante ikārasseva jhasaññattāti idaṃ pana visesanattena vattu manicchite yujjati.

Why was it said that the substitution of `ṭa` is over-applied? Surely, when it applies to an aggregate ending in that, according to the rule 'chaṭṭhiyantassa' (1-17), it applies only to the final part. In that case, there is no over-application. So why was it said that it is over-applied? That is true. However, while it was possible to say 'jhissa,' because 'issa' was stated, by the force of that, it was said that the substitution of `ṭa` for the whole aggregate is over-applied. But surely, even if 'jhissa' were said, that over-application would remain the same? That is true. Nevertheless, if the substitution of `ṭa` for the whole aggregate were intended, then why mention 'jha'? One could just say 'issa,' and it would not be over-applied. However, the mention of 'jha' gives the designation 'jha' only to the 'i' at the end of a name; this is fitting when one does not wish to state it as a qualification.

94. Vevo

94. Vevo

Sahacaritañāyassāti “taṃsahacaritā taggahaṇena gayhantī”ti ñāyassa.

The principle of association means the principle that 'those associated with it are grasped by the grasping of it.'

95. Yomhi

95. Yomhi

Hetukurusaddehi yosu iminā ṭādese “lopo”tīminā yolope vā sampatte “paccayanissitaṃ bahiraṅga”nti yolopato “pakatinissitamantaraṅga”nti “antaraṅgabahiraṅgasu antaraṅgavidhi balavā”ti paṭhamaṃ ṭādese nimittābhāvāva lopā bhāvoti dassetumāha-‘hetukurusaddehi’ccādi.

After the words 'hetu' and 'kuru', when the substitution of `ṭa` for 'yo' or 'su' by this rule, or the elision of 'yo' by the rule 'lopo' are both applicable, the following maxims apply: 'what is dependent on a suffix is external' (referring to the elision of 'yo'), and 'what is dependent on the base is internal.' To show that 'between internal and external rules, the internal rule is stronger,' and that therefore the substitution of `ṭa` occurs first, and due to the resulting absence of its condition, the elision does not occur, he says: 'After the words hetu and kuru,' etc.

99. Sabbā

99. Sabbā

Nanu katarādayova sabbādisaddavacanīyā honti samāsenābhihitattā, na tu sabbasaddo saddasse (potthake) tyāha-‘avayavene’tyādi,yadipi ‘sabba saddo [M 0.0127] ādi yesa’nti avayavena viggaho, tathāpi samudāyovāssattho bhavati… yesantyanena samudāyassa parāmāsāti bhāvo, itīti hetumhi, ko bhavantānaṃ dvinnaṃ bahunnaṃ vā eko deva datto kaṭhādīhi vā atthe dvīhi bahūhi vā ekassa niddhāraṇe sati kimhā niddhāraṇe ratara ratamesu ṇādivuttiyaṃ “ekatthatāya”nti (2-119) vibhattilope “rānubandhentasarādissā”ti (4-132) antasarādilope kiṃsaddassa rūpasiddhīti dassetumāha katamā’tiādi, ubho aṃsā assāti atthe “ayubhadvitīhaṃse”ti (4-49) aye“saro lopo sare”ti (1-26) saralope rūpasiddhīti āha-‘ubho aṃsā’iccādi, kāyaṃ vavatthā nāme tyāha-‘sābhidheyyā’tyādi, avadhiccādinā tassevātthaṃ vibhāveti, adhaṃso abhaṭṭhatā avadhibhāveyevāvaṭṭhānaṃ, sābhidheyyā pekkhāti ettha so sako abhidheyyo attho disādi sābhidheyyoti gahitoti āha-‘pubbādīna’ntiādi, sābhidheyyanti kammato parā apapubbā ‘ikkha=dassane’tīmasmā “kvacaṇa”iti (5-41) aṇpaccaye sābhidheyyāpekkho, so vāvadhiniyamoti dassetumāha-‘tamapekkhati’ccādi, tatthādhippāyaṃ vivarati ‘tathāhi’ccādinā, ettha ca parādisaddābhidheyyo-ttho disādesādi pubbādisaddābhidheyyassātthassa disāya desādino vāvadhibhāvena niyamavasena pavattati, yo cāvadhibhāvo niyamavasena pavattati, socāvadhibhāvo niyamavasena pavatto pubbādisaddavacanīyaṃ disādesādi mapekkhatīti sābhidheyyāpekkhovadhiniyamoyeva vavatthāti vuccatītyayamadhippāyo, na tu abhidheyyāyanti asambhavā, asambhavameva dassento āha-‘yo hi’ccādi, kosallena nimittenāti kusala saddassa pavattinimittena kosallena, uttarākuravo uttarakurudīpa vāsino, deso vā, ‘nāññañca nāmappadhānā”ti (2-136) aneneva saññāyaṃ sabbādikāriyassa nisiddhatte kimasaññāyaṃbhyanenetyāha ‘nāññañce’tyādi, kiñci pubbattādikamuddissa kesañci pubboparotyādikā atthānugatā saññā anvatthasaññā.

Surely, are not 'katara' and so on what is meant by the term 'sabbādi' (sabba, etc.), because they are stated concisely, and not the word 'sabba' itself? To this, he says: 'by a part,' etc. Although the analysis is by a part—'those of which the word sabba is the beginning'—nevertheless, the meaning is the whole aggregate; the sense is that by 'of which,' the aggregate is referred to. Thus, in the sense of a reason: when there is a determination of one from two or many—such as 'Who among you two or many is Devadatta?' or in the sense of 'kaṭha,' etc.—to show the establishment of the form from the word 'kiṃ' in the context of determination with 'ratara' and 'ratama', after the elision of the case ending by 'ekatthatāya' (2-119) and the elision of the final vowel and the following consonant by 'rānubandhentasarādissā' (4-132), he says: 'katamā,' etc. In the sense 'he has two parts (aṃsa),' the form is established by the elision of the vowel by 'saro lopo sare' (1-26) after the 'aya' substitution by 'ayubhadvitīhaṃse' (4-49); thus he says: 'ubho aṃsā,' etc. What is this arrangement (vavatthā) by name? He says: 'It is dependent on its denotation' (sābhidheyyāpekkhā), etc. He clarifies its meaning with 'limit' (avadhi), etc. 'Adhaṃso' means non-violation, non-transgression; it is establishment precisely in the state of being a limit. Here, in 'sābhidheyyāpekkhā,' 'sābhidheyya' is taken as its own denotable object, such as a direction; thus he says: 'of pubbādi,' etc. 'Sābhidheyyāpekkho' is formed with the suffix 'aṇa' by 'kvacaṇa' (5-41) from the root 'ikkha' (to see), which follows an object and is preceded by 'apa'. To show that this is a restriction by a limit, he says: 'it is dependent on that,' etc. He explains the intention there with 'for thus,' etc. And here, the denotable object of a word like 'parādi' (other, etc.)—a direction, region, etc.—functions by way of a limit and restriction in relation to the denotable object of a word like 'pubbādi' (east, etc.), which is a direction, region, etc. And that which functions by way of a limit and restriction, that state of being a limit, functioning by way of restriction, is dependent on what is expressed by words like 'pubbādi' (a direction, region, etc.). Thus, the arrangement (vavatthā) is said to be precisely a restriction by a limit that is dependent on its denotation; this is the intention. It is not 'for the denotation,' for that is impossible. Showing this very impossibility, he says: 'For he who,' etc. 'By the characteristic of skillfulness' means by the skillfulness that is the ground for the use of the word 'kusala.' 'Uttarākuravo' are the inhabitants of the Uttarakuru continent, or the country itself. Since the function of 'sabbādi' is already prohibited for proper names by 'nāññañca nāmappadhānā' (2-136), why is there the phrase 'asaññāyaṃ' (not in a proper name)? He says: 'nāññañce,' etc. When, with reference to some 'easternness,' etc., certain names like 'pubbāpara' (eastern and western) follow the meaning, this is an 'anvatthasaññā' (a name corresponding to its meaning).

104.Ti

104. Three

“Vānekaññatthe”ti (3-17) [M 0.0128] vikappānuvattanato ayuttattābhāvaṃ dasseti‘nayidamayutta’nti, yuttatā cāssa pāṭhe byabhicāra dassanatoti vattumāha-‘napuṃsake’ccādi, pāṭhānugatā hi suttaracanā, vikappānuvattiyā anapuṃsakamidameva vacanaṃ tassa kvaci byabhicāratte ñāpakanti vattumāha-‘tassa cā’tiādi, avassamevamettha attho gahetabbo, aññathā yathāvaṭṭhitapāṭhānukkamenātthaggahaṇe sati suttassa suttassā (potthake) mukhyattappatītito kathantamaññassa ñāpakaṃ bhaveyya, mukhyabhāve hi ñāpakatthaṃ na yujjeyya.

Regarding 'Vānekaññatthe' (3-17), by following the option it shows the absence of inappropriateness, stating, 'this is not inappropriate.' And to show that its appropriateness in the reading is from seeing an exception, it says, 'napuṃsake,' etc. For the composition of the rule follows the reading. And to indicate that this very non-neuter word, by following the option, is an indicator of its occasional exception, it says, 'tassa cā,' etc. The meaning here must necessarily be understood in this way. Otherwise, if the meaning were grasped by following the established sequence of the reading, since the primary meaning of the rule would be apparent, how could it be an indicator of something else? For if it were primary, its function as an indicator would not be suitable.

108. Ate

108. Ate

Nanu ca “lakkhaṇapaṭipadavuttesu paṭipadavuttasseva gahaṇa”ntīmāya paribhāsāya lakkhaṇikassākārassa gahaṇaṃ na pappotītyāsaṅkiya paṭipādayamāha-‘rassākāre’ccādi, paribhāsāya cassāyamattho “lakkhīyateneneti lakkhaṇaṃ, sādhvasādhujānana hesuttā sutta sattha muccate, paṭigatampadaṃ paṭipadaṃ, uccāritamañjasetyattho, lakkhaṇañca paṭipadañca lakkhaṇapaṭipadāni, tehi vuttāni rūpāni lakkhaṇapaṭipadavuttāni, tesu, vuttasaddo paccekamparisamāpīyate ‘lakkhaṇavuttesu paṭipadavuttesū’ti, tatrāñcasā yamaniddiṭṭhaṃ, kevalaṃ lakkhaṇadassanenāsmiṃ lakkhaṇe satyavassamanena rūpena bhavitabbanti lakkhaṇena paṭipāditaṃ, taṃ lakkhaṇavuttamityuccate, yantvañjasā saddeneva paṭipāditaṃ, taṃ paṭipadavuttanti vuccate, tasmiṃ lakkhaṇavutte paṭipadavutte ca rūpe sati paṭipadavuttasseva gahaṇaṃ, netarasse”ti, paṭipadavuttassevetyavadhāraṇena niyamarūpabhāssā paribhāsāyāvagamyate, so ca niyamo aniyamapubbake sandehe satyavatiṭṭhate, tasmā yatra lakkhaṇavuttameva kevalaṃ, na paṭipadavuttaṃ, tatra nāyaṃ paribhāsā vatiṭṭhate, yatrāpi paṭipadavuttameva kevalaṃ, na lakkhaṇavuttaṃ, sopyetissā avisayo, yatra dve rūpāni sambhavanti tatrevā yamparibhāsā sandehāpākaraṇamukhena pavattāti ñāyappattoyevā mattho [M 0.0129] imāya paribhāsāyānuvādyate, tathāhi sandehaṭhānesu yadyapyekarūpamevamabhinnamubhinnaṃ, tathāpi lakkhaṇavuttaṃ rūpaṃ lakkhaṇe nonnīyamānaṃ dhūmaggi viya jalabalākā viya cānu mānikaṃ, yantu paṭipada vuttaṃ rūpaṃ, taṃ paccakkhasiddhaṃ, paccakkhānumānesu ca paccakkhambalavantaraṃ pamāṇanti ato paṭipadavuttameva gayhatīti.

Is it not so that, according to the maxim, 'Among forms stated by characteristic and by specific word, only the one stated by specific word is to be taken,' the acceptance of a form indicated by a characteristic is not obtained? Anticipating this objection, he explains it, saying, 'rassākāre,' etc. The meaning of this maxim is as follows: A 'characteristic' (lakkhaṇa) is that by which something is marked. A 'rule' (sutta) is so called because it is a means for knowing the correct and the incorrect. A 'specific word' (paṭipada) is a word that has been uttered; the meaning is 'clearly articulated.' 'Characteristic' and 'specific word' together are 'characteristic-and-specific-word' (lakkhaṇapaṭipadāni). The forms stated by them are 'those stated by characteristic and specific word' (lakkhaṇapaṭipadavuttāni). Among these, the word 'stated' (vutta) is applied to each individually: 'in those stated by characteristic' and 'in those stated by specific word.' Therein, that which is not explicitly specified but is established by a characteristic—whereby simply by seeing the characteristic one knows that when this characteristic is present, it must have this form—is called 'stated by characteristic.' But what is established explicitly by the word itself is called 'stated by specific word.' When a form may be stated by characteristic and also by a specific word, only the one stated by specific word is to be taken, not the other. By the emphasis 'only the one stated by specific word,' this maxim is understood to be a restrictive rule. And that restriction applies when there is doubt due to a prior lack of rule. Therefore, where there is only a form stated by characteristic and not one stated by a specific word, this maxim does not apply. Also where there is only a form stated by a specific word and not one stated by a characteristic, that too is outside its scope. This maxim operates only where two forms are possible, by way of removing doubt. Thus, this meaning, which is arrived at by logic, is simply restated by this maxim. For in cases of doubt, even if there is one and the same form for both, still the form stated by characteristic, being inferred from the characteristic, is inferential, like fire from smoke or water from a line of cranes. But the form stated by a specific word is established by direct perception. And between direct perception and inference, direct perception is the stronger means of knowledge; therefore, only that which is stated by a specific word is taken.

110. Kvace

110. In some cases.

Napuṃsakaliṅge ekārena na bhavitabbanti sambandho.

The connection is that in the neuter gender, it should not be formed with the letter 'e'.

114. Lopo

114. Elision.

Akārassantaraṅgatte kāraṇamāha-‘pakatinissitattā’ti, pakatiyā idaṃ pākataṃ “ṇo”ti (4-34) ṇo, lopassa bahiraṅgatte kāraṇamāha-‘paccayanissitattā’ti, antaraṅgeccādinā “antaraṅgabahiraṅgesvantaraṅgavidhi balavā”ti paribhāsamupalakkheti, aṅgasaddo-vayavavācī, ante saddo sattamyatthe, aṅge bhavamantaraṅgaṃ vibhatthyatthe-saṅkhyasamāso “eonama vaṇṇe”ti (1-37) attaṃ rāgamo, aṅgato bahi bahiraṅgaṃ “payyapābahitiro purepacchā vā pañcamyā”ti (3-5) asaṅkhyasamāso, atra cāntaraṅgaṃ bahiraṅganti nāṅgebhavamantaraṅgaṃ, apitvantaraṅganissitaṃ kāriyamantaraṅgaṃ, nāpyaṅgato bahibhūto samudāyo bahiraṅgaṃ, kintu bahiraṅganissitaṃ kāriyambahiraṅgaṃ yathā mañcanissitesu saddāyantesu ‘mañcā saddāyantī’tyuccate taṃ viyeti atoyevā saṅkhyasamāsepi liṅgavibhattivacanantarayogo ‘antaraṅgo antaraṅgā’ti, saṅketiko hyayamasaṅkhyasamāso, na pubbapadatthappadhāno, yathā-paccakkhassākkhanissitattāvabodhatthaṃ ‘akkhamakkhampati vattate’ti vicchāya-masaṅkhyasamāsepi kate paccakkha ñāṇassākkhanissitattañāpanatthaṃ saṅketavasena kato-yamasaṅkhya samāso, na pubbapadatthappadhānoti‘paccakkho paccakkhā’ti liṅgavibhatti vacanantarayogo, tathevāya-mantaraṅganissito-yaṃ samudāyanissitoti ñāpanatthaṃ saṅketavasena kato-yamasaṅkhyasamāsoti liṅgavibhattivacanantarayogo na virujjhate, athavā antaramaṅgamassa kāriyassātthīti “saddhāditva” (4-84) tathā bahiraṅganti, antaraṅgañca bahiraṅgañca [M 0.0130] antaraṅgabahiraṅgāni, tesvantaraṅgo balavāti. Antaraṅga kāriyassa balavattaṃ sādhetuṃ ‘sabbapaṭhamaṃ vidheyyattā’tiādi vuttaṃ, idampana antaraṅgakāriyassa balavabhāvasādhane kāraṇaṃ na hoti, antaraṅgattā balavabhāvoyeva hi sabbapaṭhamaṃ vidheyyatta kāraṇaṃ, tathā cāha-‘yo lopato akārassa paṭhamameva bhavane kāraṇamāha antaraṅgattā akārassā’ti, tasmā nāyaṃ pāṭho ghaṭate, antaraṅgabalavabhāvasādhanassa pana lokato icchitattā ayamevatthe pāṭho ghaṭate”antaraṅgameva kāriyambalavaṃ loke tathādiṭṭhattā, tathā hi loko pātovā”tyādi, loke tathādiṭṭhattāti antaraṅgabalavabhāvassa loke evaṃ vakkhamānanayena diṭṭhattā, athavā kenaci vidhurappaccayopanipātena kāraṇave kallena vā kadāci kattumasakkuṇeyyattepi antaraṅgassa avassaṃ vidheyyattaṃ dassetumāha sabbapaṭhamaṃ vidheyyattā’ti, satisambhaveti nimittassānupahatattā kāriyassa sambhave sati.

He states the reason for the letter 'a' being internal: 'because it is dependent on the base.' This `ṇo` is natural from the base, as in the rule 'ṇo' (4-34). He states the reason for the elision being external: 'because it is dependent on a suffix.' By 'internal,' etc., he alludes to the maxim: 'Between internal and external operations, the internal rule is stronger.' The word 'aṅga' means a part. The word 'ante' is in the sense of the locative. What occurs in the member is 'internal' (antaraṅga); this is a numerical compound in the sense of an inflection. According to 'eonama vaṇṇe' (1-37), there is the substitution of 'a' for 'rā'. What is outside the member is 'external' (bahiraṅga); this is an unnumbered compound according to the rule 'payyapābahitiro purepacchā vā pañcamyā' (3-5). And here, 'internal' and 'external' do not mean that what occurs in the member is internal, but rather the operation dependent on an internal cause is internal; nor is the aggregate that is outside the member external, but rather the operation dependent on an external cause is external, just as when those on a bed make a sound, one says 'the beds are making a sound.' Therefore, even in an unnumbered compound, there is a connection with other genders, inflections, and numbers, as in 'antaraṅgo, antaraṅgā.' For this unnumbered compound is conventional; it is not one where the meaning of the first member is primary. For example, for the sake of understanding that 'paccakkha' is dependent on the sense organ, even when an unnumbered compound is formed by analyzing it as 'it proceeds towards the sense organ,' this unnumbered compound is made conventionally to indicate that the knowledge of 'paccakkha' is dependent on the sense organ, and it is not one where the meaning of the first member is primary; therefore, there is a connection with other genders, inflections, and numbers, as in 'paccakkho, paccakkhā.' Just so, this unnumbered compound is made conventionally to indicate that this is dependent on the internal and that is dependent on the aggregate, so a connection with other genders, inflections, and numbers is not contradictory. Alternatively, 'internal' (antaraṅga) is so called because this operation has an internal member, according to 'saddhāditva' (4-84), and likewise 'external' (bahiraṅga). 'Internal' and 'external' are 'internal-and-external' (antaraṅgabahiraṅgāni); among them, the internal is stronger. To establish the strength of the internal operation, it is said, 'because it must be applied first of all,' etc. But this is not the reason for establishing the strength of the internal operation; for its being strong because it is internal is itself the reason why it must be applied first of all. And so he says: 'He states the reason for the letter 'a' arising before the elision: due to the internality of the letter 'a'.' Therefore this reading is not suitable. But since the establishment of the strength of the internal is desired from worldly experience, this reading is suitable in this sense: 'The internal operation alone is strong, because it is seen to be so in the world. For in the world...' etc. The phrase 'because it is seen to be so in the world' means because the strength of the internal is seen in the world in the way that will be explained. Or, to show that the internal operation must necessarily be applied even when it might sometimes be impossible to do so due to the occurrence of some adverse condition or a defect in the cause, he says, 'because it must be applied first of all.' The phrase 'when possible' means: when the operation is possible because its cause is not obstructed.

116. Ye

116. Those

Ivaṇṇassāti vuttattāti ‘ye passivaṇṇassā”ti ettha ivaṇṇassāti vuttattā.

Because it has been said 'of the letter i,' therefore in the phrase 'ye passivaṇṇassā,' this is because 'of the letter i' has been said.

118. Asaṃ

118. Without Number

Liṅgavacanabhedepi byayarahitattā abyayavantaupasaṅganipātānaṃ pubbācariyasaññā, asatī saṅkhyā yesantyānyasaṅkhyānītyāha- ‘ekatte’ccādi, ekānekesūti vuttattā saṅkhyāvisese vidhīyamānāsyādayo kathamasaṅkhyehi uppajjitumussahante iccāsayenāha- ‘kathamasaṅkhyehi syādīnaṃ sambhavo’ti. Atha nissaṅkhyehi hotusyādīnamasambhavo uccaṃ rukkhassiccādotu saṅkhyāsambhave bhavitabbameva syādīhiccāha-‘saṅkhyāsambhaveve’ccādi. Vuttiganthassādhippāyaṃ vivarati ‘aññathe’ tyādinā, kimesamuppattiyampayojanaṃ yenāsaṅkhyehi taduppatti no-numīyate ccāsaṅkiyāha-‘tassañca satiya’ntyādi, asati hi syādīnamuppattiyamuccamādīnamasaṅkhyānampadattaṃ natthīti yo ādīsu padasmā paresaṃ tumhāmhasaddānaṃ savibhattīnaṃ vonoādikaṃ padanimittaṃ [M 0.0131] kāriyaṃ na siyāti ‘uccaṃ vo, uccaṃ no’tiādayo payogā na sijjhanti, sati tu syāduppattiyaṃ luttesupi tesu padattanipphattiyāyeva taduppattito padatte siddhe padalakkhaṇaṃ kāriyaṃ sijjhatevāti bhāvo. Parehi ettha ‘tassaṃ sālāya’nti vacanicchāyaṃ ‘tatra sālāya’nti yathā siyāti “abyayatvā syādino”ti (pā, 2-4-82) abyayato parassitthiyamāppaccayassāpi lopo vihito, tenāha- ‘asaṅkhyehi’ccādi, tadayuttanti āppaccayassa lopavidhāna mayuttaṃtyattho. Atha kenātra āppaccayo vidhīyate yenāssāpi lopo-nusāsīyate “itthiyamatvā”ti (3-26) ce netadatthi, itthiyamāppaccayassa vidhānato-saṅkhyānañcāliṅgattā, tasmā asaṅkhyehi āppaccayassa sambhavoyeva natthītyanatthakamāppaccayassa lopavacananti nānatthakaṃ itthiyanti (3-26) hi guṇippadhāno niddeso itthattavati āppaccayādayo vidhīyante ‘tassaṃ sālāya (micce tasmiṃ padatthe) tatre’ti asaṅkhyamidamitthattavati vattate, tasmā siyāye vetasmā āppaccayotyavassamāppaccayassa lopo vidheyyoti yo maññate, tampati āha-‘yadīpi’ccādi, visesābhidhānātyupagame vatta mānoyamasaṅkhyasamudāyo‘niddeso vattate’ti cobhayamikkhate, itthiyanti niddesassa guṇippadhānattaṃ sādhetuṃ ‘itthattavati hi āppaccayādayo’tiāha, tatretīmassāsaṅkhyassa sālāyaṃ vattanato āha- ‘itthattavati cā’ti, ayampasiddhirūpena na vattateti sambandho, yadi ayampasiddhirūpena vattate, kuto carahi itthattāvasāyotyāha- ‘itthattāvasāyo’ccādi. Idāni jinindabuddhivacanamānīya tassā yuttattamubbhāvayitumāha- ‘yopyāhi’ccādi, yadīpiccādi jinindabuddhivacanaṃ, tassāti itthattassa, padattho ca itthattaṃ siyāti yopyāheti sambandho, gammamānatthattā itisaddāppayogo, tassāyuttanti tassevaṃ vādino jinindabuddhino vacanamayuttaṃtyattho, kutoccāha- ‘evaṃ hi’ccādi, yadi itthattassa vākyatthatā itthippaccayanivattikatā, evaṃ sati sālāyamiccādisaddantarāpekkhā itthattappatīti tatretyādīsu siyāti attho, neva tathā patīyatīti bhāvo, vuttamevatthaṃ phuṭayitumāha- ‘tathāhi’ccādi, aviddasuayanti diṭṭhanto paññāso, aviddasu [M 0.0132] ayanti ubhayatrāpyatrekavacanasissa nivattiyā kataṃ yamekattaṃ, taṃ saddantarādyanapekkhameva patīyatetyattho, itthatta vuttinā sālādisaddena sāmānādhikaraṇyaṃ tatretyetassāti etāvatā āppaccayo uppajjatīti ca na sakkā vattunti dassento āha-‘samānādhikaraṇattampi’ccādi, samānādhikaraṇattampīti (itthi) vuttinā sālādisaddena sāmānādhikaraṇyampi, āppaccayādīnaṃ nāṅganti sambandho.

Even when there is a difference of gender and number, because they are without declension, it is the designation of the ancient teachers that prepositions and particles are indeclinable. He states that those for which number does not exist are 'without number' (asaṅkhyāni). Because it is said 'in the singular and plural,' the case endings beginning with 'si,' which are prescribed for specific numbers, cannot possibly arise from what is without number. With this intention, he asks: 'How is the arising of the case endings beginning with 'si' possible from what is without number?'

Well, let there be no arising of case endings from what is without number. But in cases such as 'uccaṃ rukkhassa' (high of the tree), where number is possible, the case endings must certainly arise. Thus he says: 'Only when number is possible,' etc.

He explains the intention of the Vutti text with the words 'otherwise,' etc. Having raised the doubt, 'What is the purpose in their arising, such that their arising from what is without number is not inferred?', he says: 'And when that exists,' etc. For if there were no arising of case endings, indeclinables such as 'uccaṃ' would not have the status of a 'pada' (an inflected word). Therefore, the grammatical operations conditioned by a preceding 'pada'—such as the substitution of 'vo,' 'no,' etc., for the inflected pronouns 'tumha' and 'amha' which follow a 'pada'—would not occur. Thus, usages such as 'uccaṃ vo' (high for you) and 'uccaṃ no' (high for us) would not be accomplished. But when there is an arising of case endings, even when they are elided, the status of a 'pada' is accomplished simply from that arising. Once the 'pada' status is established, the operations characterized by a 'pada' are indeed accomplished. This is the meaning.

Here, by others, so that with the desire to say 'tassaṃ sālāyaṃ' (in that hall), one may say 'tatra sālāyaṃ,' the elision of the feminine suffix '-ā' after an indeclinable has also been prescribed by the rule 'abyayatvā syādino' (Pāṇini 2.4.82). Therefore, he says: 'from what is without number,' etc. This is unsuitable, meaning that the prescription of the elision of the '-ā' suffix is unsuitable.

Now, by what rule is the '-ā' suffix prescribed here, such that its elision is also taught? If it is by 'itthiyam atvā' (Kacc. 3-26), that is not so, because the '-ā' suffix is prescribed in the feminine, and what is without number is without gender. Therefore, for what is without number, there is no possibility of an '-ā' suffix at all, so the teaching of its elision is pointless. (The opponent replies:) It is not pointless. For in the rule 'itthiyam,' the specification is secondary to the quality; the suffixes beginning with '-ā' are prescribed for a word possessing femininity. In the expression 'tassaṃ sālāyaṃ' (that is, in that word-meaning), the indeclinable 'tatra' occurs in the sense of possessing femininity. Therefore, the '-ā' suffix would arise from it, and thus its elision must necessarily be prescribed. To one who thinks thus, he replies, saying: 'Even if,' etc.

Now, bringing up the statement of Jinendabuddhi, he shows its unsuitability, saying: 'Whoever also said,' etc. The statement of Jinendabuddhi is 'Even if,' etc. The connection is: 'Whoever also says that femininity is the meaning of the word...' The word 'iti' is not used because the meaning is understood. 'That is unsuitable' means that the statement of Jinendabuddhi, who holds this view, is unsuitable. Why? He says: 'For if so,' etc. If femininity were a meaning belonging to the whole sentence, and its removal were caused by the feminine suffix, then in cases like 'tatra,' the understanding of femininity would be dependent on another word, such as 'sālāyaṃ.' But it is not understood in that way. To clarify this very point, he says: 'For thus,' etc. The example is 'aviddasu ayaṃ.' Here, the singularity that is made by the removal of the plural ending is understood without dependence on another word. And it cannot be said that the '-ā' suffix arises merely because 'tatra' has co-referentiality with a word expressing femininity, such as 'sālā.' To show this, he says: 'Even co-referentiality,' etc. 'Even co-referentiality' means that even co-referentiality with a word expressing femininity, such as 'sālā,' is not a basis for the suffixes beginning with '-ā.' This is the connection.

119. Eka

119. One

Evāti anuvattateeva, ekottho yassa pakatyādisamudāyassa so ekattho ‘assa cekatthasaddassa pavattinimittaṃ īyādi vidhānantyāha- ‘ekatthatā īyādividhāna’nti, īyādivuttiyanti vattanaṃ vutti īyādīnaṃ vutti, īyādividhāne satityattho, samāsatoti samāsitā, tenevāti “dissantaññepi paccayā”ti (4-120) sutteneva.

The word 'eva' indeed continues. That which has a single meaning, being a collection of a stem and so forth, is termed 'ekattha'. He states that the cause for the application of this term 'ekattha' is the prescription of suffixes such as '-īya', saying: 'The prescription of suffixes such as '-īya' is due to the unity of meaning.' In the phrase 'īyādivuttiyaṃ,' 'vutti' means application—the application of suffixes such as '-īya'; the meaning is 'when the prescription of suffixes such as '-īya' occurs.' 'Samāsato' means 'in summary.' 'Teneva' means by that very sutta, namely 'dissantaññepi paccayā' (4-120).

120. Pubba

120. Earlier
