Yadā cātrādhisaddappayogo tadā teneva vibhatyatthassa vuttattā na sattamī payujjate, yadā sattamī, na tadādhisaddo, tenā sakapadeneva viggaho evaṃ dassanīyoti āha- ‘itthīsu kathā pavattā’ti, itthisaddato sattamībhavane kāraṇamāha- ‘taṃsamānādhikaraṇattā’ti, tena adhisaddena samānatthattāti attho.

When an intensifying word (adhisadda) is used here, the seventh case (sattamī) is not employed because the meaning of the inflection (vibhatti) has already been stated by that word. When the seventh case is used, that intensifying word is not used. Therefore, the analysis should be shown with the word itself, as he demonstrates with the example: "A talk took place concerning women (itthīsu kathā pavattā)." He gives the reason for the seventh case arising from the word "itthi" (women) as "taṃsamānādhikaraṇattā" (because of having the same locus). This means that it has the same meaning as the intensifying word.

121. Nāto

121. Not from that.

So ca amādeso, ādesassevāti aṃādesasseva, apañcamiyāti pañcamiṃ vajjetvā. Aññatra vidhīyamāno-yamamādeso pañcamiyampaṭisiddhattā pañcamiyā paṭisedhena sayampi paṭisiddho nāma hotītyāha ‘ādesassevāyaṃ paṭisedho’ti, lopapaṭisedhassa ‘nāto’ti pubbavākyena vuttassa ayampaṭisedho neti sambandho, atha kathamidamapañcamyātyamādesenevātisambandhati na lopa paṭisedhenāti paribhāsamāha-‘anantarassa vidhi vā hoti paṭisedho [M 0.0133] vā’ti, ettha antarasaddassānekatthattepīhāntarāḷavācīti na vijjate antarammajjhamassetyanantaro, antarāḷamattapaṭisedhe payojanaṃ natthītyantarāḷagatassa vidhino paṭisedhassa cābhāvānantarotyupa carīyate anantarā gāmātyādi viya, diṭṭhatte pana majjhassa na vijjate-ntara mesanti viggahe suttepyanantarassa vidhānantarassāpi diṭṭhattā dvinnamekopyanantarotyuccate, tenevānantarassāti paribhāsāyameka vacanaṃ, itisaddo idamatthe, iti imāya paribhāsāyādesenābhisambandhatītyattho, tenāti yathāvuttaparibhāsāya vasena, yena kāraṇenādesenābhisambandhati tenātyattho, alopoti lopa paṭisedho, sāmatthiyāladdhanti dvinnamatthānaṃ vidhānāya dve vākyāni bhavanti, tatra ‘nāto’tīdaṃ paṭisedhavidhāyakamekaṃ vākyaṃ, ‘amapañcamiyā’ti dutiyamamādesassa, tatrāpañcamiyātyādesenevāti sambandhati, vuttavidhānā na lopapaṭisedhena, tathāsatyamapañcamiyātidaṃ vākyaṃ yadi na visesatthamālambate tamantarenānupapattito-ññathā kintyanenātthabalena laddhanti attho, alopoti jotetīti sambandho, vākyabhedena vivaraṇaṃ kataṃ, na ekavākyattenāti byatireko ekavākyatāyañhi kāriya dvayassapi pañcamiyampaṭisedho siyā ‘pañcamiṃ vajjetvā taṃ kāriyadvayaṃ veditabba’nti, yadipi siddhāti sambandho, yena nāppattiyātyanena “yena nāppatte vidhirārabbhate, tassa bādhanambhavatī”ti mamparibhāsamupalakkheti, kimatthamihāyaṃ paribhāsā paṭhyate iha satthe-pavādā ussagge bādhanteti niyamo, tatra cussaggā duvidhā niyatappattayo aniyatappattayo ceti, ye sabbatthāpavādavisayampavisanti, te niyatappattayo vuccante, ye kvacidevāpavādavisayamavagāhante, te aniyatappattayo vuccante, evaṃ duvidhesussaggesu ye-niyatappattayo, tesameva bādhanamicchīyate, na niyatikānaṃ, tena tappadassanatthamayamparibhāsā paṭhyateti, yenetyussaggassa niddeso, neti paṭisedhavācī nipāto, appatte asamphuṭṭhe visaye ityajjhāhāriyaṃ, yena ussaggena nāppatte patteeva samphuṭṭheeva visayetyattho… ‘dve paṭisedhā pākatamatthaṃ gamentī’ti katvā, vidhīyatīti, paṭisedho vidhānañca, ārabbhate vidhī

And that is the 'aṃ' substitution. 'Ādesasseva' means 'of the 'aṃ' substitution itself'. 'Apañcamiyā' means 'excluding the fifth case'. This 'aṃ' substitution, being enjoined elsewhere, is prohibited in the fifth case; thus, by the prohibition of the fifth case, it itself is also called prohibited. Therefore, he says: 'This prohibition is of the substitution itself.' This prohibition is not connected to the prohibition of elision, which was stated by the previous phrase 'nāto'. Then, how is this 'apañcamiyā' connected with the 'aṃ' substitution itself, and not with the prohibition of elision? He states the maxim: 'An injunction or a prohibition applies to that which is immediate.' Here, although the word 'antara' has multiple meanings, in this context it means 'interval'; thus, 'anantara' means 'that which has no interval or middle'. Since there is no purpose in merely prohibiting an interval, and since there is no injunction or prohibition that has entered an interval, 'anantara' is used metaphorically, as in 'anantarā gāmā' ('villages that are immediate to each other'), and so on. However, since it is observed, in the analysis 'na vijjate antaraṃ esaṃ' ('there is no interval between these'), and in the sutta, since both an immediate injunction and an immediate prohibition are seen, either of the two is called 'immediate'. Therefore, in the maxim 'anantarassa', the singular is used. The word 'iti' is in the sense of 'thus'. Thus, the meaning is that by this maxim, it is connected with the substitution. 'Tena' means 'by that', i.e., according to the aforementioned maxim. The meaning is 'by which reason it is connected with the substitution, by that'. 'Alopo' means the prohibition of elision. 'Sāmatthiyāladdhanti' means 'obtained by the force of context', because there are two statements for the injunction of two operations. Therein, 'nāto' is one statement enjoining the prohibition, and 'amapañcamiyā' is the second, for the 'aṃ' substitution. In this, 'apañcamiyā' is connected with the substitution itself, not with the prohibition of elision, as stated by the injunction. Thus, if this statement 'amapañcamiyā' does not rely on a specific meaning, then due to the impossibility otherwise, it is obtained by the force of context; what else could it be? 'Alopo' clarifies; this is the connection. The explanation is given by splitting the sentences, not as a single statement. The distinction is that if it were a single statement, the prohibition of the fifth case would apply to both actions: 'excluding the fifth case, those two actions should be understood.' Even if it is established, this is the connection. By 'yena nāppattiyā', he indicates the maxim: 'When an injunction is begun where [the general rule] has not applied, it obstructs that [general rule].' For what purpose is this maxim recited here? In this science, it is a rule that exceptions obstruct general rules. Therein, general rules are of two kinds: those with fixed application and those with unfixed application. Those that enter the scope of an exception everywhere are called general rules with fixed application. Those that enter the scope of an exception only in certain cases are called general rules with unfixed application. Thus, among these two kinds of general rules, the obstruction of only those with unfixed application is desired, not of those with fixed application. Therefore, this maxim is recited to show that. 'Yena' is the designation of the general rule. 'Na' is a prohibitive particle. 'Appatte' means 'in a scope not attained, not touched'—this is to be supplied. The meaning is: 'by which general rule, in a scope where it has not applied (i.e., where it has already applied or been touched)...' On the principle that 'two prohibitions convey the natural meaning', it is enjoined. Prohibition and injunction. An injunction is begun.

Yate [M 0.0134] paṭhyatetyattho, anenāpavādavidhindasseti, tasseti ādoyeneti niddiṭṭhassaussaggassabādhanambhavatyapavādena, yena tvappatte visaye ārabbhate tassa bādhanaṃ na bhavatītyattho, kutoti ce anavakāsattā, tathāhi yadi ussaggena sabbo visayo gahito siyā, ko-pavādassaañño visayo siyā, tasmā anavakāsattā (na) apa (vāde) pana tassa bādhanambhavatītyavaseyaṃ, yena tussaggena koci devāpavādavisayo-nuppattosiyā, nasabbo, tampati sāvakā sattā tambādhateti vuttaṃ hoti, ‘pañcapūlimānaye’tyatra pañcannaṃ pūlānaṃ samāhāroti visesanasamāso “nadāditovī” (3-27) samāharaṇaṃ samāhāroti samāhārassapi bhāvarūpattā āha ‘bhāvappadhānattepī’ti, guṇabhūtadabbāni pūlāni.

The meaning is 'it is recited.' By this, he shows the rule of exception. The meaning is that the obstruction of the general rule, which is designated by 'tassa' ('of that') and 'yena' ('by which'), occurs by the exception; but for that which is begun in a scope not attained, its obstruction does not occur. Why? Because there is no room for the exception. For if the entire scope were grasped by the general rule, what other scope would there be for the exception? Therefore, due to the lack of room, it should be understood that its obstruction occurs by the exception. But for a general rule where some, but not all, of the scope of the exception is not covered, it is said that [the exception] obstructs it because it [the general rule] has scope elsewhere. In the phrase 'pañcapūlimānaye,' it is 'the collection of five bundles' (pañcannaṃ pūlānaṃ samāhāro), a determinative compound. As in 'nadāditovī' (3-27), 'samāharaṇaṃ' is 'samāhāra' (collection), and because 'samāhāra' also has the nature of an abstract noun, he says 'even when the abstract noun is primary.' The bundles (pūla) are substances that have become secondary.

125. Ima

125. Ima

Sutte anitthiyanti kimatthiya (manena) paṭisedhavacanena, yato imassetvevānitthiliṅgena niddesoti manasikatvā āha-nāmaggahaṇe’iccādi, “nāmaggahaṇe liṅgavisiṭṭhassāpi gahaṇa”nti paribhāsāyaṃ, tattha liṅgena sutte niddiṭṭhato aññena kenaci visiṭṭhaṃ nāmaṃ liṅgavisiṭṭhaṃ, tassa, yattha saddasāmaññasannissayanaṃ, tattha nāmaggahaṇe satiliṅgavisiṭṭhassāpi gahaṇaṃ hoti… sāmaññe sabbavisesānuppave satotyadhippāyo, idamevāti anitthiyanti vacanameva, ñāpakanti patti pubbako paṭisedho, so itthiyampattiyaṃ sati anitthiyanti kato siyāti anitthiyanti paṭisedhavacanamevemaṃ paribhāsaṃ ñāpetīti attho, iminā imissā paribhāsāya sāmatthiyaladdhataṃ dasseti.

In the sutta, regarding 'anitthiyaṃ': what is the purpose of this prohibitive statement, since 'imassa' itself is specified in the non-feminine gender? Having considered this, he says: 'in the taking of a noun,' etc. In the maxim, 'in the taking of a noun, that which is qualified by gender is also taken.' There, a noun qualified by some gender other than that specified in the sutta is 'gender-qualified' (liṅgavisiṭṭhaṃ). Where there is reliance on the generality of the word-form, there, when a noun is taken, that which is qualified by gender is also taken... The intention is that in the general case, all specific cases are included. This very statement 'anitthiyaṃ' is an indicator (ñāpaka). An indicator means that a prohibition presupposes a possible application. Thus, since there is a possible application in the feminine, the prohibition 'anitthiyaṃ' is made. The meaning is that this prohibitive statement 'anitthiyaṃ' itself indicates this maxim. By this, he shows that this maxim is obtained by implication.

127. Simha

127. Simha

Anapuṃsakassāti pariyudāsoti anapuṃsakassāti ettha nañsaddassa pariyudāso-tthotyattho.

Regarding 'anapuṃsakassa', it is a 'pariyudāsa'. Here, the meaning of 'anapuṃsakassa' is that the negative particle 'nañ' has the sense of 'pariyudāsa'.

129. Massā

129. Massā

Tannetiādinā katthaci paribhāsāvatiraniccāti sūceti.

By 'tanna', etc., he indicates that the application of a maxim is sometimes not invariable.

130. Kevā

130. Kevā

Hotu [M 0.0135] sito-ññatrake sati sādeso, simhi tu kappaccayā paṭhamameva kato massa sādesoti tappaccaye sati ‘kevā’ti kiṃ sāmaññena sādesavidhānene tyāsaṅkiya suttassa sāmañña vidhāne phalaṃ dassetuṃ ‘kenekatthatāyaṃ’tyādimāha, kenekatthatāyanti kappaccayena saha ṇādivuttiyaṃ, pubbabhāgassāti asubhāgassa padattābhāvāti “ekatthatāyā”ti (2-119) vibhattiyā padattasādhikāyāpagamena padattābhāvā, padasaṅkhāranibandhanoti pada siddhi hetuko, “nimittābhāve nemittikassāpyabhāvo”ti ñāyassāyamattho “nimittaṃ kāraṇaṃ hetūtyanatthantaraṃ, nimittassa abhāvo nimittābhāvo, tasmiṃ nimittābhāve hetuvināsetyattho, nimittā āgato nemittiko, phalabhūto dhammo, nimitte bhāvo vā nemittiko, nimittassābhāve taṃ hetuto pavattassa nemittikassa phalassāpyabhāvo bhavatī”ti, tathāhi chattanimittachāyā chattāpāyena bhavati, padīpanimittadassanaṃ padīpāpāye na bhāti, tathehāpi nimittato pavattānaṃ nimittābhāve abhāvoyeva yutti māti maññate, aññatracāti sito aññatra ca.

Let there be the substitution of 'sa' when 'ke' follows, except for 'si'. But in the case of 'siṃ', the substitution of 'sa' for 'ma' is made first because of the 'ka' suffix. Therefore, when that suffix is present, why is 'kevā' formed? Why is there a general injunction for the substitution of 'sa'? Having raised this doubt, in order to show the result of the general injunction in the sutta, he says 'kenekatthatāyaṃ', and so on. 'Kenekatthatāyaṃ' means in a compound with the 'ka' suffix, as in the 'ṇādi' group. 'Pubbabhāgassa' means because the preceding part 'asu' does not have the status of a word (pada); because of the removal of the case ending, which establishes word-status, by the rule 'ekatthatāyā' (2-119), there is no word-status. 'Padasaṅkhāranibandhano' means it is dependent on the formation of a word. The meaning of the maxim 'in the absence of a cause, the effect also does not exist' is this: 'nimitta' (cause), 'kāraṇa' (reason), and 'hetu' (cause) are synonyms. The absence of a cause is 'nimittābhāva'. In the absence of that cause means in the destruction of the cause. 'Nemittika' is that which comes from a cause, a resultant phenomenon. Or 'nemittika' is that which exists in the cause. In the absence of the cause, the effect, 'nemittika', which arises from that cause, also does not exist. For example, the shadow caused by an umbrella does not exist with the removal of the umbrella; and the sight caused by a lamp does not appear with the removal of the lamp. Similarly, here too, it is considered logical that what arises from a cause ceases in the absence of that cause. 'Aññatraca' means 'and elsewhere than si'.

131. Tata

131. Tata

Tyaetānaṃ takārassa pariccāgāya ‘tatassā’ti vuttaṃ.

For the sake of omitting the letter 'ta' in these words, it is said 'tatassa'.

132. Ṭasa

132. Ṭasa

Imissāyātyādīsu “ssaṃ ssā ssāye”tyādinā (2-52) i, “tadādesā te viya hontī”ti paribhāsato sādyādesīnaṃ gahaṇāssāyādesādīnaṃ gahaṇasambhavepi kiṃ ssāyādiggahaṇe na suttagurukaraṇene tyāsaṅkiya‘ssāyādiggahaṇa’miccādi, vutti gantho vuttoti dassetumāha-‘nanu ce’tyādi, ṭasasmādikaṃ ‘ṭasasmāsminnannāsvimassa cā’ti vattabbaṃ, namādīnampi vidhiggahaṇāya nādīnampaviggahāya (potthake), tassā

In 'imissāya' and so on, by the rule 'ssaṃ ssā ssāye' etc. (2-52), and from the maxim 'substitutes are like their originals,' even though the taking of the substitutes beginning with `ssāya` is possible from the taking of the substitutes beginning with `sā`, why is the sutta made weighty by the inclusion of `ssāya`, etc.? Having raised this doubt, he says 'the inclusion of `ssāya`, etc.' To show that the commentary text is stated, he says 'nanu ce' etc. 'Ṭasasmādikaṃ' should be stated as 'ṭasasmāsminnannāsvimassa cā', also for the purpose of including the rule for `namādi`, etc., and for `tassā`.

Desino [M 0.0136] ādeso tadādeso, tassa, tassa ādesino gahaṇaṃ taggahaṇaṃ, tena.

The substitute of the original is `tadādeso`. The taking of that, of that original, is `taggahaṇaṃ`. By that.

134. Duti

134. Second.

Aññathāti guruniddesamakatvā aññena lahuppakārena niddisane sati, ekavibhattiniddiṭṭhattāti‘dutiyāyossā’ti ekavibhattiyā niddiṭṭhattā, aññathātiādinā nekadesotivacanapariyantenetena ‘na tvekavibhattiyuttāna’nti paribhāsekadesassa adhippāyo pakāsitoti ñātabbaṃ, etadevānuvattatītyanena tu “ekayoga niddiṭṭhānampekadeso-nuvattate”tīmassa, ekavibhattiyuttānaṃ ekadeso nānuvattateti yojanā paribhāsāyaṃ, ñāpetīti pubbe viya sāmatthiyena ñāpeti.

Regarding 'aññathā': if, not having made a weighty explanation, one explains in another, lighter manner. Regarding 'ekavibhattiniddiṭṭhattā': because it is indicated by a single case ending, as in 'dutiyāyossā'. By this statement beginning with 'aññathā' and ending with the expression 'na ekadeso', it should be understood that the intention of a part of the maxim 'na tu ekavibhattiyuttānaṃ' is revealed. But by 'etad eva anuvattati', the application in the maxim is that for this maxim 'ekayoga niddiṭṭhānaṃ ekadeso anuvattate', a part of what is connected by a single case ending does not recur. 'Ñāpeti' means, just as before, it makes known through its capability.

139. Nāññaṃ

139. Not Other.

Appadhānappaṭisedhato sabbādīnaṃ tadantavidhinā bhavitabbaṃ, aññathā hi sabbādiggahaṇe ko pasaṅgo piyasabbādīnaṃ, yato appadhānappaṭisedho, karīyate tena paramasabbeiccādi hotīti dassetumāha-‘appadhānappaṭisedho’iccādi.

Due to the prohibition of the non-principal, the `tadantavidhi` rule should apply to `sabba` and so on. Otherwise, what would be the occasion for `piyasabbādi`, etc., in the inclusion of `sabbādi`? Since the prohibition of the non-principal is made, to show that `paramasabbe`, etc., thereby occurs, he says: 'the prohibition of the non-principal,' etc.

140. Tati

140. Third.

Yatthāti yasmiṃ kattari karaṇe vā, kattari tatiyāsiddhimāha-‘karoti’ccādi, karotimhi karadhātumhi gammamāne, māsena katāti pāṭhena bhavitabbaṃ… māsena katānaṃ pubbānanti vattabbattā, pubbabhāveti pubbabhavane māsassa karaṇattaṃ, ettha tu māsena karaṇabhūtena pubbabhūtānanti attho, tenevetthāpi bhavantīti pāṭhena bhavitabbaṃ.

Regarding 'yattha': that is, in whatever agent or instrument. In the agent, he states the accomplishment of the third case: 'karoti,' etc. When the root `kar` is understood in `karoti`, the reading should be 'māsena katā'... Because it must be said 'māsena katānaṃ pubbānaṃ'. In 'pubbabhāve', that is, in prior becoming, the month has instrumentality. But here, the meaning is 'those which became prior through the month which has become the instrument.' Therefore, even here, the reading should be 'bhavanti'.

141. Cattha

141. Fourth.

Cassa attho cattho, soyevāti ettha samāsassa parāmāso, cattho ettha sambhavati kintu sabbādi na catthasamāsavisayoti pāṭhena bhavitabbaṃ.

The meaning of `ca` is `attha` (purpose), hence `cattha`. Regarding 'so yeva', here there is a reference to the compound. The reading should be: `cattha` is possible here, but `sabbādi` is not within the scope of the `cattha` compound.

144. Manā

144. The `Manas` Group.

Kiṃ bahulaṃvidhānā ‘vuddhyabhāvo’ otthābhāvo (pañcikāyaṃ) ti pāṭhena payojanaṃ yene tadatthameva [M 0.0137] “sumedhādīnamavuddhi ce”ti gaṇapāṭho kato, hemasaddena hemamayāni gahitānyabhedenatyāha- ‘hemamayānī’ti, kappana saddena sīsālaṅkārajālāni gayhanti, tāniyeva vāsasāni paṭā taṃsarikkhatāya, sakatthepi yathāgamambhavantīti sambandho, bāṇādīsu abhidheyyesu manādīsu na paṭṭhīyantīti yojanā, bāṇādīsuti bāṇa saddakkhayādīsu, ahasaddassa manādikāriyāsambhavā ahasaddo manādīsu na daṭṭhabbo, rahasīti nipātattā ikārassa ca asabbhavā rahasaddo ca manādīsu na daṭṭhabboti sajjhāhāro sambandho veditabbo, ikārassa kaccāyane smino karīyamānassa ikārādesassa ca, rahatisaddassa nipātattaṃ sabhāvato pakāsetuṃ ‘rahasītyādi’māha, rahosaddeti ettha rahasaddoti pāṭho-vagantabbo, tenāti yena ahasaddassa manādikāriyāsambhavo rahasītica nipāto, tena, ihamanādīsu.

What is the purpose of the reading 'avuddhyabhāvo' from the frequent prescription? By which, for that very purpose, the `gaṇapāṭha` 'sumedhādīnam avuddhi ce' is made. By the word `hema`, golden things are taken without distinction; he says: 'hemamayāni'. By the word `kappana`, head ornaments and nets are taken. Those very garments are cloths due to their similarity. The connection is: even in its own meaning, it occurs according to tradition. The construction is: among the things to be denoted, such as arrows, etc., they are not read in the `manādi` group. 'Bāṇādīsu' means among `bāṇa`, `sadda`, `akkhaya`, etc. Because the function of the `manādi` group is not possible for the word `ahas`, the word `ahas` should not be seen in the `manādi` group. The connection to be supplied should be understood as: because `rahasī` is a particle and because of the non-existence of the vowel `i`, the word `rahas` also should not be seen in the `manādi` group. This refers to the vowel `i` and the substitute `i` being made for `smi` in Kaccāyana's grammar. To explain the nature of the word `rahas` as a particle, he says 'rahasī', etc. Here, in `rahosadde`, the reading should be understood as `rahasaddo`. 'Tena' means: by which reason the function of the `manādi` group is not possible for the word `ahas`, and `rahasī` is a particle; by that reason, here in the `manādi` group, they are not included.

146. Bhava

146. Existence.

Geti gasaññe pare, kuto-nuiccādo bho’iti bahuvacananto nipāto, tathāsati ‘tayojanā’ti yujjati, tañca nipātattaṃ samatthetīti nipātamatteti dassetumāha- ‘bahutte’ccādi.

Regarding `ge`: when the designation `ga` follows. `Bho` in `kuto nu`, etc., is a particle with a plural ending. That being the case, 'the application of `ta`' is appropriate. And to show that this supports its status as a particle, he says: 'bahutte', etc.

148. Ntassaṃ

148. Of `nta`.

Sattamyantaṃ bhavatīti seso, nanucantassāti vutte ntantuppaccayovāvasīyati, na tadantavidhīti ntantuppaccayova nāvasīyati, tadantavidhipīti pāṭhena bhavitabbaṃ āha- ‘ntappaccaya sseve’ccādi, sutattāti sotaviññāṇena gahitattā paccakkhattāti vuttaṃ hoti, anumitassa “vidhibbisesanantassā”ti (1-26) liṅgato tadantasaṅkhāta atthadassanasaṅkhātaanumānaññāṇena viññātassāti attho.

The remainder is 'it becomes ending in the seventh case'. When 'nanu ca ntassa' is said, the suffix `nta` itself is certainly understood, not the `tadantavidhi` rule; thus he says: 'ntappaccayassa eva', etc. 'Sutattā' means because of being grasped by auditory consciousness, it is said to be 'direct experience'. Of the inferred, the meaning is 'of that which is known through inferential knowledge—which is designated as seeing the meaning and designated as `tadanta`—from the mark in the rule 'vidhi visesana ntassa' (1-26).

154. Rāja

154. King.

Daḷho dhammo dhanu assa daḷhadhammā. Rājādīsvimappaccaye paṭhite

`Daḷhadhammā` means 'one whose bow (`dhanu`) is strong (`daḷha`)'. When the suffix `ima` is read in the `rājādi` group.

Tadanto [M 0.0138] paccayaggahaṇa paribhāsāya gayhatī tyāha- ‘iminā iccādi.

That which ends in it is grasped by the maxim of taking the suffix; thus he says: 'by this,' etc.

162. Ltu

162. `Ltu`.

Paccayaiccādinā “paccayaggahaṇe yasmā so vihito tadādino tadantassa ca gahaṇa”nti ñāyaṃ dasseti, tattha yato vihito taṃ vinā na bhavati paccayotyanena ñāyena pattoyevāttho ākhyāyate ‘paccayaggahaṇe yasmā so vihito, tadādino gahaṇa’nti, “vidhibbisesanantasse”ti tadantaggahaṇaṃtyākhyāyate ‘tadantassa ca gahaṇa’nti, so pakativiseso ādi yassa samudāyassa so tadādi, so paccayo-nte yassa samudāyassa so tadanto, tādisassa tadāditadantasamudāyavisesassa gahaṇaṃ, na tu tadantamattassetyattho, iha tu tadantaggahaṇamevānurūpanti’ dassetumāha-“kattari ltuṇakā”ti iminā tyādi, tadāditadanta samudāyassa tu gahaṇe phalaṃ ‘byajigisī’tiādīsu daṭṭhabbaṃ, tañca “tuṃsmā lopocicchāyaṃ te”ti (5-4) sutte sayameva vakkhati.

By 'paccaya', etc., he shows the principle: 'In the taking of a suffix, since it is prescribed after a base, there is the taking of that which begins with that base and that which ends with that suffix.' Therein, by the principle 'a suffix does not exist without that after which it is prescribed', the meaning is explained as: 'In the taking of a suffix, since it is prescribed after a base, there is the taking of that which begins with that base.' By the rule 'vidhi visesana ntassa', the taking of that which ends in it is explained as: 'and the taking of that which ends with it.' That special base is the beginning of whichever aggregate, that is `tadādi`. That suffix is the end of whichever aggregate, that is `tadanta`. The taking is of such a special aggregate which has that as its beginning and that as its end, not merely of that which ends in it alone—this is the meaning. But here, to show that only the taking of that which ends in it is appropriate, he says by this 'kattari ltuṇakā', etc. The result of taking the aggregate which has that as its beginning and end should be seen in 'byajigisī', etc. And that he himself will state in the sutta 'tuṃsmā lopo ca icchāyaṃ te' (5-4).

165. Salo

165. Sāla.

Kaccāyane “sakamandhātādīnañce”ti (2-3-44) suttitaṃ, sopi ltvantoyevātyabhimatasiddhīti dassetuṃ vuttiyamudāhaṭaṃtyāha- ‘sakamandhātu’iccādi, ltvanto mandhātusaddo atthīti ‘sakamandhātu’ saddopi ltvantoti sajjhāhāro padasambandho daṭṭhabbo, tatopīti na kevalaṃ kattutova, mandhātusaddassa ltvantataṃ sādhetvā sakamandhātusaddampaṭipādetuṃ ‘sabbesa’ntiādimāha.

In Kaccāyana, it is stated in the sutta 'sakamandhātādīnaṃ ca' (2-3-44). To show that it too is indeed one ending in `ltu` and thus the desired conclusion is established, he says it is cited in the commentary: 'sakamandhātu', etc. The connection of words to be supplied should be understood as: because the word `mandhātu` is one ending in `ltu`, the word `sakamandhātu` is also one ending in `ltu`. 'Tatopi' means not only from `kattu`, but also from that. Having established that the word `mandhātu` ends in `ltu`, in order to explain the word `sakamandhātu`, he says 'sabbesaṃ', etc.

169. Ṭapa

169. Austerity.

Saṅkhyāsaddo yadīpi saṅkhyāne vattate, tathāpi saṅkhyānadvārenidhasaṅkhyeyye vattatītyāha-‘cuddasahi saṅkhyāhī’ti pāṭhena bhavitabbaṃ, cuddasasaddavacanīyāva pañcādisaṅkhyā, yato saṅkhyāsaddo neha pariggahitoti.

Although the word `saṅkhyā` occurs in the sense of counting, nevertheless, through counting, it occurs here in the sense of the thing counted; therefore, he says the reading should be 'cuddasahi saṅkhyāhi'. The numbers beginning with five are indeed expressible by the word 'fourteen', because the word `saṅkhyā` is not taken here in the sense of counting.

175. Divā

175. By Day.

Divasato smino ṭimhi pubbasaralope divi.

From `divasa`, when `smi` is replaced by `ṭi`, with the elision of the preceding vowel, it becomes `divi`.

181. Yonaṃ

181. Of the Ionians.

Dutiyāggahaṇenāti [M 0.0139] ‘dutiyāyossa ne vā’tyevaṃ sutta racanāyaṃ dutiyāggahaṇena.

Regarding 'dutiyāggahaṇena': by the inclusion of `dutiyā` in the composition of the sutta 'dutiyāyo ssa ne vā'.

185. Nāmhi

185. I am not.

Enādesassāsambhavāti nāssa smādesattā.

Because the substitution 'ena' is impossible, there is no substitution by 'smā' for it.

187. Gassaṃ

187. Of grass.

Ubhayavikappoti samāsāsamāsapakkhadvayavidhānaṃ, kaccāyanavutti kārassa vippaṭipattimāvīkattumāha-‘kaccāyane’ccādi, itthipumannapuṃsaka samūhoti etthāyantesaṃ sādhanakkamo ‘dvandachaṭṭhīhi samāse itthipumanapuṃsakasamūho’ti ṭhite “samāse ca vibhāsā”ti (2-2-35) pumantassa amādese “vaggantaṃ vā vagge”ti (1-42) niggahītassa vagganto.

'Ubhayavikappo' means the prescribing of two alternatives, namely, compounding and non-compounding. To reveal the disagreement of the author of the Kaccāyana commentary, it is said, 'in Kaccāyana,' and so on. Regarding 'itthipumannapuṃsakasamūho'—here, the method of derivation is as follows: when it is established that 'in a compound with dvanda or sixth-case endings, there is a collection of feminine, masculine, and neuter genders,' and when, by the rule 'samāse ca vibhāsā' (2-2-35), there is the 'am' substitution for the masculine ending, then according to 'vaggantaṃ vā vagge' (1-42), the niggahīta becomes a class-nasal.

192. Puma

192. Man.

Kammādittā enassāpi abhāvapakkheti “nā sse no”ti (2-80) kammādito nāssa enādesakaraṇato vuttaṃ.

Because it is at the beginning of a word, there is also the alternative of the absence of 'ena'; this is stated by the rule 'nā sse no' (2-80), because the substitution 'ena' is not made for 'na' when it is at the beginning of a word.

197. Ime

197. These.

Ādeso kathanaṃ, anvādeso-nukathanamiccāha-‘anvādeso kathitānukathana’mīti, kathitassānukathanaṃ kathitānukathanaṃ, anena ca neha pacchā uccāraṇamattamanvādeso, kiñcarahi ekassābhidheyyassa pubbasaddena paṭipāditassa dutiyampatipādanamanvādesoti vadati, teneha na bhavati ‘devadattaṃ bhojaya, imañca yaññadatta’nti, kenaci visesantarayogena kathitassānukathanaṃ anvādesoti sambandho. Kathampana visesantarayogo gamyateccāha- ‘sāmatthiyā’ti, kenaci visesenāyoge vuttasseva punabbacanānupapajjanaṃ sāmatthiyaṃ, tenevāha- ‘aññathe’ccādi.

Ādesa is stating; anvādesa is re-stating—thus it is said: 'Anvādesa is the repetition of what has been spoken.' The repetition of what has been spoken is 'kathitānukathana.' And by this, mere subsequent utterance here is not anvādesa. What then? It is said that anvādesa is the second expression of a single referent that has been established by a prior word. Therefore, it does not occur here as 'Feed Devadatta, and also this Yajñadatta,' because the connection is that anvādesa is the repetition of what has been spoken in conjunction with some other distinguishing feature. How, then, is the connection with a different distinguishing feature understood? He says: 'By implication.' Implication is the unsuitability of merely repeating what has been stated without some distinguishing feature. Therefore, he says: 'Otherwise,' etc.

198. Kissa

198. Of what?

Navirujjhatīti iminā “itthiyamatvā”ti (3-26) sāmaññena vidhānato syādyantamajjhepi itthiyampaccayo navirujjhatīti vadati.

By 'Navirujjhati' (it is not obstructed), it is said that because of the general prescription by 'itthiyamatvā' (3-26), the feminine affix is not obstructed even at the beginning, middle, or end of the case endings.

204. Namhi

204. I am not.

Nanu [M 0.0140] yathākkamaṃ naṃvibhattikkamenāpi sambhavati, tathāsati ‘dvinnaṃ saddānaṃ dveādesā kamene’cceva kasmā vuttaṃ tyāsaṅkiyāha ‘na naṃvibhattikkamenāpī’ti. Kāraṇamāha- ‘tassānapekkhitattā’ti, iminā nissayakaraṇamekā satthiyā yuttīti dasseti, apekkhite kathaṃ bhaveyyā tyāha- ‘yadi hi’ccādi, apekkhiti yathākkamaṃ, evamaññate “kiñcāpi jātiniddesena dvepi naṃ rūpāni gayhanti, tathāpi ‘ticatunna’nti viya byattiniddesova yathākkamopakārīyamānāna, manudesassa tathā viññayamānattāti naṃsuicceva vadeyya, na tathā vuttaṃ, tato-vasīyate ‘na yathākkamametthāpekkhita’nti.

Now, does it not occur in order even according to the order of the 'naṃ' suffixes? If so, why is it said, 'For two words, two substitutions occur in order'? Raising this doubt, he says, 'It does not occur even according to the order of the 'naṃ' suffixes.' He states the reason: 'Because it is not required.' By this, he shows that relying on one authoritative text is appropriate. If it were required, how would it be? He says: 'If indeed,' etc. 'Required' means 'in order.' Thus it is thought: 'Although both forms of 'naṃ' are taken by the specification of class, still, just as in 'of three, of four,' the specification of the individual is helpful for those adopting the order. Since the instruction is to be understood in that way, one should have said 'naṃsu' itself, but it was not stated thus. Therefore, it is inferred that 'the order is not required here.'

205. Nta

205. The suffix -nta.

Nanu ntantūnanti tadantā gayhanti paccayaggahaṇaparibhāsāya, tathā sati kāriyittena tadantāva gayhanti kathaṃ ntantūyevā tyāsaṅkiyāha- teyeve’ccādi, paccakkhatāyāti sutathāya-pañcikā sutattā, balavattā teyeva kāriyittena gayhantīti sambandho, na tadantā, dubbalāti byatirekaṃ vatvā dubbalatte kāraṇamāha- ‘anumitattā’ti, anumitattaṃ sādhetumāha- ‘anumitāhi’ccādi, bhavibhattīnanti pāṭho yutta taro, tassa antādese akāreti sambandho.

Now, by 'nta, ntū', are not the words ending in them taken, according to the maxim 'when an affix is mentioned, what ends in it is meant'? If so, since those ending in them are the subject of the operation, how is it that only 'nta, ntū' themselves are taken? Raising this doubt, he says, 'Only they,' etc. Because of being directly perceived, that is, because of being explicitly stated, and because of their strength, only they are taken as the subject of the operation—this is the connection, not those ending in them. Having stated the contrast, 'they are weak,' he states the reason for their weakness: 'because of being inferred.' To establish their being inferred, he says: 'anumitāhi,' etc. The reading 'bhavibhattīnaṃ' is more suitable; in the substitution of its final part, the connection is with the letter 'a'.

219. Yomhi

219. Regarding the case endings 'yo' and 'mhi'.

Yomhīti sattamyantajātiniddesā labbhamānatthavasena ‘pacceka’nti vuttiyaṃ vuttaṃ, tenevāha pañcikāyaṃ- ‘kathamidamavasīyate yomhīti niddesā’ti, tassadāni atthampakāsetuṃ ‘paccekanti ekekasmi’ntiādi vuttaṃ. Ekekasmiṃ yomhi dvinnaṃ ādesānaṃ sambhavā ādesīnampi bahuttasambhavoti sutte ‘dvinna’nti bahuvacananiddeso, vuttiyampana paccekaṃ yomhi paccekaṃ dvisaddasambhavā ‘dvissā’ti vuttaṃ, dutiyāyampi duve dve.

In the commentary, 'pacceka' (severally) is stated in the sense of the meaning obtainable from 'yomhi,' which is a class designation in the locative case. Therefore, it says in the Pañcikā: 'How is this understood from the designation 'yomhi'?' Now, to clarify its meaning, it is stated: ''paccekaṃ' means 'in each one',' etc. Because for each 'yomhi' there is the possibility of two substitutions, and also the possibility of a plurality of the original forms, in the sutta the designation 'dvinnaṃ' is in the plural. But in the commentary, 'dvissa' is stated because of the occurrence of two words for each 'yomhi'; and in the second case, two and two.

228. Nāsmā

228. Not from this.

Pakatavasenāti [M 0.0141] tumhāmhānamādesānamadhikatavasena, kamamanatikkamma na bhavantīti sambandho.

'Pakatavasena' (by way of what is under discussion) means by way of the authority of the substitutions for 'tumha' and 'amha.' The connection is that they do not occur without transgressing the order.

230. Caṃvā

230. Campā.

Kaccāyanācariyo tumhāmhehi parāya catutthī chaṭṭhī savibhattiyā “sassaṃ”ti (2-3-3) suttena amādesaṃ vidhāya ‘tumhaṃ amha’nti bahuvacanarūpāni sādheti… ekasmimpi attani guruādike ca gārava vasena bahuvacanarūpadassanatoti dassetumāha-tumhaṃ amha’ntiādi, tassāyuttattā ‘tamayutta’nti vatvā ayuttataṃ sādheti ‘evaṃ hi’ccādinā, imasmimpana satthe ekasmimpi sabbathā bahuvacana rūpasādhanakkamaṃ dassetuṃ ‘idha panā’tiādimāraddhaṃ.

The teacher Kaccāyana, having prescribed the 'am' substitution for the fourth and sixth cases following 'tumha' and 'amha' with their suffixes by the rule 'sassaṃ' (2-3-3), establishes the plural forms 'tumhaṃ' and 'amha.'... And to show that even for a single person, such as a teacher, plural forms are used out of respect, he says 'tumhaṃ amha' and so on. Because that is unsuitable, having said 'that is unsuitable,' he establishes the unsuitability by 'for thus,' etc. But in this treatise, to show the process of establishing plural forms in every way, even for a single person, the section beginning with 'idha pana' (but here) is commenced.

232. Apā

232. Apā: Away from.

Nenāti nakārena, padasaññāvidhāya kavacanābhāvepīti pāṇini yānamiva syādityādyantānaṃ padasaññāvidhāyakassa suttassa abhāvepi, anvatthavasena padanti gayhamāne atippasaṅgopi siyāti āha-‘ruḷhiyāvātippasaṅgā bhāvo’ti, ākhyātaṃ sābyayakāraka visesanaṃ vākyanti keci, ekākhyātikaṃ vākyantyapare, taṃ sabbaṃ ekato saṅgahetvā ‘padasamūho vākya’nti vuttikārena vuttanti dassetumāha- ‘sābyaye’ccādi, ākhyātaṃ tyādyantamāhu, abyayamasaṅkhyaṃ, ākhyātaṃ sābyayaṃ sakārakaṃ savisesanañca vākyesaññaṃ bhavatītyattho, visesananti kārakavisesanassa kiriyā visesanassa ca sāmaññena gahaṇaṃ, sābyayaṃ-saddhiṃ vacati, sakārakaṃ odanaṃ pacati devadatto pacati, sakārakavisesanaṃ-muduṃ visadamodanampacati, dassanīyo devadatto pacati, sakiriyāvisesanaṃ- muduṃ pacati, mandaṃ pacati, padasamūho vākyanti vutte ayampi adhippāyavisesovasīyatīti vattumāha-vattu’miccādi, yatheccādinā anekākhyāti kampi guṇappadhānabhāve nopakārato vākyamekambhavati… pada samūho vākyanti vuttattāti vadati, yathā vākyanānattanti sambandho. Ihāpīti vattumicchitatthetyādopi.

'Nena' means by the letter 'na'. Even in the absence of a sutta that prescribes the designation 'pada' for those ending in 'si' etc., as in the system of Pāṇini, if 'pada' were to be taken in its etymological sense, there could be over-application. Thus it is said: ‘By convention, there is no over-application.’ Some say that a sentence is a verb with an indeclinable, a kāraka, and a modifier. Others say a sentence is that which has a single verb. To show that the commentator, having gathered all this, has said, 'a collection of words is a sentence,' he states: 'sābyaye,' etc. They say a verb, etc., is the limit. An indeclinable is that which has no number. The meaning is that a verb, together with an indeclinable, a kāraka, and a modifier, receives the designation 'sentence'. ‘Modifier’ is a general term for a modifier of a kāraka and a modifier of an action. 'With an indeclinable': e.g., 'saddhiṃ vacati' (he speaks with). 'With a kāraka': e.g., 'odanaṃ pacati' (he cooks rice), 'devadatto pacati' (Devadatta cooks). 'With a modifier of a kāraka': e.g., 'muduṃ visadamodanaṃ pacati' (he cooks soft, clear rice), 'dassanīyo devadatto pacati' (handsome Devadatta cooks). 'With a modifier of an action': e.g., 'muduṃ pacati' (he cooks softly), 'mandaṃ pacati' (he cooks slowly). When it is said that 'a collection of words is a sentence,' a particular intention is also understood. To express this, he says: 'vattumicchi,' etc. As by 'yathā' etc., even a phrase with many verbs can become a single sentence due to a principal-subordinate relationship... because it is said 'a collection of words is a sentence'. The connection is 'yathā vākyanānattaṃ' (as there is a variety of sentences). Here too, in 'vattumicchitatthe' etc.

233. Yonaṃ

233. Of whom.

Higgahaṇe [M 0.0142] pañcamīhissāpi gahaṇambhaveyyāti sutte ‘apañcamyā’ti vuttaṃ, tumhehi puññaṃ pasutaṃ anappakanti gāthāpāde tumhehitiādisū tattā na voādeso, tumhe tiṭṭhatha nagareti pubbavākyato vākyantarattā ekavākyatā natthi, tumhe viya diya dissanti amhe viya dissantīti viggayha ‘disa-pekkhaṇe’ iccasmā “samānaññabhavantayādi tūpamānā disā kamme rīrikkhakā”ti (5-43) kappaccaye “nate kānubandhanāgamesū”ti (5-85) ettābhāve “syādisyādinekattha”nti (3-1) samāse ca ‘ekatthatāyaṃ”ti (2-119) vibhattilope ca “sabbādīnamā”ti (3-86) ā ‘tumhādisāna’miccādi.

Lest in taking the suffix 'hi', the 'hi' of the fifth case also be taken, it is stated in the sutta 'apañcamyā' (excluding the fifth). In the verse line 'tumhehi puññaṃ pasutaṃ anappakaṃ' (by you, much merit has been produced), because 'tumhehi' is at the beginning of the line, the substitution 'vo' does not occur. In 'tumhe tiṭṭhatha nagare' (you stay in the city), since it is a separate sentence from the previous one, there is no unity of sentence. Having analyzed 'they are seen like you, they are seen like us' from the root 'disa' in the sense of 'seeing', the suffix 'ka' is applied according to 'samānaññabhavantayādi...' (5-43); then in the absence of 'etta' by 'nate kānubandhanāgamesu' (5-85); then in a compound by 'syādisyādinekattha' (3-1); and with the elision of the case ending by 'ekatthatāyaṃ' (2-119); and the substitution of 'ā' by 'sabbādīnamā' (3-86), up to 'tumhādisāna,' etc.

235. Anvā

235. Anvā: Following.

Pacchā ādeso anvādesoti gahite kathitānukathananti kathaṃ ñāyatīti āha- ‘pacchā kathanañca kathitāpekkhanti katvā’ti.

When 'anvādesa' is taken to mean 'subsequent substitution,' how is it known to mean 'reiteration of what has been spoken'? He says: 'Because subsequent speaking is dependent on what has already been spoken.'

236. Sapu

236. Sapu: The good.

Saha vijjamāno pubbo yassa so sapubbo.

He for whom a preceding element exists is called 'sapubbo'.

237. Naca

237. And not.

Aparamparayogappatipatyatthanti ‘gāmanagarānaṃ cenā’tiādinā vuttassa paramparayogassa aggahaṇatthaṃ.

For the purpose of preventing the application of the successive connection mentioned by 'gāmanagarānaṃ cenā,' etc.

240. Nasā

240. Nasā: Nose.

Jaṭā assa atthīti jaṭilo, sova jaṭilako, jaṭilakāti ekatthe nidassitavisesavacanaṃ, māṇavakāti viya na sāmaññavacanaṃ, asatte sampatteti idaṃ “āmantaṇaṃ pubbamasantaṃ vā”ti (2-239) suttassa sāmaññatā vuttaṃ, sāmaññavacanassa paṭisedhoti iminā visesavacane jaṭilakaiccatra ‘āmantaṇaṃ pubbamasantaṃ vā”tīmassa pattindasseti, devadattādisāmaññavacaneti devadatto devadattasaddo ādi yassa, tañca taṃ sāmaññavacanañca, tasmiṃ devadattādisāmaññavacane māṇavake māṇavakasadde parabhūte sati, ubhinnampi asatteti iminā [M 0.0143] idaṃ dīpeti “devadattāti visesavacanattā paṭisedhābhāvā pubbaparānamubhinnampi “āmantaṇaṃ pubbamasantaṃ vā”tīdaṃ pappotī”ti.

He has matted hair (jaṭā), hence he is a jaṭila; that very one is a jaṭilaka. 'Jaṭilaka' is a specific term indicating a single meaning; it is not a general term like 'māṇavaka.' The phrase 'asatte sampatte' illustrates the generality stated in the sutta 'āmantaṇaṃ pubbamasantaṃ vā' (2-239). By this prohibition of a general term, it shows the application of 'āmantaṇaṃ pubbamasantaṃ vā' in the case of the specific term 'jaṭilaka.' In the case of a general term beginning with Devadatta—that is, the word 'Devadatta' and so on—when the word 'māṇavaka' follows, by the phrase 'for both, it is not a being,' it clarifies this: 'Because 'Devadatta' is a specific term, there is no prohibition; therefore, this rule 'āmantaṇaṃ pubbamasantaṃ vā' applies to both the preceding and the following.'

Iti moggallānapañcikāṭīkāyaṃ sāratthavilāsiniyaṃ

Thus in the Sāratthavilāsinī, the sub-commentary on the Moggallānapañcikā.

Dutiyakaṇḍavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Second Chapter is concluded.

3. Tatiyakaṇḍavaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Third Chapter

1. Syādi

1. Syādi

Yassātikamāvaṭṭhitassayoādiakkharasamudāyassa, kintanti āha- ‘ida’miccādi, idanti yathāvuttaṃ syādisamudāyarūpaṃ, avayavena viggaho samudāyo samāsattho, samudāye pavattā saddā avayavesupi vattantīti syādisaddo siādike avayavepi vattate, vidhiggahaṇañāyenāti “paccayaggahaṇe yasmā sa vihito tadādino tadantassa ca gahaṇa”nti ñāyena. Syādi ante yassa taṃ syādyantaṃ. Nanu ca “syādisyādinekattha”nti sāmaññena vuccamāne yaṃkiñci syādyantaṃ yenakenaci syādyantena sahekatthībhāvamarahati, tathāhi yathā gāmagatotiādo, tathā passa devadatte gāmaṃ, gato yaññadatto gurukulanti ādopi samāso tyāsaṅkiyāha-‘sāmaññena vuttepi’ccādi, yassa syādyantassayena syādyantena sambandho, tena syādyantena sahataṃ syādyantamekatthambhavatīti sambandhato viññāyati avasīyatīti yassātyādisvattho, tathā ca gāmagatotyatratthīmesa-maññamaññāpekkhālakkhaṇo sambandhotyekatthībhāvo, tatoyevetthāhu-

Regarding the collection of syllables beginning with 'si,' which is established as transcending its parts, what is it? He says: 'this,' etc. Here, 'this' refers to the aforementioned collection of syllables in the form of 'syādi.' The analysis is by its parts; the meaning of the compound is the collection. Words that apply to the collection also apply to the parts, so the term 'syādi' also applies to the parts like 'si' and so on, according to the maxim of grasping the rule—that is, the maxim: 'in grasping a suffix, from which it is prescribed, one grasps that which begins with it and that which ends with it.' That which has 'syādi' at its end is 'syādyanta.' But is it not said generally, 'syādi and syādi have a single meaning'? If so, any term ending in 'syādi' could share a single meaning with any other term ending in 'syādi.' For example, just as in 'gāmagato' (gone to the village), etc., could there also be a compound in cases like 'passa devadatte gāmaṃ' (see the village in Devadatta) and 'gato yaññadatto gurukulaṃ' (Yaññadatta went to the teacher's house)? Anticipating this doubt, it is said, 'even when stated generally,' etc. The meaning of 'yassa,' etc., is: that term ending in 'syādi' which has a connection with another term ending in 'syādi,' becomes one in meaning with that term. This is understood and determined from the connection. And so, in 'gāmagato,' there is a connection characterized by mutual expectation, which results in a single meaning. From this very point, they say—

Niyataṃ sādhanaṃ sādhye, kriyā niyatasādhanā;

Sannidhānena metesaṃ cethissā (potthake), niyamo-yampakāsatīti.

The means is fixed on the goal; the action has a fixed means. By the proximity of these, this rule is revealed.

Ayamettha attho “yato gāmamiccetaṃ sādhanaṃ sādhyaṃ kiriyaṃ taṃbyapadesajānanayogyamapekkhate gatoti, ato sādhanaṃ kāra kaṃ [M 0.0144] sādhye kiriyāya niyataṃ, yato ca kiriyā sayaṃ sādhanamapekkhate kiṃ gatoti, ato kiriyāpi niyataṃ sādhanametissāti niyatasādhanā hoti ayaṃ yathāvutto niyamo aññamaññāpekkhāvasena vattamāno etesaṃ sādhyasādhanānaṃ sannidhāna mattena aññamaññato pakāsatī”ti. Passa devadatta gāmaṃ, gato yaññadatto gurukulaṃtyatra tu gāmanti sādhanaṃ passeti sādhyamapekkhate, gatoti gamanakiriyā tu gurukulamapekkhate, tato ca gāmagatānaṃ vākyantarāvayavānaṃ natthevāpekkhāti na bhavati samāso, sabbatthevamūhanīyaṃ, sambandho hi aññamaññāpekkhālakkhaṇo sambandhyantarato-navaṭṭhitaṃ nivattetvā visese niveseti, tathāca vuttaṃ–

Here is the meaning: 'Since this means (sādhana), 'gāmaṃ' (to the village), requires the action to be accomplished (sādhyaṃ kiriyaṃ), 'gato' (gone), which is fit to be known by that designation, therefore the means (sādhana), the instrument (kāraka), is necessarily connected to the action to be accomplished. And since the action itself requires a means—as in the question 'gone to what?'—the action, too, has a necessarily connected means; thus, it is called 'niyatasādhanā' (having a necessarily connected means). This aforementioned rule, operating through mutual dependence, becomes apparent between these goals and means merely through their proximity.' But in the example 'passa devadatta gāmaṃ, gato yaññadatto gurukulaṃ' (Devadatta, see the village; Yaññadatta went to the teacher's house), the means 'gāmaṃ' requires the goal 'passa,' and the action of going, 'gato,' requires 'gurukulaṃ.' Therefore, for 'gāma' and 'gata,' which are parts of different clauses, there is no mutual expectation, so no compound is formed. This is to be inferred in all such cases. For connection, which is characterized by mutual expectation, prevents what is unconnected from arising from another connection and establishes it in a specific one. And thus it is said—

Tassa tvākaṅkhato bhede, yā pariplavamānatā;

Visese taṃ nivesento, sambandhovāvachindatīti.

For one desiring a distinction for that word, whatever fluctuation there is, the connection, establishing it in a specific meaning, cuts it off from others.

Bhede visese gāmantetaṃ sāmaññaṃ visesāpekkhaṃ ‘gāmamāsīsati, jahāti, gato’ti, tathā ‘gato gāmaṃ, vanaṃ, gurukula’nti vevamākaṅkhato-bhilasato tassa tu padhānapadassupasajjanapadassa ca yā pariplavamānatā anavaṭṭhitatā taṃ visese visiṭṭhe sambandhini nivesento patiṭṭhapento sambandhovānekappakāro kvaci sādhyasādhanabhāvalakkhaṇo kvaci pakativikārabhāvasabhāvo kvaci sassāmi sambandharūpo avachindati sambandhyantarato nivattetīti attho, yato-yamapekkhā vākyakāleyeva nirūpyate, tato yatthātthi padānamapekkhā, tattha samāsāvagamo, yatra tu natthi, tatra na bhavatītyanupadiṭṭho visayavibhāgo ñāyateti bhāvo, bāle abudhetu nissāya vicitto samāsavidhānalopādinānekappakāro paṭipattiyā sādhusaddaparijānanatthamupāyo sambhavati, paramatthato tu saddantarattā accantaṃ aññattaṃ vākyasamāsānaṃ bhedo, na hi vākye diṭṭhapadāni samāse santi, tathā ca vuttaṃ–

In making a distinction, the general term 'gāmaṃ' is dependent on a specific, as in: 'he desires the village,' 'he leaves it,' 'he has gone to it.' Similarly, 'he has gone to the village, the forest, the teacher's house.' Thus, for one who desires this, the connection—establishing that fluidity and instability of both the primary word and the subordinate word in a specific, distinct relatum—cuts it off, turning it away from another connection. This is the meaning. The connection is of various kinds: sometimes characterized by the relation of goal and means, sometimes by the nature of the relation between original and modification, sometimes in the form of the relation between owned and owner. Since this expectancy is determined only at the time of the sentence, the sense is that where there is expectancy between words, a compound is understood to occur; but where there is not, it does not. This unstated division of scope is to be known. For the sake of the foolish and ignorant, this varied means for practice—with its many types, such as rules for compounding, elision, and so on—exists for the correct understanding of words. In the ultimate sense, however, because they are different words, the distinction between sentences and compounds is absolute, for the words seen in a sentence are not present in a compound. And thus it is said—

Bāle nissāyupāyo-yaṃ, vicitto paṭipattiyā;

Bhedo vākyasamāsānaṃ, ccantaṃ ññattaṃ (potthake) saddantaraṃ yatoti.

This is a varied means for practice for the sake of the foolish; the distinction between sentences and compounds is absolute, because they are different words.

Atoyevāti [M 0.0145] yato sāmaññena vuttepiyassayena sambandhotena saha tadekatthambhavatīti sambandhato viññāyatīti nāniṭṭhaṃ kiñcipīha hoti, atoyeva hetutoti attho. Byapekkhā sāmatthiyapariggahāyeti padānamaññoññākaṅkhā byapekkhā, sāva sā matthiyaṃ, tassa pariggahāya. Samatthavacanaṃ na katanti pāṇiniyehi viya “samattho padavidhī”ti (pā, 2-1-1) samatthavacanaṃ na kataṃ. Samattho pada vidhīti paribhāsāyamayamattho “vidhīyate vidhīyatīti (potthake) vidhi, padānaṃ vidhi padavidhisamāsādi, yokocīha satthe padavidhi,so samattho viggaha vākyatthābhidhāne (satti) veditabbo”ti, tādisaparibhāsāya byāpārato tesaṃ ‘passa devadatta gāmaṃ, gato yaññadatto gurukulaṃ’ tyādo nāniṭṭhappatti, sāmatthiyañcettha dvidhātyupagamyate vākye byapekkhāvuttiyamekatthībhāvo ceti vuttiyamekatthībhāvo vākye byapekkhāceti (potthake). Tattha paṭhamassa pariggahaṃ vacanamantarena paṭipādiya dutiyassa pariggahamidāni vacanena paṭipādayamāha- ‘ekatthī bhāvo’ccādi, ekatthībhāvo bhinnatthānaṃ sādhāraṇatthatāvasena pavattiviseso, vākye hi sādhāraṇatthatā natthi bhinnatthattā, atoyevettha bhedanibandhanā chaṭṭhyupajāyate ‘rañño puriso’ti, vuttiyantūbhayapadabyavacchinnatthābhidhānato sādhāraṇatthatā bhavati, idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti “samāse visesanaṃ visessamanupavīsati ekībhavati visesanaṃ, vākye tu visesanaṃ visessato visuṃyevā vatiṭṭhate”ti. Dvandasamāsassa tu padānaṃ visesanavisessābhāvepi sakalapadatthappadhānattā ‘rañño go ca asso ca puriso cā’ti vākyato ‘rañño gavāssa purisā’ti samāsassa viseso ekatthī bhāvalakkhaṇo bhavatyeva, tathāhi tattha vākye bhinnatthanibandhana samuccayapaṭipādanāya casaddo payujjate, samāse tu nappayujjate, ekattha vacanenevāti “syādisyādinekattha” tyekatthavacaneneva, ekattībhāvoyeva bhavatīti seso, evakāro na vākye tathāhi dīpeti. Vākye kathanti āha- vākye’tiādi.

By 'Atoyeva' is meant: because, even when something is spoken generally, it becomes one in meaning with that with which it has a connection of purpose, it is understood from the connection; thus, nothing unintended occurs here. Therefore, the meaning is 'due to a cause.' 'Byapekkhā sāmatthiyapariggahāya' means: the mutual expectancy (aññoññākaṅkhā) of words is 'byapekkhā'; that itself is capability (sāmatthiya), and this is for the grasping of that. 'Samatthavacanaṃ na kataṃ' means: a statement of capability is not made, just as by the Pāṇinians, a statement of capability such as 'samattho padavidhī' (Pā. 2.1.1) is not made. The meaning of this maxim, 'samattho padavidhī,' is: 'vidhi' is that which is prescribed; 'padavidhi' is a rule concerning words, such as compounding. Whatever rule concerning words is in this treatise, that is to be understood as capable (samattho) of expressing the meaning of the analytical sentence (viggahavākya). Due to the operation of such a maxim, for them, an unintended result does not occur in cases like 'passa devadatta gāmaṃ, gato yaññadatto gurukulaṃ.' And capability (sāmatthiya) is accepted here in two ways: mutual expectancy (byapekkhā) in a sentence, and unity of meaning (ekatthībhāvo) in a compound. Therein, having established the grasping of the first without a statement, he now establishes the grasping of the second with a statement, saying: 'ekatthībhāvo,' etc. Unity of meaning is a particular mode of operation whereby things of different meanings proceed by way of a common meaning. For in a sentence, there is no commonality of meaning due to the distinctness of meanings; for this very reason, the sixth case ending, founded on difference, arises here, as in 'rañño puriso.' In a compound, however, a commonality of meaning occurs because it expresses a meaning defined by both words. This is what is said: 'In a compound, the qualifier enters into the qualified; the qualifier becomes one. But in a sentence, the qualifier remains quite distinct from the qualified.' In the case of a dvandva compound, however, even though there is no qualifier-qualified relationship between the words, because the meaning of all the words is primary, the compound 'rañño gavāssapurisā' certainly has the characteristic of unity of meaning, which is a distinction from the sentence 'rañño go ca asso ca puriso ca.' For in that sentence, the word 'ca' is used to indicate the collection based on distinct meanings, but in the compound, it is not used. It is by the single expression of meaning, as in 'syādisyādinekattha,' that unity of meaning occurs—this is the remainder. The particle 'eva' indicates that it is not so in a sentence. As to how it is in a sentence, he says: 'vākye,' etc.

Vākyeti viggahavākye, visesena gayhati ñāyatyaneneti vigga- ho[M 0.0146], so ca taṃ vākyaṃ ceti viggahavākyaṃ, visesena vā gahaṇaṃ viggaho, tadatthaṃ vākyaṃ viggahavākyaṃ, tasmiṃ, kāyaṃ byāpekkhāti āha-‘bhedādilakkhaṇā’ti, ādisaddena saṃsagga bheda saṃsaggānañca gahaṇaṃ.

By 'vākye' is meant 'in a viggahavākya' (analytical sentence). 'Viggaha' is that by which something is particularly grasped (gayhati) or known (ñāyati). That which is both a viggaha and a sentence is a 'viggahavākya'. Or, 'viggaha' is the particular grasping, and a sentence for that purpose is a 'viggahavākya'. In that, what is the mutual expectancy? He says: 'characterized by distinction, etc.' By the word 'etc.' (ādi), connection (saṃsagga), and both distinction (bheda) and connection (saṃsagga) are grasped.

Tattha sāntarehi sāmyantarehi ca byāvutti chedo, saṃvisesa sāmivisesānaṃ sambandho saṃsaggo, tadāha- ‘tathāhi’ccādinā, bhedako byāvattako, atthagahitoti kāraṇavasena bhedavādinā gahito, yadeccādinā saṃsaggavādino-dhippāyamāha yadā tūbhayampiccādinā ubhayavādino, abhimatoti “pākkaḍārāsamāso”ccanena (2-1-3) pāṇininā icchito. Pākkaḍārāti “kaḍārā kammadhāraye”ccanena (2-2-38) kaḍārāsaṃsaddanā pagevāti attho.

Therein, distinction (byāvutti) is severance (chedo) by means of difference (sāntarehi) and by means of sameness-and-difference (sāmyantarehi). Connection (saṃsagga) is the relation (sambandho) of the qualified and the qualifier, of the owner and the property. This he states, beginning with 'tathāhi.' The divider (bhedako) is the distinguisher (byāvattako). 'Atthagahito' means: grasped by the proponent of distinction by way of reason. Beginning with 'yadā,' he states the intention of the proponent of connection (saṃsaggavādino). Beginning with 'yadā tu ubhayam,' he states the intention of the proponent of both (ubhayavādino). 'Abhimato' means: intended by Pāṇini through the rule 'pākkaḍārāsamāso' (cf. Pā. 2.1.3). 'Pākkaḍārā' means: 'before' (pāg eva) the word 'kaḍārā' in the rule 'kaḍārā kammadhāraye' (Pā. 2.2.38).

‘Putha bhinno attho yesaṃ padānaṃ tāni puthagatthāni, vākye hi rañño puriso tettha rājasaddo rājatthameva vadati, purisasaddo purisatthameva, vuttiyantu rājapurisotettha rājasaddopi purisatthameva vadatīti dvinnamekatthībhāvo bhavati, aññoyevāvayavatthānvito samudāyattho pātubhavatīti tadapekkhāya cekatthībhāvo vuccate, jahamānasakatthavuttimabhyupagamma vuttaṃ- ‘visesanassa sakattha pariccāgene’ccādi, atoyeva paro codessati ‘nanu ce’ccādinā. Ekatthībhavanaṃ samasananti iminā ekatthanti samāsoti nātthantaranti dīpeti.

'Puthagatthāni' means: those words whose meanings (attho) are distinct (putha bhinno). For in the sentence 'rañño puriso,' the word 'rāja' expresses only the meaning of 'king,' and the word 'purisa' expresses only the meaning of 'man.' But in the compound 'rājapuriso,' even the word 'rāja' expresses the meaning of 'purisa'; thus there is a becoming one of two meanings. And a different collective meaning, connected with the meaning of the constituent parts, arises; and in relation to that, 'unity of meaning' is spoken of. Accepting the view of a compound in which the words abandon their own meaning, it was said: 'by the qualifier's relinquishing of its own meaning,' etc. For this very reason, another will object, beginning with 'nanu ce,' etc. By the statement 'Becoming one in meaning is compounding,' he shows that 'ekattha' (single meaning) is 'samāsa' (compound), and that there is no difference in meaning.

Jahamānāni padāni sakatthaṃ yassaṃ (sā) tathā vuttā, nāccantāya jayātīti evammaññate “pariccāgamattamabhisandhāya jahamānasakatthaṃtyuccate, na tu sabbathā pariccāgoparopakārāya tassopādānato, sabbathā ca sakatthapariccāge paropakārāsampādanato-nupādānameva payojanābhāvā tassa siyā”ti, thapati vaḍḍhatī. Atthanti rājasaddavāccaṃ. Accantapariccāgepi na doso… vākye diṭṭhassupasajjanassa vuttiyaṃ soyevāyantyanvayāvasāyato tadatthāva gatiyāti dassento āha- ‘atha ve’ccādi.

That (compound) in which the words abandon their own meaning is so called. It is understood thus: it does not abandon it completely. 'It is called "abandoning its own meaning" with the intention of mere relinquishment, not complete relinquishment, because it is employed for the benefit of another. And if there were a complete relinquishment of its own meaning without accomplishing the benefit for the other, then it would not be employed at all, as it would have no purpose.' The carpenter prospers. 'Meaning' refers to that which is expressed by the word 'rāja'. Even in complete relinquishment, there is no fault. To show that the understanding is of that very meaning of the subordinate term seen in the sentence, because of the determination of the connection 'this is that very same one' in the compound, he says: 'atha vā,' etc.

Soyevāyantyajjhavasāyo-nvayo, soyevāyaṃ rājasaddo yo vākyatāle diṭṭhoti vohārīnamekattāvasāyenāsatyapi (rājasaddassa)tthe [M 0.0147] purisassa visesanambhavissatīti bhāvo, ettheva diṭṭhantamāha- ‘yathe’ccādi.

The connection (anvayo) is the determination (ajjhavasāyo) that 'this is that very same one.' The idea (bhāvo) is that 'this is the very same word "rāja" that was seen in the context of the sentence'; thus, by the determination of oneness on the part of the speakers, even if there is no meaning of the word 'rāja', it will become a qualifier for the man (purisa). Here itself, he gives an illustration: 'yathā,' etc.

2. Asaṃ

2. Regarding the innumerable.

Abyayanti yadaññesaṃ pasiddhanti liṅgavacanabhedepi byayarahitattā upasagganipātānaṃ parehi abyayasaññākaraṇato abyayanti paresaṃ pasiddhaṃ, tesantvayaṃ samāso abyayatthapubbaṅgamattā anabyayaṃ abyayambhavatīti abyayībhāvo pasiddho, asaṅkhyassa sutattā tasseva vibhatyatthādayo visayabhāvena visesanānīti viññāyantītyāha- ‘asaṅkhye’ccādi, iminā nemesamāsatthāti dīpeti.

'Abyaya' is that which is known to others as such. Because prefixes and particles are without change (byaya) despite differences in gender and number, the term 'abyaya' (indeclinable) is made for them by others. For them, this compound, merely because it is preceded by the meaning of an indeclinable, is known as 'abyayībhāva', in which a non-indeclinable becomes an indeclinable. Because 'asaṅkhya' is stated, the meanings of the case endings and so forth of that very word are understood as its qualifiers, having it as their domain. Thus he says: 'asaṅkhye,' etc. By this, he indicates the meaning of this compound.

Tāvasaddassa kamavuttiyaṃ yo-ttho sampajjate tamāha- ‘vibhatya’ccādi, vibhatyatthe udāharitvāti vibhatyatthavisaye vattamānassāsaṅkhyassa itthisaddena samāsamadhitthīti uvāharitvā, niccayamāsāna maviggaho, asakapadaviggaho vā yutto, aññathā aniccatāpattītyāha- ‘niccasamāsattā’iccādi.

He states the meaning that results for that word in the compound, beginning with 'vibhatti,' etc. 'Vibhatyatthe udāharitvā' means: having cited 'adhitthī' as the compound of 'asaṅkhya'—which is current in the domain of the meaning of a case ending—with the word 'itthi'. For permanent compounds, non-resolution or resolution by non-constituent words is appropriate; otherwise, the fault of non-permanence would occur. Thus he says: 'niccasamāsattā,' etc.

Asakapadena anattaniyapadena aññapadena viggaho asakapadaviggaho, tena, ettha hi yathā kumbhassa samīpaṃtyaññapadavākye samīpa saddenupasaddavacanīyassa vuttattā upasaddo nappayujjate, yathā itthī sūti etthādhisaddavacanīyassā (dhā)ratthassa sattamiyā vuttattā nādhisaddoti ‘itthīsū’ti aññapadavākyaṃ vuttaṃ, kathāpavattāti tvādheyyo padassanaṃ, evaṃ sabbatthonneyaṃ, asakapadaviggahenātthova vutto,

'Asakapadaviggaho' is an analysis (viggaho) with a non-constituent word (asakapadena), that is, with a word not its own (anattaniyapadena), with another word (aññapadena). By that, here, just as in the analytical sentence with another word, 'kumbhassa samīpaṃ,' since the meaning to be expressed by the word 'upa' is expressed by the word 'samīpa,' the word 'upa' is not used. Just as here, in 'itthīsu,' since the meaning of location (ādhāra), which is to be expressed by the word 'adhi,' is expressed by the seventh case ending, the word 'adhi' is not used; thus, 'itthīsu' is stated as the analytical sentence with another word. The phrase 'kathā pavattā' is an indication of the content (ādheyya). In this way, it should be inferred everywhere. By an analysis with non-constituent words, only the meaning is stated.

Adhisaddassa pana puratovaṭṭhitassādhāre vattamānassa taṃsamānādhikaraṇena sattamyantenitthisaddena saha samāsoti dassetumāha-‘adhisaddo’ccādi.

But to show that there is a compound of the word 'adhi'—which was previously established and is current in the sense of location (ādhāra)—with the word 'itthi' which ends in the seventh case ending and is in apposition with it, he says: 'adhisaddo,' etc.

Syādilopoti adhisaddato itthisaddato ca paresaṃ sattamī bahuvacanānaṃ lopoti attho. Atta (bhāva) sampattīti sarīrasampatti adhippetāti brahmasaddassa sarīraṃ atthoti āha- ‘brahmaṃ sarīranti, katthacī uttarapadatthappadhānattāvāsaṅkhyasamāsassa ‘sampannaṃ brahma’nti viggaho vutto.

'Syādilopo' means the elision of the seventh case plural endings that come after the word 'adhi' and the word 'itthi'. 'Atta(bhāva)sampatti' is intended as bodily accomplishment; thus, it is said that the word 'brahma' has the meaning 'body'—'brahmaṃ sarīraṃ'. In some places, because the meaning of the latter word is prominent, the resolution of the asaṅkhya compound is stated as 'sampannaṃ brahma'.

Samāsavibhattiyāti [M 0.0148] samāsato uppannavibhattiyā, sakalo padesasakalo, pariggahāpekkhāti abhyupagamāpekkhāyāti attho, abhyupagamepi hi pariggahasaddo–

'By the compound's case ending' means by the case ending arisen from the compound. 'Sakalo' means a whole in respect of a part. 'Pariggahāpekkhā' means with expectation of acceptance, for the word 'pariggaha' is also used in the sense of acceptance—

Sapathe parivāre ca, mūlābhyupagamesu ca;

Ravimhi rāhugahite, dāresu ca pariggaho”ti nighaṇṭu.

In oaths, in one's retinue, and in undertaking basic principles; when the sun is seized by Rāhu, and in the acquisition of wives—thus the glossary.

Sakalassa bhāvo sākalyaṃ-sakalasaddappavattinimittaṃ, tampana nissesa matanissesa (potthake) ggahaṇā puthu bhavatītyāha- ‘asesaggahaṇa’nti, tiṇānaṃ sākalyanti viggaho, tiṇasaddena hi tiṇasahitāni gahitāni, teneva vakkhati byatirekanaye- ‘taṃ sabbaṃ tiṇasahitamajjho- haratī’ti, satiṇamajjhoharatītetthādhippāyattha māha-‘yāvā’tiādi.

The state of being whole is 'sākalya'—the ground for the application of the word 'sakala'. However, this is distinct from grasping entirely; he says it is 'grasping without remainder'. The resolution is 'the completeness of the grass'; for by the word 'grass', things accompanied by grass are grasped. For that reason, it will be said in the method of exclusion: 'He consumes all that is accompanied by grass.' To show the intended meaning here in 'he consumes it with the grass', he said 'yāvā', etc.

Tiṇasaddo upalakkhaṇaṃ sesā-najjhohāriyānaṃ, tenāha ‘tiṇādikampī’ti. Pariggahāpekkhāyantabhūtassa gahaṇatthaṃ “abyayaṃ vibhattisamīpā”disutte ‘sāgyadhīte’ti nipphādanatthamantavacana mudāhatampāṇininā, tampi sākalyeyevāharituṃ sākallenodāharituṃ sāgyadhītetyūdāhaṭanti dassetuṃ ‘tato’tyādi vuttaṃ.

The word 'tiṇa' is illustrative of the rest of the things not to be consumed; hence it is said 'tiṇādikampi'. For the purpose of grasping what is included at the limit with the expectation of inclusion, Pāṇini, in the rule 'abyayaṃ vibhattisamīpā', etc., cited 'sāgyadhīte' for the formation of a word denoting a limit. And to show that this 'sāgyadhīte' is cited to convey completeness, 'tato', etc., is stated.

Tatoti yato sakalasakale na vattati, pariggahāpekkhāya samattiyā antato sakāsā sākalyaṃ na bhijjateti sambandho, samatthiyampi ante udāharaṇanti seso.

'Tato' means: because 'sakala' does not apply to the whole in its entirety, the connection is that completeness is not broken from its own limit, due to the completion with respect to the expectation of inclusion. The rest is an example of capability even at the limit.

Aggipariyantanti aggiattho gantho tādatthiyā aggi, sopariyanto-ssa ajjheyassāti aggipariyantaṃ, yattakassājjheyassa pariggaho, tassa aggi pariyanto, agginā pariyantabhūtena sahito sakaloti viggaho, aggino sākalyanti vā.

'Aggipariyantaṃ' means a text whose subject is fire, or fire for that purpose. That is the limit of what is to be studied, hence 'aggipariyantaṃ'. Whatever extent of what is to be studied is included, fire is its limit. The resolution is 'the whole together with fire as the boundary', or 'the completeness of fire'.

Saddikānanti byākaraṇaññūnaṃ. Atthābhāveityatthaggahaṇaṃ itaretarābhāve dhammābhāve ca mā siyāti, atoyeva coccate ‘athetaretarābhāve’iccādi, itarasmiṃ itarassa abhāvo itaretarābhāvo, go asso na bhavatīti hi atthantarattaṃ nisedhīyate, na vatthubhāvo, brāhmaṇo na bhavatītyatrapibrāhmaṇattadhammo [M 0.0149] nisedhīyate, na vatthubhāvo, parattātiādinā vippaṭisedha visayamāha.

'Saddikānaṃ' means of those who know grammar. In 'in the absence of meaning', the inclusion of 'meaning' is so that it may not be understood as mutual absence or the absence of a property. Therefore, it is said: 'Now, in mutual absence,' etc. The absence of one in another is mutual absence. For in 'a cow is not a horse', the identity is negated, not the existence of the object. Similarly, in 'is not a brahmin', the property of brahmin-ness is negated, not the existence of the object. By 'parattā', etc., he states the object of contradiction.

Atikkamābhāvetī ettha atikkamāti pañcamiyā asamāsaniddesoti āha- ‘atikkamā’ti, na panuppannassa pacchāti iminā atikkamābhāvo nāma uppannassa pacchā abhāvoti dasseti.

In 'atikkamābhāve', here 'atikkamā' is an uncompounded indication in the ablative case; thus he says 'atikkamā'. And by 'not after it has arisen', he shows that 'atikkamābhāva' means the absence of something after it has arisen.

Nittiṇanti uttarapadatthappadhāno-saṅkhyasamāso. Sampatisaddassa sāmaññavacanattepi idhādhippetaṃ kālaṃ dassetumāha- ‘upabhogasse”ccādi, upabhogo kammasādhano lahupāvuraṇassa nāyamupabhogakāloti viggaho, (ati) lahupāvuraṇanti rūpasiddhīti dassetuṃ lahupāvuraṇassātiādi vuttiyaṃ vuttaṃ.

'Nittiṇaṃ' is an asaṅkhya compound where the meaning of the latter word is prominent. Although the word 'sampati' has a general meaning, to show the time intended here, he says 'for enjoyment,' etc. The resolution is: 'enjoyment' is instrumental to the action; this is not the time for enjoyment of a light covering. To show that '(ati)lahupāvuraṇaṃ' is the correct formation of the word, 'lahupāvuraṇassa', etc., is stated in the commentary.

Yoggaṃ rūpanti viggahe anurūpaṃ, nanu cātra niccasamāsattāsapadaviggahena bhavitabbaṃtyāsaṅkiyāha-‘vicchāya’miccādi, anusaddena hi yoge vicchāyaṃ “anunā”ti (2-10) dutiyā vidhīyate, vākyeyevāssa ca payogo nāññatreti vākyampi bhavatīti maññate. Sakikhīti etthāpi “akāle sakatthe”ti (3-81) sahassa so.

In the resolution 'yoggaṃ rūpaṃ', the result is 'anurūpaṃ'. Anticipating the doubt, 'But shouldn't there be a resolution here with non-constituent words, since it is an obligatory compound?', he says: 'vicchāyaṃ', etc. For in connection with the word 'anu', the second case ending is prescribed by 'anunā' (2-10) in the sense of 'vicchāyaṃ'. And since its application is only in a sentence and not elsewhere, it is thought that a sentence is also possible. Here also in 'sakikhī', 'sa' is the substitute for 'saha' by the rule 'akāle sakatthe' (3-81).

Sadiso kikhiyāti ettha kikhiyā pasiddhabhūtāya sādhiyassa sādhanabhāvena gahitāya sadhammattena koci sādhiyo sadisoti vuttoti kimidha sadiso appadhānaṃ padhānamevāti attho tathā sati puppapadatthappadhānenāsaṅkhyasamāsena sakikhīti ettha na bhavitabbanti āha-‘nanuce’tyādi, kikhiyāti sambandhe chaṭṭhī, ettha pana sadisattassa kikhīyā-ppaṭibaddhattāppadhānattaṃ. Netadatthītiādinā yathāvuttaṃ codanaṃ pariharati.

Here in 'sadiso kikhiyā', since 'kikhiyā', being well-known, is taken as the means of proving that which is to be proven, it is said that something to be proven is 'similar' by virtue of a common property. Why then is 'sadisa' not prominent here? If that were so, 'sakikhī' would not be possible here through an asaṅkhya compound where the meaning of the former word is prominent. He says: 'nanu ce', etc. 'Kikhiyā' is in the sixth case in the sense of relation. But here, the state of being similar is not prominent because it is dependent on 'kikhiyā'. By 'na etad atthi', etc., he refutes the objection as stated.

Yathā devadattoti ettha yadi samāso bhaveyya, devadattena sadiso yathādevadattanti bhaveyya, paṭisiddhattā pana (na) samāsoti, kikhīti makkaṭassābhidhānaṃ. Jeṭṭhānukkamenāti vuttattā anujeṭṭhanti tatiyantatā gamyate. Cakkena yugapadi sacakkaṃ.

As in 'yathā devadatto': here, if there were a compound, it would be 'yathādevadattaṃ' from 'devadattena sadiso'. But because it is prohibited, there is no compound. 'Kikhī' is a name for a monkey. Because 'in order of seniority' is stated, for 'anujeṭṭhaṃ' an instrumental case ending is understood. 'Cakkena yugapad' becomes 'sacakkaṃ'.

4. Yāvāvadhāraṇe

4. Yāva in the sense of limitation.

Amattānaṃ yattako paricchedo yāvāmattaṃ.

Whatever is the measure of the unmeasured things becomes 'yāvāmattaṃ'.

5. Payyapābahitiro purepacchāvāpañcamyā

5. Pari, apa, bahi, tiro, pure, and pacchā optionally with a word in the fifth case.

Pañcamyāti [M 0.0150] kasmā vuttaṃ nanu avuttepi tasmiṃ vakkhamānanayena pañcamyantattā pañcamyanteheva samāso viññāyatītyāsaṅkiyāha‘yadipi’ccādi. Tathāpiccādinā pariharati, hotu kāmaṃ ‘paripabbataṃ vijjotate’ti dutiyānisedhāya, aññatra kathanti āha ‘iha ce’tyādi.

Why is 'pañcamyā' stated? Anticipating the doubt, 'Is it not so that even if it were unstated, by the method to be explained, the compound would be known to be with a word ending in the fifth case, because it ends in the fifth case?', he says 'yadipi', etc. He refutes this with 'tathāpi', etc. Let it be so for the sake of prohibiting the second case in 'paripabbataṃ vijjotate'; but how is it elsewhere? He says 'iha ce', etc.

Ācattāro vāti āsaddo vākye, saraṇe vā, gāmo bahi tiṭṭhatītyattho, purato gāmampassāti vadanto puretyatthappaghānoyanniddeso, nasarūpappadhānoti dasseti, abhimukhe gāmampassātyattho. Avuttānametānyupalakkhaṇāni, tasmā ‘tiro gāmampassā’tipi vuttaṃ hoti, tiriyato gāmampassa, pacchato gāmampassāti attho.

The word 'ā' is used in a sentence, or in recollection. The meaning is 'the village stands outside'. One who says 'purato gāmaṃ passa' shows that this is an instruction where the meaning of 'pure' is prominent, not the form itself. The meaning is 'see the village in front'. These are illustrations of the unstated. Therefore, 'tiro gāmaṃ passa' is also said. The meaning is 'see the village from the side', 'see the village from behind'.

Apasaddayoge niccapañcantassa vikappena samāsavidhānāvābhavanenodāharaṇaṃ dinnaṃ (ettha) pañcamyāti payojanābhāvepi aññadatthaṃ kariyamānamihāpyatthavantaṃ hoti.

In connection with the word 'apa', an example is given of the optional non-compounding of that which always ends in the fifth case. Here, 'pañcamyā', although having no purpose in itself, being employed for another purpose, becomes meaningful here also.

6. Samī

6. In the sense of proximity.

“Anu yaṃ samayā”ti (2-1-15) ca “yassa cāyāmo”ti (2-1-16) ca pāṇinino vacanadvayaṃ, ayametesamattho “yassa samayā samīpavācī anusaddo, tena saha samassateti ca, anu yassāyāmavācī, tena syādyantena saha samassate”ti ca. Vatthuto tu sāmīpyāyāmavantānamaniddesepi sāmatthiyā tadākkhepoti dassento āha-‘samīpāyāmāna’miccādi.

'Anu yaṃ samayā' and 'yassa cāyāmo' are two statements of Pāṇini. This is their meaning: 'The word 'anu', when it denotes proximity to something, compounds with it; and when 'anu' denotes the length of something, it compounds with that word ending in a case marker.' But in reality, showing that even without the specification of the things possessing proximity and length, they are implied by capability, he says 'samīpāyāmānaṃ', etc.

Sambandhittāti sambandhisaddā sakatthamiva niyatapaṭiyoginamākkhapanti… tena vinā tesaṃ sakatthābhāvā. Āyāmo dīghatā, “yassa samīpāyāmesvanu”ti yathāvuttasuttadvayamākkhepenupadisati, vanassa sāmipyamanuvanaṃ, “asaṅkhyaṃ vibhattisampattisamīpa” icceva (3-2) siddhepuna samīpaggahaṇaṃ vikappatthaṃ, tena vanassānuti vākyenāpi bhavitabbaṃ.

'Sambandhittā' means that relational words, like their own meaning, indicate a fixed correlative, because without it, their own meaning would not exist. 'Āyāmo' is length. He teaches by implying the two previously mentioned suttas with 'yassa samīpāyāmesu anu'. 'Vanassa sāmipyaṃ' is 'anuvanaṃ'. Although this is already established by 'asaṅkhyaṃ vibhattisampattisamīpa...' (3-2), the inclusion of 'samīpa' again is for the sake of making it optional. Therefore, it can also be expressed by the sentence 'vanassa anu'.

Gaṅgāya [M 0.0151] āyāmo anugaṅgaṃ, bhāgavuttikāro “lakkhaṇene”ti vattate. Yassāyāmavācī anu, tena lakkhaṇena samassate anugaṅgaṃ bārāṇasī, gaṅgāya lakkhaṇabhūtāya pasiddhāyāmaguṇāya bārāṇasī lakkhīyate yāvāyatāyāmā gaṅgā tāvāyampīti sabhāvato tūpamānopameyyabhāvo samāse patīyate gaṅgā viya dīghā”ti lakkhiyalakkhaṇabhāvaṃ vaṇṇeti. Evaṃ sati bārāṇasīti paṭhamā nopapajjateti maññamāno āha-‘gaṅgāyā mena yuttā “tyādi. Anugaṅgaṃ bārāṇasiyāti bārāṇasiyā gaṅgāyāmo lakkhaṇanti attho.

The length of the Ganges is 'anugaṅgaṃ'. The commentator on the parts states: 'by means of a characteristic.' When 'anu' denotes length, it is compounded by that characteristic, as in 'anugaṅgaṃ bārāṇasī' (Varanasi along the Ganges). Varanasi is characterized by the Ganges, which is a characteristic renowned for its quality of length, meaning 'as long as the Ganges extends, so long does this city extend.' By its nature, a relationship between the standard of comparison and the object of comparison is understood in the compound, describing the relationship between the characteristic and the characterized, as in 'long like the Ganges.' Thinking that, this being the case, the nominative 'Bārāṇasī' is not suitable, he says: 'not connected with the Ganges,' and so on. 'Anugaṅgaṃ bārāṇasiyā' means that the length of the Ganges is the characteristic of Varanasi.

7. Tiṭṭha

7. Stand.

Akatasamāsācāti anena iminā katasamāsataṃ dīpeti, tiṭṭhantīti idaṃntappaccayantassātthapadanti dassetumāha-“ntokattari vattamāne”ticcādi, (5-64) āyatītīmassāttapadaṃ āyantīti, pumbhāvābhāvo nīpātanā, akāro ca nipātanā “gotva catthe cā lope”tyatra (3-46) ‘nāññāsaṅkhyatthesū’tyanuvattanato.

By 'akatasamāsā' (uncompounded), he indicates that these are not compounded. To show that 'tiṭṭhanti' (standing) is a word ending in the suffix '-nta' in the sense of an agent, he says 'the suffix -nta is in the agent in the present tense' and so on (5-64). The agentive form of 'āyati' (comes) is 'āyanti'. The absence of the masculine form is by irregular formation. And the 'a' vowel is also by irregular formation, as in 'gotva catthe cā lope' (3-46), due to the continuation of the rule 'not in the sense of another or number'.

Lūnayavādīnamettha nipātanā kālepi napuṃsakaliṅgattaṃ, saṃhaṭāyavā yasmiṃ kāle saṃhaṭayavaṃ, ummattagaṅganti saññāyamaññapadatthe vādhikārepi niccasamāso, na hi vākyaṃ saññāti, ādisaddena‘samassa sobhanattaṃ susama’miccādīnañca saṅgaho, pabhāvanaṃ pakāsanaṃ.

Here, for 'lūnayava' (reaped barley) and so on, even in the sense of time, the neuter gender is by irregular formation. 'Saṃhaṭayavaṃ' (heaped barley) refers to the time when the barley is heaped. 'Ummattagaṅgaṃ' (the maddened Ganges) is an obligatory compound even when it is a designation or in the sense of another word, for a sentence is not a designation. And by the word 'ādi' (etc.) is included 'susama' (very well-balanced), meaning 'the beauty of a compound,' and so on. 'Pabhāvanaṃ' means 'making manifest'.

8. Ore

8. On this side.

Oraṃ gaṅgāya, pāraṃ yamunāyāti samāse kate nipātanā ekāro, teneva vuttiyaṃ vuttaṃ ‘ekārantattaṃ nipātanato’ti, vuttivikappanatthatoti vuttiyā vikappo attho yassāti viggaho.

In 'oraṃ gaṅgāya' (on this side of the Ganges), 'pāraṃ yamunāya' (on the far side of the Yamuna), when the compound is formed, the vowel 'e' is by irregular formation. For this very reason, it is stated in the commentary: 'The state of ending in 'e' is from irregular formation.' The analysis of 'vuttivikappanatthato' (for the purpose of an alternative explanation) is 'vuttiyā vikappo attho yassa,' meaning 'that whose purpose is an alternative to the commentary'.

10. Amā

10. Amā (an indeclinable).

Socekatthībhāvo visiṭṭho-bhimatoti sambandho, muhuttanti accantasaṃyoge dutiyā, pādisamāsaṃ katvāti āsaddassa harasaddena vuttisaddena vuttipadena (pañcikā) kiriyākhyāpyateti asatyupasecanādikiriyāyaṃ [M 0.0152] saṅkhārakaṃ saṅkhāriyaṃ vā na bhavati, atthiceha tadubhayaṃ, tato tesaṃ sambhavāyeva samāsantobhūtakiriyā gamyateti maññate, tathāhi dadhibhojanaṃtyādo vutte adhyādino saṅkhārakattaṃ bhojanādino ca saṅkhāriyattaṃ patīyate, na copasekādimantarena saṅkhāriyasaṅkhārakabhāvo-tthīti sāmatthiyāyevupasekādippatīti.

The connection is that the state of being a single meaning is specifically intended. 'Muhuttaṃ' (for a moment) is in the accusative case in the sense of continuous connection. Having made a compound like 'pādi', it is explained that the action is expressed by the word 'āsa' (eating) or 'hara' (taking) or 'vutti' (usage). If there is no action like sprinkling, etc., then there is no conditioner or conditioned. Here, both exist; therefore, it is thought that the action inherent in the compound is understood simply from their possibility. For example, when 'dadhibhojanaṃ' (eating curd) is said, the state of curd, etc., as conditioner and the state of eating, etc., as conditioned are perceived. And the relationship of conditioned and conditioner does not exist without sprinkling and so on; thus, sprinkling and so on are understood through capability alone.

Tadapekkhāyāti gammamānopasecanādikiriyāpekkhāya. Pāṇiniyehi atthena ‘etassida’nti atthe niccasamāso-bhimato sabbaliṅgatā ca, tathā vacanābhāvamiha manasikatvā ‘katha’miccādinā vutti yaṃvuttaṃcodakavacanamāharitvā tatthādhippāyaṃvivarati ‘evamaññate’ccādinā, vidhānaṃ katanti evamaññateti sambandho, tattheccādinā añña padatthe bhavissatītyetthādhippāyaṃ vivaranto niccasamāsataṃ sabbaliṅgatañca paṭipādayati, vākyanivattisiddhāyevāti.

In dependence on that, meaning in dependence on the implied actions like sprinkling and so on.
