By the Pāṇinīyas, obligatory compounding and the state of having all genders are intended in the sense of 'this belongs to it' by meaning. Likewise, considering the absence of an explicit statement here, he explains the intention there by bringing forth the statement of the objector, which was stated in the commentary with 'how' and so on, saying 'thus it is understood' and so on. The connection is 'thus it is understood' that the rule is made. There, with 'and so on', explaining the intention that it will be in the sense of another word, he establishes obligatory compounding and the state of having all genders, because the cessation of the sentence is already established.

Atthasaddenāvagatatthatāya etassāti vattumayuttanti ‘etassa attho’ti vākyanivatti siddhāyeva, kathañcipi catutthyantā bhinnatthassa samāse katepi tattha virodhamāha- ‘catutthyantasse’tyādi.

Since the meaning is understood by the word 'attha', it is not appropriate to say 'etassa' (of this); rather, the cessation of the sentence 'etassa attho' (the meaning of this) is already established. Even if a compound is made with a fourth-case ending having a distinct meaning, he states a contradiction there, saying 'of the fourth-case ending' and so on.

Vacanampīti “atthena niccasamāso sabbaliṅgatāca”iti (3-1-36) vākyakārena patiṭṭhitavacanampi, pāṇinīyānaṃ ‘etassa ida’nti atthe samāse kate yo-ttho sampajjati, aññatthasamāsepi soyevatthoti dasseti ‘yo’ iccādinā, anupādāparinibbānanimittaṃ vāyāmoccādinā yojetabbaṃ… taṃnimittattā vāyāmādīnaṃ, tesaṃ kathādīnanti ettha tesaṃ vāyāmādīnanti vattabbaṃ… vāyāmotyādinā vuttattā so ca tannimittaṃ hoteva, ayametthādhippāyo “etassa idanti vākye atthena samāse sabbaliṅgatā ca ‘etadattho etadatthā etadattha’nti vāyāmādayo ca samāsatthā honti, etaṃ anupādāparinibbānamattho payojanametassa etissā etassāti aññapadatthepi esaṃ padānaṃ soyevatthoti nātthabhedo”ti.

The statement 'obligatory compounding by meaning and universality of gender' (3-1-36) is also a statement established by the sentence-maker. For the Pāṇinīyas, the meaning that arises when a compound is made in the sense of 'this belongs to it' is the same meaning even in other compounds, as shown by 'yo' (which) and so on. It should be connected with 'effort' and so on, as a sign of final Nibbāna without clinging... because effort and so on are the signs of that. Here, instead of 'their discussions' and so on, it should be said 'their effort and so on'... Since it is stated by 'effort' and so on, that too is indeed the sign of it. This is the intention here: in the sentence 'this belongs to it', when compounded by meaning, there is universality of gender, as in 'etadattho, etadatthā, etadatthaṃ' (this is its meaning/purpose), and effort and so on are the meanings of the compound. This final Nibbāna without clinging is the meaning or purpose of this (masculine), of this (feminine), of this (neuter); even in the sense of another word, these words have the same meaning, so there is no difference in meaning.

Idañca “avippaṭisāratthāni kho ānandaṃ kusalāni, avippaṭisāro pāmojjatthāya…pe… vimuttiñāṇadassanaṃ anupādāparinibbānatthāya etadattho [M 0.0153] vāyāmo etadatthā kathā etadatthā mantanā etadatthaṃ sotāvadhāna”ntiādi (tikaṅguttara, ānandavagga) pāḷiṃ nissāya vuttaṃ.

And this is said with reference to the Pāli text (Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.2, Ānandavagga): 'Ānanda, wholesome states are for the purpose of non-regret; non-regret is for the purpose of joy... for the purpose of the knowledge and vision of liberation; for the purpose of final Nibbāna without clinging. This is the purpose of effort, this is the purpose of discussion, this is the purpose of deliberation, this is the purpose of attentive listening,' and so on.

Pāṇiniyehi “kattukaraṇe kitantena bahula”nti (2-1-32) kitantena tatiyāsamāsavidhānā tattheva bahulaggahaṇena ‘gāmaniggatā’dīsu samāso vutto, tenetthāntodāharaṇānaṃ dvinnamadhikattaṃ, samāsābhāvo-bhimatoti pāṇinīyehi “pūraṇaguṇasuhitatthasadabyayatabbasamānādhikaraṇene”ti (2-2-11) sutte guṇa itivacanenābhimato, saditi saññā tesaṃ ntamānānaṃ.

By the Pāṇinīyas, from the rule for a third-case compound with a kṛt-ending, 'kattukaraṇe kitantena bahulaṃ' (2-1-32), and by the inclusion of 'bahulaṃ' (variously) therein, compounding is stated in examples like 'gāmaniggatā' (gone out of the village) and so on. Therefore, there is an excess of two examples here. The absence of compounding is intended by the Pāṇinīyas by the word 'guṇa' (quality) in the sūtra 'pūraṇaguṇasuhitatthasadabyayatabbasamānādhikaraṇena' (2-2-11). 'Sat' is a designation for those ending in '-nta' and '-māna'.

So kathanti iha ‘bhāvatittatthehī’ti bhāvappaccayanteneva samāsapaṭisedhavidhānā ‘brāhmaṇassa sukkā’ iccādo so samā sappaṭisedho kathaṃ sijjhatīti attho.

So how is it? Here, since the prohibition of compounding is ruled only for words ending in a 'bhāva'-suffix by the rule 'bhāvatittatthehi', how is that prohibition of compounding achieved in examples such as 'brāhmaṇassa sukkā' (the Brahmin's whiteness) and so on? This is the meaning.

Guṇattaniyevāti guṇasabhāve eva, abhimatoti vāttikakārassābhimato “tadavaṭṭhehi ca guṇehī”ti, tasaddenāssa guṇassa parāmāso tasmiṃyeva guṇe avatiṭṭhantīti tadavaṭṭhā, guṇeyeva guṇātiṭṭhanti na kadācipi soyamityabhedā dabbavuttayo sukkādayo viya te tadavaṭṭhā guṇā gandhādayo, tadavaṭṭhitehi guṇehi chaṭṭhī samassateti vattabbanti attho.

'In the nature of a quality itself' means precisely in the nature of a quality. 'It is intended' means it is intended by the Vārttikakāra, as in 'and by those qualities that abide in it.' By the word 'ta' (that), there is a reference to this quality; 'they abide in that very quality' is the meaning of 'tadavaṭṭhā' (abiding in that). Qualities abide in the quality itself; they are never separate, like expressions of substance such as 'white' etc., which are non-different from it. Those qualities abiding therein are smell and so on. The meaning is that it should be stated that the sixth case is compounded with those qualities abiding therein.

Ābhimatoti “pūraṇā”disutte abyayaggahaṇena, devadattassāti chaṭṭhiyā gurumhi sāpekkhattepi gurusaddassa sambandhisaddattā sakatthe vākye viya vuttiyaṃ byapekkhā-yāhānito vuttisabbhāvaṃ vacanantarena sādhetumāha- ‘tathācāhū’ti.

It is intended by the inclusion of indeclinables in the 'pūraṇā' and so on sūtra. Even though the sixth case 'devadattassa' (of Devadatta) is dependent on 'guru' (teacher), because the word 'guru' is a relational word, the expectancy is not lost in the compound expression, just as in its own meaning. To establish the existence of the compound expression here with another statement, he says: 'tathācāhu' (and so it was said).

Sātthevāti sakatthe viya, assāti sambandhisaddassa, sāmatthiyaṃ gamakattañcatthīti padānamaññoññāpekkhālakkhaṇaṃ sāmatthiyaṃ sāmatthiyābhāvepi viggahavākyatthassa gamakattaṃ vā atthīti attho, guruno kulaṃ dāsassa bhariyāti viggaho, athātra brāhmaṇassa ucce’iccādo sāmatthiyaṃ gamakattaṃ vā natthīti kuto-vasitaṃ, yena tadābhāvātra [M 0.0154] samāsābhāvo vaṇṇīyateccāha-‘sāmatthyādinotvi’ccādi.

By 'sātthevāti' is meant 'as in its own meaning.' By 'assāti' is meant 'of the relational word.' The meaning of 'sāmatthiyaṃ gamakattañca atthi' is: there exists either sāmatthiya, which is the characteristic of mutual expectation among words, or, even in the absence of sāmatthiya, there is gamakatta, the capacity to convey the meaning of the analytical phrase. The analysis is 'the family of the teacher, the wife of the slave.' But here, in 'the high of the brahmin,' etc., how is it ascertained that sāmatthiya or gamakatta does not exist, whereby the absence of a compound is described due to their absence? Thus it is said: 'sāmatthyādinotvi,' and so on.

Samāsābhāvo-bhimatoti “pūraṇā”disutte samānādhikarassāpi upādānato. Sehīti attaniyehi, nābhimatoti “cayuttehi sehi asamāsitehi chaṭṭhīsamāsappaṭisedhovattabbo” (vā) tyanena, puthagatthatāya bhinnatthatāyaṃ-vutti miccassavivaraṇaṃ gavādīnamasamāseti, evamassādīnaṃ samāsenālanti sambandho.

The absence of a compound is intended because of the inclusion of words in apposition in the sūtra beginning with 'pūraṇā,' etc. By 'sehi' is meant 'by one's own.' It is not intended, according to this statement: 'the prohibition of a genitive compound should be stated for uncompounded words connected with ca (and) and se (one's own)' (Vārttika). Due to having a separate meaning, 'gavādīnamasamāseti' is an explanation of what is incorrect; thus the connection is: enough of compounding assa, etc.

Yogīnanti itarītarayogīnaṃ, anenetaretarayogacatthasamāsaṃ vadati. Vuttihotītyassa vivaraṇaṃ chaṭṭhīsamāso bhavatīti, ekatthībhāveiccassa vivaraṇaṃ gavādīnañca catthasamāse satīti.

By 'yogīnaṃ' is meant 'of those mutually connected.' By this, it speaks of a copulative compound of mutual connection. The explanation of 'vuttihotīti' is 'it becomes a genitive compound.' The explanation of 'ekatthībhāve' is 'when there is a copulative compound of 'gavā', etc., with 'ca'.'

Ruḷhittāti samāsasseva kīḷāvācakattena jīvikāya ca paccāya kattena pasiddhattā, na vākyassāti ‘uddālapupphabhañjikā’tyādo ruḷhīvasena niccasamāso bhavissatīti tatra kiṃ vacaneneti maññate, sarasi ruḷhanti viggaho.

By 'ruḷhittā' is meant 'by established usage,' because a compound itself, and not a sentence, is well-known as expressing play and as a means of livelihood. He thinks: 'In "uddālapupphabhañjikā," etc., there will be a permanent compound by convention, so what is the need for a rule there?' The analysis is 'sarasi ruḷhanti' (they grow in a lake).

Ayampana amādisamāso kammadhārayadigusamāsāti sabbepi paresaṃ tappurisasadisattā tappurisā, yathā hi tassa puriso tappurisoti uttarapadatthappadhāno, tathā te siyuṃ, saṅkhyāpubbatta napuṃsakattasaṅkhātehi dvīhi lakkhaṇehi gacchati pavattatītidigu.

Now, this compound beginning with 'ama', and the kammadhāraya and digu compounds—all of them, according to others, are tappurisa compounds because they are similar to a tappurisa. For just as 'tassa puriso' is a tappurisa wherein the meaning of the latter member is predominant, so too would these be. That which proceeds or functions by means of two characteristics, namely, having a numeral as its first member and being in the neuter gender, is a digu.

11. Vise

11. Distinction.

Kintaṃ visesana micchāha-‘yami’ccādi, yaṃ avatthāpayati taṃ vuccatīti sambandho, kintaṃ visessamiccāha-‘yadaneke’ccādi, yaṃ avatthā pīyate tamabhidhīyateti sambandho, nanvekatthenetyuccamāne visesseneti kathamavagamyate, yato evaṃ vivaritavā tyāsaṅkiyāha- ‘yadipi’ccādi.

What is a `visesana` (qualifier)? He says, beginning with 'yaṃ' ('that which'). The connection is: 'That which determines is so called.' What is a `visessa` (qualified)? He says, beginning with 'yadaneka' ('that which is manifold'). The connection is: 'That which is determined is so designated.' When 'ekatthena' ('with one meaning') is stated, how is 'visessena' ('by the qualified') understood? Since it has been explained thus, anticipating this doubt, he says, 'yadipi' ('even though'), etc.

Sambandhisaddattāti evaṃ maññate “sambandhisaddā sakatthamiva niyatampaṭi-yoginamākkhipanti… tena vinā tesaṃ sakatthassāsambhavāti, vivaritavāti vivarittha, ekatthenetīmassa samānādhikaraṇena saha samāso [M 0.0155] hotīti evaṃ sājjhāhāro attho veditabbo, atthasaddassānekatthattā viseseti ‘attho abhidheyyo’ti. Kathaṃ tenattho vuccatītyāha- ‘adhikarīyati’ccādi.

Because it is a relational word, one thinks thus: 'Relational words imply their fixed correlative... without that, their own meaning is impossible.' By 'vivaritavā' is meant 'he explained.' The meaning of 'ekatthena' is to be understood as supplied thus: 'a compound occurs with that which is in apposition.' Because the word 'attha' has multiple meanings, he specifies: 'Attho is that which is denoted.' How is that meaning expressed by it? He says, beginning with 'adhikarīyati' ('it is made the basis').

Visessassa samānādhikaraṇattañca visesanāpekkhanti sambandho. Visessasaddassa visesanena saha samānādhikaraṇattaṃ visesana saddāpekkhanti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo, tattha kāraṇamāha- ‘sambandhā’ti, adhikaraṇassa samānattaṃ nāma bhinnānaṃ sambandhīnaṃ bhavati, sambandhino ca sambandhamantarena na hontī hoti (potthake) ti visesanavisessānaṃ sambandho viññāyate, evaṃ viññātā tasmā sambandhāti attho.

The connection is that the qualified's being in apposition also depends on the qualifier. Here, the meaning should be seen thus: the qualified word's being in apposition with the qualifier depends on the qualifier word. There, he states the reason: 'Because of relation.' The sameness of substratum occurs for distinct relata, and relata do not exist without a relation; thus, the relation between qualifier and qualified is understood. Thus understood, therefore, 'because of relation'—this is the meaning.

Saddabyatirekena hettha atthānaṃ visesanavisessabhāvo na sambhavati, tathā hi ‘nīlamuppala’nti pañca vatthūni sannihitāni nīlanti nīlattaṃ guṇasāmaññaṃ, nīlo guṇo, tadādhāro dabbanti tīṇi, uppalanti uppalattaṃ uppalajāti, dabbañca tannissayoti dve.

Here, apart from words, the relationship of qualifier and qualified among things is not possible. For example, in 'nīlamuppala' (blue lotus), five things are present: by 'nīla' is meant blueness, the general quality; the quality blue; and its substratum, the substance—these three. By 'uppala' is meant lotus-ness, the lotus species; and the substance which is its basis—these two.

Tattha uppalajāti guṇajātīnaṃ nīlajātiuppalajābhadhanaṃ (kātantaṭīkā) tāva na sambhavati visesanavisessabhāvo jātiyā nigguṇattā, nīlattassa ca nīlaguṇe samavāyino, uppalattassa ca uppaladabbe samavāyino samānādhikaraṇattampi natthi, uppalajātiyā nīlassa ca guṇassa atthi samānādhikaraṇattaṃ… nīla muppalanti pavattinimittānaṃ uppalajātinīlaguṇānamekamadhi karaṇaṃnissayoti, visesana visessabhāvo tu natthi jātiyā anīlattā, guṇadabbānantu sambhavativisesanavisessattaṃ dabbassānekaguṇattā, samānantu tesamparamadhikaraṇaṃ tatiyaṃ natthi, yena samānādhikaraṇattaṃ siyā, evaṃ nīladabba uppaladabbānampi aññamaññaparihārena vattumicchitānaṃ na visesana visessabhāvo, nāpi samānādhikaraṇattaṃ, kasmā aññamaññāsambandhato apekkhābhāvato, vuttapaṭipakkhato pana vakkhamānanayena saddānameva sāmānādhikaraṇyaṃ visesanavisessattañca veditabbaṃ, tenevāha-‘atoyeve’ccādi.

Here, first, the relationship of qualifier and qualified is not possible for the lotus species and the quality species, because a species is devoid of qualities. And there is no apposition for blueness, which inheres in the quality blue, and for lotusness, which inheres in the lotus substance. But there is apposition for the lotus species and the quality blue. The phrase 'nīlamuppala' has a single substratum as its basis, namely, the lotus species and the quality blue, which are the causes of its usage. However, the relationship of qualifier and qualified is not present because the species is not blue. But for qualities and substances, the relationship of qualifier and qualified is possible because a substance has many qualities. Moreover, there is no third common substratum for them, by which there could be apposition. Similarly, for the blue substance and the lotus substance, when they are intended to be spoken of by mutual exclusion, there is neither a relationship of qualifier and qualified nor apposition. Why? Because of their mutual non-relation and absence of expectation. However, from the opposite of what was stated, and by the method to be explained, it should be understood that apposition and the relationship of qualifier and qualified belong to words alone. Therefore, he says, 'atoyeva', etc.

Atoyevāti yato visessassa samānādhikaraṇattaṃ visesanāpekkhaṃ, atoyeva hetutoti attho, bhinnanimittappa yuttānamevāti [M 0.0156] sāmaññena nīlaguṇādhāre dabbe guṇeyeva vā nīlasaddassa, uppalasaddassa ca sāmaññena guṇavati dabbe vattamānattā aññamaññesu bhinnesu saddappavattiyā kāraṇesu payuttānaṃ saddānameva niṭṭhānameva (potthake).

By 'atoyeva' is meant: since the qualified's being in apposition depends on the qualifier, 'atoyeva' means 'because of that cause.' It applies only to those words used with different causes of application, because the word 'nīla' generally occurs in a substance that is the substratum of the quality blue, or in the quality itself; and the word 'uppala' generally occurs in a substance possessing qualities; thus, it applies only to words used with different causes of word-application in things distinct from one another.

Samānādhikaraṇattanti nīluppalasaddānaṃ visuṃvisuṃ yoge visiṭṭhadabba vācittassāsambhavā, nīlañca taṃ uppalaṃ ceti sāmānādhikaraṇye sannipatite sati sambhavā evaṃ tattha visiṭṭhe vatthumhi pavattānaṃ tesaṃ samānatthatā, evakārena byavacchinnamatthaṃ dassetumāha-‘natvabhinne’ccādi.

By 'samānādhikaraṇatta' is meant: because it is impossible for the words 'nīla' and 'uppala', when used separately, to denote a qualified substance, but it is possible when they are brought together in apposition as 'nīlañca taṃ uppalaṃ ca' ('that which is blue and is a lotus'); thus, for them, when applying to a qualified object, there is a sameness of meaning. To show the meaning excluded by the particle 'eva', he says, beginning with 'na tvabhinne' ('but not in what is identical').

Nanucetyādi codyaṃ, sīsampātīti sīsapā rukkhaviseso, nayida mevamiccādi parihāro.

The objection begins with 'nanu ca'. By 'sīsampāti' is meant a `sīsapā`, a particular kind of tree. The refutation begins with 'nayidamevaṃ' ('this is not so').

Atha tuccateiccādinā parassa vacanāvakāsamāsaṅkate, visesavuttīti phalassa rukkhassa ca sāmaññasaddattā bhāvena visese vutti, imesanti sīsapādīnaṃ na samodhāritāti na nicchitā, sāmaññavuttiyeva samodhāritāti adhippāyo, avasitā nicchitā vutti yesaṃ sīsapādīnaṃ te avasitavuttayo, payatanaṃ vinā tadā pappoti cāti sambandho, payatananti ‘sāmatthiyaladdhepivisesse’tivacanaṃ. Tañcanatthiccādi parihāro, sarūpamattakathanāyāti vuttatthānampi sarūpamattakathanāya ‘pūpe bahū ānaye’ti yathā, evaṃ jātīyakanti sarūpakathanappakārayuttaṃ. Upasaṃharamāha-‘tadeva’miccādi, nipātasamudāyovāyaṃ vuttena pakārenetyassa atthe vattate.

Then, by 'atha vuccati', etc., he anticipates an opportunity for another's speech. By 'visesavutti' is meant usage in a specific sense, because 'fruit' and 'tree' are general terms. By 'imesaṃ' is meant 'for these, such as sīsapā trees, it is not ascertained,' that is, 'it is not definite.' The intention is that only the general usage is ascertained. Those, such as `sīsapā`, whose usage is settled and definite are 'avasitavuttayo'. The connection is 'and then it is attained without effort.' By 'payatanaṃ' is meant the statement 'even when the specific is obtained by capability.' The refutation begins with 'tañca natthi' ('and that does not exist'). By 'sarūpamattakathanāya' is meant 'for merely stating the form' of things already mentioned, as in 'pūpe bahū ānaye' ('bring many cakes'). 'Evaṃ jātīyakaṃ' means 'endowed with the manner of stating the form.' Concluding, he says, 'tadevaṃ', etc. This is a collection of particles that functions in the sense of 'in the manner stated'.

Aññatarasambhavepi tannivattiyā vacanasabbhāvaṃ dassetumāha- ‘athapi’ccādi, aññatarasambhavepīti visesanassa visessassa vā sambhavepi, yatrapyubhinnamatthi visesanavisessabhāvasambhavo tatthapitāva bahulaṃvacanatova nivatti hoti, kimpanā-ññatarasambhaveti dassetumāha-‘yathā puṇṇo’iccādi, ettha pana aññepi puṇṇanāmakā santīti byabhicārasambhavā ubhinnampi visesanavisessabhāvasambhave bahulaṃvacanameva samāsaṃ nivatteti, evaṃ vidhepīti aññatarasambhavepi, na [M 0.0157] kevalaṃ visesanavisessabhāvasambhave, atha kho evaṃ vidhepyañña tarasambhavepityavisaddassa attho.

To show the existence of a rule for its prevention even when one of them is possible, he says, 'athapi', etc. By 'aññatarasambhavepi' is meant 'even when the qualifier or the qualified is possible.' Even where a qualifier-qualified relationship is possible for both, there too prevention occurs precisely from the rule of optionality. To show what more then when only one is possible, he says, 'yathā puṇṇo', etc. Here, however, since there are others named Puṇṇa, due to the possibility of ambiguity, even when a qualifier-qualified relationship is possible for both, the very rule of optionality prevents the compound. 'Evaṃ vidhepi' means 'even when one of them is possible'; it is not only when a qualifier-qualified relationship is possible, but rather 'even in such a case where one of them is possible'—this is the meaning of the word 'api'.

Yajjevamiccādi paccekaṃ visesanavisessabhāve sati aniṭṭhā pādanacodanā, paccekaṃ visesanaṃ siyā ubhinnampi visesanattā, tattha dosamāha-‘visessassaca pubbanipāto’ti, co-vadhāraṇe, vattabbantarasamuccaye vā, kutoccāha- ‘nāggahite’ccādi, iti kāraṇe, ato kimaniṭṭhamāyāta miccāha- ‘uppalanīlantipi siyā’ti, itthañcarahi kintyāha- ‘nīluppalanti ce’ccādi. Parihāramāha-‘nesadoso’ccādi, upapattyantaramāha- ‘atha ce’ccādi.

The objection that adduces an undesirable consequence begins with 'yad evaṃ' ('if it is so'), when there is a qualifier-qualified relationship for each individually. Each could be a qualifier, since both have the nature of a qualifier. Regarding that, he states the fault: 'and the prior placement of the qualified.' The particle 'ca' is for emphasis, or for the inclusion of another matter to be stated. And why? He says, beginning with 'nāggahite' ('when it is not grasped'); this is the reason. Therefore, what undesirable consequence arises? He says: 'There could also be "uppalanīlaṃ".' If so, then what? He says, 'nīluppalanti ce', etc. He states the resolution, beginning with 'neso doso' ('this is not a fault'). He gives another reason, beginning with 'atha ce' ('or if').

Aññamaññānupakārittāti aññamaññassa visesanavisessatte nānupakārittā sappadhānattāti attho, atha dvinnampi appadhānattaṃ kasmā na siyā tyāha- ‘appadhānattepi’ccādi, sakasakappadhānāpekkhāvantānanti sakesake padhāne attani apekkhāvantānaṃ. Atha kuto dabbasseva padhānattamasitaṃ, na tu guṇassetyāsaṅkiya ñāyamupanissayati ‘atha ce’tyādinā. Chāgotyajo vuccate, taṃ setavaṇṇamālabhetha māreyya, phusanaṃ vā kareyyāti attho, āpubbo labhi hi māraṇe phusane ca vattate, desanāyanti codanāyanti codanāvākya (potthake) vedavākyeti attho, kuto chāgato-ñño nālabbhateccāha- ‘na hi’ccādi.

'Mutual non-assistance' means that because they are qualifier and qualified in relation to each other, there is no assistance, due to each having its own predominance—this is the meaning. But why should not both be non-predominant? To this, he says: 'Even in non-predominance,' etc., meaning 'of those who are dependent on their own respective predominance.' Then, whence is the predominance of substance alone assumed, and not that of quality? Doubting this, he relies on the maxim in the passage beginning with 'But if.' A goat is called 'aja.' One should take a white-colored one, that is, kill it, or touch it—this is the meaning. For the root 'labh' with the prefix 'ā' occurs in the sense of both killing and touching. 'In the teaching' means 'in a Vedic utterance'—this is the meaning. But why is nothing other than the goat taken? To this, he says: 'For not,' etc.

Chāgābhāveti setaguṇayuttassa chāgassābhāve, piṭṭhapiṇḍimālabbhāti setaguṇayogena viṭṭhapiṇḍiṃ ālambha, na ca nālambhate tasmā guṇo appadhānanti ajjhāharitabbaṃ.

'In the absence of a goat' means 'in the absence of a goat endowed with the quality of whiteness.' 'Having taken a lump of flour' means 'having taken a lump of flour due to its connection with the quality of whiteness.' And indeed it is taken; 'therefore, the quality is non-predominant'—this should be supplied.

Puna codento āha- ‘nanu ce’ccādi, athetyadhippāyamāsaṅkate, aniṭṭhamāpādayati nīlasaddepi pasaṅgo’ti, kutoccāha- ‘sopihi’ccādi, idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti- “uppalasaddo jātivācī, na tu dabbavācī, jāti visiṭṭhadabbavācittā yadi dabbavācīti vuccate, tadā nīlasaddopi guṇavisiṭṭha dabbavācittā dabbavacanamāpajjatīti imesaṃ na koci viseso”ti, pariharanto āha ‘nedamatthi’ccādi, apāyino apagantāro dabbāti gamyate, kutoccāha- ‘satīpi’ccādi, iti kāraṇe.

Again, the objector says: 'But surely if,' etc. Suspecting the intention 'then,' he points out an undesirable consequence: 'an implication even for the word "blue."' Why? He says: 'For that also,' etc. This is what is meant: 'The word "lotus" denotes a class, not a substance. If it is said to denote a substance because it denotes a substance qualified by a class, then the word "blue," because it denotes a substance qualified by a quality, would also become a substance-word. Thus, there is no difference between these.' Refuting this, he says: 'This is not so,' etc. 'Substance' (`dabba`) is understood as 'those who depart' (`apāyino`), 'those who go away' (`apagantāro`). Why? He says: 'Even when there is,' etc. The word `iti` is in the sense of 'reason'.

Visesanamekattheneti [M 0.0158] siddhepi papañcatthaṃ paripphuṭatthañca udāharaṇabahuttaṃ dassetuṃ pāṇiniyehi bahuṃ suttitaṃ, sabbassetassa paccakkhātabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ vuttiyamudāharaṇamattaṃ dassitaṃ, tadidāni byākhyātukāmo āha- ‘pubbakāle’ccādi, chinnoca visesanantī sambandho “pubbakāleka sabbadhurapurāṇanavakevalāni samānādhikaraṇene”ti (2-1-49) te samettha suttaṃ, tatthekādīnaṃ vuttiyamudāharaṇāni na dassitānyupalakkhaṇatova viññāyantīti dassetumāha- ‘eke’ccādi, eko ca so purisocātyādinā viggaho upalakkhaṇattāyeva ca ‘satta ca te isayo ca sattisayo’ccādikañca daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Even though it is established that a qualifier has a single meaning, the Pāṇinīyas have composed many sūtras for the sake of elaboration and clarity, and to show an abundance of examples. To show the rejection of all of this, only an example is presented in the Vutti. Now, wishing to explain that, he says: 'pubbakāle,' etc. The connection is with the qualifier, as in the sūtra 'pubbakāleka sabbadhurapurāṇanavakevalāni samānādhikaraṇena' (Pāṇini 2.1.49), which is quoted here. To show that in the Vutti the examples for words like 'eka' are not given, as they are understood by implication, he says: 'eke,' etc. The analytical expression, such as 'eko ca so puriso ca,' is illustrative, and due to this being an implication, examples such as 'satta ca te isayo ca, sattisayo,' etc., should also be understood.

Upamīyate paricchijjate-nenetyupamānaṃ, upamīyatītyupameyyaṃ, tesaṃ upamānopameyyānaṃ sādhāraṇo yo dhammo sāmatātena visiṭṭhaṃ yadupameyyaṃ, taṃ vacanenetyattho upamānopameyyaccādi kassa, samāso bhavatīti seso, kāraṇamāha- ‘visese’ccādi, visesāpariggahāti visesanantyeva sāmaññena pariggahā, evambhū tassāpīti upamānarūpassāpi. Nanu satthīsaddassasatthiyaṃ vutti sāmāsaddassa tu devadattāya, ato byadhikaraṇattā kathamettha samāsoccāsaṅkīyāha- ‘yade’ccādi, samāno dhammo sāmattādi yassa so sadhammo, tassa bhāvo sādhammiyaṃ sāmattaṃ, tasmā devadattātthe vattate upacāravasena, sāmāsaddopi guṇavacanopi sāmattaṃ vatvā saddhādittavasenābhedopacārena vā devadattāyaṃ vattate, nanu ca sāmāsaddassa devadattābhidhāne caritatthatāya satthī guṇena niddiṭṭhātyaniyataguṇappatītippasaṅgo nekaguṇādhārattā satthiyātyāsaṅkiyāha- ‘yadipi’ccādi.

'That by which one compares or delimits' is the standard of comparison (`upamāna`); 'that which is compared' is the subject of comparison (`upameyya`). The meaning is: with a word for the common quality of these, the standard and subject of comparison—such as sameness—the subject of comparison is qualified. For what is the phrase 'of the standard and subject of comparison,' etc.? 'A compound is formed' is the remainder. He states the reason: 'because of a qualifier,' etc. 'Without grasping the specific' means that it is grasped generally, simply as a qualifier. This being so, it applies also to the form of the standard of comparison. 'But surely the word for sword (`satthī`) has its application to a sword, whereas the word `sāmā` has its application to Devadattā. Therefore, because they have different referents, how can there be a compound here?' Doubting this, he says: 'When,' etc. 'That which has a common property' (`sadhammo`) is that which has a common quality, such as sameness. The state of that is 'commonality' (`sādhammiya`), i.e., sameness. Therefore, it refers to Devadattā by way of metaphorical transfer. The word `sāmā` also, though a quality-word, having expressed 'sameness', refers to Devadattā by a metaphorical transfer of non-difference based on faith and so on. 'But surely, since the purpose of the word `sāmā` is fulfilled in denoting Devadattā, and the sword is indicated by a quality, there is the unwanted consequence of cognizing an unspecified quality, because a sword is the basis for many qualities.' Doubting this, he says: 'Even if,' etc.

Ihāti niddhāraṇe, etesaṃ guṇānaṃ majjheti attho, iha vā satthiyaṃ, sāmaguṇavantatāya sāmāyāti gamyate, pasiddhivasenāti satthisāmātyatropamānaṃ satthī, upameyyā devadattā, pasiddhantupamānaṃ bhavati nāppasiddhaṃ… pasiddhasādhammiyā sādhyu sādhanamupamānanti katvā satthiyeva sāmaṅguṇena pasiddhā na devadattā, tasmā sāmaguṇappasiddhiyāti attho. Sādhyute upamīyateneneti sādhanamupamānaṃ, sādhyate [M 0.0159] upadhīyateti sādhyamupameyyaṃ, pasiddhassa sādhammiyaṃ tena, sādhyassāppasiddhassa kassaci sādhanaṃ sādhyasādhanaṃ. Yatratviccādinā bahulaṃvacanasāmatthiyā sāmaññavacaneneva samāsasabbhāvaṃ vatvā aññenāsabbhāvamudāharaṇena phuṭayituṃ ‘phālā iva taṇḍulā’tyādi āraddhaṃ.

'Here' (`iha`) is in the sense of specification, meaning 'among these qualities.' Or, 'here' in the sword, it is understood as 'sāmā' due to possessing the `sāma` quality. 'By way of being well-known' means that here in 'satthi-sāmā', the standard of comparison is the sword, and the subject of comparison is Devadattā. The well-known becomes the standard of comparison, not the not-well-known. Because the standard of comparison is the means of proving the subject through a common property with what is well-known, the sword itself is well-known for the `sāma` quality, not Devadattā. Therefore, the meaning is: due to the well-knownness of the `sāma` quality. 'That by which one proves or compares' is the means of proof (`sādhana`), the standard of comparison. 'That which is to be proved or established' is the provable (`sādhya`), the subject of comparison. By that common property of the well-known, there is the proving of the subject, which is not well-known to someone; this is the 'proving of the provable'. By the passage beginning 'But where,' due to the force of the word 'variously' (`bahula`), having stated the existence of a compound even with a word for a generality, in order to clarify its non-existence with another word, the example 'grains of rice like husks,' etc., is introduced.

Taṇḍulasaddoti upameyyabhūtataṇḍulasaddo, taṇḍulattampi vatvā dabbe pavatto sāmaññavacano natu bhavatīti sambandho, dabbeti taṇḍuladabbe phāladabbe ca.

'The word taṇḍula' means the word `taṇḍula` which is the subject of comparison. The connection is: having expressed 'rice-ness', it operates on the substance, but it is not a word for a generality. 'On the substance' means on the substance of rice and the substance of the husk.

Upamānopameyyasādhāraṇasūrattādidhammavacanāppayogeti upamānopameyyānaṃ sādhāraṇo yo visāradattādidhammo tabbacanassa ‘muni ayaṃ sīho viya visārado’tyādo visāradādisaddassāppayogeti attho, kesañciti kesañci saddānaṃ majjhe, visessattameva phuṭayati. ‘Tathā ce’tyādinā, visesanavisessānaṃ yathiṭṭhattā niccaṃ sīhādīnaṃ visessatāyeva vacanicchāti pubbanipātattāppasaṅgoti bhāvo, upapatyantaramāha-‘visesanasseve’ccādi, yadipi sīho visesanameva na visessaṃ, tathāpi bahulādhikārā visesanassāpi paranipātoti bhāvo.

'When there is non-application of a word for a quality like heroism common to the standard and subject of comparison' means the non-application of a word like 'confident' etc., for a quality like confidence common to the standard and subject of comparison, as in 'this sage is confident like a lion.' 'Of some' means 'among some words,' it clarifies only the state of being the qualified. By 'And so,' etc., the sense is: because the qualifier and the qualified are as desired, and the intention of speech is always for 'lion' etc. to be only the qualified, there is no occasion for it to be placed first. He states another reason: 'Of the qualifier alone,' etc. The sense is: even though 'lion' is only a qualifier, not a qualified, nevertheless, due to the governing rule of 'variously' (`bahula`), there is also post-position of the qualifier.

Athātrāpi visesananteva samāsappaṭipādane’muni ayaṃ sīhova visārado’ccādo sāmatthiyatova samāsāppasaṅgepi upamāno pameyyānaṃ sādhāraṇavisāradattādidhammavacanāppayoge sati tappasaṅgābhāvatthaṃ vacanamārabbhanīyanti codeti ‘nanuce’tyādinā, sāmatthiyatoti sāmaññavacanappayoge sāpekkhattā samāsāppasaṅgoti sāmatthiyaṃ tasmāti attho. Sāmaññappayogatthanti samāsavākye sāmaññavacanassa sūrattādi(no), appayogatthaṃ, tathā hiccādinā sāmaññasaddappayoge sāmatthiyato samāsāsabbhāvā suttantarassānārabbhanīyabhāvaṃ sādheti.

Now, here too, in the teaching of a compound with a qualifier, he objects with 'But surely if,' etc., saying that even though there is no occasion for a compound in 'this sage is confident like a lion' due to a lack of capacity, still, when there is non-application of a word for a common quality like confidence between the standard and subject of comparison, a statement should be commenced to prevent that unwanted consequence. 'Due to capacity' means: because there is dependency when a word for a generality is used, there is no occasion for a compound; this is the capacity, therefore this is the meaning. 'For the sake of the application of a generality' means for the sake of the non-application of a word for a generality, like heroism, in the compound phrase. Similarly, by the passage beginning with 'for,' he establishes that another rule should not be commenced, because when a word for a generality is used, there is no formation of a compound due to a lack of capacity.

Visesānantabbhāvāti sāmaññassa samāse antobhāvepi tikhīṇattādito visiṭṭhassa sūrassādivacanīyassa visesassa samāse anantogadhattā appasaṅgo sāpekkhamasamatthanti. Atheti ‘saccameta’ntiādiṃ [M 0.0160] paravacanamāsaṅkiya vadati, evamādisijjhanatthaṃ samāsoti (ñāpanatthaṃ) ārabbhanīyambhavatīti sambandho.

'Because of the non-inclusion of the specific' means that even when the generality is included in the compound, there is no occasion for it, because the specific—the word 'hero' etc. which is to be stated, qualified by sharpness etc.—is not included in the compound, for a dependent word is incapable of compounding. 'Then'—anticipating the other's statement, 'This is true,' etc., he speaks. The connection is: for the sake of accomplishing such things, the compound should be commenced for the sake of making it known.

Padhānassāti ‘raññopuriso-bhirūpo’tettha abhirūpasāpekkhassa purisassa visesanattenevā visesanaṃ tenevā (potthake) ppadhānaṃ, samāsāvayavabhūtaṃ rājānaṃ pati visessabhāvenāviphalitasakatthatāya padhānabhūtassa purisassa. Ādisaddena ‘rājapurisassa dassanīyassa geha’nti saṅgaṇhāti.

'Of the predominant' means: here in 'the king's man is handsome,' the man, being dependent on 'handsome', is non-predominant precisely because it is a qualifier; yet in relation to the king, who is a member of the compound, this same man is predominant, because his own meaning is not nullified by his state as the qualified. By the word 'etc.', he includes 'the house of the handsome man of the king'.

Ettha hi gehampati visesanabhāvenāppadhānattepi rājānampati padhānabhūtassa purisassa sāpekkhassāpi samāso hoteva. Idañcañāpanatthaṃ vacanārambhappayojanañca, kāraṇamāha- ‘gamakattā’iccādi.

Here indeed, although the qualifier is non-predominant, a compound still occurs for the man, who is predominant in relation to the king, even though he is dependent in relation to the house. And this is the purpose of commencing the statement: for the sake of making this known. He states the reason: 'because of conveying meaning,' etc.

Gamakattāti viggahavākyatthassa vuttiyampatīyamānattā gamakattaṃ tasmā, naceha gamakattamatthīti ‘muni sīhova sūro’tyatra tu vākyato yottho patīyate, nāyaṃ ‘muni sīho sūro’tyato gamyateti gamakattaṃ natthī-ti attho, tathāhi munisīhasaddenevo pamānopameyyabhāvanimittassa visāradattassa sabhāvenevopādānato visāradasaddassa tena sambandhābhāvo.

'Because of conveying meaning' means that since the meaning of the analytical statement is understood in the compound expression, there is the conveying of meaning. Therefore, if there is no conveying of meaning here, then in 'a sage is courageous like a lion,' the meaning that is understood from the sentence is not conveyed by 'a sage-lion is courageous.' Thus, there is no conveying of meaning—this is the meaning. For indeed, by the very word 'munisīha,' since courage—the reason for the relationship between the standard and the subject of comparison—is included by its very nature, there is no connection of the word 'visārada' (courageous) with it.

Apavaggo nibbānaṃ, vākyameveti evakārena byavacchinnamatthampadassayamāha- ‘vuttinivattetī’ti bahulādhikārato viññāyati, nanu cātra visessabhāvāsambhavāppasaṅgoyeva vuttiyāti codeti. ‘Nanuce’tyādinā.

Apavagga is Nibbāna. In 'vākyam eva' (the sentence itself), showing the meaning delimited by the particle 'eva', he says: 'it prevents the compound expression.' This is understood from the governing rule concerning 'bahula' (variously). But with 'nanu ce,' etc., he raises an objection: 'Is it not the case that here, in the compound expression, there is precisely the contingency of the impossibility of the state of being the qualified?'

Puṇṇatābyabhicārāti puṇṇatāsaṅkhātassa bālādiavatthāvisesassa avināppavattito byabhicārī hi visessambhavati yathā nīlatāyuppalaṃ, pariharati ‘nedamatti’ccādinā, mantāṇiputtānaṃ anekattāti kevalaṃ mantāṇiyā putto puṇṇoyevāti abhāvā tesaṃ bahubhāvato, attano attano gahassa patayoti gahapatīnaṃ bahuttaṃ pākaṭameva.

Regarding the deviation from fullness (`puṇṇatā`): a qualified term can indeed be deviating, due to the non-invariable occurrence of the particular state of childhood and so forth, which is designated as 'fullness'—just as a lotus is in relation to blueness. He refutes this with 'this is not so,' etc. 'Because of the multiplicity of Mantāṇī's sons' means that since it is not the case that Puṇṇa is the only son of Mantāṇī, they are many. And the multiplicity of householders, each being the master of his own house, is indeed evident.

Vuttiyeveti evakārena byavacchinnamatthamāha-‘vākyaṃ nivattetī’ti. Visiṭṭhajātivacanāti vuttaṃ kaṇhasappajātiyā lohitasālijātiyā ca visiṭṭhattā.

In 'vuttiyā eva' (by the compound expression itself), he states the meaning delimited by the particle 'eva': 'it prevents the analytical sentence.' It is called a term for a specific species, due to the specific nature of the black serpent species and the red rice species.

Tacchako [M 0.0161] sappoti byākhyeyamupanikkhippacodayamāha- ‘nanu ce’ccādi. Tacchakabhāvānapetoti bālayuvattādisaṅkhātatacchakabhāvato abyāvutto, atthināmadheyyoti tacchako nāma koci tannāmo atthi, kiriyāsaddoti tacchatīti tacchakoti evaṃ kiriyāya pavattinimittattenopādinno vaḍḍhakīvācī tacchakasaddo, evaṃ maññate “yathāvuttanayena visesanavisessasabbhāvā samāsena bhavitabbaṃ, tathā sati kimidaṃ paccudāharaṇaṃ kata”nti. Atra kenaci na nāmadheyyassetyādi nopajāyatevātyetadavasānaṃ vuccamānamanudyataṃ nirākattukāmo āha-‘yopā he’ccādi.

Introducing the point to be explained, 'tacchako sappo' (carpenter-snake), he raises an objection with 'nanu ce,' etc. 'Not separate from the state of being a tacchaka' means not excluded from the state of being a tacchaka, which is designated as childhood, youth, and so on. 'Is there a proper name?' means: is there someone with that name, 'Tacchaka'? 'It is a word of action' means: 'he planes' (`tacchatīti`), therefore 'a planer' (`tacchako`). In this way, the word 'tacchaka', meaning a carpenter, is taken as having the action as its cause of application. He thinks thus: 'According to the method stated, since there is the existence of a qualifier and a qualified, there should be a compound. That being so, why is this given as a counter-example?' Here, someone, wishing to refute the statement being made—which was introduced beginning with 'na nāmadheyyassa' and ending with 'na upajāyate vā'—says, 'yo pā he,' etc.

Imassāyamadhippāyo “vuttanayena tacchakasaddassa kiriyā saddassātthavisayāpekkhāyābhāvato visessattābhāvā paccudāharaṇamidaṃ kata”nti.

This is the intended meaning: 'This has been given as a counter-example because, according to the method stated, the word 'tacchaka', being an action-word, lacks dependence on an object of meaning, and because it is not a qualified term.'

Kasmā ayuttamiccāha-‘yato’ccādi, nāmadheyyassa kiriyāvācino ca atthābhidhānasāmatthiyaṃ tulyaṃ vā na vā, avayavappasiddhiyā samudāyappasiddhi balavati vā navetyetaṃ vicāretuṃ yato nādhikatantyattho, kiñcarahi adhikatantyāha- ‘apitvi’ccādi, tacchakasaddonekatthavutti nānekatthoti vicāretumadhikatanti yojanā.

Why is it unsuitable? He says: 'Because,' etc. The meaning is that the point under consideration is not to investigate whether the capacity of a proper name and of a word denoting an action to express a meaning is equal or not, nor whether the conventional meaning of the whole is stronger than the conventional meaning of the parts. What then is the point under consideration? He says: 'But rather,' etc. The connection is that the point under consideration is to investigate whether the word 'tacchaka' has one meaning or multiple meanings.

Evaṃ maññate- “visesanavisessabhāvacintāyaṃ saddānamatthābhidhānasāmatthiyacintā na yujjate ‘sati sambhave byabhicāre ca visesanaṃ sātthakaṃ hotī’ti visesanaṃ maggīyate, nāsambhave nābyabhicāre yathā sītaṃ (himaṃ) uṇhoggīti, tasmā sambhavabyabhicāracintā visesanavisessabhāvacintāyamupayujjatīti tacchakasaddo-nekatthavuttivā na vetyetadeva vicāretumadhikatanti katthacipi visesanavisessa sabbhāve samāso hotevā”ti, yadipi nāmadheyyakiriyāvācīnamatulyamatthābhidhānaṃ samudāyappasiddhiyā ca balavatittaṃ, tathāpi vakkhamānanayena samāsasabbhāvā na kāci hānīti dassetumāha- ‘ettha cā’tiādi.

He thinks thus: 'In the consideration of the state of being qualifier and qualified, the consideration of the capacity of words to express meaning is not suitable. A qualifier is sought based on the principle: 'A qualifier is meaningful when there is possibility and deviation'; not when there is impossibility or non-deviation, as in 'cold snow' or 'hot fire.' Therefore, the consideration of possibility and deviation is useful in the consideration of the state of being qualifier and qualified. Thus, the relevant matter to investigate is only this: whether the word 'tacchaka' has one meaning or not; and a compound certainly occurs wherever there is the existence of a qualifier and qualified.' And even though the expression of meaning by proper names and action-words is unequal, and the conventional meaning of the whole is stronger, nevertheless, to show that there is no harm, since a compound does exist according to the method to be explained, he says, 'And here,' etc.

Etthacāti keci pakkhe ca, kañci pīḷamāvahatīti sambandho, kutoccāha ‘tathāhi’ccādi. Evaṃ maññate- “yadīpi samudāyappasiddhiyā sati kiriyāsaddatthavisayāpekkhā [M 0.0162] nopajāyate, tathāpi nāmadheyyasseva tacchakasaddassāpyanekatthavuttittamattheva… sappavisese manusse ca tannāmake nāmadheyyassa tacchakasaddassa pavattisabbhāvā(ti) visesanavisessasabbhāvato samāsappasaṅgo tadavattho yevā”ti, na kevalaṃ sappavisesasseva tacchakasaddo nāmadheyyamapitu manussānampīti pisaddattho. Tacchakasaddassānekatthavuttittepi na samudāyappasiddhiyā avayavappasiddhībādhāti dassetumāha- ‘nacā’tiādi. Co-vadhāraṇe, kutoccāha ‘kiriye’ccādi. Kamenatthappasiddhīti yaṃ, etampana sakkā viññātunti yojanā.

'And here' means: and in the view of some. The connection is: 'it brings some affliction.' Whence? He says: 'For thus,' etc. He thinks thus: 'Even though, when there is a conventional meaning of the whole, a dependence on the object of meaning of the action-word does not arise, nevertheless, the word 'tacchaka', just like a proper name, certainly has the quality of having multiple meanings. Because the proper name 'Tacchaka' is found to apply to a particular kind of serpent and to a human with that name, the contingency of a compound, due to the existence of a qualifier and qualified, remains in that very state.' The meaning of the particle 'pi' is that 'Tacchaka' is a proper name not only of a particular kind of serpent but also of humans. To show that even though the word 'tacchaka' has multiple meanings, the conventional meaning of the parts is not obstructed by the conventional meaning of the whole, he says: 'na ca,' etc. The particle 'ca' is for emphasis. Whence? He says: 'kiriye,' etc. The connection is: that which is the gradual establishment of meaning, this can be understood.

Yanti yaṃ pasijjhanaṃ, kamenāti bādhābhāvato anukkamena. Evañceti iminā nacetyādinā vuttaṃ paccāmasati… kimpaṭivihitaṃ siyā parihaṭaṃ siyāti attho, iti iminā kāraṇena ‘tacchako sappo’ti paccudāharaṇaṃ na yuttaṃ… tacchakasappoti samāsasabbhāvatoti adhippāyo, nedamevamiccādinā pariharati, yadā carati yathā vuttena visesanavisessabhāvasambhavo, tadā kathaṃtyāha- ‘yadā visesane’ccādi. Tadāpi kathaṃ vākyena bhavitabbamiccāha- ‘idañce’ccādi. Bahulaṃvacanatoyevāti adhippāyo.

'Yanti' means: that which is the establishment. 'Gradually' means: sequentially, due to the absence of obstruction. With 'Evañce' ('If so'), he reconsiders what was said with 'na ca,' etc. The meaning is: what would be counteracted? What would be refuted? Therefore, for this reason, the counter-example 'tacchako sappo' is not suitable. The intention is that 'tacchakasappo' exists as a compound. He refutes this with 'na idam evaṃ' ('it is not so'), etc. When there is the possibility of a qualifier-qualified relationship as stated, how is it then? He says: 'When in a qualifier,' etc. Even then, how should it be a sentence? He says: 'idañce,' etc. The intention is that it is only from the statement about 'bahula'.

Aññassāti kammani sambandhavacanicchāyaṃ chaṭṭhī. Avacchedakattāti ettha kattunā bhavitabbanti kāḷassāti kattari bhāvayoge chaṭṭhiyā ajjhāharitabbaṃ. Pattāpannehi dutiyantassa jīvikampatto jīvikā pannoti samāso ‘kārakaṃ bahula”nteva (caṃ-2-2-19) vihito dutiyantena tu tesaṃ samāsatthaṃ suttantaraṃ kataṃ parehi, atthañca tesamitthiliṅgānampi samāseneva, kāranivattiyā, tathā māso jātassāti viggahe parimāṇivācinā chaṭṭhiyantena parimāṇavacanānaṃ kālasaddānaṃ, tadāha- ‘pattāpannāna’miccādi, parimāṇaṃ māsādi paricchedo tamassatthīti parimāṇī jātādi.

'Aññassa' is the sixth case ending, with the desire to state a relation to the object. In 'because of being a delimiter', since it should be by the agent, 'kāḷassa' is to be supplied as a sixth case ending in the sense of agent in connection with a state. With 'patta' and 'āpanna', a compound of a word ending in the second case, such as 'jīvikaṃ patto' or 'jīvikaṃ āpanno', is prescribed by 'kārakaṃ bahulaṃ' itself (Caṃ-2-2-19). But by others, another rule has been made for the purpose of their compounding with a word ending in the second case. And the meaning of these, even when they are feminine, is by the compound itself, due to the removal of the case relation. Similarly, in the analysis 'māso jātassa', there is a compound of time-words, which denote a measure, with a word ending in the sixth case that denotes the thing measured. Thus he says: 'pattāpannānaṃ,' etc. 'Parimāṇa' (measure) is a division such as a month. 'Parimāṇī' (the measured) is that which possesses it, such as 'jāta' (born).

Ettha hi māso parimāṇaṃ paricchedakattā, jāto parimāṇī paricchejjattā, pattā jīvikānenāti patto jīvikanti pāṭhena bhavitabbaṃ vacanicchāyaṃ yo-ttho so- ñāpadatthasamāsepyatinno [M 0.0163] vacanicchābhedamantarenātidassetuṃ ‘aññapadatthe bhavissatī’ti yaṃ vuttiyaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ byākhyātukāmo āha- ‘vānekaññatthe iccevā’tiādi. Aññattha samāse kate sabbattha “itthiyaṃ bhāsite”ccādinā (3-67) pumbhāvo. Māso jātassāti vacanicchāyaṃ yo-ttho, so-ññatthasamāsepyabhinno vacanicchābheda mantarenāti dassetumāha- ‘yassa jātādino’ccādi.

Here indeed, the month is the measure, because it is the delimiter; the one born is the measured, because it is what is to be delimited. Desiring to explain what was said in the `vutti`, 'it will be in the meaning of another word'—in order to show clearly that the meaning which is in the desire to say 'livelihood was attained by him' is also present in the compound which indicates that meaning, without any difference in the desire to say—he says: 'vā aneka-aññatthe,' etc. When a compound is formed in the meaning of another word, everywhere the masculine form occurs, according to the rule 'itthiyaṃ bhāsite...' (3-67). To show that the meaning which is in the desire to say 'a month for the one born' is also undifferentiated in the compound with another meaning, without a difference in the desire to say, he says: 'yassa jātādino,' etc.

Jātasaddassatthamāha sampannoti, sampuṇṇotyattho, iminā ca māso jāto-ssāti viggahassa attho dassito, aññathāti yadi māso tassa aññapadatthassa jātādino sampuṇṇo na bhātīti attho. Ttattavantūnaṃ niṭṭhāsaññaṃ vidhāya tadantassaññatthasamāse “niṭṭhā”ti (2-2-36) suttena pubbanipāto vutto, tadāha- ‘nace’ccādi, pubbanipātappasaṅgo naca siyātisambandho, kutoccāha- ‘jāti’ccādi. Kesañciti vākyakāramāha, naca yuttanti sambandho, kāraṇamāha- ‘visesana’meccādi, tathāhiccādinā visesanassa sātthakatte samāsabbhāvamabhāve cābhāvaṃ sādheti… chaṭṭhīsamāse ‘sati sambhave byabhicāre ca visesanassa sātthakambhavatīti visesanassa sātthakattā.

He states the meaning of the word 'jāta' as 'sampanna' (complete), meaning 'sampuṇṇa' (full). By this, the meaning of the analysis 'māso jāto-ssa' (a month has passed since his birth) is shown. Otherwise, the meaning is: if the month does not appear complete for him who is the referent of the other term, 'born' etc. Having established the designation 'niṭṭhā' for words ending in 'ta' and 'tavant', the prior position of a word ending in 'niṭṭhā' in a bahubbīhi compound is stated by the rule 'niṭṭhā' (2-2-36). Therefore, he says: 'nor indeed,' and so on. The connection is that the occasion for prior position would not arise. From where? He says: 'birth,' and so on. He refers to some grammarians, and the connection is that it is not appropriate. He states the reason: 'qualifier,' and so on. Thus, by 'tathāhi' etc., he establishes that when the qualifier is meaningful, a compound exists, and when it is not, it does not. In a genitive compound, 'when occurrence and deviation are possible, the qualifier is meaningful,' hence the qualifier's meaningfulness.

Avacanepīti niyamavacane (a)satīpi, chaṭṭhīsamāsappasaṅgo carahi vuttanayena byavacchejja byavacchedakattābhāvena visesanānatthakyā na bhaveyya ce vākyenāpi na bhavitabbanti āha- ‘vākyaṃ tvi’ccādi. Ayampana visesanasamāso parehi kammadhārayoti ñāyati… yathā kammaṃ kiriyaṃ payojanañca dhāreti evamayaṃ samāso kammamiva dvayaṃ dhārayatīti.

'Even if there is no statement' means even if there is no restrictive rule. If the occasion for a genitive compound would not arise—due to the absence of the state of being the distinguished and the distinguisher in the manner stated, and due to the qualifier being meaningless—then it should not occur even as an analytical sentence. Therefore, he said, 'But the sentence,' and so on. This qualifier compound, however, is known by others as a karmadhāraya. Just as an action (kamma) bears an activity (kiriya) and a purpose (payojana), so this compound, like an action, bears two things.

12. Naña

12. Nañ

Etthevāti “ṭa nañssa”iti (3-74) sutteeva. Pāmanaputtotipāmā kuṭṭhaviseso assa atthīti pāmasaddā “dissantaññepi paccayā”ti (4-120) nappaccayo, pāmanassa putto, yadi hettha ñakāro visesanattho na karīyetha, tadā “ṭa nassā”ti suttaṃ karīyetha, tathā ca satyuttarapade parato pāmanasadde nakārassāpi ṭo

'Here itself' means in the very rule 'ṭa nañssa' (3-74). 'Pāmanaputto' (son of a leper): 'pāmā' is a type of leprosy; 'he has it' (assa atthīti), hence from the word 'pāma', the suffix 'na' is applied according to 'dissantaññepi paccayā' (4-120) to form 'pāmana'. 'Pāmanassa putto' (son of a leper). If the letter 'ñ' here were not made for the purpose of specification, then the rule would be made as 'ṭa nassā'. And in that case, when the word 'pāmana' is the following latter member, its 'na' would also become 'ṭa'.

Siyāti [M 0.0164] bhāvo, nanu ciha samāsavidhimhi ña kāroccāraṇā ña lopa rahitassa samāso na bhavatīti vattumucitaṃ, na tu “ṭa nañssā”ti visesanatthoti ññakāro etthova visesanattho, ti bhavitabba saccaṃ, kintviha samāsavidhimhi ña kārassa byavacchajjaṃ na dissate.

This is the sense of 'siyā'. (Objection:) Surely, here in the rule for compounds, is it not proper to say that because the letter 'ñ' is uttered, a compound does not occur for that which is without the elision of 'ñ', rather than that it has a specifying purpose in 'ṭa nañssā'? (Reply:) True, but here in the rule for compounds, what is to be excluded by the letter 'ñ' is not seen.

Pariyudāsavuttīti pari tulitamuggayha nisedhanīyassa asanaṃ khepanaṃ vajjanaṃ pariyudāso, tena pariyudāsena visiṭṭhe-tthe vutti asseti pariyudāsavutti, pasajjappaṭisedhavuttīti paṭisedhanīyameva pasajja patvā taṃsadisamanapekkhiya nisedho, tena vutti asseti pasajjappaṭisedha vutti.

'Pariyudāsavutti' (nominal negation): 'pariyudāsa' is the rejection (khepanaṃ) or avoidance (vajjanaṃ) of what is to be negated, after having compared (pari tulita) and grasped (uggayha) it. That which has its function (vutti) in a meaning qualified (visiṭṭhe) by such exclusion is 'pariyudāsavutti'. 'Pasajjappaṭisedhavutti' (verbal negation): having directly approached (pasajja patvā) that very thing which is to be negated, it is a negation (nisedho) without regard for anything similar to it. That which has its function (vutti) from this is 'pasajjappaṭisedhavutti'.

Yattha brāhmaṇā aññova bhavatītyevaṃ vākyenātthantaravidhānā vidhino padhānattaṃ, atthantaravidhānasāmatthiyeneva brāhmaṇassa paṭisedho patīyate, brāhmaṇassa brāhmaṇassā (potthake) nivattane tadapekkhāyāññassa vidhānayogato sakapadena nañkhyena vidhibhāgī na vuccate, kiñcarahi aññasaddena… pariyudāsanissayinoññasaddasseva vākye payogato’ añño brāhmaṇā abrāhmaṇo’ti, nañssaca syādyantena sāmatthiyaṃ, na tyādyantenetyekavākyatā… añño brāhmaṇā abrāhmaṇoti tattha tattha pariyudāsavuttittā.

Where, in the sentence 'one other than a brahmin exists', because another meaning is established, the prescription is primary. The negation of 'brahmin' is understood precisely through the capacity to establish another meaning. When 'brahmin' is removed, because the establishment of another is dependent on that, that which partakes of the prescription is not expressed by the negative particle 'nañ' with its own word, but rather by the word 'other'. Because the word 'other', which is dependent on nominal negation, is used in the analytical sentence: 'one other than a brahmin is a non-brahmin'. And the negative particle 'nañ' has syntactic capability with a word ending in a case inflection, not with a word ending in a verbal inflection; thus there is a single sentence. 'One other than a brahmin is a non-brahmin'; in such cases, it is because of the function of nominal negation.

Pasajjappaṭisedhetu paṭisedhassa padhānattā brāhmaṇo na bhavatīti vākyena brāhmaṇassa paṭisedho vidhi atthagammo vākyabhedo, sakapadena ca nañkhyena paṭisedhabhāgivācī sambajjhate. Ko so brāhmaṇā aññoti āha- ‘brāhmaṇattānajjhāsito’ccādi.

In verbal negation, however, since negation is primary, the negation of 'brahmin' is by the sentence 'is not a brahmin'; the prescription is understood from the meaning, and there is a split in the sentence. And the negative particle is connected with its own word, expressing that which partakes of the negation. Who is that one other than a brahmin? He says: 'one not endowed with brahminhood,' and so on.

Itarasminti pasajjappaṭisepekkhe, kenaci saṃsayanimittenāti upavītadassanādinā kenaci saṃsayakāraṇena, sabbampi padaṃ sakatthe payogampati ñāṇamapekkhate, tañca ñāṇaṃ dvidhā sammāñāṇaṃ micchā ñāṇañca. Ubhayampetabrāhmaṇasaddaṃ pavattayati. Tattha sammāñāṇa pubbake abrāhmaṇasaddappayoge natthi nañssa byāpāro, na hi tattha tena kiñci karīyati. Micchāñāṇapubbake tu vijjate tassa byāpā ro [M 0.0165] tattha hi tena micchāñāṇappabhavatā parassākhyāyate, micchāñāṇaṃ cendriyahetukaṃ, vinā sadisattaṃ na bhavatīti paṭisedhe sati uttarapadatthasadiso samāsattho jāyateccāha- ‘tattha sadisattaṃ vine’ccādi. Rajjuyaṃ hi sappabuddhi sadisattā.

In the other case, that is, with respect to verbal negation, 'due to some cause of doubt' means due to some reason for doubt, such as seeing a sacred thread. Every word requires knowledge for its application to its own meaning. And that knowledge is twofold: right knowledge and wrong knowledge. Both cause the word 'abrāhmaṇa' to be applied. Therein, in the application of the word 'abrāhmaṇa' which is preceded by right knowledge, there is no operation of the negative particle 'nañ', for nothing is done by it there. But when it is preceded by wrong knowledge, its operation exists, for there, by it, another is designated through the arising of wrong knowledge. And wrong knowledge is caused by the sense faculties; without similarity, it does not arise. Therefore, when there is negation, the meaning of the compound becomes similar to the meaning of the latter term. Hence he says: 'There, without similarity,' and so on. For the cognition of a snake in a rope is due to similarity.

Payogasāmatthiyāceti abrāhmaṇamānayeccādipayogasāmatthiyā ca. Evammaññate- “yadyatra brāhmaṇamattassānayanaṃ siyā pubbapadassuccāraṇamanatthakaṃ siyā, atha na kassaci ānayanaṃ evampi sabbassevā brāhmaṇasaddassānatthakattaṃ, tasmā payogasāmatthiyāpi sadisappaṭipattī”ti.

'And from the force of usage' means from the force of usage such as in 'bring a non-brahmin'. It is thought thus: 'If here there were the bringing of a mere brahmin, the utterance of the prior member would be meaningless. And if no one is brought, even so, the entire word 'abrāhmaṇa' would be meaningless. Therefore, from the force of usage also, there is the understanding of something similar.'

Taggatāti sadisatthagatā. Yathāvuttassevā-tthassupabrūhanāya viññūvacanamupaññassati ‘atoyeva vuccate’ccādi. Ayañcettha attho “nañvacanena ivasaddena ca yaṃ yuttaṃ tadaññasmiṃ tappadatthasadise-tthe paṭipattiṃ janeti, tathāhyatthasampaccayo loke dissati ‘abrāhmaṇamānayā’ti brāhmaṇasadiso khattiyādi ānīyatīti, adhikarīyati niyujjate saddo-smintyadhikaraṇaṃ. Yathāvuttena ca byākhyānena kimiṭṭhaṃ siddhantyāha- ‘tadeva’miccādi. Keci pana uttarapadatthappadhānattamiha vaṇṇenti.

'Taggatā' means pertaining to the meaning of similarity. To elaborate on the very meaning already stated, he introduces a statement of the wise: 'Therefore it is said,' and so on. And this is the meaning here: 'That which is connected with the word 'nañ' or with the word 'iva' generates an understanding of another thing that is similar in meaning to that word. Thus a connection of meaning is seen in the world: when it is said 'Bring a non-brahmin', a khattiya or someone similar to a brahmin is brought.' 'Adhikaraṇa' (locus) is that in which a word is authorized or enjoined. And by the explanation thus stated, what desired result is accomplished? He says: 'That very thing,' and so on. Some, however, describe here the primacy of the meaning of the latter member.

Samatthavādīnanti “samattho padavidhi” (pā 2-1-1) tvevaṃ vādīnaṃ. Samattha vādīnaṃ samāso vidheyyoti sambandho, vidheyyoti vacanantarena vidheyyo, tathāhi apunageyyāti gāyanena nañssa sambandho, na tu punasaddatthena. Anokāsaṃ kāretvāti karaṇena sambandho na okāsena. Amūlāmūlaṃ gantvāti gamanena, na mūlenāti asāmatthiyaṃ. Gamakattavādinoti asāmatthiyepi yatra gamakattaṃ tattha samāso hoteva, tato gamakattañca samāsassa nibandhananti yo vadati tassetyattho. Etthāpīti apunageyyātyādopi, nanvayamapyācariyo gamakattavādī, tathāsati gamakattāiccanabhidhāya bahulādhikārāti kasmāvuttanti āha-‘so ce’ccādi.

'Samatthavādīnaṃ' means of those who hold the view 'a rule concerning a word applies to a syntactically capable word' (Pāṇini 2.1.1). The connection is that for the proponents of syntactic capability, a compound is to be enjoined. 'To be enjoined' means to be enjoined by another expression. For example, in 'apunageyya', the connection of 'nañ' is with the singing, not with the meaning of the word 'puna'. In 'anokāsaṃ kāretvā' (having made no opportunity), the connection is with the making, not with 'opportunity'. In 'amūlāmūlaṃ gantvā' (having gone without finding the root), the connection is with the going, not with 'root'. Thus there is a lack of syntactic capability. 'Of one who holds the view of expressiveness' means of one who says that even where there is a lack of syntactic capability, if there is expressiveness, a compound certainly occurs; therefore, expressiveness is also a basis for compounding. 'Here too' means in 'apunageyya', and so on. (Objection:) Surely, this teacher is also a proponent of expressiveness. That being so, why is it said 'due to the governing rule of optionality' instead of stating 'due to expressiveness'? (Reply:) He says: 'And that...' and so on.

Kehicīti vuttigganthena byavacchinnamatthaṃ dassento āha- ‘kehiciyeva [M 0.0166] na sabbehī’ti, apunageyyāti “ṭa nañssā”ti (3-74) nassaṭo, atippasaṅgābhāvatoti suttantarena samāse avihitepi anabhimatatthānampatītiyā abhāvato.

Showing the meaning delimited by the text of the vutti, he says of 'kehici' (by some): 'by some only, not by all'. In 'apunageyya', 'na' becomes 'ṭa' by 'ṭa nañssā' (3-74). 'Due to the absence of over-application' means because there is no understanding of an unintended meaning even when a compound is not enjoined by another rule.

13. Kupā

13. Kupā

Syādividhinoti kārakavibhattividhānato visuṃ itthambhūtādīsuvidhānā syādividhītisaṅkhaṃ gatassa syādividhino, asyādividhimhīti pariyudāso-natthakoti codento āha ‘nanvi’ccādi, anatthakaṃ bhaveyya… lakkhaṇādyatthānaṃ samāse guṇībhūtattā samāsato kiriyāsambandhānurūpavibhattiyatthassa padhānabhāvato, pariharati ‘nayidameva’miccādinā. “Anunā”ti (2-10) vicchāyamanunā yoge dutiyā vidhānasāmatthiyā vākyampi hoti, aññathā niccasamāse dutiyā vidhānamanatthakanti bhāvo, nigamayati tasmāiccādinā, “ku pāpatthe”ti paresaṃ gaṇapāṭho, evamuparipi “dunindāyaṃ”tyādi veditabbaṃ.

Regarding `syādividhinoti`: from the `syādividhi` (rule of `syādi`), which is so designated because it is a prescription concerning `itthambhūtādi`, etc., distinct from the prescription of case-endings related to agent (`kāraka`). The objector, stating 'If there were no `syādividhi`, this is an exclusion; it is not so,' says 'nanvi,' etc. It would be meaningless... because in a compound, the meanings of characteristics, etc., are subordinate, while the meaning of the case-ending corresponding to the connection with the action is primary. He refutes this with 'nayidameva,' etc. Regarding 'Anunā' (2-10), in connection with `vicchāyamanunā`, a sentence is also formed by the power of the prescription of the second case-ending; otherwise, the prescription of the second case-ending in an obligatory compound would be meaningless—this is the import. He concludes with 'tasmā,' etc. 'Ku pāpatthe' is the recitation in the `gaṇa` list of others; similarly, above also, 'dunindāyaṃ,' etc., should be understood.

14. Cīkri

14. Cīkri

Cīsaddoti ettha cīti iminā cīppaccayantaṃ parāmasati, cīppaccayanta saddoti attho.

Regarding 'cīsaddo': here, by 'cī,' it refers to that which ends in the suffix 'cī'; the meaning is 'a word ending in the suffix cī'.

15. Bhūsa

15. Abundantly.

Pītisambhamoti pītiyā sambhamo pītipubbikā paccuṭṭhānāsana dānādivisayā turitatā, alaṃbhutvā pariyattaṃ sampuṇṇaṃ bhutvā.

'Pītisambhamo' means the excitement of joy; it is the promptness concerning matters such as rising to greet, offering a seat, and giving, which is preceded by joy. 'Alaṃbhutvā' means having eaten sufficiently, completely.

16. Aññe

16. Aññe

Purobhūya aggatobhūya. Tirobhūya antaradhānībhūya. Anaccādhāneti imassa attho ‘upariyādhānato aññatrā’ti, ādhānaṃ patiṭṭhāpanaṃ, icchantīti pāṇiniyādayo icchanti, urasi katvā pāṇinti pāṇiṃ urasi katvā.

'Purobhūya' means having become foremost. 'Tirobhūya' means having become concealed. The meaning of 'anaccādhāne' is 'other than placing above'; 'ādhāna' means establishing. 'Icchanti' means Pāṇini and others desire. 'Urasi katvā pāṇinti' means having placed the hand upon the chest.

17. Vāne

17. In the wood.

Anekaggahaṇassa payojanaṃ vattumupasakkati ‘idhe’ccādi, vivacchitekasaṅkhyāsāmaññanti vivacchitaṃ ekasaṅkhyāya sāmaññaṃ, evaṃ maññate “yadi‘syādi [M 0.0167] syādine’ti vattumicchitekasaṅkhyāsāmaññassa pariggaho na siyā tadā ihānatthaka (maneka)ggahaṇaṃ siyā tenehāne kaggahaṇasāmatthiyāyeva ‘syādisyādine’ti vattumicchitekasaṅkhyā sāmaññampariggahitanti viññāyate”ti teneccādinā idaṃ dasseti “tena yathāvuttena pubbe vutto sabbopi samāso pubbaparānaṃ dvinnaṃyeva syādyantānaṃ hotī”ti.

He proceeds to state the purpose of including 'aneka' with 'idha,' etc. 'Vivacchitekasaṅkhyāsāmaññanti' means the generality of a single number that is desired to be expressed. Thus, it is thought: 'If there were no inclusion of the generality of a single number desired to be expressed by 'syādi syādine,' then the inclusion of 'aneka' here would be meaningless. Therefore, by the very power of the inclusion of 'aneka' here, it is understood that the generality of a single number desired to be expressed by 'syādi syādine' is included.' By 'tena,' etc., he shows this: 'Therefore, by what has been said, every compound previously mentioned is of only two terms ending in `syādi`, a preceding and a succeeding one.'

Yajjevaṃ kathaṃ ‘tadahujāto’ti bahulādhikārena visesana samāsagabbhakārakasamāsena vā sijjhati, ayaṃ aññapadatthasamāso. Catthe bahunnamiṭṭhattā tadatthañcānekaggahaṇaṃ, tena ‘hotu potu pitā puttā’ti hoti uttarapade (yoni) sambandhe parato pubbapadassa “putte”ti (3-65) suttenāttena, aññathā dvinnaṃdvinnaṃ samāse sabbattha uttarapadasambhavena “vijjāyonisambandhānamā tatra catthe”ti (3-64) “putte”ti ca suttadvayenāttena‘hotā potā pitā puttā’ti āpajjeyya. Anekanti paṭhamantattā syādītīdamevānuvattate, tenevānekaṃ syādyantamicceva vuttaṃ. Athāññattheti vutte-ññassa vākyassattheti avatvā padassecceva kasmā vuttantyāsaṅkiyā ha- ‘syādyantasse’ccādi, tassevāti sāmatthiyaladdhassa syādyanta padasseva samāso viññāyatīti sambandho.

If this is so, how is 'tadahujāto' accomplished? It is accomplished by the governing rule of `bahula` or by a `kārakasamāsa` containing a `visesanasamāsa`. This is an `aññapadatthasamāsa`. In the sense of 'ca' (`and`), because a compound of many terms is desired, the inclusion of 'aneka' is for that purpose. Therefore, 'hotu potu pitā puttā' is formed, when there is a kinship (`yoni`) relation in the subsequent member, by the lengthening of the vowel of the preceding member by the rule 'putte' (3-65). Otherwise, in a compound of two by two, wherever a subsequent member is possible, by the two rules 'vijjāyonisambandhānamā tatra catthe' (3-64) and 'putte', it would result in 'hotā potā pitā puttā'. Because 'anekaṃ' ends in the first case-ending, 'syādi' is what is carried forward. Therefore, it is said that 'anekaṃ' means 'ending in `syādi`'. Now, when 'aññatthe' is stated, having raised the doubt, 'Why is it said "of a word" and not "in the meaning of another sentence"?', he says 'syādyantassa,' etc. 'Tasseva' means the compound is understood to be of that very word ending in `syādi` which has acquired the capacity; this is the connection.

Tassa guṇā tagguṇā tasseccanenāññapadattho niddisīyate, tassa aññapadatthassa ye guṇā yāni visesanāni, tesaṃ saṃviññāṇaṃ gahaṇaṃ tagguṇasaṃviññāṇaṃ, athavā so guṇo yassa so tagguṇo, tagguṇassa tagguṇayuttassāññapadatthassasaṃviññāṇaṃ, na guṇavirahitassā(ti) tagguṇasaṃviññāṇaṃ, ettha pana ‘aññapadatthe tagguṇasaṃviññāṇaṃ pyatthī’ti paribhāsīyati, tatthāyamattho “aññapadatthe samāse-ññapadattho visesanena saha viññāyati navisesanarahito”ti, kvaci atagguṇasaṃviññāṇassāpi dassane nāpisaddo, yatrāvayavena viggaho samudāyo samāsattho tattheva tagguṇasaṃviññāṇaṃ bhavati, tagguṇasaṃviññāṇato aññaṃ atagguṇasaṃviññāṇaṃ, tasmiṃ, yatrāvayavoyeva samāsattho tatrātagguṇasaṃviññāṇaṃ.

'Tassa guṇā' means `tagguṇā` (his qualities). By this 'tassa', the meaning of another word is indicated. Whatever qualities, whatever attributes belong to that meaning of another word, the comprehension or inclusion of them is `tagguṇasaṃviññāṇa`. Alternatively, he whose quality it is, is `tagguṇa`; the comprehension of the meaning of another word endowed with that quality is `tagguṇasaṃviññāṇa`, not of one devoid of that quality. Here, however, it is stated as a general rule: 'In the meaning of another word, there is also `tagguṇasaṃviññāṇa`.' Therein, this is the meaning: 'In a compound in the meaning of another word, the meaning of the other word is understood together with its attribute, not devoid of its attribute.' The word 'api' (`also`) is used because `atagguṇasaṃviññāṇa` is also seen in some cases. Where the analysis is by the constituent part and the whole is the meaning of the compound, there `tagguṇasaṃviññāṇa` occurs. Different from `tagguṇasaṃviññāṇa` is `atagguṇasaṃviññāṇa`. In that case, where the constituent part itself is the meaning of the compound, there is `atagguṇasaṃviññāṇa`.

Ettha [M 0.0168] pana bahudhanasaddo purisassa upalakkhaṇabhāvena katattā. Abhimatoti pāṇinīyānaṃ abhimato dasannaṃ samīpe āsannā dasannamiccādivākye.

Here, however, the word 'bahudhana' is used because it serves as a characteristic of a person. 'Abhimato' means that which is favored by the Pāṇinīyas, as in the sentence 'āsannā dasannam,' meaning 'near the ten,' and so forth.

Parimāṇamevasaṅkhyeyanti parimāṇalakkhaṇameva saṅkhyeyaṃ, tañca parimāṇalakkhaṇaṃ saṅkhyeyañca.

Regarding 'parimāṇameva saṅkhyeyam' (measure itself is the countable): that which has the characteristic of measure is itself the countable; and that is both what has the characteristic of measure and what is countable.

Saṅkhyānarūpanti saṅkhyānasabhāvaṃ.

'Saṅkhyānarūpam' means the nature of counting.

Parimāṇenāti pañcasaṅkhyāya paricchijjamānena saṅkhyeyasaṅkhātena parimāṇena.

'Parimāṇena' (by measure) means by a measure designated as 'countable,' which is delimited by the number five.

Saṅkhyānavuttīti tena anativattiyamānatapparicchedaka saṅkhyānarūpa saṅkhāte saṅkhyāne vutti yassā sā saṅkhyānavutti-pañcasaṅkhyā.

'Saṅkhyānavutti' is that which has its function in counting, designated as the form of counting whose own delimiter is not to be transgressed by it; for example, the number five.

Diṭṭhanteniminā imaṃ dīpeti “yathā pañca parimāṇamesanti pañcakāti ettha parimāṇarūpo-vayavabhedasamudāyasabhāvo pakatiyattho samudāyino sakunā paccayattho, tathā tidasāti etthāpi”ti, kappaccayo pakatippaccayatthabhedasambhavena.

By this example, he illuminates this: 'Just as in 'pañcaka,' meaning 'five is their measure,' the meaning of the base (`pakati`) is the nature of an aggregate of a division of parts in the form of a measure, and the meaning of the suffix (`paccaya`) is the possessor of the aggregate, namely the birds, so too here in 'tidasa'.' The suffix 'ka' is used because of the possibility of a difference in meaning between the base and the suffix.

Keci panāti iminā pāṇinīye dasseti.

By 'keci pana' (but some), he indicates the Pāṇinīyas.

Pakatippaccayatthabhedasambhavāti iminā paresaṃ pakatippaccayatthānaṃ bhedābhāvassa icchitattā saññāyaṃ sakatthe kappaccayassa vidhānaṃ dasseti.

By 'pakatippaccayatthabhedasambhavā' (because of the possibility of a difference in meaning between the base and the suffix), he shows the prescription of the suffix 'ka' in its own meaning in the case of a proper name, because it is desired by others that there be an absence of difference between the meanings of the base and the suffix.

Syādyantassāti iminā vāsaddassa padattaṃ dasseti.

By 'syādyantassa,' he shows that the word 'vā' has the status of a `pada` (an inflected word).

Tadatthepīti tassa vāiti aññapadassa atthepi, tadattho cettha vikappattho vā siyā tadā pana dvinnaṃ gahaṇe na tiṇṇaṃ, tesantu gahaṇe na dvinnaṃ, saṃsayo vā, tadā tu saṃsayassobhayā lambanarūpattā dvevāti vutte tayo, tayovāti vutte dve apekkhīyantīti buddhivisayā pañca atthā samāsābhidheyyo honti.

'Tadatthepi' means also in the meaning of that other word, 'vā'. If that meaning here were the meaning of option, then it is the taking of two, not three; or in the taking of three, not two. Or it is doubt; then, however, because doubt has the nature of depending on both, when 'two' is said, three are expected, and when 'three' is said, two are expected. Thus, five meanings, which are the objects of cognition, become the denotation of the compound.

Nāmattenāti ruḷhināmattena, abhimato pāṇiniyānaṃ, vikappitaṃ suttantarena vibhāsā sabbanāmasaññāvidhānena.

'Nāmattena' means by being a conventional name. This is favored by the Pāṇinīyas. It is made optional by another rule, through the optional prescription of the designation 'pronoun' (`sabbanāma`).

Avayavadhammenāti avayavasaṅkhātena sabhāvena.

'Avayavadhammena' (by the property of the part) means by the nature designated as 'part'.

Nanu [M 0.0169] ca samānādhikaraṇānaṃ bahubbīhi vutto pāṇiniyehi ‘pañcahi bhuttamasseti byadhikaraṇānaṃ na siyā’ti, tathā paṭhamatthaṃ vajjetvā sabbavibhatyatthesu iṭṭho ‘vuṭṭhe devegatoccatra vuṭṭhadevoti na siyā’ti tasmā kathamatra byadhikaraṇānaṃ paṭhamatthe samāso vaṇṇīyateccāsaṅkiyāha-‘byadhikaraṇānampi’ccādi, byadhikaraṇānampi yathābhidhānaṃsamāsasabbhāvato pañcahi bhuttamassetyādo bahulādhikārā anabhidhānato vā na bhavissati, tatoyeva ca pañca bhutta vanto-sseti samānādhikaraṇānampi kvaci na bhavissati, tathā paṭhamatthepi kvaci na bhavissati vuṭṭhe deve gato’ti. Tulyayoge gamyamāneti attho.

But is it not stated by the Pāṇinians that a `bahubbīhi` compound is of terms sharing the same case-relation, and so for terms with different case-relations, as in 'pañcahi bhuttamassa', it would not be formed? Similarly, it is desired in the meanings of all case-endings except that of the first, so that in 'vuṭṭhe deve gato', 'vuṭṭhadevo' would not be formed. Therefore, how is a compound of terms with different case-relations in the meaning of the first case-ending described here? Raising this doubt, he says, 'byadhikaraṇānampi,' etc. Even for terms with different case-relations, because the existence of a compound is according to usage, in cases like 'pañcahi bhuttamassa', it will not occur due to the governing rule of `bahula` or due to non-expression. For that very reason, even for terms sharing the same case-relation, as in 'pañca bhuttavanto assa', it will sometimes not occur. Similarly, even in the meaning of the first case-ending, it will sometimes not occur, as in 'vuṭṭhe deve gato'. The meaning is 'when an equal connection is understood'.

Aññatracāti tulyayogato-ññatra salomakotyādīsu ca, vijjamānāni lomānyassa, vijjamānā pakkhā assāti viggaho. Upasaṅkhyāto “syādyadhikāre-tthikhīrādīnamupasaṅkhyāna”nti (2-2-24-vā) sabhāvato eva nivatto na suttantarato, gatatthassāpi hi payoge anavaṭṭhānaṃ siyā piṭṭhapesane viya, kathañcarahi brāhmaṇe bahū ānaya, ahaṃ pacāmīti nāvassamevaṃ payogo, katthaci pana vacanasiliṭṭhatādippayojane sati hoteva.

"Elsewhere" means apart from instances of equal applicability, and in cases such as 'salomakoṭi' and the like, the derivation being "hairs exist for him," "wings exist for him." It is enumerated—"there is an enumeration in the section on sya, etc., for thikhīra and the like"—thus, it is excluded by its very nature, not by another rule. For even in the usage of what is already understood, there can be non-restriction, as in the case of 'piṭṭhapesana.' How then? For example, "bring many brahmins, I will cook"—such usage is not necessary. But in some cases, when there is a purpose such as elegance of expression, it does indeed occur.

Kaṇṭhe sambhavoti kāḷassa kaṇṭhe sambhavo. Ṭṭhasaddatthoti kaṇṭhaṭṭhasadde ṭṭhasaddattho. Oṭṭhasaddova mukhavuttītyanena gammamānatthattā dutiyassa mukhasaddassāppayogamāha, tasmā oṭṭhova mukhamassāti viggayha oṭṭhamukhoti samāso, na ca pāṇi pāṇyantarassa mukhaṃ, mukheneva ca pāṇimukhassa sadisattaṃ pasiddhanti sāmatthiyā oṭṭhamukhamiva mukhamassetyattheva tiṭṭhate, upanyasyantetyupanyāsā, visayadassanatthāti iminā’kaṇṭhe kāḷo yassā’tyādīkameva vākyanti dasseti. Samudāye vikārecāti samudāyasambandhe vikārasambandhe ca. Taṃsamāsassāti tassā chaṭṭhiyā samāsassa, tadabhidhāyinanti saṅghāta vikārābhidhāyīnaṃ, kesānaṃ saṅghāto iccādi paresaṃ vākyaṃ. Dhātuto jātaṃ dhātujaṃ, uttarapadaṃ patitasaddādi, tassa payogoti patitasaddassa payogo.

"It arises in the throat" means it arises in the throat of Kāḷa. "The meaning of the sound 'ṭṭha'" means the meaning of the sound 'ṭṭha' in the word 'kaṇṭhaṭṭha' (standing in the throat). The word 'oṭṭha' (lip) itself has the sense of 'mouth'; by this, because the meaning is understood, he states the non-usage of a second word 'mouth.' Therefore, by analyzing 'the lip is its mouth,' the compound 'oṭṭhamukha' is formed. And a hand is not the mouth of another hand, and the similarity of a 'hand-mouth' is established only through the mouth itself; thus, by implication, it stands only in the sense of 'its mouth is like a lip-mouth.' "They introduce" means introductions. "For the purpose of showing the object"—by this, he shows that "in whose throat is black," etc., is indeed the sentence. "In the aggregate and in the modification" means in relation to the aggregate and in relation to the modification. "Of that compound" means of the compound of that sixth case ending. "Denoting that" refers to those denoting aggregates and modifications. "The collection of hairs," etc., is the statement of others. "Born from an element" is 'dhātuja.' The latter member is the word 'patita' (fallen), etc.; 'its usage' means the usage of the word 'patita'.

“Nañsmātthyatthāna”nti (2-2-24) [M 0.0170] vāttikaṃ, etanāha-‘ña kārānu bandhā’iccādi. Pāṇiniyā tu avijjamānasaddo nañsamāso, padantare nāssa bahubbīhi vottarapadalopo, avijjamānā puttāssa aputtovijjamānaputtoti sādhenti, icchate pāṇinīyehi… dakkhiṇapubbā saddānaṃ nānatthattā byadhikaraṇattā, vacanepīti sutte vijjamānepi, aya maññapadatthasamāso parehi bahubbīhīti vuccati tathāhi bahavo vihayo yassa so bahubbīhi, yathā bahubbīhīti aññapadatthappadhāno tathā ayampi.

The Vāttika (2-2-24) is 'nañsmātthyatthānaṃ'; by this, he says 'ña kārānu bandhā,' etc. According to the Pāṇinīyas, however, the word 'avijjamāna' is a nañ-compound. With another word, this is not a bahubbīhi, or there is elision of the latter member. They form 'aputto' from 'avijjamānā puttā assa' (one whose sons are non-existent), not 'avijjamānaputto'; this is desired by the Pāṇinīyas... because the words 'dakkhiṇa' and 'pubba' have different meanings and are in different cases, even though they are present in the rule. This compound, where the meaning of another word is primary (aññapadatthasamāso), is called a bahubbīhi by others. For, 'he who has much rice' is 'bahuvīhi'; just as 'bahuvīhi' has the meaning of another word as primary, so too does this one.

19. Catthe

19. In the sense of 'ca'.

Samuccīti piṇḍīkaraṇaṃ, ko soti āha- ‘sādhanameka’miccādi. Ekaṃ sādhanaṃ ekaṃ kiriyaṃ vā paṭicca cīyamānatāti sambandho, kesanti āha- ‘kiriyāsādhanāna’nti, kenāti āha- ‘attarūpabhedenā”ti.
