Tattha devadatto bhuñjati tiṭṭhati pacaticāti sādhanampaṭicca kiriyānaṃ attarūpabhedena cīyamānatā veditabbā, dhave ca khadire ca palāse ca chindāti kiriyampaṭicca attarūpabhedena sādhanānaṃ cīyamānatā veditabbā.

'Samucciti' is collection, 'piṇḍīkaraṇaṃ.' What is that? He says, 'one means,' etc. The connection is that it is accumulated depending on one means or one action. Of what? He says, 'of actions and means.' By what? He says, 'by the distinction of their own forms.' Therein, it should be understood that actions, such as in 'Devadatta eats, stands, and cooks,' are accumulated with respect to a single means, distinguished by their own forms. Similarly, it should be understood that means, such as in 'he cuts dhava, khadira, and palāsa trees,' are accumulated with respect to a single action, distinguished by their own forms.

Soti samuccayo bhavatīti seso, kesanti āha- ‘tulya balāna’miccādi.

That is 'samuccaya'; 'comes to be' is what is understood. Of what? He says, 'of equal strength,' etc.

Tulyabalānanti iminā visuṃ padhānabhāvena kiriyābhisambandhā aññamaññānapekkhattamāha.

By 'of equal strength,' he states their mutual independence, which is due to their connection with the action with each having separate prominence.

Aniyatakkamayogapajjānanti kamo ca yogapajjañca, aniyataṃ kamayogapajjaṃ yesaṃ saddānaṃ tesaṃ, yathetyādinā tatthodāharaṇaṃ dasseti, etthāyamadhippāyo “ettha gavādīnaṃ visuṃ padhānabhāvenānayanakiriyābhisambandhā tulyabalatā gavādīnaṃ vuttakkameneva nayanābhāvā aniyatakkamatā gavādīnaṃ yugapadi nayanābhāvā aniyata yogapajjatā ca hoti, tathā aññaṃ tādisampī”ti. Anu pacchā padhānānurodhena (cayanaṃ) anvācayo, taṃ byañjayati ‘yatthe’ccādi, tadanurodhenāti tadanuguṇena, udāharati ‘yathe’ccādi, bhikkhāgamanamettha padhānamantaraṅgattā[M 0.0171], netaraṃ bahiraṅgattā, taṃ karaṇe yadi gāvopi passati tāpyānayati, ettha tu gossānayanaṃ bhikkhāṭanamapekkhate, netaramitarassa… vināpi tena tadanuṭṭhānato. Itarassa itarena yo go itaretarayogo, so ca etādisoti āha- ‘aññamaññe’ccādi.

'Aniyatakkamayogapajjānaṃ' is analyzed as: 'kamo ca yogapajjañca' (sequence and simultaneity); 'aniyataṃ kamayogapajjaṃ yesaṃ saddānaṃ tesaṃ' (of those words whose sequence and simultaneity are indeterminate). He shows an example there with 'yathā,' etc. Here, the intended meaning is: 'Here, for cows, etc., there is equal strength due to the connection of the act of leading with their individual prominence. Because leading does not occur in the order stated, there is indeterminate sequence for the cows, etc.; and because leading does not occur simultaneously, there is indeterminate simultaneity. Similarly, for other such cases.' 'Anvācayo' is subsequent (anu, pacchā) collection (cayanaṃ) in accordance with the primary item. This is expressed by 'where,' etc. 'According to that' means in conformity with that. He gives an example with 'yathā,' etc. Here, going for alms is primary because it is internal; the other is not, because it is external. In doing that, if one also sees a cow, one also leads it. Here, however, the leading of the cow is dependent on the alms-round, not the other on the one, because without that, this is not undertaken. The connection (yogo) of one with the other is 'itarītarayogo'; that it is of such a nature, he says, 'mutual,' etc.

Avayavappadhāno cāti sābhāvikābhidhānasāmatthiyenāputhubhūto ca, vuttivayena sāriputtasaddo moggallānattho hoti moggallānasaddo sāriputtatthopīti aññamaññatthe padhānato yugapadyadhikaraṇavacane sati cattha samāsoti so-yamadhikaraṇa samudāyo ubhayapadānugataubhayatthavasena catubbidhopi yugapadi buddhiyā gayhamāno kadāci ubbhūtāvayavabhedo teneva sābhāvikābhidhānasāmatthiyeneccevamavayavappadhāno ca, nanu ca jananamaraṇānīti viruddhānaṃ kathamekenābhidhānanti vuccate- sabbopi saddo payujjamāno (itarī) tarenāvadhāraṇaṃ vattate, tena ekeko saddo ekekassatthassa vācako, tathāpi yathā sāriputtamoggallānāti ettha bahuvacanassaññathānupapattiyā yugapadyadhikaraṇavacanatā hotī, tathātrāpi bahuvacanassaññathānupapattilakkhaṇena sāmatthiyena ekenāpyabhidhānaṃ hoti. Iti hetumhi, yato evamavayavappadhāno tatoti attho.

And 'primary in its members' means that it is not separate, due to the natural capacity of expression. In the context of a compound expression, the word 'Sāriputta' has the meaning of 'Moggallāna,' and the word 'Moggallāna' also has the meaning of 'Sāriputta.' Thus, when there is a simultaneous expression of the locus due to the prominence of the mutual meaning, it is a 'cattha' compound. This collection of loci, being fourfold according to both terms and both meanings, being grasped simultaneously by the intellect, sometimes has the distinction of its members made manifest due to that very natural capacity of expression, and thus is primary in its members. But how can contradictories like 'birth and death' be expressed by a single term? It is said: Every word, when used, functions by way of determination from the other. Therefore, each word is expressive of a single meaning. Yet, just as in 'Sāriputta-Moggallāna,' a simultaneous expression of the locus arises due to the unsuitability of the plural otherwise, so too here, expression by a single term occurs due to the capacity characterized by the unsuitability of the plural otherwise. 'Iti' is in the sense of reason; the meaning is 'because it is thus primary in its members, therefore...'

Bahuttāti kiñcāpi vākye nesaṃ vākyenevesaṃ (potthake) visuṃ bahvatthatā, na hi sāriputtamānayāti vutte moggallānassāpi sampaccayo bhavati, tathāpi yato vuttivisaye sahabhūtānamevesaṃ visuṃ bahvatthatā, tato tattha vacanīyassa atthassa saṅkhyātedena bahuttaṃ. Samāharaṇaṃ piṇḍīkaraṇavasena saṃharaṇaṃ samāhāro, so cevaṃ veditabboti dassetumāha ‘aññamaññe’ccādi.

'Plurality' means that although in a sentence there is no separate plurality of meanings for them—for when it is said 'bring Sāriputta,' there is no understanding of Moggallāna as well—yet because in the sphere of the compound expression, there is indeed a separate plurality for them as co-existent things, therefore, the plurality of the meaning to be expressed is indicated by number. 'Samāharaṇaṃ' is 'samāhāra' (collection), which is a gathering in the sense of making into a single mass. To show that this should be understood thus, he says, 'mutual,' etc.

Ettha ca kiñcāpi itarītarayogassa samāhārassa ca bhāvarūpattā adabbarūpatā, tathāpītarītarayoge tu yathā guṇavaca nānaṃ [M 0.0172] sukkaṃ vatthaṃ sukko kambalo sukkā gāvīti nissayabhedato liṅgavacanasiddhi, tathā taddhammānamabhidhānato nissayato liṅgavacana siddhi veditabbā, saṃhatippadhānattācekavacananti yadā bahunnaṃ samudāyo tirohitāvayavabhedo saṃghāto pakkamīyate, tadā samāhārocceva saṃhatippadhānattā ekavacanaṃ hotīti attho. Tadanuṭṭhānatoti tassa karaṇato. Byatikaro missatā, byatikaraṃ dasseti pāṇiccādinā, paccekaṃ parisamattiyaṃ vākyabahuttaṃ dasseti ‘tattha hiccādi.

And here, although both the mutual connection (itarītarayoga) and the aggregate (samāhāra) are non-substantive because they are of the nature of a state, still, in the case of a mutual connection, just as for adjectives the gender and number are established from the difference of the substrate—as in 'a white cloth,' 'a white blanket,' 'a white cow'—so too should the establishment of gender and number be understood from the substrate, due to the expression of those properties. And 'singular number due to the prominence of the collection' means that when a collection of many things, a mass whose distinction of members is concealed, is intended, then it is an aggregate, and thus, due to the prominence of the collection, the singular number applies. 'Tadanuṭṭhānato' means 'from the performance of that.' 'Byatikaro' is mixture. He shows mixture with 'pāṇi,' etc. He shows the plurality of sentences in the completion of each one with 'there, indeed,' etc.

Cakkhuñca sotañca, mukhañca nāsikā ca, hanu ca gīvā ca, chavi ca maṃsañca lohitañca, nāmañca rūpañca, jarā ca maraṇañcāti viggayha samāso, “samāhāre napuṃsaka”nti (3-20) sabbattha napuṃsakaliṅgaṃ, syādimhi mukha nāsikantiādīsu “syādīsu rasso”ti (3-23) rasso. Alabhatā gomukhaṃ ḍiṇḍimo bherivisesā, āḷambaraṃ paṇavo, murajo mudaṅgo, maddavo mudaṅgo. Maddavavādanaṃ paṇavavādanañca sippamassa maddaviko pāṇaviko, sammaṃ kaṃsatāḷaṃ, tāḷaṃ hatthatāḷaṃ, alasatā ca āḷambaro ca, murajo ca, gomukho ca, saṅkho ca ḍiṇḍimo ca, maddaviko ca, pāṇaviko ca, gītañca vāditañca, sammañca tāḷañcāti viggaho. Yugassa hitā yoggā goṇā, tesamidaṃ yoggaṃ kasikammaṃ, tassa aṅgaṃ. Tenāha- ‘kasibhaṇḍāna’nti, phālokasako, pācanaṃ patodo, yugo ca naṅgalañcāti viggaho. Piṇḍamāyudhaviseso, asi ca satti ca tomarañca piṇḍañcāti viggaho. Cammaṃ saravāraṇaphalakaṃ, kalāpo tūṇīraṃ, paharaṇañca āvaraṇañcāti viggaho. Ahi ca nakulo ca, bīḷāro ca mūsiko ca, kāko ca ulūko ca, nāgo ca supaṇṇocāti viggaho. Saṅkhyā ca parimāṇañca saṅkhyāparimāṇaṃ, tattha parimāṇasaññānaṃ yathādīgho ca majjhimo ca dīghamajjhimaṃ. Ekakañca dukañcāti viggaho, dukatikādīsupi esevanayo.

The eye and the ear; the mouth and the nose; the jaw and the neck; the skin, flesh, and blood; name and form; old age and death—this is the analysis of the compound. By 'samāhāre napuṃsaka' (3-20), the neuter gender applies everywhere. In 'mukha-nāsika,' etc., in the syādi declension, the vowel is shortened by 'syādīsu rasso' (3-23). The gomukha is a kind of drum, the ḍiṇḍima is a special type of drum, the āḷambara is a paṇava, the muraja is a mudaṅga, the maddava is a mudaṅga. Playing the maddava and playing the paṇava are the skills of the maddavika and pāṇavika. The samma is a cymbal, the tāḷa is hand-clapping. The alasatā, the āḷambara, the muraja, the gomukha, the conch, the ḍiṇḍima, the maddavika, the pāṇavika, singing, instrumental music, the samma, and the tāḷa—this is the analysis. Oxen suitable for the yoke are 'yogga' oxen; their work, plowing, is 'yogga,' and it is a part of that. Therefore, he says, 'agricultural implements.' The plowshare, the goad, the yoke, and the plow—this is the analysis. The piṇḍa is a special type of weapon. The sword, the spear, the javelin, and the piṇḍa—this is the analysis. Leather is a shield for warding off arrows. The kalāpa is a quiver. Striking and covering—this is the analysis. The snake and the mongoose; the cat and the rat; the crow and the owl; the nāga and the supaṇṇa—this is the analysis. Number and measure are 'saṅkhyāparimāṇa.' Therein, for the designations of measure, for example, 'long' and 'medium' become 'dīghamajjhima.' One and two—this is the analysis; the same method applies to 'dukatikādi' (two, three, etc.).

Khuddajantu siyā- naṭṭhi, athavā khuddakova yo;

Sataṃ vā pasate yesaṃ, keci ānakulā api.

A tiny creature may be one that has no bones, or one that is simply small; of which some produce a hundred offspring, and some even many families.

Kīṭo ca pataṅgo ca, kuntho ca kipilliko ca, ḍaṃso ca makaso ca, makkhikā ca kipillikācāti viggaho. Pacanacaṇḍālāti o rabbhikādīnaṃ [M 0.0173] ruḷhīsaññā. Urabbhe hantvā jīvatīti orabbhiko, evaṃ sesesu. Sānaṃ sunakhaṃ pacatīti sapāko, venā tacchakā, rathakārā cammakārā. Sādhāraṇā samānā, caraṇasaddo- yaṃ idha gayhatīti sambandho, yathā sakamajjhayanāya carīyanti vatānyetesūti caraṇāni, kaṭhādivājhānyajjhayanāni sākhāsaññakāni. Yasmā etehi carati ariyasāvako gacchati amataṃ disaṃ, tasmā caraṇāni sīlādayo paṇṇarasa dhammā. Tenāha- ‘kaṭhādīhī’tiādi, kaṭhādīhīti pasiddhivasena kamātikkamenāpi vuttaṃ, tato ādisaddena atisādayo gayhanti. Atisena bhāradvājena kaṭhena vuttaṃ vidantyadhīyanti vāti “aññasmi”ti (4-121) ṇo, “lopo”ti (4-123) lopo atisā bhāradvājā kaṭhā. Kalāpinā vuttaṃ vidantyadhīyanti vāti, teneva ṇo, kalāpā, kaṭhā ādi yesaṃ te kaṭhādayo, tehi ajjhenavisese ca purise ca upacārāti sambandho.

An insect and a grasshopper, a grub and an ant, a gadfly and a mosquito, a fly and a small ant—this is the analysis. Terms such as ‘Pacana’ and ‘Caṇḍāla’ are conventional designations for those like sheep-butchers. One who lives by killing sheep is called a sheep-butcher; similarly for the rest. One who cooks dogs is called a dog-cooker; basket-makers, carpenters, chariot-makers, and leather-workers. ‘Sādhāraṇā’ means ‘common,’ ‘samānā’ means ‘similar.’ The word ‘caraṇa’ is taken here in this connection: as observances are practiced in them for one’s own study, they are called ‘caraṇāni,’ such as the Kaṭha and other studies, which are known as branches. Because a noble disciple conducts himself by these, he goes to the deathless direction; therefore, the fifteen qualities, beginning with virtue, are called ‘caraṇa.’ Therefore it is said: ‘by the Kaṭha and others,’ etc. ‘By the Kaṭha and others’ is stated in a well-known manner, even out of sequence. From that, the word ‘ādi’ includes the Atisā and others. ‘Atisā,’ ‘Bhāradvājā,’ ‘Kaṭhā’ are those who know or study what was spoken by Atisa, Bhāradvāja, and Kaṭha, by the rule ‘aññasmi’ (4-121) which gives ‘ṇo,’ and by ‘lopo’ (4-123) which gives elision. What was spoken by Kalāpin, they know or study, by that same ‘ṇo,’ thus ‘Kalāpā.’ ‘Kaṭhādayo’ are those who have Kaṭha as their beginning. The application is in relation to both the specific study and the person.

Sīlādayotiādisaddena indriyasaṃvarādayo gayhanti. Sīlañca paññāṇañca, samatho ca vipassanā ca vijjā ca caraṇañcāti viggaho. Ekato ajjhayanametesūti ekajjhayanāni, pakaṭhāni vacanāni pāvacanāni saddhammo, ekajjhayanāni ca tāni pāvacanāni ca tesaṃ, dīgho ca dīghāgamo ca majjhimo ca majjhimāgamo ca, ekuttaro ca aṅguttarāgamo ca saṃyuttāgamo ca, khandhako ca vibhaṅgocāti viggaho.

By the word 'ādi' in ‘sīlādayo,’ restraint of the senses and the like are included. Virtue and wisdom; serenity and insight; knowledge and conduct—this is the analysis. Because these are studied together, they are called ‘ekajjhayanāni.’ Excellent statements are ‘pāvacanāni,’ which is the good Dhamma. And those ‘ekajjhayanāni’ and ‘pāvacanāni’ of theirs are: the Long Discourses and the Long Collection, the Middle Length Discourses and the Middle Length Collection, the Numerical Discourses and the Numerical Collection, the Connected Collection, the Khandhaka, and the Vibhaṅga—this is the analysis.

Tesanti iminā liṅgavisesānanti chaṭṭhiyantataṃ dīpeti, itthī ca pumā ca, dāsī ca dāso ca, cīvarañca piṇḍapāto ca senāsanañca gilānapaccayo bhesajjaparikkhāro ca, tiṇañca kaṭṭho ca sākhā ca palāso cāti viggaho. Cheko dakkho, pubbā ca parācātiādinā viggaho.

By ‘tesaṃ,’ it indicates the sixth case ending of ‘liṅgavisesānaṃ.’ A woman and a man; a female slave and a male slave; robes and almsfood, lodging, and medicine as a requisite for the sick; grass, sticks, branches, and leaves—this is the analysis. ‘Cheko’ means ‘skillful,’ ‘dakkho’ means ‘expert.’ The analysis is as in ‘the former and the latter,’ etc.

Pubbadakkhiṇantiādīsu “byañjane dīgharassā”ti (1-33) rasso. Kāso ca kuso ca usiro ca bīraṇañca, muñjañca babbajañcāti viggaho. Khadiro ca palāsocātiādinā ca, gajo ca gavajo cātiādinā ca, hatthī ca goca asso ca vaḷavācāti ca, haṃso ca balāvā cātiādinā ca, bako ca balākācāti ca. Hiraññañca suvaṇṇo ca, maṇi ca saṅkho ca muttā ca veḷuriyo ca jātarūpañca rajatañcāti ca, sāli ca [M 0.0174] yavakocātiādinā ca, sākañca suvañcātiādināca, kāsiyo ca kosalācātiādinā ca viggaho, janapadavācinā ca bahuvacanantā.

In phrases like ‘Pubbadakkhiṇa,’ etc., the vowel is shortened according to the rule ‘byañjane dīgharassā’ (1-33). Kāsa and kusa and usira and bīraṇa, muñja and babbaja—this is the analysis. Khadira and palāsa and so on; gaja and gavaja and so on; hatthi and go and assa and vaḷavā and so on; haṃsa and balāvā and so on; baka and balākā and so on. Hirañña and suvaṇṇa; maṇi and saṅkha and muttā and veḷuriya and jātarūpa and rajata and so on; sāli and yavako and so on; sāka and suva and so on; kāsiyo and kosalā and so on—this is the analysis; and these are place-names ending in the plural.

Ekavīsaticcādino ekañca taṃ vīsaticāti visesanasamāso vā siyā, ekañca vīsati ca ekavīsatīti catthasamāso vā, samāhāre napuṃsakattantu na pappoti, “nānusāsanīyaṃ liṅgaṃ sokanissayattā liṅgasse”ti loke napuṃsakaliṅgassehānabhidhānato napuṃsakaliṅgaṃ na bhavissatītyadhippāyo, sabhāparisāyāti ñāpakato vā samāhāre napuṃsakaliṅgamatra byabhicaratīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

The term ‘ekavīsati,’ etc., can be either a descriptive compound (visesanasamāso) meaning ‘one, and that twenty,’ or a coordinate compound (catthasamāso) meaning ‘one and twenty.’ But the neuter gender in a collective sense is not obtained, because, as stated in the world, ‘gender is not to be determined by rule, since gender is dependent on usage,’ the neuter gender will not occur here due to its non-specification. This is the intended meaning. Alternatively, from the indication of ‘sabhāparisā,’ it should be understood that the neuter gender deviates here in the collective sense.

Pubbappayogo-bhimatoti upasajjanasaññakassa syādīti paṭhamāya niddiṭṭhassa samāse pubbanipāto “upasajjanaṃ pubba”miccanena (2-2-31) iṭṭho kamassa padhānabhāvena vattumiṭṭhattāti “syādisyādinekattha”nti (3-1) ettha syādīti paṭhamāniddiṭṭhassāsaṅkhyādino pubbamavaṭṭhānato syādineti tatiyāniddiṭṭhassa pacchāvaṭṭhānato “syādisyādinā”ti sutte paṭipāṭiyā padhānabhāvena vattumiṭṭhattā.

The anterior usage is preferred because the anterior placement in a compound of the element designated as ‘upasajjana’ and specified in the first case as ‘syādi’ is desired by the rule ‘upasajjanaṃ pubba’ (2-2-31), as it is desired for the sequence to be stated in a primary role. And in the rule ‘syādisyādinekattha’ (3-1), because the ‘syādi’ specified in the first case is positioned before the non-numeral, and the ‘syādina’ specified in the third case is positioned after, it is desired for the sequence in the rule ‘syādisyādinā’ to be stated in a primary role.

Parappayogo-bhimatoti heṭṭhā vuttasuttena pubbanipāte patte “rājadantādīsu para”ntīminā (2-2-30) paranipāto-bhimato, vacanenāti- “bahula”nti vacanena, pubbakā layuttassa parappayogo-bhimatoti rājadantādipāṭhato evā-bhimato.

The posterior usage is preferred because, when anterior placement would otherwise be obtained by the rule mentioned below, posterior placement is preferred by this rule: ‘rājadantādīsu paraṃ’ (2-2-30). This is by the word, that is, by the word ‘bahulaṃ.’ The posterior usage of the earlier element is preferred precisely from the reading of ‘rājadantādi’ itself.

Kamampaccanādarāti iminā padhānabhāvenā-kkamassa vattumiṭṭhattamāha. Saro ādi yassa taṃ sarādi, saṅkho ca dundubhi ca vīṇā ca, udukkhalañca musalo ca, dhanapati ca rāmo ca kesavocāti viggaho. Jaṃdaṃsaddā jāyāsaddasamānatthā asaṅkhyā-jañca pati ca, dañca paticāti viggaho, avantayo ca assakāca, aggi ca indocāti viggaho, taṃnivāsimhi gahite avanti ca assakocāti ekattenapi viggaho vattati. Dvandasamāso- yaṃ dvandasadisattā dvando, dve ca dve ca padāni dvandānīti hi ubhayatthappadhāno- yaṃ dvandasaddo.

By 'disregarding the sequence,' it states that it is desirable for a non-sequential order to be stated as primary. ‘Sarādi’ is that which has sound as its beginning. A conch and a drum and a lute; a mortar and a pestle; Dhanapati and Rāma and Kesava—this is the analysis. The words ‘jaṃ’ and ‘daṃ’ are similar in meaning to the word ‘jāyā.’ ‘Asaṅkhyā-jaṃ’ and ‘pati,’ and ‘daṃ’ and ‘pati’—this is the analysis. Avanti and Assaka; Aggī and Inda—this is the analysis. When referring to their inhabitants, the analysis also holds as ‘Avanti’ and ‘Assaka’ in the singular. This Dvanda compound is called ‘dvanda’ because it resembles a pair. Indeed, because ‘dve ca dve ca padāni dvandānīti’ (two and two words are pairs), this word ‘dvanda’ is primary in both members.

21. Saṅkhyā

21. Number

Atha “samāhāre napuṃsaka”nti (3-20) vijjamāne kiṃ “saṅkhyādī” ti iminā [M 0.0175] satthagāravakarenāti āsaṅkiya codeti ‘nanuce’ccādi. Tathāhiccādinā “samāhāre napuṃsaka”nteva sijjhanaṃ samattheti. Yathāvuttacodanācālane parādhippāyaṃ parikappento’catthe’tiādimāha.

Then, while the rule 'samāhāre napuṃsaka' (3-20) exists, one raises an objection with 'nanu ce,' etc., questioning the purpose of this rule 'saṅkhyādī,' which shows great respect for the Teacher. With 'tathāhi,' etc., one supports the position that the result is accomplished by 'samāhāre napuṃsaka' alone. While refuting the aforementioned objection and imagining the other's intention, he says 'catthe,' etc.

Neti iminā catthetiādinā kataparikappanā na sijjhatīti dasseti, tattha hetumāha- ‘sambandhassa purisādhīnattā’ti, saticeccādinā ‘samāhāre napuṃsaka’ntettha visesanaggahaṇe payojanaṃ vatvā ‘saṅkhyādī’ti imassa niratthakattameva thirīkaroti.

By this, it is shown that the contrived notion, 'in the sense of ca,' etc., is not established. Therein, he states the reason: 'because the connection is dependent on the person.' With 'sati ce' etc., having stated the purpose for taking the qualifier in 'the neuter in a collective sense,' he firmly establishes the very meaninglessness of this 'saṅkhyādī'.

Payojaneti lāghavappayojane;

Sambandhīyatīti visesanaggahaṇaṃ sambandhīyati;

Etthāti etasmiṃ ‘saṅkhyādī’sutte;

Tanneti iminā yathāvuttaṃ codanaṃ nivatteti.

'Payojane' means for the purpose of brevity. 'Sambandhīyati' means the taking of the qualifier is connected. 'Ettha' means in this 'saṅkhyādī' sutta. 'Tanne' means by this, he refutes the aforementioned objection.

‘Saṅkhyādī’ti suttassa sātthakattamāha- ‘catthasamāsānantara’miccādinā. Ekattabyapadeso kātabboti “saṅkhyāpubbo digū”ti (2-1-52) saṅkhyāpubbassa samāsassa digusaññaṃ vidhāya tadatthassa “digurekavacana”ntīminā (2-4-1) ekattabyapadeso parehi viya kātabbo.

He states the meaningfulness of the 'Saṅkhyādī' sutta with 'after the compound in the sense of ca,' etc. The designation of singularity should be made. Having prescribed the designation 'digu' for a compound preceded by a numeral by the rule 'saṅkhyāpubbo digu' (Pāṇ. 2.1.52), the designation of singularity for its meaning should be made by this rule 'digurekavacana' (Pāṇ. 2.4.1), just as it is by others.

Samāharaṇaṃ samāhāroti iminā bhāvasādhano-yaṃ samāhārasaddo. Yadi samāharīyatīti samāhāroti kammasādhano siyā, tadā pañca kumāriyo samāhaṭāti vākyassātthe vutti siyā pañcakumārītyettha sakapadatthappadhānattā bahuvacanaṃ siyā “ghāpassāntassāppadhānassā”ti (3-24) appadhānarassattañca na siyā… samāhaṭānameva kumārīnaṃ padhānattā, tasmā pañca gāvo sa māhaṭātyetasmiṃ vākye samāsova natthi kammasādhanassānupagamato. Pañcannaṃ gunnaṃ samāhāro, catunnaṃ pathānaṃ samāhāroti vākye pana atthi, samāhārassekattā tu sataṃ yūthaṃ vananti ettha viya sābhāvikamekavacanaṃ siddhameveti viññāpeti.

By 'a collecting is a collection (samāhāra),' this word 'samāhāra' is derived in the sense of an action. If 'samāhāra' were derived in the sense of the object of action, as 'that which is collected,' then the compound would have the meaning of the sentence 'five maidens are collected.' In 'pañcakumārī,' because the meaning of its own constituent words would be primary, there would be the plural, and the shortening prescribed for a non-primary member by 'ghāpassāntassāppadhānassa' (Kacc. 324) would not occur, because the collected maidens themselves would be primary. Therefore, in the sentence 'five cows are collected,' there is no such compound, because the derivation in the sense of the object of action is not accepted. However, in the sentences 'a collection of five cows' and 'a collection of four paths,' it does exist. But, he explains, because the collection is a single entity, the singular is naturally established, as in 'a herd of a hundred roams the forest.'

22. Kvace

22. Sometimes

Kvacisaddassa [M 0.0176] payoganiyamanattho “paro kvicī”ti (1-27) ettha vuttanayena veditabbo. Avisesena udāharaṇepīti paresaṃ viya “chāyā”ti (2-2-73) suttayitvā vikappena ‘(kuḍḍacchāya) kuḍḍacchāyāti ca “bāhulle”ti (caṃ, 2-2-74) suttayitvā niccaṃ ‘ucchucchāyaṃ salabhacchāya’nti ca nodāharitvā sāmaññena ‘salabhacchāyaṃ sakuntacchāya’nti udāharaṇe dassitepi. Aññatthāti bahulabhāvato aññattha. Viggahasamattassāti viggahasāmaññassa, yathāsambhavanti pāsādassa chāyāiccādinā sambhavānatikkamena, saddāti saddato parāya.

The purpose of regulating the use of the word 'kvaci' should be understood according to the method stated in 'paro kvicī' (Kacc. 27). This applies even when a general example is shown, such as 'salabhacchāyaṃ' and 'sakuntacchāyaṃ,' without giving specific examples like others do—who, having formulated the rule 'chāyā' (Pāṇ. 2.2.73), give optional forms like 'kuḍḍacchāya' and 'kuḍḍacchāyā,' and, having formulated the rule 'bāhulle' (Cāndra 2.2.74), give invariable forms like 'ucchucchāyaṃ' and 'salabhacchāyaṃ.' 'Aññattha' means elsewhere, due to abundance. 'Viggahasamattassa' means of the generality of the analysis. 'Yathāsambhavaṃ' means without exceeding what is possible, as in 'pāsādassa chāyā,' etc. 'Saddā' means apart from the word.

23. Syādi

23. Syādi

Nanuceccādinā vuttaṃ codanaṃ nisedheti ‘tanne’ti. Tattha kāraṇamāha- ‘ghasaññattā’tyādi. Aghonanti ghaokāravajjitānaṃ, nanu itthi yamākāro gho, tathāsati napuṃsake so (na siyāti) parikappeti ‘napuṃsakattā ghattameva natthīti cedi’ti. Tampi neti yathā vuttampaṭikkhipitvā attheva napuṃsake ghattanti napuṃsakattanti (potthake) dassetumāha-chaṭṭhīsamāsasse’ccādi. Napuṃsake ghattassa napuṃsakattassa (potthake) sabbhāvameva samattheti napuṃsakattaṃ hi’ccādinā, pāribhāsikanti ettha suttamevādhippetaṃ, paribhāsāya nibbattaṃ pāribhāsikaṃ suttikanti attho. Ārabhitabbamevidaṃ suttaṃ (napuṃsakassāpi) rassattavidhānāyāti adhippāyo. Ghanissitampi kāriyanti “ghabrahmādīte”tyādinā (2-60) vidhiyamānamekārādikāriyampi. Etaṃ ghanissitaṃ kāriyaṃ naca yuttanti sambandho. Ayuttattepi doso-yamāpatatevākyāsaṅkiyāha-‘nāyampidoso’ccādi, na rassassa ettheva laddhāvasarattā paṭhamaṃ tena paviṭṭhe… (ghani)ssitaṃ kāriyanti nāyampi doso paribhāsāva senāti mantabbaṃ. Salabhacchāye iti padacchedo.

With 'tanne,' he rejects the objection stated with 'nanu ce,' etc. Therein, he states the reason: 'because of the designation gha,' etc. 'Aghonaṃ' means of those which are not designated 'gha' and do not end in 'o.' If one were to suppose: 'Surely, in the feminine, that which has the form of i or ī is gha; that being so, in the neuter it would not be so,' meaning, 'if you say that due to being neuter, there is no ghatta (state of being gha) at all...' He rejects that too. Having refuted what was said, to show that ghatta does indeed exist in the neuter, he says 'chaṭṭhīsamāsassa,' etc. He establishes the very existence of ghatta in the neuter with 'napuṃsakattaṃ hi,' etc. 'Pāribhāsikaṃ' here refers to a sutta itself; the meaning is that which is produced from a technical rule is a pāribhāsika sutta. The intention is that this sutta should indeed be commenced in order to prescribe shortening, even for the neuter. Also an operation dependent on gha, namely the operation of e, etc., which is prescribed by 'ghabrahmādīte' (Kacc. 260). The connection is: this operation dependent on gha is not proper. Fearing that this fault would arise even in its impropriety, he says 'nāyam pi doso,' etc., because the shortening, having found its opportunity right here, has entered first. It should be considered that this is not a fault, because the operation dependent on gha is governed by a technical rule. The word-division is 'salabhacchāye'.

24. Ghama

24. Ghama

Atoevacātiādi [M 0.0177] heṭṭhā vuttanayāvalambena vuttaṃ.

'Ato eva ca,' etc., is stated by relying on the method explained previously.

25. Gossu

25. Gossu

Sakatthapariccāgena kule pavattattāti iminā chaṭṭhīsamāsassa uttarapadatthappadhānattamāha.

By this phrase, 'because it operates in relation to the group by abandoning its own meaning,' he states the primacy of the meaning of the final member in a genitive compound.

26. Itthi

26. Feminine

Itthividhīsu “puthussa pathavaputhavā”ti (3-39) suttapariyantesu. Itthiyanti idaṃ nāmavisesanaṃ vā siyā paccayatthavisesanaṃ vā, tattha nāmavisesanamevidaṃ na paccayatthavisesananti dassetumāha- ‘nāme’ccādi. Akārantato nāmasmāti ekattādimahantatthavācito akārantato nāmasmā. Itthattanti ettha itthīti itthiliṅgaṃ vuccati. Itthiyeva hi esāti liṅgīyati saṅketīyatīti liṅgaṃ. Itthiyā esāti pasiddhimato atthassa bhāvo sāmaññaṃ bālayuvattādi lakkhaṇaṃ itthattaṃ. Kimettha liṅgaṃ nāma–

In the rules concerning the feminine, which end with the sutta 'puthussa pathavaputhavā' (Kacc. 339). This word 'itthiyaṃ' could be either a qualifier of the noun or a qualifier of the meaning of the suffix. To show that this is indeed a qualifier of the noun and not a qualifier of the meaning of the suffix, he says 'nāme,' etc. 'From a noun ending in 'a'' means from a noun ending in 'a' that expresses the meaning of singularity, etc., and greatness. 'Itthattaṃ'—here, 'itthī' is called the feminine gender. Gender (liṅga) is so called because it marks or indicates, 'this is indeed a woman.' Femininity (itthatta) is the state of the established meaning 'this is of a woman,' a generality characterized by childhood, youth, etc. What, then, is called gender here?

Eseso etamiti ca,

Pasiddhi atthesu yesu lokassa;

Thīpuṃ napuṃsakānīti,

Vuccante tāni nāmāni.

And 'this' (fem.), 'this' (masc.), 'this' (neut.)—those nouns are called feminine, masculine, and neuter in whichever meanings the world's convention holds.

Atthesu yesu esā eso etanti pasiddhi lokassa hoti etāni yathākkamaṃ itthipurisanapuṃsakaliṅgānīti lokena vuccantīti attho. Evañcakatvā vuccate “liṅgaṃ nānusāsanīyaṃ lokanissa yattā liṅgassā”ti. Tattha goiccādīsvesā esoti pasiddhiyā itthiliṅgattaṃ, acciādīsvesā etanti pasiddhiyā itthinapuṃsakattaṃ, taṭobhaṭī taṭamiccādīsveso esāetanti pasiddhiyā pumitthinapuṃsakattaṃ, mālāiccādīsvesāti pasiddhiyā itthattaṃ, rukkhoccādīsvesoti pasiddhiyā pulliṅgattaṃ, kulamiccādo etanti pasiddhiyā napuṃsakattaṃ. Samāsassāpyevaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, jotakāti dassetīti sambandho. Jotakā [M 0.0178] itthattasseti pakaraṇato viññāyati. Tato veccādinā paccayatthabhāvino ye dosā tesametthanāvakāsoti dasseti. Samānādhikaraṇattaṃ bahuvacanampi hotītisambandho. Iminā idaṃ dīpeti “itthattassa paccayatthatte sati padhānattāssa byatirekalakkhaṇāya chaṭṭhiyā ‘kumārittaṃ (devadattāyā’tibhavitabbaṃ, tato ca na siyā kumārī) devadattā’ti samānādhikaraṇattaṃ, tathā kumāriyoti bahuvacanampi itthattassekattā. Pakatiyattha visesanapakkhe tu pakatiyā itthattavisiṭṭhaṃ dabbamevoccate, āādayo tu jotakatāti tattha byatirekābhāvā chaṭṭhiyā appasaṅgo ca bahuvacanampi anekattāva dabbassa yuttanti yathāvuttadosāvasarābhāvā iṭṭhatthasiddhī”ti. Aññeti jayādicca jinindabuddhyācariyādayo dasseti.

The meaning is: in whichever meanings the convention of the world holds for 'this' (fem.), 'this' (masc.), and 'this' (neut.), those are called by the world, respectively, the feminine, masculine, and neuter genders. And having done so, it is said: 'Gender is not to be taught by rule, for gender depends on worldly usage.' In this regard, for 'go' (cow), etc., because of the convention 'esā' (this, fem.), it has feminine gender. For 'acci' (flame), etc., because of the conventions 'esā' and 'etaṃ' (this, neut.), it has feminine and neuter gender. For 'taṭo' (bank), 'bhaṭī' (basket), 'taṭaṃ' (bank), etc., because of the conventions 'eso' (this, masc.), 'esā,' and 'etaṃ,' it has masculine, feminine, and neuter gender. For 'mālā' (garland), etc., because of the convention 'esā,' it has feminine gender. For 'rukkho' (tree), etc., because of the convention 'eso,' it has masculine gender. For 'kulaṃ' (family), etc., because of the convention 'etaṃ,' it has neuter gender. For a compound, it should be understood in the same way. The connection is that 'indicative' means 'it shows.' From the context, it is understood as 'indicative of femininity.' Then, with 'tato ve,' etc., he shows that there is no occasion here for those faults which arise when it is the meaning of a suffix. The connection is that co-referentiality and also the plural number occur. By this, he explains the following: 'If femininity were the meaning of the suffix, then due to its being primary, the genitive, which has the characteristic of distinction, should be used, as in 'the femininity of Devadattā.' Consequently, the co-referential 'the girl Devadattā' would not be possible. Likewise, the plural 'girls' would also not be possible, due to the singularity of femininity. However, on the side where it is a qualifier of the meaning of the base, the substance itself, qualified by femininity, is expressed by the base, while the suffixes beginning with ā are merely indicative. In that case, due to the absence of distinction, there is no application of the genitive, and the plural is also proper due to the multiplicity of the substance. Thus, because there is no occasion for the aforementioned faults, the desired meaning is established.' 'Others' indicates teachers like Jayāditya, Jinendrabuddhi, and so on.

Itthiyamabhidheyyāyanti itthiliṅgasaṅkhāte itthatte atthabhūte, yathevahītiādinā upamāvasena yathāvuttamevatthaṃ vibhāveti. Tattha itthattamiccādinā paropavaṇṇitapakkhassāyuttattannicchindeti, no papajjate nopapajjeyya (pañcikā) devadattāsaddavacanīyassāpi itthattato abyatirittattā ‘itthattaṃ devadattāyā’ti bhinnādhikaraṇatā na yujjate, anupapattimeva samattheti ‘devadattāyāti’ccādinā. Samānādhikaraṇattameva siyā itthisaddavacanīyato anaññattā devadattā saddavacanīyassa itthī devadattāti.

The phrase 'itthiyamabhidheyyāyam' means: in the state of being female, which is designated as the feminine gender, being the actual meaning. By means of simile, as in 'yathevahi', etc., it clarifies the very meaning as stated before. Therein, by 'itthattam', etc., he refutes the unsuitability of the position praised by others. This does not hold, because even that which is denoted by the word 'Devadattā' is not distinct from femininity; hence, the expression 'the femininity of Devadattā' is not suitable due to having different referents. By 'devadattāya', etc., it establishes only its untenability. Only co-referentiality would be suitable, because that which is denoted by the word 'Devadattā' is not different from that which is denoted by the word 'itthī', as in 'the woman Devadattā'.

Atoevāti itthatte āvidhānatoyeva. Tabbatotthassāti idaṃ jayādiccādimatānugāminā nugāmī pana (potthake) vuttaṃ, tathā hi te evaṃ liṅgalakkhaṇa māhu (pā, 4-1-3 kāsikāyaṃ) “sāmaññavisesā itthattādayo gottādayo viya bahuppakārabyattiyoti sāmaññāni ca tulyajātiyapadatthasādhāraṇattā tāni visesā ca añña maññehi vijātiyeti ca visissante byāvattanteti sāmaññavisesā. byañjīyantiā etehīti byattiyo sāmaññavisesānaṃ nissayā, bahuppakārā byatti yo yesaṃ sāmaññavisesānaṃ te tathāvuttāti– (kāsikāvivaraṇa pañjikā.) te hyevaṃ maññante “yathā [M 0.0179] gottādayo samānajātiyesu sabbesvanuvattante, vijātiyehi pana nivattante, tathā itthattādayopi. Vicittattā pana sāmaññavisesanissayānaṃ byañjakānaṃ kociyeva sāmaññaviseso kenacideva nissayena byañjate, na sabbo sabbena (pati) niyatavisayattā bhāvasattīnaṃ, tattha yenatthena itthattameva byañjate na pumattaṃ nāpi napuṃsakattaṃ, sā itthiyeva bhavati na pumā nāpi napuṃsakaṃ. Yena pumattameva byañjate, so pumāyeva. Yena tu napuṃsakattaṃ taṃ napuṃsakameva. Yo tu dvinnaṃ tiṇṇaṃ (vā) byañjako, so dviliṅgo tiliṅgo ve”ti (pā, 4-1-3 kāsikāvivaraṇapañjikā) tasmā pabbato yathā vuttaitthattavato atthassa abhidheyyassāti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo.

'Atoeva' means: precisely because femininity is not explicitly enjoined. The phrase 'tabbatotthassa' is stated by the followers of the view of Jayāditya and others, for they explain the characteristic of gender thus (in Pāṇini 4.1.3, Kāśikā): 'Generalities and particulars, such as femininity and clan, have many kinds of manifestations.' They hold the opinion that just as clan and other such terms apply to all of the same kind and not to those of a different kind, so too do femininity and other such terms. However, due to the varied nature of the bases that manifest generalities and particulars, only a certain generality or particular is manifested by a certain base, not all by all, because the powers of things have fixed domains. Therein, that by which femininity alone is manifested, and not masculinity nor neuterness, is only female, not male nor neuter. That by which masculinity alone is manifested is only male. That by which neuterness is manifested is only neuter. But that which is a manifestor of two or three is dual-gendered or triple-gendered.' (Pāṇini 4.1.3, Kāśikāvivaraṇapañjikā). Therefore, the meaning here should be understood thus: of the denotable object which possesses the aforementioned femininity.

Atheccādinā yathāvuttadosaparihārāya jinindabuddhinā yadupavaṇṇi taṃ taṃ parikappeti. So eva carahiccādinā upahāsapubbakamuttara mācikkhate. Masimakkhitakukkuṭoviyāti yadā koci aññakukkuṭo aññasmā bhīto siyā, tadā vijayino kukkuṭassa mukhaṃ masiyā makkhetvā upanenti so paṭhamaṃ tato bhītopi puna aññoti mantvā yujjhitumussahate. Yathātra sova kukkuṭo byāje nopadassito, tathā trāmītyattho.

By 'atha', etc., in order to avoid the aforementioned faults, he speculates on what was described by Jinindabuddhi. By 'so eva carahi', etc., a reply preceded by ridicule is related. 'Like a rooster smeared with soot' means: when a certain rooster is frightened of another, they smear the face of the victorious rooster with soot and bring it forward. That rooster, though at first frightened of it, then thinking it is another, dares to fight. Just as here that very rooster is presented under a pretext, so also is the meaning here.

29. Ārā

29. Ārā

Puṃyogena bhariyāyaṃ vattamānatova niyamena “mātulāditvānī bhariyāyaṃ” (3-33) tyānī, iminā tvaniyamena bhariyāyamabhariyāyañca inītyaniyamena vattumāha- ‘ārāmikassa bhariyā’iccādi.

The suffix '-ānī' is used restrictively, only when denoting a wife through connection with a male, as in 'mātulādito ānī bhariyāyaṃ' (3-33). By this present rule, however, he states that the suffix '-inī' is used without restriction for both a wife and a non-wife, as in 'ārāmikassa bhariyā' (the wife of a park-keeper), and so on.

31. Kti

31. Kti

Ttimhāti ettake vuttepi ttippaccayantatoti vacane kāraṇamāha-kevalassa aññapadatthe payogābhāvā’ti. Iminā paccayaggahaṇaparibhāsamantarenāpi sāmatthiyenevāyamatthaviseso labbhatīti dīpeti.

Although only 'from -tti' is stated, he gives the reason for the expression 'ending in the suffix -tti': 'because a bare suffix is not used in the sense of another word.' By this, he shows that even without the maxim regarding the inclusion of a suffix, this special meaning is obtained precisely through inherent capacity.

32. Ghara

32. Ghara

Taṃsanniyogāti [M 0.0180] tena nīppaccayena sanniyogā ekībhāvā, ayametthādhippāyo ‘yattha nīppaccayo tattheva yalopo’ti.

'Taṃsanniyogā' means: through connection, through unification, with that suffix '-nī'. The intention here is this: 'Where there is the suffix '-nī', precisely there is the elision of 'ya'.

33. Mātu

33. Mātu

Bhariyāyanti pakativisesanattā māha- ‘bhariyāya’ntiādi. Punnāmadheyyāti purisassa samaññābhūtā, puṃyogenāti purisena saha sambandhena hetunā. Itthiyaṃ vattantīti soyamityabhedavacanicchāyaṃ yadā bhariyāsaṅkhātāyamitthiyaṃ vattante, nadādipāṭhāti vutte viññāyati ‘ākatigaṇattā nadādipāṭho honto evaṃ hotī’ti dasseti, punnāmasmāyogāapālakantāti nadādipāṭhatoti atthoti seso. Idañca nadādīsu gaṇasuttanti veditabbaṃ, tassa atthaṃ vadati-‘pumuno’iccādi, apālakantāti kiṃpasupālikā khettapālikā.

Because it is a qualifier of the base, he says 'bhariyāyaṃ', etc. 'Punnāmadheyya' means: being a name for a man. 'Puṃyogena' means: by reason of connection with a man. 'Itthiyaṃ vattanti' means: when they occur in the feminine, with the desire for an expression of identity like 'this is that', that is, when they denote a woman designated as a wife. When 'from the nadādi list' is said, it is understood. He shows: 'Being from the nadādi list, because it is an open class, it is thus'. The rest of the meaning is: 'from a masculine name, through connection, not ending in -pālaka', this is from the nadādi list. And this should be known as a gaṇasutta in the nadādi group. He states its meaning: 'pumuno', etc. What is the purpose of 'not ending in -pālaka'? To exclude words like pasupālikā and khettapālikā.

39. Puthu

39. Puthu

Puthusaddato saññāyaṃ vīppaccayaṃ samattheti‘puthubhūtā pathavīti hi mahī vuccatī”ti, puthubhūtāti hi iminā pathavīsaddassa puthusaddabhūtattaṃ viññāpeti, mahī vuccatīti iminā nadādipāṭhā saññāyaṃ vīppaccayattaṃ, puthubhūtā patthaṭāti attho.

He supports the suffix '-vī' from the word 'puthu' in the sense of a proper name, for 'the earth (mahī) is indeed called pathavī because it has become extensive (puthubhūtā)'. Indeed, by this 'puthubhūtā', he makes known that the word 'pathavī' has the nature of the word 'puthu'. By 'mahī vuccati', he indicates that the suffix '-vī' is from the nadādi list in the sense of a proper name. The meaning of 'puthubhūtā' is 'spread out'.

40. Samā

40. Samā

Parādhikārato paccayassa paravidhināva sāmīpyassa siddhattā sādhīpyavacanassantasaddassa gahaṇamanatthakaṃ siyāti mantvāvayavavacano yamantasaddo gayhatīti dassento āha- ‘tassa anto’iccādi. Avasānavati+avayavoti padacchedo, samāsaggahaṇena gahaṇe kāraṇamāha-‘avayavattā’ti. Yathāvuttacodanāya niddosattamupamāvasena dassetumāha-‘nāyaṃ doso’ccādi. Pallavitassa rukkhassa pallavānamavayavattaṃ viya samāsato uttarakālaṃ vidhīya mānassa akārassa samāsāvayavattaṃ na virujjhatīti attho.

Thinking that, since the proximity of a suffix is established by the very rule that it comes after the base, the inclusion of the word 'anta', which denotes proximity, would be meaningless, he shows that this word 'anta' is taken as denoting a part, and says: 'its end', etc. The word division is 'avasānavati + avayavo'. He states the reason for its inclusion in the compound: 'because it is a part'. To show its faultlessness with regard to the aforementioned objection, by way of a simile, he says: 'This is not a fault', etc. The meaning is: just as new shoots are parts of a tree that has sprouted, so it is not contradictory for the sound 'a', which is enjoined after the compound, to be a part of the compound.

44. Asaṃ

44. Asaṃ

Atikkantamaṅguliyoti [M 0.0181] viggaho. Dve aṅguliyo samāhaṭāti paraviggahenātthamāha, dve aṅguliyo pamāṇamassāti viggahenevaṃ samāso tato mattappaccaye tagghappaccaye vā tassa “lopo”ti (4-123) iminā lope kate visesanasamāsā akāroti dassetuṃ ‘katha’miccādinā yaṃ vuttaṃ taṃ dassetuṃ ‘aññapadatthe’ccādi vuttaṃ. Samāsavidhānaṃ atopīti mattādippaccayalopaṃ katvā “visesanamekatthene”ti (3-11) samāsavidhānā, atha nāyamaṅgulisaddenevaṃ samāso, māne paccayalopavasena vināva appaccayena niṭṭhappattīti mantvā ‘aṅgulasaddo vā’ccādinā yaṃ vuttiyaṃ vuttaṃ tattha āsaṅkaṃ viracayati ‘athe’ccādi. Dvaṅgulasaddassa pamāṇinivattanato kathañcipi aññapadatthatā siyāti ‘yathā tathā aññapadatthe vattatū’tivuttaṃ. Nanu niraṅgulantyādi sabbamaṅgulasaddena sādhetuṃ sakkā, tathā sati kimaṅguli saddā appaccayavidhānenetyāsaṅkiya payojanantaraṃ apadisitumāha- ‘sabbatthe’ccādi. Aṅgulisaddato appaccaye avihite niraṅguliccādipi siyā tannivattanamettha payojananti dasseti ‘aṅgulisaddanivattanattha’nti.

The analysis is 'atikkantamaṅguliyo'. He states the meaning with another analysis, 'dve aṅguliyo samāhaṭā' (two fingers brought together). By the analysis 'dve aṅguliyo pamāṇamassa' (that which has a measure of two fingers), the compound is thus formed. Then, after the elision of the suffix '-matta' or '-taggha' by the rule 'lopo' (4-123), to show that the suffix '-a' is added by the rule for descriptive compounds, what was stated by 'katham', etc., is shown by 'aññapadatthe', etc. The rule for compounding is also from this: after eliding the suffixes '-matta', etc., the compound is formed by the rule 'visesanamekatthena' (3-11). Then, thinking that this compound is not formed thus from the word 'aṅguli', because in the sense of measure, the desired form is achieved by the elision of the suffix even without the suffix '-a', he raises a doubt with 'atha', etc., regarding what was stated in the commentary by 'aṅgulasaddo vā', etc. Since the word 'dvaṅgula' refers back to the thing measured, so that it might somehow have the meaning of another word, it is said: 'Let it occur in the meaning of another word in whatever way'. Now, can 'niraṅgula', etc., all be formed from the word 'aṅgula'? If so, then why enjoin the suffix '-a' from the word 'aṅguli'? Raising this doubt, he points out another purpose with 'sabbattha', etc. He shows that if the suffix '-a' were not enjoined from the word 'aṅguli', then 'niraṅguli', etc., could also occur, and the purpose here is to preclude that, saying: 'for the purpose of precluding the form from the word aṅguli'.

45. Dīghā

45. Dīghā

Dīgharattantyādo nānusiṭṭhattā liṅgavisesassa kathaṃ napuṃsakattameviccāsaṅkiya codeti ‘nanuce’ccādi. Nāyaṃdosoccādinā pariharati. “Liṅgaṃ nānusāsanīyaṃ lokanissayattā liṅgassā”tīdamālamba vadati ‘loke’tiādi. Athavāti pakkhantaropadassanatthe nipāto, vibhajjāti vibhajitvā. Kvacīti yogavibhāgenāti adhippāyo.

Regarding 'dīgharattam', etc., since a specific gender is not taught, he raises an objection with 'nanu ca', etc., doubting how there can be only the neuter gender. He refutes it with 'nāyaṃ doso', etc. Relying on this statement, 'Gender is not to be taught, because gender is based on worldly usage,' he speaks with 'loke', etc. 'Athavā' is a particle for the purpose of showing another alternative. 'Vibhajjā' means 'having divided'. 'Kvaci' means the intention is 'by splitting the rule'.

Ahorattanti samāhāre (cattha) samāsā napuṃsakattaṃ. Atirattoti pulliṅge pādisamāso, samudāyasaddassāpyavayave vutti sabbhāvato ekadesavacano pubbarattādo rattisaddoccāha-‘pubbā ca sā ratti cā’tiādi. Evamekarattanti pāṭhena na bhavitabbaṃ… tassa samāhārena samāsattābhāvā. Napuṃsakaliṅgampana lokasannissa yattā viññeyyaṃ.

In 'ahoratta,' the neuter gender is due to its being a collective compound in the sense of 'ca'. 'Atiratta' is a Pādi compound in the masculine gender. Since a word for a whole can also be applied to a part, the word 'ratti' in 'pubbaratta,' etc., is a term for a part, as he says: 'pubbā ca sā ratti ca,' etc. Thus, the reading should not be 'ekaratta,' because it is not a collective compound. The neuter gender, however, should be understood as dependent on worldly convention.

Asamāsantapakkheti [M 0.0182] samāsantaappaccayassābhāvapakkhe. Pubbā atikkantā ratti pubbarattī(ti ratti saddo) nekadesavacanoti samāsantābhāvo.

'Asamāsantapakkhe' means in the case of the absence of the 'a' suffix as a compound-ending. The night that has passed is 'pubbarattī'; the word 'ratti' is not a term for a part, hence the absence of the compound-ending.

46. Gotva

46. Gotva

Nanuceccādinā yathāpāditadosaṃ nāyaṃ dosoti pariharati. Syādilopassiccādinā sulabhasyādi lopato pyasulabhataddhita lopova alopetīminā parāmaṭṭhuṃ yuttoti dasseti.

By means of 'nanu ca,' etc., he refutes the fault that was raised, saying: 'This is not a fault.' By means of 'syādilopassa,' etc., he shows that because the elision of a taddhita suffix is more difficult to effect than the easy elision of 'syā,' etc., it is proper to refer to it with the term 'alopeti' (there is no elision).

47. Ratti

47. Ratti

Rattindivaṃ bhuñjatīti payoge ādheyye bhojanasaṅkhāte apekkhite ratyādayo ādeyyasāpekkhā, tesampi iminā nipāta nenevātimatā samāsassa siddhīti dassento āha- ‘rattandiva’ntiādi, ratti ca divācāti viggaho, catthasamāse tu ra(ttindi) vā.

In the usage 'rattindivaṃ bhuñjati' (he eats night and day), when the content, designated as food, is intended, 'ratti' and so on are dependent on that content. Showing that for these too the formation of the compound is accomplished by this very irregular formation (nipātana), he said: 'rattandiva,' etc. The analysis is 'ratti ca divā ca.' In a copulative compound, however, it is 'rattindivā'.

50. Dāru

50. Dāru

Samāsattho (ettha) dāru, nāssa mukhyāhi aṅgulīhi sambandho yujjati, nanu dve aṅgulī pamāṇamassa dārunoccādiṃ mukhyo aṅgulisaddogahitoti sambandho sambhavati kimevaṃ vuccateccāsaṅkiyāha-‘yadipi’ccādi, pamāṇavacanenāti mattādipaccayatthabhūtapamāṇavācakena, aṅguli saddassa dāruno pamāṇavācakattā vuttaṃ- ‘dāruno sambandho atthī’ti. Visesanasamāsato paraṃ tadatthavisaye tasmiṃpamāṇatthavisaye “mānematto”tiādinā (4-46) mattādippaccayenabhavitabbantiattho, lopenabhavitabbanti sambandho, “asaṅkhyehi cāṅgulyā naññāsaṅkhyatthesu”iccatra (3-44) yadākhyātaṃ, tadihāpyatidisamāha-‘pubbe viyasiddha’nti, anakārantānanti bhūmiādīnaṃ, tabbidhāne tassa appaccayassa vidhāne payojanaṃsissokārotisambandho. Iminā kaccāyanānaṃ pakaraṇe payojanaṃ dassitaṃ. Athaca panettha “kvaci samāsantagatānamakāranto”ti (ka, 2-7-22) iminā akārantassa samāsante kate sāmatthiyā ‘syāca’iti (ka, 2-3-29) sissākārādesābhāvā niccamokārantarūpaṃ sampajjatīti parikappiyatassāyuttabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ yaṃ [M 0.0183] vuttaṃvuttikārena, taṃ dassetumāha‘akārantassapi’ccādi, yaṃ-vuttaṃ sissākārā desanivattane akārakaraṇe sāmatthiyaṃ, tadabhāvā sissākārādeso na nivārīyatīti dassetumāha-‘nace’ccādi. Caritatthatāya niṭṭhitappayojanatāya, teneva kaccāyanavuttikāreneva appaccayanta mudāhaṭaṃ sakkataganthānusārena, abyañjanantattāti iminā tiṇṇamesaṃ saddānaṃ sakkate byañjanantattameva bodheti, niratthakanti pubbeva akārantattā niratthakaṃ, ākāravidhānenevāti (ka, 2-7-25) “dhanumhāca” ityākāravidhāneneva.

Here, `dāru` (wood) is the meaning of the compound. A connection with primary fingers is not suitable for it. But anticipating the objection, 'In an expression such as "wood of two fingers' measure," is not the word 'aṅguli' taken in its primary sense, so that a connection is possible? Why is it said thus?', he says: 'yadipi,' etc. 'By a word expressing measure' means by a word that denotes measure, which is the meaning of suffixes such as 'matta.' Because the word 'aṅguli' denotes the measure of the wood, it is stated: 'There is a connection with the wood.' The meaning is that after a descriptive compound, in the domain of that meaning—that is, in the domain of the meaning of measure—it should be formed with suffixes like 'matta' by the rule 'māne matto,' etc. (4-46); the connection is that it should be formed by elision. What was stated in the rule 'asaṅkhyehi cāṅgulyā naññāsaṅkhyatthesu' (3-44), he applies that here too by extension, saying: 'Established as before.' 'Of those not ending in -a' means of 'bhūmi,' etc. In prescribing that, the purpose of prescribing that 'a' suffix is its connection with the 'o' of the genitive ending. By this, the purpose in Kaccāyana's treatise is shown. Furthermore, in this context, to show the unsuitability of what was supposed by the commentator—namely, that according to the rule 'kvaci samāsantagatānamakāranto' (Ka. 2-7-22), when the final vowel of a compound is made 'a,' the form always ends in 'o' due to the power of this rule to prevent the substitution of 'ā' for the genitive ending by 'syāca' (Ka. 2-3-29)—he says: 'akārantassapi,' etc. To show that the power to prevent the substitution of 'ā' for the genitive ending, which was mentioned in making the final vowel 'a,' does not in fact prevent it because that power is absent, he says: 'nace,' etc. 'Caritatthatāya' means because its purpose has been served, i.e., its function is completed. By that same commentator on Kaccāyana, an example ending in the 'a' suffix was cited in accordance with the Sanskrit texts. By 'abyañjanantattā' (because they end in a consonant), he indicates that in Sanskrit these three words do indeed end in a consonant. 'It is pointless' means it is pointless because they already end in 'a.' 'By the very prescription of ā' refers to the prescription of 'ā' by the rule 'dhanumhāca' (Ka. 2-7-25).

51. Civī

51. Civī

Aññamaññakiriyeti kiriyāparivattanamāha, iminā sutte kiriya saddābhāvepi vītiharaṇasaddeneva kiriyābyatihāreti labbhatīti dasseti.

By 'aññamaññakiriya' (mutual action), he refers to an exchange of action. By this he shows that in this rule, even in the absence of the word 'kiriya' (action), the sense of 'reciprocity of action' is obtained from the word 'vītiharaṇa' (interchange) alone.

52. Latvī

52. Latvī

Paṭimukkakambū āmukkavalayā.

She who wears a conch-shell bracelet and has put on bangles.

53. Vāñña

53. Vāñña

Kāpekkhehīti kappaccayamapekkhitehi.

'Kāpekkhehi' means by those who expect the 'ka' suffix.

54. Utta

54. Utta

Āparicchedāvasānā na pare parena (potthake) tato paraṃ ṇādikāriyavidhānā.

They extend up to the end of the chapter; there are none beyond that. After that, there is no prescription of operations such as the `ṇa` suffix.

57. Ṭanta

57. Ṭanta

Ṭādese pubbasaralopo, atisayena mahantīti viggahe “taratamissikiyiṭṭhātisaye”ti (4-64) tarappaccayo ṇādivuttiyaṃ vibhattilopo. Mahattarasaddā ‘nadāditovī” (3-27) mahato bhāvoti vākye“tassa bhāvakammesuttatā ttana ṇya ṇeyya ṇiya ṇiyā”ti (4-56) tto, vibhattilopo, chaṭṭhīsamāso, tenāha ‘rattaññūna’miccādi.

When `ṭa` is substituted, there is elision of the preceding vowel. In the analysis 'exceedingly great,' the suffix 'tara' is used in the sense of 'exceeding' according to the rule 'taratamissikiyiṭṭhātisaye' (4-64), with elision of the case ending in the `ṇādi` group. From the word 'mahattara,' [a suffix is added] by 'nadādito vī' (3-27). In the phrase 'the state of being great,' the suffix 'tta' is applied by the rule 'tassa bhāvakammesu ttatā ttana ṇya ṇeyya ṇiya ṇiyā' (4-56), with elision of the case ending, forming a genitive compound. Therefore, he says: 'rattaññūnaṃ,' etc.

58. A

58. A

Nto [M 0.0184] neti sambandho.

The connection is that one infers the `-nt` suffix.

60. Para

60. Para

Parāsaddo ettha adhikatthoti āha-‘adhikā’ti.

Here the word 'para' has the meaning 'additional'; thus he says: 'adhikā'.

63. Klu

63. Klu

Apavādavisayepīti “vijjāyonisambandhānamā tatra catthe”ti (3-64) imassa apavādasuttassa visayepi.

'Apavādavisayepi' means 'also in the sphere of an exception': that is, in the sphere of this exceptional rule (apavādasutta), 'vijjāyonisambandhānaṃ mā tatra catthe' (3-64), 'For those related by knowledge or birth, let [the operation] not be in that sense of 'ca'.'

64. Vijjā

64. Vijjā

Atha vijjāyonisambandhānamityuccamāne vijjāsambandhīnaṃ yonisambandhīnanti kathaṃ vivaraṇamiccāha-‘vijjāyoni’ccādi, vijjā ca yoni ca vijjā yonī tāsaṃ sambandho, so yesaṃ atthi te hotādayo mātādayo ca abhedopacāreneha vijjāyonisambandhisaddena gayhantīti adhippāyo, tasaddenāti tatretyatra. Te ca ltupitādayoti tasaddena parāmaṭṭhā ltupitādayo ca, atthe kāriyā sambhavā taṃvācako saddo gayhati.

Now, when 'vijjāyonisambandhānaṃ' is said, how is the explanation 'of those related by knowledge and of those related by birth' derived? He says: 'vijjāyoni,' etc. The intention is: 'knowledge' and 'birth' are 'vijjāyonī'; their connection is meant. Those who have this connection—such as the teacher and others, and the mother and others—are here designated by the word 'vijjāyonisambandhī' through a figurative identification. 'By that word' refers to the word 'tatra' in this context. And those, the father and others, are referred to by that word. Since the grammatical operation is possible in that meaning, the word denoting it is understood.

65. Putte

65. Putte

Ltupitādī (ti pubba) sutte tatreti gahitaltupitādi.

In the previous sutta beginning with `Itupitādi`, by 'tatra' is understood `itupitādi`.

66. Cismiṃ

66. Cismiṃ

Paccayaggahaṇaparibhāsāya cippaccayanteti vuttaṃ.

By the technical rule for grasping a suffix, it is said to be that which ends in the suffix ‘ci’.

67. Itthi

67. Woman

Itthisaddena itthiliṅgaṃ gahitaṃ na itthī, taggahaṇe sati ‘itthiyaṃ vattamāne’ti vuttiganthassa itthisaṅkhāte atthe vattamāneti attho gayheyya, evaṃ sati ‘kalyāṇippadhānā’ti etthāpi pumbhāvo pasajjeyya… padhānasaddassa kalyāṇiyaṃ vattamānattāti āha- ‘itthiyanti itthiliṅge’ti. Atha itthiyanti ettake vutte kathaṃ taggahaṇaṃ [M 0.0185] siyāti āha-‘visesane’ccādi, ekattheti vuttepi itthiyaṃ vattamāneti ayamattho viññāyatīti itthiyanti vacanamanatthaṃ siyāti samatthamaññathānupapattiyanti itthiyanti visesanamitthiliṅgasseva gahaṇeti āha- ‘visesane’ccādi, itthiyanti itthiliṅgasseva gahaṇanti sambandho. Byavacchejjābhāvā visesanamanatthakaṃ siyāti ekattheiccaneneva itthiyaṃ vuttiyā (gamma) bhāvatoti bhāvo. Pume pulliṅge vattamāno saddo pumāsaddo, sakaloti padesasakalo hi gayhati… kassaci suttatthassa puthabhūtattā, tenevacāha- ‘itthiyantu na vattatte’ti.

By the word ‘itthi,’ the feminine gender is taken, not a woman. If a woman were taken, the meaning of the commentary phrase ‘when occurring in the feminine’ would be understood as ‘when occurring in the sense of an entity designated as a woman.’ In that case, even in an expression like ‘kalyāṇippadhānā,’ a masculine state would result, because the word ‘padhāna’ refers to ‘kalyāṇī’ (a beautiful woman). Hence it is said: ‘By “itthiyaṃ” is meant “in the feminine gender.”’ Then, if only ‘itthiyaṃ’ were stated, how could that gender be taken? He says: ‘by a qualifier,’ etc. Even when ‘in a single meaning’ is stated, the meaning ‘occurring in the feminine’ is understood. Thus the word ‘itthiyaṃ’ would be superfluous. Therefore, because it would otherwise be inexplicable, the qualifier ‘itthiyaṃ’ must refer to the taking of the feminine gender only. Thus he says, ‘by a qualifier,’ etc. The connection is: ‘By “itthiyaṃ” is meant the taking of the feminine gender only.’ Because there would be nothing to exclude, the qualifier would be pointless; the sense is that by ‘in a single meaning’ alone, the occurrence in the feminine is already implied. A word occurring in the masculine gender is a masculine word. ‘All’ (sakalo): for a part of the whole is taken, because the meaning of some rule is distinct. Therefore he also said: ‘but it does not occur in the sense of a woman.’

69. Sabbā

69. All

Vattanaṃ ekasmiṃ atthe adhitthiccādo itthivisiṭṭhe sattamiyatthādo, vāsiṭṭhoccādo vasiṭṭhādivisiṭṭhe apaccādo, puttīyaticcādo puttādivisiṭṭhe icchādyatthe pavatti, tenāha-‘ekatthībhāvo’ti. Sāmañña gahaṇatthanti iminā mattasaddassa kasiṇatthe pavattimāha.

Occurrence in a single meaning: for example, in ‘adhitthi,’ etc., it is in the sense of the locative case, with reference to that which is characterized by a woman; in ‘vāsiṭṭho,’ etc., it is in the sense of offspring, with reference to that which is characterized by Vasiṭṭha, etc.; in ‘puttīyati,’ etc., the application is in the sense of desire, etc., with reference to that which is characterized by a son, etc. Therefore he said: ‘the state of becoming a single meaning.’ By the phrase ‘for the purpose of taking the general sense,’ he indicates the application of the word ‘matta’ in the sense of ‘the whole’ (kasiṇa).

70. Jāyā

70. Wife

Evanti iminā itarītarayoge catthasamāsaṃ vibhāveti. Jānijāyā, saddantarenāti jānisaddena tathāsaddopadiṭṭhena daṃ jaṃ saddantarena ca, kesañciti kharīgatantiādīsu ‘kharī’tiādīnaṃ kesañci, kharīti kharatthe vattamāno-yaṃ saddo niyatavisayo… gatasaddaṃ vinā aññattha adiṭṭhattā, nāyampayogoti tudampatippayogaṃ nivattetvā hetumāha- ‘āgame’ccādi, aññehi cāti iminā rūpasiddhiṃ gaṇhāti.

Thus, by this, he explains the copulative compound of mutual connection. ‘Jānijāyā’ (wife and wife). By ‘with another word’ is meant: with the word ‘jāni’ and with another word ‘jaṃ’ substituted for ‘daṃ’ as taught by the word ‘tathā’. According to some, this applies to some words like ‘kharī’ in examples such as ‘kharīgata.’ ‘Kharī’: this word, occurring in the sense of ‘rough,’ has a restricted domain, because it is not seen elsewhere without the word ‘gata.’ This is not the usage; having rejected the usage ‘tudampati,’ he states the reason: ‘by an augment,’ etc. And by ‘and by others,’ he includes the formation of the form.

75. Ana

75. Not

Nanu sutte‘sare’ti ettakaṃ vuttaṃ‘sarādo’ti kathaṃ laddhanti āha-‘sare’tiādi, vaṇṇe yantantadādoti siṭṭhavacanaṃ, vaṇṇe parabhūte yaṃ kāriyaṃ vidhīyate taṃ so vaṇṇo ādi yassa taṃ tadādi, tasmiṃ tadādo uttarapade sampajjatīti attho, khādhātuto ktappaccaye vihite rassenākārenevāyampayogo, na visuṃ akārenāti dassetuṃ na ākkhātaṃ anakkhāta “byañjane dīgharassā”ti uttarapadādi sarassa rassatta’nti vuttaṃ.

Surely, in the rule only ‘sare’ (on a vowel following) is stated; how then is ‘sarādo’ (at the beginning of a vowel) obtained? He says: ‘sare,’ etc. The principle ‘that which has it at the beginning’ is a teaching of the learned concerning a letter. When a letter follows, whatever operation is prescribed applies to that which has that letter as its beginning, meaning it applies to the following word that begins with it. To show that when the suffix ‘-ta’ is prescribed after the root ‘khā,’ the resulting word ‘anakkhāta’ (‘not told’) is formed with a short ‘a’ and not with a separate ‘a,’ it is explained as a compound of ‘na’ + ‘akkhāta.’ By the rule ‘long vowels become short before a consonant,’ it is stated that the initial vowel of the following word is shortened.

76. Nakhā

76. Nails

Saññāsaddesucātiādinā [M 0.0186] avayavatthanirapekkhānampi yathākathañci nipphattiṃ dassento sabbesameva saddānaṃ nipphannavācitañcāttano dīpeti, yathākathañci nipphatti, ruḷhiyā atthanicchayo, tena saññeccādo-dhippāyaṃ vivarati ‘yaṃkiñci’tyādinā, itthī ca pumā ca itthipumaṃ, na itthi pumanti samāse nipātaneniminā napuṃsakādeso napuṃsakaniddeso (potthake) ti dasseti ‘na itthi’ccādinā. Khī-khaye, khara-vināse cāti hi etehi ‘na khīyati na kharatī’ti atthe “bhāvakārakesva ghaṇa ghakā”ti (5-44) appaccaye’ na khaya na khara’iti ṭhite khattādesoti āha- na khīyati’ccādi.

By ‘in proper names,’ etc., showing that even for words independent of the meaning of their components there is some kind of derivation, he illuminates his own view that all words are both derived and denotative. Derivation occurs in some way; the determination of meaning is by convention (ruḷhi). Thereby he clarifies the intention of ‘proper name,’ etc., with ‘whatever,’ etc. ‘Itthī ca pumā ca’ becomes ‘itthipumaṃ.’ He shows that in the compound ‘na itthi pumā,’ the substitution of the neuter is by this irregular formation, with ‘na itthi,’ etc. The roots are ‘khī’ in the sense of ‘decaying’ and ‘khara’ in ‘destroying.’ From these, in the sense ‘it does not decay, it is not destroyed,’ when the suffix ‘a’ is applied by the rule ‘ghaṇa, ghaka in the sense of state or agent’ (5-44), and the form stands as ‘na khaya, na khara,’ he states there is the substitution of ‘khatta,’ saying ‘na khīyati,’ etc.

77. Nago

77. Mountain

Evanti iminā gacchatīti vākye kvippaccayādiṃ dasseti, viseso panettha nañssa(ṭo) vasalo caṇḍālo, sītena karaṇabhūtena.

Thus, by this, he shows the suffix ‘kvi,’ etc., in the phrase ‘gacchati’ (it goes). Here, however, the distinction is: the negative particle ‘nañ’ is in ‘vasala’ (outcaste) and ‘caṇḍāla’ (outcaste), and ‘sīta’ (cold) is the instrument.

78. Saha

78. With

Tattha tasmiṃ parabhūte, yassa ca jhattanti sambandho.

Therein, when that following term is present, the connection is also with what is immediate.

80. Apa

80. Away

Appaccakkhaṃ paccakkhañāṇenānupalabbhanīyaṃ tampanātthato-numeyyameva. Tasmiṃ gammamāne yamādesoti kenaci liṅgenādhigatenānumānañāṇenānumeyuttamagyādinoti dassetumāha- ‘kapote’ccādi. Kapotādibhāveti katthaci gharādo kapotavātamaṇḍalikādīnaṃ dassanavasena sabbhāve sati. Agyādidassanatoti aggipisācādidassanato, aññatrāpīti gharādito aññatra, kapotavātamaṇḍalikādino liṅgassa, agyādiyoganti aggiādīhi anumeyyehi sambandhaṃ. Mantvāti anumānañāṇena jānitvāpayogoti sāggisapisācāti payogo.

That which is not directly perceived, being unapprehendable by direct knowledge, is indeed to be inferred from its meaning. When that is being understood, to show that what is to be inferred, such as fire, etc., is fit to be inferred by inferential knowledge acquired through some sign, he says: ‘pigeon,’ etc. ‘The state of pigeons, etc.’ means: when there is the presence, somewhere in a house etc., on account of seeing pigeons, whirlwinds, etc. ‘From the sight of fire, etc.’ means from seeing fire, demons, etc. ‘Elsewhere too’ means elsewhere than in a house, etc. ‘Of the sign of pigeons, whirlwinds, etc.’ ‘Connection with fire, etc.’ means the connection with the inferable things, such as fire. ‘Having considered’ means having known through inferential knowledge. ‘The usage’ refers to the usage ‘sāggi’ (with fire) and ‘sapisāca’ (with a demon).

81. Akā

81. Akā

Sakatthe [M 0.0187] vattamānassa sahasaddassāti vattabbe vattamāno tappadhānoyevāti āha- ‘sakatthappadhānassa sahasaddassā’ti, vutti bhavatīti sambandho, yugapadi dhurā sadhuraṃ. Aparaṇhena sahitaṃ sahā paraṇhaṃ.

When it should be said 'of the word saha existing in its own meaning,' he says that this meaning is primary. Hence the text says: 'of the word saha when its own meaning is primary.' The connection is: 'the formation occurs.' For example, 'simultaneously with the yoke' is sadhuraṃ. 'Together with the afternoon' is sahāparaṇhaṃ.

82. Gantha

82. Gantha

“Aṭṭhādasa nimesā tu, kaṭṭhā tiṃsantu tākalā”ti vacanato āha- ‘kalā kālaviseso’ti. Kalādisaṅkhātaganthassānte sahasaddo vattatītisamāsavākyaṃ niddisati ‘kalanta’miccādi. Ganthanteccādinā āsaṅkatoyamadhippāyo “kālatthapariccāgena ganthante vattamānattā akālattho”ti. Ganthavuttipi kalādi kālasaddatthaṃ nātikkamatīti adhippāyenāha- ‘ganthavuttipi’ccādi. Adhiko māsako assāti samāsako, vikappena siddheti “sahassa so-ññatthe”ti (3-78).

Following the statement, 'Eighteen blinks of an eye are a kaṭṭhā; thirty of those are a kalā,' he says: 'Kalā is a specific measure of time.' He indicates the compound phrase 'kalanta,' etc., to show that the word saha occurs at the end of a text designated by kalā, etc. By the phrase 'at the end of the text,' etc., this intention is suggested: 'Because it occurs at the end of a text, having abandoned the meaning of time, it does not have the meaning of time.' With the intention that even the textual formation does not go beyond the meaning of words for time such as kalā, etc., he says: 'even the textual formation,' etc. 'That which has an extra māsaka' is samāsaka; it is established optionally by the rule 'sa for saha in another sense' (3-78).

83. Samā

83. Samā

Samāno pati yassā sapattinī sapattī iti nipphannānamekadeso ‘pattinī pattī’ti dassitoti vattumāha- ‘yakkhādi tvini’ccādi. Vayasaddassa “saravayāyavāsacetā jalāsayākkhayalohapaṭamanesū”ti gaṇapāṭhato akkhaye vattamānasso manādittā okārantattanti dassetumāha- ‘vayo’tiādi. Yappaccayantoti iminā nipātanena takayappaccayanto.

To say that 'pattinī' or 'pattī' is shown as a part of the derived words sapattinī or sapattī—meaning 'she whose husband is shared'—he says: 'yakkhādi tvini,' etc. To show that the word vayas, although occurring in the sense of 'imperishable' (akkhaye) according to the list of words beginning with sara ['saravayāyavāsacetā jalāsayākkhayalohapaṭamanesū'], ends in 'o' because it belongs to the manas-group, he says: 'vayo,' etc. By '[the word] ending in the suffix ya,' is meant a word ending in the suffix ya from that base by this special rule.

84. Uda

84. Uda

“Aññasmi”nti (4-121) iyappaccayavidhāyakaṃ suttaṃ.

The rule 'Aññasmiṃ' (4-121) is the aphorism that prescribes the suffix iya.

88. Tumhā

88. Tumhā

Tumhe viya dissantīti tumhādī amhādīccādiṃ “sabbādīnamā”ti (3-86) ā.

In the sense 'they appear like you,' the form is tumhādisa; in 'they appear like us,' amhādisa, etc., by the rule 'Sabbādīnamā' (3-86), which substitutes 'ā'.

90. Vidhā

90. Vidhā

Gabbhenāti iminā kucchigatena gabbhena saha dvihadayattamassāti dasseti, pubbapadeti dusadde.

By 'gabbhena,' he shows that because of the fetus in the womb, she has a two-hearted state. In the first member of the compound, there is the word du.

92. Digu

92. Digu

Guṇā [M 0.0188] paṭalā dve padāni assa iti bhavitabbaṃ dve pādā esaṃ dve satāni assa, dve sahassāni assa, dvinnaṃ satānaṃ dvinnaṃ sahassānaṃ vā samāhāroti viggaho.

The analysis is: 'of which there are two strands (dve guṇā)'; 'of which there are two layers (dve paṭalā)'; 'of which there are two feet'; 'of which there are two hundred'; 'of which there are two thousand'; or 'a collection of two hundred'; or 'a collection of two thousand'.

93. Tīsva

93. Tīsva

Dvattipattāti paṭhamantā‘pūra-pūraṇe’iccasmā karaṇatthe “bhāva kārakesva ghaṇa ghakā”ti (5-44) appaccaye syādisamāsoti dassetu māha- ‘dvattipatta’iccādi.

To show that `dvattipatta`, etc., is a `syādisamāsa` with a word ending in the first case inflection, he says, '`dvattipatta`,' etc. The word `patta` is formed from the root `pūr` in the sense of 'filling', in the instrumental sense, with the suffix `a` by the rule 'Bhāva kārakesva ghaṇa ghakā' (5-44).

94. Āsaṃ

94. Āsaṃ

Dve ca tiṃsā ca, dvīhi vā adhikā tiṃsāti viggaho.

'Two and thirty,' or 'thirty exceeded by two,' is the analysis.

96. Cattā

96. Cattā

Sampattavibhāsāyanti ayaṃyogo (sampattavibhāsāti) dasseti, sampatte vibhāsā vikappoti attho, tayo ca cattālīsā ca, tīhi vā adhikā cattālīsāccādinā viggaho, tisso cattālīsā assa ticattālīsaṃ gaṇo.

This application shows 'sampattavibhāsā' (that is, 'it is sampattavibhāsā'). The meaning is 'optionality (vibhāsā) upon attainment (sampatte)'. The analysis is by phrases such as 'three and forty' or 'forty exceeded by three.' 'A group of which there are three forties' is ticattālīsaṃ.

97. Dvissā

97. Dvissā

Sampattavibhāsattāti “āsaṅkhyāye”ccādinā (3-94) ākāre sampatte vibhāsattā.

Because it is an optional rule upon attainment (sampattavibhāsattā): that is, because there is optionality when the vowel `ā` is attained by the rule 'Āsaṅkhyāye,' etc. (3-94).

Iti moggallānapañcikāṭīkāyaṃ sāratthavilāsiniyaṃ

Thus in the Sāratthavilāsinī, the subcommentary on the Moggallāna Pañcikā.

Tatiyakaṇḍavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Third Section is finished.

Catutthakaṇḍa

Fourth Section

1. Ṇo vāpacce

1. The suffix ṇa [is used] optionally in the sense of a descendant.

Nanu [M 0.0189] ca ‘ṇo vāpacce’ti vacanato kathaṃ pakativisayāvagamo siyā. Yathākathañci pakativisayāvagamepi sāmaññavacanato pana dhammenāpaccantyādo yato kutoci dhammeniccāditopi siyā ṇā dipaccayotyāsaṅkiyāha ‘apaccavatā’ccādi. Apaccassāti apaccatthassa, apaccavatāti “ṇo vāpacce”ti vasiṭṭhādyatthasseva pariggahaṇāya sāmaññavacanato yo apaccavā tato, atthato pana asambhavā dabbācakasaddāva sāmatthiyena chaṭṭhiyantā sabbaliṅgavacanā jāyateti viññātabbaṃ. Dhammasmāpaccaṃtyādīsu ṇādippaccayo (na jāyate) ti sambandho.

But surely, following the rule 'Ṇo vāpacce,' how could the scope of the base word be understood? Even if the scope of the base word were somehow understood, from such a general statement the suffixes ṇa, etc., might be applied to any word whatsoever, such as in 'dhammenāpaccaṃ' ('descendant by means of Dhamma'). Apprehending this, he says: 'apaccavatā,' etc. 'Apaccassa' means 'of the meaning of descendant.' 'Apaccavatā' means: from that which has a descendant (apaccavā), according to the general statement in 'Ṇo vāpacce,' for the sake of including only the meaning of progenitor, such as Vasiṭṭha and others. In terms of meaning, however, since this is impossible otherwise, it should be understood that the suffix arises only from capable words denoting a substance that end in the sixth case, in any gender or number. The connection is: in cases like 'dhammasmāpaccaṃ' ('descendant from Dhamma'), the suffixes ṇa, etc., do not arise.

Dhammenāti dhammena karaṇabhūtena. Dhammāyāti dhammatthaṃ, dhammasmāti dhammahetunā, tato asambhave kāraṇamāha ‘sāpekkhattā’ti. Sāpekkhattameva samattheti ‘apaccavāhi’ccādinā, dhammenāpaccaṃ kassāti pucchitvā devadattassāti apekkhiyamānaṃ vadati. Devadattassāti apaccavā devadattādi apekkhīyateti sambandho, hisaddo hetumhi. Na hettha ṇādivutti aññattha nahetakāmantattha (potthake) sāpekkhattā kambalo vasiṭṭhassāpaccaṃ devadattassāti ettha pana vasiṭṭho-paccavāti tato chaṭṭhiyantā hoticcāsaṅkiyāha- ‘na ce’ccādi. Na ca hotīti sambandho.

'Dhammena' means 'by Dhamma as an instrument.' 'Dhammāya' means 'for the sake of Dhamma.' 'Dhammasmā' means 'because of Dhamma.' Since the suffix does not arise from that, he states the reason: 'because of its dependency.' He supports this very dependency with 'apaccavāhi,' etc. Having asked, 'Whose descendant by means of Dhamma?' he states the expected answer: 'Devadatta's.' The connection is: by 'Devadattassa' it is meant that the one who has the descendant, i.e., Devadatta, is expected. The particle hi is in the sense of a reason. Here the formation with ṇa, etc., does not occur because of dependency on something else. In the sentence, 'A blanket is the descendant of Vasiṭṭha for Devadatta,' one might apprehend that since Vasiṭṭha has the descendant, the suffix should be applied to the word ending in the sixth case. To counter this, he says: 'na ca,' etc. The connection is: 'and it does not occur'.

Kāraṇamāha- ‘asambandhā’ti. Na hettha sambandho vasiṭṭhassa kambalāpekkhattena apaccassa ca devadattāpekkhattenātthantarāpekkhāya vasiṭṭhassāpaccena sambandhābhāvāyeva vasiṭṭhassa apaccaṃ vāsiṭṭhoti ṇādivuttiyā bhāve sāmatthiyaṃ natthi, samatthañhi vasiṭṭhaṃ rājapurisādi samāsavuttiyamekatthattamiva vāsiṭṭhādiṇādivuttiyaṃ ṇādippaccayamupajanayati, nāsamatthaṃ, tato sabbamevetammanasi nidhāya vuttaṃ- ‘asambandhā’ti.

He states the reason: 'because of non-connection.' Here there is no connection. Because Vasiṭṭha is dependent on the blanket and the descendant is dependent on Devadatta, through this dependency on another meaning, there is no connection of Vasiṭṭha with the descendant. Therefore, there is no capability for the formation with ṇa, etc., to occur to mean 'Vāsiṭṭha, the descendant of Vasiṭṭha.' For a capable word, such as Vasiṭṭha in a compound formation like rājapurisa, produces a unity of meaning, and similarly in a derivative formation with ṇa, etc., such as Vāsiṭṭha, it produces the suffix ṇa, etc.; an incapable word does not. Therefore, having kept all this in mind, it was said: 'because of non-connection'.

Yadi [M 0.0190] panettha ṇādippaccayo sabbathā sambandhamapekkhate, tadā visesato yassāpaccena sambandho tatova janakato so siyāti dassetumāha- ‘yajjeva’miccādi.

To show that if the suffix ṇa, etc., here always requires a connection, then it would arise only from that progenitor who has a specific connection with the descendant, he says: 'yajjeva,' etc.

Yo janakoti yoyo yassa yassa apaccassa janako. Tatoyevāti tasmātasmā janakatoyeva. Siyāti tasmiṃ tasmiṃ apaccatthe ṇādippaccayo siyā. Tattha hetumāha- ‘tassevāpaccena yogā’ti. Yogāti apaccasambandhato, na mūlappakatitoti paramappakatito na hotīti vuttaṃ hoti. Hetumāha- ‘ayogā,ti, vacanābhāvampettha dassetuṃ ce’tyādi vuttaṃ.

'Yo janako' means: whoever is the progenitor of whichever descendant. 'Tatoyeva' means: only from that very progenitor. 'Siyā' means: the suffix ṇa, etc., may be applied in the sense of that particular descendant. There he states the reason: 'because of the connection with that very descendant.' 'Yogā' means 'because of the connection with the descendant.' 'Na mūlappakatito' means that it is said that the suffix does not arise from the ultimate base word. He states the reason: 'because of non-connection.' And to show the absence of a rule here, it is said: 'iti,' etc.

Vacananti suttaṃ, sambandhābhāvā (tādisavacanābhāvā) ca mūlappakatito ṇādippaccayassābhāvaṃ dassetvā idāni mūlappakatitovāssābhimatabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ ‘mūlappakatito’ccādi vuttaṃ.

'Vacana' means a rule. And having shown the absence of the suffix ṇa, etc., from the ultimate base word because of the absence of connection (that is, the absence of such a rule), now, to show that its application from the ultimate base word is indeed intended, it is said: 'mūlappakatito,' etc.

Kathampanidaṃ viññāyaticcādinā janakassevābyāhitassāpaccena mukhya sambandhamānīya idamayuttantyādinā byavahitajanitassāpyapaccayassa paramappakatiyābhisambandhasabbhāvaṃ vatvā taṃ sādhayitumārabhate ‘katha’miccādi, evaṃ hiccādi kathaṃpanidamiccādinā yathāvuttassa samattha navākyaṃ, hiyasmā taṃ disvā tathā pucchito devadattassavātiādinā uppādetārameva niddisati, nāttānaṃ pitāmaho, tasmā uppādetāyevāpaccena sambajjhati na pitāmahoti yojetvā adhippāyo veditabbo. Idaṃ yathāvuttamuppādetuniddisanaṃ, tena apaccena saddhiṃ uppādetuyeva janakasseva yogo sambandho paṭipādetuṃ na sakkāti sambandho.

Having first raised the primary connection of the immediate progenitor with the descendant by the question 'But how is this understood?,' and then having stated the existence of a connection of even a descendant produced by a remote progenitor with the ultimate base word by the phrase 'this is unsuitable,' etc., he begins to establish this with 'how?,' etc. The phrase 'evaṃ hi,' etc., is a new sentence supporting what was said beginning with 'But how is this understood?' Because, having seen that descendant, when asked, he indicates only the producer with 'Devadattassa,' etc., not himself, the grandfather. Therefore, the intention should be understood by construing: 'He is connected with the descendant as the producer only, not as the grandfather.' This is the indication of the producer as stated. The connection is: it is not possible to establish that the connection is only with the producer, the immediate progenitor, through that descendant.

Tantitaṃ tattha-iti (pañcikāyaṃ) pucchānimittaṃ, tenāti apaccena. Apatananti narake apatanaṃ bhavati, soti yoso yassātyaniyamaniddiṭṭho so ñātuṃ na icchitoti sambandho. Iminā idaṃ dīpeti- “napatatyanena naraketyapaccanti vuccati apaccenānena yassakassaci avisesenāpatanambhavati narake soso tāya pucchāya ñātuṃ na icchito”ti. So vāti [M 0.0191] kassāyaṃ puttoti pucchāyānurodhane so uppādetāyeva ñātumicchitoti sambandho. Tusaddo cetthāpaccena narakāpātasabba janajānanicchāvisesajotako, yadi siyāti sambandho, attānampi niddiseyya na kevalamuppādetāraṃ, atthiccādi pitāmahassa attanopi niddese kāraṇavacanaṃ, taṃ apaccaṃ nimittaṃ kāraṇaṃ, yassa taṃ taṃnimittaṃ tasmā katvā (potthake) evaṃ diṭṭhiko hiccādinā yathāvuttaṃ samattheti.

That is the sign of the question. 'Tena' means 'by the descendant.' 'Apatanaṃ' means 'non-falling into hell occurs.' 'So' means: 'he who is indicated without specification as "whose son he is," he does not wish to be known.' This is the connection. By this he clarifies: 'He is called a descendant (apacca) because one does not fall (na patati) into hell on account of him. By this descendant, there is a non-falling into hell for anyone at all without distinction; he is not the one wished to be known by that question.' Or, the connection is: in accordance with the question 'Whose son is this?', he wishes only the producer to be known. Here the particle tu indicates the distinction that by 'descendant' is meant the desire to know all people in the line of descent, which prevents the fall into hell. The connection is: if it were so, he would indicate himself as well, not only the producer. 'Atthi,' etc., is a statement of the reason for the grandfather indicating himself as well. That descendant is the sign, the cause. For whom that is the sign... Therefore, he supports what was said with 'evaṃ diṭṭhiko hi,' etc.

Byavahitajanitenāpīti byavahitena kattunā janitenāpi, karaṇe cāyaṃ tatiyā, hetumhi vā. Kasmā evaṃ diṭṭhikoti āha ‘yaṃ nimittaṃ hi’ccādi. Hisaddo yasmādatthe. Yassāti pubbajassa, tena apaccena apatanaṃ tadapatanaṃ tato, idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti “tena byavahitajanitenāpi pumunā pubbajopi narakaṃ na patati so pubbajassāpya paccaṃ bhavati yathāvuttena nibbacanenā”ti. Tasmāccassa pubbe vuttayasmātyanenābhisambandho veditabbo. Upapatyantaramāha-‘upacāratove’ccādi. Pubba pubbabhāve satīti pubbassa pubbassa vijjamānatte sati. Byavahitena janite apaccepi nimittaṃ apāyāpatakāraṇabhāvo atthiye vāti sambandho. Kesanti āha-‘pubbesanti pubbajānanti attho, ke nāti āha- ‘pārampariyenā’ti. Abhedopacārenāti pubbapubbabhāve saticcādinā vuttanayena janakassa viya pārampariyenapubbesampinimittatā vato janakasadisattā janakāva nāma te siyunti evamabhedena upacaraṇato cintanatoti attho.
