Ubhayathāti ñāyena upacārenacāti ubhayena pakārena, evamubhayathāpi mūlappakatiyā paccenābhisambandhā kathamanantara manantarādi (potthake) (tattha) potthake janitenāpaccenādipurisasambandhoyena tato ṇādippaccayo siyāti nāsaṅknīyaṃ.

'Even by one indirectly generated' means even by one generated by an indirect agent; and this is the third case ending in the sense of instrument, or in the sense of cause. Why is this view held? He says: 'For that sign,' etc. The word 'hi' is in the sense of 'yasmā' (because). 'Of whom' means of the ancestor. By that descendant, there is no falling; that is, his non-falling from it. This is what is said: 'Even by a person generated indirectly, the ancestor does not fall into hell; he becomes a descendant of the ancestor by the aforesaid method.' Therefore, its connection with the previously stated 'yasmā' should be understood. He states another reason: 'or by figurative usage,' etc. 'When there is a preceding predecessor' means when each preceding one exists. The connection is: 'Even in a descendant generated indirectly, there is a sign, that is, the state of being a cause for not falling into a state of loss, or there is indeed.' 'Of whom?' he says. 'Of the predecessors,' meaning of the ancestors. 'Of whom indeed?' he says. 'By succession.' 'By non-distinctive figurative usage' means: in the way stated by 'when there is a preceding predecessor,' etc., just as the progenitor, so too the predecessors in succession are a sign. Because they are like the progenitor, they may be called 'progenitors.' Thus, by considering them non-distinctively through figurative usage, this is the meaning. 'In both ways' means by reasoning and by figurative usage, that is, in two ways. Thus, since in both ways there is a connection with the original progenitor through the descendant, one should not doubt how there could be a connection of the original person with a descendant generated non-immediately, whereby the suffix 'ṇa', etc., would arise from that.

Tato cāti mūlappakatito ca, apaccasāmaññavacanicchāyanti itthi punnapuṃsakattavisesopaggāhi apaccasāmaññassa vacanicchāyaṃ.

'And from that' means and from the original progenitor. 'With the desire for a word for descendant in general' means with the desire for a word for 'descendant' in general, which does not take up the specific distinctions of feminine, masculine, or neuter.

Evammūlakatito- paccasāmaññena ṇādippaccayaṃ vavatthapetvā idāni apaccāditopi hoteva ṇādi sāmaññavidhānā. So ca bahulādhikārato [M 0.0192] gurujanāyattattā tanniyogācaraṇena pasatthe yevāpacce byavahitajanitepi itthivajjite siyāti dassetumāha ‘nattādīhi’ccādi. Satiyeva gurujane sappadhānabhāvena kucchite-paccetu nattādīvuttīhi vasiṭṭhādīhi ṇādippaccayo hoti vāsiṭṭhotiādi, itthiyañca na hoti vāsiṭṭhītiādi.

Thus, having established the suffix 'ṇa', etc., from the original progenitor in the general sense of 'descendant', now the suffix 'ṇa', etc., also occurs from 'grandson', etc., by the general rule. And to show that this suffix—because of the governing rule of 'variously,' because it is dependent on respected persons, and by acting on their instruction—occurs only for a praiseworthy descendant, even one indirectly generated, excluding the feminine, he says: 'from grandson, etc.' When a respected person is present as the principal factor, for a blameworthy descendant, however, the suffix 'ṇa', etc., occurs from Vasiṭṭha, etc., with the meaning of 'grandson', etc., forming 'Vāsiṭṭho', etc.; and it does not occur in the feminine, as in 'Vāsiṭṭhī', etc.

Atthatoti sāmatthiyato. Apacce vidhīyamāno paccayo apaccavatā jāyamāno tassāpaccanti atthe jāyati. Socāya matthaviseso cha(ṭṭhiyanta) tābhāve kathaṃ siyāti idamettha sāmatthiyaṃ. Anantare vāpacce putte-bhidheyya nattādo vāpacce-bhidheyyāti sasambandho. Kutoci apaccavatā nattādo eva. Idañca sabbambahulavacaneva sampajjatīti āha- ‘bahulādhikārā’ti. Apacceti ekavacanena niddese pumunā napuṃsakena kariyati, tene kasmiṃ yevāpacce siyā, na bahūsu vasiṭṭhassāpaccāni vāsiṭṭhāni, na citthi vāsiṭṭhāni, na citthiyaṃ vāsiṭṭhītyāsaṅkiyāha-‘idañce’ccādi. Idañca apaccavacanañca. Iminā cettha tathā nissayakaraṇaṃ dasseti. Tassa vacanicchābhāvatoti tassa liṅgavacanassa sutte vattumicchāyābhāvatoti attho.

'From the meaning' means from the implication. A suffix prescribed in the sense of 'descendant' arises with the meaning 'his descendant,' being generated from one who has a descendant. How could this special meaning exist without the base word being in the sixth case? This is the implication here. Or it should be stated for an immediate descendant, a son; or it should be stated for a descendant such as a grandson. This is the connection. From some progenitor, by virtue of having descendants, it means a grandson. And all this is accomplished by the word 'bahula', so he says: 'because of the governing rule of "variously".' Fearing that, since the specification 'apacce' is made in the singular, masculine or neuter, it would therefore apply only to one descendant, not to many, as in 'the descendants of Vasiṭṭha are Vāsiṭṭhas,' nor in the feminine, as in 'Vāsiṭṭhī,' he says: 'And this...,' etc. And this, that is, the word 'descendant.' By this he shows that the basis is thus established here. 'Because of the lack of desire for that expression' means because there is no desire in the rule to state that gender and number, this is the meaning.

Kiṃ pana kāraṇaṃ sutte liṅgavacanāvacanicchāyaṃ tassāppadhānattā yenakenaci liṅgādinā niddeso-vassaṃ kattabboti nānantariyakattā tassehopādānaṃ, yathādhaññatthinopalālādinopyappadhānassopādānanti. Tatoyevāha-‘upalakkhīyassettha padhānattā’ccādi. Itthipumattayuttajaññaviseso upalakkhīyo, apaccetīdamupalakkhaṇaṃ, sayanti yathāvuttamupalakkhaṇaṃ sayaṃ. Kāriyappaṭipattiyāti pume napuṃsakepacce-bhidheyye vidhi hoticcevaṃ kāriyappaṭipattiyā vattuṃ na iṭṭhaṃ.

But what is the reason? In the rule, there is no desire to state the gender and number because of their non-predominance. Since the specification must be made by some gender, etc., it is included because it is unavoidable, just as one seeking grain also takes up the non-predominant chaff, etc. Therefore he says: 'Because what is to be indicated is predominant here,' etc. The specific nature of being born with femininity or masculinity is what is to be indicated; this word 'descendant' is the indicator. 'Itself' means the aforesaid indicator itself. 'Regarding the application of the operation' means it is not desired to state, for the application of the operation, that 'the rule applies when a masculine or neuter descendant is to be denoted.'

Vacanantarepi aññasmiṃ vacane. Āṇīti ṇippaccayasuttaṃ vadati. Agottāditoti yogottassādibhūto na hoti, tato, teneva “āṇī”ti sutte (4-5) vakkhati-‘akārantamattatovāyaṃṇina gottādibhūtato’ti. Vākyasamāsāpīti yathāsaṅkhyenāha. Tasmiṃ attheti tasmiṃ vākyopadassite atthe, tanti vākyaṃ. Samāsavuttiñca nivatteyyunti sambandho.

'In another expression' means in a different statement. 'Āṇī' refers to the rule for the suffix 'ṇi'. 'From what is not the beginning of a gotra, etc.' means from that which is not the beginning of a gotra. For that reason, in the rule 'āṇī' (4-5) he will say: 'this suffix ṇi is applied only to that which ends in 'a', not to that which is the beginning of a gotra.' 'Sentence and compound' he states according to the numerical order. 'In that meaning' means in the meaning shown by the sentence; 'that' means the sentence. The connection is: 'and he should prevent the compound formation.'

Satipanāti [M 0.0193] vākāre sati tu aniccattā ṇappaccayassa. Sopīti samāsopi, samāsotiādinā pakkhantaramāha. Tena vākyasijjhanena. Pakkhe vākyasamāsāpi siyunti pakkhe samāsavuttiyā eva bādhitattā pakkhantare ṇādivutti na bādhīyatīti vākyavuttiyopi siyunti attho.

'But if there is' means if there is the particle 'vā' (or), it is because of the optionality of the suffix 'ṇa'. 'That also' means the compound also. By 'compound,' etc., he states another alternative. By that, the sentence is established. The phrase 'In the alternative, there can also be a sentence and a compound' means: since in one alternative the formation with 'ṇa', etc., is blocked by the compound formation, in the other alternative it is not blocked, so there can also be a sentence formation. This is the meaning.

2. Vacchā

2. Vacchā

Vacchakaccādinā kaccādigaṇaṃ dassetvā tassa vibhāgena nipphattiṃ dassetuṃ ‘vacchādīhī’tiādimāha. “Kaṇho brāhmaṇe”ti gaṇasuttaṃ. Tattha kaṇhasaddo brāhmaṇe vattamāno ṇānaṇāya nappaccaye uppādayatīti attho. Evamādīhiccādinā ākatigaṇattamassa dasseti. “Katāṇiyove”ti gaṇasuttaṃ, diccādīsūti yatoṇyo dissati “ṇya diccādīhī”ti (4-4), te diccādayo, tesu pāṭhāti taṃsuttappadese “katā ṇiyove”ti pāṭhābhāvepi diccā dīnamākatigaṇattā paṭhitameva nāma tanti vuttaṃ.

Having shown the gaṇa beginning with Kaccādi by the term 'Vacchakaccādi,' to explain its formation by division, he says 'vacchādīhi,' etc. ‘Kaṇho brāhmaṇe’ is a gaṇasutta. Here, the meaning is that the word 'kaṇha', when referring to a brahmin, produces the suffix `ṇa`. By 'evamādīhi,' etc., he shows that this is an ākatigaṇa. ‘Katā ṇiyo ve’ is a gaṇasutta. Regarding 'diccādīsu': because the suffix ṇya is seen in the rule 'ṇya diccādīhi' (4-4), these are the words beginning with 'dicca'. Regarding the reading among them: although the reading 'katā ṇiyove' is absent in that sutta passage, because the group beginning with 'dicca' is an ākatigaṇa, it is indeed considered as read; thus it is said.

Ṇyeti ṇyappaccaye kate. Gottādisaddāti gotte vaṃse ādibhūtā saddā. Vaṃsoti anvayo. Soyeva gāvaṃ sajāti sādhāraṇaṃ vijātivinivattanaṃ sakaṭādivacanaṃ tāyatīti gottanti vuttaṃ, tenāha-‘gottaṃ vaṃso’ti. Tassāti gottassa, tassādayo gottādayoti seso. Kete gottādayoccāha- ‘saññākārino’ccādi. Vacchādayo nattādino apaccassa apaccaṃ tadapaccādi cāti dassetumāha-‘nattādino’ccādi.

'Ṇye': when the suffix ṇya is applied. 'Gottādisaddā': words that are primary in a gotta (clan) or vaṃsa (lineage). 'Vaṃso' means lineage. That very lineage is called gotta because it protects (tāyati) the herd (go), being common to its own kind and distinguishing it from other kinds; therefore he says: 'Gotta is lineage.' 'Tassa' means 'of the gotta'; the rest of the phrase is to be supplied, making it 'tassādayo gottādayo.' To the question, 'What are these gottādayo?' he says: 'saññākārino,' etc. To show that 'Vacchādayo' means 'the descendant of a grandchild, etc.'—that is, the descendant of a descendant—he says: 'nattādino,' etc.

3. Katti

3. Kattikā

Ghapasaññantāvettha bhīyyo kattikādayoti gayhanti. Yadi panettha aññepi gayhanti, atthi paṇhiādayo keciyeva kattikādīsu antogadhā hontīti vattumāha- ‘etthā’tiādi. Vinatā supaṇṇamātā, tehīti vidhavādīhi. Vidhavādigaṇaṃ dasseti ‘bandhaka’ccādi. Vigato dhavo pati assāti vidhavā, bandhakī abhisāriṇī.

Here, since those ending in the ghapa designation are more numerous, 'kattikādayo' (the group beginning with Kattikā) are included. If others are also included here, to state that some, like the group beginning with Paṇhi, are indeed encompassed within the group beginning with Kattikā, he says: 'etthā,' etc. 'Vinatā' is the mother of the Supaṇṇas. 'Tehi' refers to 'vidhavādīhi' (by widows, etc.). He indicates the vidhavādigaṇa (the group of widows, etc.) by 'bandhakā,' etc. 'Vidhavā' is a woman whose husband (dhavo, pati) is gone. 'Bandhakī' is an unchaste woman; 'abhisāriṇī' is a woman who goes to meet her lover.

4. Ṇyadi

4. Gaggādi

Yassa [M 0.0194] ca cavaggoti sambandho, kevalaṃ gaggyoti ettakamevā dassetvā parasatthāgatagaggādigaṇekadesabhūtakuṇḍanīsaddatopi koṇḍaññoti mudāharanto so gaggādigaṇopyatrābhyupagatoti viññāpeti. Tasmā tasmiṃ gaggādikepi parasatthapaṭhite yoyo payogo āgame dissati vaccho aggivessoccādi. Sopīha veditabboti dassetumāha-‘gaggādi’ccādi. Gaggādīti gaggādi ayaṃ. Gottassa gaggavaṃsassa ādibhūtena gaggena upalakkhito gaṇo gottādigaṇo, tena gaggo nāma koci, tassatvapaccaṃ gaggīti bhavati. Paputtādovāti avadhāraṇaṃ gaggassāpaccaṃ gaggicceva yathāsiyāti.

And whoever has a connection with 'Gagga,' having shown only 'Gaggyo,' he cites 'Koṇḍañño' from the word 'Kuṇḍanī'—which is part of the Gaggādigaṇa found in another treatise—and thereby makes it known that this Gaggādigaṇa is also accepted here. Therefore, to show that whatever usage from that Gaggādigaṇa taught in other treatises is seen in the scripture—such as 'Vaccho,' 'Aggivesso,' etc.—should also be understood here, he says: 'gaggādi,' etc. 'Gaggādi' means this group beginning with Gagga. The gaṇa characterized by Gagga, the originator of the Gagga lineage of the clan, is the gottādigaṇa. Thus, there is someone named Gagga, and his descendant becomes 'Gaggī.' The phrase 'paputtādo vā' is an emphatic statement, so that the descendant of Gagga should indeed be 'Gaggī'.

5. Āṇi

5. Āṇi

Pakatassāti “māgadhaṃ saddalakkhaṇa”nti vā “nāmasmā”ti vā pakatassa. Āti nāmavisesanesati “vidhibbisesanantassā”ti tadanta vidhinā akāranto gayhatīti āha-‘visesanena cā’tiādi. Anantaramapaccanti sambandho.

'Pakatassa': of what is established as the topic, as in 'Māgadhaṃ saddalakkhaṇaṃ' or 'nāmasmā.' When there is a specification of a name (nāmavisesane sati), by the tadantavidhi (the rule concerning that which ends in it) based on the principle 'vidhibbisesanantassā,' a word ending in the letter 'a' is taken; thus he says 'visesanena ca,' etc. The connection is with 'anantaramapaccaṃ' (immediate descendant).

6. Rāja

6. Rāja

Paccayantenāti rājaññoti paccayantena. Rājaññotīmassattho khattiyajātīti, rājaññajātīti attho. Rañño apaccaṃ rājāpaccaṃ.

'Paccayantena': by the word ending in a suffix, as in 'rājañño.' The meaning of 'rājañño' is 'of the Khattiya caste'; that is, the meaning is 'of the royal caste.' 'Rañño apaccaṃ' means 'descendant of a king,' which becomes 'rājāpaccaṃ'.

8. Manu

8. Manu

Samudāyenāti paccayantasamudāyena, jātiyanti manussajātiyaṃ. Jātisaddāeteti idaṃ manusso mānusoti ettha apaccatthābhāve hetuvacanaṃ. Apaccattho ettha natthevāti ca idaṃ visuṃ manussamānusa saṅkhātassa paccatthassābhāvadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Ṇovāti manuno apaccanti atthe“ṇo vāpacce”ti (4-1) ṇappaccayova. Na jātīti byatirekamāha.

'Samudāyena': by the aggregate form ending in a suffix. 'Jātiyaṃ': in the human species. This word 'jāti' in the case of 'manusso' and 'mānuso' is a statement of the reason for the absence of the meaning of 'descendant.' And 'the meaning of descendant is not present here' is said in order to show the absence of the meaning derived from the suffix for what are designated separately as 'manussa' and 'mānusa.' 'Ṇo vā': in the sense 'descendant of Manu,' the suffix ṇa is indeed applied by the rule 'ṇo vāpacce' (4-1). 'Na jāti' states the exclusion.

9. Jana

9. Jana

Rājasambandheti [M 0.0195] raññeti vuttarājasambandhe. Pañcālānaṃ khattiyānaṃ apaccaṃ, pañcālānaṃ janapadānaṃ rājāti vā evamettha vi(bhāgo) veditabbo okkākānaṃ apaccaṃ rājā vā okkāko.

'Rājasambandhe': in connection with a king, as stated by 'raññe.' Here the analysis should be understood thus: 'Pañcālo' means 'descendant of the Pañcāla khattiyas' or 'king of the Pañcāla country.' Similarly, 'Okkāko' means 'descendant of the Okkākas' or 'king of the Okkākas'.

11. Ṇarā

11. Rāgā

Sāmaññena rattasaddassātthamāha- ‘kuṅkumādinā’ti. Aññathā ‘rāgo kusumbhādī’ti vuttattā kusumbhādināti (vuttaṃ) siyā, rañji aya matthi abhisaṅge‘bhojane ratto’ti. Atthi vaṇṇavisese ‘rattogo’ti, lohitotyattho, atthi sukkasaja vaṇṇantarāpādane‘ratto paṭo’ti. Iha tu tatiye-tthe vattamāno gayhatīti vuttaṃ- ‘vaṇṇantaramāpādita’nti. Rāgāti.

He states the general meaning of the word 'ratta': 'by saffron, etc.' Otherwise, since it is said 'dye is from safflower, etc.,' it would have been stated as 'by safflower, etc.' The root rañj exists in the sense of attachment, as in 'delighting in food.' It exists in the sense of a specific color, as in 'a red bull,' meaning 'blood-red.' And it exists in the sense of imparting another color to what was originally white, as in 'a dyed cloth.' Here, however, it is taken as occurring in this third sense; thus it is said: 'caused to take on another color.' By 'rāgā'...

Atthaggahaṇanti atthappadhānattā niddesassa vuttaṃ. Tañcācariyāna mupadesato avicchinnā (cariya) pārampariyāvagamyate, rāgāti kasāva saṅkhātaatthaniddeso. Tenāti paṭassa rattabhāve rāgassa karaṇaniddeso, rattanti paccayatthaniddeso, paccayo cāyaṃ kasā vatthato bhavatyasambhavā, tena sutte rāgāti vuttepi tabbācakā kasāvasaddāti viññāyati, rāgāti pana tenāti rāgasseva niddiṭṭhepi tabbhāvenā tabbāvakabhāvenā-ti bhavitabbaṃ ttho niddiṭṭho, tabbācakā ca honto‘tena ratta’nti atthe hotīti kasāvena rattanti viññāyatīti rāgavācino tatiyantattaṃ sampajjati, tena ‘ṇa rāgā tena ratta’nti vuttepi labbhamānatthavasena vuttaṃ- ‘rāgavācitatiyantato’ti. Sutte pana rāgena rattantetasmiṃ atthe rāgā rāgavācīsaddā tatiyantā ṇappaccayo hotīti attho. Abhidhānatoti upacāravasena kathanato. Vināpi tenāti taṃpaccayaṃ vināpi.

'Atthaggahaṇaṃ': this is said because the instruction is primarily concerned with the meaning. And this is known from the uninterrupted tradition of the teachers' instruction. 'Rāgā' is an instruction about the meaning designated as 'dye' (kasāva). 'Tena' is an instruction about the instrument, which is the dye, in the dyeing of the cloth. 'Rattaṃ' is an instruction about the meaning of the effect. And this effect is from the dye, because it is impossible for it to arise from the cloth itself. Therefore, even when 'rāgā' is said in the sutta, the word 'kasāva' (dye), which denotes it, is understood. But although only 'dye' is specified by 'tena' in 'rāgā', the meaning is specified by its nature. And since its denotative words occur in the sense 'dyed by that,' the phrase 'dyed by dye' is understood. Thus the state of being in the third case for a word signifying 'dye' is accomplished. Therefore, even when 'ṇa rāgā tena rattaṃ' is said, it is stated as 'rāgavācitatiyantato' ('from a word signifying dye in the third case') according to the meaning that is obtained. But in the sutta, in the sense 'dyed by a dye,' the meaning is that from words signifying dye in the third case, the suffix ṇa occurs. 'Abhidhānato': from being stated by way of metaphor. 'Vināpi tena': even without that suffix.

12. Nakkha

12. The Constellation

Tatiyantato vijjhatthaṃ tenāti anuvattateti sambandho. Sutte ayamattho “induyuttena nakkhattena lakkhito ce kālo, tadā tena [M 0.0196] lakkhite kāletyasmiṃ atthe tatiyantato nakkhattā ṇo hotī”ti. Suttavivaraṇe tu tañcetyādikamadhippāyavasena vuttaṃ. Tenātyanuvuttiyā tatiyantatoti labbhati nakkhattenāti sutattāti, kāleti pana atthaniddesato ṇappaccayādheyyassa kālo ādhāroti viññāyatīti ‘lakkhite kāle’ti vuttaṃ, visessagatavibhattiyā vicāritāya visesana gatā ca (vicāritā) nāmāti āha- ‘nakkhattene’ticcādi, iha keci khandhapañcakasaṅkhātaṃ kiriyāsabhāvamicchanti aniccaṃ, apare tu dabbasabhāvaṃ niccaṃ. Tasso bhayassapi kālassa candayuttena phussādinā lakkhiyabhāvā lakkhaṇe tatiyā yuttanti vattumāha- ‘kiriyā rūpo kālo’ccādi.

The connection is that 'tena' (by that) follows by inference from the third case ending, for the purpose of understanding. In the Sutta, this is the meaning: 'If the time is marked by a constellation joined with the moon, then at that time marked by it, the affix 'ṇa' comes from the word for constellation in the third case.' In the Sutta commentary, however, 'tañca' and so forth are stated with a deeper intention. By the continuous application of 'tena', the third case ending is obtained, as in 'nakkhattena' because it is stated in the Sutta. But regarding 'kāle', from the explanation of its meaning, it is understood that time is the locus (ādhāra) of the affix 'ṇa', hence 'lakkhite kāle' (at the marked time) is stated. When the case ending belonging to the qualified is examined, that belonging to the qualifier is also considered; thus it is stated: 'by the constellation (nakkhattena),' and so on. Here, some consider the nature of action, called the five aggregates, to be impermanent, while others consider the nature of substance to be permanent. And for both kinds of time, since they are marked by the moon joined with Phussa and so on, the third case is appropriate for the characteristic, thus it is said: 'Time is of the nature of action,' and so on.

Visesāvasāyoti kālassa visesāvadhāraṇatthameva hi ‘phussī ratti’ccādi. Loke payujjate. Gurunāti ettha guru jīvo, na nakkhattaṃ, candayuttatā panettha atthi… candayuttena gurunā rattiyā lakkhitattā. Kattikāya lakkhito muhuttoti ettha candaṃ vinā kattikāya tu kevalāya muhutto kālo lakkhito ‘kattikā muhutto’ti. Phussena lakkhitā atthasiddhīti ettha phusseninduyuttena atthasiddhi lakkhitā na kālo phussoti. Nakkhattayuttassa kālassa ratyādivisesāparāmāsena nakkhattavācito uppannassa paccayassa suttantarena lopaṃ vidhāya puna aññena suttena yuttāti desavidhānena sakaliṅgasaṅkhyāyuttehi-ṭṭhamabhidhānaṃ parehi, tadāha- ‘aho ratto’ccādi.

Indeed, for the purpose of specifically determining time, expressions like 'Phussī ratti' (Phussa night) are used in common parlance. Here, 'Gurunā' refers to Guru (Jupiter), not a constellation, but there is a connection with the moon here... because the night is marked by Guru (Jupiter) associated with the moon. Here, in 'Kattikāya lakkhito muhutto' (a moment marked by Kattikā), without the moon, the moment is marked solely by the Kattikā constellation, hence 'Kattikā moment.' Here, in 'Phussena lakkhitā atthasiddhi' (success marked by Phussa), the success of the purpose (atthasiddhi) is marked by Phussa joined with the moon, not the time itself as 'Phussa.' Because of not referring to the specific distinctions of time like night, etc., when associated with constellations, having made the elision of the affix arising from the word denoting the constellation by another Suttanta rule, and again, by the method of teaching that it is connected by another Sutta, the primary designation is made by others, endowed with all genders and numbers. Therefore, it is said: 'aho ratto' (oh, night!) and so on.

Ratyādivisesāparāmāsenāti phussī ratti phusso ahoti evaṃ ratyādivisesassa aparāmāsena asammassena aggahaṇena. Sakaliṅgasaṅkhyāyuttenāti phussakattikādīnaṃ yaṃyaṃ liṅgaṃ yāyā saṅkhyā, attaniyehi tehi tehi liṅgehi tāhitāhi ca saṅkhyāhi yuttena nakkhattasaddena. Na tadupalakkhito kāloti kattikā saddobahuvacananto bahutārakattā kattikāya, tāyakattikāya lakkhitokāloparehiviya na kathīyatīti attho. Atha tadupalakkhitassakālassevakattikāsaddenābhidhāne ko doso ye nevamuccateccāha- [M 0.0197] ‘ajjeti’ccādi. Iminā ca paramate doso ubbhāvito, tadatthatte satīti tadupalakkhitakālatthatte sati.

'Ratyādivisesāparāmāsena' means by not specifying, not confusing, and not grasping the distinctions of night and so on, such as 'Phussī' is night, 'Phusso' is day. 'Sakaliṅgasaṅkhyāyuttena' means by the word 'nakkhatta' (constellation) being endowed with whatever gender and number belongs to Phussa, Kattikā, etc., with their respective genders and numbers. 'Time is not indicated by that' means that because the word 'Kattikā' is plural due to the multitude of stars, time is not spoken of as being marked by Kattikā, as it is by others. This is the meaning. Then, what is the fault if time marked by it is denoted by the term 'Kattikā'? He says: 'ajjeti' (today), etc. And by this, a fault in the view of others is exposed: 'When there is the meaning of that'—that is, when there is the meaning of time marked by that.

Sattamī siyāti nakkhattasaddā taddhitalopantā phussena pāyasaṃ bhuñjeyya, phusse pāyasaṃ bhuñjeyyā’tyādo ādheyyantarāpekkhā siyā sattamī, yā suttantarena vidhīyati pāṇinīyehi, tato ‘ajjakattikā’tetthāpyādheyyantarāpekkhā sattamī siyā lopantattā ‘ajjakattikāsū’ti, na paṭhamā. Paṭhamāyeva panāyaṃ payogo ‘ajjakattikā,ti. Ajjetyadhikaraṇappadhāno ahorattakālavācī saddo, kattikāsaddopi taddhitalopena takkālābhidhāyako, tato yevaubhinnampisāmānādhikaraṇyā kattikāyopyadhikaraṇaṃ sampajjante, tañca na vinādheyyena hotītyādheyyantarāpekkhāyaṃ tesu sattamīyeva siyā, na paṭhamā (upa) pajjeyyātyadhippāyo. Attanodāni dassane sattamiyā appasaṅgaṃ paṭhamāyevopapattiṃ dassetumāha- ‘cande panūpacārene’ccādi, nādheyyantarāpekkhāccanena sattamiyā appasaṅgamāha. Evañcarahi vacanamantarena paresaṃ viya sattamīvidhāyakaṃ kathaṃ kattikāya jātoccāsaṅkiya tampaṭipādetumāha- ‘kattikāya jāto’ccādi. Bahuvacanantattepi kattikāya jātiyameka vacanantaṃ. Pakārantaramāha- ‘lopoti’ccādi. Lopenāti kattikāhi induyuttāhi lakkhito kāloti viggayha kataṇappaccayassa lopena.

The seventh case might be applicable: from words for constellations ending in the elision of a taddhita suffix, as in 'phussena pāyasaṃ bhuñjeyya' (one should eat milk-rice with Phussa) or 'phusse pāyasaṃ bhuñjeyya' (one should eat milk-rice in Phussa), etc., the seventh case would be due to the expectation of another substratum, which is prescribed by other Suttanta rules by the Pāṇinīyas. Therefore, in 'ajjakattikā' (today is Kattikā), the seventh case would also be applicable due to the expectation of another substratum, because of the elision, it would become 'ajjakattikāsu', not the first case. However, this usage is only in the first case: 'ajjakattikā'. The word 'ajja' is primarily a word denoting the time of day and night, functioning as a locative, and the word 'kattikā' also denotes that specific time through the elision of a taddhita suffix. Therefore, because both have the same syntactical relation, the locative also applies to 'kattikā', and that does not occur without a substratum. Thus, due to the expectation of another substratum, the seventh case would be applicable in those instances, and the first case would not be suitable—this is the intention. Now, to show the non-applicability of the seventh case and the suitability of only the first case in his own view, he says: 'But by the moon's figurative usage,' etc. By this, he states the non-applicability of the seventh case because there is no expectation of another substratum. If that is so, then how, without a specific statement, can one refute the possible presumption that the seventh case is prescribed for 'born on Kattikā,' just as in the speech of others? To establish that, he says: 'born on Kattikā,' etc. Even though it is plural, the word 'kattikā' is singular in 'kattikāya jāti'. He states another way: 'due to elision,' etc. 'Due to elision' means by eliding the 'ṇa' affix formed after analyzing 'the time marked by Kattikā joined with the moon'.

13. Sāssa

13. That is his.

Seti paṭhamantāti sāti niddiṭṭhapaṭhamantā, yaṃ paṭhamantanti sāceti dassitaṃ paṭhamantamāha. Paṭhamantassa devatāpuṇṇamāsittabhāvato tadatthamabhedenāha- ‘sā’ti. Kā sā devatāccāha- ‘lokappasiddhāyeva devatā’ti. Yāgasampadānampi loke devatāti pasiddhanti yāgassa yajitabbassa puroḍāsādino sampadānampi paṭiggāhako pindādi loke deyyassa puroḍāsādino devatā sāmīti pasiddhantyattho, indo devatā assa indaṃ, ādicco devatā assa ādiccaṃ, havi puroḍāsādi yāgadabbaṃ.

'Sā' is the first case ending; 'sā' is the designated first case ending. He states that which is shown as the first case ending, namely 'sā'. Because the first case ending refers to the deity and the full moon, he explains its meaning without difference, saying 'sā'. Which deity is that? He says: 'It is indeed the deity well-known in the world.' Even the recipient of a sacrifice is known as a deity in the world. That is, the recipient of the sacrifice—of the sacrificial cake and so forth to be sacrificed—the receiver of an offering given in the world, such as a lump of food, is known as the deity, the lord; this is the meaning. 'Indra is its deity' yields indaṃ; 'the sun is its deity' yields ādiccaṃ. Havi means a sacrificial substance, such as a sacrificial cake.

Mantathomanīyampi [M 0.0198] devatāti pasiddhanti yena manthena yo thūyate so tassa mantassa devatā sāmīti loke pasiddhantyattho mahindo yamo varuṇo devatā assāti viggaho. Vuttanaya mevāti “nakkhatteninduyuttena kāle”ti sutte vuttanayameva. Jātyekavacanaṃ maghāyāti, tārakarūpānampana bahuttā maghāsaddo bahuvacananto. Pāṇinīyā “sāsmiṃ puṇṇamāsīti saññāya”nti (4-2-21) suttayitvā phussī puṇṇamāsī asmiṃ phusso māso phusso addhamāso phusso saṃvaccharoti saññāyaṃ paṭipādenti, tena tesaṃ phussī puṇṇamāsī asmiṃ pañcadasaratteti ettha ca bhatakamāse ca taddhito na bhavati. Idha pana ‘saññāya’nti vacanābhāve bhatakamāsepi chaṭṭhyatthe bhavatītyāsaṅka viracayati ‘bhatakamāsepi’ccādi. Puṇṇo mā iccatra māsaddo candapariyāyoti āha- ‘māsaddene’ccādi. Puṇṇo mā assanti nibbacanāti ettha puṇṇamāsīsaddassa puṇṇo mā assanti nīharitvā vacanāti attho. Vuttiyā atthassa phuṭīkaraṇāya vuttaṃ- ‘so puṇṇo tiādi. Tassanti puṇṇamāsiyaṃ. Sāpuṇṇamāsī, bhatakassa bhatiyā kammakārakassa yo tiṃsati ratto māso paribbayaniyamito, tassa sambandhinī neti sambandho.

Even that which is praised by a mantra is known as a deity. That is, the meaning established in the world is that whoever is praised by a mantra is the lord of that mantra. The analysis is: 'Mahinda, Yama, and Varuṇa are its deities.' 'Vuttanaya meva' means just as stated in the Sutta: 'at the time when the moon is united with the constellation.' 'Maghā' is a generic singular, but because the stars are many, the word 'Maghā' is plural. The Pāṇinīyas, having formulated the Sutta 'sāsmiṃ puṇṇamāsīti saññāyaṃ' (4-2-21), establish the convention that 'Phussī full moon' means 'in this Phussa month,' 'Phussa fortnight,' or 'Phussa year.' Therefore, for them, the taddhita suffix is not applied in 'Phussī full moon' meaning 'on the fifteenth night,' nor in the case of a hired month. Here, however, in the absence of the term 'saññā,' he resolves the doubt that the suffix in the sense of the sixth case ending would apply even to the hired month, by stating 'even in the hired month,' and so forth. In 'Puṇṇo mā,' he says that the word 'māsa' is a synonym for the moon, thus: 'by the word 'māsa',' and so forth. Here, the meaning is that the word 'puṇṇamāsī' is explained by extracting 'puṇṇo mā assa' (it has a full moon). To clarify the meaning in usage, it is said: 'That is full,' and so forth. 'Tassa' refers to the full moon day. That full moon day is not related to the thirty-night month determined as wages for the hired worker, who is a worker for hire; this is the connection.

Yassañcatithīyanti aniyamena paṭipadādimāha. Atoeva ca nipātanāti imasmāva nipātanā, tenevāha- ‘sutte vacanameva nipātana’nti. Māsasutiyāccādo sādhippāyamatthaṃ vivarati ‘yadipi’ccādinā. Assāti sāmaññavacanepi ‘sāssa devatā puṇṇamāsī’ti sutte assāti avisesavacanepi soyeva puṇṇamāsīsadde sūyamāno māsoyeva chaṭṭhyattho viññāyatīti sambandho.

He states 'yassañca tithīyaṃ' (and on which tithi) referring to the first day of the lunar fortnight etc. without restriction. And for this very reason, it is a 'nipātana' (an indeclinable particle or irregular formation); therefore, he says: 'In the Sutta, the mere word itself is a nipātana'. He explains the intended meaning of 'māsasutiyā' (by the month's hearing) and so on, with 'yadipi' (although) etc. 'Assa' (its) - even in a general expression, as in the Sutta 'sāssa devatā puṇṇamāsī' (that is its deity, the full moon), even though 'assa' is a non-specific expression, the meaning of month in the sense of the sixth case is understood from the word 'puṇṇamāsī' itself when heard—thus the connection.

Pañcadasarattādoti paresaṃ saññāgahaṇena nivattitapañcadasarattādo. Atha addhamāsasaṃvaccharānampi udāharaṇatte nopaññāso kasmā na katoccāha- ‘addhamāsasaṃvaccharāna’miccādi. Evammaññate “addhamāsasaṃvaccharānaṃ na paccayenojukamabhidhānamapi tu saṃvaccharepi phussādimāsasambhavāsmiṃ saṃvacchare phussena māsena sambandhā phussotyupacārīyate, yathā ca phussādimāsassa sambandhī addhamāso phusso addhamāsotyupacārīyate[M 0.0199], na panojukanti tesamudāharaṇatte nānupādāna”nti.

'Pañcadasarattādo' (fifteen nights etc.) means that the fifteen nights etc. are excluded by the acceptance of convention by others. Then, why are half-months and years not included as examples? He says: 'addhamāsasaṃvaccharāna' etc. He thinks thus: 'There is no direct designation of half-months and years by means of an affix. Rather, even in the case of a year, because the month of Phussa etc. occurs in that year, that year is conventionally referred to as 'Phussa' due to its connection with the month of Phussa. And just as the half-month connected with the month of Phussa etc. is conventionally referred to as 'Phussa half-month,' it is not, however, a direct [designation]. Therefore, they are not included as examples.'

14. Tama

14. Tama

Nākaḍḍhanatthoti ṇassākaḍḍhanattho na hoti. Yadyākaḍḍhanattho assa, tadā cānukaḍḍhitaṃ nottaratrānukaḍḍheyyāti maññate, kociyeva hotīti hontīti ito bhinditvā ānetabbaṃ. Tadā desassāti iminā “tadādesā taggahaṇena gayhantī”ti paribhāsamupalakkheti. Katayādesassāpīti kato yādeso yassa tassa katayādesassāpīti. Ikārassāti yādesato pubbe ikārassa, iminā cādesādesīnamabhedo dassito. Tasadde nekenāpi paccekābhisambandhe siddheti evamaññate- “yathā’tena kataṃkīta’ (4-29) ntyādisutte ekova tasaddo bahūhi paccayattehi sambajjhate, tathihāpi ekameva tasaddaggahaṇaṃ ‘tamadhīte taṃjānātī’ti paccekamabhisambajjhate, tasmā kimetadatthena dvitaggahaṇene”ti. Dvitaggahaṇe payojanattayaṃ vuttaṃ, tattha paṭhamaṃ dassento jānaniccādinādhippāyamāvīkatvā dvitaggahaṇamiccādinā padatthamāha.

It does not have the meaning of drawing in; that is, it does not have the meaning of carrying forward. If it had the meaning of drawing in, then one might think that what has been drawn in should not be drawn in further elsewhere. One might think: 'It is only some.' The word 'honti' should be brought in by splitting it from here. By the phrase 'of its substitute,' he indicates the maxim: 'Substitutes for it are included by its mention.' 'Even of that for which the 'ya' substitute has been made': that is, of that for which the substitute 'ya' has been made. 'Of the vowel i': that is, of the vowel 'i' before the substitution of 'ya'. By this, the non-difference between the substitute and that which is substituted is shown. One might think that the connection with each individually is established even with a single word 'ta', as follows: 'Just as in the sutta beginning with 'tena kataṃ kītaṃ' (4-29), a single word 'ta' is connected with many suffixes, so here too a single mention of the word 'ta' is connected individually with 'he studies it' and 'he knows it.' Therefore, what is the purpose of this double mention of 'ta'?' Three purposes for the double mention of 'ta' are stated. Among these, showing the first, having revealed the intention with 'knowing,' etc., he states the meaning of the words with 'the double mention of 'ta',' etc.

Tattha-‘yo yamadhīte jānāti cā’ti iminā dvitaggahaṇābhāve paccayatthāvayavassa samuccayappasaṅgamāha. Samuccaye sati(yo) yamadhīte jānāti ca, tattheva siyā, yo panādhīte kevalaṃ, na (jānāti) tattha na siyāti bodhayituṃ byabhicāramāha‘na paccekāti sambandhene’ti. Yathā “tena kathaṃ kīta”miccādo “tena jitaṃ jayati”ccādi paccekasambandhena bhavati evammāviññāyīti yatheccādi kassāttho. ‘Tena kataṃ kīta”miccādīhi avatvā “tena jitaṃ jayati”ccādisuttekadesavacanamatthabyatti tathā vutte hotīti vuttaṃ, tena jitamiccādo jayanādikā kiriyāne kadabbasamavāyittena pasiddhāti yutto tattha paccekābhisambandho, nevamajjhena vedanā pyekadabbasamavāyittābhiyyotyadhippāyo.

Here, with 'whoever studies and knows it,' he states that in the absence of the double mention, there would be the contingency of a conjunction of the components of the affix's meaning. If there were a conjunction, the affix would apply only where one both studies and knows it. To show the deviation—that it would not apply where one only studies but does not know—he says 'not by individual connection.' So that it might not be understood to be by individual connection, just as in 'by him it was done, bought,' and so forth, and 'by him victory is won,' and so forth—this is the meaning of 'just as,' and so forth. It is said that by not stating 'by him it was done, bought,' and so forth, but by stating a portion of the sutta, 'by him victory is won,' and so forth, the meaning is clarified when stated thus. In 'by him victory is won,' and so forth, the action of winning and so on is established as inhering in a single substance, so an individual connection is proper there. The intention is that it is not so with studying and knowing, which do not inhere in a single substance.

Idāni [M 0.0200] dutiyaṃ dasseti ‘jānana’miccādi, nimitta miṭṭhāniṭṭhabodhakāraṇaṃ muhutto kattikādi, uppāto iṭṭhāniṭṭhasūcakaṃ pathavisamuddādīnaṃ sabhāvapariccāgenāññatattagamanaṃ. Jānanasāmaññeti nimittādīnaṃ jānana sāmaññe. ‘Yathāvuttajānanassa ajjhena visayatte hetumāha- ‘taṃ jānātīti tasaddena adhīyamānaparāmasato’ti. Tatiyaṃ dasseti ‘yato ce’ccādinā. Yato ca uppannena vidhinā ajjhena ñātu abhidhānampasiddhanti sambandho, potthakesu pana ajjhetuñātūsuti pāṭho dissati, etthāyamadhippāyo “katthaci pasiddhivisayo hoti tasaddo, tathā ca vuttaṃ subodhālaṅkāraṭīkāyaṃ pakkantavisayo tathā pasiddhavisayo anubhūtavisayo ca taṃsaddo yaṃ saddaṃ nā pekkhate’ti, tasmā pasiddhivisayena tasaddena puthageva pasiddhiyā upasaṅgahatthaṃ dvitaggahaṇaṃ kattabba”nti. Atthattaye vattamānassa tu tasaddassa savisayo viseso tatovātthikehi veditabbo.

Now he shows the second purpose with 'knowing,' etc. A sign is a cause for knowing the desirable and undesirable; a moment is a time such as Kattikā; a portent is an indicator of the desirable and undesirable, the going to another state through the relinquishment of the natural state of the earth, ocean, etc. 'In the general sense of knowing': in the general sense of knowing signs, etc. He states the reason why the aforementioned knowing has what is studied as its object: 'because what is being studied is referred to by the word 'ta' in 'he knows it'.' He shows the third purpose with 'and from which,' etc. The connection is: 'And since by the rule that has arisen, the designation of the one who knows what is studied is established.' However, in the books the reading 'ajjhetuñātūsu' is found. Here, this is the intended meaning: 'In some cases, the word 'ta' has a well-known object, and thus it is said in the Subodhālaṅkāraṭīkā: 'The word 'ta' whose object is departed, whose object is well-known, and whose object is experienced, does not require the word 'ya'.' Therefore, the double mention should be made for the purpose of including by means of a well-known designation, separately, with the word 'ta' that has a well-known object.' But the specific object of the word 'ta' when it occurs in three meanings should be understood from that by those concerned with the meaning.

15. Tassa

15. Tassa

Visayasaddo gāmasamudāyepi vattate, gāmasamudāyo ca nāma desoyeva, tenāha visayopi gāmasamudāyattā desoyevā’ti, iminā visayadesasaddānaṃ samānādhikaraṇattamāha. Vasāti desavāsino vasātayo, anuvāko ganthaviseso.

The word 'visaya' also occurs in the sense of a collection of villages, and a collection of villages is indeed a region. Therefore he says: 'visaya' too, being a collection of villages, is indeed a region. By this he states the syntactic agreement of the words 'visaya' and 'desa'. Vasāti: inhabitants of a region, dwellers. Anuvāka: a specific section of a text.

16. Nivā

16. Nivā

Tannāmeccādinā na kevalaṃ nivāseyeva, athakho vakkhamānesu pīti dasseti. Paccayantaṃ sebbādi. Desanāmambhavati catūsu atthesūti viññāyati, tenāha-‘nivāsādo vidhī’ti. Nivāsādoti nivāsa adūrabhavanibbattaatthiatthesu. Saṃhitanāmaṃ nāma lokiyasaddavo hārāppasaṅgamaññasaddavohārenupāttanāmaṃ.

By 'that name,' etc., he shows that it occurs not only in the sense of 'dwelling' but also in the senses about to be stated. An example of a word ending in the suffix is 'Sibbādi.' It is understood that the name of a country occurs in four meanings; therefore, he says: 'The rule is from 'dwelling' onwards.' 'From 'dwelling' onwards' means in the senses of dwelling, being not far from, produced in, and being present there. A 'saṃhitanāma' is a name adopted from conventional worldly usage and the usage of other words.

17. Adū

17. Adū

Nagarampi desoyevāti āha- ‘adūrabhava’nti.

Because a city is also a region, he says 'being not far from'.

18. Tena

18. Tena

Yathāyogatthoti vuttiyaṃ vuttayathāyogasaddassa attho.

'As is appropriate': this is the meaning of the word 'yathāyoga' stated in the commentary.

19. Tami

19. Tami

Paccayantanāmeti [M 0.0201] paccayantanāmaṃ yassa sattamyatthabhūtassa desassa hasminti attho, nāññasseti bhūmādivisiṭṭhatthayuttato aññassa paccayantanāmaṃ na hotīti attho. Badarā babbajā asmiṃ dese santīti viggaho.

'The name of that which ends in a suffix': the meaning is that the name ending in a suffix belongs to that region which is in the locative sense, as in 'in this.' 'Not of another': the meaning is that the name ending in a suffix does not belong to another that is not connected with a specific meaning such as 'place,' etc. The analysis is: 'Jujube trees and babbaja grass are in this region.'

21. Ajjā

21. Ajjā

Hīyyattanoti “saramhā dve”ti (134) dvittaṃ.

In hīyyattano: by the rule 'two from the vowel' (134), there is doubling.

23. Amā

23. Amā

Amāsaha bhavo amacco.

An amacco (minister) is one who is together with.

24. Majjhā

24. Majjhā

Majjhe bhavo majjhimo, ante bhavo antimo iccādi.

That which is in the middle is majjhimo; that which is at the end is antimo, and so on.

25. Kaṇa

25. Kaṇa

Magadhesu araññe gaṅgāyaṃ pabbate vane kule bārāṇasiyaṃ campāyaṃ mithilāyaṃ sambhavoti viggaho. “Dissantaññepi paccayā”ti (4-120) eyyakoti seso. Paccayantaradassane sati imināva suttena ito aññatrāpi paccayantarāni hontīti seso, gāme bhavo udare bhavo pañcālesu bhavo bodhipakkhe bhavoti viggaho.

The analysis is: 'born in Magadha, in the forest, on the Ganges, on the mountain, in the woods, in a family, in Bārāṇasī, in Campā, in Mithilā.' By the rule 'Other suffixes are also seen' (4-120), the remainder is the suffix -eyyaka. When other suffixes are seen, by this very rule other suffixes also occur elsewhere—this is the rest. The analysis is: 'that which is in a village,' 'that which is in the belly,' 'that which is in Pañcāla,' 'that which pertains to the factors of enlightenment'.

26. Ṇiko

26. Ṇika

Sarade bhavo, bhavā vāti viggaho.

The analysis is: 'born in autumn' or 'originating from'.

27. Tamassa

27. Tamassa

Sippasaddatthamāha-‘losalla’nti. Tameva byañjayati ‘kiriye’ccādinā, karaṇaṃ kiriyā vādanādikassa abhyāso, so pubbo yassāti samāso, vīṇādisaddehi kimuccateccāha- ‘vīṇādi’ccādi, dabbaṃ taṃtaṃsamudāyarūpaṃ. Sippañcāti vatvā tadatthaṃ vibhāveti ‘kiriyā viseso’ti. Vādanādikiriyāya visiṭṭho jānanakiriyāvisesoti attho, iminā vīṇādisaddā dabbatthavuttino vādanādikiriyaṃ kiriyā visesañca [M 0.0202] sippamupacārena vadantīti dīpeti. Itisaddo hetumhi. Sāyeveti abhyāsitabbā jānanakiriyāvisesassa pubbabhūtā vādanakiriyā, visesetuṃ yuttā vīṇādisaddenāti adhippāyo.

He states the meaning of the word sippa with 'proficiency' (kosalla). He clarifies that very thing with 'action,' etc. Karaṇa or kiriyā is the practice of playing instruments and so on; 'that which it precedes' is the compound. To the question, 'What is meant by words like vīṇā?' he says: 'vīṇā, etc.' Dabba (substance) is the form of the collection of those respective things. Having said 'and skill,' he explains its meaning as 'a specific action.' The meaning is: a specific action of knowing that is distinguished from the action of playing instruments and so on. By this he shows that words like vīṇā, which denote a substance, metaphorically speak of the action of playing instruments, etc., and the specific action, which is skill. The word iti is in the sense of cause. 'That very thing': the action of playing, which is to be practiced and is prior to the specific action of knowing, is fit to be specified by the word vīṇā, etc.—this is the intention.

Yuttatā cettha… vīṇādivādanavasena sippassa gahetabbabhāvato, kathaṃ vīṇādisaddehi dabbavuttīti vādanā vuccatīti āha- ‘vīṇādi visayattā’ti, vādanavuttivīṇādisaddānaṃ sippavuttittaṃ yathāvuttasso pamāvasena vattumāha- ‘yathe’ccādi. Vīṇādivādananti yatheti sambandho. Vuttameva phuṭayanto vuttiganthassa mukhaṃ vivarīyati ‘kiriye’ccādinā. Kiriyātyāsapubbakaṃ ñāṇakkhamaṃ kosallaṃ vādanakiriyā visayattā vīṇāvādanamiccanena kiriyāsaddena vuccatītyattho. Mudaṅgaṃ mudaṅgavādanaṃ sippamassa, vaṃso sippamassāti viggaho. Sīlamaddabbaṃ kathaṃ paṃsukūlādi(no) sīlatthasamānādhikaraṇattenābhidhānantyāha- ‘paṃsukūlādidhāraṇa’miccādi. Tañca sīlanti sambandho.

And the suitability here... is because skill is to be understood in terms of playing the vīṇā, etc. To the question, 'How is playing spoken of by words like vīṇā, which denote a substance?', he says: 'Because it has the vīṇā, etc., as its object.' To state that words like vīṇā, which denote playing, also denote skill by way of the aforesaid simile, he says: 'Just as,' etc. The connection is with 'just as... the playing of the vīṇā, etc.' Elucidating what has been said, the introduction to the Vutti text is opened with 'action,' etc. The meaning is: proficiency (kosalla) capable of knowledge, preceded by action and effort, is called 'lute-playing' by the word 'action' because its object is the action of playing. The analysis is: 'mudaṅga' means 'one whose skill is playing the mudaṅga (drum)'; 'vaṃsa' means 'one whose skill is the vaṃsa (flute)'. To the question, 'How is virtue (sīla), which is not a substance, designated by words like paṃsukūlika (rag-robe wearer) through apposition with the meaning of virtue?', he says: 'The wearing of rag-robes, etc.' The connection is: 'And that is virtue'.

Appicchatāyāti paccayappicchatāya. Santuṭṭhitāyāti catūsu paccayesu dvādasavidhasantuṭṭhiyā. Anuvidhīyamānaṃ karīyamānaṃ. Phalanirapekkhanti iminā idha loke cīvarādihetu paṇidhāya paṃsukūla dhāraṇādiṃ paṭikkhipati, sīlaṃ tapparabhāvena sevanā. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti “paṃsukūlādidhāraṇaṃ paṃsukūlādivisayanti paṃsukūlādisaddenopacārenābhidhīyate, sīlaṃ paṃsukūladhāraṇavisayanti paṃsukūlādi saddenopacārenoccatī”ti. Ticīvaraṃ sīlamassāti viggaho tesaṃ guḷo paṇyamassāti viggaho tomaraṃ, muggaro paharaṇamassāti viggaho, upadhīyatyupariādhīyatīti rathaṅgaṃ vuccati. Kāmakkhandhakilesābhisaṅkhārā vā upadhi upadadhāti sukhaṃ dukkhaṃvāti katvā.

'By fewness of wishes' means by fewness of wishes for requisites. 'By contentment' means by the twelve kinds of contentment regarding the four requisites. Anuvidhīyamānaṃ means being done accordingly. 'Without expectation for the fruit': by this he rejects the wearing of rag-robes, etc., in this world with an aspiration for robes, etc., and the cultivation of virtue with that as its primary aim. This is what is said: 'The wearing of rag-robes, etc., has rag-robes, etc., as its object and is designated metaphorically by the word paṃsukūla, etc.; virtue has the wearing of rag-robes as its object and is spoken of metaphorically by the word paṃsukūla, etc.' The analysis is: 'one whose virtue is the three robes.' The analysis is: 'one whose merchandise is molasses.' The analysis is: 'one whose weapon is a spear or a club.' That which is placed on, placed upon, is called a chariot-wheel. Or the aggregates of sensual pleasure, the defilements, and volitional formations are the upadhi (substratum), because they place upon one happiness or suffering.

28. Taṃhanti

28. One kills it.

Bahumhi bhūtānagatesupi paccayabhāve kāraṇamāha-‘saṅkhyākālānamavivacchitattā’ti, sutte vuttāya ekasaṅkhyāya vuttamānakā lasseva ca vattumanicchitattāti attho.

Although there are many past and future conditions, he states the reason as: 'because number and time are not intended to be expressed.' The meaning is that the singular number and the present tense mentioned in the rule are not intended to be exclusively expressed.

Tadupādānantūti [M 0.0203] tesamekavacanādīnamupādānantu. Taṃ nānantarīya kattāti upalakkhaṇavasena tesaṃ vacanakālantarānamavinābhāvittāti adhippāyo. Hanticcādityādyantassa kiriyāppadhānatte kathaṃ ṇādīnaṃ tadatthe jāyamānānaṃ sādhanappadhānatta miccatra hetumāha ‘sabhāvato’ti. Mīne hantīti meniko. Ajivhā animisā ca macchā, diṭṭhova sandiṭṭhanti iminā saṃsaddassa visuṃ atthabhāvaṃ dasseti. Lokuttaradhammoti navavidho lokuttaradhammo, phaladhammopi heṭṭhimo sakadāgāmivipassanādīnaṃ paccayabhāvena uparimaggādhigamassa upanissayabhāvato pariyāyato dissamānova vaṭṭabhayaṃ nivatteti, bhāvanābhisamayavasena maggadhammo sacchikiriyābhisamayavasena nibbānadhammo.

Tadupādānantūti means the taking up of their singular number, etc. Taṃ nānantarīyakattāti: the intention is that, as a characteristic mark, they are inseparable from other numbers and tenses. When the action is primary in verbs ending in -ti such as hanti, how is it that suffixes like -ṇa, which arise in that meaning, are primarily denoting the agent? To this, he states the reason: 'by its own nature.' Mīne hantīti meniko: 'A menika is one who kills fish.' 'Fish are tongueless and unblinking; the seen is the directly seen': by this he shows that the prefix saṃ- has a distinct meaning. The supramundane Dhamma is the ninefold supramundane Dhamma. Even a lower fruition Dhamma, by being a condition for the insight of a once-returner and so on, and a decisive support for the attainment of the higher paths, is seen indirectly to avert the fear of the round of rebirth. The path Dhamma is by way of the full understanding of development; the Nibbāna Dhamma is by way of the full understanding of realization.

Vaṭṭabhayanti kammakilesavipākasaṅkhātaṃ tividhavaṭṭabhayaṃ. Vidhāna vacananti appatte-tthe niyogasaṅkhātavidhino pakāsataṃ ehipassa vacanaṃ. Parisuddhattāti kilesamalavirahena sabbathā visuddhattā. Amanuññampi kadāci sappayojanaṃ yathāsabhāvappakāsanena dassetabbaṃ bhaveyyāti tadabhāvaṃ dasseti. Tenāha ‘vijjamānampi ce’ccādi. Nanu ca ehipassāti tyādyantā, tasmā neteti paccayo pappoti, tathāhi pāṭipadikato paccayavidhānampaṭipāditaṃ, na tyādyantato nāpi vākyato, tasmā kathamehipassikoti hotīti āha-‘ehipassasaddocāya’miccādi. Padasamudāyassānukaraṇoti padasamūhassa anukaraṇabhūto eko ehipassasaddo. Athavā ehi āgaccha imaṃ dhammaṃ passāti yo appatte-tthe niyogasaṅkhāto vidhi, tabbācako yannipāto ehipassāti, ehipassavidhiṃ arahatīti ehipassiko, athavā ehicceva nipāto, dassanaṃ ñāpanaṃ passo, ehīti passo ñāpanaṃ ehipasso, ehipassaṃ arahatīti ehipassiko.

'The fear of the round' (vaṭṭabhayaṃ): the fear of the round, designated as the threefold round of kamma, defilements, and results. 'An injunctive utterance' (vidhānavacanaṃ): the utterance 'come and see' (ehipassa), which proclaims the injunction called vidhi in the sense of something not yet attained. 'Because of purity' (parisuddhattā): because of being completely pure through the absence of the stain of defilements. He shows the absence of that disagreeable nature, for even what is disagreeable might sometimes be beneficial and should be shown by revealing its true nature. Therefore he says: 'even if it is existing,' etc. But isn't it the case that ehipassāti ends in -ti, etc.? Therefore the suffix -ika is not obtained. For the prescription of a suffix is taught from a nominal stem, not from a word ending in -ti, etc., nor from a sentence. Therefore, how does ehipassiko come about? To this he says: 'This word ehipassa...,' etc. 'An imitation of a collection of words' means the single word ehipassa is an imitation of a group of words. Alternatively: ehi means 'come,' passa means 'see this Dhamma.' The particle ehipassa is what expresses the injunction called vidhi in the sense of something not yet attained. An ehipassiko is one who is worthy of the 'come and see' injunction. Or, ehi itself is a particle; passo is showing, making known. Ehipasso is the making known of 'come.' An ehipassiko is one who is worthy of ehipassa.

29. Tena

29. By that.

Ekībhāvoti muggehi saṃsaṭṭhānaṃ māsānamiva missībhāvo. Esoti saṃsaggo, ukkaṃsenāti ukkaṃsādhānena utkaṃsasādhanena (potthake) ca bhavitabbanti sambandho[M 0.0204]. Saṃsaggaukkaṃsānaṃ sahabhāvassa anekanti katte kāraṇamāha- ‘asucidabbe’ccādinā. Byatirekamāha- ‘nukkaṃso’ti yattha saṃsaggarahitaṃ kevalamabhisaṅkhattamatthi, tattha paccayamudāharaṇena dassetvā vijjāya saha saṃsaggassāvijjamānatte kāraṇaṃ vadati ‘rūpī dhammattā’tiādi. Rūpaṃ bhūtopādāyabhedamassa atthīti rūpī, ghatādi saṃsaṭṭhaṃ bhattādi. Tassa dhammo sabhāvo saṃsaggo, tassa bhāvo tattaṃ, tasmā, tassāti saṃsaggassa, vijjātvarūpī… yathāvutta rūpasabhāvābhāvā, tenāha- ‘vijjāya ca arūpittā’ti caraiccandhātuyeva carati.

'Unification' (ekībhāvo) is the state of being mixed, like beans mixed with mung beans. 'This' (eso) is association; 'by eminence' (ukkaṃsena) means it should be by way of eminence—this is the connection. He states the reason for the non-absolute co-existence of association and eminence with 'in an impure substance,' etc. He states the negative instance: 'no eminence' (nukkaṃso), where there is only something prepared, devoid of association. There, having shown an example of a condition, he states the reason for the non-existence of association with knowledge, saying 'because of its nature as a material thing' (rūpī dhammattā), etc. 'Material' (rūpī) is that which has materiality—divided into primary elements and derived matter—for example, rice, etc., mixed with ghee, etc. Its nature is association; its state is thatness. Therefore, 'of that' (tassā) means of association. But knowledge is immaterial because of the absence of the aforesaid material nature. For that reason, he says: 'and because knowledge is immaterial.' The root 'car' itself moves thus.

Vācasikaṃ mānasikanti “manādīnaṃ saka, yaṃkiñcīti satādikaṃ yaṃkiñci. Bāhulakenevetthāvadhāraṇaṃ labbhatīti vuttaṃ- ‘tato vā’ti, devadattena kītoti so attho tadattho, tassa appatīti abhidhānasattivekallena vuttiyamanavagamo, devadattikoti hi vutte devadattena kītotyayamattho nappatīyate… tādisa saddasattivekallena tadatthassānamidhīyamānattā, avagamo ca nāma sati sāmatthiye siyāti imamatthaṃ saṅkhepato dassetumāha- ‘tadatthāppatītiyā’tiādi.

'Verbal and mental' means 'one's own of the mind, etc.'; 'whatever' means 'whatever of mindfulness, etc.' It is said: 'Here the specification is obtained through prevalence.' 'From that, or...': 'bought by Devadatta'—that is the meaning, its meaning. 'Its non-cognition' means non-comprehension of the expression due to a deficiency in the power of the term to denote. For when 'devadattika' is said, the meaning 'bought by Devadatta' is not cognized, because its meaning is not expressed due to such a deficiency in the power of the word. 'And comprehension might be, when there is the capacity'—to show this meaning in brief, he says: 'because of the non-cognition of its meaning,' etc.

Abhidhānalakkhaṇattanti abhidhānaṃ sati sāmatthiye vākye vacanīyassātthassa vuttiyā kathanaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ sabhāvo yesante abhidhānalakkhaṇā, tesaṃ bhāvo tattaṃ, tabbādisamāpyevameva daṭṭhabbā. Maricena abhisaṅkhataṃ saṃsaṭṭhaṃ vāti, salākāya jitanti viggaho.

'Because of having the characteristic of denotation' means: those whose characteristic or nature is the stating, by means of an expression in a sentence, of the meaning to be conveyed, when there is the capacity, are 'those with the characteristic of denotation.' Their state is thatness. It should be seen in this same way also in taddhita and other compounds. 'Prepared with or mixed with pepper.' 'Won by a ticket'—this is the analysis.

30. Tassa

30. Of that.

Yo “dissantaññepi paccayā”ti (4-120)

That which [is stated in the rule]: 'And other conditions are also seen' (4-120).

34. Ṇo

34. No.

Pavuttepīti kaccāyanena pavuttanti atthe “aññasmiṃ”tismiṃṇo hotevāti adhippāyo.

'Even when it has been said': The intention is that in the sense 'said by Kaccāyana,' the particle `ṇo` occurs in the meaning of 'in another'.

35. Gavā

35. Cattle.

Duno rukkhassa.

Of the Duna tree.

38. Mātā

38. Mother.

Mātāpitunnaṃ [M 0.0205] mātāpitaroti mātuyā mātāpitaro pitussa mātāpitaro, na ekamekato dvīsūti ekato ekato vuttanayena dvīsudvīsu atthesu na bhavatīti attho.

'The parents of the parents' means: the mother's parents and the father's parents. The meaning is that it is not 'two from each one'; that is, it is not in the sense of two and two in separate instances, according to the method stated for each one.

39. Hite

39. Welfare.

Mātu hito, pitu hitoti viggaho.

'Welfare for the mother,' 'welfare for the father'—this is the analysis.

40. Ninda

40. Reproach.

Sena rūpena ñātepi visesarūpena aññāto aññātaviseso. Kaṭṭhādimayā yā paṭimā tampaṭicchandakaṃ. Sambandho sassāmīlakkhaṇo assa atthīti sambandhi kassāti kiṃ saddaniddiṭṭho, sova viseso, sambandhiviseso visayo assa aññāṇassāti samāso. Payogāsambhavāti ayamassoti vutta assappakatiyāpi payogā sambhavā. Tathāhi yadi yassāccantamajānanaṃ siyā tathā sati sabbathā vatthujānanābhāve pakatiyeva na siyā, na hi sabbathā aviññātattho saddo payogamaharati, tasmā sarūpena ñātassa yassa viseso aviññāto, soyevidha aññāto-timatoti viññāyate, aññāto-ssokassa aññāto sesaññassa (potthake) vā kutotivā kiṃ sabhāvo veti hi assakoti. Kappaccayanto hatthikaiccayannāmadheyyaṃ nāmaṃ yassa hatthiviyāti dassitapaṭibhāgassa so kappaccayantanāmadheyyo. Abhinivesena vā sijjhanti yathā ajjunādivesadhārini ajjunādisaddenāti adhippāyo.

'One whose specific aspect is unknown' is one who is unknown in a specific form even though known in its own form. An image made of wood, etc., is a likeness of that. 'Related' (sambandhī) is that which has a connection characterized by ownership. 'Whose?'—indicated by the interrogative pronoun—is the specific aspect. 'The specific aspect of the related thing is the object of ignorance'—this is the compound. 'Because of the impossibility of usage'—this is said of it, because usage of its very nature is possible. For if there were absolute ignorance of something, then, with the complete absence of knowledge of the object, its nature itself would not exist, for a word whose meaning is entirely unknown is not fit for usage. Therefore, that which is known in its general form but whose specific aspect is unknown, that alone is understood here as 'unknown.' For it is asked of this 'unknown' thing: 'Whose is it?' or 'Whence is it?' or 'What is its nature?' That which has a name ending in the suffix '-ka' is one whose counterpart is shown as 'like an elephant' (e.g., hatthika). Or, they are established by convention, as for example, the word 'Ajjuna, etc.' for one who wears the guise of Ajjuna, etc.—this is the intention.

Paṭimāyāti ettha pūjanatthā eva paṭimā gahitā, morasamāna nāmattā moroviyāti yojanā, cañcā tiṇapuriso, idha pana taṃ sadiso puriso manusso cañcā. Akasmā eva ākasmikaṃ “sakatthe”ti (4-122) ṇiko. Yaṃkiñci abuddhipubbakaṃ, tamākasmikaṃ, tasmiṃ ākasmikebhidheyyo sati ivasaddatthe vattamānato īyo hotīti attho. Kāko ca tālañca phalaṃ kākatālāni, tesamiva milanaṃ. Ajākhaggānamiva milanaṃ yadākasmikaṃ, kiñci tama jākhaggīyaṃ[M 0.0206], ṇo ivatthe. Sakkaranti “saṃyoge kvacī”ti (4-125) vuddhyabhāvo. Munīva, bālova, kulisamiva, ekasālāivāti viggaho, lohitova lohitiko phaṭikamaṇi.

'In the case of `paṭimā`': here an image for the purpose of worship is taken. Because of having a name similar to a peacock, the construction is 'like a peacock.' `Cañcā` is a man of grass; here, however, a man, a person similar to that, is `cañcā`. From 'without cause' (akasmā) comes 'accidental' (ākasmikaṃ); the suffix `ṇika` is in the sense of 'its own meaning.' Whatever is not preceded by intention is 'accidental.' The meaning is that when 'accidental' is what is to be expressed, the suffix `īya` occurs from a word that is in the sense of 'like' (iva). 'A crow and a palm fruit' are `kākatālāni`; their meeting is like that. The accidental meeting like that of a goat and a sword is `ajākhaggīyaṃ`; the suffix `īya` is in the sense of 'like.' 'In `sakkaroti`': according to the rule 'sometimes in a conjunct,' there is an absence of vṛddhi. 'Like a sage,' 'like a child,' 'like a diamond,' 'like a single hall'—this is the analysis. 'Like blood' becomes `lohitiko`, a ruby.

41. Tamassa

41. Tamassa

Doṇādītyādisaddena khārasatādayopi parimāṇavisesā gayhanti. Saṅkhyā asītipañcādayo, aññaṃ vā yaṃkiñcīti upaḍḍhakāyādi, soḷasa doṇā ekā khārī. Nanu pañcakaṃ ganthajātanti vatvā aññaṃ vā saṅghādikanti vuttaṃ taṃ kathaṃ pāṇiniyehi viya “saṅkhyāya saññāsaṅghasuttājjhayanesū”ti (5-1-58) suttitattābhāvāti manasi nidhāya ‘saṅkhyāvācīhi’ccādi vuttaṃ. “Ādasahi saṅkhyeye vattantī”ti pañcasaddassa saṅkhyeye vuttattā āha- ‘pañcāvayavā’ti. Parimāṇasaddasannidhāne saṅkhyānepi pañcasaddoti maññamāno āha- ‘pañcasaṅkhyānañce’ti. Pañcā vuttayoti pañcavārā, rūpānīti ca pariyāyantarena āvuttisaddasse vātthaṃ byattaṃ karoti.

By the word 'doṇa, etc.,' specific measures such as a hundred khāris and so on are also included. 'Number' means eighty-five and so on, or whatever else, such as 'half a body,' etc. Sixteen doṇas make one khārī. Now, it was stated that 'a pentad is a collection of texts' or 'the Sangha, etc.' How can this be, since—unlike for the followers of Pāṇini, for whom it is formulated by the rule 'saṅkhyāya saññāsaṅghasuttājjhayanesū' (Pāṇini 5.1.58)—there is no such rule? Bearing this in mind, it was said: 'by words denoting number,' etc. Because the word 'pañca' is stated in the sense of 'what is to be counted' by the phrase 'Ādasahi saṅkhyeye vattantī,' he says: 'having five components.' Thinking that in the proximity of a word for measure, the word 'pañca' is also a numeral, he says: 'and if it is the number five.' `Pañcāvuttayo` means 'five times'; and by 'forms,' he clarifies the meaning of the word 'āvutti' with a synonym.

44. Kimhā

44. Why?

Nanu sutte saṅkhyāyanti na vuttaṃ katyādayo ca payogā saṅkhyā parimāṇeyeva dissanti kathaṃ nāmetthāyaṃ vidhīti āha- ‘bahule’ccādi. Saṅkhyāparimāṇeyevāyaṃ vidhīti kiṃ sadde saṅkhyāparimāṇa visayeyeva vattamāne ayaṃ ratyādiko vidhīti attho, nanu cettha kiṃ saddo pañhe vattamāno kathaṃ saṅkhyāparimāṇe vattateti vuccate, yajjapi saṅkhyāparimāṇe na vattate, tathāpi saṅkhyāparimāṇassa pucchiyamānattā saṅkhyāparimāṇavisaye vattate vāti. Bahulādhikāra payogasāmatthiyahetunidassane phalamāha- ‘yatratvi’ccādi, paricchedakattena parimāṇakattena. Ayametthādhippāyo “yadākimidaṃ saṅkhyā parimāṇamesaṃ dasannaṃ na kiñci appakamevetanti saṅkhyāparimāṇameva kiṃ saddena nindīyate, tadāpi saṅkhyā parimāṇassa nindīyamānattā saṅkhyāparimāṇavisayattameveti khepe vattamānāpi kiṃ saddā raticcādi siyā, bahulādhikārāditova panettha na siyā”ti. Rakārānubandhā isaddalopatthāti yojanā.

Now, since 'from a number' is not stated in the rule, and usages such as `katyādayo` are seen only with number and measure, how then is this rule applicable here? He says: 'bahulaṃ,' etc. This rule applies only to number and measure. The meaning is that this rule concerning `rati`, etc., applies only when the word `kiṃ` is used in the domain of number and measure. Now, here the word `kiṃ` is used in a question; how is it said to be used in the sense of number and measure? Although it is not used in the sense of number and measure, still, because number and measure are being asked about, it is said to be used in the domain of number and measure. In indicating the reason for the power of usage under the governing rule of `bahulaṃ`, he states the result with 'yatratu,' etc., meaning by way of delimitation, by way of measurement. This is the intention here: 'When number and measure are censured by the word `kiṃ`, as in "What is this number or measure of these ten? It is nothing, just a small amount," then too, because number and measure are being censured, it is indeed within the domain of number and measure. Thus, even when the word `kiṃ` is used in censure, the suffixes `rati`, etc., could occur, but they do not occur here precisely because of the governing rule of `bahulaṃ`, etc.' The connection is that the anubandha `ra` is for the purpose of eliding the sound `i`.

45. Sañjātaṃ

45. Arisen.

Bubhukkhāpipāsappakatīhi [M 0.0207] khasantāhi akammavacanicchāyaṃ “gamanatthā kammakādhāre cā”ti (5-59) kattari kte ñimhi ca bubhukkhito pipāsitoti siddhepi vattamāne payogatthaṃ bubhukkhāpipāsāti pāṭho.

From the roots `bubhukkhā` (to be hungry) and `pipāsā` (to be thirsty), which are afflicted and intransitive in meaning, the forms `bubhukkhito` (hungry) and `pipāsito` (thirsty) are established in the agentive sense with the suffixes `kta` and `ṇi` by the rule 'gamanatthā kammakādhāre cā' (Kaccāyana 5.59). Even though these are established, the reading is `bubhukkhāpipāsā` for the sake of usage in the present context.

46. Māne

46. In measurement.

Sabbamparicchedarūpanti ummānaparimāṇādikaṃ sabbaṃ paricchedarūpaṃ. Tatra ca uccattena mānamummānaṃ, sabbato mānaṃ parimāṇaṃ.

'All that is of a delimiting nature' means that everything such as upward measurement, overall measurement, and so on, is of a delimiting nature. Among these, `ummāna` is measurement by height, while `parimāṇa` is measurement from all sides.

47. Taggho

47. Indeed.

“Pamāṇaparimāṇehi saṅkhyāyacāpi saṃsaye mattovattabbo”ti (5-2-37) pāṇiniyavattabbakāravacanaṃ, tattha pamāṇa māyāmo. Saṅkhyāyāti pañcamī. Etehi saṃsaye matto vattabboti attho. Vidatthimattaṃ ratanamattaṃ vātiādīni kamena tatthodāharaṇāni.

The statement 'The suffix `matta` should be stated in case of doubt concerning `pamāṇa` (linear measure), `parimāṇa` (capacity measure), and also `saṅkhyā` (number)' (Pāṇini 5.2.37) is a Pāṇinian statement concerning what should be stated. Therein, `pamāṇa` means linear measure. `Saṅkhyāya` is in the ablative case. The meaning is that `matta` should be stated when there is doubt concerning these. Examples thereof, in order, are `vidatthimattaṃ` (about a span) or `ratanamattaṃ` (about a cubit), and so on.

Na vattabbanti yathāvuttavattabbavacanaṃ paṭikkhipati. Paṭikkhitte tasmiṃ vidatthimattaṃ ratanamattaṃ vātiādi(nā) yaṃkiñci daṇḍapubbaṇṇādikaṃ paṇṇādikaṃ (potthake) saṃsayitaṃ, tena mānasaṅkhātassa paricchedassābhāvā kathamete payogā siyunti āsaṅkiya tattha kāraṇamāha- ‘tathābhyūhanato siddhattā’ti. Tathābhyūhanatoti vidatthimānampamāṇamassa ratanammāna massātyādinā tenappakārena abhyūhanato abhyupagamatoti attho. Saṃsayo ca nāma ubhayapakkhaparāmasane sati siyāti yathāvuttamabbhūhanaṃ sādhetumāha-nāntarene’ccādi. Pakkhadvayehīti vidatthi mānamassa ratanammānamassāti evamādikehi pakkhadvayehi. Abhyūhanaṃ saṃsayassāti gamyate. Jaṇṇu mānamassa jaṇṇutagghaṃ.

By 'it should not be stated,' he rejects the aforementioned statement concerning what should be stated. When that is rejected, one might suspect: 'Regarding something doubtful—such as 'about a span' (`vidatthimattaṃ`), 'about a cubit' (`ratanamattaṃ`), or anything like a staff, a forehead ornament, etc.—how can these usages be valid, since there is no determination known as 'measure' for it?' In response, he states the reason: 'Because it is established through such conjecture.' 'Through such conjecture' means: because of acceptance through conjecture in that manner, such as 'its measure is a span,' 'its measure is a cubit,' etc. And since doubt arises when there is consideration of both sides, in order to establish the aforesaid conjecture, he says: 'not without,' etc. 'By both sides' means by the two sides, such as 'its measure is a span,' 'its measure is a cubit,' etc. It is understood that this is the conjecture of doubt. The analysis of `jaṇṇutagghaṃ` is 'a knee is its measure' (i.e., knee-high).

48. Ṇoca

48. And not `ṇa`.

Puriso pamāṇamassāti viggaho.

The analysis is: 'A man is its measure'.

49. Ayū

49. Ayu.

Upādhyantaropādānāti ‘aṃse’ti nimittantaropādānā nivattatīti yojanā.

Regarding 'the grasping of another substratum': the connection is that by specifying 'on the shoulder' (`aṃse`), the grasping of another sign is precluded.

50. Saṅkhyā

50. Number.

Saccutīsāsadasantāya [M 0.0208] saṅkhyāya paṭhamantāya asmiṃ satasahasse adhikā saṅkhyāti atthe ḍo bhavatīti suttattho. Saccutīsā sadasantāti paṭhamāvacanaṃ paṭhamantato vidhiñāpanatthaṃ. Nanu ca sutte ‘satasahassa satasahasse ḍo’ti na vuttaṃ, tathā sati vuttiyaṃ kathaṃ ‘sataṃ sahassaṃ satasahassaṃ vā’ti vuttantyāsaṅkiyāha-ubhayathāvagamā’tiādi. Ubhayathāvagamāti sataṃ sahassanti ca satasahassanti ca ubhayappakārenāvagamā, ubhayathāvagamo payoga dassanañcettha evaṃ vivaraṇe kāraṇanti adhippāyo. Paccayatthena samānajātiye pakatyatthe satīti yenakenaci suvaṇṇakahāpaṇādinā paccayatthena samānajātiye. Suvaṇṇamāsakadīna suvaṇṇakahāpaṇādīnaṃ (potthake) masamāna jātiyānaṃ. Akevalaṃ codāharaṇaṃ dassetuṃ ‘ekavīsa’nti vuttaṃ. Anipphannattā saddānamidha paccayaggahaṇaparibhāsāvatāro natthi.

The meaning of the sutta is: after a number in the nominative case ending in `sacca`, `uti`, `īsa`, `ada`, or `asa`, the suffix `ḍo` occurs in the sense of 'a number greater than this hundred thousand.' The phrase `saccutīsāsadasantā` is in the nominative singular to indicate that the rule applies to a word in the nominative. Now, since the sutta does not state '`ḍo` after `satasahassa`,' one might ask how the commentary can say 'a hundred thousand (`sataṃ sahassaṃ`) or a hundred-thousand (`satasahassaṃ`)'. In response, he says: 'because it is understood in both ways,' etc. 'Because it is understood in both ways' means that it is understood in both forms: `sataṃ sahassaṃ` and `satasahassaṃ`. The intention is that this twofold understanding and the evidence from usage are the reason for this explanation. 'When the meaning of the base is of the same kind as the meaning of the suffix': this means of the same kind as the meaning of the suffix, with regard to anything whatsoever, such as gold kahāpaṇas. Gold māsakas and so on are of a different kind. 'Twenty-one' is stated to show a non-exclusive example. Because the words are not regularly derived, the meta-rule concerning the taking of a suffix does not apply here.

51. Tassa

51. Of that.

Nanu ca saṅkhyāsaddo saṅkhyāne saṅkhyeyye ca vattate, kathamettha saṅkhyānevasitā vutti yenevaṃ vivaraṇaṃ katamiccāha- ‘yadipi’ccādi, paccāsannaṃ saṅkhyāsaddassāti adhippāyo. Iminā ca karaṇasādhano-yaṃ pūraṇasaddoti viññāpeti. Yatoti vuttayaṃ saddasambandhinā taṃsaddena seti ulliṅgitassa saṅkhyātiatthamupadassiya sāyeva pūrīyatetīmassa kammabhāvena tiṭṭhatīti dassetuṃ tena pūraṇena pūrīyate’ti āha.

But does not the word 'number' (`saṅkhyā`) apply to both the act of counting (`saṅkhyāna`) and the thing counted (`saṅkhyeyya`)? How then is its usage here confined to the act of counting alone, for which this explanation is given? He says, 'Although...' etc. The intention is that this is proximate to the word for number. And by this he makes it known that this word for an ordinal is a derivative in the instrumental sense. Because 'which' (`ya`) is stated, he indicates the meaning 'number' which is referred to by the connected pronoun 'that' (`sā`), and in order to show that this very number stands as the object of 'is filled,' he says, 'it is filled by that ordinal.'

Sampajjateti pūrīyatetyassatthamācikkhati. Anenetaṃ dasseti “(na) ghaṭikādīnamiva dabbānaṃ dabbantare nātirittīkaraṇaṃ saṅkhyāya pūraṇaṃ kiñcarahi tassa samappattiyevā”ti. Atha kāyaṃ vacoyutti ‘sāsaṅkhyā pūrīyate yene’ti, yāvatā sāti yasmā paccayo vihito tassa saṅkhyāsaddassa parāmāso tassa ca pūraṇena abhedoccāsaṅkiyāha- ‘abhedenoccate saṅkhyā pūrīyate yenetī’ti abhidhānābhidheyyānamabhedopacārena vuccatītyattho, saṅkhyeyyapūraṇe [M 0.0209] ḍo na hotīti vatvā tadatthaṃ vibhāvetumāha- ‘dvādasanna’miccādi. So ghaṭo tāsaṃ ghaṭikānaṃ pūraṇo dabbānaṃ dabbantare nāti rittīkaraṇavasena. Vīsatiyā pūraṇotiādinā viggaho.

‘It is accomplished’ explains the meaning of ‘is filled.’ By this he shows the following: 'The filling of a number is not, as in the case of small pots and so on, the making of one substance an excess with another substance; rather, it is the very attainment of that number.' Then what is the verbal formulation: 'that number which is filled by it'? Insofar as 'that' (`sā`) is a reference to the word 'number' from which the suffix is prescribed, and suspecting an objection on account of its non-difference from the ordinal, he says: 'It is stated with non-difference: "the number which is filled by it."' The meaning is that this is stated by way of a figurative identification of the term and its referent. Having said that the suffix `ḍo` does not occur in the filling of the countable, in order to clarify its meaning, he says: 'Of twelve,' etc. That pot is the filler of those small pots in the sense of making one substance an excess with another. The analysis is by means of 'the filler of twenty,' and so on.

54. Chā

54. Chā.

Kaccāyanena “dvitīhi tiyo”ti (2-8-42) suttena dvitisaddehi tiyappaccayaṃ vidhāya “tiye dutāpi cā”ti (2-8-43) dvitīnaṃ dutādesena dutiyaṃ tatiyanti ca “catuchehi thaṭhā”ti (2-8-41) suttena catuto thappaccayaṃ vidhāya dvittena catutthanti ca nipphāditaṃ. Idha tathā bhāvena kathaṃ te sijjhantīti āsaṅkiya vuttiyaṃ ‘katha’miccādi vuttanti dassetumāha ‘saṅkhye’ccādi. Vuttiyaṃ ‘dutiyassā’tiādinā suttekadesā dassitāti tāni sampuṇṇaṃ katvā dassetuṃ ‘dutiyassā’tiādinā ‘catutthatatiyāna’miccādinā ca vuttāni.

By Kaccāyana, the forms `dutiya` and `tatiya` are produced by prescribing the suffix `tiya` after the words `dvi` and `ti` with the rule 'From `dvi` and `ti`, `tiya`' (Kacc. 2.8.42), and by substituting `duta` for `dvi` with the rule 'And also `duta` for `dvi` when `tiya` follows' (Kacc. 2.8.43). And `catuttha` is produced by prescribing the suffix `tha` after `catu` with the rule 'From `catu` and `cha`, `tha` and `ṭha`' (Kacc. 2.8.41), with doubling. Suspecting, 'Here, in the absence of that process, how are they accomplished?', in order to show that 'How...' etc. is stated in the commentary, he says, '`saṅkhye`...' etc. Since parts of the rules are shown in the commentary by 'of the second,' etc., in order to present them in full, they are stated as 'of the second,' etc., and 'of the fourth and third,' etc.

55. Ekā

55. One.

Saṅkhyāvacanassa gahaṇe ko dosoccāha-‘saṅkhyāvāci’ccādi. Bahuttavisaye payogo na siyāti saṅkhyāvacanassa ekatthe niyatattā vuttaṃ. Ekākīhiccassa atthamācikkhati padhānabhūteheva’ccādinā. Upapajjake bahuttavisaye payogotyapekkhate.

What is the fault in taking this as a word for a number? To this, he says: 'Because it expresses number,' etc. It is said that its use in a plural sense would not be possible, because a word for a number is fixed in the singular sense. He explains the meaning of `ekākī` with 'indeed, by what is foremost,' etc. One expects its use in a plural sense with the base word.

56. Vacchā

56. Calves.

Taro hotīti vuttepi tehi taro hotīti viññāyati, vacchādīhīti sutattā pana vacchādīnanti ca viññāyatīti vacchādīnantiādinā vuttiganthopadassanaṃ. Nanu tanutte vavacchādīhi paccayo vidhīyate, ye ca sarīrena kisāvacchādayo, tatrāpyavisesena payogo pasajjati payopasajjane (potthake) visesānupādānato, tasmā kathamatra sabhāvasseva tanuttaṃ viññāyate yenevaṃ vivaṭamiccāha- ‘vacchādisaddāna’ micca-di, vacchādīhi pakatīti paccaye vidhīyamāne tāsaṃ pavattinimittaṃ vayovisesādi, yasmiṃ sati vacchādayo saddā dabbe-bhinivisante, taṃ paccayā-sannaṃ, na ca kisattassa bhāvā dabbe vacchādisaddā pavattante. Ato [M 0.0210] tasseva saddappavattinimittassa tanutte yuttaṃ paccayena bhavituṃ, (na) tanuttamatteti maññate. Pavattinimittaṃ sambandhi āsannanti samānādhikaraṇāni.

Although it is said 'becomes `-tara`,' this is understood as 'becomes more so than them.' However, since 'from `vaccha`, etc.' is heard in the rule, it is also understood as 'than `vaccha`, etc.' Thus the commentary passage is shown with 'than `vaccha`, etc.' and so on. Now, is not the suffix prescribed after '`vaccha`, etc.' in the sense of 'thinness'? For those calves, etc., that are emaciated in body, an indiscriminate application would also follow, since no distinction is mentioned. Therefore, how is 'thinness' here understood as being of its very nature, for which it is thus explained? To this, he says: 'Of the words `vaccha`, etc....' etc. When the suffix is prescribed from '`vaccha`, etc.' as the base, their ground of application—such as a specific age, in the presence of which the words '`vaccha`, etc.' are applied to a substance—is proximate to the suffix. But the words '`vaccha`, etc.' are not applied to a substance because of the state of emaciation. Therefore, he thinks it is proper for the suffix to occur in the sense of the thinness of that very ground of application of the word, not in the sense of mere thinness. 'The ground of application,' 'related,' and 'proximate' are in apposition.

Vaccho paṭhamavayo, tassa tanuttaṃ dutiyavayappatti. Dutiyañhi vayaṃ pappontassa vacchassa paṭhamo vayo vacchasaddassa pavattinimittaṃ kiñcimattāvasesaṃ bhavati amumevāha-‘susuttasse’ccādinā. Ukkhotaruṇodutiyavayappatto vuccate, tassa tanuttaṃ tatiyavayappatti. Tatiyañhi vayappattakāle dutiyassa vayassa ukkhasaddappavatti nimittassa kiñcimattā vasesato vasissate (potthake) jātisaṅkarattā gaddabhajātiyā vaḷavājātiyā ca missattā. Bhāravāhakattampati yo samattho, so usabhotyuccate, yadātu tassa bhāravāhakatte sāmatthiyaṃ mandaṃ bhavati parikkhīṇaṃ, tadā tanuttambhavatītyāha- ‘sāmatthiyassa tanuttaṃ appabalatā’ti.

A calf (`vaccha`) is the first stage of life; its 'thinness' is the attainment of the second stage of life. For when a calf is reaching the second stage of life, the first stage of life—the ground of application for the word 'calf'—becomes a mere remnant. This is what he refers to with 'of the very subtle...' etc. A young bull (`ukkho taruṇo`) is said to be one who has attained the second stage of life; its 'thinness' is the attainment of the third stage of life. For at the time of attaining the third stage of life, only a remnant of the second stage of life—the ground of application for the word `ukkha`—remains. One who is capable of bearing burdens is called a bull (`usabha`). But when his capacity for bearing burdens becomes weak and diminished, then 'thinness' occurs. Hence he says: 'The "thinness" of capacity is weakness.'

57. Kimhā

57. Why?

Samudāyo nāma dvyavayavo vā siyā bahukāvayavo vā, tattha dvyavayavasamudāyā niddhāraṇe sāmatthiyā ekasseva niddhāraṇaṃ viññāyati tamevānusarati. Bahukāvayavasamudāyāpye ‘kassa niddhāraṇe’ti sutte ekassāti vacanābhāvepi ekasseva niddhāraṇaṃ viññātabbaṃ teneva kataro bhavataṃ devadatto’tyādikamudāharaṇamadāsi. Kataro bhavataṃ devadatto kataro bhavataṃ kaṭhotyādyudāharaṇabahuttena niddhāraṇavācīnamabahutthepi niddhāriyamānavācīhī’ti bahuttena vuttaṃ. Apaccaparaṃparāya pavattaṃ gottaṃ vaṃso, tadabhi dhāyino apaccappaccayantāpi abhedopacārena gottaṃ, tevāpaccā paccavantasambandhadvārenāpacce pavattāti sambandhisaddā bhavanti, caraṇasaddā ca kaṭhā yo kiriyāsaddā bhavanti kaṭhādīhi vuttajjhayanatthaṃ yathā sakaṃvatacaraṇakiriyānimittattenājjhetūsu pavattāti tesaṃ sambandhisaddānaṃ kesañci atthassa kiriyāsaddānaṃ cātthassa asatyapi jātitte jātinibandhanaṃ loke kāriyamiṭṭhaṃ taduttaṃ “gottañca cara- ṇehi [M 0.0211] sahā”ti. Tatthāpi jātittamparibhāsitaṃ, tenāha- ‘kaṭhassa caraṇattā jātittaṃ gotattā jātitta’nti ca.

A collection may be of two components or of many components. There, in distinguishing from a collection of two components, by the capacity of the distinguishing word, the distinguishing of one alone is understood; it refers to that one alone. Even when distinguishing from a collection of many components, the distinguishing of one alone should be understood, even if the word 'of one' is absent in the rule. For that reason, the example 'Which of you is Devadatta?' and so on was given. Due to the abundance of examples such as 'Which of you is Devadatta? Which of you is Kaṭha?', although the words indicating distinction are not in the plural, it is said in the plural 'by the words being distinguished'. Lineage (gotta) or family (vaṃso) is that which proceeds through a succession of descendants.
