Words that express that, even those ending in a descendant-suffix, are metaphorically called 'lineage' by way of non-distinction. Those descendants, through the connection with those who have descendants, apply to descendants, and thus they become relative words. And words for conduct, such as Kaṭha, are action-words, because for the purpose of the recitation taught by Kaṭha and others, they apply to the reciters as a designation for the action of their own respective conduct. Although there is no actual basis in birth for the meaning of some of these relative words and action-words, a function based on birth is considered desirable in the world. Thus it is said: 'Lineage together with conduct.' There too, 'basis in birth' is conventionally defined. Therefore, he says: 'Because of the conduct of the Kaṭhas, there is a basis in birth; and because of lineage, there is a basis in birth.'

58. Tena

58. Therefore:

Lokiyāti parasaddasatthakāre sandhāyāha. Iha tu avisesena vuttanti sambandho. Niruttiyaṃ sāmaññena vuttattāti yojanā. Sāmaññena vuttākāraṃ dassetuṃ ‘katha’ntiādi vuttaṃ. Devehi datto brahmunā dattotiādīni kattari karaṇe vā viggahavākyāni. Devadatto devadattiko deviyo devalotiādīni vuttipadāni.

He says 'worldly' with reference to the authors of other grammatical treatises. Here, however, it is said 'without distinction'; this is the connection. The construction is: because in etymology it is stated generally. To show the manner in which it is stated generally, 'how?' and so on is said. 'Given by the devas,' 'given by Brahmā,' and so on are analytical phrases in the agentive or instrumental case. 'Devadatta,' 'Devadattika,' 'Deviya,' 'Devala,' and so on are derivative words.

Tattha niruttipiṭakāgatānaṃ ‘devadattā devadattiko’tiādīnaṃ vuttipadānamaññathā nipphattimupadassiya devalo deviyotiādīnampana vacanantareneva nipphattiṃ dassetuṃ ‘devehi datto’tiādi vuttaṃ. Parasaddasatthakārānampi devalo deviyoti vacanantareneva sādhanaṃ sādhanākārañca tesaṃ dassetuṃ ‘kecīhī’tiādi vuttaṃ. Ekadesatoyeva paccayamicchanti tena tesaṃ devalo deviyo datti loccādi bhavati. Kappanāgāravoti dattasaddalopanāmekadesavasena kappanāgāravo.

Therein, having shown a different formation for derivative words from the Niruttipiṭaka such as 'Devadattā' and 'Devadattiko,' the phrase 'given by the devas' and so on is stated in order to show the formation of 'Devalo,' 'Deviyo,' and so on by means of another expression. And in order to show the derivation of 'Devalo' and 'Deviyo' and their manner of derivation by means of another expression for the authors of other grammatical treatises as well, 'by some' and so on is said. They desire the suffix only partially; therefore, for them, the forms 'Devalo,' 'Deviyo,' 'Datti,' 'Locca,' etc., arise. 'Respect for the concept' means respect for the concept by way of the partial elision of the word 'datta'.

59. Tassa

59. Of that:

Na ca sabbetiādinā bahulādhikāre phalaṃ vuttaṃ. Bhāvasaddo katthaci kiriyāyaṃ vattate ‘bhāve ayaṃ vidhī’ti. Katthaci adhippāye ‘ayametesaṃ bhāvo bhāvodhippāyo’ti. Katthaci padatthe ‘ime bhāvā’ti. Katthaci sattāmatte‘tiṇānaṃ bhāvo’ti. Tenāha-‘bhāvasaddasse’ccādi. Rūpasādhana dvārenāti bhāvasaddassa rūpasādhanadvārena, sappanti pakāsenti attha manenāti saddo. Sova abhidhānaṃ abhidhīyate-nenatthoti katvā. Bujjhati atthasarūpanti buddhi, sāva patīyate-nenāttho pacceti attha miti vā paccayoti vuccati.

And by the phrase beginning 'And not all,' the result in the section on general applicability is stated. The word 'bhāva' sometimes refers to action, as in 'this rule applies in the case of a state (bhāve)'; sometimes to intention, as in 'this is their intention (bhāvo)'; sometimes to the meaning of a word, as in 'these are the meanings (bhāvā)'; and sometimes to mere existence, as in 'the existence of grass (tiṇānaṃ bhāvo).' Therefore, he says: 'Of the word bhāva,' etc. 'Through the means of morphological derivation' means: through the means of the morphological derivation of the word 'bhāva.' A 'word' (sadda) is that by which they convey or reveal meaning. That itself is a 'designation' (abhidhāna), because meaning is designated by it. 'Understanding' (buddhi) is that which understands the nature of the meaning. That itself is called a 'basis' (paccaya) because meaning is arrived at by it, or one goes towards the meaning by it.

Nanu ca ‘bhavanti etasmā buddhisaddā’ti vuttaṃ tasmā pavattinimittamubhinnampi bhavati, tathāsati ‘saddappavattinimitta’nti saddasseva pavattinimittatā kasmā [M 0.0212] vuttāti vuccate. Pākaṭabhāvena abhidhānābhidheyyasambandhassa saddasseva pavattinimittataṃ vatvā visuṃ buddhiyā nimittassa rūpānugatattaṃ visesetvā pavattinimittatamassā dīpetuṃ ‘nimittavasāhi’ccādimāha. Dabbeguṇoti dabbe vuttiyaṃ guṇo nimittanti sambandho. Guṇasaddasseva jātisaddattenodāharaṇadvayaṃ dattaṃ… guṇassa jātiyā visuṃ jātinimittassābhāvato nidhittassa bhāvato. Kiriyādītiādisaddena dabbādīnaṃ gahaṇaṃ, keci pana kiriyāsaddānaṃ kiriyā pavattinimittantyāhu. Tesaṃ devadattādīnaṃ avatthāvisesena avatthābhedena sāmaññaṃ tadavatthā visesasāmaññaṃ. Tenāha- ‘devadattassā’tiādi. Vijjamāno padattho visayo yesaṃ devadattādīnaṃ saññāsaddānaṃ tesaṃ pavattinimittaṃ jātilakkhaṇamācikkhitampaṭipāditanti attho.

But was it not said, 'From this, words and understanding arise'? Therefore, the ground of application pertains to both. This being so, why is it said 'the ground of application of the word,' stating that the ground of application belongs to the word alone? It is said: Having stated that the ground of application belongs to the word alone due to the manifest nature of the relationship between the signifier and the signified, he then says 'by the power of the characteristic,' etc., in order to clarify that it is the ground of application for understanding by distinguishing that the characteristic for understanding is that which follows the form. 'In a substance, a quality' means: when referring to a substance, the quality is the characteristic; this is the connection. Two examples of a quality-word as a class-word are given because for a quality, there is no characteristic of class separate from the class itself. By 'etc.' in 'action, etc.,' substance, etc., are included. Some, however, say that for action-words, the action is the ground of application. For them, the generality of 'Devadatta,' etc., is a specific state or a difference of state; it is the generality of that specific state. Therefore, he says: 'Of Devadatta,' etc. The meaning is: for those proper nouns like 'Devadatta,' etc., whose object is an existing word-meaning, their ground of application, which has the characteristic of a class, is explained and established.

Anena ca devadattādayo saññāsaddāpi samānā jātisaddāti vuttaṃ hoti. Yadi carahi saññāsaddāpi jātivacanā siyuṃ, pañcavidhattamesaṃ parihāyatīti. Nedamevaṃ viññeyyaṃ… pasiddhatarajātyābhidhāna kaṭhagovīhiyavādisaddā jātisaddattena visuṃ pariggayhanti.

And by this, it is said that proper nouns like 'Devadatta,' etc., while being such, are also class-words. If, then, proper nouns were also expressive of class, their fivefold nature would be lost. This should not be understood thus: words that are more famous as designators of class, such as 'Kaṭha,' 'cow,' 'rice,' and 'barley,' are taken separately as class-words.

Sambandhibhedatoti ghaṭādisambandhīnaṃ bhedato. Abhāvassabhedatoti ghaṭapaṭādīnaṃ sambandhīnaṃ bhedena abhāvassa bhedato abhedepi bhedā upacaritā santīti yojanā. Yassa sāmaññassa vasā, tesu upacaritabhedesvākāsādīsu. Niravayavāvijjamānavisayānantiye ākāso viya niravayavā abhāvo viya asantā ca, te visayo yesaṃ saddānaṃ tesanti attho. Sāmaññaṃ bhāvoti puthujjanādisāmaññaṃ bhāvoti attho. Alasassa bhāvo kiriyāsambandhittaṃ, brahmaññaṃ jāti cāpalyaṃ nepuññaṃ guṇo vā. Vuttiyaṃ sakatthekantāti “sakatthe”ti (4-122) iminā sakatthe katakappaccayantāti attho. Na daṭṭhabbanti sambandho. Pattakālova pattakallaṃ. Karuṇā eva kāruññaṃ.

'Because of the difference of the relatum' means: because of the difference of the relatum of a pot, etc. 'Because of the difference of absence' means: because of the difference of absence due to the difference of the relata, such as a pot, a cloth, etc. The construction is: even when there is no difference, differences exist metaphorically. By the power of which generality, in those things such as space, etc., in which difference is metaphorical. The meaning of 'of those whose objects are partless and non-existent' is: of those words whose objects are partless like space and non-existent like absence. 'Generality is a state' means: the generality of common people, etc., is a state. 'The state of being lazy' is connection with action; 'brahminhood' is class; 'fickleness' or 'skill' is a quality. 'Ending in -ka in its own meaning' in the Vutti means: ending in the suffix -ka applied in its own meaning by the rule 'in its own meaning.' 'Should not be seen'; this is the connection. 'The proper time' (pattakālo) is just 'the proper time' (pattakallaṃ). 'Compassion' (karuṇā) is just 'compassion' (kāruñña).

62. Aṇvā

62. Minute

“Ekayoganiddiṭṭhānaṃ sahavāpavatti sahavā nivattī”ti ‘bhāva kammesū’ti [M 0.0213] anuvattate. Tathāpi bhāvetīmināvettha sappayojanattaṃ dassetumāha- ‘bhāvakammesu’ccādi.

‘Of those designated by a single formulation, there is co-occurrence and co-cessation.’ Herein, the phrase ‘in states and actions’ is carried forward. Nevertheless, to show its purposefulness in this context, he says: ‘in states and actions,’ and so on.

64. Tara

64. Tara

Yajjapi sīdhātussa kevalassa supane pavatti, tathāpyatipubbassa ukkaṃse pavattīti āha- ‘atisayo ukkaṃso’ti. So ca atisayo kassa sambhavaticcāha- ‘so ca kiriyāguṇāna’nti. Kathaṃ tesamatisayoccāha- ‘ādhārabhūtadabbavasā’ti. Kutoccāha- ‘anapekkhite’ccādi. Anapekkhito kiriyāguṇānaṃ nissayo dabbasaṅkhāto yesanti viggaho, dabbassa nissayabhūtassā-tisayattaṃ hontampi nissitānaṃ kiriyā guṇānaṃ vaseneva siyā nāññathāti vattumāha-‘paccadhikaraṇa’ntiādi.

Although the root sī by itself occurs in the sense of sleeping, nevertheless, when preceded by ati, it occurs in the sense of excellence. Thus it is said: ‘Excellence is preeminence.’ And for what does this excellence exist? It is said: ‘It is of actions and qualities.’ How is there excellence of these? It is said: ‘By virtue of the substance that is the basis.’ Whence is this? It is said: ‘Without dependence,’ etc. The analysis is: ‘those for whom the basis of actions and qualities, designated as substance, is independent.’ To state that even when there is excellence of the substance that has become the basis, this is so only by virtue of the dependent actions and qualities and not otherwise, it is said: ‘by means of the counter-foundation,’ etc.

Nanu ca yadi kiriyāguṇānamevātisayo, tadā na sijjhati ‘gotaro’ti nesa doso, no cettha jātiyātisayo, kassa carahi guṇassa go ayaṃ yo sakaṭaṃ vahati, gotaro-yaṃ yo sakaṭaṃ vahati sirañcāti, jātiyā hi niccāyekarūpāya nokkaṃsāpakaṃsayogo sambhavatīti dabbassāpi nātisayasambhavo. Tathāhi tulyappamāṇassa guṇakatova mūlato ukkaṃso dissati samānepi hi āyāme vitthāre ca paṭassa kāsikassāññovāggho bhavati māthurassāñño vāti. Dabbassāpi sātisayehi yuttatāmattena sātisayattassupaṭṭhāpitattā vuttaṃ- ‘tenevāhā’tiādi. Yadaggena kiriyāguṇānaṃ nissitānamatisayavasena nissayabhūtampi dabbaṃ kathañcidapyatisaye vattati nāma, tadagge tabbācikāpi pakati attano vacanīyatthavasena tattha vattatiyeva nāmāti ‘atiyaye vattamānato’ti pakativisesanavasena vuttaṃ, tenevāha- ‘iminā pakati visesanattañcāhā’ti. Sakatthikānaṃ pakatiattho jotanīyo hotīti sambandho.

But surely, if excellence belongs only to actions and qualities, then ‘gotaro’ is not established. This is not a fault. If there is no excellence of birth-species here, then of what quality is this ox that pulls a cart? This is a better ox (gotaro), one that pulls a cart and also a load on its head. For with a birth-species, which is constant and uniform, a connection with superiority and inferiority is not possible; thus, for a substance too, the existence of excellence is not possible. For indeed, even with things of equal measure, excellence is seen to be created by quality from the very basis. For though the length and width of a cloth are the same, the value of a Kāsika cloth is different from that of a Māthura cloth. Since the excellence of a substance is established merely by its association with things that possess excellence, it is said: ‘Therefore it is said,’ etc. When a substance, though it is the basis, operates in some way in the sense of excellence by virtue of the excellence of the dependent actions and qualities, then the root that expresses it also indeed operates in that sense by virtue of its own expressible meaning. Thus it is said, ‘because it operates in the sense of surpassing,’ by way of qualifying the root. Therefore it is said: ‘By this, he also stated the qualification of the root.’ The connection is: ‘The meaning of the root should be illuminated by those that have their own meaning.’

Sakatthikānanti kattari chaṭṭhī sambandhavacanicchāya, sakatthikehīti attho. Hetumāha- ‘pakativisesanantī’ti. Itisaddo hetumhi, yasmā [M 0.0214] ‘atisaye vattamānato’ti, pakativisesanaṃ, tato pakatyatthabhūte-tisaye jātattā sakatthikehi yathāvuttanayena pakatyatthabhūtetisayo jotanīyo hotīti attho. Tattha nābhidheyyoti byatirekamāha, tathā ca vakkhati- ‘atisayajotakātarādayo’ti.

‘Sakatthikānaṃ’: this is the sixth case ending (genitive) in the sense of the agent, with the desire to express a relation; the meaning is ‘by those with their own meaning’ (instrumental). He states the reason: ‘because it is a qualification of the root.’ The word ‘iti’ is in the sense of reason. Since the phrase ‘because it operates in the sense of surpassing’ is a qualification of the root, therefore, because it has arisen in the sense of surpassing which has become the meaning of the root, the meaning is that this surpassing, which has become the meaning of the root, should be illuminated in the aforesaid manner by those things that have their own meaning. Herein, he states the exclusion by saying ‘it is not directly expressed.’ And so it will be said: ‘The suffixes -tara, etc., are illuminators of surpassing.’

Atha pakativisesanatte kasmā nābhidheyyo jotanīyoccāha ‘pakatiyāyeva’ccādi. Ukkaṃso samānaguṇavisayeyeva loke diṭṭho paviṭṭho (potthake) tena sāmaññavacanepi tādithavisayeyeva soyeva kāraṇa vasena hotīti dassetumāha- ‘atisayene’ccādi. Dvinnamekassā-tisayeccādinā ‘dvibahūsukkaṃse taratamā”ti (caṃ 4-3-45) sakkatasuttatthassādhippāyaṃ vivarati. Taraiyāti sakavohārena vuttaṃ, tesantu īyappaccayo. Evamihāvidhānaṃ sukhasānettanti sambandho.

Now, if it is a qualification of the root, why is it to be illuminated and not directly expressed? He says: ‘By the root itself,’ etc. Excellence is seen in the world only in the sphere of similar qualities. Therefore, to show that even in a general statement it occurs in such a sphere by way of a cause, he says: ‘By surpassing,’ etc. With the phrase ‘in the surpassing of one of two,’ etc., he explains the intended meaning of the Sanskrit sūtra: ‘Tara and tama occur in the sense of excellence among two or many’ (Cāndra 4.3.45). ‘Taraiyā’ is said according to their own usage; for them, there is the suffix ‘-īya.’ Thus, the connection is: ‘Here, the absence of such a rule is for easy accomplishment.’

Ayametthādhippāyo ‘yathāvuttasuttatthavasena dvinnamekassa ukkaṃsābhāvā ‘māthurā pāṭaliputtakehi sukumāratarā’ccādo tarappaccayo na hotīti eko māthuro dutiyo pāṭaliputtako imesaṃ sukumārānaṃ dvinnameko māthuro-tisayena sukumāro sukumārataro, ekamaññesaṃ dvinnamukkaṃsetathāññesaṃ dvinnamekassāti evaṃ dvinnaṃdvinnamekekassa ukkaṃse tarappaccayo bhavati, ubhayatra tvavayavāpekkhambahuvacanaṃ, tathāhi sukumārattenukkaṃsiyamānānaṃ samudāyānamavayavā māthurā bahavo pāṭaliputtakāpi nikkaṃsiyamānā tathevāvayavā bahavo honti, evaṃ māthurā pāṭali puttakehi sukumāratarā’ti tarappaccayena sijjhati. Imasmiṃ gāme aḍḍhatarā vāṇijjāccādopi kathitena ñāyena dvinnaṃdvinnamekekassa ukkaṃse tarappaccayo bhavati, bahuvacanantu katthaci avayavāpekkhanti sabbaṃ sakkate kicchena sādhenti. Iha tu tathāvidhassa suttassā vidhānā “taratamissikiyiṭṭhātisaye”ti tarādīnamatisaye sāmaññena vidhānā sabbattha tarappaccayena sukhasādhanaṃ hotī”ti.

This is the intended meaning here: According to the meaning of the aforementioned sūtra, because there is no excellence of one of two, the suffix -tara would not occur in a statement like ‘The Māthurans are more delicate than the Pāṭaliputtakans.’ The explanation is: one is a Māthuran, the second a Pāṭaliputtakan; of these two delicate ones, one, the Māthuran, is exceedingly delicate, hence ‘more delicate’ (sukumārataro). When one of another pair is praised, and similarly when one of another pair is praised, in this way the suffix -tara occurs in the sense of the excellence of one member of each pair. In both cases, however, the plural is used with reference to the constituent members. For, when the Māthurans are being praised for their delicacy, the members of the community, the Māthurans, are many; and similarly the Pāṭaliputtakans who are being disparaged are also many members. Thus, ‘The Māthurans are more delicate than the Pāṭaliputtakans’ is established by the suffix -tara. Similarly, in the case of ‘The merchants in this village are richer,’ etc., according to the method described, the suffix -tara occurs in the sense of the excellence of one member of each pair. The plural, however, is sometimes used with reference to the constituent members. All this they establish in Sanskrit with difficulty. But here, due to the absence of such a sūtra and the general provision for -tara, etc., in the sense of surpassing by the rule ‘in the sense of surpassing, tara, tama, issika, iya, iṭṭha occur,’ the easy establishment by the suffix -tara is possible everywhere.

Avatthābhedenāti [M 0.0215] paṭutarāvatthāvato paṭuavatthāya bhinnattā vuttaṃ, tathāhi tamevāvatthantarayuttaṃ vattāro bhavanti aññe ‘bhavaṃsūavattho’ti. Pakārantarenapi sādhane hetumāha- ‘atisayamatte vā vidhānato’ti. Anavaṭṭhitattamāha- (‘atisayavāpi’ccādi). Pañcasvetesūti etesaṃ yathāvuttānaṃ tarādīnaṃ pañcannaṃ majjhe, rūpāni guṇavacanassa vuttiyamudāharitāni. Kiriyāvacanassa tu ‘atisayena pācakataro pācakatamo’ti. Issika iyaiṭṭhā sarādī tato (aññato) na honti bahulādhikārā.

‘By a difference of state’: this is said because the state of being ‘more clever’ is different from the state of being ‘clever.’ For indeed, speakers say of that same person, when connected with a different state, that he is another. He states a reason for the establishment by another method as well: ‘Or because of the provision in the sense of mere surpassing.’ He states its unfixed nature, saying: ‘Or also surpassing,’ etc. ‘Among these five’: among these five aforesaid suffixes, -tara, etc., the forms have been illustrated in the section on adjectives. But for a verbal noun, it is: ‘exceedingly a better cook, a best cook.’ The suffixes issika, iya, and iṭṭha are not formed from these (verbal nouns), because of the governing rule of ‘variously.’

66. Tassa

66. Of that

Tassāti sāmaññena vuttepi vikārasambandhīyeva chaṭṭhiyanto gayhati, chaṭṭhiyantasambandhīyeva ca vikāro gayhati sambandhavasāti dassetumāha ‘yassā’ccādi. Kosakārakapāṇavisesehi kato koso. Pāṇayo sattā, osadhyophalapākantā, rukkhā pupphaphalūpagāti rukkhosadhīnaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ vadanti tallakkhaṇenettha rukkho sadhayo na gayhanti, kiñcarahi osadhisaddena latādipi gayhati, rukkhasaddena (vanappa)tayopi, vanappatayo hi phalavantā na pupphavantā. Kathaṃ gāvassa vikāre purise mayoccāha- ‘aññasmi’ntiādi. Gāvassa idaṃ gomayaṃ.

‘Of that’: even when this is stated generally, a word ending in the genitive case is understood only in relation to modification, and modification is understood only in relation to a word ending in the genitive case, due to the force of the connection. To show this, he says: ‘of which,’ etc. A sheath is made by particular sheath-making creatures. Creatures are beings; herbs are those that perish after their fruit has ripened; trees are endowed with flowers and fruit—this, they say, is the characteristic of trees and herbs. By this characteristic, ‘tree’ and ‘herb’ are not meant here. What then? By the word ‘herb,’ creepers and the like are meant; by the word ‘tree,’ forest trees are also meant, for forest trees bear fruit but not flowers. How, in the case of a modification of a cow, is the suffix `maya` used for a man? He says: ‘in another,’ etc. This is cow-dung, a modification of a cow.

67. Jatu

67. Jatu

Upapatyantaranti paccayalopato yutyantaraṃ.

Regarding `upapatyantara`: it is another derivation due to the elision of a suffix.

68. Samū

68. Samū

Tīsuttaresu ca vattateti sambandho. Rājaññamanussānampi jātiyamapacce ññassappaccayānaṃ vidhānā vuttaṃ ‘gottappaccayantā’ti āha- ‘rājaññānaṃ samūho’ccādi. Ukkho usabho. Oṭṭho kharato, urabbho meso, evamiccādinā ‘ukkhānaṃ samūho’ccādi. Vākyamapadisati. Kākānaṃ samūhoti viggaho, ṇikaacittāti iminā ṇiko acittavāca keheva dissatīti ñāpeti. Apūpo piṭṭhapūpo, saṃkulanti (guḷa) missakakhajjakaviseso.

The connection is that it also applies in three suttas. Because the `ñña` suffix is prescribed in the sense of ‘descendant’ from an ‘origin’ for nobles and humans, it is said ‘from a word ending in a suffix denoting lineage’; he says: ‘a group of nobles,’ etc. `Ukkha` is a bull. `Oṭṭha` is a camel, `urabbha` is a ram; and so on, thus: ‘a group of bulls,’ etc. He indicates the phrase. ‘A group of crows’ is the analysis. By the rule `ṇika-acittā`, it is shown that the `ṇika` suffix is seen only with words denoting non-sentient things. `Apūpa` is a flour cake; `saṃkula` is a particular kind of confection mixed with molasses.

69. Janā

69. Janā

“Tadassaṭṭhānamīyo [M 0.0216] cā”ti (2-8-13) kaccāyanasuttassāya mattho “tadassaṭṭhānamiccetasmiṃ atthe chaṭṭhiyantato īyappaccayo hotī’ti. Tena madanassa ṭhānaṃ madanīyaṃ bandhanassa ṭhānaṃ bandhanīyaṃtyādikaṃ sādhenti. Idha pana tathāvidhassābhāvā kathaṃ taṃ sijjhatītyāsaṅkiya ‘madanīya’ntiādikaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ dassetumāha- ‘madanīyādippasiddhiyā’ccādi. Sādhanakkamaṃ dassetumāha- ‘evamaññate’ccādi.

This is the meaning of the Kaccāyana sutta (2-8-13) ‘Tadassaṭṭhānamīyo cā’: ‘In the sense of “that is its place,” the suffix `īya` occurs after a word ending in the genitive case.’ By this, they form such words as `madanīyaṃ` from `madanassa ṭhānaṃ` (place of intoxication) and `bandhanīyaṃ` from `bandhanassa ṭhānaṃ` (place of bondage). But here, since there is an absence of such a genitive form, how is it derived? Raising this doubt, `madanīya`, etc., is mentioned. To explain this, he says: ‘because of the established usage of `madanīya`, etc.’ To show the process of derivation, he says: ‘it is understood thus,’ etc.

Ṭhānanti kāraṇaṃ. “Upamatthāyitatta”nti (2-8-14) kaccāyanasuttassāyamattho “upamatthe āyitattappaccayo hotī”ti tena dhūmo viya dissatīti dhūmāyitattaṃ timiramiva dissatīti timirāyitattaṃtyādikaṃ sādhentīti vuttanayameva. Tampihaccādikaṃ dvīsu sādhanakkamadassanaṃ, dhūmo viya dissatīti dassito yo kammattho sopi dhūmāyīti kattuvasena sakkā parikappetunti kattusādhanato dhūmāyitasaddā sakatthettappaccayepi dhūmo viya dissatīti atthe āyitatthappaccayepi nātthabhedo-ññatravacanicchābhedāti daṭṭhabbaṃ, bhāvattho pana tesaṃ bhāvappadhānavasena labbhati, dhūmasseva dassananti viggahe āyitattena vā.

`Ṭhāna` means cause. This is the meaning of the Kaccāyana sutta (2-8-14) ‘Upamatthāyitatta’: ‘In the sense of a simile, the suffix `āyitatta` occurs.’ By this, they form such words as `dhūmāyitattaṃ` from `dhūmo viya dissati` (it appears like smoke) and `timirāyitattaṃ` from `timiramiva dissati` (it appears like darkness), in the way already explained. Herein, the process of derivation is shown in two ways. The objective sense shown by ‘it appears like smoke’ can also be conceived of as being formed as `dhūmāyī` from an agentive derivation. Therefore, it should be understood that whether the word `dhūmāyita` is formed with the `tta` suffix in its own sense, or with the `āyitattha` suffix in the sense ‘it appears like smoke,’ there is no difference in meaning, apart from a difference in the desired expression. Their abstract sense, however, is obtained by way of the predominance of the abstract state, or in the analysis ‘the very appearing of smoke’ by means of the `āyitatta` suffix.

70. Iyo

70. Iyo

Aññasminti aññasmimpi atthe iyoti yojanā.

`Aññasmiṃ`: in another sense also. The application is `iyo`.

74. Kathā

74. Kathā

Pavāse dūragamane sādhu pavāsiko, upavāse ratyabhojane sādhu upavāsiko.

One who is proficient (`sādhu`) in travelling abroad (`pavāse`), that is, in going to a distant place, is a `pavāsiko`. One who is proficient in observing a fast (`upavāse`), that is, in abstaining from food at night, is an `upavāsiko`.

75. Pathā

75. Pathā

Pathe sādhu upākārakaṃ pātheyyaṃ, maggopakaraṇaṃ, sapatimhi dhana patimhi sādhu upakaraṇaṃ sāpateyyaṃ dhanaṃ.

What is good and helpful (`sādhu upākārakaṃ`) on the path (`pathe`) is `pātheyyaṃ`, that is, provisions for a journey. Wealth (`dhanaṃ`) that is good and helpful for one's master (`sapatimhi`) is `sāpateyyaṃ`.

77. Rāyo

77. Rāyo

Tumantakiriyāyāti ghātetuṃ (tyādītu) mantakiriyāya. Vā saddo samuccayo, ghātetuṃ vātiādinā yojetabbo.

Regarding `tumantakiriyāya`: by a verbal action ending in the `tum` suffix, such as 'to kill.' The word `vā` is conjunctive; it should be connected as in 'to kill, or...' and so on.

78. Tame

78. Tame

Itisaddena [M 0.0217] byavacchinnamatthamupadassayamaññanāpekkhaṃ sappadhānaṃ mantvādi vidhimhidamatthadvayaṃ byāpārīyaticcāha-‘ettha assa atthī’ti. Nanu ca yaṃ yassa hoti taṃ tasmimpi hoti (yaṃ yasmiṃ hoti) tassāpi taṃ hoti teneva vuccate- ‘chaṭṭhīsattamīnamaviseso’ti, tatrañña taraniddeseneva siddhe kimatthamiha chaṭṭhīsattamīnaṃ bhedenopādānaṃ karīyatīti vuccate-yatrāvayavāvayavibhāvo, tattheva chaṭṭhīsattamīnamatthassa aviseso vatthuto (potthake) yathā ‘rukkhesākhā rukkhassa sākhā’ti. Sassāmibhāvajaññajanakabhāvādo tu nāvassamādhārādheyyabhāvoti dvinnamevatthānamupādānanti.

He says, 'Herein it is / it has this,' to show that in this rule concerning `mantu`, etc., a twofold meaning is operative, with one being primary. Now, is it not the case that what belongs to someone (`yassa`) is also in that person (`tasmiṃ`), and what is in something (`yasmiṃ`) also belongs to it (`tassa`)? For that reason it is said: 'There is no difference between the genitive and locative.' In that case, since the point is established by specifying just one or the other, why are the genitive and locative taken up separately here? It is said: Only where there is a relation of part and whole is there no difference in meaning between the genitive and locative, as in 'a branch in the tree' (`rukkhe sākhā`) and 'a branch of the tree' (`rukkhassa sākhā`). But in the case of the relation of owner and property, or of produced and producer, etc., there is not necessarily a relation of container and contained. Thus, both meanings are taken up.

Nanu ca sambhave byabhicāre ca sati visesanaṃ sātthakaṃ bhavati yathā ‘nīlamuppala’nti, nevātthittassātthi byabhicāro, tathā ca vuttaṃ- ‘na sattaṃ padattho byabhicaratī’ti, tasmā byavecchejjābhāvā niratthakamatthītivisesanantyāha- ‘padatthasse’ccādi. Sattāyaṃ abyabhicāre pīti sambandho. Kālantarā byabhicāratthamatthītivisesananti dassetumāha- ‘kāle’ccādi.

Now, is it not the case that a qualifier is meaningful when there is both possibility and deviation, as in 'blue lotus'? But there is no deviation from existence. And so it is said: 'The meaning of a word does not deviate from being.' Therefore, due to the absence of anything to be excluded, the qualification 'exists' is meaningless. Hence he says: 'of the word's meaning,' etc. The connection is: 'even with the non-deviation of being.' To show that the qualification 'exists' is for the purpose of indicating deviation in another time, he says: 'in time,' etc.

Nanu ca suttesu kālo padhānaṃ na hoti, “tena kataṃ kītaṃ”tyādinā hi paccayattho dassito, tathā hi kāyikaṃvācasikaṃ tyādo na kālasampaccayo, evamihāpi sattāmatte bhavitabbaṃ, atthīti tu vattamānasattāya eva pariggaho kathamavasīyate yena kālavisesanaṃ siyāti. Saccaṃ, kintu padatthassa sattābyabhicārābhāvepi atthītivisesanopādānasāmatthiyātra visiṭṭho sattā atthīti visesanattenopāttā, na sattāmattanti patīyate, sā pana visiṭṭhā sattā sampatisattā, atthi ca tassā byabhicāro sāmaññasattāyāti yujjateva visesanavisessabhāvoti maññate. Upādhīti visesanaṃ.

Now, is it not the case that in the suttas, time is not primary? For the meaning of the suffix is shown by such phrases as 'done by him,' 'bought by him,' etc. For thus `kāyikaṃ`, `vācasikaṃ`, etc., are not conditioned by time. So here too, it should be in the sense of mere being. But how is the inclusion of 'exists' determined to be of present being only, such that it would be a qualification of time? True. But even though the word's meaning does not deviate from being, by the force of taking up the qualification 'exists', it is understood that a specific being is taken up as a qualification by 'exists', not mere being. And that specific being is present being, and there is a deviation of it from being in general. Thus, the relationship of qualifier and qualified is indeed fitting, one thinks. `Upādhi` means qualifier.

Na bhuñjaticcādiviyāti yathā na bhuñjatīti nañssa paṭisedhattā viruddhatthapadassa sannidhāne-tthantarassa paṭisedharūpassatthassāvagati padanibandhanassa vidhino abādhikā bhavati, tamivākyattho. Adhippāyattha māha- [M 0.0218] ‘atthivacanicchāya yo visayo tassa niyamo’ti. Kati payasambhave na pana gomā rukkhavāti yojanā, tehīti pasaṃsāpahūtehi. Kakude āvatto kakudāvatto, nindito kakudāvatto assa atthīti kakudāvattī. Kathaṃ ninditattamassiccāha-‘kakudā vatto’ccādi. Saṃsatto daṇḍo assa atthiccanena gehaṭṭhitena vijjamānenapi daṇḍena daṇḍīti nābhidhīyatīti vadati. Dabbebhidheyyeti jātisannissayagopiṇḍaassapiṇḍādisaṅkhāte dabbe-bhidheyye, bhavaṃ bhaveyyāti yadākadāci bhavanto yadi bhaveyya.

Like 'he does not eat,' etc.: just as in 'he does not eat,' because `nañ` is a negation, the understanding of another meaning which has the form of a negation, in the proximity of a word with a contradictory meaning, does not obstruct the rule based on the word—such is the meaning of the sentence. He states the intended meaning: 'There is a restriction of the scope according to the desired expression of existence.' The connection is: 'when there is the possibility of some milk, but not that one is a possessor of cows or a possessor of trees.' `tehi` means 'by those senses of praise and abundance.' `Kakudāvatta` is a whirl on the hump. `Kakudāvattī` means 'he has a censured whirl on the hump.' How is it censured? He says: 'a whirl on the hump,' etc. He says that by the meaning 'he has an associated stick,' one is not called 'a stick-bearer' merely because of a stick that exists in the house. When a substance is to be denoted: that is, when a substance designated as a collection of individuals of a species, such as a herd of cows or a heap of almsfood, is to be denoted. `bhavaṃ bhaveyya` means 'if at some time you should be a possessor'.

79. Vantva

79. Having vomited.

Paññavā “byañjane dīgharassā”ti (1-33) rasso.

`Paññavā`. By the rule 'a long vowel is shortened before a consonant' (1-33), the vowel becomes short.

80. Daṇḍā

80. Daṇḍā

Dve hontīti iko īceti dve honti, ekamekaṃvāti ubhinnaṃ. Vāsaddo dve hontīti etthāpi daṭṭhabbo. Uttamīṇeva dhanā ikoti gaṇasuttaṃ vivarati ‘uttamīṇevā’tiādi. Kenettha samāsoti āha- ‘syādisyādinekatthanti samāso’ti. Uttamīṇo dhanasāmī. Asannihite atthāti gaṇasuttaṃ, asannihitetīmassa atthaṃ vivarati ‘appatte’ti. Asampatteti attho. Asannihiteti ca attho iccassa visesanaṃ. Atthanaṃ asannihite atthe āsisanaṃ attho, so assa atthīti atthiko atthī. Tadantācāti gaṇasuttaṃ, asannihitetyanuvattate, asannihitopādhikā atthantā ca ika īppaccayo bhavatītyattho. Vaṇṇantāīyevāti gaṇasuttaṃ, brahmānaṃ devānaṃ vaṇṇoti vā samāso. Hatthadantehi jātiyanti gaṇasuttaṃ.

Because there are two, `ika` and `ī` are two; `vā` applies to each of the two. The word `vā` should also be understood here as meaning 'there are two.' The gaṇasutta 'from `uttamīṇa`, `ika` [is added] in the sense of wealth' explains 'from `uttamīṇa`,' and so on. What is the compound here? He says: 'A compound is when words with their case endings have a single meaning.' `Uttamīṇa` means a creditor, the owner of the wealth. The gaṇasutta is 'in the sense of an unobtained object.' He explains the meaning of 'unobtained' (`asannihite`) as 'unacquired' (`appatte`). The meaning is 'unacquired.' And 'unobtained' is a qualifier of the word `attha`. The meaning is the desire for an unobtained object; one who has this is an `atthika` or `atthī`. The gaṇasutta is 'and from that which ends in it.' The word 'unobtained' is carried forward. The meaning is that the suffixes `ika` and `ī` come after a word ending in `attha` when it is qualified by 'unobtained.' The gaṇasutta is 'from a word ending in `vaṇṇa`, `ī` is added.' Or it is a compound meaning 'the praise of the gods by the brahmins.' The gaṇasutta is 'from `hatthadanta`, `iya` [is added] in the sense of origin'.

Jātiyanti paccayavisesanaṃ. Vaṇṇato brahmacārimhīti gaṇasuttaṃ. Brahmasaddena niyamaviseso vuccaticcāha-‘vijje’ccādi. Tasmiñcaniyamavisesacaraṇe tiṇṇaṃ brāhmaṇādīnamevādhikāro, nasuddassāti dassento āha- ‘tañce’ccādi. Tevaṇṇiko vaṇṇīti vuccatīti sambandho. Tīsu vaṇṇesu bhavo tadantogadhattā tevaṇṇikoti bhavatthe ṇiko. Vaṇṇasaddo brāhmaṇādivaṇṇavacano. Tatra brahmacārimhityanena suddo byavacchijjate.

`Jātiyaṃ` is a qualifier of the suffix. The gaṇasutta is 'from a `brahmacārin` in the sense of `vaṇṇa` (caste).' By the word `brahma`, a specific rule is stated; he says: 'in knowledge,' etc. Showing that in the practice of that specific rule, only the three castes, brahmins and so on, have the right, not the śūdra, he says: 'and that if,' etc. The connection is that one of the three castes (`tevaṇṇika`) is called `vaṇṇī`. One who exists among the three castes is a `tevaṇṇika` because of being included within them; the suffix `ṇika` is in the sense of 'existing in.' The word `vaṇṇa` denotes the castes, such as brahmin and so on. Therein, by the phrase 'from a `brahmacārin`,' the śūdra is excluded.

Athavā [M 0.0219] brahmanti nibbānaṃ tadattho ganthopi, taṃ brahmaṃ nibbānaṃ dhammaṃ vā tepiṭakaṃ caratīti brahmacārī, yati. Yatayopi hi vaṇṇīti brahmacārinoti vuccanti. Vaṇṇīliṅgīti hi vutte tiliṅgavāti attho. Vaṇṇa saddo panettha yathāvutta brahmapariyāyo. Pokkharādito deseti gaṇasuttaṃ. Deso cettha yattha(tthi pokkharādīni so). Padumagaccha pokkharaṇīnaṃ vācakassāti iminā padumāni assaṃ santīti paduminīti pokkharaṇīpi vuccatīti dasseti. Nāvā atthīti nāviko, yāgame nāvāyiko. Sukhadukkhā ī, balā bāhūrupubbā ceti ca gaṇasuttāni.

Alternatively, `brahma` is Nibbāna, and the textual passage also has that meaning. One who fares according to that `brahma`—Nibbāna or the Dhamma, the Tipiṭaka—is a `brahmacārī`, an ascetic (`yati`). For ascetics too are called `brahmacārins` in the sense of `vaṇṇī` (possessing quality). When `vaṇṇīliṅgī` is said, the meaning is 'one with the three characteristics.' Here the word `vaṇṇa` is a synonym for `brahma`, as has been said. The gaṇasutta is 'from `pokkhara`, etc., in the sense of place.' And here, 'place' is where things like `pokkhara` exist. By '[the word] `padumagaccha` (a clump of lotuses) is a designator of lotus ponds,' he shows that a lotus pond is also called `paduminī` because 'lotuses exist in it.' 'He has a boat' (`nāvā atthi`) makes `nāvika`; in the sense of journeying (`yāgame`), it is `nāvāyika`. 'From `sukhadukkha`, `ī` is added,' 'from `bala`,' and 'preceded by `bāhu` and `ūru`' are also gaṇasuttas.

82. Mukhā

82. Mukhā

Ihāpi pasajjeyya madhu asmiṃ ghaṭe atthīti etthāpi payoge madhuranti rappaccayo pāpuṇeyya madhumhi abhidheyyati adhippāyo. Na gacchantīti nagā. Yajjapi ūsavāccādo pahūtādivisayāyātthitāya sambhavo, tathāpi ñusādivato paccaya(ttha)ttena vacanicchābhāvā ñusavā ghaṭoccādi na sijjhati tasmā pahūtādivisayātthitāsambhavepi taṃvato-tthassa paccaya(ttha)ttena ñusaro desoti vattu micchāyaṃ paccayo yathā siyā aññatramābhaviccevamattho veditabboti āha- ‘iti’ccādi. Kuñjavātiettha kuñjasaddo tiṇalatādyacchāditapabbatekadese vattate.

Here too an issue would arise: in the usage 'there is honey (`madhu`) in this pot,' the suffix `ra` would be obtained, yielding `madhura`, when `madhu` is the intended meaning; this is the point. 'They do not go' (`na gacchanti`), hence `nagā` (mountains). Although its existence is possible in the sense of abundance, etc., from `ūsa`, etc., nevertheless, because there is no desire to state the meaning of a suffix like `ñu`, etc., `ñusavā ghaṭo`, etc., is not accomplished. Therefore, even when its existence is possible in the sense of abundance, etc., it should be understood that this suffix does not occur elsewhere, so that it may be used when one wishes to say 'a land of `ñusara`' with the meaning of that suffix. Thus he says 'iti,' etc. Here, in `kuñjavāti`, the word `kuñja` refers to a region of a mountain covered with grass, creepers, and so on.

87. Picchā

87. Picchā

Parehi vācāsaddā ālo vihito nindāyaṃ, neha tatheti codanamubbhāvayati ‘nindāya’miccādinā.

By other [grammarians], from the word `vācā`, the suffix `āla` is prescribed in the sense of censure. He raises the objection, 'It is not so here,' with the words 'in the sense of censure,' etc.

88. Sīlā

88. Sīlā

Sīlamassa atthi, kesā assa santīti viggaho. Aṇṇā niccanti niccavidhyutthaṃ gaṇasuttaṃ. Gāṇḍīrājīhi saññāyanti saññāvisayaniyamanatthaṃ gaṇasuttaṃ. Gaṇḍassa gaṇḍamigasiṅgassa ayaṃ gāṇḍī, sā assa atthīti gāṇḍīvo.

'He has virtue' (`sīlam assa atthi`), 'he has hair' (`kesā assa santi`)—this is the analysis. The gaṇasutta 'from `aṇṇa` in the sense of constant' is for prescribing constancy. The gaṇasutta 'from `gāṇḍī` and `rāji` in the sense of designation' is for restricting the object of designation. `Gāṇḍī` is this [bow] made from the horn of the Gaṇḍa beast (rhinoceros); 'he has it' (`sā assa atthi`), hence `gāṇḍīva`.

90. Sissa

90. Sissa

Samassa atthīti suvāmī,saṃ sakiyaṃ.

'He has his own property' (`saṃ assa atthi`), hence `suvāmī` (master). `Saṃ` means 'one's own' (`sakiyaṃ`).

91. Lakkhyā

91. By the mark.

Akārādeso [M 0.0220] ca ṇasanniyogenāti iminā yattha ṇakāro tatthevāyamakārādesoti dasseti. Upādānatoti iminā nissayakaraṇameko satthiyo ñāyoti dasseti. Antassa avidhānasāmatthiyācāti iminā satipi pubbalopena payoga nipphattiyaṃ akāraṃ vidhāya tassa lopo niratthakoti dasseti. Lakkhī sirī assa atthīti lakkhaṇo.

By the rule 'and the substitution of `a` is in conjunction with `ṇa`,' he shows that wherever there is the letter `ṇa`, this substitution of `a` also occurs. By 'from the source text,' he shows that making it a basis is one method of the teachers. And by 'due to the power of not prescribing it at the end,' he shows that even though the form of the word is accomplished by the elision of the preceding vowel, it would be pointless to prescribe the letter `a` and then its elision. 'He has fortune (`lakkhī`) and splendor (`sirī`)', hence `lakkhaṇa`.

94. Imiyā

94. By this.

Kappo yogyatā assa atthīti kappiyo, jaṭā hānabhāgo, senā assa atthīti viggaho.

'He has suitability (`kappo yogyatā`)', hence `kappiya`. Likewise for `jaṭā` (matted hair) and `hānabhāga` (a portion to be given up); the analysis for `senā` is 'he has an army' (`senā assa atthi`).

95. Topa

95. Heat.

‘Ohāka cāge’ iti sakakārassa hādhātuno payoge toppaccayaṃ nisedhetvā‘satthā hīyate satthā hīno’ti udāharaṇaṃ dassitaṃ. Tenāha- ‘sakkateccādi. Dassetuṃ tatiyampanudāharaṇanti sambandho. Cīppaccayāvasānānanti “abhūtatabbhāve karāsabhūyoge vikārācī”ti (4-119) vutto cīppaccayo avasāne ye santi viggaho. Jātiyavajjitānanti “tabbati jātiyo”ti (4-113) suttena jātiyappaccayena vajjitānaṃ. Kaccāyane tu toādīnaṃ vibhatti saññattā na tato puna vibhattuppatti.

Having negated the `ta`-suffix in the usage of the root `hā` (listed as `ohāk` with the letter `k`) in the sense of 'abandoning,' the example 'the teacher is abandoned' (`satthā hīyate`), 'the teacher was abandoned' (`satthā hīno`) is shown. Therefore he says: 'in the sense of honoring,' etc. The connection is 'to show a third example.' The analysis of `cīppaccayāvasānānaṃ` (of those ending in the `cī`-suffix) is: 'those at the end of which is the `cī`-suffix spoken of in the rule "In the sense of becoming what it was not before, in connection with `kar` and `bhū`, `cī` is added after a word denoting a modification"' (4-119). `Jātiyavajjitānaṃ` means 'of those devoid of the `jātiya`-suffix' by the sutta 'from that, `jātiya` is added' (4-113). In Kaccāyana's grammar, however, since suffixes like `to`, etc., are designated as inflections, there is no further arising of inflections from them.

96. Ito

96. From this.

Vuttiyaṃ ‘etassa ṭa eta’ iti atoiccatra etassa ṭādeso etto iccatra etaādesoti attho.

In the Vutti, the phrase ‘etassa ṭa eta’ means that in the case of `ato`, `ṭa` is the substitute for `etassa`, and in the case of `etto`, `eta` is the substitute.

97. Abhyā

97. From `abhi`, etc.

Nanu ca kiṃ iminā suttena, pañcamyantā “to pañcamyā”ti (4-95) bhavissati, apañcamyantātu “ādyādīhī”ti (4-98) netadevaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. “To pañcamyā”ti (4-95) pakativisesānamaparāmāsato kutoci pañcamyantā hotu, apañcamyantā pana “ādyādīhī”ti sutte sasaṅkhyassādisaddassa [M 0.0221] gahaṇena taṃsadisā sasaṅkhyāevopalakkhīyantītipi viññāyeyya tato apañcamyantehi abhyādīhi to na siyāti abhitoccādi na sijjhatīti “abhyādīhī”ti suttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Now, what is the purpose of this sutta? One might argue that for stems ending in the fifth case, the suffix is prescribed by '`to` after the fifth case' (4-95), while for those not ending in the fifth case, it is prescribed by 'from `ādi`, etc.' (4-98). But it should not be understood in this way. The sutta '`to` after the fifth case', since it does not specify particular stems, can apply to any stem ending in the fifth case. However, in the sutta 'from `ādi`, etc.', because the word `ādi` is included along with a number, it might be understood that only similar numbered stems are indicated. Therefore, the suffix `to` would not be applied to stems not ending in the fifth case, such as `abhi`, etc., and thus forms like `abhito`, etc., would not be accomplished. For this reason, it should be understood, the sutta 'from `abhi`, etc.' was stated.

98. Ādyā

98. From `ādi`, etc.

Nanu ca toicceva sāmaññena suttite yatokutoci pañcamyantā vā apañcamyantā vā bahulaṃ vā tomhi iṭṭhappasiddhīti kiṃ ādyādīhīti suttenāti saccaṃ, tathāpi vibhāgena dassite vibhāgaso visesāvasāyo siyāti na dosoti. Yanti paṭhamantā tomhi yato.

Now, one might ask: since the suffix `to` has been taught in a general way, and the desired form is accomplished by means of the suffix `to` from any stem whatsoever, whether ending in the fifth case or not, or by the principle of varied application, what is the need for the sutta 'from `ādi`, etc.'? This is true. Nevertheless, when the rules are shown with distinctions, a specific determination can be made for each division; thus there is no fault. The words beginning with `yanti` are stems ending in the first case from which the suffix `to` is added.

100. Katthe

100. Where?

Pubbenevāti “sabbādito” (4-99) ccādināva. Etassāti etasaddassa, imassāti imasaddassa.

By the preceding rule itself, namely, 'from `sabba`, etc.' (4-99) and so on. `Etassā ti` refers to the word `eta`; `imassā ti` refers to the word `ima`.

101. Dhi

101. `dhi`

Vāvidhānāti vikappena dhippaccayassa vidhānā.

`Vāvidhānā` means: because the suffix `dhi` is prescribed optionally.

102. Yā

102. `yā`

Yatrāti vutte yatthāti uppalakkhitameva siyāti na vuttaṃ. Evamuparipi.

When `yatrā` is stated, it is not explicitly said that `yatthā` is also to be understood. The same applies in the subsequent cases.

104. Kuhiṃ

104. `kuhiṃ`

Hiñcanaṃ vidhīyate “hiṃ haṃ hiñcana”nti (2-5-9) suttena. Hiñciādīnanti hiñcidācirahaciādīnaṃ.

The suffix `hiñcana` is prescribed by the sutta '`hiṃ haṃ hiñcana`' (2-5-9). `Hiñciādīnaṃ` refers to the group beginning with `hiñci`, `dāci`, and `rahaci`.

105. Sabbe

105. All.

Etasmiṃ kāle ekadāiccādi daṭṭhabbaṃ.

In the sense of 'at this time', the forms `ekadā`, etc., are to be understood.

106. Kadā

106. `kadā`

Kudāsaddo canaṃsaddayogeva dissati kudācananti.

The word `kudā` is seen only in conjunction with the word `cana`, as in `kudācana`.

107. Ajja

107. `ajja`

Nimittanimittīnanti kāraṇakāriyānaṃ, samāneti sādhāraṇe. Samānameva bodheti ‘taṃyathe’ccādinā. Ettha pana mammatāḷanaṃ nimittaṃ pāṇa haraṇaṃ [M 0.0222] nimittī, tassāti anajjatanassa. Upari tyādikaṇḍe karahasaddo tu cisaddasaṃyuttova dissati karahacīti.

`Nimittanimittīnaṃ` refers to cause and effect; `samāne` refers to when they are common. This commonality is illustrated by `taṃyathā`, etc. Here, however, striking from possessiveness is the cause (`nimitta`), and the taking of life is the effect (`nimittī`). `Tassā` refers to the non-present. In the preceding `tyādi` section, the word `karaha` is seen only in conjunction with the word `ci`, as in `karahaci`.

110. Dhāsaṃ

110. `dhāsaṃ`

Saṅkhyāvācino saddā saṅkhyāsaddena gahitāti āha- ‘atthe’ccādi. Pakāro dabbaguṇadhisayopi atthi, tattha yadi sopi gayheyya dabba guṇānaṃ liṅgasaṅkhyāhi yogā dhāppaccayanta(mpi tabbisayoyeveti) cettha (potthake (pakāravācakaliṅgasaṅkhyāhi yogā) aliṅgamasaṅkhyañca dhāppaccayantamaliṅgamasaṅkhyañca-iti kāsikāvuttipañjakāyaṃ na siyā, evañca satyabyayattamabhimatantassa na siyā, tañciṭṭhaṃ, kiriyāvisaye tu tasmiṃ gayhamāne ekadhābhuñjati dvidhābhuñjati dvidhāgacchaticcādo bhojana gamanādikiriyāya sabbathā liṅgasaṅkhyāhi yogābhāvā yathāvutta doso na siyāti pāṇinīyavuttikārena jayādiccena kiriyā visayoyevettha pakāro gahito. Tampati āha- ‘dabbe’ccādi. Kasmā panevamāhāti āha- ‘navadhādabba’miccādi. “Navadhā dabbaṃ, bahudhā guṇo”ti vesesikānaṃ saṅketo.

He states, beginning with `atthe`, that words denoting number are included under the term 'number-word.' There is also a type (`pakāra`) which is the domain of substance and quality. If that too were included, then since substance and quality are connected with gender and number, the form ending in the `dhā` suffix would also pertain to that domain, and it would not be without gender and number. If that were so, its desired status as an indeclinable would not be obtained, and that status is what is desired. However, when this `pakāra` is taken in the sphere of action—as in `ekadhā bhuñjati` (he eats in one way), `dvidhā bhuñjati` (he eats in two ways), `dvidhā gacchati` (he goes in two ways), etc.—since actions such as eating and going are entirely unconnected with gender and number, the aforementioned fault does not arise. Thus, the Pāṇinian Vutti-writer Jayāditya has taken `pakāra` here to pertain only to the sphere of action. Regarding this, he states, beginning with `dabbe`. But why does he say this? He explains, beginning with `navadhādabbaṃ`. 'Substance is ninefold, quality is manifold' is the convention of the Vaiśeṣikas.

Tattha puthabyāpotejovāyvākāsakāladisāttamanānīti nava dabbāni. Rūpa rasa gandha phassa saṅkhyāparimāṇa puthuttasaṃyogavibhāga parattāparattabuddhisukhadukkhecchādosapayatanā ca guṇā, casaddena gurutta davattasinehasaṅkhāradhammādhammasaddā ceti catubbīsati bahudhā guṇo. Atrāpi yathāvuttakāsikāvuttiyā pañcikākārena jinindabuddhinā navadhā dabbaṃ bahudhā guṇotyatrāpi “kiriyājjhāharitabbā navadhā dabbaṃ bahudhā guṇo upadisīyati viññāyati byākhyāyate vijjatevā”ti kiriyāvisayoyeva pakāro paṭipādito, payogadassanato byavacchejjabhāvā sabbattha kiriyeveti visesanopādānamayuttanti sambandho.

Therein, the nine substances are: earth, water, fire, air, space, time, direction, self, and mind. The qualities are: form, taste, smell, touch, number, measure, separateness, conjunction, disjunction, remoteness, nearness, intellect, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort; and by the word `ca` are included heaviness, fluidity, viscosity, formations, righteousness, unrighteousness, and sound—thus the twenty-four qualities are manifold. Here too, according to the aforesaid Kāśikā-vutti, Jinindabuddhi, the author of the Pañcikā, has presented the `pakāra` (type) as pertaining only to the sphere of action, even in the case of 'substance is ninefold, quality is manifold,' because an action is to be supplied, as in: 'substance is taught as ninefold... is known... is explained... or exists as ninefold.' The connection is this: since from observing the usage there is nothing to be excluded and it is always action, the inclusion of the specification that `pakāra` pertains to action is inappropriate.

Navadhā dabbaṃ bahudhā guṇoti payogadassanato dabbaguṇavisayānampakārānaṃ gayhupagattā byavacchedayitabbānaṃ dabbaguṇavisayānampakārānaṃ bhāvā sabbasmiṃ dabbaguṇavisaye jinindabuddhinā vuttanayena kiriyā [M 0.0223] atthevāti kiriyāvisayova pakāro gayhatīti vuttikāra pañjikākārānaṃ visesanopādānamayuttanti attho.

The meaning is this: From the observation of the usage 'substance is ninefold, quality is manifold,' since the types relating to the sphere of substance and quality are fit to be taken up, and since there exist types relating to the sphere of substance and quality that are to be distinguished, and since, according to the method stated by Jinindabuddhi, there is indeed an action in every case concerning substance and quality, the inclusion of the specification by the Vutti-writer and the Pañcikā-writer—that the type taken pertains only to the sphere of action—is inappropriate.

Tatoyevāti yato visesanopādānamayuttaṃ tatoyeva dvīhiccādikamāheti attho. Ayametthādhippāyo “dvidhā karotīti kiriyāpayogepi pakāro dabbaguṇavisayo… dabbavisayassa guṇavisayassa vā dvidhābhāvassa karīyamānattā, natu kiriyāvisayo… dvidhābhāvassa karaṇakiriyāvisayassettha vattumanicchitattā. Tatoyeva kiriyāpakāropādāne pakārotisayane (potthake) atra dhāppaccayantappayogo na siyāti viññāpetuṃ ‘dvīhi’ccādikamāhe”ti tenāha‘atre’ccādi.

The meaning of 'Tatoyeva' is: because the inclusion of the specification is inappropriate, for that very reason he states 'dvīhi', etc. This is the intention here: 'Even in the usage of the action 'dvidhā karoti' (he makes twofold), the type has substance and quality as its sphere, because what is being made twofold is a substance or a quality, not the action itself, since what is intended to be expressed here is not the action of making which has twofoldness as its object. For that very reason, to make it known that the suffix 'dhā' should not be used here when expressing a type of action, he states 'dvīhi', etc.' Therefore he says 'atra', etc.

Dabbaguṇavisaye pakāre gayhamāne yoyaṃ doso sambhāvito parehi, taṃ dāni nirākattumāha ‘satipice’ccādi. Sabhāvato aliṅgamasaṅkhyañcāti sambandho, saṅkhyantarāpādane gamyamāne dhāppaccayo vihito pāṇiniyehi, tadāha- ‘dabbasse’ccādi saṅkhyāntarāpādanepīti pubbaṃ yā vavatthitā saṅkhyā, tato- ññaṃ saṅkhyāntaraṃ tassāpādanaṃ karaṇaṃ saṅkhyantarāpādanaṃ, tasmimpīti attho.

Now, to refute the fault supposed by others when the type is taken as having substance and quality for its sphere, he says 'satipi ca', etc. The connection is: 'By nature, it is without gender and number.' The Pāṇinīyas have prescribed the suffix 'dhā' when the introduction of another number is understood. Therefore, he says 'dabbassa', etc., meaning 'even in the introduction of another number.' The meaning is as follows: the previously established number is 'saṅkhyā'; a number other than that is 'saṅkhyāntara'; the introduction or application of that is 'saṅkhyantarāpādana'; 'tasmim pi' means 'in that case as well'.

113. Tabba

113. Tabba

So pakāro assāti tabbā, tasaddena pakārassa parāmaṭṭhattā tabbatītettha pakāravatīti attho vuttoti āha- ‘tasaddene’ccādi. Pakāravatīti pakāravati atthe. Muduppakāravā mudujātiyo.

'Tabbā' means 'one who has that kind'. Because 'kind' is referred to by the word 'ta', here in 'tabbā', the meaning 'possessing kind' is stated; thus he says, 'by the word ta', etc. 'Pakāravatī' is in the sense of 'possessing kind'. 'Muduppakāravā' means 'of a gentle kind' or 'of a gentle species'.

115. Kati

115. How many?

Kiṃ saṅkhyānamparimāṇamesanti atthe “kimhā rati rīvarīvataka rittakā”ti (4-44) suttena ratippaccayaṃ vidhāya katīti siddhattā vuttaṃ- ‘saṅkhyāparimāṇavisaye sādhitattā’ti, kati ca so saṅkhyā parimāṇavisayattā saṅkhyā ceti katisaṅkhyā, tāya.

In the sense of 'what is their number or measure?', since 'kati' is established by prescribing the suffix 'rati' by the sutta (4-44) beginning 'kimhā rati...', it is said, 'because it is formed in the sphere of number and measure'. And 'kati' is that number; because it is in the sphere of number and measure, it is a number, thus 'katisaṅkhyā' (the number 'kati'); by that.

116. Bahu

116. Many

Paccāsattīti sambandhimhi ekamhi dassite dviṭṭhattā sambandhassa paro sambandhī [M 0.0224] viññāyamāno parova viññāyati yuttitoti ‘sambandhatovā’ti vuttaṃ.

Proximity means that when one of two related things is shown, because a relationship has two terms, the other related thing, being understood, is understood as the other; thus it is fitting, and so it is said, 'or from the relationship.'

117. Sakiṃ

117. Once

Nipātanassāti sakinti nipātanassa.

Regarding 'nipātanassa': this refers to 'sakiṃ' being a particle.

118. So

118. So

Khaṇḍaṃ khaṇḍaṃ khaṇḍaso, puthu pakāro puthuso.

Piece by piece is 'khaṇḍaso'; a different kind is 'puthuso'.

119. Abhū

119. Existed

Nanu ca abhavanannāma sabbathā anuppattiyā vā avatthantarena vā, tathā satyabhūtasaddo-nuppannamattavacanopīti kathamabhūtasaddo-vatthantare nābhūte vuttoccāha- ‘abhūtassi’ccādi. Kathamavatthāva tasaddena parāmasīyatīti ce abhūtasaddo yadyanuppannavācī siyā, tadā tasaddappa yogoyeva na siyā… tasaddenābhūtasseva gahaṇato, abhūtabhāveccādinā suttitaṃ siyā, tena tasaddappayogasāmatthiyā avatthāva tasaddena parāmasīyati, tapparāmaṭṭhañcāvatthantaramabhūta saddo apekkhate, tenāha- ‘tabbhāvetivacanā’iccādi. Bhavanaṃ bhāvo tāya avatthantare bhāvo tabbhāvo tasmiṃ. Tenāha ‘abhūtasse’ccādi. Bhāveti visayasattamī, saṃsattamī vāti āha- ‘visaye gammamāne vā’ti. Kuṇḍalattenāti kuṇḍalasabhāvena.

But is not 'non-becoming' (abhavana) either non-arising in every way, or by an altered state? If so, then the word 'abhūta' would also mean merely 'that which has not arisen'. How then is the word 'abhūta' said to refer to an altered state, or to what was not? He says, 'of the non-existent', etc. If it is asked how the state itself is referred to by the word 'ta': if the word 'abhūta' were to mean only 'that which has not arisen', then there would be no application of the word 'ta' at all, since by 'ta' only the non-existent would be grasped, and it would be formulated in a rule through terms like 'the state of non-existence' (abhūtabhāva), etc. Therefore, by the power of the application of the word 'ta', the state itself is referred to by the word 'ta', and the word 'abhūta' expects that altered state referred to by 'ta'. Hence he says, 'because of the expression "tabbhāve"', etc. Becoming is 'bhāvo'; the state in that altered state is 'tabbhāvo'; in that. Therefore he says, 'of the non-existent', etc. Regarding 'bhāve', it is either the locative of sphere (visayasattamī) or the locative of association (saṃsattamī), thus he says, 'when understood as a sphere or in association'. 'Kuṇḍalattena' means 'by the nature of a coil'.

120. Dissa

120. Dissa

Dissantīti vutte payoge dissantīti ayamattho viññāyatīti āha ‘disi’ccādi, idaṃ suttaṃ vijjhaṅga paribhāsā bhavatīti seso. “Ṇovā-pacce”tiādinā (4-1) suttena vuttesvanekavidhesu atthesu pari samantato bhāsatīti paribhāsā, vidhino paccayassa aṅgabhūtā paribhāsā vijjhaṅgaparibhāsā. Vidhiyevāti suttamidanti sambandho. Vakkhamānasuttadvayanti “aññasmiṃ sakatthe”ti suttadvayaṃ.

When 'dissantīti' is said in usage, the meaning 'they appear' is understood; thus he says 'disi', etc. The remainder is that this sutta becomes a 'vijjhaṅgaparibhāsā' (an explanatory rule for a part of a rule). Among the many kinds of meanings stated by the sutta (4-1) beginning with 'Ṇovā-pacce', 'paribhāsā' means 'that which speaks comprehensively all around'. A 'paribhāsā' that is an auxiliary part of a rule is a 'vijjhaṅgaparibhāsā'. The connection is that this sutta is the rule itself. The two suttas to be stated are the two suttas beginning 'aññasmiṃ sakatthe'.

125. Saṃyo

125. Saṃyo

Antarasaddo-nekatthopīhāntarāḷavācī majjhavācī gayhati, na vijjatentaramesanti antarāḷamattapaṭisedhepayojanaṃ natthīti katvāntarā ḷaṭṭhassābhāvāntarāḷaṃ [M 0.0225] natthītyupacarīyati, evañhi loke payujjate ‘anantarā ime gāmā anantarā ime pāsādā’ti antarāḷagatassa ññassa gāmassaññassa pāsādassa vābhāvā tathā byapadisīyate, tathevamihāpyantarāḷagatassaññassa byañjanassābhāvā anantarā ityuccante, athavāntarasaddo byavadhānavācī byavadhānābhāvato-nantarā iti vuccante. Antaraṃ karotīti vā khādiippaccayaṃ ṇippaccayaṃ (potthake) vidhāya antarāyati byavadhānaṃ karotīti kattari appaccayaṃ vidhāya antaro byavadhāyako natthetesanti anantarā. Yathā ‘rukkhā vanante’ttha rukkhā samuditāvekavanabyapadesaṃ labhante, tathātrāpi byañjanā samuditāvete saṃyogabyapadesagocarattaṃ paṭipajjante.

Although the word 'antara' has many meanings, here it is taken to mean 'interval' or 'middle'. Since there is no purpose in merely negating 'there is no interval for these', it is figuratively said 'there is no interval' due to the absence of something in the interval. For thus it is used in the world: 'these villages are without interval, these palaces are without interval,' because there is no other village or palace in between, it is so designated. Similarly, here too, due to the absence of another consonant in the interval, they are called 'anantarā' (without interval). Alternatively, the word 'antara' means 'obstruction', and due to the absence of obstruction, they are called 'anantarā'. Or, from 'antaraṃ karoti' (makes an interval), by prescribing the suffix '-i', one gets 'antarāyati' (makes an obstruction); from this, by prescribing the suffix 'a' in the agentive sense, one gets 'antaro' (an obstructer). 'Anantarā' means 'there are no such obstructers'. Just as in the phrase 'trees in the forest', the trees, being collected, obtain the designation 'a single forest', so too here, these consonants, being collected, attain the state of being the object of the designation 'saṃyoga' (conjunction).

Saṃyogoti hi samudāyappadhāno niddeso byañjanātyavayavappadhāno, tasmā byañjanāti bahuvacanena saṃyogoti ekavacananiddeso ghaṭate, nanu ca vaṇṇānamuccāritappadhaṃsittā yogapajjamaṭṭhitamānānaṃ na sambhavati samudāyattanti samudāyattamayuttanti nāyuttaṃ, tathāhi uttaruttaraggāhini buddhi pubbaparībhūte byañjanāvayave samudāyarūpena saṅkappentī samudāyavohārampavattayīti.

Indeed, 'saṃyoga' is a designation where the aggregate is primary, while 'byañjanā' is one where the components are primary. Therefore, the singular designation 'saṃyoga' is fitting with the plural 'byañjanā'. But is it not so that since sounds perish upon being uttered, it is not possible for those that have attained conjunction to have the nature of an aggregate? To the objection that the nature of an aggregate is unfitting, the reply is that it is not unfitting. For the mind, which grasps successively, conceiving the consonant components that have previously ceased as an aggregate form, brings about the conventional usage of an aggregate.

Ṇānubandheti ditisaddassa saṃyogāvisayattā deccoti ‘sarānamādissā’ti visayo, uḷumpasaddassa saṃyogavisayattā oḷumpikoti etassa visayoti tattha rāghavo venateyyo meniko decco dosaggānti rūpāni. Idha tu oḷumpiko koṇḍaññoti yujjanti. Teneva ca tattha pañcikā ettha, ettha ca pañcikā tattha upanetabbāti.

Regarding the indicatory 'Ṇa', since the word 'diti' is not within the sphere of saṃyoga, 'decca' is formed; 'sarānamādissā' is its sphere. Since the word 'uḷumpa' is within the sphere of saṃyoga, 'oḷumpika' is formed; this is its sphere. There, the forms are Rāghava, Venateyya, Menika, Decca, and Dosagga. Here, however, 'Oḷumpika' and 'Koṇḍañña' are fitting. For that very reason, the Pañcikā there should be brought to bear here, and the Pañcikā here should be brought to bear there.

127. Kosa

127. Kosa

Kosajjanti ettha tassa jattañca nipātanā, ajjavanti etthha “uvaṇṇassā vava sare”ti (4-129).

Here in 'kosajjaṃ', its transformation to 'ja' is by special formation. Here in 'ajjavaṃ', it is by the rule 'uvaṇṇassā vava sare' (4-129).

135. Jovu

135. Jovu

Yakārassa dvitte jeyyo.

When the letter 'y' is doubled, the result is 'jeyyo'.

137. Kaṇa

137. Kaṇa

Atisayena appo, atisayena yuvāti viggaho.

Exceedingly small; exceedingly young—this is the analysis.

139. Ḍesa

139. Ḍesa

Satissāti [M 0.0226] vutte satisaddo viññāyati satyantepi visesanattena vattumicchitesatyanto kathaṃ viññāyaticcāsaṅkiya “saṅkhyāya saccutīsāse”ccādinā (4-50) satyantādīhi ḍo vihito, tasmiñca ḍetinimittenopādinne tadupādānasāmatthiyāsatyantova viññāyatīti dassetumāha- ‘ḍeti nimittopādānā’tiādi.

When 'satissa' is said, the word 'sati' is understood. But even when one wishes to speak of a word ending in 'sati' with a specific meaning, having raised the doubt, 'How is a word ending in 'sati' to be understood?', by the rule beginning 'saṅkhyāya saccutīsāse...' (4-50), the suffix 'ḍa' is prescribed after words ending in 'sati' and so on. And when that 'ḍa' is taken up as a sign, by the power of its being taken up, it is understood as being precisely a word ending in 'sati'. To show this, he says: 'Because of taking up 'ḍa' as a sign,' and so on.

142. Adhā

142. Adhā

Dhātuto añño saddo adhātu tassa. Pañcikāyampana pakatipi saddoyevāti dhātutoiccādinā adhātusaddassa atthamattaṃ vuttaṃ.

A word other than a root is a 'non-root'; that is its meaning. But in the Pañcikā, it is said that 'a base, too, is just a word,' so by the phrase beginning 'from a root,' only the meaning of the word 'non-root' has been stated.

Tassāti adhātuppakatiyā, adhātusaddassāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tenacāti kakārena ca, tasmāti tena kāraṇena. Pubbaggahaṇamantarenātipāṇininā ikārādesavidhāyake imasmiṃyeva suttekakārato pubbassa ikārādesavidhānatthaṃ pubbaggahaṇaṃ kataṃ, taṃ pubbassātivacanaṃ vināti attho. Sacetiādinā kathayatīti sambandho. “Byañjane dīgharassā”ti (1-33) rasso vutto, assāti jātiniddese tu ākārassacikāro bhavatyeva, siyā etanti bahuparibbājakāti etaṃ rūpaṃ hoti. Syādyatra byavahito… kakārato pubbe syādi, na syādi kakārā paroti.

'Of that' means of the non-root base; that is to say, of the non-root word. 'And by that' means and by the letter 'k'. 'Therefore' means for that reason. Even without taking up 'pubba', by Pāṇini too, in this very sutta which prescribes the substitution of the letter 'i', the term 'pubba' is used to prescribe the substitution of 'i' for what is before the letter 'k'; the meaning is 'without the superfluous word pubbassa'. The connection is that he speaks with the words beginning 'If...', and so on. Shortening is stated by the rule 'Before a consonant, a vowel can be long or short' (1-33). But in the generic statement 'assa', the substitution of 'i' for 'ā' does indeed occur. The form is bahuparibbājikā, meaning 'it might be this'. Syādi here is separated... syādi is before the letter 'k', not after the letter 'k'.

Nanu ca asyāditoti ettha pasajjappaṭisedho naña kasmā gahito, na pariyudosoti āsaṅkiya pariyudāsesmiṃ gahite sati dosaṃ vattumārabhate ‘pariyudāse’iccādinā. Syāditoti syādyantato paribbājakasaddato. Paribbājakasaddohi syādyanto vākye syādyantattā, teneva vakkhati- ‘paribbājakasaddato ettha syādyuppattī’ti. Asyādismā paroti katvā bahuparibbājakasaddato na syādyuppattīti sambandho.

Well now, here in the phrase 'asyādito', why is the negative particle `nañ` taken as a prohibitory negation and not as an exclusionary one? Having raised this doubt, he begins to state the fault that occurs when the exclusionary sense is taken, with the words beginning 'pariyudāse...'. 'Syādito' means 'from the word paribbājaka which ends in syādi'. For the word paribbājaka is one that ends in syādi because in the sentence it has a syādi ending. For that very reason he will say: 'Here, from the word paribbājaka, there is the arising of syādi.' If it were taken as 'from that which is other than syādi', the connection is that there would be no arising of syādi from the word bahuparibbājaka.

Tatocāti bahuparibbājakasaddato ca. Pasajjappaṭisedhena nañasaddena [M 0.0227] aññapadatthasamāsepi siyāva dosoti dassento āha- ‘avijjamānosyādi’ccādi.

'And from that' means 'and from the word bahuparibbājaka'. Showing that even when the negative particle `nañ` is a prohibitory negation, there would still be a fault in a compound with the sense of another word, he says: 'avijjamāno syādi...' and so on.

Iti moggallānapañcikāṭīkāyaṃ sāratthavilāsiniyaṃ

Thus in the Sāratthavilāsinī, the subcommentary on the Moggallāna-pañcikā,

Catutthakaṇḍavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

the explanation of the fourth chapter is concluded.

Pañcamakaṇḍa

The Fifth Chapter

1. Tija

1. Tija

Khamāvīmaṃsāsūti pakativisesanameva kathamicchitanti āha- ‘sambandhassi’ccādi, padānamaññamaññasambandhassa purisādhīnattāti attho, pakati visesananti tijamāha saddānaṃ visesanaṃ, kimpana pakativisesane phala miccāha- ‘pakativisesanopādāna’miccādi. Yajjatra ‘khamāvīmaṃsāsū’ti pakativisesanaṃ, kasmiṃ atthe carati khasā vidhīyanticcāha- ‘atthantarassā niddesā’iccādi. Atthantarassāti nisānādiatthantarassa. “Sutānumitesu sutasambandhova balavā”ti paribhāsamupalakkheti ‘sutānumitāna’miccādinā. Tenevāti kiriyārūpāsu khamāvīmaṃsu khasānaṃ vīdhāneneva, sakatthe vidhāneneti vuttaṃ hoti. Titikkhakiriyattāti iminā paresaṃ viya khādyantānaṃ dhātusaññāvidhāna manatthakanti dasseti.

When it is asked how 'Khamāvīmaṃsāsu' ('In patience and investigation') is intended to be merely a qualification of the base, he says: 'Of the connection,' etc. The meaning is that the mutual connection of words is dependent on the speaker. A qualification of the base is a qualification of the three words he mentions. But what is the result of qualifying the base? He says: 'The taking up of the qualification of the base,' etc. If 'in patience and investigation' is a qualification of the base, in what sense does it operate and for what are the khasa suffixes prescribed? He says: 'Because of the indication of another meaning,' etc. 'Of another meaning' means of another meaning such as 'sharpening,' etc. He indicates the maxim, 'Between what is heard and what is inferred, the connection with what is heard is stronger,' with the words 'of what is heard and inferred,' etc. 'By that very means' refers to the very prescription of the khasa suffixes for patience and investigation, which are forms of action; that is to say, it is a prescription in their own meaning. By the phrase 'because it is the action of enduring,' he shows that, as with other formations like the desiderative of the root khād, the prescription of the designation 'root' is not meaningless.

Titikkhā khamā, titikkhati khamati, vīmaṃsā upaparikkhā, vīmaṃsati upaparikkhatīti attho. Sutte tijaiti niddesā bhūvādikassa gahaṇaṃ. Niccaṇyantassa curādikassa hi tādise payojane sati bahulaṃ vidhīyamānepi niccattamattano nātivattati. Athavā curādimānenābyabhicārinā sāhacariyā tijopi curādikova, taṃ yathā ‘gāvassa dutiyenāttho’ti. Vuttegoyevopādīyate, nāsso, na gadrabho. Kadāci pana assādinopi dutiyassa gahaṇaṃ siyā atthappakaraṇā dippabhāvato.

'Endurance' (titikkhā) is patience (khamā); 'to endure' (titikkhati) is to be patient (khamati). 'Investigation' (vīmaṃsā) is examination (upaparikkhā); 'to investigate' (vīmaṃsati) is to examine (upaparikkhati)—this is the meaning. Because of the designation 'tija' in the sutta, the Bhūvādi group is included. For a root of the Curādi class, which always takes the `-ṇe-` suffix, even when frequently prescribed for such a purpose, does not transcend its own invariable nature. Alternatively, because of its invariable association with the Curādi class, the Tija group is also treated as belonging to the Curādi class. This is like the saying, 'The purpose is with the second of "cow".' When this is said, only 'cow' is understood, not 'horse' or 'donkey'. Sometimes, however, even 'horse' and so on might be taken as the second, due to the force of the meaning, context, and so on.

Nanu [M 0.0228] ca vīmaṃsāyaṃ sappaccayavidhāna manupapannamitaretaranissayadosa duṭṭhattā, tathāhi siddhe vīmaṃsāsadde sappaccayo uppajjate, sati ca tasmiṃ vīmaṃsāti rūpaṃ sampajjatīti itaretaranissayo, itaretara nissayāni ca kāriyānī nopakappantīti tenāha- ‘anuvādarūpāna’miccādi. Anādikālasaṃsiddhasaddānuvāto natthi itaretaranissayo dosoti bhāvo. Payojakabyāpāraṇippaccayābhāve tejateti rūpaṃ.

But surely, in the case of vīmaṃsā, the prescription of the `sa` suffix is inappropriate, as it is vitiated by the fault of mutual dependence. For the `sa` suffix arises when the word vīmaṃsā is already established, and when that suffix exists, the form vīmaṃsā is accomplished; this is mutual dependence. And operations based on mutual dependence are not valid. Therefore he says: 'of those which are forms of restatement,' etc. The sense is that in the restatement of a word that has been established since beginningless time, there is no fault of mutual dependence. In the absence of the causative `-ṇi` suffix, the form is tejati.

2. Kitā

2. Kitā

Pubbeviya pakativisesanādītyanena “sambandhassa purisāyattattā ‘tikicchāsaṃsayesū’ti pakativisesananti āha- ‘tikicchāya’miccādi’tyādikaṃ sabbaṃ yathāyogametthāpi vattabbantyatidisati. Vissatthoti visaddassa attho. Atha kimitthaṃ chappaccayantasseva dvidhodāharaṇantyāsaṅkiyāha- ‘atthabhedā dvidhodāharaṇa’nti. Niketo nivāso, saṅketo lakkhaṇaṃ.

As before, by means of 'qualification of the base, etc.,' he applies by extension the following: just as it was said, 'because the connection depends on the person, in "medical treatment and doubt" it is a qualification of the base,' so too all that was said, such as 'in medical treatment,' etc., should be stated here as appropriate. `Vissattho` has the meaning of the word `visadda`. Then, anticipating the objection, 'Why is the example twofold only for that which ends in the suffix `cha`?', he says: 'The example is twofold because of a difference in meaning.' `Niketo` is a dwelling; `saṅketo` is a sign.

3. Nindā

3. Nindā

Ninda=garahāyaṃ tato “itthiyamaṇattikayakyā ce”ti (5-49) appaccaye tato “itthiyamatvā”ti (3-26) āppaccaye rūpaṃ. Bandhatīti badhako.

The root `nind` is used in the sense of censure. From this, the form is derived with the suffix `a` according to the rule `itthiyamaṇattikayakyā ce` (5-49), and then with the suffix `ā` according to `itthiyamatvā` (3-26). `Bandhatīti` means `badhako`, 'one who binds'.

4. Tuṃsmā

4. Tuṃsmā

Tuṃsmātīha paccayaggahaṇamācikkhati ‘tuṃtāye’ccādinā. Tato ceti yato tuṃsmāti paccayasseva gahaṇaṃ yato ca visesana niddeso, tatoti attho. Paccayaggahaṇe tadādiggahaṇaṃ viññāyate… “paccayaggahaṇe yasmā so vihito tadādino gahaṇa”nti ñāyato. Visesanattena vattumicchitattā tadantaggahaṇaṃ… “vidhibbisesanantassā”ti (1-13) vacanābhi manasi nidhāyāha- ‘yato kiriyatthā’iccādi. So kiriyattho ādi yassa samudāyassa so tadādi so paccayonte tassa (so tadanto). Tadāditadantasamudāyavisesassa gahaṇaṃ, (natu) tadantamattasse tyattho[M 0.0229]. Nanu ca tuṃsmāiti visesanattena vattumicchite bhavatu “vidhibbisesanantasse”ti tadantaggahaṇaṃ paccayaggahaṇe tu kathaṃ tadādino gahaṇaṃ vacanābhāvatoccāha- ‘tadavinābhāvittā’ti. Yato vihito tena vinā na bhavati sīleneti tadavinābhāvī tassa bhāvo tasmā. Imāya yuttiyā viññāyate-ttho, yamākhyāyate ‘paccayaggahaṇe yasmā so vihito tadādino gahaṇa’nti. Bhavatvevaṃ tadādino tadantassa ca gahaṇaṃ, tato kipphalaṃtyāha- ‘tene’ccādi.

Here, in the rule `tuṃsmā`, he indicates the taking of a suffix by means of `tuṃtāye`, etc. And the meaning of `tato` is: for the reason that the suffix `tuṃsmā` itself is taken, and that there is a specification as a qualifier. When a suffix is mentioned, what begins with it is also understood to be taken, according to the maxim: 'When a suffix is mentioned, that which begins with the element after which it is prescribed is also taken.' Because of the desire to speak of it as a qualifier, what ends with it is also taken. Keeping in mind the statement `vidhibbisesanantassā` (1-13), he says: `yato kiriyatthā`, etc. That aggregate which has the meaning of an action as its beginning is `tadādi` (beginning with that); that which has the suffix at its end is `tadanto` (ending with that). The meaning is that the specific aggregate that both begins with the base and ends with the suffix is taken, not merely that which ends with the suffix. Now, since it is desired to speak of `tuṃsmā` as a qualifier, let what ends with it be taken according to `vidhibbisesanantassā`. But when a suffix is mentioned, how is what begins with it taken, since there is no explicit statement? He says: 'Because of its inseparability from that.' Because it is prescribed after a base, it does not exist without it; this is its nature. Therefore, it is inseparable from it. By this reasoning, the meaning is understood, which is stated as: 'When a suffix is mentioned, that which begins with the element after which it is prescribed is also taken.' Let it be so that both what begins with it and what ends with it are taken. What is the result of that? He says: `tena`, etc.

Sapāditoti pādisahitato. Kha cha suppattābhāvāti kha cha sānaṃ uppattiyā abhāvā. Vuttappakārasseva tuṃppaccayantassa pakatibhāvena gahaṇā sapādito kha cha sānamanuppattīti adhippāyo. Vipubbā ‘ji-jaye’iccasmā tuṃpaccayantā ‘vijetumicchatī’ti atthe “tuṃsmā”iccādinā(so), tuṃssaca lopo, nemittike ekāre nivatte ‘jisa jisa iti dvitte anādibyañjanalopo “jiharānaṃ gī”ti (5-102) gī. Jigīsappakatito “bhūte īūṃ”iccādinā (6-4) ī. Tasmiṃ aña. “Ā ī ū mhā ssā ssamhānaṃ vā”ti (6-33) īssa rasse byajigīsi. Yadi tu sapādito sassa uppatti siyā, tadā byajigīsīti ettha dvibbacanaṃ karīyamānaṃ sappaccayantassa paṭhamassekassarassa dvibbacanaṃ bhavatīti “kha cha sāna”miccādinā (5-69) vijiya iti samudāye ādibhūtassa visaddassa siyā īmhi ca vihite sapādino pakatibhāvoti visadda pubbe añāgamo siyā, tato ca avivijisīti aniṭṭhampasajjeyya.

`Sapādito` means 'together with the prefix.' `Kha cha suppattābhāvāti` means 'because of the non-occurrence of `kha`, `cha`, and `sa`.' The intention is that because that which ends in the suffix `tuṃ` is taken in its natural state in the manner stated, `kha`, `cha`, and `sa` do not occur after that which has a prefix. From the root `ji` ('to conquer') preceded by `vi`, in the sense of `vijetum icchati` ('he wishes to conquer'), the suffix `sa` is added by `tuṃsmā`, etc., and `tuṃ` is elided. Upon reduplication, `gī` is substituted for the root by `jiharānaṃ gī` (5-102), yielding `jigīsa`. From this base `jigīsa`, the aorist ending `ī` is added by `bhūte īūṃ`, etc. (6-4), and after that, the augment `a`. By `Ā ī ū mhā ssā ssamhānaṃ vā` (6-33), with the shortening of `ī`, the form is `byajigīsi`. If, however, the suffix `sa` were to occur after that which has a prefix, then when reduplication is performed for `byajigīsī`, according to `kha cha sāna...` (5-69), the reduplication would be of the first syllable of the entire complex ending in `sa`, that is, of `vi` in the aggregate `vijisa`. And when the ending `ī` is prescribed, since that which has a prefix is treated as a natural unit, the augment `a` would be prefixed to `vi`, which would result in the undesirable form `avivijisī`.

Tuṃsmā icchāyanti ca pakatippaccayatthānamupadiṭṭhattā tena sabhāva liṅgena kha cha sappaccayā tadanto ca anumito na pana tuṃ, tumiha sutoti āha- ‘na tadanto, nāpi cha chasā’ti. Jighacchāiccatra dvitte pubbassa ghassa “catuttha dutiyānaṃ tatiyapaṭhamā”ti (5-78) go. Tassa “kavaggahānaṃ cavaggajā”ti (5-79) jo. Pāṇinināpīha sappaccaya vidhāyake sutte vākyampi yathā siyāti vāvacanaṃ kataṃ, tadayuttanti nirākattumāha- ‘vākyampi’ccādi. Pakatyādityatra ādi saddena atthaviseso gahetabbo, pakati viseso tumanto, icchattho-tthaviseso[M 0.0230]. Idaṃ lakkhaṇanti “tuṃsmā lopo cicchāyaṃ te”iti idaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ. Niyogatoti niyamena. Āsaṅkāyamupasaṅkhyāna”nti (3-1-7) vākyakārena vuttaṃ nirākattumāha- ‘āsaṅkāya’miccādi.

And because in `tuṃsmā icchāyaṃ` the meanings of the base and suffix are indicated, by that natural sign the suffixes `kha`, `cha`, `sa` and what ends in them are inferred, but not `tuṃ`, for `tuṃ` is explicitly stated here. Thus he says: 'Not what ends in that, nor `cha`, `kha`, `sa`.' In `jighacchā`, during reduplication, the initial `gha` becomes `ga` by `catuttha dutiyānaṃ tatiyapaṭhamā` (5-78). That `ga` then becomes `ja` by `kavaggahānaṃ cavaggajā` (5-79). Pāṇini too, in the sūtra that prescribes the suffix `sa`, made the statement optional so that a full sentence might also be possible. To refute that as unsuitable, he says: `vākyampi`, etc. In `pakatyādi`, by the word `ādi` ('etc.'), a specific meaning should be taken: the specific base is that which ends in `tuṃ`; the specific meaning is the sense of 'desire.' This is the rule: `tuṃsmā lopo cicchāyaṃ te` is this rule. `Niyogato` means 'by rule.' To refute what was said by the Vārttikakāra, `āsaṅkāyām upasaṅkhyānam`, he says: `āsaṅkāyaṃ`, etc.

Acetanattā kūlassa icchāyāsambhavoti ‘kūlappatitumicchatī’ti vākyamevecchāpakāsanamasiddhaṃ, tenāsiddhena vākyenāsiddhānaṃ kha cha sānaṃ sādhanaṃ asiddhenāsiddhasādhanaṃ. Icchāvacanicchāti icchāya vattumicchā. Icchāyapavattito upaladdhīti icchāya upaladdhi upālambo parijānanaṃ pavattitoti attho. Cetanāvaticāti vuttaṃ tasmā cetanāvati pavattito upaladdhiṃ dassetvā tadapadese nācetanepi dassetuṃ ‘yopesā’tiādimāha. Devadatte rajju khīlādipāṇinā uyyogo, kūle mattikāvikīraṇādi. Rajju guṇo. Khīlo kīla (pañcikā) saṃkvādi.

Because a riverbank is non-sentient, desire is impossible for it. Thus the sentence `kūlaṃ patitum icchati` ('the bank wishes to collapse') is itself an unestablished expression of desire. Therefore, to prove the unestablished suffixes `kha`, `cha`, and `sa` by means of that unestablished sentence is to prove the unestablished by means of the unestablished. `Icchāvacanicchā` means the desire to express a desire. `Icchāya pavattito upaladdhi` means the occurrence of comprehension, understanding, or recognition through desire. It was said 'in a sentient being.' Therefore, having shown the occurrence of comprehension in a sentient being, in order to show it also in a non-sentient being by transference of attribution, he says `yopesā`, etc. In the case of Devadatta, the effort is with a rope, stake, etc., in hand; in the case of the bank, it is the scattering of earth, etc. `Rajju` is a rope. `Khīlo` is a stake, etc.

Pulo tiṇādīnaṃ saṅghāto. Sā sunakho mimarisatīti mara=pāṇacāge’icchāyaṃ tumantā so. “Ñi byañjanasse”ti (5-170) ñi. Dvitte pubbato-ññassa lopo “kha cha sesvī”ti (5-76) dvitte pubbassāssa imimarisati. Tathā pipatisatīti ‘patapatha=gamena’ iccassa. Sā mimarisatīti satipi sacetanatte visattajīvitassa sunakhassa maraṇicchā sambhavatīti paṭipāditaṃ. “Icchāsantā paṭisedho vattabbo”ti (3-1-7) pāṇinīyavāttikakārena vuttaṃ, tannirākattumāha- ‘bubhukkhitu’miccādi. Jātipadatthanissayena nivuttimpaṭipādayamāha- ‘jātipadatthe’ccādi. Itaro icchattho.

`Pulo` is a bundle of grass, etc. `Sā sunakho mimarisati` ('That dog wishes to die'): from the root `mar` in the sense of 'giving up life,' in the sense of desire, the suffix `sa` is added to the base ending in `tuṃ`. The derivation proceeds with reduplication. Similarly, `pipatisati` is formed from the root `pat` or `path` in the sense of 'going.'
