Regarding `sā mimarisati`, it is explained that even though a dog is a sentient being attached to life, the desire for death is possible for it. To refute what was said by the Pāṇinian Vārttikakāra, `icchā-sanoḥ pratiṣedho vaktavyaḥ` ('A prohibition should be stated for the suffix `san` when it means desire'), he says `bubhukkhitum`, etc. Relying on the meaning of the word `jāti`, he explains the cessation, saying `jātipadatthe`, etc. The other is the meaning of desire.

5. Īyo

5. The suffix īya.

Karīyati sambandhīyatīti kammaṃ. Tañca nāma jāti guṇakiriyādabba sambandhato pañcadhā bhavati. Tattha nāmakammaṃ’ ḍittho ḍavitthoti nāmena piṇḍassa sambandhā. Jātikammaṃ goassoti gottādijātiyā piṇḍassa sambandhā. Guṇakammaṃ sukkonīloti sukkādinā guṇena dabbassa [M 0.0231] sambandhā. Kiriyākammaṃ pācako pāyakoti pācakādikiriyāya dabbassa sambandhā. Dabbakammaṃ daṇḍīvisāṇīti daṇḍādinā dabbena piṇḍassa sambandhā. Evaṃ kammassa pañcappakārasambhavepicchāyamatthe īyassa vidhānato icchāsambandhiyeva kammaṃ gayhatīti kiriyākammamevātra gayhate amukamevatthamupadassento āha- ‘yadipi’ccādi. Ayañca nipāta samudāyo visesābhidhānanimittāsyupagame vattate.

That which is made or connected is called 'kamma.' And that is fivefold based on connection through name, kind, quality, action, or substance. Here, name-kamma is like 'Dittha, Davittha'—the connection of a mass through a name. Kind-kamma is like 'cow, horse'—the connection of a mass through lineage or kind. Quality-kamma is like 'white, blue'—the connection of a substance through qualities such as whiteness. Action-kamma is like 'cooker, cook'—the connection of a substance through actions like cooking. Substance-kamma is like 'staff-bearer, horn-bearer'—the connection of a mass through things like a staff. Thus, even though kamma can arise in five ways, due to the prescription of the suffix 'īya' in the sense of desire, only kamma connected with desire is understood here; specifically, action-kamma is taken here to indicate that very meaning, as stated: 'even if' etc. This collection of particles functions when there is an occasion for a special designation.

Tathāpītilokavuttirayaṃvisesābhidhānārambhe. Taṃsambandhiyevāti icchāsambandhieva. Attanoputtamicchatītyādivacanicchāyamattasambandhiniputtādo attanotyanuvattiyasuttantarenapaccayovidhīyatepāṇininā, ettha tva(tta)ggahaṇamantarenātta sambandhinyeva puttādo kathaṃ viññāyate visesavacanābhāve hi parasambandhinyapi pappotītīmaṃcodyamubbhāvaya māha- ‘attasambandhini’ccādi. Īyassa parasambandhinyapi pasaṅgoti sambandho. Kutocāha-īyassāitidhānā’ti. Atthaggahaṇassāvacane īyassānabhidhānāti bhāvo.

Nevertheless, this is the worldly usage at the commencement of a special designation. It is connected precisely to that—that is, connected to the desire itself. When one desires to say, 'He desires a son for himself,' and so forth, Pāṇini prescribes a suffix by another rule for 'son' etc. when related to oneself, by carrying over the word 'attano' (of oneself). Here, without the inclusion of the word 'atta' (self), how is it understood that it applies only to a son, etc., related to oneself? For in the absence of a specific word, it would extend even to what is related to another. Raising this objection, he says: 'because it is related to oneself,' etc. The connection is that the suffix 'īya' would also apply to what is related to another. Why is that? He says, 'because of the non-designation of īya.' The sense is that if the meaning is not stated, there is non-designation of the suffix 'īya'.

Appattiyāti karaṇe hetumhi vā tatiyā. Etthāti attano puttamicchatītetthāpi. Na iṭṭhoti īyappaccayo nābhimato. Nevettha bhavitabbanti vadato-dhippāyāmāha ‘sāpekkhatta yeveti bhāvo’ti. Yadi attano puttamicchatīti vattumicchāyaṃ sāpekkhettepi siyā, tadāyamaniṭṭhappasaṅgoti dassetumāha- ‘yadicettha’iccādi.

`Appattiyā` ('By non-application') is the third case in the sense of instrument or cause. `Ettha` ('Here') also includes the case of 'he desires his own son.' `Na iṭṭho` ('Not desired') means the suffix 'īya' is not approved. To explain the intention of one saying, 'Nor should it be here,' he says: 'The sense is that it is simply a state of dependency.' To show that if, in the desire to say 'he desires his own son,' the suffix were to apply even in a state of dependency, an undesirable consequence would follow, he says: 'If, here,' etc.

Aniṭṭhappasaṅgassa sarūpamāha- ‘attano puttīyatīti siyā’ti. Uppajjamānena īyeneva attatthassābhihitattā attasaddassāppayogoti cetampi na saṅgatanti paṭipādayamāha ‘na ca sakkā’tiādi. Kasmādevaṃ vattuṃ na sakkāti āha- ‘pakati’ccādi. Apūpādikāya pakatiyā samānatthasseva visesanassa vuttipade antobhāva dassanāti attho. Kvapanevaṃ diṭṭhantyāha- ‘taṃyathe’ccādi. “Tamassa sippaṃ sīlaṃ paṇyaṃ paharaṇaṃ payojanaṃ”ti (4-27) ṇike āpūpiko. Natu bhinnatthassāti byatirekaṃ dassetvā taṃ diṭṭhantena sādhetumāha- ‘devadattassi’ccādi. Kāraṇamāha- ‘sāmyantare’ccādi. Devadattassa [M 0.0232] dhuruno kulanti sāmyantarabyavacchedāya devadattasaddasso pādānato gurukulanti vuttipadena devadattatthassānto bhāvoti attho. Tametthopi samānantūpadassento āha- ‘tathehāpi’ccādi. Athāttano puttamicchatītyetasmiṃ vākye padassānvākhyānato attasaddassāpphayogo kinna siyāti dassetumāha- ‘nacāpi’ccādi.

He states the nature of the undesirable consequence: 'It might be 'attano puttīyati'.' If it is thought, 'Since the meaning of 'atta' (self) is expressed by the arising suffix 'īya' itself, the word 'atta' is not used,' he demonstrates that this is also not consistent, stating, 'nor is it possible,' etc. Why is it not possible to say this? He states, 'because of the base,' etc. The meaning is that it is seen that a qualifier having the same meaning as the base, such as 'cake', is included within the derived word. Where is this seen? He explains, 'for example,' etc. By the rule 'That is his craft...' (4-27), with the suffix 'ṇika,' the form is `āpūpiko` (cake-maker). But not of that which has a different meaning. Having shown the contrast, he proves it with the example, 'of Devadatta,' etc. He gives the reason, 'because of another owner,' etc. The meaning is that in 'the family of Devadatta's burden-bearer,' the word 'Devadatta' is used to exclude another owner; therefore, the meaning of 'Devadatta' is not included in the derived word. Showing that the same applies here also, he states, 'similarly here,' etc. Then, to show why, in the sentence 'he desires his own son,' the word 'atta' should not be unused due to the grammatical analysis of the word, he says, 'nor indeed,' etc.

Padassāti puttīyādino padassa. Nacāpi appayogoti sambandho. Kāraṇamāha- ‘īyantassā’tiādi. Īyanto puttīyādi, niyogato na pappotīti sambandho. Tabbācīsaddappayoganti aññavācīsaddayogaṃ. Sutaggahaṇanti asutattāti vuttasutaggahaṇaṃ. Atthappakaraṇādyupalakkhaṇantyanena atthato pakaraṇāditopi puttassatta niyatā gamyate, sutasaddassa tu gahaṇamupalakkhaṇatthanti vadati.

'Padassa' refers to a word such as 'puttīya'. Nor is there non-application; this is the connection. He states the reason: 'of that ending in īya,' and so on. That which ends in 'īya,' such as 'puttīya,' is not necessarily obtained; this is the connection. 'Tabbācīsaddappayogaṃ' means the application of a word expressing something else. 'Sutaggahaṇaṃ' means the taking of the word 'suta' as mentioned, because it is not heard in this context. By this, which indicates meaning, context, and so on, the fixed nature of being a son is understood from the meaning, context, etc., but the taking of the word 'suta' is for the purpose of illustration, he says.

Nanu ca sutte kammāti vuttattā kammasamudāyatopīyo siyā tyāsaṅkiyeva (mabhā)vaṃ sādhayamāha- ‘kammā’tiādi. Vattuṃ iṭṭhā ekasakhyā yassa kammasāmaññassa taṃ tathāvuttaṃ. Vattumiṭṭheka saṅkhyassa gahaṇamāha- ‘kammasamudāyato’ti. Kimpanāvayavato na siyā’ mahantamputtamicchatī’ccatra puttamiccatoccāsaṅkiyāha ‘avayavatopi sāpekkhattāyevā’ti. Na bhatīti sambandho. Evañcarahi idampi na sijjhatīti codento āha ‘carahi’ccādi. Mahā cāyaṃ puttoceti mahāputtamicchatīti yadevaṃ karīyati tadāyampayogoti dassento āha- ‘bhavitabbameve’ccādi.

Indeed, since it is said 'kamma' in the sutta, might the suffix īya not also be from a collection of kammas? Anticipating this doubt, he establishes its absence and says: 'kammā,' etc. That generality of kamma for which a single designation is desired to be expressed is so called. To indicate the taking of that for which a single designation is desired to be expressed, it is said: 'from the collection of kammas.' Why might it not be from a part? Anticipating the doubt regarding 'puttamicchati' in 'mahantaṃ puttamicchati,' he says: 'because even from a part, there is dependence.' It is not so; this is the connection. If so, then this too is not accomplished. Raising this objection, he says: 'carahi,' etc. When it is done thus: 'This is a great son' and 'one desires a great son,' then this application is possible. Showing this, he says: 'it must indeed be so,' etc.

6. Upamā

6. Simile

Upamīyate paricchijjati sādhīyatītyattho. Kīdisantamupamānamiccāha- ‘pasiddhasādhamyā’iccādi. Pasiddho gavādi, tassa sādhamyā samāna rūpatāya yampasiddhassa gavayādino sādhiyassa sādhanaṃ tamupamānantyattho. Samāno dhammo-sseti sadhammo, gavādiyeva. Tassa bhāvo sādhamyaṃ. Sādhyate upamīyate-neneti sādhanamupamānaṃ gavādi. Sādhute upamīyateti sādhiyo, gavayādi. Tassa sādhanaṃ sādhiyasādhanaṃ.

It is compared, it is delimited, it is established; this is the meaning. What kind of thing is the standard of comparison? He says: 'by well-known similarity,' and so on. The well-known thing is a cow, etc. By its similarity—that is, by its common form—that which is the means of establishing the not well-known thing to be established (sādhya), such as the gavaya, is the standard of comparison (upamāna); this is the meaning. It has a common quality (samāno dhammo), hence 'sadhammo,' which is the cow itself, etc. The state of that is 'sādhamyaṃ.' That by which something is established or compared is the 'sādhanaṃ' (means of establishing), the 'upamānaṃ' (standard of comparison), such as the cow. That which is established or compared is the 'sādhiyo' (thing to be established), such as the gavaya. The means of establishing it is 'sādhiyasādhanaṃ'.

Puttamivācaratīti [M 0.0233] ettha ‘āvasathamāvasati’ccādo viya ādhāratthassa viññāyamānattā putte viya māṇavake madhurannapānadānādikamācaraṇaṃ karoticcevamatthasambhavena dvinnampi upamānopameyyabhāvotyavagamayitumāha- ‘putte’iccādi. Pasiddhena sādhanabhāvenupamānabhūte putte ācaraṇampi pasiddhanti āha- ‘tampasiddha’nti. Tadācaraṇena tena ācaraṇena puttamāṇavakavisayamācaraṇaṃ vā puttamāṇavaka saddenupacārato gahetvā visayīvasena visayabhāvavohārotipi yujjati. Vākyattho panetasmiṃ pakkhe ‘puttamiva puttavisaya māṇavakamiva ācarati māṇavakavisayamācaraṇaṃ karotī’ti, vuttiyantu yathāvuttamatthadvayaṃ yathāyogaṃ yojetvā veditabbaṃ.

Here, in 'Puttamivācarati,' just as in 'āvasathamāvasati,' etc., because the meaning of a basis is understood, and because the meaning 'he performs conduct such as giving sweet food and drink to the student as if to a son' is possible, in order to explain that there is a relationship of standard of comparison and thing to be compared between the two, he says: 'putte,' etc. In the case of the son, who has become the standard of comparison by being a well-known means, the conduct is also well-known; thus he says: 'that is well-known.' By that conduct, or by taking the words 'son' and 'student' metaphorically, the designation of 'object' by means of the 'possessor of the object' is also fitting. However, in this case, the meaning of the sentence is: 'He acts towards the student as if towards a son; he performs conduct directed towards the student as if directed towards a son.' But in the commentary, the two meanings as stated should be understood by connecting them as is appropriate.

Nanu ca yajjatropamānopameyyabhāvo vuttiyaṃ īyeneva jotitoti ivasaddo nivattate, tadopamānopameyyabhāvo putta saddeva vattate, taṃ kathamupameyyavacanassa māṇavakasaddassa vuttatthassa payogo yuttoccāsaṅkiyāha- ‘upamānavacanato’ccādi.

Indeed, if here the relationship of standard of comparison and thing to be compared is illuminated in the compound by the suffix `īya` alone, then the word `iva` is eliminated. In that case, the relationship of standard of comparison and thing to be compared is expressed by the word `putta` alone. How then is the application of the word `māṇavaka`, which expresses the thing to be compared, to the expressed meaning, justified? Anticipating this doubt, he says: 'From the word for the standard of comparison,' etc.

Tabbisiṭṭhācaraṇeti tenopamānena visiṭṭhe ācaraṇe. Upamānopameyyabhāvassānivattattāti etthāyamadhippāyo ‘upamāna visiṭṭhācaraṇe upamānavacanato īyassa vidhāne nopameyyavacanamantarenopamānavacanassa pavattīti upamānopameyyabhāvassānivattī”ti. Aññathāti yadyupamānopameyyabhāvassa īyeneva jotitattā tadantassupameyye vutti siyātyattho. Pabbatāyatīti “kattutāyo”ti (5-8) āyo. Upameyyassānivattattā upameyya kattusāmaññe tippaccayo.

'Tabbisiṭṭhācaraṇe' means: in conduct distinguished by that standard of comparison. As for 'upamānopameyyabhāvassānivattattā' (because the relationship of standard of comparison and thing to be compared is not eliminated), the intention here is this: 'When the suffix `īya` is prescribed after a word for the standard of comparison in the sense of conduct distinguished by it, the word for the standard of comparison is applied without the word for the thing to be compared; thus, the relationship of standard of comparison and thing to be compared is not eliminated.' 'Aññathā' means: if, because the relationship of standard of comparison and thing to be compared were illuminated by `īya` alone, the word ending in that suffix were to function in expressing the thing to be compared. In 'Pabbatāyati,' the suffix is `āyo` by the rule 'kattuto āyo' (5-8). Because the thing to be compared is not eliminated, the suffix `ti` is applied in the sense of a general agent that is the thing to be compared.

7. Ādhā

7. Basis

Yathānantarasutte upamāne upameyyassa māṇavakassa payogo upapanno, tathātrāpi ‘pāsāde kuṭiya’nti copameyyassapayogoti atidisanto āha- ‘heṭṭhāviye’ccādi. Upamāne upameyyassānantobhāvāti attho. Nanu kimatthamidamuccate yavatāyo pāsāde [M 0.0234] ivācarati so pāsādamivācaratītipi vattuṃ sakkāti nātthabhedo-ññatra vacanicchābhedāti pubbenevetthāpi īyo siddho, tato nāttho-nena vacanene ccāsaṅkiyāha- ‘yadipi’ccādi.

Just as in the immediately preceding sutta the application of the `māṇavaka`, the thing to be compared, with the standard of comparison was appropriate, so here too, extending the rule to the application of the thing to be compared, as in 'a hut in a palace,' he says: 'heṭṭhā viya,' etc. The meaning is that the thing to be compared is not included within the standard of comparison. Indeed, why is this said? Insofar as one who acts as if in a palace can also be said to act like a palace, there is no difference other than a difference in the desire for expression. Therefore, the suffix `īya` is established here too by the previous rule, so there is no need for this statement. Anticipating this objection, he says: 'yadipi,' etc.

8. Kattu

8. Agent

Ettha kattutoiti vacanā kammāti nivattate, āyaggahaṇā īyo. Kadā pana kattuviseso-vasīyaticcāha-‘yatthyādisaddasamānādhikaraṇatte’tiādi. Pabbatāyati hatthiccevamādinā hatthyādi saddena samānādhikaraṇatte satīti attho.

Here, from the word 'kattuto' (from the agent), 'kamma' (object) is discontinued, and from the taking of `āya`, `īya` is discontinued. But when is the specific agent understood? He says: 'When there is co-referentiality with a word such as `hatthi`,' etc. The meaning is: when there is co-referentiality with a word such as `hatthi`, as in 'Pabbatāyati hatthī' (the elephant behaves like a mountain), etc.

9. Jhatthe

9. In the sense of jha

Koyaṃ cyatthoccāsaṅkiya “abhūtatabbhāve karāsabhūyoge vikārācī”ti (4-119) cīssa abhūtatabbhāve karādiyogesati vidhānā ‘abhūtatabbhāvo karādivisiṭṭho’ti āha. Abhūta tabbhāvassa karādivisiṭṭhattā karotyatthanivattiyāvassaṃ pāṇiniyā viya bhuviggahaṇaṃ kattabbamaññathā karotyatthepi siyātyāsaṅkiya nivattihetumāha- ‘tenevā’tiādi. Yeneva karotyādivisiṭṭho abhūtatabbhāvocyattho teneva hetunāti attho. Bhavatyatthe-nena kāraṇena laddhe karotyatthopyaniṭṭho labbhaticcāsaṅkiya tannivattimpaṭipādayamāha- ‘karotyatthe’ccādi. Adhavalaṃ dhavalaṃ karoti dhavalīkaroticceva cīppaccaye kattabbe kammeneva karotissābhisambandhassa diṭṭhattāti attho. Kāraṇantaramāha- ‘iha ce’ccādi. Itisaddo hetumhi yasmā iha kattutoti vattate tatoceti attho.

Anticipating the question 'What is this meaning of `cya`?', he says: 'the state of becoming what it was not is distinguished by `karādi`,' because `cī` is prescribed by the rule 'abhūtatabbhāve karāsabhūyoge vikārā cī' (4-119) in the sense of 'becoming what it was not' when there is a connection with `karādi`. Because the state of becoming what it was not is distinguished by `karādi`, for the purpose of eliminating the meaning of `karoti`, it is necessary to take `bhū`, as in Pāṇini's grammar; otherwise, it might also be in the sense of `karoti`. Anticipating this, he states the reason for the elimination: 'teneva,' etc. The meaning is: for the very reason that the meaning of `cya` is the state of becoming what it was not, distinguished by `karoti`, etc. When the meaning of `bhavati` is obtained by this reason, anticipating that the undesired meaning of `karoti` might also be obtained, he demonstrates its elimination, saying: 'karotyatthe,' etc. The meaning is: because when the suffix `cī` is to be applied, as in 'adhavalaṃ dhavalaṃ karoti' (he makes the non-white white) or 'dhavalīkaroti' (he whitens), the connection of `karoti` is seen only with the object. He states another reason: 'iha ce,' etc. The word `iti` is in the sense of reason; the meaning is: because here 'kattuto' is current.

Asatyatthassa pana bhavatyattheyevāntobhāvā na tannivatti paṭipāditā. Tappakaraṇeti dhātuppaccayappakaraṇe. Dvibbacananti paṭaiccassa dvibbacanaṃ tato “dissantaññepi paccayā”ti (4-120) rāppaccayo. “Rānubandhentasarādissā”ti (4-132) antasarādissa lopo. Cyantā paccayābhāvatthaṃ- ‘acīto’ti paccayavidhānasutte paṭisedho na kato, tenāha-‘acītoti paṭisedhābhāvā’ti. Cīti bhusoiti

However, the elimination of the meaning of `asati` (non-being) is not demonstrated, because it is included within the meaning of `bhavati`. 'Tappakaraṇe' means in the section on roots and suffixes. 'Dvibbacananti' means the reduplication of `paṭa`; then, by 'dissantaññepi paccayā' (4-120), the suffix `rā` is applied. By 'Rānubandhe'ntasarādissā' (4-132), there is elision of the final vowel and the beginning of the suffix. So that there may be a suffix after a stem ending in `cya`, the prohibition 'acīto' was not made in the rule prescribing the suffix. Therefore, he says: 'because of the absence of the prohibition 'acīto'.' 'Cī' means 'intensely'.

Paṭhamantācī[M 0.0235]. Ṇādivuttittā “ekatthatāya”nti (2-119) vibhattilopo. Iheceti ‘cyatthe” itīmasmiṃyeva. Na ca vuccateti sambandho.

The suffix `cī` is applied after a word ending in the first case. Because it is a `ṇādi` compound, there is elision of the case ending by the rule 'ekatthatāya' (2-119). 'Iha ce' means precisely in this very rule, 'cyatthe'. And 'is not said'; this is the connection.

10. Saddā

10. Sounds

Nanu ca asati sutte dutiyāggahaṇe dutiyantehiccāyaṃ viseso kuto labbhate yena ‘saddādīhi dutiyantehī’ti vivaraṇaṃ katanti saccaṃ, tathāpi paccayavidhimhi yuttepi pañcamiyā niddese ‘saddādīnī’ti dutiyāyopādānasāmatthiyā tathā vivaraṇaṃ kataṃ.

Indeed, when the sutta does not mention the second case, from where is this specific meaning, 'from those ending in the second case,' obtained, by which the explanation is given as 'from sounds, etc., ending in the second case'? This is true. Nevertheless, even though in the prescription of a suffix the specification by the fifth case is proper, the explanation is made thus due to the power of the employment of the second case in 'saddādīni'.

Sabbatthāti “tamadhīte taṃ jānāti kaṇikācā”do (4-14) sabbattha. Kiriyāvātyavadhāraṇena yaṃ byavacchinnaṃ, tamupadassento āha- ‘na kāle’ccādi. Yadīpi adhīteccādīsu vattamānakālena kattunā ekavacanena ca niddeso, tathāpi tesamappadhānattā aññasmimpi bhūtādike kāle kammādo sādhane bahuvacanena ca paccayo siyā eveti bhāvo.

'Everywhere' means everywhere in such rules as (4-14): 'He studies that, he knows that....' Pointing out what is excluded by the restriction to the meaning of action, he says: 'not in time,' etc. Although in 'he studies,' etc., the instruction is with the present tense, the agent case, and the singular number, still, because these are not primary, the sense is that the suffix may also occur in another time, such as the past, etc., in another syntactic role, such as the object, etc., and in the plural number.

Nanu ca “dhātvatthenāmasmī”ti (5-12) ippaccaye patte-yamārabbhate assapi dhātvattheyeva vidhānaṃ, tato ca saddādīhi dhātvatthe ippaccayena na bhavitabbaṃ, dissate ca ippaccayapayogoccāsaṅkiya ‘nāyamippaccayassa bādhako’ti paṭipādetumāha- ‘dhūvaṃ karoti’ccādi. Nānābhinnaṃ vākyaṃ nānāvākyaṃ, tassa bhāvena, tena bhinnavākyabhāvenāyassa ippaccayassa ca samuccayatoti attho. “Dhātvatthenāmasmī”tyekaṃ vākyaṃ, “saddādīni karotya”paraṃ. Etāni dve bhinnavākyāni- ‘dhātvatthe nāmasmā ippaccayo bhavati, saddādīni karoticcasmiṃ atthe āyo bhavatī’ti paccekamākhyātāpekkhāya vākyaparisamattiyā bhinnatā, abhinne hi kiriyāpadekavākyatā, bhinnetu nānāvākyatā, nānāvākye ca sati samuccayo. Na hi sāmaññavisesabhāvena vidhānameva bādhāhetu, kiñcarahi ekavākyatāpi, taṃ yathā-‘brāhmaṇānaṃ dadhi diyyataṃ, takkaṃ koṇḍaññāye’ti. Nānāvākye tu samuccayo, taṃ yathā- ‘brāhmaṇā bhojīyantu, māḍharāya vatthayugalaṃ dīyatū’ti māḍharo brāhmaṇabhāvena bhojīyate vatthayugalañca labhate, tenojukaṃ [M 0.0236] vuttena vatthayugaladānena sāmaññavuttaṃ bhojanaṃ na bādhīyate, tathehāpi ujukaṃ vihitenāyena sāmaññavihito ippaccayo na bādhīyate lakkhiyānurodhena satthakārassa vākya bhedābhedoti nānavaṭṭhitidosoti maññate. Timhi le ca siddhanti sambandho.

But indeed, concerning the rule (5-12) 'From a noun in the sense of a root, the suffix `i` is added,' when the `i` suffix is applicable, this `āya` suffix is introduced. The prescription of `āya` is also in the sense of a root; therefore, with 'sound,' etc., the `i` suffix should not occur in the sense of a root. But since the usage of the `i` suffix is seen, and this is questioned, in order to establish that 'this (`āya`) is not an obstructor of the `i` suffix,' he says: 'he makes firm,' etc. A sentence divided in various ways is a 'diverse sentence.' By its nature, that is, by the nature of being separate sentences, there is a combination of the `āya` suffix and the `i` suffix—this is the meaning. 'From a noun in the sense of a root, the suffix `i` is added' is one sentence; 'from "sound," etc., in the sense of "makes"' is another. These are two distinct sentences: 'From a noun in the sense of a root, the suffix `i` occurs,' and 'From "sound," etc., in the sense of "makes," the suffix `āya` occurs.' The separateness is due to the completion of the sentence with respect to each verb. For when there is a single verb, it is a single sentence, but when the verbs are different, there are diverse sentences. And when there are diverse sentences, there is combination. For the cause of obstruction is not merely the prescription by the relationship of general and specific, but also the state of being a single sentence, as in: 'Let yogurt be given to the brahmins, but buttermilk to Koṇḍañña.' In the case of diverse sentences, however, there is combination, as in: 'Let the brahmins be fed, and let a pair of cloths be given to Māḍhara.' Here, Māḍhara is fed by virtue of being a brahmin and also receives a pair of cloths. Thus, by the directly stated giving of a pair of cloths, the generally stated feeding is not obstructed. Similarly here too, by the directly prescribed `āya` suffix, the generally prescribed `i` suffix is not obstructed. It is considered that, in accordance with the examples, the author's division or non-division of sentences is not a fault of inconsistency. And the connection with `ti`, `mi`, and `le` is established.

Yappaccayo na vihito pāṇinīādīhi viyāti adhippāyo. ‘Jala dala- dittiyaṃ’. “Māno”ti (5-65) māno, “kattari lo”ti “parokkhāyaṃ ce”ti (5-70) caggahaṇena ‘dala dala’itidvittaṃ “loponādibyañjanassa” (5-75) “saramhā dve”ti (1-34) dassalassa ca dvibhāve daddallamānā. Jalamānāti aṭṭhakathāvacanatoti iminā kiriyāsamabhihāre yappaccayābhāvaṃ dasseti. Iminā ca sakkate viya bhusābhikkhaññepi kiriyāsamabhihāro kiriyāparivattanaṃ, tañca yadā kiriyamaññena kattabbamañño karoti, tena kattabbañcetaro, tadā bhavatīti viññeyyaṃ. “Sāmaññavihitā vidhayo payogamanusarantī”ti iminā lakkhaṇena ‘dala-dittiya’nti imasmā “māno”ti sāmaññena vihito mānappaccayo bhusatthe ābhikkhaññe ca bhavissati. Daddalla mānāti ettha bhusaṃ jalamānā, punappuna jalamānāti ca attho veditabbo.

The intention is that the `ya` suffix is not prescribed as it is by Pāṇini and others. From the root list: '`jal` and `dal` in the sense of shining.' The form `daddallamānā` is derived thus: by the rule 'māno' (5-65), the `māna` suffix is prescribed; by 'la in the agent'; by the inclusion of 'ca' in 'parokkhāyaṃ ce' (5-70), there is reduplication as 'dala dala'; by 'loponādibyañjanassa' (5-75) and 'saramhā dve' (1-34), with the doubling of the `d` and `l`. By the commentary's statement 'shining,' he shows the absence of the `ya` suffix in the sense of repetition of action. By this it is shown that, as in Sanskrit, in the sense of 'intensely' and 'frequently,' repetition of action can also mean exchange of action. And it should be understood that this occurs when one person does an action that should be done by another, and the latter does what should be done by the former. By the maxim, 'General rules follow the usage,' from this root '`dal` in the sense of shining,' the `māna` suffix, which is generally prescribed by the rule 'māno,' will occur in the sense of 'intensely' and 'frequently.' Here, the meaning of `daddallamānā` should be understood as 'shining intensely' and 'shining again and again'.

11. Namo

11. Homage

Namo karoti namosaddamuccāreti, saddaṃ karoti saddamuccāretīticcevamattho (na) gahetabbe anissayanato anabhidhānato vā.

'He does homage' means 'he utters the word namo'; 'he makes a sound' means 'he utters a sound.' This meaning should not be accepted, either because it is not the primary sense or because it is not the expressed meaning.

12. Dhātvā

12. The Meaning of the Root

Aparinipphannoti anipphanno asiddhāvatthoti attho. Kārakasādhiyoti yathālābhaṃ kārakehi sādhiyo. Asatvabhūtoti adabbabhūto. Ayantu kiriyārūpo padattho pacatyādīnaṃ vikledanādipadhānakiriyārūpo ca tadavayavarūpā pubbaparībhūtauddhanāro panādikādayo tādatthiyā ca pacatyādivacanīyā. Tasmā yathā vuttalakkhaṇe dhātvatthe dhātuto vidhīyamāno tyādippaccayo tathābhūtameva [M 0.0237] vadatīti bhedābhāvā abhedasaṅkhyāyekavacanenoccate, ‘na bahuvacanena, tenettha ‘ṭhīyate devadattena, ṭhīyate devadattehī’ti bhavati. Na yatokutocītiādinā yato yattha na dissati, tato tattha na hotīti dīpeti. Yato yattha vidhi, sa tassa sambandhī bhavatīti nāmehi vacanīyatthato-tthantarabhūto yoyaṃ dhātvattho kamādīnamatthabhūto, so sakatthoti sakattheyevāyamippaccayo curādiṇiviyāti veditabbo.

'Unaccomplished' means not completed, in a state of not being achieved. 'To be accomplished by causal factors' means to be accomplished by the causal factors as they are available. 'Not having being' means not being a substance. This meaning of a word, which is in the form of an action, such as the primary action of cooking, which is dissolving, etc., and its component parts, the preceding and subsequent actions of placing on the fire, etc., are also, because they are for that purpose, expressible by the word 'cooks,' etc. Therefore, the suffixes `ti`, etc., being prescribed after a root in the sense of the root-meaning with the characteristics as described, express just such a state. Due to the absence of division, it is expressed by the singular number, which indicates non-difference, not by the plural. Hence, here it is said: 'It is stood by Devadatta' and 'It is stood by the Devadattas.' By the phrase 'not from anywhere whatsoever,' etc., he shows that where something is not seen, it does not occur there. Wherever a rule is prescribed, it is related to that. This root-meaning, which is the meaning of the root `kam`, etc., being something other than the meaning expressible by nouns, is its own meaning. It should be understood that this `i` suffix is in its own meaning, like the `ṇi` suffix of the `cur` group.

Tassacāti ekārassa ca. Atha atihatthayaticcādo pādivisiṭṭhe eva dhātvatthe ippaccayassa vidhānā tadatthavihiteneva ippaccayena pādivisiṭṭho dhātvattho vutto, tena kimattho ippaccayantassa pādiyogoccāsaṅkiya payojanamākhyātumāha- ‘atihatthayati’ccādi. Na sāmatthiyanti samatthatā natthīti attho.

And 'of that' (`tassa`) means 'of the letter `e`.' Now, in 'atihatthayati,' etc., since the `i` suffix is prescribed in the root-meaning that is specified by a `pa`-group prefix, the root-meaning specified by the `pa`-group prefix is already expressed by that very `i` suffix prescribed for that meaning. Therefore, questioning 'what is the purpose of combining a `pa`-group prefix with a stem ending in the `i` suffix?', in order to state the purpose, he says: 'atihatthayati,' etc. 'Na sāmatthiyan'ti means 'there is no capability'.

13. Saccā

13. The sac group

Atthamācikkhati, vedamācikkhatīti viggaho. Sukhāpeticcādo sukhaṃ vedayaticcādinā viggaho. Vāpāṭhāti vikappena pāṭhato.

The analysis is: 'He explains the meaning; he explains the Veda.' The analysis of sukhāpeti (he makes happy), etc., is by way of sukhaṃ vedayati (he feels happy), etc. Vāpāṭhā means 'by alternative recitation'.

15. Curā

15. The cur group

Asati sutte sakattheti kathaṃ labbhatīti āha- ‘atthānati desā’ti. Atthā-natidesāti atthavisesassa kassaci sutte aniddesāti attho. Atthavisesassā-natidesamattena sakatthoyeva ṇinā vāccoti kathaṃ viññāyateccāha- ‘sakatthassa ca sutattā’ti. Cura=theyye iccādīsu theyyādikassa sakatthassa sutattāti attho. Yogavibhāgatoti ‘ṇī’tiyogavibhāgato, rajjaṃ kāretīti ettha sāmyamaccādikaṃ sattaṅgaṃ rajjaṃ pavattetīti vā attho, payojakabyāpāre ṇi.

When there is no rule, how is 'in its own meaning' obtained? He says: 'By non-indication of the meaning.' 'Non-indication of the meaning' means the non-specification in any rule of a particular meaning. How is it known that by the mere non-indication of a particular meaning, it is to be expressed by the affix ṇi in its own meaning? He says: 'And because it is heard in its own meaning.' In cases like 'cur in the sense of theft,' etc., the meaning is that 'theft,' etc., which is its own meaning, is heard. 'By division of the rule' means from the division of the rule for ṇī. In rajjaṃ kāreti, the meaning is either 'he causes the seven-limbed kingdom, including the king and ministers, to proceed,' or ṇi is in the sense of the instigator's activity.

16. Payo

16. The Instigator

Payojako codako byāpārakoti attho nanu ca vuttiyaṃ ‘kattāraṃ payojayatī’ti vuttaṃ kathaṃ payujjamānassa kattuttaṃti āha- ‘payujjamāno’ccādi. Nāvassaṃ kiriyāpavattakatteneva yoggatāmattenapi [M 0.0238] kattuttaṃ siyāti dassento āha- ‘kiriyāya yoggo’tiādi. Pāsāṇambalenuṭṭhāpeti’ccādīsu hi yogyatāyapi kattuttāvasāyosiyā, kopanāyaṃ payojakabyapāroti āha- ‘pesane’ccādi. Dāsādino hīnassa katthaci atthe niyojanaṃ pesanaṃ. Guruādino sakkārapubbaṃ byāpāraṇamajjhesanaṃ. Taṃ pesanajjhesanādikaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ sabhāvo yassa so tathā vutto.

The meaning is 'instigator,' 'inciter,' 'one who engages.' But since it is stated in the commentary, 'he instigates the doer,' how can the one being instigated be a doer? He says, 'the one being instigated,' etc. To show that being a doer can exist not necessarily by initiating an action but also by mere fitness for it, he says, 'fit for action,' etc. For in examples like 'he makes a stone rise up by force,' agency can be determined even from mere capability. What, then, is this instigator's activity? He says, 'in sending,' etc. Directing an inferior person like a slave in some matter is 'sending.' Respectful engagement of a superior like a teacher is 'requesting.' That whose characteristic, whose nature, is sending, requesting, and so on, is what is meant thereby.

Ādisaddena ānukūlyabhāgino byāpārassa gahaṇaṃ, tathā ca ‘bhikkhā vāsayati kārīso-jjhāpesī’ti sijjhati. Bhikkhā hi pacurabyañjanavatī labbhamānā vāsānukūlaṃ tittivisesamupajanayati. Kārīsopi nivāte padese suṭṭhu pajjalitojjhayanavirodhi sītakatamupaddavamapanayanto-jjhayanānukūlasāmatthiyamādadhāti tato tesampi yuttampayojakattanti.

By the word ādi (etc.), the inclusion of a favorable activity is understood. And so, 'bhikkhā vāsayati' (the almsfood makes one dwell) and 'kārīso jhāpesi' (the cow dung caused to burn) are established. For almsfood, when obtained with abundant curries, produces a special satisfaction conducive to dwelling. And cow dung, well-kindled in a windless spot, removing the affliction of cold which is contrary to burning, provides a capacity conducive to burning. Therefore, for these too, it is fitting that they are instigators.

Payojakabyāpāretīdaṃ paccayavisesanaṃ vā siyā pakativisesanaṃ vā. Tattha yadi pakativisesanaṃ siyā, tadā payojakabyāpāre vattamānā ṇīṇāpī vidhīyantīti (gamanaṃ) pati yo niyogo tadattho gami, na gatyattho, tassa cāyaṃ payojjoti ‘gamayati māṇavakaṃ gāma’nti gatyatthassa payojje “gatibodhāhāre”ccādinā (2-4) vihitā dutiyā na pappoti, tato pakatyatthavisesanapakkho duṭṭhoti paccayavisesanapakkhaṃ dassetumāha- ‘paccayavisesanaṃ vedaṃ na pakativisesana’nti.

'The instigator's activity'—this could be either a qualifier of the affix or a qualifier of the base. In that case, if it were a qualifier of the base, then the affixes ṇī and ṇāpi would be prescribed for what exists in the instigator's activity. The root gam would then have the meaning of the command regarding going, not the meaning of motion, and this one is the instigated. Thus, in 'gamayati māṇavakaṃ gāmaṃ' (he makes the boy go to the village), the accusative case for the instigated object, prescribed for roots with the meaning of motion by the rule 'gatibodhāhāre...' (2.4), would not be obtained. Therefore, the position that it is a qualifier of the base's meaning is flawed. To show the position that it is a qualifier of the affix, he says: 'This is a qualifier of the affix, not a qualifier of the base.'

Payojakamattaggahaṇeti mattasaddo sāmaññavācī, yathā ‘kaññā mattaṃ vārayatī’ti. Kattāraṃ yo payujjati yo ca karaṇādīnaṃ payojako tesaṃ sāmaññena gahaṇe satīti attho. Byāpāretvevāti payojakaggahaṇamantarena byāpāreicceva vacanaṃ kattabbaṃ siyāti bhāvo, tanti payojakaggahaṇaṃ, visiṭṭho visayo yassa payojakaggahaṇassataṃtathāvuttaṃ. Kopanāyaṃvisiṭṭho visayoccāha- ‘yo loke’iccādi. Itovāti vakkhamānassa hetuno parāmāso. Tanti curādīhi ṇividhānaṃ. Evaṃsaddo vakkhamānāpekkho. Taṃ [M 0.0239] visuṃ curādīhi ṇividhānameva vakkhamānappakārena saphalaṃ siyā nāññathāti attho. Tameva pakāraṃ dasseti‘yadiminā’ccādi.

In 'payojakamattaggahaṇe', the word matta denotes generality, as in 'kaññāmattaṃ vārayati'. The meaning is: when there is a general inclusion of one who instigates the agent and one who is the instigator of the instrument, etc. 'Byāpāre tveva' means that without the inclusion of 'instigator,' the statement would have to be just 'byāpāre' (in the activity). Therefore, the inclusion of 'instigator' has a specific scope; it is stated as such. What then is this specific scope? He says: 'yo loke,' etc. 'Itovāti' is a reference to the reason about to be stated. 'Tan' refers to the prescription of ṇi after the cur group, etc. The word evaṃ anticipates what is to be stated. The meaning is that this separate prescription of ṇi after the cur group, etc., becomes fruitful only in the manner to be stated, not otherwise. He shows that very manner with 'yad iminā,' etc.

17. Kyotā

17. The kya group

Kattari vihitesupi mānantatyādīsu parabhūtesu kyo bhavatīti viññāyeyyāti ‘bhāvakammesū’ti na kyassa visesananti āha- ‘mānantatyādīna’miccādi.

So that it may be understood that the affix kya occurs even after the affixes māna, nta, tya, etc., although they are prescribed in the active voice, when they are followed, he says that 'bhāvakammesu' (in the sense of state and object) is not a qualifier of kya, but of 'mānantatyādīnaṃ' (of māna, nta, tya, etc.).

Yadi hi kattari vihitesu siyā, tathā sati tesamubhinnaṃ padhānattenābhidhīyamānānamaññamaññānapekkhattā asambandho siyā, na ce vambhūtānamabhidhānamatthi, na hi ‘ṭhīyate’ccasmā bhāvo kattā ca patīyate, nāpi ‘gamyate’ccasmā kammaṃ kattāca. Api tu bhāvakammāneva gamyante, tenāha- ‘tasmā’iccādi.

For if it were prescribed in the active voice, then, since both would be expressed as primary, there would be no connection due to their mutual independence. And there is no expression of such things. For from 'ṭhīyate' (it is stood), both the state and the agent are not understood; nor from 'gamyate' (it is gone to), both the object and the agent. Rather, only the state and the object are understood. Therefore, he says: 'tasmā,' etc.

Tesamevāti mānantatyādīnameva. Parasamaññābhi paresaṃ kaccāyanā naṃ parokkhāicceva nāmaṃ. Tabbajjitesūti parokkhāsaññipaccayavajjitesu. Aparokkhesūti ettha parasamaññāvasena parokkhāiccanena saha samāsaṃ dassetvā idāni aññathāpi paṭipādetuṃ ‘athavā’tiādimāha. Parokkheti indriyāvisaye kāle. Parokkhevihitā paccayāti iminā upacārena taddhitappaccayavasena vā parokkhāti saddanipphattimāha. Te pana‘a u’ iccādayo. Tatoti parokkhappaccayato.

'Tesam eva' means 'of māna, nta, tya, etc., only.' By 'parasamaññābhi' (by the designation of others), for other Kaccāyana grammarians, its name is parokkhā. 'Tabbajjitesu' means 'excluding the affixes designated as parokkhā.' Here, regarding 'aparokkhesu', having shown the compound with 'parokkhā' by way of the designation of others, he now says 'athavā' (or), etc., to establish it in another way. 'Parokkha' means 'at a time beyond the range of the sense faculties.' He states the derivation of the word parokkhā either by this figurative expression 'parokkhe vihitā paccayā' (affixes prescribed for the parokkha tense) or by way of a taddhita affix. And those are a, u, etc. 'Tato' means 'from the parokkhā affix'.

Nanu pubbapakkhe ‘aparokkhesū’ti ettha ‘parokkhāvajjitesū’ti attha vacanaṃ yujjati, dutiyapakkhe pana ‘parokkhavajjitesū’ti, tathā sati kathamettha ‘parokkhāvajjitesū’ti atthavacanaṃ yujjatīti āha- ‘tepanā’tiādi. Idhāti aparokkhesūti imasmiṃ. Nanu ca “parokkhe a u”iccādisutte (6-6) ‘parokkhe’ti pakativisesananti paccayānaṃ parokkhe vihitatā kathanti manasi nidhāyāha ‘parokkhe’iccādi. Bhavanaṃ bhāvo kiriyādhātvattho.

Surely, in the first position, the explanation of the meaning of 'aparokkhesu' as 'parokkhāvajjitesu' (excluding parokkhā) is fitting, but in the second position, it is 'parokkhavajjitesu' (excluding parokkha). That being so, how is the explanation of the meaning as 'parokkhāvajjitesu' fitting here? He says: 'te pana,' etc. 'Here' means 'in this word aparokkhesu.' But surely, in the rule 'parokkhe a u...' (6.6), since 'parokkhe' is a qualifier of the base, how is there the prescription of the affixes in the parokkha tense? Keeping this in mind, he says: 'parokkhe,' etc. 'Bhavanaṃ' is bhāvo, being, the meaning of the action-root.

Sādhīyamānāvatthoti iminā siddhāvatthā nirassate. Pubbaparībhūto padhānakiriyāvayavabhūto kiriyārūpo attho lakkhaṇaṃ sabhāvo [M 0.0240] yassa dhātvatthassa so tathā vutto. Satvabhūtoti ettha patīyatīti seso. Bahuvacanampi hoti pākāpāketi adhippāyo, karīyatīti kammaṃ, tañca yadipi nāmādikammamatthi, tathāpi kriyatthāiccādhikārato mānādīnamaññatthālabbhanato ca kiriyā sambandhova gayhate, su-savane sūyamānaṃ.

By this, 'sādhīyamānāvattho' (the state of being accomplished), the state of having been accomplished is rejected. That meaning of the root is so called whose characteristic and nature is the meaning in the form of an action, which has become a component of the principal action, and which is comprised of prior and subsequent stages. Here, in 'sattvabhūto', 'is understood' is the ellipsis. The intention is that there is also the plural, as in 'pākāpāke'. 'That which is done' is the object (kammaṃ). And although there is the object in the form of a noun, etc., still, because of the governing rule concerning the meaning of action and because other meanings for māna, etc., are not obtained, only the connection with action is taken. Su in the sense of hearing: sūyamānaṃ (being heard).

Pāṇiniyehettha “bhindati kusūlaṃ’tyādo yā bhedanādikiriyā kammani dissate, sā yadā sukarattamattena sappadhānattavacanicchāyaṃ kattuttepyupalabbhati ‘bhijjate kusulo sayameve’ccādinā, tadāssa kattuno suttantarena kammasarikkhabhāvo vidhīyate ‘kammanissayaṃ kāriyaṃ yathā siyā’ti. Tannissāyāha- ‘yadā kammameve’ccādi. Yadā kammameva kattubhāvena vivacchīyateti sambandho. Kathaṃ katvā tathā vivacchīyateccāha- ‘attasamavetāya’iccādi. Attasaddena kammamatra vivacchitaṃ, attani samavetā ekadesībhūtā attasamavetā, tassā kiriyāya kammaṭṭhakiriyāyāti vuttaṃ hoti.

Here in the Pāṇinian system, in examples like 'bhindati kusūlaṃ' (he breaks the granary), the action of breaking, etc., is seen in the object. When that action—due to its mere ease of accomplishment and with the desire to speak of it as if it were primary—is also found in the agent, as in 'bhijjate kusulo sayameva' (the granary breaks by itself), then for this agent, a state of being like the object is prescribed by another rule, so that 'the action might be dependent on the object.' Relying on that, he says: 'yadā kammameva...' (when the object itself...). The connection is: 'when the object itself is intended to have the nature of an agent.' How is it so intended? He says: 'attasamavetāya...' (by the action inhering in itself). By the word atta (self), the object is intended here. Attasamavetā means inhering in itself, having become a part of it. By 'that action,' what is meant is 'the action residing in the object' (kammaṭṭhakiriyā).

Subhedattādineti hetumhi karaṇe vā tatiyā. Atthatoti ‘kammeyeva kyo’ti (na sakkhi) tasmā vuttanti adhippāyo. Tathāhi ‘bhijjateti savanā kammatāvagamyate’ti iminā atthato kammeyevakyotipaṭipāditameva. Vuttameva phuṭīkaramāha- ‘bhijjate iccasmiṃ pade’iccādi. Aññathāti yadi kammeyeva tepaccayo na siyā. Atoti bhijjate iccasmā. Upasaṃharamāha- ‘tasmā’iccādi. Kiṃ vacanenāti pāṇinīyānamiva kiṃ suttattarenāti attho.

In 'subhedattādinā', the third case ending is in the sense of cause or instrument. 'Atthato' (implicitly) means the intention is that it is said (though not explicitly) that 'kyo is only in the sense of the object.' Indeed, by this statement, 'from hearing 'bhijjate', objectivity (kammatā) is understood,' it is established implicitly that kya is only in the sense of the object. Making clear what has been said, he says: 'in the word bhijjate,' etc. 'Otherwise' means: if the affix te were not only in the sense of the object. 'Ato' means 'from bhijjate.' Concluding, he says: 'tasmā,' etc. 'What is the use of the statement?' means 'what is the use of another rule, as the Pāṇinians have?'

Vacanābhāvepi kammakattari padasaṅkhārakkamopadassanamukhena vutti ganthaṃ vivaritumāha- ‘vākyato’iccādi. Vākyato uddharitvā padesaṅkhariyamāneti ‘bhijjate kusūlo sayameve’ti vākyato visuṃ katvā bhijjate’ti pade saṅkhariyamāne nipphādīyamāneti attho. Tadevāti padatthasāmaññameva. Tannipphādaneti tassa saṅkharimānassa padassa saṅkharaṇe. Sayantīmassātra attanāti attho. Na kevala manenetadeva vuttaṃ- ‘kammeyeva paccayo’ti, kiñcarahi aññampatthīti dassetumāha- [M 0.0241] ‘anena ce’ccādi. Co vattabbantarasamuccaye. Anenabhijjateti savanāiccādinā idañcāhāti attho. Kintadiccāha ‘kamma kattuno’ccādi, na padamudāharaṇanti kammakattuno vākyamevodāharaṇaṃ… vākyeneva tassa patītiyā maññate. Padamevodāharaṇaṃ kasmā na siyāti āha- ‘padehi’ccādi. Dutiyamudāharaṇaṃ dassetumāha- ‘kattunissayo pi’ccādi.

To explain the commentary text, he says 'vākyato', etc., by way of showing the process of word formation for the agent-like object, even in the absence of an explicit statement. The meaning of 'vākyato uddharitvā pade saṅkhariyamāne' is: when the word 'bhijjate' is separated from the sentence 'bhijjate kusūlo sayameva' (the granary breaks by itself) and is being formed. 'Tadeva' means 'just the general meaning of the word.' 'Tannipphādaneti' means 'in the formation of that word which is being formed.' Here, the meaning of 'sayan' is 'attanā' (by itself). To show that not only is it said by this that 'the affix is only in the sense of the object,' but that there is something else as well, he says: 'anena ca,' etc. The word ca is for the inclusion of another statement. The meaning is: by this, namely 'bhijjate iti savanā', etc., he also says this. What is that? He says: 'kammakattuno', etc. The word is not the example; the sentence is the example for the agent-like object, for he thinks its understanding comes only from the sentence. Why should the word itself not be the example? He says: 'padehi,' etc. To show the second example, he says: 'kattunissayo pi,' etc.

Asmiṃ pakkheti asmiṃ kattuttena vivacchite pakkhe. Tabbisayattanti kammavācīsayaṃ saddavisayattaṃ. Bhāvakammesūtīmassa kattariccassa ca paccayavisesanatthe sati sāmatthiyaladdhampayojanaṃ dassetumāha- ‘bhāvakammesū’tiādi. Iminā anena ca visesisattāti sambandho. Kintaṃ visesitanti āha- ‘mānanta tyādīsū’ti. Kintampayojananti payojanaṃ dassetumāha- ‘tyādīna’miccādi. Yadi bhāvakammesu kattari ca tena tena dhānena suttena mānādayo na siyuṃ, kathantaṃ visesitesu mānādīsu paresu kyādayo siyuntīminā sāmatthiyena ( ) (sati) bhāvakammesu kattari ( ) (ti) ca “vattamāneti anti”ccādippabhutikehi (6-1) suttehi yathālābhaṃ bhāvādīsu paccayā hontīti viññāyatīti bhāvo.

In this case, that is, in the case which is intended in the sense of the agent. 'That it has that as its object' means that it has the sphere of the word expressive of the object, that is, the domain of the word. To show the purpose obtained by capacity when this phrase 'in the sense of state and object' and 'in the agent' serves to qualify the suffix, he says: 'in the sense of state and object,' etc. The connection is that it is qualified by this and that. What is qualified? He says: 'in māna, nta, etc.' What is the purpose? To show the purpose, he says: 'of ti, etc.' If, in the sense of state and object and in the agent, māna and so on were not formed by that particular sutta, how then, when māna, etc., are qualified, could kya and so on follow? By this capacity, it is to be understood that in the sense of state and object and in the agent, by suttas such as 'vattamāne ti, anti...' (6-1), suffixes are formed in the senses of state, etc., as is appropriate. This is the meaning.

Natadatthaṃ vacanamāraddhanti bhāvakammesu kattari mānantatyādividhānatthaṃ pāṇiniyehi viya suttantaraṃ nāraddhanti attho. Atha bhāvakammesu kattari ca mānādividhānatthaṃ vacanaṃ nāraddhaṃ dhātuniyamanaṃ dhātuniyamatthaṃ tvassa vattabbanti tañca sāmatthiyāva (labbhateti) dassetumāha- ‘kiriyatthaniyamopi’ccādi. Akammakā dhātuto bhāve kattari ca sakammakā kamme kattari ceti kiriyatthaniyamo yathāvuttena sāmatthiyā labbhateti sambandho. Akammakānaṃ kammavirahā, sakammakānañca satopi bhāvassāppadhānattā akammakā kattari bhāve ca bhavanti na kamme, sakammakā kammasabbhāvā kattari kamme ca bhavanti na bhāvetīdaṃ sāmatthiyaṃ.

The statement is not begun for that purpose, meaning: a separate sutta is not begun for the purpose of prescribing māna, nta, etc., in the sense of state and object and in the agent, as is done by the Pāṇinians. Now, although a statement for the purpose of prescribing māna, etc., in the sense of state and object and in the agent has not been begun, the regulation of roots should be stated for it. And to show that this is obtained by capacity, he says: 'also the regulation of the meaning of the action,' etc. The connection is that the regulation of the meaning of the action—namely, from intransitive roots in the sense of state and in the agent, and from transitive roots in the sense of object and in the agent—is obtained by the aforementioned capacity. This is the capacity: because intransitive roots lack an object, and because for transitive roots, even though the sense of state exists, it is not primary, intransitive roots occur in the agent and in the sense of state, not in the object; transitive roots, due to the presence of an object, occur in the agent and in the object, not in the sense of state.

Kammamapekkhateti [M 0.0242] pacādito kattari paṭhamapurisekavacane kate pacaticcādīsu pacādino pacanādikiriyā odanādikaṃ kammamapekkhate. Kattuttamapekkhateti bhavaticcādīsu bhūādīnaṃ bhavanādikiriyā kattumattamapekkhate.

'It expects an object': When the third person singular in the agentive sense is formed from the root pac, etc., in cases like pacati, the action of cooking, etc., of the root pac, etc., expects an object such as rice. 'It expects only an agent': In cases like bhavati, the action of becoming, etc., of the root bhū, etc., expects only an agent.

20. Ṇiṇā

20. By the suffix ṇya.

Yadatthanti yaṃpayojanaṃ.

‘For what purpose’ means ‘what is the purpose.’

23. Jyā

23. To perish.

Jinantoti “byañjane dīgharassā”ti (1-33) rasso. Sabbattheva yattha kattari paccayo tattha vikaraṇāpi kattariyeva, yattha bhāvakammesu tattha vikaraṇāpi bhāvakammesuyeva,… ekāya pakatiyā kārakabhede(na) paccayassāsambhavato. Tasmā sahābhidhānānaṃ mānādivikaraṇānaṃ kathannāma sahāsambhavaṃ gaccheyyunti vidhīyante.

In the word jinanto, the vowel is shortened by the rule 'A long vowel before a consonant is shortened' (1-33). Everywhere, where the suffix is in the agentive sense, the conjugational sign is also in the agentive sense; where it is in the sense of state and object, the conjugational sign is also in the sense of state and object, because a suffix is impossible from a single base with a difference in kāraka. Therefore, how indeed could there be a co-occurrence of the conjugational signs māna, etc., which are expressed together? Thus they are prescribed.

27. Bhāva

27. State.

Vivacchābhedenāti sakammakākammakavacanicchābhedena. Ubhayatthāti bhāvakammesu. Karīyatīti kattabbo karaṇīyo. “Apavāda visaye ussaggo nābhinivisatī”ti eso ussaggadhammo. Tabbādīnantu kesañcussaggānampi apavādavisaye pavatti hoti bahulādhikārā. Yathā “bhāvakammesu tabbānīyā”ti ussaggo, “vadādīhiyo”ti (5-30) apavādo taṃvisayepi tabbānīyā honti ‘gantabbo gamanīyo’ti veditabboti.

‘By the distinction of intention to speak’ means by the distinction of the desire to express a root as transitive or intransitive. ‘In both cases’ means in the sense of state and object. ‘Karīyati’ means ‘what should be done,’ ‘what is to be done.’ ‘A general rule does not apply in the sphere of a special rule’—this is the nature of a general rule. However, for some general rules such as those for tabba, etc., application occurs even in the sphere of a special rule because of the governing influence of ‘variously.’ For example, ‘tabba and anīya in the sense of state and object’ is a general rule; ‘ya after vad, etc.’ (5-30) is a special rule. Even in the sphere of the latter, tabba and anīya occur, as in gantabbo, gamanīyo. This should be understood.

28. Dhyaṇa

28. Absorption.

Kāriyaṃ “ñi byañjanassā”ti (5-170) ñi.

In kāriyaṃ, the suffix is ṇya by the rule 'ṇya for a consonant' (5-170).

30. Vadā

30. To speak.

Annatotīminā ‘bhoggamañña’ntettha aññaṃ nāma annavatā aññanti atthamāha.

By this word 'annato' (from food), he states that here in the word 'bhoggamañña,' the word 'añña' (other) is so called because it is other than one who possesses food (annavatā).

31. Kīcca

31. Duty.

Kammakaro [M 0.0243] bharitabbatāyeccādinā kiriyāsaddattaṃ bhaccasaddassa dassento saññābhāvamapākaroti. “Saññāyaṃ bharā”ti ca gaṇasuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ, tenāha- ‘saññāyaṃ bharā’tiādi.

By stating that a servant (bhacca) is one who should be supported (bharitabba), etc., he shows that 'bhacca' is a verbal derivative and rejects its being a mere conventional name. And it should be understood that 'bhara in the sense of a name' is a gaṇasutta; therefore, he says: 'bhara in the sense of a name,' etc.

Abharitabbāpiccādinā idaṃ dīpeti duvidhā saññāsaddā keci daccanta vigatāvayavatthā yathā ḍitthādayo, kecidavayavatthānugatāyathā sattapaṇṇādayo, tattha bhariyāsaddassa kammampavattinimittaṃ ‘bharitabbā bhariyā’ti, yathā satta paṇṇāni assāti sambandho pavattinimittaṃ sattapaṇṇasaddassa, etañca pavattinimittaṃ saddanipphattikiriyāyamevopadisīyate, kvacideva tvatthavisese satyasati vā tasmiṃ nimitte saddo vattatī”ti. Okārassāti “yuvaṇṇāname oppaccaye”ti (5-82) kataokārassa.

By the phrase 'even one who should not be supported,' etc., he clarifies this: Conventional terms are of two kinds. Some have their component meaning completely lost, like Ḍittha, etc.; some follow their component meaning, like sattapaṇṇa, etc. Among these, for the word bhariyā (wife), the ground for application is the object: 'a bhariyā is she who is to be supported,' just as the connection 'it has seven leaves' is the ground for application of the word sattapaṇṇa. And this ground for application is taught only in the activity of word formation. But the word applies only in a specific meaning, whether that ground is present or absent. 'Of the o-sound' means of the o-sound that was made by the rule 'o for yu and u when o follows' (5-82).

32. Guhā

32. Cave.

Saddikānanti pāṇiniyakaccāyanādiveyyākaraṇānaṃ. Pesanaṃ sakkārapubbakaṃ vā niyojanaṃ. Kāmacārānuññāti kattumicchato yathiccha manujānanaṃ atisaggonāmāti attho. Nimittabhūtassāti “bhotā kaṭo kattabbo’ccādīsu kaṭakaraṇādino kāraṇabhūtassa.

‘Of the grammarians’ means of the grammarians such as Pāṇini, Kaccāyana, and others. Commanding (pesana) is commissioning or assigning preceded by respect. ‘Permission to act as one wishes’ (kāmacārānuññā) means allowing one who wishes to act to do as they please; this is called ‘granting leave’ (atisagga). ‘Of that which has become the cause’ means of that which has become the cause of making a mat, etc., in such phrases as ‘A mat should be made by you, sir.’

Nanu ca sāmaññena vihitā e(te), tathā ca sati vijjhatthavihi tehi eyyādīhi te bādhīyanticcāha- ‘nace’ccādi. Vidhivisesatte pīti vidhānaṃ vidhi niyojanaṃ kiriyāsu byāpāraṇā, tassa vidhino pesādīnaṃ visesattepi, nāvassantiādi jayādiccabyākhyānaṃ nissāya vuttaṃ, vuttañhi tena “kimatthaṃ pesādīsu kiccasaññino tabbaanīyaṇyatyappaccayā vidhīyante, na sāmaññena bhāvakammesu vihitā, evamete vihitāeva, vo-kāsikāvutti pesvādīññasvatra ca bhavissantīti visesavihitena vidhyādīsu paccayena bādhīyante, vāsarūpavidhinā bhavissanti evañcarahi etaṃ ñāpeti ‘itthīadhikārato parena vāsarūpavidhi nāvassambhavatī’ti kimatthamiccādi codya, vicasasavihiteccādi parihāro, kiccā hi sāmaññena vihitā, pañcamī tu pesādinātthavisesena, ato tena visesavihitena kiccā pesādivisaye bādhīyeranti punabbiyate, vāsarūpeccādinā parihāraṃ vighaṭayati. evaṃ carahiccādinā pesādīsu kiccavidhānassa ñāpakattaṃ dassayati. (jinindabuddhinu 21 sa). Asarūpavidhi [M 0.0244] asarūpāpavādappaccayo vā vikappena bādhako hoti ussaggassāti etaṃ avassaṃ na hotīti ñāpanatthampi na vidhīyateti yojanā. “Vā-sarūpo-nitthiyaṃ”ti (pā, 3-1-94) parasuttaṃ. Dhātvadhikārevihito asarūpo apavādappaccayo ussaggassa bādhako bhavati itthi adhikāre vihitappaccayaṃ vajjayitvāti attho. Heṭṭhā vuttānusārenedaṃ viññātabbaṃ.

But are not these prescribed generally? And that being so, they would be blocked by eyyādi, etc., which are prescribed for the meaning of injunction. To this he says: 'And if not,' etc. 'Even when there is a specific kind of injunction': an injunction (vidhi) is a prescription (vidhāna), a commissioning (niyojana), a directing towards actions. Even when there is a specific kind of that injunction, namely commanding (pesana), etc. This is said relying on the commentary of Jayāditya on 'na avassanti,' etc. For it has been said by him: 'For what purpose are the suffixes tabba, anīya, ṇya, and ya, which are designated as kicca, prescribed in the senses of commanding, etc.? Are they not prescribed generally in the sense of state and object? In that case, they would occur in the sense of commanding, etc., and also elsewhere. They would be blocked in the sense of injunction, etc., by a specifically prescribed suffix. They will occur by the vāsarūpa rule. If so, this then indicates that after the section on the feminine, the vāsarūpa rule does not necessarily apply.' The construction is: it is not prescribed even for the purpose of indicating that this does not necessarily happen, namely that a dissimilar rule—that is, a special rule with a dissimilar suffix—optionally blocks the general rule. 'A dissimilar [suffix] optionally [blocks a general one], but not in the feminine section' (Pā. 3.1.94) is the next sutra. The meaning is: a dissimilar special-rule suffix prescribed in the section on roots blocks a general rule, excluding a suffix prescribed in the section on the feminine. This should be understood according to what has been stated below.

Bhotā khalu kaṭo kātabboccādi pesane. Tvayā kaṭo kātabboti anuññāyaṃ. Pattakāle paramudāharaṇaṃ. Ettha pana kaṭakaraṇe kālārocanamattameva viññāyati, na pesādi. “Sattyarahesveyyādī”ti (6-11) suttaṃ visesavihitaṃ, tenāha- ‘sāmañña vidhānato’ccādi. Sattivisiṭṭheccādinā vuttamatthaṃ vivarati ‘sattī’tiādinā. Kathaṃ sattivisiṭṭhatā kattunoti āha- ‘taṃyogā’ti. Tāya sattiyā yogo taṃyogo. Avassakādhamīṇatāvisiṭṭhe tu kattari kiccānaṃ tadaññesañca bhāvāya visuṃ- suttitaṃ, tena, vuttaṃ ‘āvassakādhamīṇatā visiṭṭheva kattarī’ti. Sabbatthevettha ‘uddhaṃ muhuttato’tiādinā ekekamudāharaṇaṃ kamena dassitaṃ. Bhotā rajjaṃ kātabbanti arahe, bhavatā rajjaṃ kātabbanti attho. Bhavaṃ arahoti pana arahakattuttappakāsanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Evamuparipi. Sabbametaṃ bahulaggahaṇānubhāveneti viññeyyaṃ.

‘A mat should indeed be made by you, sir,’ etc., is an example of commanding. ‘A mat should be made by you’ is an example of permission. The latter is an example of ‘at the proper time.’ Here, however, only the announcement of the time for making the mat is understood, not commanding, etc. The sutta ‘eyyādi in the sense of ability and worthiness’ (6-11) is a special prescription; therefore he says: ‘than the general prescription,’ etc. He explains the meaning stated by ‘distinguished by ability,’ etc., with ‘ability,’ etc. How is the agent distinguished by ability? He says: ‘Through connection with it.’ Connection with that ability is ‘connection with it.’ But for the existence of kicca suffixes and others in the case of an agent distinguished by necessity and indebtedness, it is taught in a separate sutta. Therefore it is said: ‘in an agent distinguished only by necessity and indebtedness.’ Here in every case, each example is shown in sequence with ‘after a moment,’ etc. ‘The kingdom should be administered by you, sir’ is an example of worthiness; the meaning is ‘the kingdom should be administered by your honor.’ But ‘Your honor is worthy’ is said to show that the agent is worthy. The same applies above as well. All this, it should be understood, is by the power of the inclusion of ‘variously.’

33. Katta

33. The doer.

Galecopakoti alopasamāso. Abhimato parehi. Arahādīsu vihitappaccayehīti “sattyarahesveyyādī” (6-11) ca “sīlābhikkhaññāvassakesu ṇī”ti (5-53) ca arahādīsu vihitappaccayehi. Upādānasīlo sikkhāpanasīlo. Muṇḍanaṃ dhammo sabhāvo yesaṃ te muṇḍanadhammā. Vadhuṃ katapariggahaṃ sāviṭṭhāyanā muṇḍayanti etesaṃ kuladhammo.

`Galecopakoti` is a compound without elision. It is approved by others. By the suffixes prescribed for the arahant group and others, as stated in the rules ‘sattyarahesveyyādī’ (6-11) and ‘sīlābhikkhaññāvassakesu ṇī’ (5-53), by which suffixes are prescribed for the arahant group and others. One whose nature is grasping; one whose nature is teaching. Those whose nature or disposition is shaving are the muṇḍanadhammā. The Sāviṭṭhāyanas shave the bride who has been formally accepted; this is their family custom.

35. Āsiṃ

35. I was.

Kāpanāyamāsiṃsā nāmeccāha- ‘appattasse’ccādi. Kiriyā visesakattuvisayāti kiriyāvisesassa yo kattā so visayo [M 0.0245] yassā sā tathā vuttā. Kiriyāvisesakattuvisayattameva phuṭī kattumāha- ‘assā’iccādi. Assā jīvanakiriyāya nandana kiriyāya bhavanakiriyāya vā kattā taṃkiriyaṃ sampādento bhaveyya bhavatūti attho. Jīvatu nandatu bhavatūti āsiṃsāyaṃ payogena jīvaka nandaka bhavakasaddānaṃ taṃsamānatthatā dassitā.

In the sense of kāpanā (desire), the wish is named, saying, ‘of that which is not obtained,’ etc. `Kiriyāvisesakattuvisayā` means that whose sphere is the agent of a specific action. To make clear the very fact of being the sphere of the agent of a specific action, he says, ‘assā,’ etc. The meaning is: may he be, or let him be, the agent of the action of living, the action of delighting, or the action of becoming, accomplishing that action. Through the use of the expression of wishing, ‘may he live, may he delight, may he become,’ the words jīvaka, nandaka, and bhavaka are shown to have the same meaning.

Akenevāsiṃ sanatthassa gamitattāti āsiṃsanā eva attho, tassa akappaccayeneva gamitattā avabodhitattā. Nāsiṃ sanatthassa payogoti āsiṃsanā attho yassa jīvatu nandatu bhavatviccādino saddantarassa, tassa nappayogoti attho.

Because the meaning of wishing is conveyed by the suffix aka alone, the meaning is simply wishing, since it is conveyed and understood by the suffix aka alone. The meaning is that there is no application of another word, such as ‘may he live, may he delight, may he become,’ which has the meaning of wishing.

36. Karā

36. The maker.

Karoti attano phalanti kāraṇaṃ.

That which produces its own fruit is a cause.

37. Hāto

37. Abandoned.

Jahanti udakanti vīhīsu hāyanasaddassa pavattinimittaṃ dasseti. Jahāti bhāve padattheti imināpi saṃvacchare. Bhāveiccassatthamāha ‘padatthe’ti. Nipphattimattaṃ kiriyopādānanti keci.

He shows the reason for the application of the word hāyana in the context of rice plants as ‘they shed water.’ Also, in the context of a year, it means ‘it sheds’ in the sense of bhāva (state), that is, in the meaning of a word. He states the meaning of ‘in the sense of bhāva’ as ‘in the meaning of a word.’ Some say it is merely the accomplishment or the undertaking of an action.

39. Vito

39. Vito.

Nanu ca vitoti pañcamīniddiṭṭhattā ‘vito parasmā ñāiccasmā’ti vattabbaṃ kathaṃ vipubbāti vuttanti āha- ‘vito paro’iccādi. Vipubbo yassaso vipubbo. Visaddato dhātumhi parabhūte sati visaddo pubbo nāma hotīti attho.

But since vito is indicated in the ablative case, should it not be said, ‘from ñā, etc., which is after vito’? How then is vipubbā said? He says: ‘after vito,’ etc. `Vipubbo` means that which has vi as its prefix. The meaning is: when the root is subsequent to the word vi, then the word vi is indeed prior.

40. Kasmā

40. Why?

Sabbaṃ jānāti, kālaṃ jānātīti viggaho.

He knows all; he knows the time—this is the analysis.

41. Kvaca

41. Sometimes.

Nāmajātiguṇakiriyā dabbasambandhato pañcavidhattepi kammassa kriyatthassāvadhirayamupādinnoti kriyatthasambandhā kiriyākammasseha gahaṇaṃ. Tañca nibbattivikatipattibhedena tividhaṃ, tividhassāpyetassa visesānupānato gahaṇanti kamenudāharanto āha- ‘karakaraṇe’iccādi.

Although the object is fivefold through its connection with name, genus, quality, action, and substance, here the object of an action is taken in relation to the purpose of the action, as this is taken as the limit. And that is threefold, divided into production, alteration, and attainment. Since the distinctions of even these three are included, illustrating this in sequence, he says: ‘karakaraṇe,’ etc.

Lokavidūtiādidassanato [M 0.0246] kvaciggahaṇe payojanaṃ vattumāha- ‘kammato’ccādi. Nanu ca kvaciggahaṇeneva ‘ādiccaṃ passati’ccādopi (nivatti) vattuṃ sakkā kasmā ‘bahulādhikārā’ti vuttanti āha ‘tene’ccādi. Tenāti yena kvaciggahaṇaṃ kutociyevāti dassanatthaṃ kataṃ tenāti attho. Tenāti vā kvaciggahaṇena. Atha ādiccaṃ passaticcādo viya kammakarādīsupi nivattimadassetvā ‘kvacīti kiṃ kammakaro’ti kasmā vuttanti āha- ‘yajjeva’miccādi.

To state the purpose of taking kvaci, from the example of lokavidū, etc., he says, ‘kammato,’ etc. But since even with the taking of kvaci, it is possible to state the non-application in cases like ‘he sees the sun,’ etc., why is it said ‘due to the extensive scope’? He says, ‘tena,’ etc. `Tena` means: by that by which the taking of kvaci was done to show that it is from anywhere whatsoever; this is the meaning. Or, `tena` means by the taking of kvaci. Then, without showing the non-application in cases like kammakaro, etc., as in ‘he sees the sun,’ etc., why is it said, ‘kvaci—what about kammakaro?’ He says, ‘yajjevaṃ,’ etc.

Tassāti bahulavacanassa, mahādhikārattāti mahāvisayattā. Kutociyevāti kutoci dhātutoyeva. Atheha kasmā na hoti devadatto sayati dāttena lunāti sunakhānaṃ dadāti nagarā apeti thāliyaṃ pacati mātu saratī”ti, sabbamevedaṃ kiriyā (yā) bhisambandhīyatīti yadipevaṃ, tathāpi kammatteneva yaṃ vattu micchitaṃ na kārakantarattena nāpi sambandhabhāvena, tasseva kammasaddena gahaṇaṃ kammavacanasāmatthiyā, aññathā syāditocceva vadeyya kiṃ kammāti vacanenāti.

`Tassa` refers to the frequent usage; `mahādhikārattā` means due to its vast scope. `Kutociyeva` means from any root whatsoever. Then why does it not occur here: ‘Devadatta sleeps,’ ‘he cuts with a sickle,’ ‘he gives to the dogs,’ ‘he departs from the city,’ ‘he cooks in a pot,’ ‘he remembers his mother’? Even if all these are indeed connected with an action, nevertheless, that which is intended to be expressed specifically as the object, and not as another grammatical factor nor by way of a mere connection, that alone is taken by the word kamma due to the power of the word kamma. Otherwise, one would just say ‘from syādi, etc.’; what is the use of the word kamma?

42. Gamā

42. Villages.

Vedanti ettha atthamāha vittinti, tuṭṭhinti attho.

Here, he states the meaning of vedanti as vitti, meaning tuṭṭhi (satisfaction).

43. Samā

43. Equal.

Tañceti upamānassa parāmāso. Bhedena vivaraṇanti samānādīhīti avatvā bhedena vivaraṇaṃ. Tulyatāyupalabbhamānassa sadisādisaddavacanīyattā avayavatthānugamenāttano-bhidheyye sadisādisaddānampavatti veditabbā.

`Tañca` is a reference to the standard of comparison. Explaining by division means explaining by division without saying ‘by samāna, etc.’ Because what is found to be similar can be expressed by words like sadisa, etc., the application of words like sadisa, etc., to their own referents should be understood by following the analysis of the parts.

44. Bhāva

44. Being.

Kārakaṃ sādhakaṃ nibbattakanti anatthantaraṃ. Karoti kiriyaṃ nibbatteti nimittabhāvenāti kārakaṃ. Kattādīnaṃ kiriyānimittattantu sayameva ‘tattha kattā’tiādinā bhedena pakāsayissati. Kiriyānimittaṃ… nibbattakesu kattādīsu chasupi ruḷhattā tenettha kattāvāttappadhāno, karaṇādayopyappadhānā kārakabyapadeso labbhante… [M 0.0247] aññathā kārakasaddena tesaṃ gahaṇaṃ na siyāti. Kimidaṃ kārakantyāha- ‘sattikāraka’nti. Evaṃ carahi dabbādīnaṃ kathaṃ kārakattamiccāha- ‘tadadhikaraṇā’tiādi. Tassā sattiyā ādhārā nissayāti attho, puṃ napuṃsake adhikaraṇasaddo. Tesu dabbā dīsu tiṭṭhatīti tatraṭṭhā, satti. Tassā bhāvo tatraṭṭhatā, tāya. Atha dabbādīnaṃ mukhyato kārakatte sati kimāyātantyāha ‘yadi’ccādi.

Kāraka (grammatical factor), sādhaka (accomplisher), and nibbattaka (producer) are not different in meaning. That which performs or produces an action by being a cause is a kāraka. The fact that the agent and others are causes of an action, he himself will explain by distinguishing them with ‘there, the agent,’ etc. Since the six producers, the agent and others, are established by usage as causes of an action, here the agent is primary, while the instrument and others, being secondary, also obtain the designation kāraka. Otherwise, they would not be included by the term kāraka. What is this kāraka? He says: ‘power-kāraka.’ If so, then how is the kāraka-ness of substances, etc., to be understood? He says: ‘that which has it as its basis,’ etc. The meaning is: they are the supports, the reliance of that power. The word adhikaraṇa (locus) is masculine and neuter. That which stands in those substances, etc., is ‘that which stands there,’ namely, the power. Its state is ‘the state of standing there’; by that. Now, if substances, etc., are primarily kārakas, what follows? He says: ‘if,’ etc.

Tesanti kattādikārakānaṃ. Aññamaññabyāvuttarūpattāti aññamaññato byāvuttaṃ nivattaṃ rūpaṃ karaṇādisabhāvo yesaṃ kattādi kārakānaṃ te tathā vuttā, tesaṃ bhāvo tattaṃ tasmā. Karaṇa rūpanti karaṇaṃ rūpaṃ sabhāvo yassa adhikaraṇassa taṃ tathā vuttaṃ. Evañcasatiko dosoccāha ‘tathā ce’ccādi. Kenaci sukarattena sappadhānattavacanicchāyaṃ ‘thālī pacatī’ti bhavati. Tatrevukkaṃsavaca nicchāyaṃ ‘thāliyā pacatī’ti.

`Tesaṃ` refers to the agent and other kārakas. Because of their mutually distinct nature—that is, the agent and other kārakas, whose nature, the disposition of the instrument, etc., is distinct and separate from one another, are said to be such; the state of being so is that, therefore. `Karaṇarūpaṃ` means that locus whose nature is the instrument is said to be such. And if this is so, what is the fault? He says, ‘if so,’ etc. Due to some ease and the desire to state the principal thing, it becomes ‘the pot cooks.’ In that very case, with the desire to state excellence, it becomes ‘he cooks with the pot.’

Evañcakatvāti nipātasamudāyo-yaṃ hetvattho. Tasmāti attho. Kattā nimittanti sambandho. Kattuṭṭhakiriyānimittassa kattuno udāharaṇaṃ ‘hasati naccatī’ti. Tadattheti tāya kammasamavāyiniyā pacanādikiriyāya atthe adhissayanādayo pavattento kiriyāya nimittanti sambandho. Evamuparipi.

`Evañcakatvā` is a collection of particles in the sense of cause. The meaning is ‘therefore.’ The agent is the cause—this is the connection. An example of the agent as the cause of an action arising from the agent is ‘he laughs, he dances.’ In that meaning: in the meaning of that action, such as cooking, etc., which inheres in the object, one who brings about actions such as placing the pot on the fire, etc., is the cause of the action—this is the connection. And similarly in the following cases.

Odanaṃ pacati devadattoti kammaṭṭhakiriyāya nimittabhūtassa kattuno udāharaṇaṃ. Bhājanasaṅkharaṇamadhissayanaṃ. Ādisaddena taṇḍulavapanaindhanāpaharaṇādayo gayhanti. Dvidhāpattiyanti rukkhādīnaṃ dvidhā pavattiyaṃ.

‘Devadatta cooks rice’ is an example of the agent who is the cause of an action residing in the object. Preparing the vessel and placing it on the fire. By the word ādi (etc.), putting in the rice grains, fetching firewood, and so on, are included. `Dvidhāpattiyaṃ` means in the twofold occurrence of trees, etc.

Byāpaneti sambandhe. Giradhātuto appaccaye- “eonama vaṇṇe”ti (137) sutte ‘avaṇṇeti yogavibhāgato gakāre ikārassa attaṃ hotīti dassetumāha- ‘avaṇṇeti yogavibhāgā attaṃ issā’ti. Aññathāpi paṭipādetumāha- ‘essa vā’tiādi. Essāti “lahussupanthassā”ti (5-87) kataessa. Sakalenāti ‘eonama vaṇṇe”ti sakalena suttena. Purīti nipāto.

In connection with `byāpane` (spreading). From the root gir with the suffix a—in the rule ‘eonama vaṇṇe’ (137), to show that in avaṇṇeti, by splitting the rule, the i of the letter ga becomes a, he says: ‘in avaṇṇeti, by splitting the rule, the i becomes a.’ To explain it differently, he says: ‘or essa,’ etc. `Essā` means the essa made by the rule ‘lahussupanthassā’ (5-87). `Sakalena` means with the entire rule ‘eonama vaṇṇe.’ `Purī` is a particle.

Īsakkaroti [M 0.0248] bindulopo, dvittaṃ, sāmaññena vidhānatoti paresaṃ visesavidhānasabbhāvamāha. Gaṇikālayaṃ gaṇikānaṃ gehaṃ. Nepathyamākappo. Dattoladdhoti paccayassa kammasādhanattaṃ dīpetuṃvuttaṃ. Vināliṅgavacanehi pāṭipadikatthaṃ niddisituṃ na sakkāti bhāveti sabbaliṅgasaṅkhyāsambandhayoggapāṭipadikatthasāmaññe paccayanimittattena gahitepi sāmaññe caritatthattā liṅgavacanaṃ nappadhānanti iṭṭhiāvudhantī itthi napuṃsakebhāve, pākāti bahuvacanepi bhāve bhavati eva.

By the general provision, 'slight elision of the dot, doubling,' he states the existence of a special provision for others. 'Gaṇikālayaṃ' means the house of courtesans. 'Nepathya' means adornment. 'Datta' (given) and 'laddha' (obtained) are stated to indicate that the suffix has the sense of the object. He considers that the meaning of the nominal stem cannot be specified without gender and number; for although the general meaning of the nominal stem, which is suitable for connection with all genders and numbers, is taken as the cause for the suffix, gender and number are not primary, since its purpose is fulfilled in that generality. Thus, 'iṭṭhi' (woman) and 'āvudha' (weapon) exist in the feminine and neuter states respectively; 'pākā' occurs even in the plural in the sense of state.

45. Dādhā

45. The Tusk

Sapādīhi apādīhicāti pādisahitehi pādirahitehi ca dādhāhi.

“With those having feet and with those without feet”: that is, by the tusks of those endowed with feet and those devoid of feet.

46. Vamā

46. Vomit

Sāpānadoṇiyanti sārameyānaṃ bhuñjanakaambaṇe. Ṭhitasupāna vamathuviyāti pavattasunakhacchaddanaṃ viya.

“In a dog’s trough”: in a vessel for dogs to eat from. “Like the vomit of a standing dog”: like the spread-out vomit of a dog.

47. Kvi

47. The Suffix Kvi

Yathādassananti ācikkhatīti yojanā. Tena kutoci dhātutoti. Gaṇhantīti gaha=upādāneccassa. Salākāsaddassa salākanti. Sabhāsaiccassa antabyañjanalope sabhāpakatito “itthi yamatvā”ti (3-26) āppaccayo. Pabhātīti ā=dittiyamiccassa.

“As seen” means “he explains”; this is the construction. Therefore, “from some root.” “They take”: this is from the root 'gah' in the sense of “grasping.” “Of the word salākā”: this means 'salākā'. Of the word 'sabhāsa', with the elision of the final consonant, it is from the base 'sabhā'; the suffix 'ā' is added according to the rule “in the feminine, after yam, etc.” (3-26). “It shines”: this is from the root 'ā' in the sense of “shining.”

48. Ano

48. The Suffix Ano

Calanādīnaṃ sīlādīsu nipphādanatthaṃ visuṃ suttitaṃ parehi, idha pana bahulaṃ vacanenevāti dassetumāha- ‘calanādīsū’tiādi.

For the purpose of forming words denoting movement and so on in the sense of habit and so on, a separate rule has been formulated by others. But here, to show that this is accomplished simply by the force of the general statement, he says: “in movement, etc.” and so on.

49. Itthi

49. The Feminine

Klikayakiccatra kakārabahuttā kakārāti bahuvacanaṃ. Titikkhā iccādo titikkhanamiccādinā viggaho “itthiyamatvā” (3-26). Apari paṭhitoti dhātupāṭhe aparipaṭhito. Pāṇivisesoti sattaviseso. Iminā ca “yathākathañci nipphatti, ruḷhiyā atthanicchayo”ti dasseti.

In the action of 'klikaya', because of the abundance of the letter 'ka', the plural “the letters ka” is used. In the case of 'titikkhā' and so on, the analysis is “endurance,” etc., formed according to the rule “in the feminine, after yam, etc.” (3-26). “Not listed”: not recited in the List of Roots (Dhātupāṭha). “A particular kind of living being”: a particular kind of creature. And by this he shows: “However the derivation may be, the determination of the meaning is by convention.”

Āsiṃ [M 0.0249] sāyaṃ gammamānāyaṃ saññāvisaye dhātūhi tippaccayo kiccappaccayo ca yathā siyāti “tikiccāsiṭṭhe”ti (7-2-3) suttitaṃ kaccāyanena. Tamiha sāmaññena vidhānāva siddhanti nirūpayitumāha- ‘kaccāyanena pane’ccādi. Tabba anīyaṇya teyya riccappaccayānaṃ “te kiccā”ti (7-1-22) kiccasaññaṃ vidhāya sesānaṃ “aññekitī”ti (7-1-23) kitsaññā katā kaccāyanena. Tenāha- ‘kita sañño’ti.

So that the suffix 'ti' and the 'kicca' suffixes may be applied to roots in the sense of blessing, in the evening, when being understood, and in the sphere of designation, it has been formulated by Kaccāyana in the rule “In blessing, ti and kicca” (7-2-3). To investigate how that is established here by a general injunction, he says: “But by Kaccāyana,” etc. Having enjoined the designation 'kicca' for the suffixes 'tabba', 'anīya', 'ṇya', 'teyya', and 'ricca' by the rule “Those are kicca” (7-1-22), the designation 'kit' has been made for the remaining ones by Kaccāyana with the rule “The others are kit” (7-1-23). Therefore he says: “designated as kit.”

Tabbādippaccayo ca vihitoti sakiyavohārenāha. Sakiya satthe avuttadosaṃ suttadosaṃ pariharitvā vakkhamānanayena yutyabhāvā tathā vidhāne ayuttataṃ dassento ‘nacāsiṃ sāya’miccādimāha. Guhanaṃ, rujanaṃ, modananti viggaho. Sayanaṃ vā seyyā. Vajadhātuno vassa bakārena bhavitabbaṃ, so kathaṃ yakāre parabhūte asatīti āha- ‘cavaggabayañātiyogavibhāgā vassa bo’ti.

He speaks in his own terminology, saying: “And the suffixes beginning with tabba have been enjoined.” Avoiding the fault of not stating it in his own treatise, and showing the unsuitability of such an injunction due to the lack of justification according to the method to be explained, he says: “na ca āsiṃ sāyaṃ,” etc. The analysis is: “concealing,” “afflicting,” “rejoicing.” 'Seyyā' means “a bed” or “lying down.” From the root 'vaj', 'va' should become 'ba'. How can this not happen when 'ya' follows? He says: “By split-application of the rule concerning 'cavagga', 'ba', and 'ya', 'va' becomes 'ba'.”

51. Karā

51. The Suffix Karā

Ririyappaccaye ādirakārassa anubandhattā āha- ‘antasarādi lopo’ti.

In the case of the suffix 'ririya', because the initial 'ra' is an indicatory letter, he says: “elision of the final vowel and the beginning of the suffix.”

52. Iki

52. The Suffix Iki

Atha sarūpeccetāvati vutte- ‘kiriyatthassa sarūpe’ti kathaṃ viññāyaticcāha- ‘kiriyatthā’ticcādi. Nanu ca lo-yaṃ kattari vidhīya mānokathamettha siyātyāha- ‘akattaripi’ccādi. Abhimato kaccāyanassa. Paṭipādayitumāha- ‘tatthā’tiādi. Karaṇaṃ uccāraṇaṃ, assa karoti samāsavākyaṃ. Na hi eva dīhi kāro vihitoti akkhare heva kārassa vihitattā akkharasamudāyato na pappotīti bhāvo. Atha ceti matappadāne. Evādisaddavācakā evakārādayo sādhavoti atha matanti attho.

Now, when this much has been said, “in its own form,” how is it to be understood as “in its own form which has the meaning of an action”? He says: “having the meaning of an action,” and so on. But is not this suffix 'lo' enjoined in the sense of the agent? How then can it occur here? He says: “even when not in the sense of the agent,” and so on. This is approved by Kaccāyana. To establish this, he says: “there,” and so on. 'Karaṇaṃ' means “utterance”; 'assa karoti' is the compound phrase. The suffix 'kāra' is not enjoined after words like 'eva' and 'ādi'. Since 'kāra' is enjoined only after a single letter, it is not obtained after a collection of letters; this is the meaning. The words 'atha ca' are used to present another opinion. The meaning is: “Another opinion is that words such as 'evakāra', which denote words like 'eva', are valid.”

Tatthāti tathā abhimate tasmiṃ. Niyamahetuno abhāvāti akkhareheva kārappaccayo vidheyyo na pana evādīhiccassa niyamassa yo hetu tassa hetuno abhāvā.

“There” means in that which is so approved. “Due to the absence of a restrictive cause” means: because of the absence of a cause for the restriction that the suffix 'kāra' should be enjoined only after single letters and not after words like 'eva'.

53. Sīla

53. Habit

Kimidasīlamiccāha- [M 0.0250] ‘sīlampakatisabhāvo’ti. Tañca sīlamanumānena viññāyaticcāha- ‘tañce’ccādi. Kiriyāvisayarucivisesānumitanti uṇhabhojanasaṅkhātā kiriyā visayo yassa so (kiriyā) visayo ruciviseso, tena anumitanti attho. Kimidamābhikkhaññanti āha- ‘ābhikkhañña’miccādi. Punappunabhāvo ponopuññaṃ. Āse vā tapparatāti tamevābhikkhaññaṃ pariyāyehi phuṭīkaroti.
