What is this “habit”? He says: “Habit is one’s natural disposition.” And that this habit is known by inference, he says: “And that…” etc. “Inferred from a particular inclination towards the object of an action” means: it is inferred from that particular inclination whose object is an action, such as eating hot food; this is the meaning. What is this “repetition”? He says: “Repetition,” etc. 'Ponopuññaṃ' is the state of occurring again and again. “Or devotion to that” clarifies that very repetition by way of synonyms.

Yajjevanti yadi ābhikkhaññaṃ tappato vuccate. Tassīlyamidaṃ hotīti iminā- ‘sīlābhikkhaññādi”sutte sīlasaddenevābhikkhaññassa gahitattaṃ dīpeti. Aññathāpi sīlato aññamevābhikkhaññanti dassetumāha- ‘yasmiṃ dese’tiādi.

'Yajjevaṃ' means: if repetition is spoken of as devotion to that. By this, “this is its habit,” he indicates that in the rule “in the sense of habit, repetition, etc.,” repetition is included by the word “habit” itself. To show that repetition is also something other than habit, he says: “in whatever country,” etc.

Gammamāneti patīyamāne. Patīti ca atthappakaraṇasaddantarādīhi. Abhimatoti pāṇiniyehi abhimato. Āvassakaggahaṇāyeva siddhoti vuttaṃ kathametthāvassambhāvo patīyati ccāha- ‘tañcā’tiādi.

“Being understood” means being cognized. And cognition arises from meaning, context, other words, and so on. “Approved” means approved by the Pāṇinīyas. It has been said: “It is established simply by the inclusion of the sense of necessity.” How, then, is the state of necessity understood here? He says: “And that…” etc.

Yogavibhāgāti ‘ṇī’ti yoga vibhāgā. Sādhuṃ karoti, brahmaṃ vadati, asaddhaṃ bhuñjati, paṇḍitamattānaṃ maññatīti viggaho. Sādhunti kiriyāvisesanaṃ. Assaddhabhojīti vate. Vatañca bhojane atthitāyaṃ saddhaassaddhabhojanavisayāyaṃ pavattiyaṃ yadi bhuñjati assaddhameva bhuñjati na saddhanti satthe vuttaniyamo, assaddhaṃ bhuñjati evāti nottarapadāvadhāraṇaṃ… evañhi viññāyamāne yadevāssaddhaṃ na bhuñjati tadeva vatalopo siyāti atthitāya (bhojanākaṅkhitattā) yathecchaṃ sāmaññena bhojane pavattiyaṃ mattāyaṃ asaddhabhojanaṃ satthavihitamupalabhamānassa saddhato nivattitvā visese hi saddhe pavattiniyamo vatamuccate, niyamocātraduvidho sambhavati-asaddhaṃ bhūñjati eva, athaddhamo bhuñjatīti vā, tatrādime niyame yadevā saddhaṃ na bhuñjati tadevavata loposiyā (ra-3-228) kātantapañjikā. Aññathāpi paṭipādayitumāha- ‘ghaṇantādīhi’ccādi.

“By split-application of the rule”: this is from the split-application of the rule for 'ṇī'. The analysis is: “he acts well,” “he recites the Veda,” “he eats faithlessly,” “he considers himself a scholar.” 'Sādhuṃ' is an adverb. The word 'assaddhabhojī' is in the sense of a vow. And a vow, in the context of eating, is a rule stated in the treatises that if one eats, one eats only faithlessly, not with faith. Thus, it is not an exclusive determination of the final member of the compound, as in “he eats only what is faithless.” For if it were understood in this way, there would be a breach of the vow whenever he does not eat something that is faithless. To establish it in another way, he says: “from 'ghaṇanta', etc.”

54. Thāva

54. Thāva

Sayameva attanāeva. Kammakattarīti ubhayatthāpi kammakattari paccayo bahulādhikārāti adhippāyo. Ettha pana ekopi padattho kammañca [M 0.0251] hoti kattāca kārakasattibhedato. Yathā ‘pīyamānaṃ madhu madayatī’ti ekassāpi sattibhedā kammattaṃ kattuttaṃ, tathā trāpīti viññeyyaṃ. Yo paraṃ bhañjati tatthapi siyā sāmaññavidhānatoti āha- ‘nipātanassi’ccādi. Dosandhakāraṃ bhindatīti dosandhakārabhiduro.

By oneself indeed, by oneself alone. 'Kammakattari' means: in both cases, the suffix is in the reflexive agent sense because of the governing rule of 'bahula' (variously); this is the intention. Here, however, even a single word's meaning can be both object and agent due to the distinction in the power of the case-role. Just as in 'the honey being drunk intoxicates,' for a single thing there is both object-ness and agent-ness due to a distinction in power, so too here it should be understood. Where one breaks another, there too it could be by a general rule; thus he said: 'nipātanassa,' etc. 'He who shatters the darkness of hatred' is a 'dosandhakārabhiduro'.

55. Katta

55. Katta

Bhūtasaddenetthādhippetatthamupadassetumāha- ‘bhūtamatīta’miccādi. Aññathāti yadyatikkantavacano na siyāti attho.

To show the intended meaning here by the word 'bhūta,' he says: 'bhūta means past,' etc. 'Otherwise' means: if there were not a word expressing the past; this is the meaning.

Nanucātretaretaranissayadoso pasajjate, satī hi bhūtādhikāretto vidhīyate, sati ca tte bhūtasaddassa nipphattīti phuṭo yevitaretaranissayadosoti. Nesadoso, saṅketāti byatto saddatthasambandho cirakālappavatto, nāssa kiñci asādhuttaṃ, atikkante cāssa vutti saddasattisabhāvato veditabbā. Ktavantā dayopi carahi saddasattisabhāvato bhūteeva bhavissantīti na vattabbaṃ. Bhūtasaddo-yamatikkantatthe pasiddho ktavantādayotvappasiddhā, ato tena pasiddhatthenāppasiddhānamanvākhyānaṃ karīyatīti. Bhūteti cāyaṃ pakativisesanaṃ vā siyā ‘bhūtatthe vattamānā’ti, paccayattha visesanaṃ vā’bhūte kattarī’ti, tatra kassidaṃ visesananti āhabhūteti pakativisesana’nti. Kutoccāha- ‘sambandhassa ce’tyādi. Atha paccayatthavisesane ko dosoccāha- ‘paccayatthavisesane hi’ccādi. Paccayatthassa kattuno anabhikkantattā ayanti payogo nopapajjateti bhāvo. Abhidheyyeti iminā payojanādiṃ byavacchindati.

But does not the fault of mutual dependence arise here? For the suffix '-ta' is prescribed by the governing rule 'bhūte' (in the past), and when there is the suffix '-ta', the word 'bhūta' itself is formed. Thus the fault of mutual dependence is indeed obvious. This is not a fault. The relationship between word and meaning, established by convention, is manifest, has been current for a long time, and there is nothing incorrect about it. And its occurrence in the past should be known from the inherent power of the word. Then it should not be said that even the suffixes '-tavant' and others would be only in the past due to the inherent power of the word. This word 'bhūta' is well-known in the sense of 'past,' whereas '-tavant' and others are not well-known. Therefore, the explanation of the not well-known is made by means of that which is well-known. And this 'bhūte' could be a qualifier of the base, meaning 'occurring in the sense of the past,' or a qualifier of the suffix's meaning, meaning 'in a past agent.' Regarding which of these it qualifies, he says: ''bhūte' is a qualifier of the base.' Why? He says: 'sambandhassa ce,' etc. But if it were a qualifier of the suffix's meaning, what would be the fault? He says: 'paccayatthavisesane hi,' etc. Because the agent, which is the meaning of the suffix, is not past, this usage is not tenable; this is the sense. By 'what is denoted' (abhidheyya), he excludes purpose and so on.

56. Kto

56. Kto

Kamme guṇībhūtattāti kamme sati bhāvassāppadhānattā. “Guṇamukhyesu mukhyeyeva kāriyasampaccayo”ti mukhye kammeyeva paccayo, na tu bhāve tassetthāppadhānattā.

'Because of being subordinate in the sense of object (kamma)' means: because when there is an object, the state (bhāva) is not primary. 'Among subordinate and primary things, the effect pertains only to the primary.' Thus the suffix is only in the sense of the primary object, not in the sense of the state, because the latter is subordinate here.

57. Katta

57. Katta

Nanucārambheti [M 0.0252] vuttaṃ- ‘kiriyārambhe’ti kathanti āha- ‘soce’ccādi. So ca ārambho. Kiriyāyeva ārambhokiriyārambho tasmiṃ. Kiriyārambheti sāmaññena vuttattā kiriyatthavisesanaṃ vā etaṃsiyā paccayatthavisesanaṃ vā ubhayathāpi na dosoti dassetumāha- ‘kiriyatthavisesanaṃ ceta’ntiādi. Paccayatthavisesanapakkhepi sāmatthiyā ārambhe kiriyatthassāpi pavattī hotīti dassetumāha- ‘kiriyatthassāpi’ccādi. Sāmatthiyaṃ dasseti ‘sāmatthiyampanā’tiādinā. Anantarasuttena yo vihito kto, sopi sāmaññena vacanato bhāvakammesu ārambhepi hotīti yojanā. Sāmaññena vacanatoti “kto bhāvakammesū”ti (5-56) sāmaññena vacanato. Bhāvakammesuceti evaṃ na vuttanti ‘yathāpattañce’ti vadatā vuttikārenevaṃ na vuttanti attho.

But is it not stated 'ārambhe' (in inception)? How then 'kiriyārambhe' (in the inception of an action)? He says: 'so ca,' etc. And that is the inception. The inception of an action is just the action's inception; in that. Because 'in the inception of an action' is stated generally, it could be a qualifier of the action's meaning or a qualifier of the suffix's meaning. To show that in either case there is no fault, he says: 'and this is a qualifier of the action's meaning,' etc. To show that even in the alternative where it qualifies the suffix's meaning, the occurrence of the action's meaning is also present in the inception due to capacity, he says: 'of the action's meaning also,' etc. He shows the capacity with 'sāmatthiyam pana,' etc. The construction is: the suffix '-ta' which is prescribed by the immediately following rule also occurs in the inception in the sense of state and object, because of the general statement. 'Because of the general statement' means: because it is stated generally as 'the suffix -ta in the sense of state and object' (Kaccāyana 5.56). The meaning is: by saying 'and according to what is obtained,' the commentator indicates that it is not stated as 'in state and object also'.

Kasmā evaṃ na vuttanti āha- ‘pubbasmiṃ viyā’ti ādi. Aniyamuppatti saññāya sati ñāpananti tannisedhetumāha- ‘punabbacanato’tiādi. Māsaṅkīti kammani, tenevuppattīti paṭhamā. Evaṃ maññate “bhāvakamma gahaṇaṃ cākārenānukaḍḍhiya ‘bhāvakammesu cā’tyanena ktevidhīya māne idamāsaṅkīyate ‘pubbeneva sāmaññena siddhe punabbacanā punabbacanaṃ kiriyatthāniyamena ttassuppattī’ti, yathāpattañceti hyuccamāne cakārena yathāpattampi kāriyamanuññāyateti pubbeneva vacanena bhāvakammesvārambhepi yathāpatto kto bhavatīti viññāyate”ti. Evañcarahi bhāvakammesvārambhepi pubbeneva siddhattā “kattariārambhe”icceva vucceyya kiṃ cakārene ccāsaṅkiyāha- ‘padānamavadhāraṇa phalattā’ccādi.

Why is it not said thus? He says: 'as in the previous,' etc. To deny the notion that this indicates an unrestricted occurrence, he says: 'because of the repetition,' etc. 'Do not suspect' is the object; 'its arising by that' is the subject. He thinks thus: 'When the suffix '-ta' is being prescribed by 'and in state and object,' drawing in the taking up of 'state' and 'object' with the particle 'ca,' this doubt is suspected: "Since it is already established by the previous general rule, the repetition is for the purpose of the unrestricted arising of the suffix '-ta' for the action's meaning." For when 'and according to what is obtained' is said, what is obtained is also permitted by the particle 'ca.' Thus it is understood that by the previous statement itself, the suffix '-ta' that is obtained occurs even in the inception in the sense of state and object.' If so, then since it is already established by the previous rule even in the inception in the sense of state and object, it should just be said 'in the inception in the sense of agent.' Why the particle 'ca'?' Having suspected this, he says: 'because words have determination as their result,' etc.

Nanucādibhūto kiriyākkhaṇo ārambho nāma, bahūhi kiriyākkhaṇehi kaṭe parisamatteyeva bhūto kālo ca bhavatīti kiriyāphalassāparinipphannattā vattamānova kāloti tatrakto na pappoticcāsaṅkiyāha- ‘kiriyāphalassi’ccādi. Kaṭekadesassāpi kaṭattā [M 0.0253] tassa ca nibbattattā bhūtavacanicchāti bhāvo. Nanucādisūte kiriyākkhaṇakāle kaṭo nābhinibbatto, kaṭakāraṇabhūtā bīraṇāva hi tadā santi, na ca tadavatthā te eva kaṭoti kathaṃ ‘pakato kaṭo’ti bhūtakālena pakatasaddena kaṭasaddasamānādhikaraṇattamiccāha- ‘ādibhūtene’ccādi. Tattha tasmiṃ visese. Pakattuṃ ārabhi, pakattuṃ ārabhīyittha, pasottuṃ ārabhi, pasottuṃ ārabhananti atthe tto.

But is not the initial moment of action what is called 'inception' (ārambha)? And the past tense occurs only when the mat is completed by many moments of action. Because the fruit of the action is not yet accomplished, it is still the present time, and therefore the suffix '-ta' is not obtained. Suspecting this, he says: 'of the fruit of the action,' etc. The sense is: because even a part of the mat is a mat, and because it has been produced, the use of a word for the past is desired. But at the time of the initial moment of action in weaving, the mat is not yet produced. For at that time there are only the reeds which are the cause of the mat, and they in that state are not the mat. So how can there be co-referentiality of the word 'kaṭa' with the word 'pakata' (begun) in the past tense, as in 'pakato kaṭo' (the mat is begun)? He says: 'by the initial,' etc. There, in that specific case, the suffix '-ta' is used in the sense of: 'he began to make,' 'it was begun to be made,' 'he began to weave,' or 'it was begun to be woven.'

58. Ṭhāsa

58. Ṭhāsa

Anārambhatthaṃvacananti ārambhe pubbeneva siddhattā. Apādinopisilisassa sakammakattā- ‘yebhuyyenā’ti vuttaṃ. Sakammakatthanti vatvā sakammattamesaṃ pādiyoge sati hotīti dassetumāha- ‘pādisahitā’ccādi. Khaṭopikā mañco.

'A statement for the meaning of non-initiation' is so called because for initiation, it is already established by the previous rule. Even for the root `slis` without a prefix, due to its nature, it is said, 'for the most part.' Having stated that they are transitive, to show that their transitivity occurs when there is a connection with a prefix, he says: 'accompanied by a prefix,' etc. A khaṭopikā is a couch.

59. Gama

59. Gama

Avivacchitakammo cehākammakoti kathayamāha- ‘avijjamāne’ccādi. Yātavanto yātā, yānaṃ yātaṃ. Ayoyitthāti yā to. Kto na vidhātabbo pāṇiniyehi viya. Kāraṇasāmaggiyaṃ bhūtāyanti sassādihetubhūtasamiddhiyaṃ bhūtāyaṃ. Sā ca bhūtā yevātīminā kāraṇasāmaggiyā atītakālikattamāha.

If the object is not intended to be expressed, it is intransitive. Saying this, he states: 'when it is non-existent,' etc. Those who have gone are 'the gone'; a vehicle is 'what has gone.' ‘Ayoyitthā’ means ‘she who has gone.’ The suffix kta should not be prescribed as it is by the Pāṇinians. ‘In the assemblage of causes that has occurred’ means in the fulfillment that has become the cause of grain, etc., that has occurred. And by this, he states the past-time nature of the assemblage of causes, since it has indeed occurred.

60. Āhā

60. Āha

Ādhāreceti anuvuttiyā ettha cakārato ‘yathāpattañce’ti sambandhā vuttanti seso. Evaṃ na kutoci apakassanaṃ siyāti evamādhārādike anuvattamāne sati kutoci ādhārādito apakassanaṃ visuṃ karaṇaṃ na siyāti attho. Tathā sati heṭṭhā suttenekayogameva kareyyāti adhippāyo. Bhāvakammesūti sambajjhateti yojanā.

Here, by the continuation of 'in the locative,' and from the word 'ca,' the connections are stated as 'and as is appropriate'; this is the remainder. Thus, there would be no drawing away from anywhere. The meaning is that when 'in the locative, etc.' is being continued, there would be no separate making of a drawing away from the locative, etc. That being the case, the intention is that one should make only a single combination with the sutta below. The construction is that it is connected with 'in the sense of state and object.'

Bahulassa bhāvo kammaṃvāti bahvatthādānamevātra bahulasaddassa pavattinimittaṃ bhāvo kammaṃceti tattha paccayo. Kecīti pāṇiniye yeva sandhāyāha. Tassāpi bhūteyeva pavattimupadisati ‘sopi’ccādi

The state or action of 'much.' Here, the taking up of many meanings is the cause for the application of the word 'bahula'; 'state' and 'action' are the meanings of the suffix in that case. By 'some,' he refers only to the Pāṇinians. He teaches its application only in the past, saying 'that too,' etc.

Nā[M 0.0254]. Bhijjamānanti paccamānaṃ. Pararūpena passinnoti yojanā. Keciti teyeva. “Matibuddhipūjatthehi ce”ti (3-2-188) tesaṃ sutte casaddākaḍḍhite dasseti ‘yathā’tiādinā. Akkocchi tanti kamme viggahamāha, tanti kammapadaṃ, evamuparipi curādiṇilope “nimittābhāve nemittikassāpyabhāvo”tyākāranivatti. Kasirayaṃ gatyādyane kattho, kaṭṭhaṃtyatra kimatthoti āha- ‘ettha hiṃsattho’ti.

Nā. 'Being broken' means 'being tormented.' The construction is 'one who sees with another's form.' 'Some' means those very ones. In their sutta 'And in the meanings of thought, understanding, and honor' (Pāṇini 3.2.188), he shows by 'as,' etc., what is drawn in by the word 'ca.' 'He reviled': he gives the analysis in the objective case. 'Taṃ' is the objective word. Similarly above, with the elision of ṇi of the curādi-group, there is the removal of the ā-sound according to the maxim 'when the cause is absent, the effect is also absent.' Kasira has many meanings, such as 'going.' As for 'kaṭṭhaṃ' here, what is the meaning? He says: 'Here it has the meaning of harming.'

Hetunoti dukkhaphalassa hetuno agyādino. Kaṭṭhasaddassa phalahetubhūte agyādike vattamāne evaṃ hotu phalevattamāne kathanti āha- ‘yadāpanā’tiādi. Kodhātiko idha.

'By the cause' means by the cause of the fruit of suffering, such as fire, etc. Let it be so when the word 'kaṭṭha' refers to fire, etc., which has become the cause of the result. But how is it when it refers to the result? He says: 'but when,' etc. Here it is derived from the root √kudh.

61. Tuṃtā

61. Tuṃtā

Nanu ca bhāveiti bhavatināyaṃ ghaṇantena niddeso karīyatīti bhavativisayova paccayatthaniddeso kato bhavati, tato ca bhavatino yo bhāvo tasmiṃyeva vācce paccayo siyā, so ca bhavatito yevuppajjamānena paccayena sakkābhidhātuṃ tato tasmāva paccayena bhavitabbaṃ, tasmā kathaṃ pacituṃ pāko cāgo rāgotipacādīhibhavati ccāha- ‘bhavanaṃbhāvo kiriyādhātvattho’ti.

But is it not so that when it is said 'in the sense of state,' this designation is made with a word ending in the suffix `ghañ` derived from the root of `bhavati`? Thus the designation of the meaning of the suffix is made only with respect to 'bhavati.' And therefore, the suffix would be in the sense of whatever is the state of 'bhavati.' And that state can be expressed only by a suffix arising from 'bhavati' itself; therefore, the suffix must come from that root itself. Therefore, how can these forms come from roots like √pac, etc., to form 'pacituṃ,' 'pāko,' 'cāgo,' 'rāgo'? He says: 'Becoming, state, action is the meaning of a root.'

Kiriyāsāmaññañhi sabbadhātvatthānugataṃ bhavatissattho, tena kiriyāsāmaññavācinātthaniddeso karīyamāno sabbadhātuvisaye kato bhavati tasmā pacādīhipi bhavatītyadhippāyo.

For 'action in general,' which is inherent in the meaning of all roots, is the meaning of 'bhavati.' Therefore, when the designation of meaning is made by that which expresses 'action in general,' it is made with respect to all roots. Thus, the intention is that it also comes from roots like √pac, etc.

Nanu cātra tumādayo bhāve bhavantīti vutte na viññāyate kiṃvisesite bhāve tumādayo bhavanticcāha- ‘yato’ccādi. Tassāti dhātuno. Yo vattabbo bhāvoti yo vācco bhāvo. Kutoccāha- ‘sambandhā’ti. Tumādīnaṃ yā pakati tāya vācceneva bhāvena saha sambandhāti attho. Ṭhātabbanti bhāve tabbo. Atha kriyāyaṃtyanena tabbādyabhihitassa dabbarūpāpannassa bhāvassa kathaṃ gahaṇaṃtyāha- ‘yadipi’ccādi. Sakanissayakiriyābyapadesoti dabba rūpassa attano nissayabhūtāya kiriyāya byapadeso daṭṭhuṃ cakkhuccādo bhavanakiriyāya patīyamānattā tumādayo bhavanteva.

But is it not so that here, when it is said that the suffixes tuṃ, etc., occur in the sense of state, it is not understood in what specific state they occur? He says: 'from which,' etc. 'Of that' means of the root. 'The state which is to be expressed' means the state which is the meaning. From where? He says: 'From connection.' The meaning is that there is a connection of the suffixes tuṃ, etc., with the state that is expressed by their own base. 'Ṭhātabbaṃ' is formed with tabba in the sense of state. Then, by 'in action,' how is there the grasping of the state—which is expressed by tabba, etc., and has assumed the form of a substance? He says: 'even if,' etc. 'Designation by the action which is its own basis': the designation of the substantive form is by the action which is its own basis, for example, 'an eye to see with.' Because the action of becoming is understood, the suffixes tuṃ, etc., do indeed occur.

Nanu [M 0.0255] ca tumādīnaṃ bhāve vihitattā kiriyāyeva padhānattanti kamma kārakaṃ nappatīyateti kathaṃ ‘kaṭaṃ kātuṃ gacchatī’ti siyāccā saṅkiya paṭipādetumāha- ‘yadipi’ccādi. Dhātvatthakato kiriyāsaṅkhātena dhātvatthena kato. Atthīti iminā yattha ‘supyate deva dattene’ccādo natthi, tattha na kammampatīyateti dasseti.

But is it not so that since the suffixes tuṃ, etc., are prescribed in the sense of state, action is primary, and thus the objective case-relation is not understood? So how could there be the expression 'he goes to make a mat'? Having raised this doubt, to explain it, he says: 'even if,' etc. 'Made by the meaning of the root' means made by the meaning of the root, which is called action. By 'there is,' he shows that where there is no object, as in 'it is slept by Devadatta,' there the object is not understood.

“Icchatthesu samānakattukesu tavetuṃ vā”ti (4-2-12) kaccānena atadatthāyampikiriyāyaṃ tumādayo yathāsiyunti visuṃ suttitaṃ, tenāha- ‘icchatthesmi’ccādi. Yathā ‘bhottuṃ pacatī’tyādo bhojanakiriyā payojanā pacanakiriyā hoti, nevamettha tappa yojanā icchā… pacanakiriyāyaviyatappayojanattābhāvatoti ayamassādhippāyo. Puneccādinā vuttāniṭṭhapātassāsaṅkaṃ viracayamāha- ‘atadatthāyampi’ccādi.

By Kaccāyana, the sutta 'In the sense of wishing, when the agents are the same, tavetuṃ vā' (Kacc. 4.2.12) was formulated separately so that the suffixes tuṃ, etc., might be used for an action that is not for that purpose. Therefore, he says: 'in the sense of wishing,' etc. Just as in 'he cooks in order to eat,' the action of cooking has the action of eating as its purpose, so here the wish does not have that as its purpose, because it does not have that as its purpose in the way the action of cooking does. This is his intention. Dispelling the doubt about the undesirable consequence mentioned, he says: 'even for that which is not for that purpose,' etc.

Icchatthassa dhātuno payogāti iminā ‘icchanto karotī’ti ettha icchantoti icchatthassa dhātuno payogatthameva, na icchāya payojanaṃ karaṇanti dīpeti. Devadattaṃ bhuñjamānamicchatītettha bhottunti na hoti samānakattukesūti vacanato, bhojanassa devadatto kattā, icchatissa aññoyevātipi suttassa visuṃ payojanaṃ na vattabbanti dassento āha- ‘devadatta’miccādi.

By this 'application of a root with the meaning of wishing,' he indicates that in 'wishing, he does,' 'wishing' is merely for the purpose of applying the root with the meaning of wishing, not that the doing has wishing as its purpose. In 'he wishes Devadatta to eat,' 'bhottuṃ' is not used because of the rule 'when the agents are the same.' Devadatta is the agent of eating, while the one who wishes is someone else. Showing that a separate purpose of the sutta need not be stated, he says: 'Devadatta,' etc.

Icchatissāti’devadattaṃ bhuñjamānamicchatī’ti ettha icchatīti vuttaisissa. Sādhanaṃ ‘devadattaṃ bhuñjamāna’nti vuttakammasaṅkhātaṃ attho payojanaṃ yassa so sādhanattho-icchati. Tassa bhāvo tattaṃ, tasmā. Kammamevicchāya payojanabhāve ṭhitanti bhāvo. Niratthakanti etadatthameva samānakattukaggahaṇaṃ kataṃ tañca yathāvuttena pasaṅgābhāvā niratthakanti adhippāyo.

Of 'icchati': of the one stated as 'icchati' in the phrase 'he wishes Devadatta to eat.' The instrument, called the object, stated as 'Devadatta eating,' is the meaning or purpose of that verb; so it is 'sādhanattha-icchati.' The state of that is -ttā. Therefore, the state is that the object itself stands in the position of the purpose for the wishing. 'Useless': The inclusion of 'having the same agent' was made for this very purpose, and the intention is that this is useless because, as stated, the occasion does not arise.

Sakādyatthesu dhātū sūpapadesu dhātu mattā tumādayo suttantarena vihitā pāṇiniyehi, tenāha- ‘sakādidhātuppayoge’tiādi. Siddhāti tumādayo siddhā. Bhujikiriyatthāti bhujikiriyā attho yassā sattiyā sā bhujikiriyatthā patīyate. Patīya mānatte [M 0.0256] kāraṇamāha- ‘asatopi hi’ccādi. Parehettha akiriyatthopapadattho punārabbhoti vaṇṇitaṃ. Tadetaṃ vighaṭayitumāha- ‘tene’ccādi. Paresamayamadhippāyo “sakkoti bhottuṃtyādo kosalyaṃ gamyate. Gilāyati bhottuṃti tadasatti. Ghaṭate bhottuṃtyādo yogyatā. Ārabhate bhottuṃtyādobhujisse vādyavatthākiriyantaraṃ. Labhate bhottuṃti appaccakkhānaṃ. Atthi bhottuntiādīsu sambhavamattaṃ. Vaṭṭati bhottuṃtyādo dosā bhāvo gamyate. Sakkoticcādino upapadassa bhojanādikiriyatthatā na gamyate tasmā akiriyatthesupi sakādīsūpapadesu tumādayo bhavantī”ti.

By the Pāṇinians, the suffixes tuṃ, etc., are prescribed by another sutta from a mere root when roots with the meaning of 'sak,' etc., are upapadas. Therefore, he says: 'in the application of roots like sak,' etc. 'Established' means the suffixes tuṃ, etc., are established. 'Having the action of eating as its purpose': that power which has the action of eating as its purpose is understood as 'having the action of eating as its purpose.' He states the reason for its being understood: 'for even when it is non-existent,' etc. Here, it has been described by others that 'the meaning of an upapada not having the meaning of an action is a new topic.' To refute this, he says: 'therefore,' etc. The intention of others is this: in 'sakkoti bhottuṃ,' skill is understood. In 'gilāyati bhottuṃ,' inability. In 'ghaṭate bhottuṃ,' suitability. In 'ārabhate bhottuṃ,' another action, the initial stage of eating itself. In 'labhate bhottuṃ,' non-refusal. In 'atthi bhottuṃ,' etc., mere possibility. In 'vaṭṭati bhottuṃ,' etc., the absence of fault is understood. The upapada 'sakkoti,' etc., is not understood to have the action of eating, etc., as its purpose. Therefore, the suffixes tuṃ, etc., occur even when 'sak,' etc., are upapadas with meanings other than action.

Patīyamānesvapyetesvatthantaresu tādatthiyamatthiyevāti pubbena vihitassa tumādinotra na bādheti dassetumāha- ‘yadipi’ccādi. Tādatthiyamatthiyevāti bhojanakiriyatthatā sakkotiādīnaṃ atthi yevāti attho siddhāyeva “tuṃtāye”ccādinā. Alamatthavisiṭṭhesu pariyattivacanesūpapadesu dhātuto tumādayo vihitā parehi, tatthāha ‘alamatthavisiṭṭhe’iccādi. Pahusaddampi antogadhaṃ katvā ‘samatthādī’ti vuttaṃ, bhavatissa sambhavo “pubbekakattukāna”nti (5-63) ettha byākhyāyissate. Abhimatāti kaccāyanena “arahasakkādīsu ce”ti (4-2-13) casaddena abhimatā imassāti ‘kālo bhottuṃ’tiādino. Yathā bhottumanotiādinā paresampi ayameva nipphattikkamoti dīpeti. Abyabhicāratoti avinābhāvato, bhavati bhojanaṃ bhāvoti bhojanaṃ bhuñjanaṃ bhāvo bhavatīti attho. Natugamissakiriyātadatthāti gamanakiriyā bhojanatthā na hotīti attho. Atthasaddohyayaṃ payojanavacano yañca yamuddissa pavattati, taṃ tassa payojanaṃ bhavati. Nacāyaṃ bhojanamuddissa gamissati, kiñcarahi kāriyantaraṃ, kevalaṃ tena nimittena sambhāvīyate. Yadā tu bhojanatthamevārabbhate gamanakiriyā, tadā bhavatyeva’gamissati bhottu’nti.

To show that even when these other meanings are understood, the meaning 'for that purpose' still exists, and thus it does not contradict the rule for tuṃ, etc., prescribed previously, he says: 'even if,' etc. The meaning of 'the meaning "for that purpose" still exists' is that the state of having the action of eating as a purpose still exists for 'sakkoti,' etc. This is already established by 'tuṃtāye,' etc. By others, the suffixes tuṃ, etc., are prescribed from a root when words expressing sufficiency, qualified by the meaning 'alam,' are upapadas. Regarding that, he says: 'when qualified by the meaning alam,' etc. Including also the word 'pahu,' it is said 'samatthā, etc.' Its occurrence will be explained there in 'pubbekakattukānaṃ' (Kacc. 5.63). 'Intended': intended by Kaccāyana by the word 'ca' in 'arahasakkādīsu ce' (Kacc. 4.2.13) are examples for this rule, such as 'kālo bhottuṃ.' By 'as in bhottumano,' etc., he indicates that for others too this is the very same process of derivation. 'From non-deviation' means from invariable connection. 'Eating becomes the state' means the eating which is the act of consuming becomes the state. 'But the action of 'he will go' is not for that purpose' means the action of going is not for the purpose of eating. The word 'attha' here means purpose, and whatever one undertakes aiming at something, that becomes its purpose. And this one will not go aiming at eating, but rather at some other task; it is merely supposed by that sign. But when the action of going is undertaken for the very purpose of eating, then 'gamissati bhottuṃ' does indeed occur.

Tuṃvisaye ṇakopi vihito pāṇiniyehi, tatrāha- ‘kārako vajati’ccādi. Parihāramāha- ‘pubbe’ccādinā. ‘Kattariltu’ccādinā yoyaṃ [M 0.0257] ṇako tīsupi kālesu sāmaññena vihito, kriyatthā yaṃ kriyāyaṃ upapade kattuno-bhidhānaṃ siddhaṃ, na cāssa visesavihitena tuṃpaccayena bādhā bhinnattā, tuṃpaccayassa hi bhāve vidhānaṃ ṇakassa tu kattarīti. Pubbaṇakeneva siddhepi ltvādinivattiyā so vidheyyova, no ce ltvādayopi siyunti codakappasaṅgamāsaṅkiyāha- ‘naceva’miccādi. Avagamābhāvameva phuṭayitumāha- ‘nahiṃ’ccādi. Hi yasmātyatthe yo eso vajati so kattā, yo eso vajati so vikkhipotyayamattho-tra gamyate, na pana tehi tādatthiyaṃ gamyateti attho. Codako ltvādīhi sāmyamāpādayituṃ sāmarisaṃ vuttavidhinevāppattiṃ ṇakassāpyāha- ‘ṇakopi’ccādi. Agatthaṃ apakatatthaṃ (potthake) yadipi ṇakena tādatthiyaṃ na gamyate pakaraṇato gamyateti ṇako bhavissatītyāsaṅkiya codako āha- ‘athe’ccādi. Pubbeccādinā vutto-yaṃ ‘ṇako na vidheyyo’ccassa na parihāro… sottarattā yathāvuttena, kintu‘tasmā nevi’ccādinā iminā vuccamānovaparihārotiviññātabbaṃ. Tadevaṃltvādīnampipattitoṇakaltvādīhi tādatthiyānavagame vinicchite tādatthiyavisesena tesaṃ sambhavoti anatthakaṃ “ṇakassa kiriyatthopapadassavidhānaṃ ltvādipaṭisedhanattha”nti vākyakāravacananti satthakāro nigamayamāha- ‘tasmā”ccādi. Bhavatu pakaraṇatova cāpaccayabhova tādatthiyāvagamo, tathāpiṇako paro vidheyyotyadhippāyenāha- ‘athāpi’ccādi. Gatattaṃ. Bhavissati kāle kriyatthāyaṃ kriyāyamupapade bhāve ca ṇappaccayādayo vihitā, tatrāha- ‘pākāya vajati’ccādi. Avihitesupi tādatthiyā siddhameveti adhippāyo.

In the domain of the `tuṃ` suffix, the `ṇaka` suffix is also prescribed by the Pāṇiniyas; there, it is said, 'the agent goes,' etc. He states the refutation with 'pubbe,' etc. By 'kattari tu,' etc., this `ṇaka` suffix is generally prescribed in all three tenses. When a verb signifying the purpose of an action is in proximity, the expression of the agent is established, and there is no contradiction by the specifically prescribed `tuṃ` suffix, because their domains are different. For the `tuṃ` suffix is prescribed in the sense of the abstract noun (bhāva), whereas the `ṇaka` suffix is in the sense of the agent (kattari). Even though it is established by the preceding `ṇaka` suffix, it must still be prescribed for the exclusion of the `ltvā`, etc., suffixes. If not, the `ltvā`, etc., suffixes would also apply. Thus, anticipating the opponent's objection, he says, 'nacevaṃ,' etc. To make clear the lack of comprehension, he says, 'nahi,' etc. For (`hi` in the sense of `yasmā`), 'he who goes is the agent,' 'he who goes is the one who scatters'—this meaning is understood here, but the sense of purpose is not understood from them (the suffixes); this is the meaning. The opponent, in order to establish similarity with the `ltvā`, etc., impatiently points out the same non-applicability for the `ṇaka` suffix as well, by the stated method, saying '`ṇako`pi,' etc. Anticipating the argument that even if the sense of purpose is not conveyed by the `ṇaka` suffix, it is understood from the context, and thus the `ṇaka` suffix will apply, the opponent says, 'atha,' etc. What was stated by 'pubbe,' etc., is not a refutation of 'the `ṇaka` suffix should not be prescribed'... because it has a subsequent answer, as has been stated. Rather, it should be understood that the refutation is what is being stated by this 'tasmā nevi,' etc. Thus, since the applicability of `ltvā`, etc., is established, and it is determined that the sense of purpose is not understood from `ṇaka`, `ltvā`, etc., their occurrence is due to a specific sense of purpose. Therefore, the statement of the Vākyakāra, 'The prescription of the `ṇaka` suffix when a verb signifying the purpose of an action is in proximity is for the sake of prohibiting `ltvā`, etc.,' is meaningless. The author concludes by saying 'tasmā,' etc. Let the understanding of the sense of purpose come from the context alone; even so, the `ṇaka` suffix should be prescribed subsequently. With this intention, he says 'athāpi,' etc. This is understood. In the future tense, when a verb signifying the purpose of an action is in proximity, the `ṇa` suffix and others are prescribed in the sense of the abstract noun (bhāva). There, it is said—'he goes for the purpose of cooking,' and so on. Even when not specifically prescribed, the sense of purpose is indeed established—this is the intended meaning.

62. Paṭi

62. Paṭi: towards, against, in relation to, about, back.

Sotunādīsu ‘savanaṃ kātuna’iccādinā viggaho. Suteneti savananti viggaho.

In the case of `sotuna`, etc., the analysis is by means of '`savanaṃ kātuṃ`' (to make a hearing), and so on. The analysis for `savanaṃ` is `sutena` (by that which is heard).

63. Pubbe

63. Before.

Veti nātisambajjhate vidhino niccattā. Ekasaddassānekatthattā viseseti [M 0.0258] ‘sakhyāvacanoyamekasaddo’ti. Kutoccāha-‘saddāna’miccādi. Ekasaddassa saṅkhyāvacanatte yottho sampajjate, tamāha ‘ekasaṅkhyāvacchinno’ti, tadatthāti kriyatthassatthā. Yadipi ‘pubbaṃ byāpāra’nti samudāye ekadesabhūto byāpāro niddhāriyamānoti vuttaṃ, tathāpi pubbasaddena byāpāravācako kriyattho vuccate upacārā, teneva ‘tesu yo pubbo tadatthato kriyatthā’ti vuttiyaṃvuttaṃ. Nanu ca satti kārakaṃ, aññā ca pubbakālakiriyāya satti, aññā uttara kālakiriyāya, tasmā kuto ekakattukattamiccāsaṅkiya paṭipādento āha- ‘yadipi’ccādi. Sattimato dabbassāti devadattādino sattimato dabbassa. Tadajjhāropāti ekattassa ajjhāropā. Eka kattukānaṃ byāpārānaṃ kamābhidhānāya tunādayo vidhīyamānā bhāveyevuppannā sakkonti kamamabhidhātunti bhāvetyatrābhisambajjhate.

The particle `va` is not closely connected, because the rule is constant. Because the word 'eka' has multiple meanings, it is specified as 'this word "eka" expresses number.' Whence is this? He says, 'saddānaṃ,' and so on. When the word 'eka' expresses number, the meaning that results is stated as 'delimited by the number one'; `tadatthā` means for the purpose of that which has the purpose of an action. Although it is said that by 'prior action' an action that is part of a whole is being specified, still, by the word 'prior,' the action-purpose that denotes the action is expressed figuratively; for that very reason, it is said in the commentary, 'among them, that which is prior is, from its meaning, from the action-purpose.' But surely, capacity is the agent; the capacity for a prior action is one thing, and the capacity for a subsequent action is another—so how can there be a single agent? Anticipating and explaining this doubt, it is said: 'yadipi,' and so on. 'Of the substance possessing capacity' means of the substance possessing capacity, such as Devadatta. 'That superimposition' means the superimposition of oneness. For expressing the sequence of actions performed by a single agent, the `tuna`, etc., suffixes, being prescribed, are indeed capable of expressing sequence, having arisen in the sense of the abstract noun (`bhāve`)—here, it connects with `bhāve`.

Ekakattukānanti bahuvacanattā ‘bhutvā pitvā vajatī’tipi bhavati. Bhuttasmintettha anekakattukattā bhuñjitvāpi bhavati. Pāṇini yānamiva visuṃ vacanamantarena tunādividhippaṭipādayamāha- ‘mukhaṃ byādāya supati’ccādi. Byādāyāti dādhātussa viāpubbassa tvāppaccaye “pyo vā tvāssa samāse”ti (5-064) tvāssa pyādese rūpaṃ, mukhavivaraṇaṃ katvātyattho, byavadhāyakakālassāti byādāna supanānamantareyo kālo tassa, bhedānupalakkhaṇanti bhedassādassanaṃ. Bhedassīnaṃ kesañcivijjamānattā’kehīcī’ti vuttaṃ. Sahabhāvepīti byādānasupanānaṃ sahabhāvepi. Vaḍḍhitako bhattarāsi.

Because `ekakattukānaṃ` is in the plural, the expression '`bhutvā pitvā vajatī`' (having eaten, having drunk, he goes) also occurs. Here, in `bhuttasmiṃ`, because there are multiple agents, `bhuñjitvā` also occurs. Like the Pāṇiniyas, without a separate statement, he explains the rule for `tuna`, etc., saying: '`mukhaṃ byādāya supati`' (he sleeps with his mouth open), and so on. `Byādāya` is the form of the root `dā` preceded by `vi` and `ā` with the `tvā` suffix, where `tvā` is replaced by `pya` according to the rule '`pyo vā tvāssa samāse`' (5-064); the meaning is 'having made an opening of the mouth.' '`byavadhāyakakālassa`' means: of the time that is between the opening of the mouth and the sleeping. '`bhedānupalakkhaṇan`' means the non-perception of a difference. Because the difference exists for some, it is said, 'by some.' '`Sahabhāvepi`' means even when there is simultaneity of the opening of the mouth and the sleeping. `Vaḍḍhitako` means a heap of rice.

Abhimatā pāṇiniyānaṃ, parāya nadiyā pabbato-varo visesī yateti appatvā nadimpabbato’ti vutte nadiyā orabhāge pabbatoti attho. Bhavati, tato ca pārebhūtanadīvisiṭṭho pabbato patīyate. Avarena pabbatena parā nadī visesīyateti atikkamma pabbataṃ nadīti vutte pāre nadiyā ore pabbatoti attho patīyate, tato ca orabhāge pabbatavisiṭṭhā nadī viññāyate. Bhavatino sabbattha sambhave sati ekakattukatā pubbakālatā yathā gamya te [M 0.0259] tathā dasseti ‘paṭhamaṃ na pappoti’ccādi. Nigamayati ‘tadeva’miccādinā.

This is the view of the Pāṇiniyas. When it is said, '`appatvā nadiṃ pabbato`' (the mountain, not having reached the river), the meaning is that the mountain is on the near side of the river, because the mountain on the near side is distinguished by the river on the far side. This is so, and from that, the mountain is understood as being distinguished by the river which is on the far side. When it is said, '`atikkamma pabbataṃ nadī`' (the river, having surpassed the mountain), the meaning is understood that the river is on the far side and the mountain is on the near side, because the river on the far side is distinguished by the mountain on the near side. And from that, the river is known as being distinguished by the mountain which is on the near side. When there is a possibility of this everywhere, he demonstrates how single agency and prior time are understood, as in 'first, it does not reach,' and so on. He concludes with '`tadevaṃ`,' and so on.

Bhutvā bhutvā gacchatīti pare-ññathā nipphattimākaṅkhanti pāṇiniyādayo, tatrāha- ‘ekakattukāna’miccādi. Ābhikkhaññāvagame kāraṇaṃ pucchati ‘yajjeva’miccādi. Vuttameva phuṭayati ‘yehi’ccādinā. Yehīti veyyākaraṇehi. Jivaggāhaṃ agāhayiccādo pareññathā paṭipannātadāha- ‘kamma’miccādi. Sakaṅgeti pāṇipādādike-ttaniyevayave. Ṇaṃ paccayo abhimatoti sambandho. Kiṃ ṇampaccayenāti idaṃ vuttaṃ hotīti sambandho. Aññathā siddhippakāramāha- ‘jīvassi’ccādi. Kiṃ visiṭṭhanti pucchitvā jīvaggāhena visiṭṭhanti dassetuṃ jīvaggāha’nti āha. Jīvaggāhasaṅkhātaṃ gahaṇamakāsīti attho.

Regarding '`bhutvā bhutvā gacchati`' (having eaten repeatedly, he goes), others, like the Pāṇiniyas, desire a different derivation. There, he says: '`ekakattukānaṃ`,' and so on. He asks the reason for the understanding of repetition with '`yajjeva`,' and so on. He clarifies what was said with '`yehi`,' and so on. `Yehi` means 'by the grammarians.' Regarding '`jivaggāhaṃ agāhayi`,' and so on, others have understood it differently; therefore, he says: '`kamma`,' and so on. '`Sakaṅge`' refers to one's own limbs, such as hands and feet. The `ṇaṃ` suffix is desired—this is the connection. 'What is the use of the `ṇaṃ` suffix?'—this is what is meant; this is the connection. He states the manner of accomplishment otherwise with '`jīvassa`,' and so on. Having asked, 'Distinguished by what?', to show that it is distinguished by '`jīvaggāha`' (seizing alive), he says, '`jīvaggāhaṃ`.' The meaning is: he performed the act of grasping known as 'seizing alive'.

Ākhyātanti agāhayīti ākhyātaṃ kattabbarūpanti imānā gahaṇa kiriyāya kammattaṃ bodheti. Tabbisesanampīti kattabbarūpāya gahaṇa kiriyāya visesanampi. Tathābhūtamevāti kattabbarūpameva. Tathā ceti kiriyāvisesane dutiyāya ṇamante jāte sati. Ṇamanta rūpanti ṇamantassa rūpaṃ yassāti viggaho. Ṇaṃpaccayeniha kiñcineti sambandho. Iheti imasmiṃ byākaraṇe. Kiñci payojanaṃ. Pacāditotiādisaddena tehi avihitaṇampaccayā gahitā.

The finite verb (`ākhyātaṃ`), that is, `agāhayi`, indicates the objecthood of the action of grasping by this form which is to be made (`kattabbarūpaṃ`). 'Its qualifier also' means it is also the qualifier of the action of grasping which is to be made. 'Being just so' means it is precisely the form that is to be made. 'And so' means: this being the case, when the `ṇamanta` ending is in the accusative case as an adverb. '`Ṇamantarūpaṃ`' is a compound whose analysis is 'that which has the form of a `ṇamanta`.' The connection is: 'Here, there is no purpose whatsoever for the `ṇaṃ` suffix.' 'Here' means in this grammar. 'No whatsoever' means no purpose. 'From `pac`, etc.': by the word `ādi`, the `ṇaṃ` suffixes not prescribed by them are included.

64. Nto

64. The `nta` suffix.

Yo sādhayitumāraddho naca niṭṭhamupagatoti yo kaṭādisādhayituṃ nibbattayituṃ āraddho niṭṭhaṃ parisamattiṃ na copagato nappatto. Pavatto-nuparatovāti yo pabbatādi niccappavato-avirato teneva niṭṭhaṃ nopagatosovattamānoti vuccateti yojanā. Tabbi sayakiriyādvārenāti yathāvuttakaṭādivisaya kiriyāmukhena, idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti “yathāvuttakaṭādīnaṃ vattamānattā tabbisayā kiriyāpi vattamānā evāti taṃdvārena kriyatthavisesana”nti.

‘He who has begun to accomplish but has not reached completion’ means: one who has started to accomplish or produce something like a mat, etc., but has not reached or attained completion or perfection. Or, ‘active and not ceased’ means: one who is ever-active and unceasing, like a mountain, etc., and for that very reason has not reached completion; such a one is called ‘present’ (`vattamāna`). This is the construction. ‘Through the activity related to its object’ means: through the activity concerning the aforementioned object, such as the mat. This is what is said: ‘Because the aforementioned mat, etc., are in a present state, the activity pertaining to them is also in a present state. Thus, through that means, it is a qualifier of the meaning of the verb.’

Bhuñjati devadattoti ettha yajjapi bhuñjamāno hasati khajjati vadati pāniyaṃ pivati, tathāpi yuttā vattamānatā kattumicchitassārambho na [M 0.0260] parisamattoti vuttaṃ- ‘sādhayitumāraddho na ca niṭṭhamupagato’ti. Tiṭṭhanti pabbatātiādīsu niccesu pabbatādīsu bhūtānāgatānamasambhavā tannisedhino vattamānassāpyasambhavā yadīpi kālavibhāgo na viññāyate, tathāpi āraddhassa ṭhānassāparisamattiyā vattamānā evāti vuttaṃ- ‘pavatto-nuparato vā’ti. Kattuvisesane sati ko dosoccāha- ‘kattu visesane’ccādi. Ihāpi siyā kattuno vattamānattā, vattamānatta mevāssa pakāsetumayanti vuttaṃ. “Apaṭhamā samānādhikaraṇe”tyādīhi (3-2-124) anekehi suttehintappaccayo pāṇiniyehi vihito.

Here, regarding 'Devadatta eats' (Bhuñjati Devadatto), even though while eating he laughs, chews, and drinks water, still, the present tense is appropriate, because the beginning of what is desired to be done is not completed. Thus it is said: 'begun to be accomplished but not yet reached completion.' In cases like 'Mountains stand' (Tiṭṭhanti pabbatā), regarding eternal things like mountains, since past and future are impossible, and because of the impossibility of a present that negates them, even if the division of time is not discerned, still, because the begun standing has not come to completion, it is indeed present. Thus it is said: 'ongoing or uninterrupted.' When there is a specification of the agent, what fault arises? He says: 'in specifying the agent,' etc. Here too, it may be due to the present state of the agent, and it is said that they wish to make clear its very present state. By many sūtras such as 'Apaṭhamā samānādhikaraṇe' (3-2-124), the 'nta' suffix is prescribed by the Pāṇinīyas.

Idha pana sāmaññena vihitattā āha- ‘sāmaññenā’tiādi. Santo ‘asa-bhuvi’ntappaccayo. “Kattari lo” (5-18) “ntamānānti yiyuṃsvādilopo”ti (5-130) akārassa lopo. Tapanto ‘tapa-santāpe’. Jappanto ‘jappa=vacane’. Paṭhanto ‘paṭha=uccāraṇe’ pacanto ‘paca=pāke’dhārayanto ‘dhara=dhāraṇe’. Payojakabyāpāre ṇi, dharituṃ payuñjamāno dhārayanto. Dissanto disa dusa=appitiyaṃ” divādīhi yaka” (5-12) yajanto ‘yaja-devapūjāyaṃ’. Arahanto ‘araha-pūjāyaṃ. Yathācātiādinā apaṭhamāsamānādhikaraṇādīsu ‘saṃvijjamāno virocamānaṃ jappamāno’ccādīsu māno nto viya daṭṭhabboti vadati.

Here, however, because it is prescribed generally, he says: 'generally,' etc. 'Santo' (being) is from the root 'as-bhuvi' (to be) with the 'nta' suffix. According to the rules 'Kattari lo' (5-18) and 'ntamānānti yiyuṃsvādilopo' (5-130), the elision of the vowel 'a' occurs. 'Tapanto' (practicing austerity) is from 'tapa-santāpe' (to heat). 'Jappanto' (muttering) is from 'jappa-vacane' (to speak). 'Paṭhanto' (reciting) is from 'paṭha-uccāraṇe' (to utter). 'Pacanto' (cooking) is from 'paca-pāke' (to cook). 'Dhārayanto' (upholding) is from 'dhara-dhāraṇe' (to hold). In the activity of a causative agent, 'ṇi' is used; one who causes another to hold is 'dhārayanto'. 'Dissanto' (appearing) is from 'disa' (to see) or 'dusa-appītiyaṃ' (to be displeased), with the suffix 'ya' from the 'divādi' group (5-12). 'Yajanto' (sacrificing) is from 'yaja-devapūjāyaṃ' (to worship the gods). 'Arahanto' (being worthy) is from 'araha-pūjāyaṃ' (to be worthy of worship). By 'yathā ca,' etc., he states that in cases where there is no agreement with the nominative, etc., such as in 'saṃvijjamāno,' 'virocamānaṃ,' 'jappamāno,' etc., the suffix 'māna' should be understood to be like 'nta'.

65. Māno

65. The 'māna' suffix

Kālakato avatthāviseso vayo. Mānovāti imināntappaccayābhāvamāha. Yujjhamānā’yudha=sampahāre’ “divādīhi yaka” (5-12) “tavaggavaraṇāna”miccādinā (1-48) dhassa jho”vaggalasehi te”ti (1-49) yassa ca. “Catutthadutiyesvesa”ntiādinā (1-35) jhassa jo. Naccamānā ‘nacca=naccane’.

Age is a specific state determined by time. By 'Māno vā,' he indicates the absence of the 'nta' suffix. 'Yujjhamānā' (fighting) is from the root 'yudha-sampahāre' (to strike). The suffix 'ya' is added according to 'divādīhi yaka' (5-12); 'dh' becomes 'jh' by 'tavaggavaraṇāna...' (1-48), and the 'y' is treated by 'vaggalasehi te' (1-49). Then 'jh' becomes 'j' by 'Catutthadutiyesvesa...' (1-35). 'Naccamānā' (dancing) is from 'nacca-naccane' (to dance).

67. Tessa

67. Of that

Savisayeti kattari bhāve kammeca.

In its own sphere, that is, in the sense of agent, state, and object.

68. Ṇvāda

68. Ṇva, etc.

Ṇvādayoti [M 0.0261] ‘ṇvādayo’ccanena suttena. Katipayadhātvādipariggahenāti dhātavo pakatibhūtā ādī yeyaṃ kālādīnaṃ te dhā tvādayo tesaṃ pariggahenāti attho. Kālo vattamānādi, kārakaṃ kattādi pakaṃsena niyamena paccayo karīyate etasmāti pakati. Kākriyaṃ āyukādi.

The term 'Ṇvādayo' is from the rule 'ṇvādayo.' 'By the inclusion of certain roots, etc.' means by the inclusion of those roots, etc., where roots are the basic elements which are the beginning of time, etc. Time is the present, etc.; the kāraka is the agent, etc. 'Pakati' (base) is so called because the suffix is formed from it with excellence and by rule. What is action? Life-duration, etc.

Kāriyavisesanti ādesādikāriyavisesaṃ. Kāru sippijāti viseso. Tacchakādayo (tacchakakamma) kāratantavāyarajakanahāpitā pañca kāravo cārudāruti vattamāne kālaniyamenāññatrāpi bhavissati. Evaṃ kāruādīsupi.

'A specific action' means a specific action such as substitution, etc. A 'kāru' (craftsman) is a specific type of artisan. Carpenters (and their work, carpentry), smiths, weavers, dyers, and barbers—these five are craftsmen. In the present, by the rule of time, this may also apply elsewhere. The same applies to craftsmen, etc.

69. Khacha

69. Kha, cha

Khachasānanti vutte tadantaggahaṇaṃ kathamiccāha- ‘paccayaggahaṇe’ccādi. Byākhyātatthaṃ, nanu sutte ekassaroti pulliṅgena niddeso, ādīti ca tabbisesanaṃ, evaṃ sati napuṃsakena vivaraṇaṃ kathaṃ yujjatīti āha- ‘sadde’ccādi, atha jāgareccādo puthagavayavekassarassa jāgarasaddassa ca paccekaṃ kasmā na dvibhāvoccāha- ‘teneve’ccādi.

When 'Khachasāna' is mentioned, how is it understood to refer to that which ends with them? He says: 'when a suffix is mentioned,' etc. The meaning has been explained. Now then, in the rule, the designation 'ekassaro' (of one syllable) is in the masculine gender, and 'ādi' (first) is its qualifier; this being so, how is the explanation in the neuter gender appropriate? He says: 'regarding the word,' etc. Then, in 'jāgara,' etc., why is there no reduplication separately for each single-syllable component and for the word 'jāgara' itself? He says: 'for that very reason,' etc.

Tenevātiādīti ekassaroccassa visesanattahetunāva. Avayavekassarassāti visesanasamāso ‘avayavo ca so ekassaro ce’ti. Athādīhi ekassaravisesanattepyavayavekassarassa kasmā na dvibhāvoccāha- ‘ekassevādittā’ti.

By 'teneva,' etc., it is meant solely for the reason that 'ekassaro' is a qualifier. 'Avayavekassarassa' is a descriptive compound: 'a component which is of a single syllable.' Then, even though 'ekassaro' is qualified by 'ādi,' etc., why is there no reduplication of the single-syllable component? He says: 'Because it is the beginning of only one.'

Itarassāti paṭhamekassarato-ñāssāvayavekassasarassa. Dosaduṭṭhattā nettha visesanasamāsoti vattumāha- ‘ekassaroti’ccādi. Tathā sati ko dosoti āha- ‘eko ce’ccādi. Sarodīti ca vutte ‘īha-ghaṭane’ccādīnameva siyā.

'Of the other' means of the single-syllable component other than the first single syllable. To state that there is no descriptive compound here because it is flawed by a fault, he says: 'ekassaro,' etc. That being so, what is the fault? He says: 'if one,' etc. And if it were said 'beginning with a vowel,' it would apply only to roots such as 'īha-ghaṭane,' etc.

Nanu ca pacatimhi yenevākārena pacasaddo ekassaro teneva tadavayavāpi acsaddo pasaddo ca ekassaro, tatovāvayavānampi paccekaṃ dvibbacanaṃ pappoti… dvibbacanakāriyino ādissa ekassarassa sāmaññena niddesā, evañca samudāyassa tadavayavānañcekassarānaṃ visuṃ dvibbacane [M 0.0262] kate aniṭṭhampappotītīdamapākattumāha- ‘sakiṃsatthappavattiyā sāvayavassa samudāyassa gahaṇa’nti. Sakiṃ satthappavattiyā ekavāraṃ dvibbacanasuttassa pavattiyā dvibbacanakaraṇenāti vuttaṃ hoti.

Now, in 'pacati', in the same way that the word 'paca' is of a single syllable, so too are its components, the words 'ac' and 'pa', of a single syllable. Therefore, reduplication would apply to each of the components individually... because of the general designation of the initial single-syllable element which undergoes reduplication. And thus, if reduplication were performed separately for the aggregate and for its single-syllable components, an undesirable result would be obtained. To avert this, he says: 'by a single application of the rule, the aggregate together with its components is taken.' 'By a single application of the rule' means, it is said, by performing the reduplication through one application of the rule for reduplication.

Sāvayavassāti yathāvuttāvayavehi saha vattamānassa na vinā tehi. Evaṃ maññate “yassa dvibbacane karīyamāne sabbesamavayavānaṃ gahaṇaṃ bhavati, tasseva samudāyassa dvibbacanaṃ yuttaṃ nāvayavānaṃ, tesañhi dvibbacane ekāya dvibbacanassuppattiyā na sabbesaṃ gahaṇaṃ kataṃ hoti nāvayavantassa samudāyassa ca katanti puna tesaṃ dvibbacanāya satthappavattiyā bhavitabba”nti. Upapattantaramāha- ‘athave’ccādi. Iha ṭhāne dvibbacanaṃ dvippayogo dvibbacananti dve pakkhā. Tatra ṭhāne dvibbacanapakkhe dosadassanato dvippayogo dvibbacanantyayameva pakkhobbhupagatoti dassento paṭhamantāva ṭhāne dvibbacanapakkhe bhāvinaṃ dosamāha- ‘paṭhamassekassarassi’ccādi. Dvisaddo saṅkhyeyye vattate.

'With its components' means existing together with the aforementioned components, not without them. Thus it is thought: "When reduplication is to be performed, if all the components are included, reduplication is appropriate for the aggregate itself, not for the components. For in the reduplication of the components, by the production of a single reduplication, not all are included, nor is the aggregate with its components formed; therefore, for their reduplication, the rule would have to be applied again." He states another reason with 'or else,' etc. Here, there are two views on reduplication: reduplication as a substitute for a locus, and reduplication as a double utterance. Therein, seeing the fault in the view of reduplication as a substitute for a locus, and showing that this very view of reduplication as a double utterance is accepted, he first states the fault that would arise in the view of reduplication as a substitute for a locus: 'of the first single syllable,' etc. The word 'dvi' (two) refers to that which is numbered.

Saṅkhyeyyañcettha saddarūpamuccāraṇaṃ vā, tattha uccāraṇe saṅkhyeyye ṭhāne dvibbacanaṃ na sambhavati… uccāraṇassa saddā(nugata) dhammattā. Saddarūpe saṅkhyeyye ṭhāne dvibbacanaṃ, tattha tañca (potthake) doso. Tathā cāha- ‘rūpadvaye vidhīyamāne’ti. Tathā sati nivuttidhamme ṭhānī bhavatīti ṭhānino nivuttiyā bhavitabbaṃ, nivuttiyā ca dhātuttā nivutti, tenāha- ‘pakatippaccayavibhāgābhāvato’ti. Tena ppaccaye pare pakatiyā vidhīyamānaṃ kāriyaṃ na siyā, tena vuttaṃ- ‘assa ittaṃ na siyā’ti. Pipāsati ‘pā=pāne’. Icchāyaṃ pātuntitumantā “tuṃsmā”ccādinā (5-61) so. ‘Pāsa pāsa’ iti dvitte pubbato-ññassa lopo, “rasso pubbassa” (5-74) ‘kha cha sesvassi. Dvippayoge tu dvibbacane nāyaṃ doso samāvisatīti āha- ‘āvuttiyaṃ ti’ccādi. Dvidhā bhūtassā tidhinā dhātusseva dvidhābhūtattaṃ dīpeti.

And here, what is to be numbered is either the sound-form or the utterance. In that regard, if the utterance is what is numbered, reduplication as a substitute for a locus is not possible... because utterance has the nature of following sound. If the sound-form is what is numbered, there is reduplication as a substitute for a locus, and therein lies a fault. And thus he says: 'when a pair of forms is prescribed.' That being so, the locus would have the nature of being replaced, so the locus would have to be replaced; and by its replacement, its status as a root would be replaced. Hence he says: 'due to the absence of a division into base and suffix.' Therefore, when a suffix follows, an operation prescribed for the base would not occur. Thus it is said: 'its transformation to 'i' would not occur.' 'Pipāsati' (he wishes to drink) is from 'pā-pāne' (to drink). In the sense of desire, the suffix 'sa' is added by 'tuṃsmā...' (5-61). When 'pāsa' is reduplicated, there is elision of the latter part of the root from the first part, shortening of the first by 'rasso pubbassa' (5-74), and 'i' by 'khachasesvassi'. However, in reduplication as a double utterance, this fault does not arise, so he says: 'in repetition,' etc. By the rule, it shows that the root itself has become twofold.

70. Paro

70. Following

Yogavibhāgā ‘a ña’ādīsu gamyate. Yadi hyatrāpi chaṭṭhī abhimatā siyā tadā “kha cha sa parokkhānamekassarodidve”ti ekameva yogaṃ [M 0.0263] kareyya. Parokkhe vihitā añaādayo dhātutova, nāññatoti parokkhāvacanasannidhānā casaddena dhātuvihitappaccayāva gayhantīti āha- ‘aññasmimpi dhātuvihitappaccaye’ti. Yadi pana bhusattho ābhikkhaññattho vā vattumiṭṭho siyā, tadā bhūsatthādīsu ca daddallaticcādikaṃ hotīti veditabbaṃ. Caṅkamati momūhacittānīti bhusatthassa yujjamānattā tyādayo bhusatthe bhavanti bahulādhikārāti vattuṃ sakkāti.

From the splitting of the rule, it is understood in regard to 'a', 'ña', and so on. For if here too the sixth case ending were intended, then one would make only one rule: 'kha cha sa parokkhānamekassarodidve.' The affixes 'a', 'ña', and so on are prescribed after a root in the perfect tense, not otherwise; thus, due to the proximity of the term 'parokkha' (perfect tense), by the word 'ca' (and), only suffixes prescribed after a root are to be understood. Hence, he says: 'even in the case of another suffix prescribed after a root.' However, if one wishes to express an intensive or frequentative meaning, then it should be understood that in the intensive sense and so on, forms such as 'daddallati' occur. Since 'caṅkamati momūhacittāni' is applicable in the intensive sense, it can be said that the endings `ti` and so on occur in the intensive sense due to the governing force of the `bahula` principle.

71. Ādi

71. The Beginning

Paṭhamo dutiyoti ca dve ekassarā. Tattha “khachasānamekassarodi dve” (5-69) “parokkhāyaṃ ce”ti (5-70) paṭhamassekassa rassa dvibbacanaṃ ‘ādismā sarā”ti tu dutiyassa, tasmā kathamaññassuccamāneaññassabādhakaṃsiyā tasmā katepidutiya dvibbacanepaṭhamadvibbacanaṃ sambhavatvevātinapaṭhamadvibbacanāpavādo-yaṃ yogoccāsaṅkiyāha- ‘paṭhame’ccādi. Kriyatthādhikārā kriyatthānanti chaṭṭhiyā dutiyenekassa renaca sambandhā paṭhamadvibbacanassavidhāya kamaññavākyamaññaṃ dutiyassāti na vākyabhedoti āha- ‘eke’ccādi. Assāti ‘ādismā sarā”ti assa yogassa, pubbayogeti pubbehi dvihi suttehi. “Ādismā sarā”ti saramadvittenupādāya sāmaññena saddarūpassa dvibbacanavidhānato pubbe viya byañjanayuttasseva vidhānaṃ tatheviṭṭhatthattāti paṭhamadvibbacana sambandhino byañjanassa dvibbacanabādhātyavagantabbaṃ.

The first and the second are two single vowels. Therein, the rules 'khachasānamekassarodi dve' (5-69) and 'parokkhāyaṃ ce' (5-70) prescribe the reduplication of the first single short vowel, while 'ādismā sarā' prescribes it for the second. Therefore, how could one, being stated, be an obstacle to the other? Thus, even when the reduplication of the second has been done, the reduplication of the first is still possible. Hence, suspecting that this rule is an exception to the reduplication of the first, he says: 'paṭhame,' etc. Because of the governing principle of the meaning of the action, the sixth case ending in 'kriyatthānaṃ' is connected with the second case ending by a single vowel. Since the prescription of the first reduplication is one sentence and the prescription for the second is another, there is no sentence split. Thus he says: 'eke,' etc. 'Assa' means 'of this rule,' that is, of the rule 'ādismā sarā.' 'Pubbayoge' means 'in the preceding rule,' that is, by the two preceding suttas. Since the rule 'ādismā sarā,' by not specifying 'vowel,' generally prescribes the reduplication of the sound-form, just as before, the prescription is for the vowel together with its consonant, as that is the intended meaning. Therefore, it should be understood that this obstructs the reduplication of the consonant connected with the first reduplication.

72. Napu

72. Napu

Paṭinimittanti nimittaṃ nimittaṃ pati paṭinimittaṃ, nimitte satīti attho.

The counterpart-sign means a sign corresponding to a sign; that is, when the sign is present.

73. Yathi

73. As

Paṭhamekassarassa paṭhamadvibbacanaṃ visayo, dutiyekassarassa dutiyadvibbacanaṃ, tenāha- ‘yathā visaya’nti. Paṭhama dutiya tatiya dvibbacananti ettha puiti paṭhamaṃ saddarūpaṃ, ttiiti dutiyaṃ, yisiti tatiyaṃ.

The sphere of operation for the first single vowel is the first reduplication; for the second single vowel, it is the second reduplication. Therefore he says: 'yathāvisayaṃ' (according to the respective sphere of operation). Regarding 'first, second, and third reduplication,' here 'pu' is the first sound-form, 'tti' is the second, and 'yisi' is the third.

76. Kha cha

76. Kha cha

Khappaccayādi karīyatīti seso.

The rest is to be supplied as: 'is done on account of the suffix `kha`, etc.'

82. Yuva

82. Yuva

Catthaparattāti [M 0.0264] catthasamāsā parabhūtattā. Tena paccekāti sambandhena. Samānādhikaraṇattena visesananti sambandho. Ācariyena yovibhattilopeneva niddiṭṭhattā āha- ‘luttayovibhattiko vā niddeso’ti.

'Catthaparattā' means 'because of being preceded by a Catuṭṭhī (dative/genitive) tatpurisa compound.' Therefore, it is connected with 'pacceka' (each). The connection is as a qualifier through apposition. Since the teacher has stated it with the elision of the `yo` case ending, he says: 'or the statement has an elided `yo` case ending'.

83. Lahu

83. Light

Dhūpāyatīti dhūpitā, paccayassāti tippaccayassa. Kānubandhakaraṇamanatthakaṃ siyāti ghakvikaraṇassa paccayattābhāve (taṃ) nibandhanassa kāriyassābhāvā ‘na te kānubandhanāgamesū”ti (5-85) paṭisedhā bhāvoti kakārānubandhamanatthakaṃ siyā.

'Dhūpitā' is from 'dhūpāyati' (it smokes). 'Paccayassa' means 'of the suffix `ti`.' The making of the indicatory letter `ka` would be meaningless. Because if the making of `gha` and `kvi` are not considered suffixes, the operation dependent on them would not occur. Due to the absence of the prohibition 'na te kānubandhanāgamesu' (5-85), the indicatory letter `ka` would be meaningless.

85. Nate

85. Not for Them

Pucchīyitthāti viggayha tto, tassa “pucchādito”ti (5-143) ṭho. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva. E onampaṭisedhamukhenāti eonampaṭisedhassa pakatattā vuttaṃ. Cinitabbantiādīsu cīyittha cīyati vātiādinā viggaho. Cinituntiādīsu cinanā yāti(ādinā). Nanu ca (ñiāga)mo, na paccayoti kathampaccaye “lahussupantassā”ti (5-83) eo papponti kathañce sampaṭisedhoccāsaṅkiyāha- ‘ñisse’ccādi. Nanucādimhi na yuvaṇṇābhi kathametthappasaṅgoti āha- ‘sakāpānaṃ kukkūṇeti’ccādi.

Having analyzed 'pucchīyitthā,' for its `ttha`, `ṭha` is substituted by the rule 'pucchādito' (5-143). The rest is just as has been explained. 'E onampaṭisedhamukhenāti' is stated because the prohibition of `e` and `o` is the topic under discussion. In cases like 'cinitabbaṃ,' the analysis is by means of 'cīyittha' or 'cīyati vā,' and so on. In cases like 'cinantī,' it is by 'cinanā yāti,' and so on. Now, `ñi` is an augment, not a suffix. So how could `e` and `o` be obtained by 'lahussupantassā' (5-83), which applies when a suffix follows? And how could there be a prohibition of them? Suspecting this, he says: 'ñissa,' etc. But if there are no `yu`-vowels at the beginning, how could this be applicable here? He says: 'sakāpānaṃ kukkūṇeti,' etc.

Pattokārassāti dhusadde ukārassa pattokārassa. Yuvaṇṇeccādināpattassāti (tabba) tuṃ paccayesu ca ṇino pattassa. Vā vidhānā na ñi. Dhunāpetabbantiādipāṭhe ñimhi akate “aññatrāpī”ti (5-87) paṭisedhābhāvo. Dhunāpetīti pāṭhetimhi le ca “kvaci vikaraṇāna”nti (5-161) vikaraṇalope ca ekāro. Asati nāgame “yuvaṇṇe”ccādinā ettaṃ siyā tampināgame upantattā netyadhippāyenāha- ‘tathāpi’ccādi. Pakkhantaramāha- ‘nāgame’ccādi.

'Pattokārassa' means 'of the `u` vowel in the word `dhu` that has become `o`.' 'Pattassa' by 'yuvaṇṇe,' etc., means 'of the `ṇi` that has been obtained in place of the suffixes `tabba` and `tuṃ`.' Because 'vā' (optionally) is prescribed, `ñi` is not applied. In the reading 'dhunāpetabbaṃ,' etc., when `ñi` is not applied, there is no prohibition by 'aññatrāpi' (5-87). In the reading 'dhunāpeti,' when `ti` and `le` follow, the `e` vowel results from the elision of the class sign by 'kvaci vikaraṇānaṃ' (5-161). If the `n` augment were not there, there would be the substitution of `e` by 'yuvaṇṇe,' etc., but that is not the case because it is penultimate to the `n` augment. With this intention, he says: 'tathāpi,' etc. He states another alternative: 'nāgame,' etc.

87. Añña

87. Other

Sama dama-upasame. Sametīti samako, dametīti damako, jana-janane, janetīti janako badha=bandhane, badhatīti badhako.

The root `sam` in the sense of 'calming'; the root `dam` in the sense of 'taming.' 'He is calm,' thus `samaka` (one who is calm). 'He tames,' thus `damaka` (tamer). The root `jan` in the sense of 'begetting.' 'He begets,' thus `janaka` (progenitor). The root `badh` in the sense of 'binding.' 'He binds,' thus `badhaka` (binder).

92. Padā

92. Padā

Nipajjati [M 0.0265] nipajjanaṃ. Pamajjate pamajjitabbaṃ. Pamajjanāya pamajjituṃ. Pamajjati pamajjanaṃ.

He lies down, the act of lying down. He is negligent, what should be neglected. For negligence, to be negligent. He is negligent, the act of being negligent.

93. Maṃvā

93. Maṃvā

Rundhituntiādīsu rodhanāyāti viggaho.

In the case of 'rundhituṃ' and so forth, the analysis is 'rodhanāya'.

94. Kvimhi

94. Kvimhi

Nanu kimatthamantaggahaṇaṃ yato “kvimhi lopo-ntabyañjanassā”ti vuttaṃ, “chaṭṭhiyantassā”ti (1-17) antasseva lopo siyāti codanaṃ manasi nidhāya taggahaṇe payojanaṃ dassento āha- ‘antaggahaṇa’miccādi. Lopavidhīsūti (vīādilopavidhīsu, chaṭṭhī niddiṭṭhanti) “vīmantu vantū”nti (4-138) chaṭṭhīniddiṭṭhaṃ. Bhadantavidhicaritattabyāpāraṃ tadantavidhicirabhedanāccanabyāpāraṃ (potthake) nissāyāha- ‘chaṭṭhiyantassā”tī byāpārā’ti. Antassāti vīādīnamīkārādino. Aññathāti sabbāpahārilopaññāpanābhāve. Anatthakaṃ siyā “chaṭṭhiyantassā”timassa byāpārasambhāvā. Idāni chaṭṭhīniddiṭṭhānaṃ visesena vattumicchittaṃ antasseva lopapattidosaṃ dassetumāha- ‘tadante’ccādi.

Now, for what purpose is the inclusion of 'anta'? Since it is stated 'kvimhi lopo-ntabyañjanassā' (when `kvi` follows, there is elision of the final consonant), and by 'chaṭṭhiyantassā' (1-17) the elision would be of the final part only. Bearing this objection in mind, he shows the purpose of its inclusion by saying 'antaggahaṇam' and so forth. In the rules of elision (such as the elision rules for 'vī' and so forth, where the sixth case is specified), as in 'vīmantu vantū' (4-138), the sixth case is specified. Relying on the venerable one's method of exposition, he says, 'chaṭṭhiyantassā' (of that which ends in the sixth case) — by way of operation. 'Antassa' means of 'vī' and so forth, of those ending in 'ī' and so forth. Otherwise, if there were no indication of complete elision, it would be meaningless, given the possibility of the operation of 'chaṭṭhiyantassā'. Now, wishing to state specifically concerning those specified with the sixth case, he points out the fault of elision occurring only at the end by saying 'tadante' and so forth.

101. Para

101. Para

Atha dvitteti kathamavasīyate sadde abhāvetiāha- ‘para’iccādi. Anantarasutte “paripaccasamo hī”ti vuttattā tato parassāti kinnāvasīyatīti codana mubbhāviya tadayuttataṃ dassetumāha- ‘nanuce’ccādi.

Then, how is it determined to be 'dvitta'? Because the word is absent, it is said—'para' and so forth. Since it is stated in the immediately following sutta, 'paripaccasamo hī' (indeed, equal to ripening), why is it not determined from that to be 'parassa' (of the other)? To show the inappropriateness of that objection, he says—'nanu ce' and so forth.

103. Dhāssa

103. Dhāssa

Apacurappayogattāti abahuppayogattā.

Apacurappayogattā means 'due to not being of frequent use'.

104. Kimhi

104. Kimhi

Kto dūsidhātuto dūsayatīti atthe.

From the root 'dūs', in the sense of 'dūsayatī' (defiles).

106. Muha

106. Muha

“Vaṇṇe [M 0.0266] yantaṃ tadādo”ti paribhāsāya ayamattho “vaṇṇe pare yaṃ kāriyaṃ taṃ tadādo tasmiṃ vaṇṇe ādibhūte hotī”ti teti takāre pare.

By the maxim, “Vaṇṇe yantaṃ tadādo,” this is the meaning: “When a letter follows, whatever operation is to be done, that operation occurs at the beginning of that letter.” In the case of ‘te,’ this occurs when the letter ‘ta’ follows.

107. Vaha

107. Vaha

Tetvevāti vatvā paccudāharaṇaṃ dasseti ‘vuyhatī’ti. Vuttivacanaṃ mulliṅgiya atthaṃ vadati ‘ussā’tiādi.

Having said ‘tetveva,’ he shows the counter-example ‘vuyhatī.’ The word from the Vutti, referring to its original gender, states the meaning: ‘ussā,’ and so forth.

108.

108.

Nidhīyitthāti viggaho.

‘Nidhīyittha’ is the analysis.

109. Gamā

109. Gamā

Rānanti vutte ‘rā-ādāne’iccassa gahaṇampi viññāyeyyāti āha- ‘rāna’ntiādi.

When ‘rāna’ is stated, lest the taking of the root ‘rā’ in the sense of ‘ādāne’ (in giving) also be understood, he says: ‘rāna,’ and so forth.

110. Vacā

110. Vacā

Sutte ‘vassā’ti sassarova gayhatīti dassetumāha- ‘vassāti hī’tiādi.

To show that in the sutta, ‘vassā’ is taken as the form with the letter ‘sa,’ he says: ‘vassāti hi,’ and so forth.

112. Vaddha

112. Vaddha

Vatta=vattanetīmasmā ttippaccaye vā ukāro na vihitoti āsayena ‘katha’miccādi vuttanti dassento āha- ‘vattavattaneti’ccādi. Vuttimatteti nipātanāti “sabbādayo vuttimatte” tettha (3-69) ‘vuttimatte’ti nipātanā. Ṭhā=gatinivattiyanti ettha ‘gatinivattiya’nti nipātanā pakkhe ukāro na hoti, tenāha- ‘vattī’tiādi. Vattanaṃ vutti vatti.

He says ‘vattavattaneti,’ etc., to show that the question ‘kathaṃ,’ etc., was asked with the intention that from this root ‘vatta’ in the sense of ‘vattane,’ the letter ‘u’ is not prescribed for the ‘tti’ suffix. ‘Vuttimatte’ is an irregular formation, for in the sutta “sabbādayo vuttimatte” (3-69), ‘vuttimatte’ is an irregular formation. The root ‘ṭhā’ is in the sense of ‘gatinivatti’ (cessation of movement); here, because ‘gatinivattiya’ is an irregular formation, in that case the letter ‘u’ is not present; therefore, he says: ‘vattī,’ etc. Vattanaṃ is vutti or vatti.

113. Yaja

113. Yaja

Kassa sabbassāti āha- ‘ya akārāna’nti.

To the question, “Kassa sabbassa?” he says: “ya akārāna.”

115. Gāpā

115. Gāpā

Byattiniddesenāti iminā jātiniddesassānissitattaṃ dasseti. Īsseccādinā vuttiganthassādhippāyaṃ vivarati.

By this, ‘byattiniddesena’ (by designation of the individual), he shows the non-reliance of the designation of genus. With ‘īssa,’ etc., he explains the intention of the Vutti text.

117. Sāsa

117. Sāsa

Satthaṃ [M 0.0267] “byañjane dīgharassā”ti (1-33) rasso.

In the word ‘satthaṃ,’ the vowel is shortened by the rule “byañjane dīgharassā” (1-33).

120. Ñā

120. Ñā

“Nto kattari vattamāne”ti (5-64) ntoti sambandho.

The word ‘nto’ from the sutta “Nto kattari vattamāne” (5-64) is to be connected here.

121. Sakā

121. Sakā

Kukppaccaye antakakāro kuppaccaye ādikakāro antāvayavattho.

In the suffix ‘kuk,’ the final letter ‘ka’ is the initial letter ‘ka’ in the suffix ‘ku’; it has the meaning of the final part.

122. Nīto

122. Nīto

Nāññatracayādīsūti nicchayato-ññesu aññasmiṃ cayādīsvatthesu cho na bhavatīti attho.

The meaning of ‘nāññatracayādīsu’ is that the suffix ‘cha’ certainly does not occur in meanings other than ‘caya’ and so forth.

123. Jara

123. Jara

Īmhi jasadde akārassa lopo, le tu jīrāpayati. Tassātikyassa.

When ‘ī’ follows, there is elision of the letter ‘a’ of the word ‘jara.’ But when ‘le’ follows, it becomes ‘jīrāpayati.’ This is the exception.

124. Disassa

124. Disassa

Diṭṭhi dassanaṃ, dassanāya daṭṭhuṃ. “Saramhā dve”ti (1-34) dvitte duddaso. “Ā ī”ccādinā (6-33) īssa rasso (addakkhi). Dakkhissati “bhavissati ssati”ccādinā, (6-2) ssati.

‘Diṭṭhi’ is seeing; ‘dassanāya’ is for seeing; ‘daṭṭhuṃ’ is to see. By the rule “saramhā dve” (1-34), with reduplication, the form is ‘duddaso.’ By the rule “ā ī,” etc. (6-33), the long ‘ī’ is shortened (as in ‘addakkhi’). ‘Dakkhissati’ is formed with ‘ssati’ by the rule “bhavissati ssati,” etc. (6-2).

125. Samā

125. Samā

Vādassareti vikappena dakārassa rādese.

In the case of ‘vādassara,’ there is the optional substitution of the letter ‘ra’ for the letter ‘da.’

127. Ana

127. Ana

Dassātyananuvattamānepi dasseva pappoti vacanabalenāti dassetuṃ pakkhantaramāha- ‘ādissā’tiādi. Anaghaṇsu paresu āparīhi dassāniyamena ḷoccāsaṅkiya nevaṃ, yathākkamameva nissitoti dassetumāha- ‘anaghaṇsu’ccādi. Āparassāti ākārato parassa dassa.

To show that even though ‘dassāti’ is not carried forward, ‘dassa’ itself is obtained by the force of the statement, he states another alternative: ‘ādissā,’ etc. Lest it be suspected that, in the case of forms not taken that follow, by the rule of showing through what follows, ‘ḷo’ would also apply, he says ‘anaghaṇsu,’ etc., to show that it is not so and that it is based on the proper order. ‘Āparassa’ means: of the root ‘dassa’ which follows the letter ‘ā’.

128. Atyā

128. Atyā

Vuttiyaṃ etasmiṃ visayeti ettha etasminti tyādintavajjitapaccaya visayeti attho. Viññāyamānattā ñāpito hotīti gamyate. Na [M 0.0268] ñāpakatoti iminā idaṃ dasseti “kiñci vacanānusārato viññāyamānatāmattena ñāpīyate kiñci ñāpakena, asmimpakkhe vuttānusārato katthaci kassaci dhātuno appayogo viññāpīyatī”ti. Pakkhantaramāha- ‘ñāpakattāyeva vā’tiādi. Samattheti tathāhiccādinā. Asassāppayogoti asadhātussa kismiñci tabbādike paccaye pare bhavitabbantiādīnamappayogoti attho.

In the commentary, in the phrase `etasmiṃ visaye`, the meaning of `etasmin` is 'in the sphere of suffixes, excluding those ending in `tya`, and so on'. It is understood that it is made known because it is cognized. By this phrase, `na ñāpakato`, he shows the following: “Something is made known merely by being cognized in accordance with a statement, while something else is made known by an indicator. In this alternative, in accordance with what has been said, the non-application of some root in some case is made known.” He states another alternative: “or just by being an indicator,” etc. He supports this with `tathāhi`, etc. `Asassa appayogo` means the non-application of the root `as` when a suffix such as `tabba` follows, that is, the non-application of forms such as `bhavitabbaṃ`.

Vināpi suttanti “atyādī”tiādikaṃ suttaṃ vināpi. Evaṃ maññate “asassa bhūādesena sādhīyamānaṃ sabbamiṭṭhaṃ bahulādhikārato bhūdhātunāva sijjhati vināpi bhūādesasuttantaranti katthaci kassaci appayogassa ñāpakattampissa yujjati aññattha karīyamānamihāpi atthavantaṃ siyā”ti.

`Vināpi suttaṃ` means even without the sutta beginning with `atyādi`, etc. One thinks thus: “All desired forms, being accomplished by the substitution of `bhū` for `as`, are achieved by the root `bhū` itself, due to the governing rule of `bahula`, even without another sutta for the substitution of `bhū`. Its role as an indicator of non-application in some cases is also fitting; what is done elsewhere might also be meaningful here.”

Yeti dhātuppayogā yasminti visaye, pātissāti ‘pā-rakkhaṇe’tīmassa, nappayogo pāyayati pāyayitabbantiādippayogo na hotīti. Evamuparipi yathāyogaṃ ñeyyaṃ. Brūssāti ‘brū=vacane’iccassa. Adissāti ‘ada-bhakkhaṇe’iccassa. Īādīti bhūte īādi. Etissa ca īādīsūti sambandho.

`Ye` refers to the sphere in which the application of roots occurs. `Pātissāti` refers to this root `pā` in the sense of ‘to protect’; `nappayogo` means non-application, that is, the application of forms like `pāyayati`, `pāyayitabbaṃ`, etc., does not occur. Thus, what follows should also be understood as appropriate. `Brūssāti` refers to this root `brū` in the sense of ‘to speak.’ `Adissāti` refers to this root `ada` in the sense of ‘to eat.’ `Īādi` means `ī`, etc., in the past tense. And this is connected with `īādīsu`.

Avabodhe etissa ṇisesu ca īādīsu ca, ajjhene etissa parokkhāsu ca ṇisesu ca īādīsucāti yojetabbaṃ. Sabbattha nappayogoti yojetvā attho veditabbo. Bahulaṃvidhānato ñātabbāti yojanā. Yakvikaraṇena niddesā ‘asa-kkhepanetī massā’ti vuttaṃ, tadāha- ‘asassā’tiādi.

It should be construed thus: in the sense of `avabodha` (understanding), this (non-application) is in the case of `ṇi` suffixes and `ī`, etc.; in the sense of `ajjhena` (study), this is in the case of the perfect tense, `ṇi` suffixes, and `ī`, etc. The meaning should be understood by construing it as ‘non-application everywhere.’ The connection is that it should be known from the `bahula` provision. Because of the designation with the `ya` class-sign, it is said of this root `asa` in the sense of ‘to throw’; therefore, he says: `asassa`, etc.

129. Aā

129. Aā

Ssāti jātiniddesoti āha- ‘ssaiti’ccādi.

`Ssāti` is a generic designation; thus he says: `ssaiti`, etc.

130. Nta

130. Nta

Pubbasaralope rūpassa samānattā antinā antu ca gahitoti ‘santi santū’ti udāharaṇadvayaṃ dassitaṃ.

Due to the similarity of form after the elision of the preceding vowel, `antu` is also included by `anti`; therefore, the two examples `santi` and `santū` are shown.

131. Pādi

131. Pādi

Te ca pādayo jotentīti sambandho. Anvayabyatirekehi kiriyā yadipi dhātunāva vuccatīti sambandho. Kiṃ visiṭṭhā kiriye ccāha- [M 0.0269] ‘sāmaññabhūtā visiṭṭhā vā’ti. So visesoti yena visesena visiṭṭhā kiriyā dhātunāva vuccati so viseso. Vācaka bhedatoti sāmaññāya ca kiriyāya visiṭṭhāya ca vācakānaṃ dhātūnaṃ bhedato tenāpīti kaccānenāpi. Saṇṭhānaṃ saṇṭhiti.

The connection is: “And those prefixes (`pādi`) illuminate.” The connection is: “Although the action is expressed by the root itself, by means of positive and negative concomitance…” He asks what qualifies the action, saying: “whether general or specific.” That specific quality is the specific quality by which the qualified action is expressed by the root itself. `Vācakabhedato` means because of the difference of the roots that express both the general and the specific action. `Tenāpi` means “by him also,” that is, by Kaccāyana also. `Saṇṭhāna` is `saṇṭhiti` (disposition).

141. Kasa

141. Kasa

Kiṭṭhamadatīti kiṭṭhādo, kiṭṭhasaddenupacārato kasitaṭṭhāne uṭṭhita sassaṃ vuccati.

`Kiṭṭhādo` means one who eats grain (`kiṭṭha`). By metaphorical use of the word `kiṭṭha`, the crop that has grown in a plowed place is meant.

142. Dhasto

142. Dhasto

Ṭhassābhāvattaṃ nippaccanteti ajjhāhāro.

The ellipsis to be supplied is that the state of not having `ṭha` is produced.

144. Sāsa

144. Sāsa

Anusāsīyitthāti anusiṭṭho kamme kto “sā sassa sisvā” (5-117) sāsanāya sāsituṃ.

`Anusiṭṭho` is formed from `anusāsīyittha` with the suffix `kta` in the passive, according to the rule “`sā sassa sisvā`” (Kacc 5.117), meaning “to instruct with instruction.”

147. Baha

147. Baha

Atha bahassāti ḍhādesasambandhe chaṭṭhī kasmā na viññāyateti āha- ‘bahassā’tiādi. Ḍhayogapajjenāti ḍhakārena saha yogapajjena ekībhāvenāti attho.

Now, why is the genitive not understood for `bahassa` in connection with the substitution of `ḍha`? He says: `bahassā`, etc. `Ḍhayogapajjenāti` means by being inseparably connected with the letter `ḍha`, that is, in a state of unity.

148. Ruhā

148. Ruhā

Ḷocāti vuttattāti evaṃ maññate “yadāyaṃ paccayādeso siyā tadā ete samāsene-kato niddiseyyā”ti, tenāha- ‘haḷāti vadeyyā’ti.

Because it is said “and `ḷo`,” one thinks thus: “If this were a substitution for a suffix, then he would have designated these together in a compound.” Therefore, he says: “He would say `haḷā`.”

149. Muhā

149. Muhā

Muddhoti “dho hetehī”ti (5-145) tassa dho.

`Muddho` is formed by the rule “`dho hetehī`” (Kacc 5.145), where `ha` becomes `dha`.

150. Bhidā

150. Bhidā

Imassāti ‘pī-tappane’tīmassa, ihāti imasmiṃ ṭhāne. Pinayīti thūlo ahosīti attho sūyīti itisaddo ādyattho, tena adīyi aḍīyi alīyi alūyītime saṅgayhanti. Yāva ktiggahaṇāti “lopo vaḍḍhāktissā”ti (5-158) ktivacanāvadhi.

`Imassa` refers to this root `pī` in the sense of ‘to satisfy, swell.’ `Iha` means ‘here, in this place.’ `Pinayī` means ‘he became stout.’ In `sūyī`, the word `iti` has the sense of ‘etc.,’ by which `adīyi`, `aḍīyi`, `alīyi`, and `alūyī` are included. `Yāva ktiggahaṇā` means up to the limit of the mention of `kti` in the rule “`lopo vaḍḍhāktissā`” (Kacc 5.158).

151. Dātvī

151. Dātvī

Adīyitthāti [M 0.0270] dinno, adadīti dinnavā.

`Dinno` (given) is formed from the passive aorist `adīyittha`; `dinnavā` (one who has given) is formed from the active aorist `adadi`.

152. Kirā

152. Kirā

Akirī, akirīyitthāti vā kiṇṇo, akirīti kiṇṇavā. Apurī purīyitthāti puṇṇo, apurīti puṇṇavā. Akhiyīti khīṇo khīṇavā.

`Kiṇṇo` (scattered) is formed from `akirī` or `akirīyittha`; `kiṇṇavā` (one who has scattered) is from `akirī`. `Puṇṇo` (filled) is from `apurī` or `purīyittha`; `puṇṇavā` (one who has filled) is from `apurī`. From `akhiyī` are formed `khīṇo` (destroyed) and `khīṇavā` (one who has destroyed).

153. Tarā

153. Tarā

Atarī, ajīrīti kamena viggaho. Cīyitthāti ciṇṇo, cinīti ciṇṇavā.

The analysis for `tiṇṇo` and `jiṇṇo` is from `atarī` and `ajīri` respectively. `Ciṇṇo` (piled up) is from `cīyittha`; `ciṇṇavā` (one who has piled up) is from `cinī`.

157. Mucā

157. Mucā

Asakkhīti satto sattavā. ‘Saja=saṅge’tī massāpi satto sattavāti hoti.
