From `asakkhī` are formed `satto` (able) and `sattavā` (one who was able). Also for this root `saj` in the sense of ‘attachment,’ the forms are `satto` (attached; a being) and `sattavā` (one who was attached).

158. Lopo

158. Elision

Vaḍḍhanaṃ vaḍḍhi.

Increase is growth.

159. Kvi

159. Kvi

Abhibhavatīti abhibhū.

He overcomes, therefore he is a conqueror.

162. Māna

162. Māna

Massa lopoti sambandho.

The connection is with the elision of `ma`.

163. Ññila

163. Ññila

Gahetvā ‘gaha-upādāne’gahaṇaṃ katvā gahetvā.

Having grasped: from the root `gah` in the sense of 'to grasp'; having made a grasping, one gets 'having grasped'.

164. Pyo

164. Pyo

Ossaṭṭhānubandhassāti pariccattānubandhassa. Yakāramattassa nivattanatthoti visesanatthotīmassa adhippāyatthamāha. Tathāhi visesanaṃ kevalayakārato visuṃ karaṇaṃ attho yassāti añña padatthe sati kevalayakārassa nivattanaṃ viññāyate. Yakāramatte gahite ko dosoti āha- ‘yo vā tvāssa samāsetihī’tiādi. Patvāti ‘pata patha=gamane, pada=gamane’iccassa vā.

`Ossaṭṭhānubandhassā`'ti means 'of one whose connection is abandoned.' `Yakāramattassa nivattanattho`'ti means 'for the purpose of excluding the mere letter `ya`'; this states its intended meaning. For a qualifier is that which has the meaning of making something distinct from the mere letter `ya`; when the meaning of another word is present, the exclusion of the mere letter `ya` is understood. 'What fault is there if only the letter `ya` is taken?' he asks, beginning with 'yo vā tvāssa samāsetihī...' and so on. `Patvā`'ti means 'having reached,' and is derived from the roots `pat`, `path`, or `pad`, meaning 'to go'.

165. Tuṃ

165. Tuṃ

Tayopīti tuṃyāna raccā.

The three are also `tuṃ`, `yāna`, and `ra`.

169. Disā

169. Direction

Nāppakketi [M 0.0271] na appatte patteyevāti attho. Ñāpakālopoti “titālīsā”ti (1-1) ñāpakatoyeva ktvāppaccayassa yo vakāro tassa lopoti attho.

`Nāppakke`'ti does not mean 'unreached'; the meaning is 'indeed reached.' Elision by an indicator means that on the authority of the indicator 'titālīsā' (1-1), the `va` of the suffix `-tvā` is elided.

171. Rā na

171. Rā, na

Nanu nassāti vutte paccayanakārassāti kathaṃ viññāyatīti āha- ‘nassā’tiādi,ntamānatyādīnaṃ paccayānaṃ nassa “nantamānatyādīna”nti (5-172) ṇattapaṭisedhā viññāyati pakaraṇatoti pakāroti (potthake) āha- ‘paccayanakārovā’ti.

He asks: 'Surely, when `nassa` is stated, how is it understood as referring to the `na` of a suffix?' He replies: beginning with 'nassā' and so on, it is understood from the context—from the prohibition of cerebralization in the rule 'nantamānatyādīnaṃ' (5-172)—that it is the `na` of suffixes such as `-nta`, `-māna`, `-tya`, etc., that is meant. Or he says: 'it is the `na` of a suffix'.

173. Gama

173. Gama

Icchīyateti icchitabbaṃ. Esanaṃ icchā. Icchīyitthāti icchitaṃ, āsanamāsitabbaṃ. Āsanāya acchituṃ. “Byañjane dīgharassā”ti (1-33) rasso.

`Icchīyate`'ti means 'it should be desired.' Seeking is desire. `Icchīyitthā`'ti means 'it was desired'; a seat is to be sat upon. To sit on a seat. By the rule 'Byañjane dīgharassā' (1-33), the vowel is shortened.

177. Kara

177. Kara

Amānaparacchakkatte kuruādesena nodāhaṭaṃ. Karānoti “mānassamassā”ti (5-16) malopo. Kasmā ntapubbachakkesu kuru ādesena nodāhaṭanti āha- ‘vavatthite’ccādi.

When it is not a matter of pride or envy of others, it is not exemplified with the substitution of `kuru`. Regarding `karāno`, there is elision of `ma` by the rule 'mānassa massā' (5-16). He asks: 'Why is it not exemplified with the substitution of `kuru` in the preceding cases involving `-nta`?' and replies: 'Because it is established,' etc.

179. Ṇo

179. Ṇo

Niggahītassāti “mañcarudhādīna”nti (5-19) kataniggahītassa. Gahaṇīyaṃ gaṇhitabbaṃ.

`Niggahītassā`'ti refers to the `niggahīta` formed by the rule 'mañcarudhādīnaṃ' (5-19). `Gahaṇīyaṃ` means 'what should be grasped'.

Iti moggallānapañcikāṭīkāyaṃ sāratthavilāsiniyaṃ

Thus in the Sāratthavilāsinī, the subcommentary on the Moggallānapañcikā.

Pañcamakaṇḍavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Fifth Chapter is concluded.

Chaṭṭhakaṇḍa

The Sixth Chapter

1. Vatta

1. Present Tense

Tadatthassevāti tassa kriyatthassa. Yo kiriyāsaṅkhāto atto tasseva. Etena ādhārametaṃ kriyatthassāti ñāpeti. Nahiccādinā tadatthasseva visesane kāraṇamāha. Suttaṃvinātiparesaṃviya [M 0.0272] suttaṃ vinā. Tāpi vattamāneyeva bhavissantīti iminā vattumiṭṭhattāti ettha sesavacanamavabodheti. Evakārenā (ti vattamānassevāti ettha evasaddena.) Tabbivacchāti vattamānavacanicchā.

`Tadatthassevā`'ti means 'of that very meaning of action.' For that very meaning which is designated as action. By this, he indicates that this is the basis for the meaning of action. Beginning with 'nahi...,' he states the reason for the qualification 'of that very meaning.' Like others without a sutta, it is without a sutta. With the words 'Even they will exist only in the present,' he explains the implied meaning here in the phrase 'because it is desired to be said.' By the word `eva` (that is, by the word `eva` in `vattamānasseva`). `Tabbivacchā`'ti means 'the desire to speak in the present'.

Taṃsamīpassāti ettha tasaddena mahākassapassa subhaddavacanānussaraṇasaṅkhāto maraṇappattihetu dukkhānubhavasaṅkhāto ca kiriyāviseso pariggahito, te vā vattamānakiriyāvisesāti tesamubhinnamāsannāni kamena adhammadīpanamaraṇāni, tenāha-dīpana maraṇānamāsannattā’ti. Evaṃ maññate “takkālavattamānakiriyāvisesassa dīpanamaraṇasaṅkhātaṃ taṃsamīpatāvipi kiriyantaraṃ vattamānaggahaṇena taṃsāmīpyaṃ gayhati, yathā (gaṅgāsamīpo) deso gaṅgāti vuccati tato ‘gaṅgāyaṃ gāvo’ti siyā”ti. Pure iccādinā pakkhantaraṃ viracitaṃ vuttikārena, tadupadassetuṃ mukhayati ‘sabhāvato’ iccādi.

Here, in 'taṃsamīpassa', the word 'taṃ' is taken to refer to the specific action which is the recollection of Subhadda's words by Mahākassapa, and to the specific action which is the experience of suffering, the cause of his approaching death. Or, it refers to those two specific actions as occurring in the present. For those two, the expounding and death are imminent, respectively. Therefore, he says: 'because of the imminence of the expounding and death.' Thus it is thought: 'By the term 'present,' the proximity is grasped of the specific action occurring at that time, designated as the expounding and death, and even of another action in its proximity, just as a region near the Ganges is called 'Ganges,' from which one might say, 'cows in the Ganges'.' Previously, beginning with 'pure...', the commentator constructed another alternative; to introduce that, he begins with 'sabhāvato...' etc.

Kiriyākāloti vattamānakiriyākālo. Avasissatīti purepurāsaddehi dīpitaanāgatakālato avasissati. Kiriyā kāleti dīpanamaraṇakiriyākāle. Tassāti dīpanamaraṇassa. Vattamānattāti ettha vattamāneyeva bhavissantīti seso. Anenāti pureccādivuttivacanena. Purepurāsaddehi anāgatakālāvagame sati dippati maratīti ettha dīpanamaraṇakiriyākālo mukhye tadā vattatītiāha- ‘mukhyaṃ vattamānattamāhe’ti. Puna pakkhantaramupanītaṃ kāleccādinā vuttikārena, tamupadassetuṃ mukhamāvattayati ‘anāgate’ccādi.

'The time of action' means the present time of action. 'Avasissati' means it remains from the future time indicated by the words 'pure' and 'purā'. 'At the time of action' means at the time of the action of expounding and dying. 'Of that' means of the expounding and dying. 'Because it is present': here the ellipsis implies 'they will exist in the present itself.' 'By this' means by the commentator's statement beginning with 'pure...'. When the future time is understood through the words 'pure' and 'purā', then in 'dippati marati' (he expounds, he dies), the time of the action of expounding and dying is primarily present at that time; hence he says: 'he states it is the primary present.' Again, another alternative is introduced by the commentator with the word 'kāle...'; to show that, he directs attention to it, beginning with 'anāgate...'.

Vuttiyaṃ kālabyattayoti kālātivattanaṃ, vattamānakālātikkamena anāgatakālepi bāhulakātyādayo hontīti adhippāyo. Tadeva samattheti ‘bhavanteva’iccādinā. Tyādayotīminā sabbesaṃ ākhyātikānaṃ gahaṇaṃ. Lassa dīghoti sambandho. Gacchatīti sakkassa sahabhāvaṃ gamissatīti attho.

In the commentary, 'kālabyattayo' means the transgression of time; the intention is that, by the principle of varied application, suffixes such as -tya and so on also occur in future time, transgressing the present. He supports this very point beginning with 'bhavanteva...'. By 'tyādayo', all verbal endings are included. The connection is with the lengthening of 'la'. 'Gacchati' means 'he will go to companionship with Sakka'.

3. Nāme

3. On Nāma

Paṭijānissantīti vattamāne anāgatavacanaṃ, paṭijānantīti attho. Itarampana bhūte bhavissatīti āsi, karissatīti akari, cete ssasīti [M 0.0273] cetitā asi, bhuñjissasīti bhuñjitā asi. Anokappanā assaddhā. Amarisanaṃ akkhamā. Imināvāti atthivacane upapade kodhā saddhāsu gammamānesva-satīpi vacanantare imināva sāmaññavacanena siddhanti attho. Garahāvamāti tassa hetuvacanaṃ. Tathāhiccādinā garahāvagamameva samattheti. Atthināma īdisanti atthināmāti (potthake) ābhidosikassa kummāsassa paribhuñjanaṃ vijjate nāmāti attho. Vijjamānampi taṃ asaddahanto amarisanto evaṃ vadati. Natthīti maññeti adhippāyo, tenāha- ‘paccakkhamapī’ti īdisampīti ādi. Yopīti saddassa sopīti tasaddena sambandho veditabbo. Atthīti vijjamānattheti vuttavijjamānattho vakkhamānapakkhattayepi daṭṭhabbo.

'They will acknowledge': this is a future tense expression used in the sense of the present; the meaning is 'they acknowledge.' Similarly, in other cases, for the past tense, 'there will be' means 'there was'; 'he will do' means 'he did'; 'you will think' means 'you have thought'; 'you will eat' means 'you have eaten.' 'Anokappanā' is lack of faith. 'Amarisanaṃ' is intolerance. 'By this very': when the word 'atthi' is a preceding word, and when anger and faith are understood, even if another word is absent, the meaning is accomplished by this general expression. 'Garahāvamā' is the reason for that. By 'tathāhi,' etc., it supports the understanding of blame. 'Is there indeed such a thing?': the meaning is, 'Does the partaking of stale porridge indeed exist?' Although it exists, one who lacks faith and is intolerant speaks thus. The intention is, 'he thinks it does not exist'; therefore it is said, 'even when directly perceived,' etc. The word 'yopi' should be understood as connected with the word 'so' in 'sopi.' 'Atthi' is in the sense of 'existing'; this stated sense of 'existing' should be seen also in the three alternatives to be mentioned.

Nanu atthināma tātāti ettake vutte paṭhamo atthinukhoccādiko nisīditvāti saddapariyanto ca, dutiyo atthinukhoccādiko nisīditvāti saddapariyanto ca tatiyo atthimaññeccādiko jigucchaneyyanti saddapariyanto ca vacanappabandho kathaṃ labbhatīti manasi nidhāyāha- ‘sopanā’tiādi. Imināti ‘atthiyevihāpi nindāvagamo’ti vacanena. Ṭhānabhojane garahatīti sambandho. Vuttaṃ sakkatānusārena. Nissāyanissāyāti yattha bhagavā nisinno taṃ ṭhānaṃ nissāya nissāya.

When only 'But isn't there, dear?' has been said, keeping in mind the question, 'How is the connected discourse obtained, consisting of the first part beginning with "is there, I wonder?" and ending with the word "having sat down"; and the second part beginning with "is there, I wonder?" and ending with the word "having sat down"; and the third part beginning with "thinking it is" and ending with the word "one would be disgusted"?', he said: 'the staircase,' etc. 'By this' means by the statement 'there is understanding of blame even from a bone.' The connection is: 'he blames the place and the meal.' It is said in accordance with the honored tradition. 'Relying and relying' means: relying again and again on the place where the Blessed One was seated.

4. Bhūte

4. In the Past Tense

Kiriyārūpeti kiriyāsabhāve, evamaññatrāpīti agami agamitthātīmehi aññatra agamuṃ iccādike agamoccādike ca. Anudarā alomikāti santamapyudarādikaṃ mahattābhāvapaṭipādanāya bahuttā bhāvapaṭipādanāya ca na vattumicchīyate.

'In the form of an action' means in the nature of an action. 'Thus elsewhere too' means: elsewhere than these, 'agami' (he went) and 'agamitthā' (he/she went), such as in 'agamuṃ' (they went), etc., and 'agamo' (he went), etc. 'Without a belly, without hair': although a belly and so on exist, it is not wished to be stated in order to demonstrate the absence of greatness and to demonstrate the absence of abundance.

5. Ana

5. Ana

Aññapadatthavuttiyāti vuttamaññapadatthaṃ dasseti ‘vakkhamānalakkhaṇo’ccādinā. Vakkhamānalakkhaṇotivuttikārena “āñāyyā”ccādinā vakkhamānalakkhaṇo. Antokatvāti iminā āsaddassābhividhimhi pavattimāha. Aharubhayataḍḍharattaṃ vāti ettha vāsaddo pakkhantare. Aḍḍharattasaddena [M 0.0274] rattiyā catuttho bhāgo-tra vattumiṭṭho, aho ca tassa aḍḍharattañcāti attho. Imassādhippāyatthamāha- ‘atīteccādi. Ubhayattha adhippāyaṃ vivarati‘aya’miccādinā. Pañcayāmoti atītāya rattiyā pacchimapañcacattālīsavināḍikādhikaghaṭikāttayaṃ anāgatāya purimapañcacattālīsavināḍikādhikaghaṭikatthayañceti aḍḍhādhikasattaghaṭikāparimāṇo eko yāmo ahassa cattāroti pañca yāmā pahārā assāti pañcayāmo.

'Functioning with the meaning of another word': he shows the stated meaning of another word with 'having the characteristic to be explained,' etc. 'Having the characteristic to be explained': by the commentator, with 'āñāyya,' etc., it has the characteristic to be explained. 'Having included': by this, he states the application of the word 'ā' in the sense of 'inclusive limit.' 'Both day and half the night': here the word 'vā' indicates an alternative. By the word 'aḍḍharatta' (half-night), a fourth part of the night is intended to be expressed here; the meaning is 'a day and its half-night.' To clarify the meaning of this, he says: 'past,' etc. He explains the intention in both cases with 'this,' etc. 'Having five watches' (pañcayāmo): three ghaṭikās plus forty-five vināḍikās of the last part of the past night, and three ghaṭikās plus forty-five vināḍikās of the first part of the coming night—thus one watch (yāma) is a measure of seven and a half ghaṭikās. Since a day has four, 'it has five watches (yāma) or periods (pahāra),' thus 'pañcayāmo'.

Gatāyapacchimo yāmo, pacchimaddhamimassa vā;

Pahāro-nāgatāyādī, tadaddhamapi vā tathā.

The last watch of the night that has passed, or the latter half of this day; a watch is the beginning of the night that has not yet come, or likewise half of that as well.

Vuttakālāvadhi majjho, kālo so-jjatano mato;

Tannisedhena yotvañño, so-najjatano mato.

The time in the middle, with the limits just stated, is considered 'today'; whatever other time there is, by the negation of that, is considered 'not today'.

Agamatthātiādīsu aīssaādīnaṃ sambandhibyañjanassābhāvā na iña. Byāmissepīti ajjatanamissepi bhūte. Nañsamāsanissaye byāmisse yathā pappotīti dassento āha- ‘pariyudāsetāve’ccādi.

In cases like 'agamatthā,' because of the absence of a connecting consonant for 'a-ī,' etc., it is not 'i-ña.' 'Even in a mixed tense': even in the past mixed with the 'today' tense. Showing how it applies in a mixed tense dependent on a negative compound, he says: 'pariyudāsetāve,' etc.

Ajjatananissayoti byāmisse ajjatanabhāgīnissayo. Atthuti pañhe tu tadaññanissayoti byāmisseyeva tato ajjatanato itarānajjatana nissayo aññatrāti byāmissato aññatra bhūtakāle. Pasaṅgoti ā ñuādīnaṃ pasaṅgo. Ajjahiyyovāti byāmissatādassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ.

'Dependent on 'today'': in a mixed tense, it is dependent on the part that is 'today.' But in the question 'atthu,' it is 'dependent on the other': in a mixed tense itself, it is dependent on the 'not today' part, which is other than the 'today' part. 'Elsewhere' means in past time, other than the mixed tense. 'Application' means the application of 'ā,' 'ñu,' etc. 'Ajjahiyyo vā' is said to show the state of being mixed.

6. Paro

6. Remote Past

Samāsoti chaṭṭhīsamāso kārakasamāso vā. Nipātanatā cāssa visesatoti. Etañcāti parokkheti etañca. Kriyatthassa upādhi visesanaṃ kriyatthopādhi, tassa kriyatthopādhino bhūtā najjatanassa sādhanadvārena visesanaṃ, na tūjukaṃtyattho. Kasmā nojukaṃ visesanaṃ tyāha ‘byavacchejjābhāvā’ti. Tameva phuṭayitumāha- ‘tathāhi’ccādi.

'Compound': it is a genitive compound or a case compound. And its specialty is its being an irregular formation. 'And this': and this in 'parokkhe' (in the remote past). A qualifier of the meaning of the action is a 'kriyatthopādhi.' For that 'kriyatthopādhi,' the qualification of the past that is not 'today' is by way of the means of accomplishment, not directly; this is the meaning. Why is it not a direct qualification? He says: 'because there is nothing to be distinguished.' To make that clear, he says: 'for indeed,' etc.

Sādhiyamānāti iminā dhātvatthassāparinipphannataṃ bodheti. Te santi indriyānaṃ. Santo vijjamāno visayo yesaṃ indriyānaṃ te sambhāvo [M 0.0275] tattaṃ, tasmā. Neti paṭisedhe, sādhanadvārena visesanatte byavacchejjasabbhāvā yathāvuttadoso na bhavatīti attho. Dosā bhāvameva dassetumāha- ‘yassi’ccādi. Yassāti dhātvatthassa. Tatthāti tasmiṃ appaccakkhe dhātvatthe. Kārakānaṃ sattisabhāvattā sāpi apaccakkhā vāti codeti nanuceccādinā. Asattoti asamattho.

'Being accomplished': by this he indicates the uncompleted nature of the root-meaning. They exist for the faculties. The faculties for which an existing, present object exists—that is their state, their essence; therefore. 'Na' is in the sense of negation. Because there is something to be distinguished when there is qualification by way of the means of accomplishment, the aforesaid fault does not arise; this is the meaning. To show the very absence of the fault, he says: 'yassa,' etc. 'Yassa' refers to the root-meaning. 'Tattha' means in that unperceived root-meaning. Because agents have the nature of a capacity, that too is unperceived—thus he raises an objection with 'nanu,' etc. 'Asatto' means incapable.

Attānāma attano paccakkhoti tabbisaye amhakārakassa vidhānamayuttanti manasi nidhāya yaṃ vuttaṃ vuttikārena, tamupadassetumāha- ‘nanuce’ccādi. Attabodhanīyāpi hi kiriyā yadā cittavikkhepato nopalakkhīyate, tadāyaṃ parokkhā bhavati, tenuttamavisayepi parokkhabhāvo tassā bhavatveva. Jāgaratopi yadā madā manobyātaṅgato anupaladdhi, tadāpi bhavatyeveti dassetuṃ vuttaṃ byāsattavacanaṃ. Abhinibbattikāleti kiriyā nibbattikāle, ‘sutto-haṃ kiṃ vilalāpa, matto-haṃ kiṃvilalāpe’ti idamatrodāharaṇaṃ. Citta cikkhepavisayappadassanāyettha suttavacanaṃ.

Keeping in mind that 'the self, indeed, is directly perceived by oneself, so in that sphere the prescription of the first person is inappropriate,' to show what was said by the commentator, he says: 'nanu,' etc. For even an action that should be known by oneself, when it is not noticed due to mental distraction, becomes remote. Therefore, even in the sphere of the first person, its remoteness certainly occurs. To show that it also occurs even for one who is awake, when there is non-perception due to intoxication or mental affliction, the statement about being engrossed is made. 'At the time of its production' means at the time the action is produced. 'Did I, while sleeping, babble something? Did I, while intoxicated, babble something?'—this is the example here. Here, the word 'sleeping' is to show the sphere of mental distraction.

7. Eyyā

7. Eyyā

Eyyādotīminā eyyādyattho gahitoti bodhetuṃ yeneccādikaṃ vuttaṃ. Nimittasaddāpekkhāya tanti vattabbe visayasaddāpekkhāyasoti vuttaṃ. Tesanti eyyādīnaṃ. Visayaṃ dasseti ‘hetuphalesviccādiko’ti. Ādisaddena pañhapatthanādayo gahitā. Athātra kriyaggahaṇābhāve kriyātipattiyanti kathaṃ labbhaticcāha- ‘kriyāti pattiya’nti ādi. Kriyātipattiyanti vivaraṇaṃ katanti sambandho.

The phrase beginning with 'yena' is stated to show that by 'eyyādo,' the meaning of 'eyyādi' is grasped. Although it should be stated with reference to the indicative word, it is stated with reference to the word for the domain. 'Tesaṃ' refers to 'eyyādīnaṃ.' He shows the domain with 'in cause and effect,' etc. By the word 'ādi,' questions, requests, and so on are included. Now, since 'action' is not mentioned here, how is 'transgression of action' obtained? He says: 'transgression of action,' etc. The connection is that 'transgression of action' is made as an explanation.

Abhidheyyadvārenāti kiriyāsaṅkhātaatthamukhena, pakatakriyattha visesanattāti kriyatthādhikārato adhikatassa dhātussa visesanattā. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti “atipattiyanti adhikatakriyatthavisesanaṃ, visesanañca hontaṃ nojukaṃ bhavitumarahati kiñcarahi abhidheyyadvārena, tathāhi atipatanaṃ nāma kriyāya hoti, na kriyatthassa ayujjanato, tasmā atipattiyantivuttekriyātipatti yanti [M 0.0276] idaṃ kriyatthavisesanaṃ hontaṃ abhidheyyadvārena hotīti kriyātipattiyanti vivaraṇaṃ kata”nti. Vidhurappaccayopanipātatoti viruddhappaccayasamavāyāti attho.

‘Through the means of what is expressed’ means through the aspect of the meaning designated as ‘action.’ ‘Because it is a qualifier of the established meaning of the action’ means because it is a qualifier of the root that has an additional meaning on account of the governing rule concerning the meaning of action. This is what is meant: ‘transgression’ is a qualifier of the additional meaning of the action. And being a qualifier, it cannot be direct. How so? Through the means of what is expressed. For ‘transgression’ pertains to an action, not to a non-conjunction with the meaning of the action. Therefore, when ‘transgression’ is stated, this qualification of the meaning of the action occurs through the means of what is expressed. Thus, ‘transgression of action’ is stated as an explanation. ‘Due to the occurrence of a contrary condition’ means ‘due to the conjunction of opposing conditions’; that is the meaning.

Kāraṇavekallatovāti hetumato phalassa yo hetu tassa vikalattena. Tatretīmassa attho vattamānavisayeti. Kriyātipattiyanti bhūtādi kriyātipattiyaṃ. Liṅgatoti nimittena. Gamakena liṅgena gammāyātipattiyā bujjhanakālaṃ vattamāno kālo na tiṭṭhati atikkamatīti āha- ‘vattamānatāya byatikkamā’ti. Tadeva phuṭayati ‘samakāla’ntiādinā. Samakālanti ekakkhaṇe. Vattamānassa kriyātipatyasambhavā tadavasiṭṭhātītānāgatesveyyādīnambhāvo (aññathā) nupapattiyāti vuttaṃ vuttiyaṃ ‘sāmatthiyātiādi.

‘Due to a deficiency in the cause’ means due to the deficiency of the cause of an effect that has a cause. The meaning here concerns the present domain. ‘Transgression of action’ means transgression of action in the past, etc. ‘By a sign’ means by an indicator. Since the present moment does not stand still at the time of understanding the transgression—which is to be inferred by an indicative sign—but passes by, he says: ‘due to the passing of the present state.’ He clarifies this same point with ‘simultaneous,’ etc. ‘Simultaneous’ means in a single moment. Because transgression of action is impossible in the present, the occurrence of ‘eyyādi’ in the remaining past and future would otherwise be inexplicable. Thus it is said in the commentary: ‘by capacity,’ etc.

Liṅgenāti ettha pubbe dakkhiṇena gamane sati sakaṭissāpariyā bhavanadassanaṃ dakkhiṇena gamanassa sakaṭāpariyābhavanahetutte liṅgaṃ, dakkhiṇena gamanassātipattiyā aññato gamanādi liṅgaṃ. Sakaṭā kiriyābhavanātipattiyā sakaṭe garubhārāropanādi liṅgaṃ. Paṭhamavaye arahattabhavanaṃ taṃhetubhūtañca pabbajjaṃ paresaṃ paṭhamavaye pabbajjānimittārahattappattiliṅgena viññāya pabbajjāyātipatti gharakammabyāvaṭatādiliṅgena, arahattassātipatti ca pabbajjānimittābhāvena bhāvavirahena (potthake) liṅgenāvasīyateti liṅgena bhūta kriyātipatti pana veditabbā, yadi panevamabhiññālābhī payuñjati tadā paccakkhañāṇeneva sabbaṃ viññāya payuñjatīti veditabbaṃ. Liṅgatovasīyamānāyanti pana bāhullena vuttaṃ.

‘By a sign’: Here, when there was a previous going to the right, the observation that the cart did not turn is a sign that going to the right is the cause for the cart's not turning. The transgression of going to the right is indicated by a sign such as going elsewhere. The transgression of the non-occurrence of the cart's action is indicated by a sign such as loading a heavy burden on the cart. For others, the transgression of the going forth in the first stage of life—which is a sign for attaining arahantship—is known by a sign such as being occupied with household work; and the transgression of arahantship is determined by the sign of the absence of the indicator for going forth. Thus the transgression of a past action should be understood by a sign. But if one who has attained the higher knowledges uses this, it should be understood that they use it having known everything directly by personal knowledge. However, ‘being determined by a sign’ is said in a general sense.

8. Hetu

8. Cause

Niccabhavanaṃ hetu (tyādinā) hetuphalabhāvoyevettha, nāti pattīti dīpeti. Sabbappaccayodāharaṇavasenāti sabbesaṃ eyyādīnampaccayānaṃ udāharaṇavasena. Hetuphalānaṃ sabbhāvatoti vuttattā hetuphalāni dasseti hananamiccādinā. Evaṃ hetuphalasabbhāvato sabbakāle [M 0.0277] ca vidhānato ettha vattamānepi pappotīti bhāvo. So ca hetuhetumantabhāvo ca.

By the phrase ‘the cause is always productive,’ etc., he shows that here there is just the state of cause and effect, not transgression. ‘By way of example of all conditions’ means by way of example of all the conditions for ‘eyyādi,’ etc. Because it is said ‘due to the existence of cause and effect,’ he shows the causes and effects with ‘killing,’ etc. Thus, because of the existence of cause and effect and because of its application at all times, the sense is that it obtains even in the present. And that is the state of cause and that which has a cause.

9. Pañhe

9. In a Question

Pacchimaṃ pacchimaṃ padantiādīsu pañhoti purimaṃ padaṃ, sampucchanāti pacchimaṃ padantiādinā daṭṭhabbaṃ. Samecca aññamaññaṃ pucchanā sampucchanā, yācanaṃ dehī tyādinā yācanamatthaṃ, iṭṭhassāsampattassātthanamiṭṭhāsiṃsanaṃ. Pattakālavasena ca visayabhedena bhinnāya pīti yojetvā attho daṭṭhabbo. Pattakālaṃ dasseti nimittabhūtassātiādinā. Nimittabhūtassāti taṃtaṃkiccasampajjane kāraṇabhūtassa. Vidhi nāma diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyika nimantaṇāmantaṇājjhesanapesanāni. Ettha ca anuññāpattakālesu ca pañcamī vihitā parehi, diṭṭhadhammikādīsu pañcasu sattamī. Idha pana te dvepi vidhivisesāyevāti vidhimhi antokaritvā eyyādiṃ vidhātuṃ yaṃ vuttaṃ vuttikārena, tadidāni vattukāmo āha- ‘anuññāpattakālesupi’ccādi. Vidhippatītimeva pakāseti ‘evaṃ kareyyāsī”ticcādinā. Anujānantopi dīpentopi kiriyāsu byāpāretiyevāti byāpāraṇampatītitoti yojetvā attho veditabbo.

In ‘the latter, the latter phrase,’ etc., ‘question’ is the former phrase, and ‘mutual questioning’ is the latter phrase; this should be understood in this way. Mutual questioning is questioning one another after coming together. Requesting is asking with ‘give,’ etc. Wishing for the agreeable is for the purpose of attaining a desired but unattained object. The meaning should be understood by connecting it, differentiated as it is by way of the appropriate time and the division of the domain. He shows the appropriate time with ‘of that which has become an indicator,’ etc. ‘Of that which has become an indicator’ means of that which has become the cause for the accomplishment of this or that task. ‘Instruction’ means invitation, prompting, request, and sending on missions concerning things seen in this life and in the next. Here, the fifth case ending is prescribed by others in the senses of permission and appropriate time, and the seventh in the five senses beginning with things seen in this life. But here, since both these two are just specific kinds of instruction, the commentator, wishing now to state what was said about prescribing ‘eyyādi’ by including them under ‘instruction,’ says: ‘even in the senses of permission and appropriate time,’ etc. He reveals the very sense of instruction with ‘you should do thus,’ etc. The meaning should be understood by connecting it thus: since one engages others in actions even when permitting or explaining, it has the sense of ‘engagement’.

Pesanepi kesañci byākaraṇaññūnaṃ sattamīvidhicchitotivuttikārena yaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ dāni vattumāha- ‘pesane pi’ccādi. Samūlatanti kesañci saddikānaṃ sattamīvidhividhānamūlena samūlataṃ. “Anumatiparikappatthesu sattamī”ti (3-1-11) kaccānasuttaṃ. Kattumicchato parassa anujānanaṃ anumati, parikappanaṃ sallakkhaṇaṃ nirūpanaṃ parikappo hetuphalakiriyā sambhavo ca, tasmiṃ anumatyatthe ca parikappatthe ca sattamīvibhatti hotīti attho. Atthaggahaṇena vidhinimantaṇāmantaṇājjhesana patthanāpattakālesu ca.

Wishing now to state what was said by the commentator—that for some who know grammar, the prescription of the seventh case ending is desired even in the sense of ‘sending’—he says: ‘even in sending,’ etc. ‘With a basis’ means it has a basis in the root of the prescription of the seventh case ending for some grammarians. The Kaccāyana sutta says: ‘The seventh case ending is used in the senses of permission and consideration.’ Permission is allowing another who wishes to act. Consideration is examination, determination, planning, and the possibility of cause, effect, and action. The meaning is that the seventh case ending occurs in this sense of permission and in the sense of consideration. By the inclusion of the meaning, it also applies in the cases of instruction, invitation, prompting, request, aspiration, and appropriate time.

10. Tu antu

10. Tu, antu

Udāhaṭāti gacchatu gacchantuādinā udāhaṭā. Dadātūti yācane.

`Udāhaṭā` means illustrated by such examples as `gacchatu` and `gacchantu`. `Dadātu` is in the sense of requesting.

11. Satya

11. Satya

Arahatthe cāyameva payogo, tena bhavaṃ khalu rajjaṃ kareyya bhavaṃ arahoti yojetvā daṭṭhabbo.

This very usage is in the sense of worthiness. Therefore, it should be understood by connecting it thus: 'The venerable one should indeed rule the kingdom; the venerable one is worthy.'

12. Sambhā

12. Sambhā

Yoggatājjhavasānantīmassātthapadaṃ[M 0.0278], sattisaddahananti sāmatthiyassa saddahananti attho. Payogānusāritaṃ dīpetī sambandho. Gammamāneti sambhāvemiccādinā bhvādidhātūhi avuccamānepi gamyamāne. Udāhaṭaṃ ‘apipabbataṃ sirasā bhindeyyā’ti. Mahābalatāya hatthihanane alamatthavisaye sambhāvane satyapi alaṃ saddo-trālamattho yuttoti na bhavantetyādayo hanissati. Dhātunāti ettha dhātuggahaṇena bhvādayo gayhante tattha dhātusaddassa ruḷhattā pubbācariyasaññāya vā. Udāhaṭanti bhuñjeyya bhavaṃ tyādinā.

`Yoggatājjhavasāna` (determination of suitability) is the meaning of this term; `sattisaddahana` means belief in one's capability. The connection clarifies that it is in accordance with usage. `Gammamāne` means: when it is understood even though not expressed by roots of the `bhū` group, as in `sambhāvemi`, etc. An example is: 'One could even split a mountain with one's head.' Although in the context of conjecture regarding killing an elephant due to great strength, the word `alaṃ` is in the sphere of meaning 'sufficient,' here the word `alaṃ` is not fitting in the sense of 'sufficient'; therefore, forms like `hanissati` are not used. `Dhātunā`: here, by the taking up of `dhātu`, the `bhū` group is taken, either because of the conventional meaning of the word `dhātu` or by the designation of previous teachers. An example is: 'The venerable one might eat,' etc.

13. Māyo

13. Māyo

Sūti māsūti ettha susaddo. Ettha imasmiṃ udāharaṇe. Nivatteti māsaddoti seso. Āraddhanti iminā vattamānaṃ vanagamanaṃ dasseti. Antobhūtaṇyatthāti ṇippaccayābhāvepi attani antobhūtaṇyattha dhātuto. Īādīnaṃ āādīnañca sakakālonāma bhūto kālo. Dhātusambandho visesanavisessabhāvo, tenāha- ‘dhātvattha sambandhe visesana visessabhāvalakkhaṇe’ti. Sabbatthākhyāta vāccottho visesso syādyantavācco visesanaṃ.

Regarding `māsu`: here the word is `su`. Here in this example, the word `mā` prevents; this is the remainder. Regarding `āraddhaṃ`: by this, he indicates the going to the forest that has been started. Regarding `antobhūta-ṇi-attho`: from the root itself, it has the meaning of the causative included within it, even in the absence of the `ṇi` suffix. The proper time of the endings `ī`, etc., and the augment `ā`, etc., is the past tense. The connection with the root is a relationship of qualifier and qualified; therefore he said: 'in the connection with the root's meaning, which is characterized by the relationship of qualifier and qualified.' Everywhere, the meaning expressed by the finite verb is the qualified; the meaning expressed by the nominal ending is the qualifier.

Iṭṭhoti paresamiṭṭho. Jānanatthavasena gamanatthattāti “gamanatthā kammakā”ti (5-59) sutte gamanatthasaddena ‘ye gatyatthā te buddhyatthā’ti jānanatthopi gahitoti evaṃ gahitajānanatthavasena gamanatthattāti attho. Abhimatāni pāṇiniyānaṃ. Tathā saddassatthamāha- ‘anantarena gatattha’(nti ana)ntare vuttena karaṇabhūtenāti attho. Abhimatoti pāṇiniyānameva idhādhippetasamuccayaṃ vattumāha- ‘samuccayo’iccādi. Athātra kathamanekāsaṃ kiriyānaṃ cīya mānatā yāvatā ekāvāṭanakiriyājjhayanakiriyā cetyāsaṅkiyāha- ‘sādhanabhedane’ccādi. Maṭhādisādhanānambhedenāṭana kiriyāyapi bhedoti attho. Takkiriyāppadhānassāti sā lavanakiriyā padhānamassa kattuno. Yo- yamaññepi niyojento viya kiriyaṃ karoti so nā-ññakiriyāpadhāne yutto, takkiriyāppadhāneyeveti.

`Iṭṭha` means pleasing to others. Regarding `gamanatthattā`: In the sutta 'those with the meaning of going take an object' (5-59), the term `gamanattha` also includes the meaning of knowing, based on the principle 'those that have the meaning of going also have the meaning of understanding.' Thus, the meaning is that it has the meaning of going by virtue of having the meaning of knowing, which has been included in this way. These are the views of the Pāṇinians. Similarly, he states the meaning of the word: regarding `anantarena gatattha`, the meaning is 'understood by what is immediately preceding,' that is, by what was stated immediately before, which has become the instrument. To state the collection intended here, which is indeed the view of the Pāṇinians, he says: `samuccayo`, etc. Now here, raising the doubt, 'How can there be an accumulation of many actions, since there is only one action of wandering and one action of studying?', he says: `sādhanabhedena`, etc. The meaning is that due to the difference of instruments, such as monasteries, etc., there is also a difference in the action of wandering. Regarding `takkiriyāppadhānassa`: that action of cutting is primary for this agent. He who performs an action as if engaging another is not engaged in another primary action, but only in that primary action.

14. Pubba

14. Former

Mahāvākyarūpattā [M 0.0279] pakaraṇassa tadapekkhāya vākyekadesattaṃ “vattamāne tianti, bhavissati”ccādīnaṃ vākyānanti āha ‘vākyekadesehī’ti. Atoyevamāha-vākyāvayavoparo-dhunā karīyate’ti. Vidhivākyattamassa dassetvā niyamavākyattaṃ dāni dassetuṃ ‘athavā niyamatthamidantyādīna’ntyāha. Niyamasuttattameva phuṭayati ‘tehi’ccādinā. Tehi tehi suttehīti “vattamāne ti anti”ccādīhi tehi tehi suttehi. Imināti “pubbaparā”dinā iminā suttena. Nanu tumhāmhasesesūti ettake vuccamāne ‘tumhāmhasaddavacanīyesu tadaññasaddavacanīyesu ca kārakesū’ti ayaṃ viseso kuto gamyate yenevaṃ vivaṭaṃtyāha- ‘kattukamme’ccādi. Kattādīsu vidhānañca vakkhati.

Because a treatise has the form of a major sentence, he says `vākyekadesehī` (by parts of the sentence), referring to sentences such as `vattamāne ti anti, bhavissati...`, etc., which are parts of a sentence in relation to it. Therefore he says this: 'It is now done by the component part of the sentence.' Having shown its nature as an injunctive statement, now to demonstrate its nature as a restrictive statement, he says: 'Or, this is for the purpose of restriction,' etc. He clarifies its very nature as a restrictive rule with `tehi`, etc. Regarding `tehi tehi suttehi`: by those very suttas, such as `vattamāne ti anti`, etc. Regarding `iminā`: by this sutta, the one beginning with `pubbaparā`. Now, when only `tumhāmhasesesu` is stated, from where is this distinction understood: 'in the factors expressed by the words `tumha` and `amha`, and in the factors expressed by other words'? Thus he explains it with `kattukamme`, etc. And he will state the rule regarding the agent, etc.

Kattukammānamevāti iminā bhāvaṃ byavacchindati. Tathā ca vakkhati- ‘tumhāmhasaddavacanīyattābhāvā’ti. Asatvabhūtāyeccādikamekavacana sambhave kāraṇaṃ, tumhāmheccādikantu paṭhamapurisasambhave. Tumhāmhasesesu hontā majjhimuttamapaṭhamā kathaṃ bhāvādīsu viññāyanti kathañca tumhāmhādisaddavacanīyassa kārakatthassākhyātena tattha vihitena saññāvibhattā tumhāmhādisaddappayogābhāvoccāsaṅkiya yaṃ vuttaṃ vuttiyaṃ taṃdāni vivarantena ‘yadi bhāvādīsu mānādayo na vidhīyante tadāmānādīsu paresu bhāvādīsu kyalādīnaṃ vidhānameva nopapajjatī’ti iminā sāmatthiyena tumhādīsu kārakesu majjhimādīnaṃ bhāvo viññāyati teneva tumhādikārakatthassa tattha vihitenākhyātena saññāpitattā tumhādisaddappayogo nāma na hotīti dassetuṃ ‘tumhādisvi’ccādikamāraddhaṃ. Yajjevaṃ tumhādisaddappayogoyeva na siyā ccāha- ‘yajjeva miccādi. Parihāramāha- ‘sasaddenā’ti. Tumhādisaddena. Brāhmaṇāiccanenābhihitameva bahuttaṃ bahavoti vacanenānujjate. Vacanābhāve kathaṃ tulyādhikaraṇattaṃtyāha- ‘anujjamānassi’ccādi. Anujjamānassātianuvaditabbassa gacchaticcādinā niddiṭṭhassa kattuno.

By `kattukammānam eva` (of agent and object only), he excludes the impersonal construction (`bhāva`). And he will say so: 'because it cannot be expressed by the words `tumha` and `amha`.' The reason for the possibility of the singular is `asatvabhūtāya`, etc., while `tumha`, `amha`, etc., are in the case of the possibility of the third person. How are the second, first, and third persons, which occur in relation to `tumha`, `amha`, and the remainder, understood in impersonal constructions, etc.? And how, when the meaning of the factor expressed by words like `tumha` and `amha` is designated by the finite verb prescribed for it, is the non-use of words like `tumha` and `amha` suspected? Raising this doubt, what was said in the commentary is now explained: 'If suffixes such as `māna`, etc., are not prescribed in impersonal constructions, etc., then the prescription of suffixes like `kyala`, etc., in other impersonal constructions, etc., would not be justified.' By the force of this, the existence of the second person, etc., is understood in factors such as `tumha`. Therefore, to show that the use of words like `tumha` is not found because the meaning of the factor `tumha`, etc., is already designated by the finite verb prescribed for it, the section `tumhādisu`, etc., was started. If so, the use of words like `tumha` would not occur at all, he says: `yajjevam`, etc. He states the refutation: `sasaddena`. By the word `tumhādi`. The plurality already expressed by `brāhmaṇā` is repeated by the word `bahavo`. If there is no word, how can there be co-referentiality? He says: `anujjamānassa`, etc. Regarding `anujjamānassa`: of the agent indicated by `gacchati`, etc., which is being referred back to.

Anuvādenāti [M 0.0280] (tumhādi) anuvādena. “Nāmamhi payujjamānepi tulyādhikaraṇe paṭhamo”ti (3-1-5) kaccānavacanaṃ, tenāha- ‘tenevi’ccādi. Asamānādhikaraṇattā hi ‘tayāpaccate’ccādo na bhavati. Tathāhi tayeccetaṃ kattuvācī paccateccetaṃ kammavācī kamme ākhyātappaccaya vidhānato.

`Anuvādena` means by anaphoric reference to `tumha`, etc. The saying of Kaccāyana is: 'Even when a noun is used, the first case ending is used when it is co-referential' (3-1-5). Therefore he says: `tena eva`, etc. Indeed, because they are not co-referential, `tayā paccate`, etc., does not occur. For `tayā` expresses the agent, while `paccate` expresses the object, because the finite verb suffix is prescribed in the sense of the object.

‘Ehi maññe rathena gamissasī’ti pāṇiniyātimatanipphādanakkamo (nirassa) te ‘parihāse’ccādinā. Maññatissa payogeti upapadavasena manadhātussa payoge. Dhātumhāti gamiādito. Uttama purisekavacane patteti gamissāmīti patte. Majjhimobhimatoti gamissasītyabhimato. Majjhime patteti maññaseti patte, uttamekavacana miṭṭhanti maññetiṭṭhaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti “maññase tvaṃ rathena gamissāmīti vattabbe maññe tvaṃ rathena gamissasīti bhavatīti (vutta”nti). Ehi maññeccādi na kiñci vuttaṃ vuttiyaṃ. Yathāsavisayevamajjhimuttamā sampajjanti, tathāsambandhamupadassayamāha- ‘evametthābhisambandho’ccādi. Parābhimataṃ sambandhaṃ kurumāno āha- ‘natveva’miccādi. Athoccateccādinā parādhippāyamāha- ‘yade’ccādi.

The procedure for forming `ehi maññe rathena gamissasi` (Come, I think you will go by chariot) according to the view of the Pāṇinians is refuted for you by `parihāse`, etc. Regarding `maññatissa prayoge`: in the usage of `maññati` means in the usage of the root `man` as a subordinate word. Regarding `dhātumhā`: from a root means from `gam`, etc. Regarding `uttama purisekavacane patte`: when the first person singular is obtained means when `gamissāmi` is obtained. Regarding `majjhimo abhimato`: the second person is intended means `gamissasi` is intended. Regarding `majjhime patte`: when the second person is obtained means when `maññase` is obtained; the desired first person singular is `maññe`. This is what is said: 'When one should say `maññase tvaṃ rathena gamissāmi` (You think, "I will go by chariot"), it becomes `maññe tvaṃ rathena gamissasi` (I think you will go by chariot).' Nothing is said in the commentary about `ehi maññe`, etc. Just as the second and first persons are accomplished in their respective domains, so, showing the connection, he says: 'Thus here is the connection,' etc. Making the connection according to another's view, he says: 'But not so,' etc. Then by `atho uccate`, etc., he states the other's opinion: `yade`, etc.

Yadevamabhisambandhoti ‘maññase tvaṃ rathena gacchāmī’ti yadā evamabhisambandho karīyatītyattho. So cevamanugatoti ‘maññe ahaṃ tvaṃ rathena gacchasi’ccevaṃ so ca payogo anugatotyattho. Pakārantarakappanāyāti ‘maññase tvaṃ rathena gacchāmī’ti antarakappanāya.

Regarding `yadevamabhisambandho`: the meaning is, when the connection is made thus: 'You think, "I go by chariot."'. Regarding `so cevamanugato`: the meaning is, and that usage follows thus: 'I think you go by chariot.' Regarding `pakārantarakappanāya`: for the imagining of another form, that is, for the internal imagining of 'You think, "I go by chariot."'

15. Āī

15. Āī

Tenacāti samāsitattena ca,ssatyādīnamaggahaṇanti yadi tesaṃ gahaṇaṃ siyā āīssādīsūti na samāsena vadeyya.

Regarding `tena ca`: and because it is compounded. Regarding `aggahaṇaṃ ssatyādīnaṃ`: The non-inclusion of `ssati`, etc., means that if they were included, he would not have stated `ā-ī-ss-ādīsu` in a compound.

17. Bhūssa

17. Bhūssa

Katākatappasaṅgīyo vidhi so nicco-niccā balavāti paṭhamaṃ vuka bhavatīti dassetumāha- ‘katākatappasaṅgittā’ccādi.

The rule concerning what is done and not done is strong because it is permanent over the impermanent; to show that this comes first, he says: 'Because of the connection of what is done and not done,' etc.

18. Pubba

18. Pubba

Aādyapekkheti aādīsūti anuvattaaādyapekkhe.

Regarding `aādyapekkhe`: this has reference to `a`, etc., which is carried forward in the phrase `aādīsu`.

23. Kara

23. Kara

Nanu ca ‘sossā’ti kasmā vuttaṃ “kvaci vikaraṇāna “micceva (5-161) lopo [M 0.0281] siyāti ‘karassa ku’nti vattabbanti codanamanasi nidhāyāha- ‘kvaci vikaraṇānaṃ tyādi. Aññatrapayogānusaraṇā payogānusaraṇaṃ vinā olopo viññātuṃ na sakkāti sambandho.

Now, why was `sossā` said? Keeping in mind the objection, 'Since according to the rule `kvaci vikaraṇānaṃ... lopo siyā` (5-161), one should state `karassa ku`,' he says: `kvaci vikaraṇānaṃ`, etc. The elision of `o` cannot be understood without following the usage elsewhere; this is the connection.

25. Hāssa

25. Hāssa

Kāriyaṃ āhaṅsaṅkhātamassa atthīti kāriyī, tena aparo kāriyī haññati hiṃsīyatīti attho.

He for whom there is that which is called an action (`kāriya`) is a `kāriyī` (one who has an action); by him, another `kāriyī` is struck or harmed—this is the meaning.

Sahossehīti karassa okārena ssena ca saha hāssa ssena sahāti attho. Atha kathaṃ ossehi saheva vuttā desotiviññāyatīccāsaṅkiyāha- ‘sahavacanasāmatthiyā’ti. Saha saddassa sahattha(ssa ca) sossa ssenāti kathanasāmatthiyāti attho. Adhippāyaṃ vivarati ‘evaṃ maññate’ccādinā. Evaṃ maññate- ossāna manādesitte iccādinā pāṭhena bhavitabbamiva lakkhīyate… teneva pāṭhenasahavacanasāmatthiyassa patītisabbhāvato. Na tu ‘evaṃmaññateossānamantādesatte hāssacāti vacanamanatthakaṃ siyā hā to cetveva vadetya ossānamanādesitte’ccādinā pāṭhena… ossānamantādesappasaṅgassevābhāvato. Nahetthādesādesi sambandhachaṭṭhī atthi… sossāti visesanachaṭṭhiyāppadhānāya ssenāti sahatthe tatiyāya ca niddiṭṭhattā. Ubhayatthāti ssatyādīsussādīsu ca.

'Sahossehīti' means: together with the 'o' and 'ssa' of 'kara', and together with the 'ssa' of 'hāssa'. Then, how is it understood that it is a substitute said together with 'ossehi'? Having raised this doubt, he says: 'By the power of the word saha.' The meaning is: by the power of stating 'saha' with 'sossa' and 'ssena'. He clarifies the intention with 'he thinks thus,' and so on. He thinks thus: it seems it should be by the reading beginning with 'ossānaṃ anādesitte' (when 'ossa' is not a substitute)... because by that very reading, the understanding of the power of the word 'saha' is present. But not by the reading beginning with 'evaṃ maññate ossānaṃ antādesatte hāssa cāti vacanaṃ anatthakaṃ siyā hā to cetveva vadetya ossānaṃ anādesitte'... because there is no occasion for 'ossa' being a final substitute. For here there is no genitive case expressing the relationship of substitute and that for which it is substituted... because 'sossa' is specified by a non-primary genitive of specification, and 'ssena' by the instrumental in the sense of 'together with'. 'In both places' means in 'ssati' etc. and 'ussa' etc.

28. Āī

28. Āī

Pubbasaralopoti vikaraṇalopo ākārādese ca dvīsu vāresu pubbasaralopo.

Elision of the preceding vowel means: the elision of the conjugational sign; and in the case of the substitution of `ā`, and in two instances, there is elision of the preceding vowel.

29. Gami

29. Gami

Agāti īmhi lalopo, ākārādese ca pubbasaralopo.

In `Agā`: when `ī` follows, there is elision of `l`; and upon the substitution of `ā`, there is elision of the preceding vowel.

30. Ḍaṃsa

30. Ḍaṃsa

Agañchā agacchīti niggahītāgamena.

`Agañchā`, `agacchī`: by the augment of `niggahīta`.

32. Ṇānā

32. Various.

Ujjhitānubandhānanti pariccattānubandhānaṃ.

`Ujjhitānubandhānaṃ` means: of those whose indicatory letters have been abandoned.

33. Āī ū

33. Āī ū

Sutte [M 0.0282] āti iminā ubhayattha paṭhamapurisekavacanaṃ gahitanti āha- ‘ā’tiādi.

By this `ā` in the rule, it is said that in both places the third person singular is taken, as in `ā`, etc.

34. Kusa

34. Kusa

Abhirūhīti “byañjane dīgharassā”ti (1-33) dīgho.

In `Abhirūhī`: by the rule 'byañjane dīgharassā' (1-33), there is lengthening.

35. Ā ī ssa

35. Ā, ī, ssa

Parokkhāparanāmadheyyānanti parokkhātiaññanāmānaṃ.

`Parokkhāparanāmadheyyānaṃ` means: of those whose other name is `parokkha`.

38. Eyyā

38. Eyyā

Tehevāti heṭṭhā vuttasuttadvayeheva, sahacaritañāyenāti “bhūte ī uṃ”iccādo (6-4) paracchakke paṭhama purisekavacanaākārena “anajjatane āñu”iccādo (6-5) pubbacchakke paṭhamapurisekavacana ākārena ca sahacaritākārānameva paccāsattiyā sahacaritā pattivasena pavattañāyena gahaṇanti attho. Gahitattā tvādi sambandhī gayhateti sambandho. Nissayakaraṇaṃ nāma byattivaseneva, na sāmaññavasenāti āha ‘etenā’tiādi.

`Teheva` means: by those very two rules mentioned below. `Sahacaritañāyena` means: by the principle of association, in the latter group of six tenses, with the `ā` that is the third person singular in the rule beginning 'bhūte ī uṃ' (6-4), and in the former group of six tenses, with the `ā` that is the third person singular in the rule beginning 'anajjatane ā ñu' (6-5), only the associated `ā`s are taken, by the principle which proceeds by way of attainment of association due to proximity. This is the meaning. Because it is taken, the connection is that what is related to `tu`, etc., is to be taken. The making of a basis is by way of the individual instance, not by way of the general category; thus he says 'by this', and so on.

40. Eo

40. Eo

Antasarādilopo “rānubandhentasarādissā”ti (4-132).

Elision of the final vowel and what follows it occurs by the rule 'rānubandhe antasarādissa' (4-132).

42. Ossa

42. Ossa

Ādesānanti aādīnamādesānaṃ.

`Ādesānaṃ` means: of the substitutions beginning with `a`.

46. Iṃssa

46. Iṃssa

Pubbasminti akāsinti ettha.

Here, in `pubbasmiṃ` and `akāsiṃ`.

52. Tassa

52. Of that.

Kriyatthavihitānampi dhātuvihitānampi aññesaṃ tabbādīnaṃ paccayānaṃ na gahaṇanti sambandho.

There is no inclusion of other suffixes beginning with `tabba`, neither those enjoined for the purpose of an action nor those enjoined after a root. This is the connection.

54. Mimā

54. Mimā

Amhītiādīni vattamāne tvādīsu vā mimānamudāharaṇāni.

`Amhi`, and so on, are examples of the `mimā` endings in the present tense, or in `tu`, etc.

57. Himi

57. Himi

Muyhāmi [M 0.0283] muha=vecitte “divādīhi yaka” (5-21).

`Muyhāmi`: from the root `muha` in the sense of 'to be bewildered', by the rule 'divādīhi yaka' (5-21).

61. Ñāssa

61. He would know.

Jānāti “ñāssa ne jā” (5-120)

`Jānāti`: by the rule 'ñāssa ne jā' (5-120).

67. Hanā

67. Hanā

Cha ca khā ca cha khā.

Cha and khā, and cha khā.

70. Kayi

70. Kayi

Iminā katā kayirāti ajjhāharitabbaṃ.

By this which was done, 'it should be done' is to be supplied.

71. Ṭā

71. Ṭā

Eyyumādīnaṃ eyyassāti vuttattā upādivajjitassāti viññāyati.

Since it is said 'eyyassa' of 'eyyum' and so forth, it is understood as being devoid of 'upādi'.

74. Guru

74. Heavy (syllable)

Okāro guruti saṃyogapubbattā vuttaṃ.

It is said that the letter 'o' is heavy because it is preceded by a conjunct consonant.

76. Ovi

76. Ovi

Vikaraṇasaddassa aññathāpi byavacchedakattasambhave idhādhippetaṃ byavacchedakattampaṭipādetumāha- ‘yadipi’ccādi.

Even though the term 'vikaraṇa' can also serve as a differentiator in other contexts, here it is used to establish the intended differentiation, as he says: 'yadipi' and so forth.

78. Eyyā

78. Eyyā.

Aññatrāpīti bhaveyyāmubhaveyyāmaiccatrāpi.

Also elsewhere, as in 'bhaveyyāmu' and 'bhaveyyāma' (we might be).

Iti moggallānapañcikāṭīkāyaṃ sāratthavilāsiniyaṃ

Thus in the Sāratthavilāsinī, a subcommentary on the Moggallāna-pañcikā.

Chaṭṭhakaṇḍavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the sixth chapter is concluded.

Niṭṭhitā ca sabbathā sāratthavilāsinī ṭīketi.

And thus the Sāratthavilāsinī subcommentary is completed in every respect.

Nigama

Conclusion.

1.

1.

Sabbadā [M 0.0285] subhadāyittā, sattānantanisevite;

Pasatthe-nvatthasaññāya, paññāte subhasaññite.

Always bestowing welfare, frequented by countless beings; praised for its meaningful name, known by its auspicious name.

2.

2.

Cāgavikkamapaññānuddayādiguṇasālinā;

Subhasenādhināthena, kārite vasatā satā.

By Subhasena, the lord, endowed with qualities such as generosity, heroic effort, wisdom, and compassion, this was caused to be made, where the good dwell.

3.

3.

Paṭisallānasāruppe, vihāre sādhugocare;

Manonukūle yogīnaṃ, vare vikkamasundare.

In a dwelling suitable for seclusion, a resort for the good; pleasing to the minds of yogis, excellent and beautifully heroic.

4.

4.

Therena racitā sāyaṃ, sāsanujjotanatthinā;

Ṭīkā gurupadambhoja, rajomatthakasevinā.

This subcommentary was composed by the Elder, who desired to illuminate the Dispensation, and who served the dust of the lotus feet of his teachers by placing it on his head.

5. Bahussutānaṃ viññūnaṃ, paramatthāvagāhinaṃ.

5. For the learned and discerning, who have penetrated the ultimate meaning.

Pavattatu ciraṃ ceto, rañjayantī nirantaraṃ.

May it long continue, continuously delighting the mind.

6.

6.

Yesaṃ na sañcitā paññā, nekasattantarocitā;

Sammohabbhahatāvete, nāvabujjhanti kiñcipi.

Those whose wisdom is not accumulated, nor has it taken delight in the welfare of many beings; overwhelmed by the cloud of delusion, they understand nothing at all.

7.

7.

Kintehi pādasussūsā, yesaṃ natthi gurūniha;

Ye tappādarajokiṇṇā, teva sādhūvivekino.

What is the service of feet to those who have no teachers here? Only those who are covered with the dust of their feet are truly discerning.

8.

8.

Puññena sattharacanājanitena tena,

Sambuddhasāsanavarodayakāraṇena;

Lokāmisesupi kilesamalā alaggo,

Sambuddhasāsanavarodayamācareyyaṃ.

By the merit generated by the composition of this treatise, by that which is the cause for the rise of the supreme Buddha's Dispensation; may I, unattached to the stains of defilements even amidst worldly allurements, bring about the rise of the supreme Buddha's Dispensation.

9.

9.

Ye-nantatantaratanākaramanthanena,

Manthāca lollasitañāṇavarena laddhā;

Sārāmathāti sukhitā sukhayanti caññe,

Teme jayanti guravā guravo guṇehi.

Those who, by churning the endless ocean of jewel-like texts, obtained the essence with their excellent, brilliant wisdom as a churning rod; happy with that essence, they make others happy—those teachers, weighty with virtues, my teachers, are victorious.

10.

10.

Ṭīkāyo vinasādinaṃ viracayī yo kaṇṭhabhūsāparo,

Viññūnaṃ jinasāsanāmalamatīso-kāsi cānākulaṃ;

Santosakkamanomanomakamano sabbhāvanīyo mahā,

Sāmī me gurupuṅgavo vijayate sārīsuto-yaṃ bhuvi.

He who composed subcommentaries, dispelling darkness, another Kaṇṭhabhūsā; who made the Victor's pure Dispensation clear and unconfused for the wise; delightful to the minds of the contented, revered by all, my great master, this chief of teachers, Sāriputta, is victorious on earth.

11.

11.

Rājā [M 0.0286] vikkamabāhu bāhitaripū tātvassa bhātāssa lokissaro,

Sammittānihano tisīhaḷapatī yoyaṃ mahāvikkamo;

Nibbhīto tisūro vijayādibāhu vijayī so āsi laṅkissaro,

Taṃ nissāya phalaṃ cirāya phalatañcetaṃ sataṃ santataṃ.

King Vikkamabāhu, who drove out his foes, lord of the world; destroyer of enemies, lord of the three Siṃhalas, he of great prowess; the fearless Vijayabāhu, victorious, he was the lord of Laṅkā. Relying on him, may this fruit for the good ripen for a long time, continuously.

Siddhi ratthu

May there be success!

1.

1.

Aggammotivaṃsena, abhayārāmasāminā;

Pañcikāvaṇṇanābhūtā, sā sāratthavilāsinī.

By the lord of Abhayārāma, of the Aggammoti lineage, this Sāratthavilāsinī, which is an explanation of the Pañcikā, was composed.

2.

2.

Mrammakkharamāropetvā, visodhetvā yathābalaṃ;

Sakiyabyavahārena, tithīvasu karindunā.

Having transcribed it into Burmese characters and corrected it according to my ability; by the Sākiyan reckoning, in the year given by 'tithi', 'vasu', and 'karindu'.

3.

3.

Yutte vasse laṅkādīpā, saraṭṭhamāhatā puna;

Bhāssappadīpakātanta, kāsikāpañcikādihi.

In the appropriate year, having again brought them from the island of Laṅkā to one's own country, along with the Bhāssappadīpaka, the Kāsikāpañcikā, and so forth.

4.

4.

Saṃsanditvā vicāretvā, vācetvāca punappunaṃ;

Ūnādhikādi dosāni, apanetvā sinesine.

Having compared, examined, and recited again and again, the faults of deficiency, excess, and so forth were gradually removed.

5.

5.

Suddhaṭṭhake ca vassesā, pāpitā pakatiṭṭhitiṃ;

Suddhāsuddhaṃva dassentī, sodhetu pāṭhasuddhiyā.

And in the pure eighth year, it was brought to its natural state; displaying both the pure and the impure, may it be purified for the purity of the text.
